modules.title: What Wine Is
modules.description: What wine is, how it is made in the simplest terms, where it comes from and how to drink it well.

lessons.title: What is wine?
lessons.subtitle: The simplest definition, and why it matters
objectives: Explain why wine is made from Vitis vinifera
Place a wine's alcohol within the normal range

steps.title: Fermented grape juice
steps.body: Wine is the drink you get when yeast ferments the juice of fresh grapes. Drinks made from other fruit, or from rice, can be delicious, but in law they are not simply called wine: in the EU the word on its own is reserved for fermented fresh grapes or grape must.

steps.title: One species, thousands of varieties
steps.body: Almost every wine comes from one species of vine, Vitis vinifera, native to the area between the Black Sea and the Caspian. Within that species there are thousands of varieties, such as Chardonnay or Merlot. Grapes suit wine because a ripe berry holds 20 to 25% sugar, enough acid to stay fresh and the yeast it needs on its own skin.
steps.highlight: Species: Vitis vinifera. Variety: the type within it.

steps.prompt: Which of these drinks is wine, in the strict sense?
steps.explanation: Fermented fresh grape juice is the definition. Fermented apple juice is cider, distilled grape spirit is brandy, and pasteurised juice never fermented, so it has no alcohol.

steps.title: How strong is wine?
steps.body: Most still wines sit between 11 and 14.5% alcohol by volume. Light styles such as Moscato d'Asti can be around 5.5%, while fortified wines like Port reach 19 or 20% because grape spirit is added. The number is always on the label as abv.

steps.prompt: A wine labelled 13.5% abv is most likely a fortified wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. 13.5% sits comfortably inside the range of ordinary still wine. Fortified wines usually start at 15% and often reach 20%, because spirit is added.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wine is the fermented juice of fresh grapes
Nearly all wine comes from varieties of Vitis vinifera
Most still wines have 11 to 14.5% alcohol

lessons.title: From grape to glass
lessons.subtitle: Fermentation in a few minutes
objectives: Explain what yeast does to grape sugar
Put the main winemaking steps in order
Explain why riper grapes give stronger wine

steps.title: What yeast does
steps.body: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. In grape juice it eats sugar and gives off alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. In a still wine the gas escapes into the air. When the sugar runs out, or the alcohol gets too high for the yeast, fermentation stops.
steps.highlight: Sugar plus yeast gives alcohol, CO2 and heat

steps.title: More sugar, more alcohol
steps.body: Roughly 17 grams of sugar per litre turn into 1% of alcohol. Juice with 230 g/l of sugar, typical of ripe grapes, can make a wine of about 13.5%. Warm, sunny places ripen grapes further, so their wines tend to be stronger; cool places give lighter, fresher wines.
steps.highlight: About 17 g/l of sugar makes 1% alcohol

steps.prompt: Unfermented grape juice on its way to becoming wine is called ____.
steps.explanation: Must is the juice, with or without skins, before and during fermentation. Lees are the dead yeast left after it, and marc is the pressed skins and seeds.

steps.title: The five steps
steps.body: Every wine follows the same basic path. The grapes are harvested, then crushed or pressed to free the juice. Yeast ferments it. The wine then rests for weeks or years in steel, concrete or oak, which is called maturation. Finally it is bottled.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of making a wine in order.
steps.explanation: The fruit is picked, the juice is freed, yeast turns it into wine, the wine rests, and only then is it bottled. Maturation always comes after fermentation.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat
Harvest, pressing, fermentation, maturation and bottling come in that order
Riper grapes hold more sugar, so they make stronger wine

lessons.title: Where wine comes from
lessons.subtitle: The places where vines grow well
objectives: Locate the two bands where most wine is made
Explain why vines need a cool season and a warm one
Tell Old World from New World producers

steps.title: Two bands around the world
steps.body: Most wine is made between roughly 30 and 50 degrees of latitude, north and south of the equator. Closer to the equator there is no winter for the vine to rest; further away the summer is too short to ripen the grapes. France, Italy and Spain sit in the northern band; Argentina, South Africa and Australia in the southern one.
steps.highlight: Most vineyards lie between 30 and 50 degrees latitude

steps.title: Why the vine needs seasons
steps.body: A vine sleeps through winter, buds in spring, flowers, sets fruit and ripens it through summer. Each step needs the right temperature. Below about 10 degrees Celsius the vine barely grows. Too much heat ripens sugar quickly but burns off acidity, so the best wines come from places with warm days and enough coolness to keep the fruit fresh.
steps.highlight: Warm enough to ripen, cool enough to stay fresh

steps.prompt: Why is little fine wine made very close to the equator?
options: There is no cool season for the vine to rest
Grapes cannot grow in the tropics
steps.explanation: The vine needs a dormant winter to regulate its yearly cycle. Near the equator it never rests. Grapes do grow there, but making balanced wine is much harder.

steps.title: Old World and New World
steps.body: Old World means the countries where wine culture began, mainly in Europe, with centuries of rules tied to place. New World means the countries where Europeans planted vines from the 16th century on, such as the United States, Chile, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The terms describe history, not quality.
steps.highlight: Old World and New World describe history, not quality

steps.prompt: Which of these are New World wine countries?
steps.explanation: Chile and New Zealand planted vines with European settlers. Portugal, Italy and Spain have made wine for over two thousand years.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Most wine comes from between 30 and 50 degrees latitude, north and south
The vine needs a winter rest and a summer warm enough to ripen fruit
Old World and New World describe history, not quality

lessons.title: Drinking responsibly
lessons.subtitle: How to enjoy wine and stay well
objectives: Work out how much alcohol is in a glass
Explain why food and water change the effect of wine

steps.title: A unit of alcohol
steps.body: In the UK, one unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol. A 175 ml glass of 13% wine holds about 2.3 units, and a 750 ml bottle about 10. UK health guidance suggests no more than 14 units a week, spread over several days. Other countries use different measures, but the idea is the same: know how much is in your glass.
steps.highlight: Units = volume in ml x abv / 1000

steps.title: Why food and water help
steps.body: Alcohol is absorbed mostly through the small intestine. A meal slows the stomach, so alcohol reaches the blood more slowly and the peak is lower. The liver breaks down roughly one unit an hour, whatever you do; coffee and cold showers don't speed it up. Water doesn't change that rate, but it helps with thirst and pacing.
steps.highlight: The liver clears about one unit an hour

steps.prompt: Drinking a strong coffee makes the liver clear alcohol faster.
steps.explanation: Not true. Coffee can make you feel more alert, but the liver works at roughly the same speed, about one unit an hour. Only time lowers the alcohol in your blood.

steps.body: At a tasting, professionals spit. It isn't rude: it lets you taste thirty wines and still judge the last one clearly. Most of what matters, aroma and structure, you get without swallowing.

steps.prompt: Roughly how many units are in a 750 ml bottle of 13.5% wine?
steps.explanation: 750 multiplied by 13.5 and divided by 1000 gives just over 10 units. That's why a bottle shared by two is already a lot for one evening.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol; a bottle of wine holds about 10
Food slows absorption, and only time clears alcohol from the blood
Spitting lets you taste many wines and keep your judgement

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from What Wine Is
objectives: Define wine and its alcohol range
Describe how wine is made and where it grows

steps.prompt: What makes a drink wine in the strict, legal sense?
options: The fermentation of fresh grapes or must
steps.explanation: Wine is the fermentation of fresh grapes or grape must. The alcohol level describes most wines but doesn't define them, and distillation makes spirit, not wine.

steps.prompt: Put the winemaking steps in order.
steps.explanation: Fermentation turns juice into wine; maturation is the rest that follows, before bottling.

steps.prompt: Grapes from a warmer place usually make a wine with more alcohol.
steps.explanation: Yes. More heat and sun means more sugar in the berry, and more sugar becomes more alcohol, about 1% for every 17 g/l.

steps.prompt: Which of these are New World wine countries?
steps.explanation: Argentina, South Africa and Australia planted vines with European settlers. Spain and Germany are part of the Old World, where wine culture began.

steps.prompt: The liver clears roughly ____ unit of alcohol per hour.
steps.explanation: About one unit an hour. Coffee, water and fresh air don't change that speed.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wine is fermented fresh grape juice, usually 11 to 14.5% alcohol
Harvest, pressing, fermentation, maturation and bottling make every wine
Most wine grows between 30 and 50 degrees latitude, in the Old and New Worlds
Know the units in your glass, eat, and spit when tasting

modules.title: Types and Styles
modules.description: Still, sparkling and fortified, and the words that describe a wine's style: colour, sweetness, body.

lessons.title: Still, sparkling, fortified
lessons.subtitle: The three families of wine
objectives: Name the three families of wine

steps.title: Three families
steps.body: Every wine belongs to one of three families. Still wine has no noticeable bubbles and is most of what you drink. Sparkling wine holds dissolved carbon dioxide. Fortified wine has had grape spirit added. Inside each family you'll find white, rosé and red, dry and sweet.

steps.title: Where the differences come from
steps.body: Fermentation always makes carbon dioxide. Let it escape and the wine is still. Ferment in a sealed bottle or tank and the gas dissolves, building up to about 6 atmospheres in Champagne, roughly three times a car tyre. Add grape spirit and the wine rises to 15 to 22% alcohol; if that happens mid-fermentation, the yeast dies and the wine stays sweet.
steps.highlight: Trapped CO2 makes bubbles; added spirit makes fortified

steps.prompt: Match each family to what defines it.
steps.explanation: The family depends on what happens to the gas and whether spirit is added.

steps.title: Spirit added early or late
steps.body: When spirit goes in during fermentation, the yeast stops and natural sugar remains. That is how Port stays sweet. When spirit is added after a dry fermentation, the wine stays dry, as with Fino Sherry. Same idea, different moment, opposite results.
steps.highlight: Spirit during: sweet. Spirit after: dry.

steps.prompt: Every fortified wine is sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. If the spirit is added after the yeast has eaten all the sugar, the wine stays dry. Fino Sherry is fortified and bone dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wines are still, sparkling or fortified
Bubbles come from carbon dioxide trapped during fermentation
Fortified wines have added spirit, and timing decides if they are dry or sweet

lessons.title: White wine styles
lessons.subtitle: Crisp, aromatic and rich
objectives: Describe three broad styles of white wine
Explain how skins are kept out of white wine
Link a white style to climate and winemaking

steps.title: Three ways a white can taste
steps.body: White wines fall into three broad styles. Light and crisp, like Muscadet or Pinot Grigio, with high acidity and little aroma. Aromatic, like Riesling or Gewürztraminer, with intense floral or fruity smells. Full and rich, like oaked Chardonnay, with a weighty, creamy texture.

steps.title: How a white is made
steps.body: For white wine the grapes are pressed quickly and the juice is fermented without the skins, so it picks up almost no colour or tannin. Fermentation is usually cool, around 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, which keeps fresh fruit aromas. Fermenting or ageing in oak barrels, as many Chardonnays are, adds body and notes of vanilla and toast.

steps.prompt: Why does a white wine have almost no tannin?
options: The juice ferments without the skins
steps.explanation: Tannin comes mostly from skins and seeds. White wine juice is separated from them before fermentation, so very little is extracted.

steps.title: Climate shapes the style
steps.body: Cool climates keep acidity high and alcohol moderate, giving crisp whites such as Chablis. Warm climates give riper fruit, more alcohol and a rounder feel, as in many Chardonnays from California or Australia. The same grape can land in different styles depending on where it grows and how it's made.

steps.prompt: Which of these push a white wine towards a fuller, richer style?
steps.explanation: Warmth gives riper fruit and more alcohol, and oak adds texture and flavour. Early picking and cool climates both keep a wine lighter and crisper.

steps.title: What you learned
points: White wines are broadly crisp, aromatic or rich
The juice ferments without skins, so whites have almost no tannin
Cool climates give crisp whites; warmth and oak give richer ones

lessons.title: Red wine styles
lessons.subtitle: Light, medium and full
objectives: Describe light, medium and full-bodied reds
Explain where colour and tannin come from
Match a red style to its grape and climate

steps.title: Three weights of red
steps.body: Light reds, like Beaujolais or many Pinot Noirs, are pale, juicy and low in tannin. Medium reds, like Chianti or a Merlot from Bordeaux, have more grip and flavour. Full reds, like Barossa Shiraz or Napa Cabernet, are deep in colour, high in tannin and often high in alcohol.

steps.title: Skins make the red
steps.body: The pulp of almost every black grape is pale. Red wine gets its colour by fermenting the juice with the skins for days or weeks. The longer and warmer this contact, the more colour, tannin and flavour come out. Red fermentations run warmer than white, often 25 to 30 degrees Celsius, to help that extraction.
steps.highlight: Colour and tannin come from the skins

steps.prompt: Red wine takes its colour from the grape ____.
steps.explanation: The colour is in the skins. The pulp of nearly all black grapes is pale, which is why a gentle press can make white juice from black grapes.

steps.title: Thick skins, big reds
steps.body: Grapes with thick, dark skins, such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Syrah, give more colour and tannin than thin-skinned ones like Pinot Noir or Gamay. Warm climates add ripeness and alcohol. So a thick-skinned grape from a hot place usually makes the fullest red.
steps.highlight: Thick skin plus heat gives the fullest reds

steps.prompt: Which wine is most likely to be light-bodied?
steps.explanation: Gamay is thin-skinned and Beaujolais comes from a moderate climate, so the wine is pale and light. Shiraz and Cabernet from warm places are full-bodied.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Reds range from light and juicy to full and tannic
Colour and tannin come from fermenting with the skins
Thick skins and warm climates make the fullest reds

lessons.title: Rosé styles
lessons.subtitle: Pink wine, three ways
objectives: Explain how rosé gets its colour
Describe the three ways to make rosé
Explain why blending red and white is rare

steps.title: Pink from the skins
steps.body: Rosé is made from black grapes whose juice touches the skins only briefly, usually from 2 to 20 hours. That's enough for a little colour and fruit, but very little tannin. Most rosé is dry, like those of Provence, though some, like White Zinfandel, are sweet.
steps.highlight: Rosé: black grapes, short skin contact

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body: Direct pressing squeezes black grapes gently, giving the palest rosés. Short maceration leaves the juice on the skins for some hours, then runs it off to ferment like a white. Saignée, French for bleeding, draws juice off a red wine tank early; the rosé is a by-product and the remaining red becomes more concentrated.

steps.prompt: Match each rosé method to how it works.
steps.explanation: All three methods limit skin contact. Provence is the region most associated with pale, dry rosé.

steps.body: Mixing red and white wine to make rosé is banned for most European wines. Rosé Champagne is the famous exception, where a little red wine is often blended in.

steps.prompt: In saignée, the main goal of the producer is often the red wine, not the rosé.
steps.explanation: Yes. Bleeding off some juice leaves a higher ratio of skins to juice in the tank, so the red becomes deeper. The rosé is a useful by-product.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rosé gets its colour from a short contact with black grape skins
It is made by direct press, short maceration or saignée
Blending red and white is banned for most European rosé, except Champagne

lessons.title: Sweetness and body
lessons.subtitle: Two words for any wine
objectives: Explain what gives a wine body
Describe any wine by sweetness and body

steps.title: Sweetness is sugar
steps.body: Sweetness measures residual sugar, the grape sugar left when fermentation stops. Dry wines have so little you can't taste it, usually under 4 g/l. Off-dry wines have a touch. Sweet wines can have over 100 g/l. Fruit aromas are not sweetness: a wine can smell of ripe peach and be completely dry.

steps.title: Body is weight
steps.body: Body is how heavy the wine feels in your mouth, like the difference between skimmed milk, whole milk and cream. Alcohol is the biggest contributor, because it is more viscous than water. Sugar, tannin and extract add to it. A 14.5% Chardonnay feels much fuller than an 11% Riesling.
steps.highlight: Alcohol is the main source of body

steps.prompt: A wine smells of ripe peaches and honey, but there is no sugar on the palate. How would you describe its sweetness?
steps.explanation: Sweetness is about sugar you taste, not aromas you smell. Ripe fruit aromas can make a dry wine seem sweet before you sip it.

steps.title: Putting it together
steps.body: With two words you can describe almost any wine. Muscadet is dry and light. Oaked Chardonnay is dry and full. Moscato d'Asti is sweet and light. Sauternes is sweet and full. Use the colour, then sweetness, then body, and you have a sketch that anyone can picture.

steps.prompt: Which of these make a wine feel fuller-bodied?
steps.explanation: Alcohol, sugar and tannin all add weight. Acidity makes a wine feel fresher and lighter, not heavier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweetness is residual sugar; dry wines have almost none
Body is the weight of the wine, driven mostly by alcohol
Colour, sweetness and body sketch any wine

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Types and Styles
objectives: Sort a wine into its family
Explain how colour and style are made
Describe a wine by sweetness and body

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its family or style.
steps.explanation: Family first, then style. Port and Fino are both fortified, but the spirit goes in at different moments.

steps.prompt: What decides whether a black grape gives a white, rosé or red wine?
options: How long the juice touches the skins
steps.explanation: No skin contact gives white juice, a few hours gives rosé, and days or weeks give red.

steps.prompt: A dry wine can smell sweet.
steps.explanation: Yes. Aromas of ripe fruit or honey can suggest sweetness, but dry is about sugar on the palate, not the nose.

steps.prompt: Which are typical of a full-bodied red?
steps.explanation: Thick skins and warmth give colour, tannin and alcohol. Low alcohol points to a lighter wine.

steps.prompt: The rosé method that bleeds juice from a red tank is called ____.
steps.explanation: Saignée means bleeding. It gives a rosé and a more concentrated red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wine is still, sparkling or fortified
Skin contact decides white, rosé or red
Sweetness is sugar; body is weight
Climate and grape shape the style within each colour

modules.title: The Principal Grapes
modules.description: The eight grapes behind most of the wine you'll ever be offered, and what each one tastes like.

lessons.title: What a grape variety is
lessons.subtitle: Why the name of the grape tells you so much
objectives: Explain what a grape variety is
Explain how varieties are kept identical
Explain why a variety predicts a style

steps.title: A variety is a recipe
steps.body: A grape variety is a distinct type of vine within Vitis vinifera, with its own berry size, skin thickness, acidity and aromas. Chardonnay, Merlot and Riesling are varieties. Knowing the variety tells you a lot about how the wine will taste before you open it.
steps.highlight: Variety: a type of vine with its own character

steps.title: Cuttings, not seeds
steps.body: A seed from a Chardonnay grape would grow into a new, different vine, because vines don't breed true. So growers plant cuttings, pieces of an existing vine, which are genetically identical to the parent. A Chardonnay vine in Chile is effectively a copy of one in Burgundy. Most vines today are also grafted onto American rootstocks to resist phylloxera, an insect that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s.
steps.highlight: Vines are copied by cuttings, not grown from seed

steps.prompt: A vine grown from a Merlot seed will produce Merlot grapes.
steps.explanation: Not true. Vines don't breed true from seed, so the seedling would be a new variety. That's why vineyards are planted with cuttings.

steps.title: Single variety or blend
steps.body: A varietal wine is made mainly from one variety and often names it on the label, like a Chilean Sauvignon Blanc. A blend mixes varieties for balance, like Bordeaux, which combines Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. In the EU and many other places, a wine that names one variety must contain at least 85% of it.
steps.highlight: Varietal labels usually mean at least 85% of that grape

steps.prompt: A Chilean label names only Cabernet Sauvignon. What can you expect?
options: It is 100% Cabernet Sauvignon by law
It is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, possibly with a little of another grape
It is a blend with no main grape
It is Cabernet grown from seed
steps.explanation: Naming one variety usually means at least 75 to 85% of it, depending on the country. A small share of another grape is allowed.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A variety is a type of vine with its own character
Vines are propagated by cuttings, so each variety stays identical
A varietal wine names the grape that makes up most of it

lessons.title: Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc
lessons.subtitle: Two white grapes, two ways to be white
objectives: Explain why Chardonnay changes so much with winemaking

steps.title: Chardonnay, the chameleon
steps.body: Chardonnay has a neutral character of its own, so it reflects where it grows and how it is made. In cool places like Chablis it tastes of green apple and lemon, lean and crisp. In warmer places it gives peach, pineapple and melon. It is also the main grape of many sparkling wines, including most Blanc de Blancs Champagne.

steps.title: Sauvignon Blanc, the aromatic one
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc is intensely aromatic, with gooseberry, passion fruit, cut grass and green pepper. The green notes come from compounds called pyrazines, which survive best in cool climates. It is almost always made without oak to keep that freshness. Sancerre in France and Marlborough in New Zealand are its two best-known homes.
steps.highlight: Sauvignon Blanc: grass, gooseberry, high acidity

steps.prompt: Which aroma is most typical of Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: Grassy and gooseberry aromas come from pyrazines and thiols in Sauvignon Blanc. Butter and toast come from oak and winemaking, as in some Chardonnays.

steps.title: What the winemaker adds
steps.body: Because Chardonnay is neutral, it takes winemaking well. Oak barrels add vanilla, toast and spice. Malolactic conversion, where bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, gives a buttery note. Stirring the dead yeast, the lees, adds creaminess. Sauvignon Blanc rarely gets this treatment.
steps.highlight: Oak, malolactic and lees shape Chardonnay

steps.prompt: Match each flavour to its likely source.
steps.explanation: Fruit comes from the grape and climate; butter, vanilla and toast come from the winery.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay is neutral and reflects climate and winemaking
Sauvignon Blanc is aromatic, grassy and crisp, usually unoaked
Oak, malolactic and lees give Chardonnay toast, butter and cream

lessons.title: Riesling and Pinot Grigio
lessons.subtitle: Purity and lightness
objectives: Describe Riesling's acidity and range of sweetness
Describe Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris
Explain how Riesling changes with age

steps.title: Riesling, the high-acid white
steps.body: Riesling comes from Germany and has very high acidity, flowery aromas and flavours from lime to peach. It is almost never oaked. It can be bone dry, as in much of Alsace and Austria, or lusciously sweet, as in German late-harvest wines. That acidity keeps even sweet Rieslings fresh.
steps.highlight: Riesling: high acidity, dry to sweet

steps.title: Why Riesling ages so well
steps.body: High acidity protects a wine as it ages. Good Riesling can develop for 20 years or more, gaining notes of honey, toast and a smell often called petrol. That petrol note comes from a compound called TDN, which forms more in grapes exposed to strong sun. Many lovers of Riesling look for it.
steps.highlight: Petrol in Riesling comes from TDN

steps.prompt: Riesling's ability to age comes mainly from its high ____.
steps.explanation: Acidity acts as a preservative. Riesling has very little tannin and often modest alcohol, so acidity does the work.

steps.title: One grape, two names
steps.body: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape, with a greyish-pink skin. The Italian name usually signals a light, crisp, neutral wine picked early, as in north-east Italy. The French name, from Alsace, usually means a riper, rounder wine with notes of pear, spice and honey. Producers elsewhere borrow the name to signal the style.
steps.highlight: Grigio: light and crisp. Gris: rich and round.

steps.prompt: A label says Pinot Gris and the wine comes from Alsace. Which style is most likely?
options: Rich and round, with ripe pear and spice
steps.explanation: Pinot Gris from Alsace is usually riper and fuller. The Italian name, Pinot Grigio, is the one linked to the light, crisp style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling has high acidity and ranges from bone dry to sweet
Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are one grape, named by style
Good Riesling ages for decades, developing honey and petrol notes

lessons.title: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
lessons.subtitle: The Bordeaux pair
objectives: Describe Cabernet Sauvignon's flavours and structure
Describe Merlot and how it differs
Explain why the two are often blended

steps.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon has small, thick-skinned berries, which give deep colour, high tannin and high acidity. Its flavours are blackcurrant and black cherry, with mint, cedar and sometimes green pepper. It ripens late, so it needs a warm site. Bordeaux's Médoc made it famous, and Napa Valley made it a star of the New World.

steps.title: Merlot
steps.body: Merlot has bigger, thinner-skinned berries and ripens about two weeks earlier than Cabernet. Its tannins are softer and its flavours are plum, red and black cherry, with a rounder feel. It suits cooler, clay soils that would leave Cabernet unripe, as on Bordeaux's Right Bank in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion.
steps.highlight: Merlot: plum, softer tannin, earlier ripening

steps.prompt: Which grape is more likely to give a wine with firm tannin and blackcurrant aromas?
steps.explanation: Cabernet's small, thick-skinned berries give more tannin, and blackcurrant is its signature aroma. Merlot is softer, more plum and cherry.

steps.title: Why blend them
steps.body: Cabernet brings structure and length; Merlot fills the middle with fleshy fruit. Together they make a more complete wine. Blending also spreads risk: if a cool year leaves Cabernet short of ripeness, Merlot, which ripens earlier, can make up the difference. That's the logic of most Bordeaux reds.
steps.highlight: Cabernet gives the frame; Merlot fills it in

steps.prompt: Which of these describe Merlot rather than Cabernet Sauvignon?
steps.explanation: Merlot ripens earlier, is softer and plummy, and copes with cool clay. Thick skins, high tannin and blackcurrant are Cabernet's signature.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Sauvignon gives blackcurrant, high tannin and acidity
Merlot gives plum and softer tannins, ripening earlier
Blending them balances structure and fruit, and spreads risk

lessons.title: Pinot Noir and Syrah
lessons.subtitle: Elegance and spice
objectives: Describe Pinot Noir's style and its demands
Tell the two apart by colour and flavour

steps.title: Pinot Noir
steps.body: Pinot Noir has thin skins, so it gives pale, low-tannin reds with red cherry, raspberry and, with age, earthy and mushroom notes. It needs a cool climate; in heat it loses its delicacy. It is fragile in the vineyard, prone to rot and sensitive to frost. Burgundy is its home, and it is also a key grape of Champagne.
steps.highlight: Pinot Noir: pale, red fruit, cool climate

steps.title: Syrah and Shiraz
steps.body: Syrah is a thick-skinned grape from the northern Rhône, giving deep colour, firm tannin and flavours of blackberry, black pepper and smoked meat. In Australia it is called Shiraz, and the warmer climate of places like the Barossa gives riper, sweeter fruit, chocolate and more alcohol. The pepper note comes from rotundone, more common in cooler sites.
steps.highlight: Syrah: black fruit and black pepper

steps.prompt: Syrah and Shiraz are two different grape varieties.
steps.explanation: Not true. They are the same grape. The name often hints at style: Syrah for a cooler, peppery wine, Shiraz for a riper, fuller one.

steps.body: Hold the glass over a white page. If you can read print through a red wine, you're likely looking at Pinot Noir or another thin-skinned grape. If it's nearly opaque, think Syrah or Cabernet.

steps.prompt: A red is pale, with raspberry and a light earthiness, and gentle tannin. Which grape is most likely?
steps.explanation: Pale colour, red fruit and low tannin point to Pinot Noir. Syrah, Shiraz and Cabernet are all deeply coloured and more tannic.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir is pale, low in tannin and needs a cool climate
Syrah gives deep colour, black fruit and pepper; in Australia it's Shiraz
Colour and tannin help you tell the two apart

lessons.title: Same grape, different places
lessons.subtitle: How climate changes the wine
objectives: Explain how climate changes a grape's flavour
Compare cool and warm climate versions of one grape
Predict style from a grape and a place

steps.title: Cool and warm
steps.body: Climate is the long-term pattern of a place. In a cool climate, grapes ripen slowly, keeping high acidity and giving lighter body and fresher, sometimes green, fruit. In a warm climate, grapes ripen fully, with more sugar, lower acidity and flavours of ripe or even jammy fruit.
steps.highlight: Cool: fresh, tart. Warm: ripe, full.

steps.title: Why acidity falls in heat
steps.body: As grapes ripen, sugar rises and acidity falls. Heat speeds both up, and warm nights let the vine burn off malic acid, one of the grape's main acids. That's why a Chardonnay from Chablis may have 12% alcohol and sharp acidity, while one from a hot valley might reach 14.5% with soft acidity and tropical fruit.
steps.highlight: Heat raises sugar and burns off acid

steps.prompt: A Chardonnay is lean, with green apple and 12% alcohol. Where does it most likely come from?
steps.explanation: Green apple, high acidity and moderate alcohol are signs of slow ripening in a cool place. A hot valley would give riper fruit and more alcohol.

steps.title: The grape and the place together
steps.body: Read a label as two clues. The grape tells you the basic character: aromas, skin, tannin. The place tells you how ripe it got. Sauvignon Blanc from the cool Loire tastes of grass and citrus; from warmer parts of Chile it leans towards passion fruit and melon. Same grape, different sun.
steps.highlight: Grape gives character; place gives ripeness

steps.prompt: Which are signs of a warm-climate wine?
steps.explanation: Heat gives more sugar, so more alcohol and riper fruit, and it lowers acidity. Sharp acidity is a cool-climate sign.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cool climates give fresher, lighter wines; warm ones riper and fuller
Heat raises sugar and lowers acidity
Grape gives the character, place gives the ripeness

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from The Principal Grapes
objectives: Recognise the eight principal grapes by their flavours
Explain how varieties are propagated and labelled
Predict a wine's style from grape and climate

steps.prompt: Match each grape to a typical aroma.
steps.explanation: Each grape has a signature you can learn to recognise.

steps.prompt: Why are vineyards planted with cuttings rather than seeds?
options: Vines don't breed true from seed
steps.explanation: A seedling would be a new variety. Cuttings keep every vine identical to the parent.

steps.prompt: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape.
steps.explanation: Yes. The Italian name usually signals a light, crisp style; the French name a richer, rounder one.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are normally deeply coloured and tannic?
steps.explanation: Cabernet and Syrah have thick skins. Pinot Noir is pale and low in tannin, and Riesling is white.

steps.prompt: Merlot ripens ____ than Cabernet Sauvignon, which helps in cooler years.
steps.explanation: Merlot ripens about two weeks earlier, so it is the safer half of a Bordeaux blend in a cool year.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Eight grapes cover most wine: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Grigio, Cabernet, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Syrah
Varieties are copied by cuttings and named on varietal labels
Grape gives the character; climate gives the ripeness

modules.title: Tasting Basics
modules.description: Look, smell, taste: a simple order that lets you describe any wine and compare two of them.

lessons.title: Why taste with a method
lessons.subtitle: Drinking versus tasting
objectives: Explain why a method helps you taste
Name the three steps of tasting
Set up good conditions for tasting

steps.title: Tasting is paying attention
steps.body: Drinking is enjoying. Tasting is noticing what you're enjoying, in an order that lets you compare. The method is simple: look, smell, taste. Doing it the same way each time builds a memory of wines you can draw on later.

steps.title: Why the order matters
steps.body: Each step prepares the next. The look hints at age and body. The nose works before the palate because most of what we call flavour is smell: the tongue senses only sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. When you sip, aromas travel up the back of the throat to the nose, a route called retronasal smell.

steps.prompt: Why do you smell a wine before you taste it?
options: Most of what we call flavour is smell
steps.explanation: The tongue registers five basic tastes. Everything else, from cherry to vanilla, is detected by smell, before and during the sip.

steps.body: Taste in daylight or under white light, against a white background, with a clean, plain glass. Avoid perfume, coffee and toothpaste just before. Small changes like these make a bigger difference than expensive gear.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of tasting in order.
steps.explanation: Swirling releases aromas between looking and smelling. The conclusion comes once you've taken everything in.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A method turns drinking into tasting you can compare
Most flavour is smell, so the nose comes before the palate
White light, a plain glass and no strong smells help

lessons.title: Look
lessons.subtitle: What the colour tells you
objectives: Judge a wine's clarity and intensity
Explain what tears in the glass mean

steps.title: Clarity, intensity, colour
steps.body: Tilt the glass over a white surface. Check that the wine is clear, not hazy. Then judge intensity, from pale to deep, by looking at the core. Finally name the colour: lemon, gold or amber for whites; purple, ruby, garnet or tawny for reds.

steps.title: Colour changes with age
steps.body: Young reds look purple, because their pigments are fresh. With time, pigments bind with tannins and drop out, so the wine turns ruby, then garnet with an orange rim, and finally tawny. Whites go the other way: they deepen from pale lemon to gold and amber as they oxidise slowly.
steps.highlight: Reds lose colour with age; whites gain it

steps.prompt: A red wine has a garnet core and an orange-brown rim. What does this suggest?
steps.explanation: Purple means youth. Garnet with an orange rim shows years of development, when pigments slowly change and drop out.

steps.title: Legs mean alcohol, not quality
steps.body: After swirling, drops called legs or tears run down the glass. They form because alcohol evaporates faster than water at the edge, changing surface tension. More and slower legs usually mean more alcohol or sugar. They tell you nothing about quality.
steps.highlight: Legs show alcohol or sugar, not quality

steps.prompt: Thick, slow legs on the glass show that a wine is of high quality.
steps.explanation: Not true. Legs are physics: they come mostly from alcohol and sugar. A cheap, strong wine can have thicker legs than a great, lighter one.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Look for clarity, intensity and colour
Reds fade from purple to tawny; whites deepen to gold and amber
Legs show alcohol or sugar, never quality

lessons.title: Smell
lessons.subtitle: Training your nose
objectives: Judge the intensity of a wine's aromas
Sort aromas into primary, secondary and tertiary
Smell in a way that finds more aromas

steps.title: Intensity first
steps.body: Before naming aromas, judge how strong they are: light, medium or pronounced. Then ask what they remind you of. A young Sauvignon Blanc jumps out of the glass; a young Chardonnay from a cool place may be much quieter. Neither is better, but it tells you about the grape and style.

steps.title: Three families of aroma
steps.body: Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbs. Secondary aromas come from winemaking: vanilla and toast from oak, butter from malolactic, bread from lees. Tertiary aromas come from age: leather, mushroom, honey, nuts, dried fruit. Naming the family tells you how the wine was made and how old it is.

steps.prompt: Vanilla and toast in a wine usually come from:
steps.explanation: Vanilla and toast are secondary aromas from oak barrels. Bottle age gives tertiary notes like leather and honey instead.

steps.title: How to smell
steps.body: Swirl to lift aromas, then take short sniffs rather than one long one; your nose tires within seconds. Start with broad groups, like fruit or flowers, then narrow down: red fruit, then strawberry or cherry. Smelling real fruit, herbs and spices at home is the fastest way to build your vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Which of these are tertiary aromas, from age?
steps.explanation: Dried fruit, leather and mushroom develop with years in bottle or barrel. Fresh lime and green apple are primary fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Judge intensity before naming aromas
Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking, tertiary from age
Short sniffs, broad to narrow, build skill fastest

lessons.title: Taste
lessons.subtitle: Structure on the palate
objectives: Judge the length of the finish

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: On the palate you judge the wine's structure: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body. Sweetness is felt on the tip of the tongue. Acidity makes your mouth water. Tannin dries your gums, like strong tea. Alcohol gives warmth at the back of the throat.

steps.title: What each one is
steps.body: Tannins are compounds from skins, seeds and oak that bind to proteins in your saliva. That's why your mouth feels dry and rough. Acidity, mainly tartaric and malic acid in wine, triggers saliva, which is why acidic wines feel refreshing. Alcohol above about 14% starts to feel hot.
steps.highlight: Tannin binds saliva; acid makes it flow

steps.prompt: After a sip, your mouth waters for several seconds. Which element are you tasting?
steps.explanation: Acidity triggers saliva. Tannin does the opposite, drying the mouth.

steps.title: The finish
steps.body: After you swallow or spit, notice how long the flavours last. A short finish fades in a few seconds. A long finish lingers for 10 seconds or more. Length is one of the clearest signs of quality, because only concentrated, well-balanced wines hold their flavour that long.

steps.prompt: A wine that makes your gums feel dry and rough is high in ____.
steps.explanation: Tannin binds to proteins in saliva, leaving that drying, gripping feel. Acidity would make your mouth water instead.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body make up structure
Acid makes the mouth water; tannin dries it
A long finish is one of the clearest signs of quality

lessons.title: Describing what you find
lessons.subtitle: Turning impressions into words
objectives: Write a short, useful tasting note
Compare two wines with the same words

steps.title: A note in four lines
steps.body: A useful tasting note has four parts. Look: clarity, intensity, colour. Nose: intensity and main aromas. Palate: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavours, finish. Conclusion: is it good, and is it ready to drink? Short, specific words beat long poetic ones.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: A wine is balanced when no element sticks out. Fruit should carry the acidity, tannin should be supported by fruit, alcohol shouldn't burn. Sweet wines need high acidity, or they feel cloying. A Sauternes can have 130 g/l of sugar and still feel fresh because its acidity is high.

steps.prompt: A very sweet wine can feel balanced if its acidity is high enough.
steps.explanation: Yes. Acidity cuts sugar, which is why great sweet wines feel fresh rather than syrupy.

steps.body: Compare two wines side by side, using the same order and the same words. Differences that you'd miss in one glass become obvious next to another.

steps.prompt: Which of these is the most useful line in a tasting note?
options: Lovely, a real joy to drink
Medium acidity, high tannin, blackcurrant and cedar, long finish
Tastes like a holiday in the sun
steps.explanation: Specific words about structure and flavour let you, and anyone else, picture the wine and compare it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A good note covers look, nose, palate and a conclusion
Balance means no single element sticks out
Comparing side by side with the same words sharpens your judgement

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Tasting Basics
objectives: Taste a wine in a consistent order

steps.prompt: Put the tasting steps in order.
steps.explanation: Look, swirl to release aromas, smell, taste and only then conclude.

steps.prompt: A white wine is deep gold. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It has some age or oak
steps.explanation: Whites deepen in colour with age and time in oak. Very young, unoaked whites are pale lemon.

steps.prompt: Aromas that come from age, like honey, leather and nuts, are called ____ aromas.
steps.explanation: Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking and tertiary from time.

steps.prompt: Which are part of a wine's structure?
steps.explanation: Structure is what you feel: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body. Aromas and colour are separate parts of the note.

steps.prompt: Legs on a glass are a reliable sign of quality.
steps.explanation: Not true. They show alcohol and sugar, nothing about quality. Length of finish and balance tell you much more.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Look, smell, taste and conclude, every time
Colour tells age; aromas tell grape, winemaking and time
Structure is felt: acidity waters, tannin dries, alcohol warms
Balance and length are the clearest signs of quality

modules.title: Storing and Serving
modules.description: Keeping a bottle well, serving it at the right temperature and saving what's left.

lessons.title: Storing a bottle
lessons.subtitle: What wine needs while it waits
objectives: Name the four conditions for good storage
Explain why bottles are stored on their side
Decide which wines are worth keeping

steps.title: Cool, dark, still, steady
steps.body: Wine keeps best somewhere cool, ideally 10 to 15 degrees Celsius, dark, free of vibration and with a steady temperature. A cupboard away from the oven is better than the top of the fridge or a sunny shelf. Strong light, especially sunlight, can damage wine in days.

steps.title: Why heat and swings hurt
steps.body: Heat speeds up the chemistry of ageing, so a wine kept at 25 degrees ages several times faster and can taste cooked. Swings in temperature make the wine expand and contract, pushing air past the cork. Light, especially ultraviolet, breaks down compounds in the wine and causes a fault called light strike, which smells of cabbage.
steps.highlight: Heat and light age wine too fast

steps.prompt: Which of these are good conditions for storing wine?
steps.explanation: Cool, steady, dark and still. Sun and the oven bring heat and light, the two main enemies.

steps.title: Side or standing
steps.body: Bottles with natural cork are stored on their side so the wine keeps the cork moist; a dry cork shrinks and lets air in. Screw caps can stand up. And most wine is made to drink within a year or two. Only a small share, such as good Bordeaux or vintage Port, improves for decades.
steps.highlight: Cork on its side; screw cap any way

steps.prompt: Most wines improve if you keep them for ten years.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most wine is made to be drunk young, within a year or two. Only wines with enough concentration, acidity or tannin improve over many years.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Store wine cool, dark, still and at a steady temperature
Heat, light and temperature swings damage wine
Lay corked bottles on their side, and drink most wines young

lessons.title: Serving temperatures
lessons.subtitle: Why a few degrees change a wine
objectives: Name the right temperature for each style
Chill or warm a wine quickly

steps.title: A rough guide
steps.body: Sparkling wines are best well chilled, 6 to 10 degrees Celsius. Light whites and rosés, 7 to 10. Fuller whites, 10 to 13. Light reds, 13 to 15. Medium and full reds, 15 to 18. Room temperature in a modern heated home, often 21 or more, is too warm for most reds.

steps.title: What temperature does
steps.body: Cold hides aromas and makes tannin and bitterness feel harsher, but it lifts freshness and keeps bubbles fine. Warmth releases aromas and softens tannin, but too much makes alcohol taste hot and flabby. That's why light whites go cold and tannic reds go warmer.

steps.prompt: Why is a tannic red usually served warmer than a white?
steps.explanation: Cold emphasises tannin and bitterness. A few degrees warmer and the red feels smoother and more aromatic.

steps.body: Fifteen minutes in the fridge brings a red from a warm room down to cellar temperature. To chill a white fast, put it in a bucket of ice and water, not ice alone; water touches the whole bottle.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its serving temperature.
steps.explanation: Bubbles coldest, full reds warmest, everything else in between.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Serve sparkling coldest and full reds warmest
Cold sharpens tannin and hides aroma; warmth releases aroma
Ice plus water chills fast; a short spell in the fridge helps reds

lessons.title: Glasses and opening
lessons.subtitle: The tools that help
objectives: Choose a glass that helps a wine show well
Open still and sparkling wines safely

steps.title: The right glass
steps.body: A good glass has a bowl that narrows at the top, to gather aromas, and a stem so your hand doesn't warm the wine. Fill to about a third so you can swirl. Larger bowls suit aromatic reds; narrower ones keep whites cool. A tall flute keeps bubbles but hides aroma, so many prefer a white wine glass for Champagne.
steps.highlight: Bowl that narrows, a stem, a third full

steps.title: Why a sparkling cork flies
steps.body: A bottle of Champagne holds about 6 atmospheres of pressure. If the cork is released fast, it can leave at over 40 km/h. Keep a thumb on the cork, point it away from people, and twist the bottle, not the cork, letting the gas out with a sigh rather than a pop.
steps.highlight: Twist the bottle, not the cork

steps.prompt: Put the steps for opening a sparkling wine in order.
items: Loosen the wire cage, thumb on the cork
Tilt the bottle away from people
Let the cork ease out with a sigh
steps.explanation: Keeping the thumb on the cork from the moment the cage loosens is the key safety step.

steps.title: Decanting
steps.body: Pouring a wine into a decanter does two jobs. It separates an old red or vintage Port from its sediment, the solids that form with age. And it gives a young, tight wine air, which can open up its aromas. Pour slowly in front of a light and stop when you see sediment reach the neck.
steps.highlight: Decant for sediment or for air

steps.prompt: Decanting is only useful for very old wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Old wines are decanted for sediment, but young, tannic reds are often decanted for air, which helps their aromas open.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A bowl that narrows, a stem and a third full help any wine
Open sparkling wine by holding the cork and twisting the bottle
Decant old wines for sediment and young ones for air

lessons.title: Leftover wine
lessons.subtitle: Making an open bottle last
objectives: Explain what happens to an open bottle
Know how long each style lasts once open

steps.title: Air is the enemy
steps.body: Once opened, wine meets oxygen. At first that can help, but over days it flattens fruit and turns the wine dull, nutty or vinegary. Bacteria can turn alcohol into acetic acid, the acid of vinegar. Cold slows all of this, so the fridge is the best place for any open bottle, red included.

steps.title: How long each lasts
steps.body: Light whites and rosés usually stay pleasant for 2 to 3 days in the fridge with the cork back in. Reds, 3 to 5 days, because tannin protects them. Sparkling wine keeps its fizz for 1 to 3 days with a proper stopper. Fortified wines last longest: an opened tawny Port or Madeira can keep for weeks, Madeira for months.

steps.prompt: Which opened wine is likely to keep longest?
steps.explanation: Madeira has already been exposed to heat and oxygen in its making, and its high acidity and alcohol protect it. It can last months once opened.

steps.body: Pour leftovers into a smaller bottle so there's less air above the wine. Less air, slower decline. The spoon in the neck of a sparkling bottle is a myth; a hinged stopper works.

steps.prompt: Leftover red wine keeps longer if stored in the ____.
steps.explanation: Cold slows oxidation and bacteria. Take a red out half an hour before serving.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Oxygen slowly flattens an open wine
Keep open bottles closed and in the fridge, reds included
Fortified wines last longest; light whites and sparkling the least

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Storing and Serving
objectives: Serve each style at the right temperature
Open, decant and keep wine properly

steps.prompt: Which conditions damage a stored wine?
steps.explanation: Light, heat and swings age or damage wine. Darkness is what it needs.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its best temperature.
steps.explanation: Bubbles coldest, full reds warmest.

steps.prompt: Why are corked bottles stored on their side?
steps.explanation: A moist cork stays tight. A dry one shrinks and lets air in.

steps.prompt: Young, tannic reds can benefit from decanting.
steps.explanation: Yes. Air helps a tight young red open up. Old wines are decanted mainly for sediment.

steps.prompt: Order these opened wines from shortest to longest life in the fridge.
steps.explanation: Bubbles fade first, then light whites. Tannin helps reds, and Madeira's making leaves it almost immune to air.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Store wine cool, dark, still and steady
Serve sparkling coldest and full reds warmest
Decant for sediment or for air
Recork and refrigerate leftovers; fortified wines last longest

modules.title: Food and Wine
modules.description: What food does to wine, and the few rules that make a pairing work.

lessons.title: How food changes wine
lessons.subtitle: Why the same wine tastes different with dinner
objectives: Explain why food changes how wine tastes
Name the food elements that matter most
Explain the idea of matching weight

steps.title: Food changes the wine
steps.body: Taste a wine on its own, then with food, and it often changes. A red can turn harsh after a bite of something sweet, or soft after a bite of salty cheese. Pairing isn't about finding a perfect match; it's about avoiding clashes and finding combinations where both taste better.

steps.title: The mechanism
steps.body: Your palate adapts to what it has just tasted. After sugar, the next thing tastes less sweet and more sour. After salt, it tastes less bitter and acidic. Fat coats the mouth, so tannin and acidity feel softer and cleaner. These effects are reliable enough to plan around.
steps.highlight: The palate adjusts to the last bite

steps.prompt: After eating something salty, a wine is likely to seem:
steps.explanation: Salt reduces our sense of bitterness and acidity, which is why salty dishes make many wines seem softer and fruitier.

steps.title: Weight with weight
steps.body: A simple rule that rarely fails: match the weight of the food to the body of the wine. A delicate fish needs a light white; a rich stew needs a fuller red. Big flavours overpower light wines, and big wines flatten delicate food. Colour matters far less than weight.
steps.highlight: Light with light, rich with rich

steps.prompt: Which of these food elements make a wine seem harder, more bitter or more acidic?
steps.explanation: Sweetness and umami make wine feel harsher. Salt and acidity in food make it feel softer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Food changes how wine tastes, for better or worse
Sugar and umami harden wine; salt and acid soften it
Match the weight of the food to the body of the wine

lessons.title: Sweetness and umami
lessons.subtitle: The two that make wine harder
objectives: Explain why sweet food clashes with dry wine
Fix a sweet or umami pairing

steps.title: Sweet food, dry wine
steps.body: Sweetness in food makes a dry wine taste more acidic, more bitter and less fruity. A dry Champagne with a sweet dessert often tastes thin and sour. The rule: the wine should be at least as sweet as the food. That's why sweet wines are served with dessert.
steps.highlight: Wine at least as sweet as the food

steps.title: Umami, the savoury taste
steps.body: Umami is the savoury taste of glutamates, found in mushrooms, ripe tomatoes, aged cheese, soy sauce and cured meat. Like sweetness, it makes wine taste more bitter, astringent and acidic, and less fruity. Asparagus and eggs are tricky for the same reason. Salt counteracts it, which is why salty umami dishes are easier to match.

steps.prompt: A dry sparkling wine is the ideal match for a very sweet chocolate dessert.
steps.explanation: Not true. The sweetness of the dessert makes the dry wine taste sour and thin. A wine at least as sweet as the dessert works far better.

steps.title: Fixing it
steps.body: With sweet dishes, choose wines like Sauternes, Tokaji or tawny Port. With umami, reach for fruity, lower-tannin wines, such as Pinot Noir, and add salt or acidity to the dish, like a squeeze of lemon or a little soy. The dish and the wine can both be adjusted.
steps.highlight: Sweet wine for sweet; salt for umami

steps.prompt: You're serving mushroom risotto. Which wine is the safest choice?
options: A dry fino Sherry served warm
steps.explanation: Umami in mushrooms makes tannin feel harsher, so a fruity, low-tannin red like Pinot Noir handles it best.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweet food needs a wine at least as sweet
Umami makes wine more bitter and astringent
Fruity, low-tannin wines and a little salt help with umami

lessons.title: Acid, salt and bitterness
lessons.subtitle: The elements that make wine softer
objectives: Explain why acidic food needs acidic wine

steps.title: Acid in the food
steps.body: Acidic food, like a tomato salad or a dish with lemon, makes a wine taste less acidic, richer and fruitier. But if the wine has lower acidity than the dish, it can taste flat and flabby. So acidic food needs a wine with at least as much acidity, like Sauvignon Blanc or Chianti.

steps.title: Salt and bitterness
steps.body: Salt makes wine feel softer and fruitier, which is why salty cheeses and charcuterie are so easy to pair. Bitterness works the other way: bitter food adds to bitterness in the wine. Grilled radicchio or very charred meat can make a tannic red taste harsh, because tannin itself tastes slightly bitter.

steps.prompt: Match each food element to its effect on wine.
steps.explanation: Salt and acidity soften a wine. Sweetness and bitterness harden it.

steps.body: Salty blue cheese with a sweet wine, like Roquefort with Sauternes, is one of the great pairings. Salt softens, sweetness balances salt, and the wine's acidity cuts the fat.

steps.prompt: A tomato salad with lemon dressing needs a wine with high ____.
steps.explanation: Acidic food makes a wine seem less acidic, so the wine needs plenty of acidity to stay fresh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Acidic food needs wine with at least as much acidity
Salt is wine-friendly, softening and lifting fruit
Bitter food adds to the bitterness of tannic wines

lessons.title: Chilli heat
lessons.subtitle: Spice and wine
objectives: Explain the role of alcohol and tannin

steps.title: Heat and wine
steps.body: Chilli heat, from capsaicin, is not a taste but a feeling of burning. In the mouth it makes alcohol feel hotter, and it makes tannin and bitterness more aggressive. A high-alcohol, tannic red with a hot curry can feel like fire. The wine also loses fruit.

steps.title: Why sugar helps
steps.body: Sugar and low alcohol calm the burn. Capsaicin dissolves in alcohol and fat, so strong drinks spread it around the mouth. A touch of sweetness and moderate alcohol soothe instead. An off-dry Riesling at 9 or 10% alcohol is a classic match for spicy Thai or Sichuan food.
steps.highlight: Off-dry and low alcohol calm the heat

steps.prompt: Which wine is the best match for a hot Thai curry?
steps.explanation: Lower alcohol and a touch of sugar calm chilli heat. High alcohol and tannin make it burn more.

steps.title: Other good options
steps.body: Fruity, aromatic whites like Gewürztraminer handle spice well. Among reds, choose low-tannin, juicy wines served slightly cool, such as Beaujolais. Fruity rosé also works. Avoid big oak, high alcohol and firm tannin.
steps.highlight: Fruity, aromatic, low tannin, moderate alcohol

steps.prompt: Which features make a wine harder to pair with chilli?
steps.explanation: High alcohol, firm tannin and heavy oak all clash with heat. Sugar and lower alcohol help.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chilli heat makes alcohol, tannin and bitterness feel stronger
Off-dry, lower-alcohol wines calm the burn
Choose fruity, aromatic, low-tannin wines with spicy food

lessons.title: Building a pairing
lessons.subtitle: A method for any table
objectives: Analyse a dish before choosing a wine
Pair with confidence for a full meal

steps.title: Start with the dish
steps.body: Look at the dominant elements, not the main ingredient. Chicken in cream sauce is about fat and richness; chicken with lemon and herbs is about acidity. The sauce, the cooking method and the seasoning often matter more than the meat or fish itself.
steps.highlight: Pair the sauce, not the protein

steps.title: Match or contrast
steps.body: You can match, like a rich oaked Chardonnay with lobster in butter, or contrast, like a crisp Champagne cutting through fried food. High acidity and bubbles act like a squeeze of lemon, cleaning the palate of fat and salt. Tannin works similarly with fatty red meat, which softens it.
steps.highlight: Acid and bubbles cut fat; tannin loves fat

steps.prompt: Why does a tannic red work well with a fatty steak?
steps.explanation: Fat coats the mouth and tannin binds with protein and fat, so each softens the other.

steps.body: When in doubt, ask where the dish comes from. Regional pairings grew up together over centuries, like Muscadet with oysters or Chianti with tomato-based pasta.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of choosing a wine for a dish in order.
steps.explanation: Start with what's on the plate, rule out clashes, then fine-tune the style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pair the dominant elements, especially the sauce
Match richness or contrast with acidity and bubbles
Regional pairings are a safe starting point

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Food and Wine
objectives: Build a pairing for a dish

steps.prompt: Match each food element to its effect on wine.
steps.explanation: Sweetness, umami and chilli make wine harder; salt and acidity soften it.

steps.prompt: Which wine is best with a sweet dessert?
options: A wine at least as sweet as the dessert
steps.explanation: Sweet food makes dry wine taste thin and sour.

steps.prompt: High acidity and bubbles help cut through fried and fatty food.
steps.explanation: Yes. They work like a squeeze of lemon, refreshing the palate.

steps.prompt: Which wines suit a spicy curry?
steps.explanation: Aromatic, off-dry, lower-alcohol whites calm heat. Big, tannic, high-alcohol reds burn.

steps.prompt: When choosing a wine, focus on the sauce more than the ____.
steps.explanation: The sauce sets the dominant elements, like acid, fat or sweetness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweetness and umami harden wine; salt and acidity soften it
Chilli needs lower alcohol and a touch of sugar
Match weight, then match or contrast the dominant elements
Tannin and fat, acidity and frying, sweet and salty work well together

modules.title: The Vineyard
modules.description: Climate, weather, soil and the grower's choices: everything that shapes a grape before it is picked.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a grape
lessons.subtitle: What each part of the berry gives
objectives: Name the parts of a grape berry
Explain what each part gives to wine

steps.title: Four parts
steps.body: A grape berry has skin, pulp, seeds and, around the bunch, stems. The pulp is mostly water, sugar and acid, and makes up most of the juice. The skin holds colour, tannin and most of the aroma. Seeds contain bitter, harsh tannins. Stems add tannin and a green note if they go into the fermenter.
steps.highlight: Pulp: sugar, acid. Skin: colour, tannin, aroma.

steps.title: Why size matters
steps.body: Small berries have more skin compared with juice. Since colour, tannin and aroma sit in the skin, small-berried grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon give more concentrated wines than large-berried ones. This is also why drought years, which shrink berries, often produce deeper, more tannic reds.

steps.prompt: Match each part of the grape to what it gives.
steps.explanation: Most of the character of a red wine comes from the skins; most of the juice from the pulp.

steps.title: Crushing gently
steps.body: Winemakers crush gently to avoid breaking the seeds, which would release bitter tannins. Some keep whole bunches, stems and all, in red fermentations for extra structure and a fresh, herbal lift. This is common for Pinot Noir and Syrah in some cellars, but only works when the stems are ripe and brown, not green.
steps.highlight: Ripe stems can add freshness; seeds stay whole

steps.prompt: A grape with small berries tends to give a more concentrated red wine than one with large berries.
steps.explanation: Yes. Small berries mean more skin compared with juice, so more colour, tannin and flavour per litre.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A grape has skin, pulp, seeds and stems
Pulp gives sugar and acid; skins give colour, tannin and aroma
Small berries give more concentrated wine

lessons.title: The growing year
lessons.subtitle: From winter to harvest
objectives: Put the stages of the vine's year in order
Explain the risks at each stage

steps.title: The cycle
steps.body: In the northern hemisphere, the vine rests in winter. Buds break in March or April. Shoots and leaves grow, then the vine flowers in late May or June. Flowers that are pollinated become berries, called fruit set. In late summer the berries soften and change colour. Harvest comes from September to October.
steps.highlight: Budburst, flowering, fruit set, veraison, harvest

steps.title: Veraison and ripening
steps.body: Veraison is the moment berries soften and change colour: black grapes turn from green to purple, white grapes become translucent. From then on, sugar rises fast, acidity falls, tannins and aromas mature. This takes about 6 to 8 weeks, depending on the weather and the grape.

steps.prompt: Put the stages of the vine's year in order.
steps.explanation: Rest in winter, then buds, flowers, berries, colour change and finally harvest.

steps.title: Risks along the way
steps.body: Spring frost can kill young shoots after budburst. Cold, wet weather at flowering leads to poor fruit set, called coulure, or uneven berries, called millerandage. Hail can shred leaves and fruit. Rain near harvest can swell berries and cause rot. Each stage has its danger.

steps.prompt: What is veraison?
options: When berries soften and change colour
steps.explanation: Veraison is the start of ripening, marked by colour change and softening. Budburst and flowering come months earlier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The vine moves from dormancy to budburst, flowering, fruit set, veraison and harvest
Veraison marks the start of ripening, when sugar rises and acidity falls
Frost, poor fruit set, hail and rot threaten each stage

lessons.title: Climate and weather
lessons.subtitle: Long-term patterns and single years
objectives: Describe cool, moderate and hot climates

steps.title: Climate versus weather
steps.body: Climate is the average pattern of a place over decades. Weather is what happens in a single year. Climate decides which grapes can ripen in a region; weather decides how good a particular vintage will be. Burgundy's climate suits Pinot Noir every year, but a wet, cold summer can still make a thin vintage.
steps.highlight: Climate decides the grape; weather decides the vintage

steps.title: Measuring climate
steps.body: One common measure is the average temperature of the growing season. Below about 16 degrees Celsius is cool, 16 to 18.5 is moderate, 18.5 to 21 is warm, and above that is hot. Champagne and the Mosel are cool; Bordeaux is moderate; the Barossa and much of southern Spain are warm to hot.

steps.prompt: Which statement describes weather, not climate?
options: 2021 was a wet, cold year in France
Bordeaux has a moderate maritime climate
steps.explanation: A single year's conditions are weather. The other statements describe long-term patterns.

steps.title: Vintage variation
steps.body: In cool and moderate regions, weather swings a lot from year to year, so vintages vary. That's why vintage charts matter in Bordeaux or Germany. In warm, dry, irrigated regions, conditions are more reliable, so vintages differ less. Wines that blend several years, like most Champagne, smooth out these differences.
steps.highlight: Vintages vary most in marginal climates

steps.prompt: Where are vintages likely to vary the most?
steps.explanation: Cool and moderate regions depend on weather to ripen grapes, so years differ. Hot, irrigated regions are more consistent.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Climate is the long-term pattern; weather is a single year
Climates are cool, moderate, warm or hot by season temperature
Vintages vary most in cool and moderate regions

lessons.title: Heat, sunlight and water
lessons.subtitle: What the vine needs to ripen
objectives: Explain the role of heat and sunlight
Explain how water stress affects quality
Name the natural influences that cool or warm a site

steps.title: Heat and sunlight
steps.body: The vine needs warmth to grow and to ripen sugar, tannin and aroma. Sunlight drives photosynthesis, the process that makes sugar in the leaves. Too little heat and grapes stay sour and green. Too much and sugar races ahead of flavour, while acidity drops. Balance is what growers look for.

steps.title: Water: not too much, not too little
steps.body: A vine needs about 500 to 700 mm of water a year. Too much and it grows leaves instead of fruit, with large, diluted berries. Mild water stress after veraison is good: berries stay small and the vine focuses on ripening. Severe drought shuts the vine down. In dry regions, drip irrigation lets growers control the dose.
steps.highlight: Mild stress concentrates; drought stops ripening

steps.prompt: A small amount of water stress after veraison can improve grape quality.
steps.explanation: Yes. Mild stress keeps berries small and pushes the vine to ripen fruit instead of growing more leaves.

steps.title: Natural influences
steps.body: Large bodies of water moderate temperatures, keeping winters milder and summers cooler, like the Atlantic in Bordeaux. Cold ocean currents cool coastal regions, like the Humboldt current in Chile. Altitude cools a site by roughly 0.6 degrees per 100 m, which is why Mendoza's vineyards at 1,000 m keep their freshness. Fog does the same in Napa and Sonoma.
steps.highlight: Water, currents, altitude and fog cool a site

steps.prompt: Why does Mendoza make fresh wines despite its warm, sunny latitude?
options: Its vineyards sit at high altitude
It is close to the equator
steps.explanation: Altitude cools the air, about 0.6 degrees per 100 m, so cool nights preserve acidity even in strong sun.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Heat ripens grapes and sunlight makes sugar
Mild water stress after veraison improves quality
Water, ocean currents, altitude and fog cool a site

lessons.title: Soils and slopes
lessons.subtitle: The ground beneath the vine
objectives: Explain what soil does for the vine
Describe the effect of drainage and heat retention

steps.title: What soil does
steps.body: Soil anchors the vine and supplies water and nutrients. The best vineyard soils are often poor, which limits vigour so the vine puts energy into fruit, not leaves. Drainage matters most: vines hate standing water, which suffocates roots and dilutes berries.

steps.title: Warm and cool soils
steps.body: Stony and gravel soils drain fast and store heat, releasing it at night, which helps ripening in cooler areas like the Médoc. Clay soils hold water and stay cool, which suits early-ripening grapes like Merlot. Dark slate in the Mosel absorbs warmth. Chalk drains well yet stores water deep, ideal for Champagne.

steps.prompt: Match each soil to its effect.
steps.explanation: Each soil changes water and heat around the roots, and so the ripening.

steps.title: Why slopes matter
steps.body: Slopes drain well and catch more sunlight when they face the sun: south or south-east in the northern hemisphere, north in the southern. Cold air flows downhill, so slopes avoid the frost that settles in valley floors. That's why Burgundy's best vineyards lie on the middle of the slope, and the Mosel's on steep south-facing banks.
steps.highlight: Slopes: drainage, sun and less frost

steps.prompt: Why are slopes often better vineyard sites than valley floors?
steps.explanation: Slopes drain, catch the sun and let cold air flow away. Valley floors usually have deeper, more fertile soils, which can lead to too much vigour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Poor, well-drained soils focus the vine on its fruit
Gravel and slate store heat; clay stays cool and wet
Slopes give drainage, sun and protection from frost

steps.title: Yield
steps.body: Yield is how much fruit a vineyard produces, usually measured in hectolitres per hectare. Lower yields often mean more concentrated fruit, because the vine's energy goes into fewer grapes. Many European appellations set a legal maximum: Grand Cru Burgundy reds are capped well below basic Bourgogne. But very low yields aren't automatically better; balance is the goal.

steps.title: Training and canopy
steps.body: Training is how a vine is shaped: low bush vines without wires, common in hot, dry places, or vines trained along wires, which makes the work and the sun exposure more even. The canopy is the leaves and shoots. Growers trim, position and thin leaves to give the right amount of sun and air to the bunches, preventing rot and sunburn.
steps.highlight: Training shapes the vine; the canopy shades the fruit

steps.prompt: Why might a grower remove some leaves around the bunches in a cool region?
options: To improve sun exposure and airflow
To make the vine grow faster
steps.explanation: In a cool, damp place, more sun and air help ripening and reduce rot. In hot regions growers often keep leaves to shade the fruit.

steps.title: Green harvest
steps.body: Some growers cut off bunches in summer, called green harvesting, to lower the yield and concentrate the rest. Others prune hard in winter for the same effect. The choice depends on the grape, the vintage and what the wine is for: a fresh, everyday wine needs a different vineyard from a long-ageing one.

steps.prompt: Cutting off some bunches in summer to concentrate the rest is called green ____.
steps.explanation: Green harvesting removes unripe bunches so the vine ripens the remaining fruit more fully.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Lower yields often concentrate flavour, within balance
Training and canopy work control sun and air on the fruit
Green harvesting and pruning adjust the crop to the goal

lessons.title: Harvest
lessons.subtitle: Choosing the moment
objectives: Explain how growers decide when to pick
Explain why picking time shapes style

steps.title: When to pick
steps.body: Growers measure sugar, acidity and pH, and taste the berries for flavour, seed ripeness and tannin. Pick early and the wine is fresh and lower in alcohol, but may taste green. Pick late and it is rich and riper, but can lose acidity and turn jammy. The date is one of the most important decisions of the year.
steps.highlight: Picking date is a style decision

steps.title: Hand or machine
steps.body: Hand picking is gentle and selective: pickers choose healthy bunches and can keep them whole, essential for Champagne and many fine wines. Machines shake the vine and collect berries, working fast and at night when it is cool, but they need flat, accessible vineyards and break the skins. Steep slopes like the Douro or the Mosel must be picked by hand.
steps.highlight: Hand: selective. Machine: fast and cool.

steps.prompt: Why are grapes for Champagne picked by hand?
options: Machines are banned everywhere in France
Whole bunches avoid colour and bitterness from broken skins
steps.explanation: Champagne presses whole bunches of black and white grapes gently, so broken skins would release colour and harsh compounds. Hand picking is required there.

steps.body: In hot regions, many growers harvest at night or before dawn. Cool fruit reaches the winery fresher, and less energy is spent cooling it down.

steps.prompt: Picking grapes later in the season usually raises sugar and lowers acidity.
steps.explanation: Yes. As grapes hang, sugar builds and acidity falls. That's why the harvest date shapes alcohol, freshness and style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Growers measure sugar and acid and taste for ripe flavour and tannin
Hand picking is selective; machines are fast and work at night
Earlier picking means fresher wine; later picking means riper wine

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from The Vineyard
objectives: Explain how the grape and the vine's year shape wine
Describe the effects of climate, soil and site

steps.prompt: Put the vine's yearly stages in order.
steps.explanation: Buds, flowers, berries, colour change and then the harvest.

steps.prompt: Match each factor to its effect.
steps.explanation: Each of these changes the temperature and so the ripening.

steps.prompt: What does the skin of a black grape mainly give the wine?
steps.explanation: Skins hold most of the colour, tannin and aroma; pulp holds sugar, acid and water.

steps.prompt: Very fertile soils usually give the best quality grapes.
steps.explanation: Not true. Fertile soils push the vine to grow leaves. Poorer, well-drained soils focus it on the fruit.

steps.prompt: Which choices tend to increase concentration in the fruit?
steps.explanation: Lower yields, removing bunches and mild stress all help. Heavy irrigation dilutes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Skins give colour, tannin and aroma; small berries concentrate them
Climate sets the grape; weather sets the vintage
Soil, slope and altitude shape heat and water
Yield, canopy and picking date are the grower's key decisions

modules.title: The Winery
modules.description: Fermentation, extraction, oak and time: the steps that turn the same fruit into very different wines.

lessons.title: Fermentation
lessons.subtitle: Yeast, temperature and vessels
objectives: Explain how temperature changes a fermentation

steps.title: Controlling the process
steps.body: Fermentation is yeast turning sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. The winemaker's main tool is temperature. Cool fermentations, 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, keep fresh, fruity aromas in whites. Warmer ones, 25 to 32, extract colour and tannin in reds. Above about 35 degrees, yeast can die and fermentation may stop.
steps.highlight: Temperature is the winemaker's main dial

steps.title: Which yeast
steps.body: Wild or ambient yeasts live on grapes and in the winery. Many winemakers rely on them, saying they add complexity, but they are less predictable. Cultured yeasts are selected strains, chosen for reliability, speed or particular aromas. Either way, the dominant species is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
steps.highlight: Ambient for complexity, cultured for control
