steps.prompt: Why are most white wines fermented cool?
steps.explanation: Low temperatures keep delicate aromas. Warmer fermentations suit reds, which need colour and tannin.

steps.title: Vessels
steps.body: Stainless steel is inert and easy to cool, keeping pure fruit. Concrete holds a stable temperature and allows a little air. Oak barrels add flavour and let small amounts of oxygen in. Clay vessels, like amphorae or Georgian qvevri, are ancient and returning to fashion.

steps.prompt: Match each vessel to its main effect.
steps.explanation: The vessel shapes texture and flavour as much as the yeast does.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Temperature controls the speed and style of fermentation
Ambient yeasts add complexity; cultured yeasts add reliability
Steel, concrete, oak and clay each shape the wine differently

lessons.title: Making a white
lessons.subtitle: From press to bottle
objectives: Describe the steps of white winemaking
Explain skin contact and its effect

steps.title: The steps
steps.body: White grapes are crushed and pressed, usually soon after picking. The juice settles to drop solids, then ferments cool, often in stainless steel. The new wine may rest on its lees, then is clarified, stabilised and bottled. Many aromatic whites are bottled within months to keep them fresh.
steps.highlight: Press, settle, ferment cool, clarify, bottle

steps.title: Protecting freshness
steps.body: Juice browns quickly in air, like a cut apple, and loses fruit. Winemakers use cold, inert gases like carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide to protect it. Some leave skins and juice together for a few hours before pressing, called skin contact, to draw out aroma, but too long adds bitterness and colour.
steps.highlight: Cold, inert gas and sulphur protect the juice

steps.prompt: Put the steps of making a white wine in order.
steps.explanation: White wines are pressed before fermentation, unlike reds.

steps.title: Orange wines
steps.body: Ferment white grapes on their skins, like a red, for days or months, and you get an orange or amber wine. It has tannin, deeper colour and flavours of dried fruit, tea and nuts. The method is ancient in Georgia and returned in Friuli and elsewhere from the 1990s.
steps.highlight: White grapes, red method, orange wine

steps.prompt: In white winemaking, the grapes are usually pressed before fermentation.
steps.explanation: Yes. For whites, the juice is separated from the skins first. Reds are pressed after fermentation, because skin contact is needed for colour and tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: White grapes are pressed first, then the juice ferments cool
Cold, inert gas and sulphur keep the juice fresh
Long skin contact turns white grapes into orange wine

lessons.title: Making a red
lessons.subtitle: Colour, tannin and pressing
objectives: Describe the steps of red winemaking
Explain the ways to extract colour and tannin

steps.title: The steps
steps.body: Black grapes are destemmed and crushed. Juice, skins and seeds ferment together, often at 25 to 30 degrees. The skins float to the top and form a cap. After fermentation the wine may stay on the skins to extract more, then is pressed. The free-run wine and the press wine are kept separate.

steps.title: Managing the cap
steps.body: The cap of skins must be kept in contact with the juice to extract colour and tannin and to stop it drying out and spoiling. Punching down pushes the cap under. Pumping over sprays juice from the bottom over the top. Rack and return drains the tank and pours the juice back. Each gives a different intensity of extraction.
steps.highlight: Punch down, pump over, rack and return

steps.prompt: Why must the cap of skins be managed during red fermentation?
options: To extract colour and tannin and avoid spoilage
steps.explanation: A floating cap dries out and can spoil. Keeping it wet extracts colour, tannin and flavour.

steps.title: Carbonic maceration
steps.body: In carbonic maceration, whole bunches go into a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Fermentation starts inside each berry, without yeast at first. This gives soft, low-tannin reds with bright aromas of banana, bubblegum and cherry. It is the classic method of Beaujolais, where many wines use a partial version.
steps.highlight: Whole berries, CO2, fruity soft reds

steps.prompt: Which are ways to extract colour and tannin from the cap?
steps.explanation: Cold settling is used to clear white juice, not to manage a red cap.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Reds ferment with their skins, then are pressed
Punching down, pumping over and rack and return manage extraction
Carbonic maceration gives soft, fruity reds like Beaujolais

steps.title: Short contact
steps.body: Most rosé is made from black grapes with skin contact of a few hours, then the juice is run off and fermented cool like a white. Direct pressing gives the palest colour, with juice just touched by the skins during the press. Longer maceration gives deeper colour and more fruit.
steps.highlight: Hours of contact, then made like a white

steps.title: Colour as a choice
steps.body: Rosé colour depends on grape, contact time and temperature. Thin-skinned Grenache gives pale pink quickly; thick-skinned Syrah colours fast. Provence's pale rosés, many with less than 6 hours of contact, now set the market fashion, so producers plan colour as carefully as flavour.
steps.highlight: Grape and contact time set the colour

steps.prompt: The rosé method that draws juice off a red wine tank is called ____.
steps.explanation: Saignée means bleeding. Pigeage and remontage are cap management methods for reds; dosage belongs to sparkling wine.

steps.title: Blending red and white
steps.body: In the EU, mixing red and white wine to make still rosé is not allowed. Champagne is the exception: most rosé Champagne is made by adding a small amount of still red wine to the white base. Outside Europe, blending is allowed in many countries.
steps.highlight: Blending is banned for most EU still rosé

steps.prompt: Which wine can legally be made by blending red and white wine in the EU?
steps.explanation: Rosé Champagne is the exception. Still rosé in the EU must be made from skin contact or saignée.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Most rosé is made with a short skin contact, then fermented like a white
Grape and contact time set the colour
Blending red and white is banned for EU still rosé, except Champagne

lessons.title: Oak and its alternatives
lessons.subtitle: Flavour, texture and oxygen
objectives: Explain what oak adds to wine
Compare new and old, French and American oak
Name the cheaper alternatives to barrels

steps.title: What oak adds
steps.body: Oak does two things. It adds flavour: vanilla, toast, clove, smoke and coconut. And, in barrels, it lets a little oxygen in slowly, which softens tannins and helps the wine develop. Small barrels, like the 225-litre Bordeaux barrique, have more effect than large casks.

steps.title: New or old, French or American
steps.body: New barrels give the most flavour; after three or four uses they add little but still allow oxygen. Toasting the inside over fire changes flavours from vanilla to smoke. French oak, Quercus petraea and robur, gives subtle spice and fine tannin. American oak, Quercus alba, gives stronger vanilla and coconut, typical of traditional Rioja.

steps.prompt: Match each oak choice to its effect.
steps.explanation: The age, origin and toast of a barrel decide what it adds.

steps.title: Cheaper alternatives
steps.body: Barrels are expensive, around 1,000 euros each for French oak. For wines at lower prices, winemakers add oak chips or staves to a steel tank. They give oak flavour quickly but not the slow oxygen of a barrel. Micro-oxygenation can supply that separately.
steps.highlight: Chips and staves: flavour without the barrel

steps.prompt: Oak chips give a wine both oak flavour and the slow oxygen exchange of a barrel.
steps.explanation: Not true. Chips and staves add flavour, but in a sealed steel tank there's no slow oxygen through the wood. That's why barrels remain prized.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Oak adds flavour and, in barrels, slow oxygen
New, small, toasted barrels add the most
Chips and staves are cheaper and add flavour only

steps.title: Two ways to mature
steps.body: Reductive maturation keeps oxygen out, in steel tanks or full vessels, preserving fresh, primary fruit. Oxidative maturation lets some air in, in barrels or partly filled vessels, which softens tannin and adds notes of nut, caramel and dried fruit. Most wines sit between the two.

steps.title: Why blend
steps.body: Blending combines wines to make a better whole. Grapes add different qualities: Cabernet for structure, Merlot for fruit. Plots add different notes. Vintages, in Champagne or Port, give consistency. Vessels, oak and steel, bring balance. A good blend is more than the sum of its parts.
steps.highlight: Blend grapes, plots, vintages or vessels

steps.prompt: Which of these are common reasons to blend?
options: To keep a house style consistent across years
To make every wine identical worldwide
To raise the legal alcohol limit
steps.explanation: Blending balances grapes, plots and vessels, and blending vintages keeps a house style steady, as in Champagne. It has nothing to do with legal limits or global uniformity.

steps.title: Ageing in bottle
steps.body: Once bottled, a wine keeps changing slowly. Fruit fades, tannins soften and tertiary notes like leather, earth and honey develop. Only some wines gain from it, mainly those with high acidity, tannin or sugar and plenty of concentration. Some regions require bottle ageing before release, as Rioja Gran Reserva does.
steps.highlight: Bottle age softens and adds complexity

steps.prompt: Which wine is most likely to improve with ten years in bottle?
options: A concentrated, tannic red from a top vineyard
steps.explanation: Long ageing needs concentration and structure, like tannin and acidity. Light, fruity wines are made to drink young.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Reductive maturation keeps fruit fresh; oxidative adds development
Blending combines grapes, plots, vintages or vessels for balance
Only structured, concentrated wines gain from long bottle age

lessons.title: Bottling and closures
lessons.subtitle: The last steps
objectives: Explain why wine is clarified and stabilised
Compare cork, screw cap and other closures
Explain the effect of the closure on ageing

steps.title: Clarifying and stabilising
steps.body: Before bottling, wine is made clear and stable. Fining adds an agent like bentonite clay or egg white that binds haze-causing particles. Filtration strains them out. Cold stabilisation chills the wine to drop tartrate crystals, the harmless wine diamonds sometimes found in bottles. Some producers skip these steps, accepting a little haze.

steps.title: Closures and oxygen
steps.body: Natural cork lets in tiny amounts of oxygen, but about 1 to 3% of bottles can be tainted by TCA, which smells of damp cardboard. Screw caps let in very little oxygen and cannot cause cork taint, so they keep fruit fresh; they are standard in New Zealand and Australia. Technical corks and glass stoppers sit in between.
steps.highlight: Cork breathes a little; screw caps barely at all

steps.prompt: What are the crystals sometimes found in a bottle of white wine?
steps.explanation: Tartrates are natural salts of tartaric acid. They are harmless and show the wine wasn't cold stabilised.

steps.body: A screw cap isn't a sign of a cheap wine. Many top Rieslings, Sauvignon Blancs and even fine reds use them to keep the wine exactly as the winemaker intended.

steps.prompt: Wines sealed with screw caps cannot suffer from cork taint.
steps.explanation: Yes. TCA, the cause of cork taint, comes from natural cork. Screw caps avoid it, although other faults are still possible.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fining, filtration and cold stabilisation make wine clear and stable
Corks let in a little oxygen but risk TCA
Screw caps keep wine fresh and avoid cork taint

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from The Winery
objectives: Explain how whites, reds and rosés are made
Describe the effects of oak and maturation
Explain the final steps before bottling

steps.prompt: Put the steps of making a red wine in order.
steps.explanation: Reds ferment with skins first and are pressed afterwards.

steps.prompt: Match each technique to its result.
steps.explanation: Each method creates a different style from the same fruit.

steps.prompt: What does a new oak barrel add that oak chips do not?
steps.explanation: Chips can add flavour, but only barrels let oxygen in slowly through the wood.

steps.prompt: Most white wines ferment at warmer temperatures than reds.
steps.explanation: Not true. Whites ferment cool to keep aromas; reds ferment warmer to extract colour and tannin.

steps.prompt: Which steps prepare a wine for bottling?
steps.explanation: Punching down is part of red fermentation, not the bottling stage.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Whites are pressed before fermentation; reds after
Rosé is made with short skin contact; blending is rare in Europe
Oak and maturation add flavour, oxygen and complexity
Fining, filtering and closures prepare and protect the wine

modules.title: White Grapes and Their Places
modules.description: The principal white grapes, the regions that made them famous and how place changes the wine.

lessons.title: Chardonnay around the world
lessons.subtitle: From Chablis to California
objectives: Name Chardonnay's classic regions in Burgundy
Compare cool and warm climate Chardonnay
Recognise the effect of oak and malolactic

steps.title: Burgundy, the template
steps.body: Chardonnay comes from Burgundy, where it makes almost all the white wine. Chablis, in the cool north, gives lean, steely wines with green apple and lemon, often unoaked. The Côte de Beaune, with Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, gives richer, nutty wines fermented and aged in oak. The Mâconnais, further south, gives rounder, fruitier, good-value wines.
steps.highlight: Chablis: steely. Côte de Beaune: rich.

steps.title: Beyond Burgundy
steps.body: Chardonnay grows almost everywhere. In warm places like California's Central Valley or parts of Australia it gives tropical fruit, high alcohol and often lots of oak. Cooler sites, like Sonoma Coast, Tasmania, Adelaide Hills or Limarí in Chile, now make tighter, fresher styles. Since the 2000s, many producers have cut back on new oak and malolactic.
steps.highlight: Cool sites: citrus. Warm sites: tropical.

steps.prompt: Which Burgundy area is known for lean, steely, often unoaked Chardonnay?
steps.explanation: Chablis is the coolest part of Burgundy, and its wines are typically crisp and mineral. Meursault is richer and oaked.

steps.title: The winemaker's touch
steps.body: Chardonnay takes winemaking well. Barrel fermentation and new oak add vanilla and toast. Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into soft lactic acid, adding a buttery note. Lees stirring gives a creamy texture. Unoaked versions are fresh and fruity. The label rarely tells you which, but the region and price are good clues.
steps.highlight: Oak, malolactic and lees shape the style

steps.prompt: Which flavours suggest a warm-climate, oaked Chardonnay?
steps.explanation: Tropical fruit comes from heat; vanilla, toast and butter from oak and malolactic. Green apple and lime point to a cool climate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy is Chardonnay's home: Chablis lean, the Côte de Beaune rich
Cool sites give citrus; warm sites give tropical fruit
Oak, malolactic and lees add toast, butter and cream

lessons.title: Sauvignon Blanc around the world
lessons.subtitle: Loire, Marlborough and beyond
objectives: Compare Loire and Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc
Explain where green and tropical aromas come from

steps.title: The Loire
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc's classic home is the Loire's Central Vineyards, mainly Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. Their cool climate and chalky or flinty soils give high acidity, citrus, green apple and a smoky, stony character. The wines are usually unoaked and restrained.

steps.title: Marlborough and the aroma chemistry
steps.body: Marlborough, in New Zealand, put Sauvignon on the world map in the 1980s with intense passion fruit, gooseberry and cut grass. Sunny days and cold nights give ripe fruit and high acidity together. The green notes come from pyrazines; the tropical notes from thiols, released during fermentation. Machine harvesting and skin contact can increase them.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Sauvignon Blanc its green, grassy aromas?
steps.explanation: Pyrazines give grass and green pepper. Thiols give passion fruit and grapefruit. Terpenes are the floral compounds of Muscat and Riesling.

steps.title: Bordeaux and Fumé Blanc
steps.body: In Bordeaux, Sauvignon is blended with Sémillon for dry whites, sometimes in oak, as in Pessac-Léognan. That gives fuller, waxy wines that can age. In California, Robert Mondavi named his oaked Sauvignon Fumé Blanc in the 1960s, borrowing from Pouilly-Fumé. Chile and South Africa also make fine examples from coastal sites.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Sauvignon Blanc style.
steps.explanation: The same grape gives very different wines, from restrained to exuberant.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Loire gives restrained, mineral Sauvignon
Marlborough gives intense passion fruit and grass
Bordeaux blends it with Sémillon, sometimes in oak

lessons.title: Riesling around the world
lessons.subtitle: Germany, Alsace, Austria, Australia
objectives: Explain why Riesling expresses place clearly

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: Riesling is Germany's great grape. In the cool Mosel, on steep slate slopes, it gives light wines, often 7.5 to 9% alcohol, with high acidity and some sweetness. In the Rheingau and Pfalz, warmer and broader, it gives fuller, more often dry wines. Labels may use Prädikat terms, like Kabinett or Spätlese, for ripeness at harvest.

steps.title: Why Riesling shows place
steps.body: Riesling is rarely oaked, rarely put through malolactic, and is almost never blended. With nothing to mask it, the vineyard speaks clearly: slate, granite and limestone sites give recognisably different wines. Its high acidity, often above 8 g/l, also keeps it fresh for decades, from dry to sweet.
steps.highlight: No oak, no blend: pure place

steps.prompt: Most German Riesling labelled Kabinett is fermented in new oak.
steps.explanation: Not true. Riesling is almost always made without new oak, to keep its pure fruit and acidity. Kabinett refers to ripeness at harvest, not winemaking.

steps.title: Alsace, Austria, Australia
steps.body: In Alsace, Riesling is mostly dry, fuller and riper, from a dry, sunny valley sheltered by the Vosges. Austria's Wachau and Kamptal make dry, powerful versions on steep terraces above the Danube. Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys give dry, lime-scented wines that develop toast and petrol notes with age.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Riesling.
steps.explanation: Each place gives a distinct style, from light and off-dry to powerful and dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany's Mosel gives light, high-acid, often off-dry Riesling
Alsace, Austria and Australia make mostly dry Riesling
Riesling shows place clearly because it's rarely oaked or blended

lessons.title: Pinot Grigio and Gewürztraminer
lessons.subtitle: Pink-skinned, very different
objectives: Compare Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris styles
Explain the challenges of aromatic grapes

steps.title: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris
steps.body: Pinot Gris has pinkish-grey skin. In north-east Italy it is picked early for light, neutral, crisp Pinot Grigio, one of the world's best-selling whites. In Alsace it is picked riper for fuller, richer wines with pear, honey and spice, sometimes off-dry. Oregon makes a middle style. The name on the label usually signals the style.

steps.title: Gewürztraminer
steps.body: Gewürztraminer, from the Traminer family of north Italy, has pink skin and intense aromas of lychee, rose and ginger, from compounds called terpenes. It ripens to high sugar and often reaches 14% alcohol with low acidity, which can make it feel heavy. Alsace is its home, from dry to late-harvest sweet.
steps.highlight: Lychee and rose, low acidity, high alcohol

steps.prompt: Which aroma is most typical of Gewürztraminer?
steps.explanation: Lychee and rose are Gewürztraminer's signature, from terpenes. Gooseberry points to Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.body: Gewürztraminer is a classic with Munster cheese in Alsace, and its exotic perfume suits mildly spiced dishes, especially when a touch of sweetness balances the heat.

steps.prompt: Gewürztraminer's main challenge is its naturally low ____.
steps.explanation: It ripens to high sugar and alcohol but loses acidity, so growers must pick carefully to keep balance.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Grigio is light and crisp; Pinot Gris is riper and richer
Gewürztraminer smells of lychee and rose
Aromatic grapes like Gewürztraminer need care to keep acidity

lessons.title: Chenin Blanc and Sémillon
lessons.subtitle: Two grapes, many styles
objectives: Describe Chenin Blanc's range in the Loire
Explain Sémillon's styles in Bordeaux and Australia

steps.title: Chenin Blanc
steps.body: Chenin Blanc has very high acidity and flavours of apple, quince and honey. In the Loire's Anjou and Touraine it makes every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling. Vouvray can be any of these; Savennières is dry and long-lived; Coteaux du Layon is sweet, often from noble rot. South Africa grows more Chenin than any other country.
steps.highlight: Chenin: high acid, dry to sweet

steps.title: Sémillon
steps.body: Sémillon has thin skins, low acidity and a waxy, lemony texture. Thin skins make it prone to noble rot, the fungus Botrytis cinerea, which shrivels berries and concentrates sugar. That's why it is the main grape of Sauternes. In Australia's Hunter Valley, picked early at about 10 to 11%, it makes lean whites that turn toasty and honeyed after ten years, without oak.

steps.prompt: Which styles can Chenin Blanc make in the Loire?
steps.explanation: Chenin is made dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling in the Loire. Fortified wines aren't a Loire tradition.

steps.title: Blends and roles
steps.body: In Bordeaux, Sémillon is blended with Sauvignon Blanc: Sémillon gives body and texture, Sauvignon gives acidity and aroma. South Africa's Chenin often comes from old bush vines in Swartland and Stellenbosch, giving concentrated dry wines, sometimes oaked, that now rank among the country's best.
steps.highlight: Sémillon for body, Sauvignon for lift

steps.prompt: Why is Sémillon so suited to making Sauternes?
options: Its thin skins are prone to noble rot
steps.explanation: Thin skins let Botrytis cinerea attack, concentrating sugar. That's what makes Sauternes sweet.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chenin Blanc makes dry, sweet and sparkling wines in the Loire
South Africa grows the most Chenin, often from old vines
Sémillon gives body, ages well in the Hunter and suits noble rot

lessons.title: Viognier and Albariño
lessons.subtitle: Perfume and the Atlantic
objectives: Describe Viognier and its home in Condrieu

steps.title: Viognier
steps.body: Viognier comes from the northern Rhône, where Condrieu makes full-bodied whites with apricot, peach and violet aromas, low acidity and often 14% alcohol. By the 1960s barely 14 hectares were left; it has since spread to California, Australia and the south of France. In Côte-Rôtie, a little Viognier may be co-fermented with Syrah.
steps.highlight: Viognier: apricot and violet, full body

steps.title: Albariño
steps.body: Albariño grows in Rías Baixas, in Galicia, on Spain's wet Atlantic coast. Thick skins resist the damp, and vines are often trained high on pergolas to let air circulate. Its wines are crisp, light to medium-bodied, with lemon, peach and a salty edge. In Portugal it is called Alvarinho, the star grape of Monção e Melgaço in Vinho Verde.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its grape.
steps.explanation: Viognier belongs to the northern Rhône; Albariño and Alvarinho to the Atlantic north-west of Iberia.

steps.title: Two opposite whites
steps.body: Viognier needs heat to develop its perfume, but must be picked before acidity falls too far. Albariño needs a cool, damp climate and thick skins to stay healthy and fresh. One is generous and soft; the other is bright and salty, a classic with Galician seafood.
steps.highlight: Viognier: warm and soft. Albariño: cool and bright.

steps.prompt: Why are Albariño vines often trained on high pergolas?
options: To get more sun on the leaves
To let air circulate and reduce rot in a damp climate
steps.explanation: Rías Baixas is very wet. Raising the canopy lets air move through, keeping grapes healthy.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier gives full, perfumed wines, at home in Condrieu
Albariño gives crisp, salty wines on the Atlantic coast
One needs warmth; the other thrives in cool, damp air

lessons.title: Other whites to know
lessons.subtitle: Five grapes that matter
objectives: Name a classic region for each grape

steps.title: Grüner Veltliner and Assyrtiko
steps.body: Grüner Veltliner is Austria's signature grape: crisp, with citrus, green apple and white pepper, from light to powerful in the Wachau. Assyrtiko, from Santorini in Greece, keeps very high acidity even in hot sun, and grows on volcanic soil, giving firm, mineral, citrus wines.
steps.highlight: Grüner: white pepper. Assyrtiko: acid and volcanic.

steps.title: Muscat and Torrontés
steps.body: Muscat is a family of grapes that tastes like fresh grapes, thanks to terpenes like linalool and geraniol. It makes light, sweet Moscato d'Asti at 5.5% and rich, fortified wines in southern France. Torrontés, Argentina's white grape, a cross that includes Muscat of Alexandria, gives floral wines in high Salta, up to 3,000 m.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its home.
steps.explanation: Each grape has a region where it shows best.

steps.title: Melon and Garganega
steps.body: Melon de Bourgogne makes Muscadet, near the Loire's mouth: light, crisp and often aged on its lees, labelled sur lie, which adds texture and a slight spritz. Garganega is the main grape of Soave, in the Veneto, giving almond, lemon and a light texture, and sweet Recioto di Soave from dried grapes.
steps.highlight: Muscadet sur lie; Soave from Garganega

steps.prompt: Muscadet is made from the Muscat grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. Despite the name, Muscadet is made from Melon de Bourgogne. Muscat is a different, aromatic family.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grüner Veltliner and Assyrtiko are crisp, high-acid whites
Muscat and Torrontés are floral, grape-scented whites
Muscadet comes from Melon; Soave from Garganega

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from White Grapes and Their Places
objectives: Link each grape to its classic regions

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its classic region.
steps.explanation: Every grape has a place that set its benchmark.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Sauvignon Blanc passion fruit aromas?
steps.explanation: Thiols give tropical notes; pyrazines give green ones.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are usually made without oak?
steps.explanation: Côte de Beaune Chardonnay is classically fermented and aged in oak.

steps.prompt: Sémillon's thin skins make it prone to noble rot.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why it is the main grape of Sauternes.

steps.prompt: Pinot Grigio in Italy is usually light and crisp, while Pinot ____ in Alsace is richer.
steps.explanation: Same grape, Pinot Gris, with the French name linked to the richer style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc change with climate and winemaking
Riesling and Chenin make every style from dry to sweet
Aromatic grapes like Gewürztraminer and Viognier need careful picking
Each grape has a benchmark region worth knowing

modules.title: Black Grapes and Their Places
modules.description: The principal black grapes, the regions that made them famous and how place changes the wine.

lessons.title: Cabernet Sauvignon around the world
lessons.subtitle: The grape that travelled furthest
objectives: Describe Cabernet in Bordeaux's Left Bank

steps.title: The Left Bank
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, born in Bordeaux in the 17th century. On the gravel soils of the Médoc, which drain well and store heat, it leads the blend in wines like Pauillac and Margaux. The style: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin and acidity, built to age.

steps.title: Late ripening
steps.body: Cabernet buds and ripens late. In cool years it can keep a green pepper note, from pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness. That's why it needs warm, well-drained sites. Warm regions like Napa Valley give riper blackcurrant, softer tannins and 14.5% alcohol or more.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon thrive on the gravel of the Médoc?
options: Gravel drains and stores heat, helping a late ripener
steps.explanation: Gravel warms the roots and drains water, both helping a late-ripening grape in a moderate climate.

steps.title: Napa, Chile and Australia
steps.body: Napa Valley made Cabernet famous in the New World after the Judgment of Paris in 1976. Chile's Maipo gives ripe blackcurrant with a minty note. Australia's Coonawarra, on red terra rossa soil, gives eucalyptus and mint; Margaret River gives an elegant, Bordeaux-like style.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet character.
steps.explanation: Cabernet keeps its blackcurrant core while place changes the rest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet leads the blends of Bordeaux's gravelly Left Bank
As a late ripener it needs warmth, or it tastes green
Napa, Maipo, Coonawarra and Margaret River each give a distinct style

lessons.title: Merlot around the world
lessons.subtitle: Softness and the Right Bank
objectives: Describe Merlot on Bordeaux's Right Bank

steps.title: The Right Bank
steps.body: Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux. On the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, it leads the blend. Clay and limestone soils hold water and stay cool, suiting an early-ripening grape. The wines show plum, black cherry and a velvety texture; Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot.

steps.title: Why Merlot suits cooler soils
steps.body: Merlot buds and ripens about one to two weeks before Cabernet Sauvignon. That lets it ripen on cool clay where Cabernet would struggle. But early budding brings frost risk, and its thin skin makes it sensitive to rot. In warm places it can overripen fast, losing freshness and turning jammy.

steps.prompt: Merlot ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Merlot ripens one to two weeks earlier, which is why it suits cooler clay soils.

steps.title: Beyond Bordeaux
steps.body: Merlot is grown widely: in Italy, notably in Tuscany's Bolgheri and in Friuli; in Chile and California for soft, fruity reds; in Washington State for structured, fresh versions; and in New Zealand's Hawke's Bay. The 2004 film Sideways hurt its reputation in the United States, though great Merlot never went away.

steps.prompt: Which wine is famous for being made almost entirely from Merlot?
steps.explanation: Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot. Margaux is Cabernet-led; Sassicaia is Cabernet-based; Vega Sicilia is Tempranillo-led.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot leads the Right Bank blends of Pomerol and Saint-Émilion
It ripens early, suiting cool clay soils
It's grown widely, from Italy to Washington and New Zealand

lessons.title: Pinot Noir around the world
lessons.subtitle: The cool-climate red
objectives: Name its key New World regions
Explain why Pinot needs a cool climate

steps.title: Burgundy
steps.body: Pinot Noir is Burgundy's red grape. On the Côte d'Or's limestone and marl slopes, it gives wines that can be light in colour yet intense in aroma: red cherry, raspberry, and with age, earth, game and forest floor. Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée and Pommard are famous villages.

steps.title: Why cool climates
steps.body: Pinot's thin skins and early ripening make it fragile. In heat, it ripens too fast, losing its delicate aromas and acidity, and turns jammy. In cool places, the long, slow season builds complexity. It is also prone to rot, frost and virus, and mutates easily; Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations of it.
steps.highlight: Thin skins, early ripening, cool sites

steps.prompt: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour ____ of Pinot Noir.
steps.explanation: They arose as natural mutations of the skin colour. Genetically, they are almost identical to Pinot Noir.

steps.title: Beyond Burgundy
steps.body: Pinot thrives in Oregon's Willamette Valley, California's Sonoma Coast and Santa Barbara, New Zealand's Central Otago and Martinborough, Germany, where it's called Spätburgunder, and in Champagne as part of the blend. Each gives a different balance of fruit, earth and spice.

steps.prompt: Which region is NOT a well-known home of Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: The Barossa is hot and best known for Shiraz. The others are cool regions famous for Pinot Noir.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy's Côte d'Or is Pinot Noir's benchmark
Thin skins and early ripening need a cool climate
Oregon, Sonoma, Central Otago and Germany grow fine Pinot

lessons.title: Syrah and Grenache
lessons.subtitle: The Rhône pair
objectives: Compare Syrah in the Rhône and Australia

steps.title: Syrah
steps.body: In the northern Rhône, Syrah grows on steep granite slopes in Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage, giving firm, peppery, blackberry wines. In Australia it's Shiraz, the country's most planted grape. The Barossa makes ripe, full wines with chocolate and spice; cooler sites, like the Yarra or Canberra, give peppery styles closer to the Rhône.
steps.highlight: Rhône: pepper. Barossa: chocolate and ripe fruit.

steps.title: Grenache
steps.body: Grenache, from Spain, where it's called Garnacha, loves heat and drought. Its thin skins give paler wines with red fruit, spice and high alcohol, often 15%. Grown as bush vines on poor soils, it can live over 100 years. It is the main grape of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Priorat and many rosés, and part of sweet fortified wines like Banyuls.
steps.highlight: Grenache: heat, red fruit, high alcohol

steps.prompt: Which feature best describes Grenache?
options: Thin skins, red fruit and high alcohol
steps.explanation: Grenache has thin skins and reaches high sugar levels. It's paler than Syrah but strong in alcohol.

steps.title: GSM blends
steps.body: Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre, often called GSM, are blended across the southern Rhône and in Australia. Grenache brings red fruit and alcohol, Syrah brings colour and structure, Mourvèdre brings tannin, meaty notes and dark fruit. Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 varieties, but most wines are led by Grenache.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to what it brings to a GSM blend.
steps.explanation: Each grape fills a gap in the blend. Viognier belongs to the northern Rhône, co-fermented with Syrah.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah is peppery in the Rhône and riper as Barossa Shiraz
Grenache gives red fruit, spice and high alcohol, and loves heat
GSM blends combine Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre

lessons.title: Tempranillo and Sangiovese
lessons.subtitle: Spain's and Italy's great reds
objectives: Describe Tempranillo in Rioja and Ribera

steps.title: Tempranillo
steps.body: Tempranillo is Spain's leading red grape, early-ripening, as its name, from temprano, suggests. In Rioja it is often blended with Garnacha and aged in oak, traditionally American, giving vanilla, coconut and red fruit. In Ribera del Duero, high on the plateau, it's called Tinto Fino and gives darker, more powerful wines. In Portugal it's Tinta Roriz or Aragonez.

steps.title: Sangiovese
steps.body: Sangiovese is Italy's most planted red. Its thin skins and high acidity give medium colour, firm tannin, sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried herbs. It's the grape of Chianti and Chianti Classico, of Brunello di Montalcino, which must be 100% Sangiovese, and of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Its acidity makes it great with tomato-based food.
steps.highlight: Sangiovese: sour cherry and high acidity

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its description.
steps.explanation: Tempranillo leads in Spain; Sangiovese in central Italy.

steps.body: When you taste a red with sour cherry and tea-like tannin that makes you crave pasta with tomato sauce, think Sangiovese. If it smells of vanilla, leather and strawberry, think Rioja.

steps.prompt: Brunello di Montalcino must be made entirely from Sangiovese.
steps.explanation: Yes. Brunello di Montalcino is 100% Sangiovese by law, unlike Chianti, which can include other grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo leads Rioja and Ribera del Duero, often with oak
Sangiovese gives Chianti and Brunello their sour cherry and acidity
Both have regional names and long ageing traditions

lessons.title: Nebbiolo and Malbec
lessons.subtitle: Tannin and altitude
objectives: Describe Nebbiolo in Barolo and Barbaresco
Describe Malbec in Cahors and Mendoza

steps.title: Nebbiolo
steps.body: Nebbiolo, from Piedmont, is pale in colour but very high in tannin and acidity, with aromas of rose, tar, cherry and dried herbs. It ripens very late, often in October, in the fog, or nebbia, that may give it its name. Barolo and Barbaresco are its great wines, and both need long ageing to soften.
steps.highlight: Pale colour, huge tannin, rose and tar

steps.title: Malbec
steps.body: Malbec comes from south-west France, where Cahors makes dark, tannic wines once called black wine. In Argentina's Mendoza, at 800 to 1,500 m, it found new life. Strong sun and cool nights give deep purple colour, ripe plum and violet, and softer tannins. Argentina now grows more Malbec than anywhere else in the world.

steps.prompt: Why is a Barolo pale in colour yet very tannic?
options: Nebbiolo has few colour pigments but lots of tannin
It's aged in white wine barrels
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo's skins are low in stable colour pigments yet rich in tannin. Colour isn't a good guide to its power.

steps.title: Altitude in Mendoza
steps.body: Every 100 m of altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees. In high vineyards like Valle de Uco, at up to 1,500 m, nights are cool, so grapes keep acidity. The intense ultraviolet light thickens skins, adding colour and tannin. That's why Mendoza Malbec is ripe and dark yet fresh.
steps.highlight: High altitude: cool nights, intense light

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its key region.
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo stays at home in Piedmont; Malbec has an Old World home in Cahors and a New World one in Mendoza.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo is pale but very tannic, and makes Barolo and Barbaresco
Malbec comes from Cahors and found fame in Mendoza
Altitude gives Mendoza Malbec colour and freshness

lessons.title: Other reds to know
lessons.subtitle: Five grapes that complete the map
objectives: Name a classic region for each

steps.title: Zinfandel and Pinotage
steps.body: Zinfandel, the same grape as Italy's Primitivo, came from Croatia and became California's heritage red, with ripe bramble fruit and high alcohol, often from old vines in Lodi and Sonoma. Pinotage is South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, made in 1925, giving dark, smoky wines with red fruit.

steps.title: Gamay and Carmenère
steps.body: Gamay is the grape of Beaujolais, light and fruity, often with carbonic maceration. Carmenère, once grown in Bordeaux, was nearly lost there after phylloxera. In 1994 it was found in Chile, where it had been mistaken for Merlot. It gives dark fruit and a green, peppery note when not fully ripe.
steps.highlight: Carmenère was found in Chile in 1994

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its country of fame.
steps.explanation: Each grape is closely tied to one country's identity.

steps.title: Touriga Nacional and Tannat
steps.body: Touriga Nacional is Portugal's finest red grape, giving dark, floral wines in the Douro and Dão, and a key grape in Port. Tannat, from south-west France, has very high tannin; Uruguay adopted it as its national grape. Its name is close to the word tannin, and with good reason.

steps.prompt: Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile after being mistaken for Merlot.
steps.explanation: Yes. In 1994, DNA analysis and ampelography showed many Chilean Merlot vineyards were actually Carmenère.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Zinfandel is California's heritage red; Pinotage is South Africa's own
Gamay makes Beaujolais; Carmenère is Chile's rediscovered grape
Touriga Nacional leads in Portugal; Tannat in Uruguay

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Black Grapes and Their Places
objectives: Link each grape to its classic regions
Explain how climate and soil shape each

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its classic region.
steps.explanation: Each grape has a benchmark place.

steps.prompt: Which grape is pale in colour yet very tannic?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo has few stable pigments but lots of tannin and acidity.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are part of a classic GSM blend?
steps.explanation: GSM stands for Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.

steps.prompt: Merlot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why Merlot suits the cooler clay of the Right Bank.

steps.prompt: In Spain's Ribera del Duero, Tempranillo is called Tinto ____.
steps.explanation: Tinto Fino is the local name. Tinta Roriz is the Douro's name, and Tinto Cão is a different Portuguese grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet and Merlot shape Bordeaux's two banks
Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo need special sites and time

modules.title: Reading the Label
modules.description: What a label must tell you, what it only implies and how quality systems differ between Europe and the rest of the world.

lessons.title: What a label must say
lessons.subtitle: The compulsory information
objectives: List the information most labels must show

steps.title: The essentials
steps.body: Most wine labels must show the producer or bottler, the country of origin, the alcohol by volume, the volume of the bottle and allergen warnings. Wines with a geographical indication must name it. Since December 2023, EU labels must also give nutrition and ingredient information, often through a QR code.

steps.title: Vintage and sulphites
steps.body: The vintage is the year the grapes were picked. In the EU, if it is stated, at least 85% of the grapes must be from that year. Wines with over 10 mg/l of sulphur dioxide must say contains sulphites. Almost all wines do, since sulphur dioxide protects against oxygen and bacteria, and yeast makes a little naturally.
steps.highlight: Vintage: at least 85% from that year in the EU

steps.prompt: What does the vintage on a European label mean?
options: The year the wine was bottled
The year at least 85% of the grapes were harvested
The year the vineyard was planted
The year the wine was released
steps.explanation: Vintage is the harvest year. In the EU, at least 85% of the grapes must come from the stated year.

steps.title: Allergens
steps.body: Wines fined with egg or milk products must say so if any residue remains. Many vegans look for wines fined with bentonite clay or pea protein instead, or unfined wines. Some producers now state vegan on the label, but that term isn't regulated everywhere.
steps.highlight: Egg and milk fining must be declared

steps.prompt: A wine labelled contains sulphites has had unusually large amounts of chemicals added.
steps.explanation: Not true. The warning applies above 10 mg/l, which covers almost every wine. Yeast produces some sulphur dioxide itself.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels must show producer, origin, abv, volume and allergens
In the EU, a stated vintage means at least 85% of grapes from that year
Contains sulphites applies to almost all wines

lessons.title: Geographical indications
lessons.subtitle: Place as a legal promise
objectives: Explain what a geographical indication is
Explain why place names are protected

steps.title: What a GI is
steps.body: A geographical indication, or GI, is a legally defined area whose name can only be used by wines from there. Champagne, Rioja and Napa Valley are all GIs. Using the name promises origin, and often more: in Europe, rules may set grapes, yields and winemaking.
steps.highlight: A GI is a protected place name

steps.title: PDO and PGI
steps.body: The EU has two levels. PDO, Protected Designation of Origin, is stricter: grapes must all come from the area, and rules cover varieties, yields, methods and ageing. PGI, Protected Geographical Indication, covers larger areas with looser rules: at least 85% of grapes from the area, and wider grape choices. Each country has its own names for them.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Each step down the ladder gives producers more freedom and the consumer less information about place.

steps.title: Why protection matters
steps.body: Place names became valuable, so others copied them. Before protection, sparkling wines worldwide called themselves Champagne. Today, EU agreements protect GIs in many countries. In the US, some older semi-generic names like California Champagne can still appear on bottles approved before 2006, but no new ones.
steps.highlight: Protection stops others using famous names

steps.prompt: What does PDO require that PGI does not?
options: All grapes from the defined area
steps.explanation: PDO requires all grapes from the area and stricter rules. PGI requires at least 85%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A GI is a legally protected place name
PDO is stricter than PGI
Protection stops famous names being copied

lessons.title: European quality systems
lessons.subtitle: AOC, DOCG, DO and Prädikat
objectives: Name the national terms for PDO and PGI
Explain the extra tiers in Italy and Spain

steps.title: National names
steps.body: Each EU country names its levels. France: AOC or AOP for PDO, IGP or Vin de Pays for PGI. Italy: DOCG and DOC for PDO, IGT for PGI. Spain: DOCa or DOQ and DO for PDO, Vino de la Tierra for PGI. Portugal: DOC for PDO, Vinho Regional for PGI.
steps.highlight: AOC, DOC, DO: the PDO family

steps.title: Extra steps
steps.body: Italy's DOCG is a top tier, with stricter rules and tasting approval; Barolo and Chianti Classico are DOCG. Spain's DOCa, for Rioja and Priorat, works similarly. Germany's PDO wines are graded partly by sugar in the grapes at harvest: Qualitätswein, then Prädikatswein with six levels, from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese.
steps.highlight: DOCG and DOCa sit above DOC and DO

steps.prompt: Match each term to its country.
steps.explanation: Every EU country uses its own words for the same two levels, sometimes with extra tiers.

steps.body: When a label from Europe names a region and nothing else, it's usually a PDO. Look up the rules once and you'll know the grape for life: Chablis is Chardonnay, Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, Barolo is Nebbiolo.

steps.prompt: Order Germany's Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Eiswein sits beside Beerenauslese in required ripeness, but is made from frozen grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Each EU country has its own names for PDO and PGI
Italy's DOCG and Spain's DOCa are top tiers
Germany grades Prädikatswein by ripeness at harvest

lessons.title: New World labels
lessons.subtitle: Grape and place, fewer rules
objectives: Explain how New World labels work
Describe the AVA and GI systems

steps.title: Grape first
steps.body: New World labels usually lead with the grape variety and the brand. GIs exist but generally only define the area; they don't set grapes, yields or methods. A Napa Valley wine can be any variety, made any way, as long as the grapes come from Napa.

steps.title: Percentage rules
steps.body: Labelling rules set minimums. In the US, a varietal label needs 75% of the named grape, and an AVA name needs 85% of the grapes from that area. In Australia, Chile, New Zealand and South Africa, the figure is usually 85% for variety, vintage and region. A state or county name in the US needs 75%.

steps.prompt: A Californian wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon must contain at least how much of that grape?
steps.explanation: US federal law requires 75% for a varietal label. Many other New World countries use 85%.

steps.title: Reading the extras
steps.body: Terms like Reserve, Private Selection or Old Vines usually have no legal meaning in the New World. A few exceptions exist: in Washington, Reserve must be a small part of production, and South Africa's Wine of Origin seal certifies origin. Treat most extra words as marketing.

steps.prompt: An AVA in the United States sets which grapes may be grown.
steps.explanation: Not true. An AVA defines only the area. Growers can plant any grape and make wine as they choose.

steps.title: What you learned
points: New World labels lead with grape and brand
GIs define area, not style or grapes
Percentage rules set minimums for variety, vintage and region

lessons.title: Ageing and style terms
lessons.subtitle: Words that tell you more
objectives: Explain Spanish and Italian ageing terms
Recognise terms with no legal meaning

steps.title: Ageing terms
steps.body: Some terms set minimum ageing. In Spain, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva each require more time in oak and bottle; Rioja Gran Reserva reds need at least five years, with two in oak. In Italy, Riserva means longer ageing than the standard wine, with rules set for each DOC. Portugal's Reserva requires higher alcohol and quality approval.

steps.title: Sweetness terms
steps.body: Sparkling wines use a scale based on grams of sugar per litre: Brut Nature up to 3, Extra Brut up to 6, Brut up to 12, Extra Dry 12 to 17, Dry 17 to 32, Demi-Sec 32 to 50, Doux over 50. Still wines use terms like sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux in France, or trocken and halbtrocken in Germany.

steps.prompt: Which sparkling wine term means the driest of these?
steps.explanation: Brut, up to 12 g/l, is drier than Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l. The naming is confusing but legal.

steps.title: Words without rules
steps.body: Many attractive words have no legal meaning in many countries: Reserve outside Europe, Old Vines, Natural and Premium. Organic, by contrast, is regulated: certified organic wine must follow rules on farming and winemaking, including lower sulphur limits in the EU.
steps.highlight: Organic is regulated; Old Vines usually isn't

steps.prompt: Which terms have a legal ageing meaning in Spain?
steps.explanation: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are regulated. Old Vines has no legal definition.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spanish and Italian terms like Reserva and Riserva set minimum ageing
Sparkling sweetness terms follow a sugar scale, with Brut dry
Many attractive words, like Old Vines, have no legal meaning

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Reading the Label
objectives: Interpret European and New World systems

steps.prompt: In the EU, a stated vintage means at least what share of grapes from that year?
steps.explanation: 85% in the EU, and in many New World countries too.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its country.
steps.explanation: Every country has its own terms for protected places.

steps.prompt: A PGI wine has stricter rules than a PDO wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. PDO is stricter; PGI covers larger areas with looser rules.

steps.prompt: Order these sparkling wine terms from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, which surprises many people.

steps.prompt: Which of these are usually defined by law?
steps.explanation: Gran Reserva and Organic are regulated. Old Vines and US Reserve generally aren't.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels must show producer, origin, abv, volume and allergens
PDO is stricter than PGI; each country names them differently
New World GIs define area only
Ageing and sweetness terms are regulated; many others are marketing

modules.title: Sparkling Wine
modules.description: Where the bubbles come from, and how each method gives a different wine.

lessons.title: How the bubbles get there
lessons.subtitle: Trapping carbon dioxide
objectives: Explain where the bubbles come from
Name the main methods of making sparkling wine

steps.title: Second fermentation
steps.body: Most sparkling wines start as a dry, still base wine. Yeast and sugar are added, and a second fermentation takes place in a sealed vessel, a bottle or a pressurised tank. The carbon dioxide can't escape, so it dissolves in the wine. Champagne reaches about 6 atmospheres; Prosecco and other lighter styles often less.
steps.highlight: Second fermentation in a closed vessel

steps.title: The methods
steps.body: The traditional method makes the second fermentation in the bottle you buy. The transfer method ferments in bottle, then empties the wine into a tank to filter it. The tank method ferments in large pressurised tanks. The cheapest way is carbonation, injecting gas like soda, which gives large, short-lived bubbles.

steps.prompt: Match each method to how it works.
steps.explanation: Each method traps carbon dioxide in a different way.

steps.title: Why method matters
steps.body: Fermenting in bottle leaves the wine in contact with dead yeast, the lees, for months or years. That adds bread, brioche and biscuit flavours and finer bubbles. Tank fermentation is fast, often weeks, and keeps fresh, fruity, floral aromas. Neither is better: they suit different grapes and styles.

steps.prompt: All sparkling wines get their bubbles from a second fermentation.
steps.explanation: Not true. The cheapest are carbonated, with gas injected directly. Their bubbles are coarser and fade faster.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bubbles come from carbon dioxide trapped during a second fermentation
Traditional, transfer, tank and carbonation are the main methods
Bottle fermentation adds toasty notes; tank keeps fresh fruit

lessons.title: The traditional method
lessons.subtitle: Champagne's way
objectives: Put the steps of the traditional method in order

steps.title: The steps
steps.body: A dry base wine is blended, then bottled with sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage. The bottle is sealed with a crown cap. A second fermentation raises alcohol by about 1.2 to 1.5% and makes carbon dioxide. The wine then rests on its lees, from 15 months for non-vintage Champagne to many years for top wines.
steps.highlight: Tirage, second fermentation, ageing on lees

steps.title: Getting the yeast out
steps.body: Riddling, or remuage, slowly turns and tilts the bottles until the dead yeast slides into the neck. It once took weeks by hand; machines called gyropalettes now do it in about a week. The neck is frozen and the cap removed: pressure pushes out the plug of ice and yeast. This is disgorgement. Then sweetened wine, the dosage, is added.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of the traditional method in order.
items: Add sugar and yeast, and seal
steps.explanation: The order ensures the yeast does its work, adds flavour, and is then removed cleanly.

steps.title: Dosage
steps.body: Dosage is a mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement. It balances the high acidity of the base wine and decides the final sweetness: most Champagne is Brut, with up to 12 g/l. Brut Nature has none added. The traditional method is used for Champagne, Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and many others.

steps.prompt: What is disgorgement?
options: Removing the frozen plug of yeast from the neck
steps.explanation: Disgorgement removes the yeast sediment, using the wine's own pressure to push out a frozen plug.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The second fermentation happens in the bottle you buy
Riddling moves the yeast to the neck; disgorgement removes it
Dosage balances acidity and sets the sweetness

lessons.title: The tank method
lessons.subtitle: Fresh and fruity bubbles
objectives: Explain how the tank method works
Explain why it suits aromatic grapes
Compare it with the traditional method

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: In the tank method, also called Charmat or Martinotti, the base wine goes into a sealed, pressurised tank with sugar and yeast. The second fermentation takes days or weeks. The wine is then filtered under pressure and bottled. The whole process can take as little as a month.
steps.highlight: Second fermentation in a pressurised tank

steps.title: Why aromatic grapes suit it
steps.body: Glera, Muscat and similar grapes have delicate floral and fruit aromas. Long contact with yeast would cover them with bready notes. The tank method keeps them fresh. It is also cheaper and faster, so the wines are affordable, made to drink young, and usually show larger, softer bubbles than Champagne.
steps.highlight: Tank: fresh fruit, made to drink young

steps.prompt: Which wine is typically made by the tank method?
steps.explanation: Prosecco is made by the tank method. Champagne, Cava and Franciacorta use the traditional method.

steps.body: Keep tank-method wines in a cool place and drink them within a year or two. Their charm is freshness, and it doesn't last.

steps.prompt: What are typical features of tank-method sparkling wine?
steps.explanation: Bread and biscuit notes come from long ageing on lees in bottle, typical of the traditional method.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The tank method ferments in sealed tanks, often in weeks
It preserves fresh fruit and floral aromas
It's faster and cheaper, and the wines are best young

lessons.title: Champagne and its rivals
lessons.subtitle: Traditional method around the world
objectives: Describe the Champagne region and its grapes

steps.title: Champagne
steps.body: Champagne lies about 150 km north-east of Paris, one of the coolest wine regions in France. Grapes ripen barely, giving very high acidity, perfect for sparkling wine. The main grapes are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. Most Champagne is a blend of several years, called non-vintage, to keep a consistent house style.
steps.highlight: Cool climate, high acidity, three grapes

steps.title: Chalk and ageing
steps.body: Champagne's chalk soils drain well yet hold water deep, and the chalk cellars dug beneath Reims and Épernay stay at about 10 to 12 degrees all year, ideal for long ageing on lees. Non-vintage must age at least 15 months, vintage at least 3 years. That ageing gives the toasty, brioche notes.

steps.prompt: The three main grapes of Champagne are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot ____.
steps.explanation: Pinot Meunier, often just Meunier, is the third main grape, giving fruit and roundness.

steps.title: The rivals
steps.body: Cava, mostly from Catalonia, uses local grapes like Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada, with 9 months minimum on lees. Crémant is made in eight French regions, like Alsace, Burgundy and the Loire. Franciacorta, in Lombardy, uses Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. England's south, on chalk like Champagne's, is a rising star.

steps.prompt: Match each sparkling wine to its origin.
steps.explanation: All of these use the traditional method, with different grapes and rules.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne is cool and chalky, with three main grapes
Non-vintage ages at least 15 months on lees; vintage at least 3 years
Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and English sparkling use the same method

lessons.title: Prosecco and Asti
lessons.subtitle: Italy's lighter bubbles
objectives: Explain how Asti keeps its sweetness

steps.title: Prosecco
steps.body: Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, in the Veneto and Friuli. It must be at least 85% Glera. Most is made by the tank method, giving pear, apple and white flower aromas, light body and fresh acidity. The top area is Conegliano Valdobbiadene, a DOCG of steep hills, with the single slope of Cartizze at its peak.
steps.highlight: Glera, tank method, pear and flowers

steps.title: Asti
steps.body: Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from Piedmont and are made from Moscato Bianco. Instead of a second fermentation, the juice is chilled and stored, then fermented once in a sealed tank. Fermentation is stopped by cooling and filtering, leaving sugar and only 5 to 7% alcohol. Asti is fully sparkling; Moscato d'Asti is gently fizzy, frizzante.

steps.prompt: Asti is made with a second fermentation, like Prosecco.
steps.explanation: Not true. Asti uses a single fermentation in a sealed tank, stopped early to keep sugar and low alcohol.

steps.title: Serving them
steps.body: Both are made to drink young and well chilled. Prosecco suits aperitifs and light dishes; Extra Dry is the most common style, slightly sweeter than Brut. Moscato d'Asti, sweet and low in alcohol, suits fruit desserts and, in Piedmont, sometimes breakfast pastries.

steps.prompt: Which grape is the main grape of Prosecco?
steps.explanation: Prosecco must be at least 85% Glera. Moscato Bianco is the grape of Asti.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco is mostly Glera, made by the tank method
Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from one fermentation, stopped early
Both are best young and chilled

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Sparkling Wine
objectives: Compare the traditional and tank methods

steps.prompt: Put these traditional method steps in order.
steps.explanation: Yeast first does its work, then is moved and removed, and the wine is topped up.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its method.
steps.explanation: Method shapes flavour, bubble and price.

steps.prompt: What gives traditional method wines their bready, toasty notes?
steps.explanation: Long contact with dead yeast in the bottle releases those flavours.

steps.prompt: Which are traditional method sparkling wines?
steps.explanation: Prosecco is mostly made by the tank method.

steps.prompt: Moscato d'Asti is fermented to dryness and then sweetened.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its fermentation is stopped early, leaving natural sugar and low alcohol.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bubbles come from a second fermentation in a closed vessel
The traditional method gives toasty, fine bubbles; tank keeps fruit fresh
Champagne, Cava, Crémant and Franciacorta use the traditional method
Prosecco uses the tank method; Asti a single, stopped fermentation

modules.title: Sweet Wine
modules.description: Four ways to keep sugar in a wine, and why the best sweet wines are never cloying.

lessons.title: Keeping the sugar
lessons.subtitle: How a wine ends up sweet
objectives: Explain the two routes to a sweet wine
Explain why acidity matters in sweet wine

steps.title: Two routes
steps.body: A wine is sweet when sugar remains after fermentation. There are two routes. Stop fermentation before the yeast has eaten all the sugar, by chilling, filtering or adding spirit. Or concentrate the sugar in the grapes so much that yeast can't finish, stopping naturally at around 11 to 14% alcohol with plenty of sugar left.
steps.highlight: Stop the yeast, or overload it with sugar

steps.title: Concentrating sugar
steps.body: Grapes can be concentrated in four main ways: by noble rot, a fungus that dries the berries; by late harvesting, leaving grapes on the vine; by freezing them on the vine, for ice wine; or by drying them after picking. Each removes water, so sugar, acid and flavour all become more intense.
steps.highlight: Noble rot, late harvest, freezing, drying

steps.prompt: Which methods concentrate sugar in the grape before fermentation?
steps.explanation: Adding spirit stops fermentation; it doesn't concentrate the grape. That's how fortified wines like Port keep their sugar.

steps.title: Balance with acidity
steps.body: Sugar without acidity tastes cloying, like syrup. The great sweet wines have high acidity to balance it: Riesling, Chenin Blanc, Furmint and Sémillon blended with Sauvignon are typical. That's why a Mosel Auslese or a Tokaji can feel fresh despite 100 g/l of sugar or more.

steps.prompt: Why do the best sweet wines not taste cloying?
options: They have high acidity to balance the sugar
They have no sugar at all
steps.explanation: High acidity cuts through sugar, keeping the wine fresh and lively.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweet wines either stop fermentation early or start with concentrated grapes
Noble rot, late harvest, freezing and drying concentrate sugar
High acidity keeps sweet wines from tasting cloying

lessons.title: Noble rot
lessons.subtitle: A fungus that makes great wine
objectives: Name the great noble rot wines

steps.title: Botrytis cinerea
steps.body: Noble rot is the fungus Botrytis cinerea. On ripe, healthy grapes in the right conditions, it pierces the skin, letting water evaporate. Berries shrivel, sugar and acidity concentrate, and new flavours appear: honey, marmalade, apricot and ginger. The same fungus in wet weather becomes grey rot, which ruins the crop.
steps.highlight: Botrytis: noble when dry, grey when wet

steps.title: Misty mornings, sunny afternoons
steps.body: Noble rot needs humid, misty mornings, often from rivers or lakes, to let the spores grow, followed by warm, dry afternoons that stop it turning into grey rot. Infection is uneven, so pickers pass through the vineyard several times, choosing only shrivelled berries. Yields can be tiny, sometimes a glass per vine.
steps.highlight: Mist then sun; picking in several passes

steps.prompt: Which conditions favour noble rot rather than grey rot?
options: Misty mornings and dry, sunny afternoons
steps.explanation: Morning humidity lets the fungus grow; dry afternoons stop it becoming destructive grey rot.

steps.title: The great wines
steps.body: Sauternes and Barsac, in Bordeaux, use Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, near the cool Ciron river. Tokaji Aszú, in Hungary, uses Furmint. In Germany and Austria, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are made from botrytised berries. The Loire's Coteaux du Layon and Quarts de Chaume use Chenin Blanc.
steps.highlight: Sauternes, Tokaji, TBA, Coteaux du Layon

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its main grape.
steps.explanation: Each of these is made from noble rot grapes, with a high-acid grape at its heart.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Noble rot is Botrytis cinerea concentrating ripe grapes
It needs misty mornings and dry afternoons
Sauternes, Tokaji Aszú and TBA are its great wines

lessons.title: Late harvest and ice wine
lessons.subtitle: Time and frost
objectives: Explain how late harvest wines are made
Explain how ice wine is made
Name the main regions for each

steps.title: Late harvest
steps.body: Leave grapes on the vine past normal ripeness and they keep gaining sugar, then start to shrivel, losing water. This is late harvest. Labels show it as Vendanges Tardives in Alsace, Spätlese and Auslese in Germany, or simply Late Harvest elsewhere. Some late harvest wines also have a share of noble rot.
steps.highlight: Late harvest: longer on the vine

steps.title: Ice wine
steps.body: Ice wine, Eiswein in Germany and Austria, is made from grapes left on the vine until they freeze, at minus 7 degrees Celsius or colder. They are picked and pressed while frozen. The water stays as ice, so only drops of very sweet, acidic juice flow. Canada's Niagara Peninsula and Okanagan, and Germany, are the main producers.
steps.highlight: Ice wine: picked frozen, at minus 7 or colder

steps.prompt: For true ice wine, grapes must freeze naturally on the vine.
steps.explanation: Yes. In Canada, Germany and Austria, the law requires natural freezing. Freezing grapes artificially, called cryoextraction, cannot be labelled ice wine there.

steps.body: Ice wine tastes of pure fruit, like peach and lemon, because it rarely has noble rot. If you taste honey and marmalade, think botrytis instead.

steps.prompt: Why is the juice of frozen grapes so sweet?
options: The water stays frozen, so only concentrated juice flows
steps.explanation: Pressing frozen grapes leaves most of the water behind as ice, so the juice that flows is rich in sugar and acid.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Late harvest grapes gain sugar and shrivel on the vine
Ice wine grapes are picked and pressed frozen
Canada, Germany and Austria are the main ice wine producers

lessons.title: Dried grapes
lessons.subtitle: Raisins and passito
objectives: Explain how dried grapes can make dry wines

steps.title: Drying after picking
steps.body: Grapes can be dried after harvest, on straw mats, in lofts or racks, or in the sun. Over weeks or months they lose 30 to 50% of their weight. The method is ancient and found all around the Mediterranean. In Italy it is called appassimento, and the wines are called passito.

steps.title: Sweet and dry
steps.body: Most dried grape wines are sweet: Vin Santo from Tuscany, Recioto della Valpolicella, Sicily's Passito di Pantelleria, and Spain's Pedro Ximénez, dried in the sun. But fermentation can run to dryness too. Amarone della Valpolicella is made from dried Corvina grapes fermented nearly dry, giving a powerful red of around 15 to 16% alcohol.

steps.prompt: Amarone is made from dried grapes, but fermented to be nearly ____.
steps.explanation: Unlike Recioto, Amarone's fermentation continues until almost all the sugar is gone, giving a powerful, dry red.

steps.title: Why drying changes flavour
steps.body: Drying doesn't just concentrate sugar. The berries start to oxidise and dry out, adding raisin, fig, dried cherry and chocolate notes. Some grapes get a touch of botrytis in drying lofts too. The result is rich, often high in alcohol, and long-lived.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its region.
steps.explanation: Drying grapes is a Mediterranean tradition, from Spain to Sicily.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Drying grapes after picking concentrates sugar, acid and flavour
Vin Santo, Recioto and Pedro Ximénez are sweet dried grape wines
Amarone is made from dried grapes but fermented nearly dry

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Sweet Wine
objectives: Explain how sweet wines keep their sugar

steps.prompt: Match each method to a wine.
steps.explanation: Each method concentrates sugar in a different way.

steps.prompt: What stops grey rot from developing instead of noble rot?
steps.explanation: Dry afternoons stop the fungus from turning destructive.

steps.prompt: Amarone is a sweet wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It is made from dried grapes but fermented nearly dry. Recioto is its sweet sibling.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are known for great sweet wines thanks to high acidity?
steps.explanation: Gewürztraminer can make sweet wines, but its naturally low acidity is a weakness, not a strength.

steps.prompt: Ice wine grapes must freeze naturally at minus ____ degrees Celsius or colder.
steps.explanation: Minus 7 degrees is the common legal threshold in Canada and Germany.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sweet wines stop fermentation early or start with concentrated grapes
Noble rot, late harvest, freezing and drying concentrate sugar
High acidity keeps great sweet wines fresh
Amarone shows that dried grapes can also make dry wine

modules.title: Fortified Wine
modules.description: Spirit added before or after fermentation, and the families that follow.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: Fortification means adding grape spirit to wine, raising its alcohol to 15 to 22%. The spirit is usually neutral, around 77% for Port, or around 95% elsewhere. More alcohol kills yeast and bacteria, so fortified wines are very stable and last long once opened.

steps.title: Timing decides sweetness
steps.body: Add spirit during fermentation and the yeast dies, leaving natural sugar: Port, Banyuls and Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise are made this way. Add it after the yeast has fermented the wine dry, and the wine stays dry: that's the starting point for Sherry. Some Sherries are sweetened later by blending.

steps.prompt: How does Port keep its sweetness?
options: Spirit added during fermentation stops the yeast
steps.explanation: Spirit added mid-fermentation kills the yeast, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine.

steps.title: Why it began
steps.body: Fortification spread in the 17th and 18th centuries, when wine travelled by ship for months. Extra alcohol stopped it spoiling. British merchants shaped Port in the Douro, Sherry in Jerez and Madeira on its island. The trade explains why so many Port and Sherry houses have English names, like Taylor's, Graham's and Harveys.

steps.prompt: All fortified wines are sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. Fino and Manzanilla Sherry are fortified after a dry fermentation and stay bone dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fortification adds grape spirit, raising alcohol to 15 to 22%
Spirit during fermentation keeps sugar; after, the wine stays dry
It began as a way to protect wine on long voyages

lessons.title: Sherry
lessons.subtitle: Flor, solera and Palomino
objectives: Describe where Sherry is made and from what

steps.title: Jerez and Palomino
steps.body: Sherry comes from the area around Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María, in Andalusia. The main grape is Palomino, which makes a neutral, low-acid base wine. The chalky white soil, called albariza, holds water through hot, dry summers. Sweet styles use Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel.

steps.title: Flor and the solera
steps.body: After fermentation the wine is fortified. Wines for Fino are taken to about 15%; at this level a layer of yeast called flor grows on the surface, protecting the wine from oxygen and adding notes of bread, almonds and salt. Wines for Oloroso go to 17%, which stops flor, so they age with oxygen. Most Sherry ages in a solera, a system of barrels where young wine tops up older wine.

steps.prompt: What does flor do to a Fino Sherry?
options: Protects it from oxygen and adds bready, salty notes
steps.explanation: Flor is a layer of yeast that shields the wine from air and adds its own distinctive flavours.

steps.title: How a solera works
steps.body: A solera is a set of barrels in tiers. Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest tier, called the solera, but never more than about a third at a time. That tier is topped up from the next oldest, called the first criadera, and so on, with new wine entering at the youngest tier. The blend keeps a steady style and gains average age.
steps.highlight: Old tier drawn, refilled from younger

steps.prompt: Put the solera's movements in order, starting with bottling.
items: Draw wine from the oldest tier
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill that from the second criadera
Add new wine to the youngest tier
steps.explanation: Each tier passes some of its wine to the older one, so the style stays consistent year after year.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sherry is made from Palomino on the albariza soils of Jerez
Flor protects Fino from air; Oloroso ages without it
The solera blends wines of many ages for consistency

steps.title: Making Port
steps.body: Port comes from the Douro valley in northern Portugal, from many local grapes, led by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca. Fermentation is fast and intense, often by foot treading in stone tanks, called lagares, or by machines. After two or three days, at about 6 to 9% alcohol, spirit is added, leaving around 90 to 110 g/l of sugar and about 19 to 22% alcohol.

steps.title: Ruby and tawny
steps.body: Ruby styles age briefly in large vats, keeping dark colour and fresh black fruit. Tawny styles age for years in small casks, so oxygen turns them tawny brown, with nuts, caramel and dried fruit. Aged tawnies carry an indication of age: 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old, an average style, not an exact age.
steps.highlight: Ruby: fruit. Tawny: nuts and caramel.

steps.prompt: Match each Port style to its character.
steps.explanation: How a Port ages, in vat, cask or bottle, defines its style.

steps.title: Vintage and LBV
steps.body: Vintage Port comes from a single, exceptional year, declared by each house, about three times a decade. It is bottled after two years and ages for decades in bottle, throwing a heavy sediment. Late Bottled Vintage, or LBV, is from a single year but spends 4 to 6 years in wood, so it is ready to drink sooner.
steps.highlight: Vintage: bottle aged. LBV: wood aged longer.

steps.prompt: Which statements about Port are true?
options: It comes from Portugal's Douro valley
Tawny styles age mainly in bottle
steps.explanation: Tawny Ports age in small casks, not bottle. Vintage Port throws a sediment and needs decanting.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Port is fortified during fermentation, leaving sweetness
Ruby styles are fruity; tawnies are nutty from cask ageing
Vintage Port ages in bottle; LBV is ready earlier

lessons.title: Madeira
lessons.subtitle: Heat, air and immortality
objectives: Name the noble grapes and their sweetness
Explain why Madeira lasts so long

steps.title: Heated wine
steps.body: Madeira comes from the Portuguese island of the same name, in the Atlantic. On long voyages through the tropics, merchants found the wine improved with heat and movement. Today producers recreate this in two ways: estufagem, heating the wine in tanks to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, and canteiro, ageing in casks in warm lofts for years.
steps.highlight: Estufagem: heated tanks. Canteiro: warm lofts.

steps.title: The grapes and their sweetness
steps.body: Four noble white grapes name the main styles, from dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, also spelled Bual, and Malvasia, or Malmsey. All keep striking acidity. Most Madeira, though, is made from Tinta Negra, a versatile black grape. Spirit is added during or after fermentation, depending on the sweetness wanted.

steps.prompt: Order the noble Madeira grapes from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Sercial is the driest style, Malvasia the richest.

steps.title: Why it lasts
steps.body: Madeira has already been heated and exposed to oxygen, so it is almost impossible to spoil. Bottles from the 18th and 19th centuries are still sound. Its high acidity keeps even the sweetest styles fresh. Once opened, a bottle can last for months.

steps.prompt: Why does an open bottle of Madeira last so long?
options: It has already been heated and oxidised in its making
steps.explanation: Madeira's making exposes it to heat and air, so further oxygen does little harm.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Madeira is heated by estufagem or aged by canteiro
Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to sweet
Heat and oxygen in its making make it nearly indestructible

lessons.title: Sweet fortified wines of France
lessons.subtitle: Vins doux naturels
objectives: Explain what a vin doux naturel is
Name the main Muscat and Grenache styles

steps.title: Vins doux naturels
steps.body: In the south of France, sweet fortified wines are called vins doux naturels. Spirit is added during fermentation, as for Port, keeping natural sugar and reaching 15 to 18% alcohol. They are made from Muscat or Grenache, mostly in the Roussillon and the southern Rhône.
steps.highlight: Fortified during fermentation, Muscat or Grenache

steps.title: Muscat and Grenache
