steps.body: The Alentejo covers much of southern Portugal: hot, dry, with wide plains. Its reds are ripe and fruity, from Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, a red-fleshed grape. Whites use Antão Vaz. Some producers still ferment in talhas, large clay pots, a Roman tradition that the DOC now recognises as Vinho de Talha.

steps.prompt: Colares vines grow ungrafted because phylloxera cannot survive in sandy soils.
steps.explanation: Yes. Phylloxera struggles to move through sand, so Colares vines grow on their own roots.

steps.title: Native grapes
steps.body: Portugal has around 250 native grapes, and few international ones. Many are known by different names: Tempranillo is Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo. Field blends, with many varieties mixed in old vineyards, are common. This diversity gives Portugal a distinct identity.

steps.prompt: What is unusual about Alicante Bouschet?
steps.explanation: Alicante Bouschet is a teinturier, with red flesh, giving very deep colour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bairrada makes Baga reds and sparkling wines; Colares grows ungrafted in sand
The Alentejo makes ripe reds and keeps the talha tradition
Portugal has around 250 native grapes

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Spain and Portugal
objectives: Explain Spain's ageing and quality system
Link Iberian regions to their grapes
Compare north and south in both countries

steps.prompt: Order Spain's red ageing categories from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Each category requires more time in oak and bottle.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its main grape.
steps.explanation: Iberia's regions each have their own identity.

steps.prompt: What soil defines Priorat?
steps.explanation: Llicorella forces roots deep and keeps yields tiny.

steps.prompt: Which are regions of Portugal?
steps.explanation: Rioja is in Spain.

steps.prompt: In the Alentejo, Tempranillo is called Aragonez.
steps.explanation: Yes. In the Douro it's Tinta Roriz; in Spain, Tempranillo or Tinto Fino.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spain's ageing terms run from Joven to Gran Reserva
Rioja and Priorat are Spain's DOCa regions
Green Iberia makes fresh whites; the plateau and the south make ripe reds
Portugal's native grapes give it a unique identity

modules.title: Germany, Austria and Hungary
modules.description: Steep slopes, cold rivers, labels that measure ripeness and the oldest classified sweet wine in the world.

steps.title: Graded by ripeness
steps.body: German law grades wine partly by the sugar level of the grapes at harvest, measured in degrees Oechsle. Deutscher Wein and Landwein are the basic levels. Qualitätswein comes from one of 13 regions. Prädikatswein, the top level, adds a ripeness term: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein or Trockenbeerenauslese.

steps.title: Ripeness, not sweetness
steps.body: A Prädikat says how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. A Spätlese can be fermented dry, with trocken on the label, or left off-dry. Trocken means up to 9 g/l of sugar, halbtrocken up to 18 g/l. Feinherb is an unofficial term for off-dry. Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are always sweet.

steps.prompt: What does Spätlese on a German label tell you?
options: The grapes were picked at a higher ripeness level
steps.explanation: Spätlese means late harvest, a ripeness level. The wine can be dry or sweet.

steps.title: The VDP
steps.body: The VDP, an association of about 200 leading estates, created its own vineyard classification, much like Burgundy: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. Dry wines from Grosse Lage sites are labelled Grosses Gewächs, or GG. This system is private, but widely respected.

steps.prompt: A Grosses Gewächs from the VDP is always a sweet wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. Grosses Gewächs is the VDP's term for a dry wine from a top vineyard.

steps.title: What you learned
points: German law grades Prädikatswein by ripeness at harvest
Prädikat terms show ripeness, not sweetness
The VDP ranks vineyards; GG means dry wine from a top site

lessons.title: The Mosel
lessons.subtitle: Slate, slopes and Riesling
objectives: Describe the Mosel's slopes and soils

steps.title: Steep slate
steps.body: The Mosel winds through western Germany at about 50 degrees north, one of the coolest regions for quality wine. The best vineyards rise on steep, south-facing slopes above the river, some over 60 degrees, like the Bremmer Calmont. Dark slate soils absorb heat and the river reflects light, helping Riesling ripen.

steps.title: The Mosel style
steps.body: Mosel Riesling is light, often 7.5 to 10% alcohol, with high acidity, green apple, peach and floral notes. Many are off-dry or sweet, with sugar balancing fierce acidity. They age for decades. Working these slopes is mostly by hand and costs several times more than on flat land.

steps.prompt: Match each Mosel feature to its effect.
steps.explanation: Every feature helps a cool region ripen Riesling.

steps.body: A Mosel Kabinett at 8% alcohol is one of the best lunchtime wines in the world. Light, refreshing and great with spicy food.

steps.prompt: Why can Riesling ripen in a region as cool as the Mosel?
options: Steep south-facing slate slopes capture heat and light
steps.explanation: Slope, aspect, slate and the river all add warmth and light.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Mosel's steep slate slopes help Riesling ripen at 50 degrees north
Mosel Riesling is light, high in acidity and often off-dry
Its tributaries, the Saar and Ruwer, are even cooler

lessons.title: The Rhine
lessons.subtitle: Rheingau, Pfalz and Rheinhessen
objectives: Compare their styles with the Mosel

steps.title: The Rheingau
steps.body: Where the Rhine turns west for about 30 km, the Rheingau faces south across the river, sheltered by the Taunus hills. Riesling covers about 80% of plantings, with Spätburgunder, Germany's Pinot Noir, at Assmannshausen. The wines are fuller and drier than the Mosel's. Schloss Johannisberg claims the discovery of Spätlese in 1775, when the harvest messenger arrived late.

steps.title: Pfalz and Rheinhessen
steps.body: The Pfalz, south of Rheinhessen, is Germany's warmest and sunniest region, sheltered by the Haardt mountains, an extension of the Vosges. It makes rich dry Rieslings, Pinot Noir and many other grapes. Rheinhessen is Germany's largest region, once known for cheap Liebfraumilch, now a source of exciting dry wines from young producers.
steps.highlight: Pfalz: warm and dry. Rheinhessen: large and reborn.

steps.prompt: Which statements about the Pfalz are true?
options: It is one of Germany's warmest regions
It is sheltered by the Haardt mountains
It continues the Alsace landscape north
steps.explanation: The Pfalz makes mainly dry wines; its mountains are an extension of the Vosges.

steps.title: Compared with the Mosel
steps.body: Rhine wines are generally riper and fuller than Mosel wines, with more alcohol and more often dry. The Mosel's slate gives a lighter, more delicate style; the Rheingau and Pfalz, with warmer sites and varied soils, give broader wines. Pinot Noir is increasingly important in the Pfalz and Baden.

steps.prompt: Which region claims the discovery of Spätlese?
steps.explanation: Schloss Johannisberg in the Rheingau tells the story of the late messenger in 1775.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Rheingau makes fuller Riesling on south-facing slopes
The Pfalz is warm and dry; Rheinhessen is large and revived
Rhine wines are generally riper and drier than the Mosel's

steps.title: Lower Austria
steps.body: Most Austrian wine comes from Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, along the Danube. Grüner Veltliner, Austria's signature grape, gives peppery, citrus whites. The Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal make powerful dry Rieslings and Grüners on terraces of granite, gneiss and loess. The DAC system now labels regions by their typical style.

steps.title: The Wachau's terms
steps.body: The Wachau uses its own terms through the Vinea Wachau association. Steinfeder is light, up to 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel is medium, 11.5 to 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald lizard, is the ripest, over 12.5%. All are dry. These terms are by alcohol, unlike Germany's ripeness at harvest.

steps.prompt: The ripest and fullest of the Wachau's dry styles is called ____.
steps.explanation: Smaragd is over 12.5% alcohol. Steinfeder is the lightest, Federspiel sits in the middle, and Ausbruch is a sweet wine from Rust.

steps.title: Reds and sweet wines
steps.body: Burgenland, in the east, is warmer, near the Hungarian border. Blaufränkisch gives structured, peppery reds; Zweigelt, a cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, gives soft, cherry reds. Around the shallow Neusiedlersee lake, mists favour noble rot, and Rust is famous for sweet Ausbruch.

steps.prompt: Which is Austria's signature white grape?
steps.explanation: Grüner Veltliner covers about a third of Austria's vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Austria's Danube regions make Grüner Veltliner and dry Riesling
The Wachau uses Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd
Burgenland makes Blaufränkisch reds and noble rot sweet wines

lessons.title: Tokaj
lessons.subtitle: Hungary's great sweet wine
objectives: Explain how Tokaji Aszú is made

steps.title: The place
steps.body: Tokaj is in north-east Hungary, where the Bodrog and Tisza rivers meet. Autumn mists rise from the rivers, then warm, dry afternoons follow, perfect for noble rot. The soils are volcanic. Furmint is the main grape, with high acidity, joined by Hárslevelű and Sárgamuskotály, a Muscat.

steps.title: Aszú
steps.body: Aszú berries, shrivelled by noble rot, are picked one by one. They are mixed into a base wine or fermenting must, and soaked for a day or two to extract sugar and flavour. Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, equal to the old 5 puttonyos. Wines age at least 18 months in oak.

steps.prompt: What is Tokaj's main grape?
steps.explanation: Furmint dominates Tokaj and gives the high acidity that balances the sugar.

steps.title: The first classification
steps.body: Tokaj was among the first wine regions to classify its vineyards, from 1730, and was legally demarcated in 1737. Its sweet wines were served at European courts; Louis XIV is said to have called it the wine of kings and the king of wines. After decades of communist state control, private estates revived quality from the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Which statements about Tokaj are true?
options: Noble rot is helped by river mists
steps.explanation: Tokaj makes both sweet and dry wines, but Aszú is the most famous.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tokaj's river mists and volcanic soils suit noble rot
Aszú berries are soaked in base wine; at least 120 g/l of sugar
Tokaj was classified from 1730 and demarcated in 1737

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Germany, Austria and Hungary

steps.prompt: Order these Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Each level demands riper grapes at harvest.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its country or region.
steps.explanation: Each place has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Trocken on a German label means the wine is dry.
steps.explanation: Yes. Trocken allows up to 9 g/l of sugar, usually balanced by acidity.

steps.prompt: Which is Austria's most planted white grape?
steps.explanation: Grüner Veltliner is Austria's signature and most planted grape.

steps.prompt: Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must contain at least ____ g/l of sugar.
steps.explanation: 120 g/l, equal to the old 5 puttonyos.

steps.title: What you learned
points: German Prädikats show ripeness; trocken means dry
The Mosel is light and steep; the Rhine fuller and drier
Austria's Wachau terms grade dry wines by alcohol
Tokaj's Aszú is one of the world's oldest classified sweet wines

modules.title: North America
modules.description: How California, Oregon, Washington and Canada built their own wine cultures in under a century.

steps.title: AVAs
steps.body: An American Viticultural Area, or AVA, is a defined grape-growing area with distinct geography. There are over 270. AVAs set boundaries only, not grapes, yields or methods. They can nest: Oakville sits inside Napa Valley, which sits inside the larger North Coast AVA.

steps.title: Labelling
steps.body: A wine naming an AVA needs at least 85% of grapes from it. A varietal name needs 75% of that grape, though Oregon requires 90% for most varieties. A vintage needs 95% from that year when an AVA is named. A state name, like California, needs 100% from that state.

steps.prompt: What does an AVA control?
steps.explanation: An AVA only defines where the grapes grow. Producers choose grapes and methods freely.

steps.title: After Prohibition
steps.body: From 1920 to 1933, Prohibition banned the sale of alcohol in the US. Most wineries closed, vineyards were replanted with table grapes or thick-skinned varieties for home winemaking. The industry restarted slowly. Modern fine wine in California really grew from the 1960s, with Robert Mondavi founding his Napa winery in 1966.

steps.prompt: In Oregon, a wine labelled Pinot Noir must contain at least 90% of that grape.
steps.explanation: Yes. Oregon sets a stricter rule than the federal 75% for most varieties.

steps.title: What you learned
points: An AVA defines a place, not grapes or methods
Labels need 85% from an AVA and 75% of a named grape
Prohibition set American wine back by decades

lessons.title: Napa and Sonoma
lessons.subtitle: California's North Coast
objectives: Describe Napa Valley's climate and sub-AVAs

steps.title: Napa Valley
steps.body: Napa Valley, north of San Francisco, is about 50 km long. Cool air and fog come in from San Pablo Bay in the south, so the south, Carneros, is cool, and the north, Calistoga, is hot. Cabernet Sauvignon is the star. Sub-AVAs include Oakville, Rutherford and Stags Leap District on the valley floor, and Howell Mountain and Spring Mountain in the hills.

steps.title: Fog
steps.body: The cold California Current chills the Pacific. As inland valleys heat up, they draw cool, damp air and fog in through gaps in the coastal hills. Fog keeps mornings cool and preserves acidity; it burns off later, letting the sun ripen grapes. It explains why North Coast wines can be ripe yet balanced.

steps.prompt: Why is Carneros cooler than Calistoga?
options: Closer to the cool bay and fog
steps.explanation: Carneros, at the southern end, gets more cool air and fog from San Pablo Bay.

steps.title: Sonoma
steps.body: Sonoma, west of Napa, is larger and more varied. The Russian River Valley and Sonoma Coast, cooled by fog, make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Dry Creek Valley and Alexander Valley, warmer, make Zinfandel and Cabernet. Old-vine Zinfandel is a Sonoma speciality.
steps.highlight: Cool coast to warm inland valleys

steps.prompt: Match each AVA to its signature grape.
steps.explanation: Each part of the North Coast has its own climate and grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Napa runs from cool Carneros to hot Calistoga, with Cabernet the star
Pacific fog keeps North Coast wines fresh
Sonoma ranges from cool Pinot Noir to warm Zinfandel

lessons.title: The Central Coast
lessons.subtitle: Santa Barbara to Monterey
objectives: Explain the transverse valleys of Santa Barbara

steps.title: A long coast
steps.body: The Central Coast runs from San Francisco Bay to Santa Barbara. Monterey's Salinas Valley is cool and windy, good for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Paso Robles is warmer, with large day and night swings, making Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Rhône grapes, a movement known as the Rhône Rangers.

steps.title: Transverse valleys
steps.body: In Santa Barbara County, the Santa Ynez Valley runs east to west, unusual on the American coast. This lets cold Pacific air flow straight in. The Sta. Rita Hills, near the sea, are cool enough for fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; further inland, Happy Canyon is warm enough for Bordeaux grapes.
steps.highlight: East-west valleys bring in the ocean

steps.prompt: Santa Barbara's valleys run east to west, letting ocean air flow inland.
steps.explanation: Yes. That orientation brings cool Pacific air deep into the valleys, making them ideal for Pinot Noir.

steps.body: The film Sideways, set in Santa Barbara County in 2004, made Pinot Noir sales jump in the US, and hurt Merlot's reputation for years.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are associated with the Rhône Rangers in Paso Robles?
steps.explanation: Rhône Rangers grow Rhône grapes like Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Viognier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Central Coast runs from cool Monterey to Santa Barbara
Santa Barbara's east-west valleys let in cool Pacific air
Paso Robles grows Rhône grapes, Zinfandel and Cabernet

lessons.title: Oregon
lessons.subtitle: Pinot Noir in the north-west
objectives: Explain why Pinot Noir suits Oregon
Explain Oregon's labelling and farming culture

steps.title: Willamette Valley
steps.body: Oregon's wine centre is the Willamette Valley, south of Portland, at about 45 degrees north, the same latitude as Burgundy. The climate is cool and maritime, with wet winters and dry summers. David Lett planted Pinot Noir there in 1965, and his 1975 wine did well against Burgundy in a 1979 Paris tasting.

steps.title: Pinot's natural home
steps.body: Pinot Noir is over 60% of Oregon's plantings. The cool climate keeps acidity and red fruit, and long, dry autumns ripen it slowly. Volcanic Jory soil in the Dundee Hills and marine sediments in places like Yamhill-Carlton give different styles. Pinot Gris and, increasingly, Chardonnay are the main whites.

steps.prompt: Why does Pinot Noir thrive in the Willamette Valley?
options: A cool climate and long, dry autumns
steps.explanation: Cool conditions keep acidity and fruit purity, while dry autumns let grapes ripen slowly.

steps.title: A small-producer culture
steps.body: Oregon wineries are mostly small and family-run. The state requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than federal rules. Sustainable, organic and biodynamic farming are widespread. Burgundian houses like Maison Joseph Drouhin invested from 1987, a sign of respect for the region.

steps.prompt: Match each Oregon feature to its detail.
steps.explanation: Oregon's history is short but focused.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Willamette Valley lies at Burgundy's latitude
Pinot Noir is over 60% of plantings
Oregon is mostly small producers, with strict labelling

lessons.title: Washington and Canada
lessons.subtitle: Desert vineyards and ice wine
objectives: Explain how ice wine shaped Canada

steps.title: Washington
steps.body: Washington's vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, which block Pacific rain. The Columbia Valley is a desert, with under 200 mm of rain a year, so all vines are irrigated from rivers. Long summer days at 46 degrees north give ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling and Chardonnay lead.

steps.title: Cold winters and sandy soils
steps.body: Winter can drop below minus 20 degrees, damaging vines. Growers plant on slopes for air drainage and bury canes in some cases. Sandy, wind-blown soils mean phylloxera struggles, so most vines grow on their own roots. Walla Walla, Red Mountain and Yakima Valley are top AVAs.

steps.prompt: Which statements about Washington are true?
options: Most vineyards lie east of the Cascades
Many vines grow on their own roots
steps.explanation: Sandy soils keep phylloxera at bay, so own-rooted vines are common.

steps.title: Canada
steps.body: Canada's main regions are Ontario's Niagara Peninsula, moderated by Lake Ontario, and British Columbia's Okanagan Valley, a dry, warm valley in the interior. Reliable hard winters made Canada the world's leading ice wine producer, especially from Vidal and Riesling. The VQA system sets quality and origin rules.

steps.prompt: Which grape is widely used for Canadian ice wine?
steps.explanation: Vidal, a hardy hybrid, and Riesling are the main ice wine grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Washington's vineyards are an irrigated desert east of the Cascades
Cold winters and sandy soils mean many own-rooted vines
Canada leads in ice wine from Niagara and the Okanagan

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from North America
objectives: Link each region to its grapes

steps.prompt: Match each region to its signature grape.
steps.explanation: Each region has found its grape in under a century.

steps.prompt: What does an AVA define?
steps.explanation: AVAs are about place only.

steps.prompt: Washington State vineyards rely on irrigation.
steps.explanation: Yes. East of the Cascades, rainfall is too low for vines without it.

steps.prompt: Which help cool California's coastal vineyards?
steps.explanation: California summers are dry. Fog, ocean currents and valley orientation do the cooling.

steps.prompt: Prohibition in the United States lasted from 1920 to ____.
steps.explanation: 1933. Fine wine only really grew again from the 1960s.

steps.title: What you learned
points: AVAs define place; labels need 85% from the area
California's fog and valleys shape its styles
Oregon is Pinot Noir country; Washington an irrigated desert
Canada is the world's leader in ice wine

modules.title: South America
modules.description: Irrigation, altitude and the Andes: Chile, Argentina and their neighbours.

lessons.title: Chile's valleys
lessons.subtitle: Between the Andes and the Pacific
objectives: Explain the role of irrigation and the Andes

steps.title: A long, narrow country
steps.body: Chile is about 4,300 km long but rarely more than 180 km wide, between the Andes and the Pacific. Its isolation, protected by the Atacama desert in the north, the mountains, the ocean and Antarctic ice, has kept phylloxera out, so most vines grow on their own roots. The Central Valley holds most vineyards.

steps.title: Water from the Andes
steps.body: The Central Valley has a Mediterranean climate, with dry summers. Rivers fed by Andean snowmelt provide irrigation. Cold air flowing down from the mountains at night gives a wide day and night swing. Maipo, near Santiago, is Chile's historic Cabernet region; Colchagua and Cachapoal, in the Rapel Valley, make ripe reds.

steps.prompt: Why are most Chilean vines grown on their own roots?
steps.explanation: Natural barriers have kept phylloxera out, so grafting isn't needed.

steps.title: Carmenère
steps.body: Carmenère came from Bordeaux in the 19th century and was mixed up with Merlot. In 1994 it was identified, and it became Chile's signature grape. It needs a long, warm season; when ripe it gives dark fruit, spice and soft tannin; when unripe, a strong green pepper note.

steps.prompt: Match each Chilean valley to its focus.
steps.explanation: Chile's valleys differ by distance from the sea and the Andes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chile is long, narrow and free of phylloxera
Andean snowmelt irrigates the dry Central Valley
Carmenère, identified in 1994, is Chile's signature grape

lessons.title: Chile's cool fringes
lessons.subtitle: Coast, north and south
objectives: Explain the influence of the Humboldt Current

steps.title: The Humboldt Current
steps.body: The cold Humboldt Current runs north along Chile's coast, cooling the air and bringing morning fog. Coastal valleys like Casablanca, San Antonio and Leyda are among Chile's coolest, ideal for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. This east to west contrast matters more than north to south.

steps.title: Costa, Entre Cordilleras, Andes
steps.body: In 2011 Chile added three descriptors to its regions: Costa, for coastal areas; Entre Cordilleras, between the mountain ranges; and Andes, for the foothills. A Costa wine is likely to be fresh and lower in alcohol; an Andes wine to have firm tannin and freshness from altitude.

steps.prompt: In Chile, distance from the coast often matters more than latitude for climate.
steps.explanation: Yes. The cold Humboldt Current cools coastal areas, while inland valleys get warmer before the Andes cool them again.

steps.title: North and south
steps.body: In the north, Limarí and Elqui have limestone soils and coastal fog, making mineral Chardonnay and Syrah. In the south, Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco are cooler and wetter, with old dry-farmed vines of País and Cinsault, and new plantings of Riesling and Pinot Noir.
steps.highlight: Limarí in the north; Itata in the south

steps.prompt: Which Chilean region is best known for cool, coastal Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: Casablanca's coastal location brings fog and cool air, perfect for crisp whites.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Humboldt Current cools Chile's coast
Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes describe position
Limarí and Itata extend Chile north and south

steps.title: A desert at the foot of the Andes
steps.body: Mendoza produces about 70% of Argentina's wine. It is a high desert with under 250 mm of rain a year, sitting in the Andes' rain shadow. Irrigation comes from rivers fed by snowmelt, historically through channels built by the Huarpe people and later the Spanish. Hail is a constant threat; nets protect many vineyards.

steps.title: Altitude
steps.body: Mendoza's vineyards lie from about 700 to 1,500 m. Higher sites have cooler nights, preserving acidity, and stronger ultraviolet light, which thickens skins for more colour and tannin. That's why Malbec there is dark and ripe yet fresh. The Zonda, a hot, dry wind, can harm flowering in spring.

steps.prompt: What protects many Mendoza vineyards from a frequent hazard?
steps.explanation: Summer hailstorms are common in Mendoza; nets shield the grapes.

steps.title: Sub-regions
steps.body: Luján de Cuyo, south of Mendoza city, was the first DOC in Argentina, in 1989, known for old-vine Malbec. Maipú is nearby and historic. The Valle de Uco, at 900 to 1,500 m, has Argentina's most acclaimed new sites, like Gualtallary, Paraje Altamira and Los Chacayes, now recognised as geographical indications.
steps.highlight: Luján de Cuyo and the Valle de Uco

steps.prompt: Match each Mendoza area to its feature.
steps.explanation: Mendoza's quality grows with altitude and site detail.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mendoza is a high, irrigated desert making 70% of Argentina's wine
Altitude gives cool nights and strong light
Luján de Cuyo and the Valle de Uco are key sub-regions

lessons.title: Argentina beyond Mendoza
lessons.subtitle: North and south
objectives: Name San Juan and other regions

steps.title: Salta
steps.body: In the far north, Salta's Calchaquí Valleys hold some of the world's highest vineyards, from 1,700 to over 3,000 m. Cafayate is the centre. Torrontés, a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, gives floral, aromatic whites. Malbec and Cabernet there are dark and intense, thanks to strong sun and cold nights.

steps.title: Patagonia
steps.body: In the south, Patagonia's Neuquén and Río Negro are low, about 300 m, but at 38 to 39 degrees south, cooled by latitude and strong winds. The wind keeps grapes healthy and thickens skins. Pinot Noir, Malbec and Merlot make fresher, more elegant wines than in Mendoza. Some Río Negro vines date from the early 20th century.

steps.prompt: What keeps Patagonia cool, compared with Salta?
steps.explanation: Patagonia is low, so its coolness comes from latitude and constant wind.

steps.body: The same grape, Malbec, from Salta, Mendoza and Patagonia makes a great tasting lesson. Altitude, latitude and wind each leave a mark.

steps.prompt: Which statements about Salta are true?
steps.explanation: Mendoza is by far Argentina's largest region.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Salta has vineyards up to 3,000 m and floral Torrontés
Patagonia is cooled by latitude and wind
Argentina's styles vary with altitude and latitude

lessons.title: Uruguay and Brazil
lessons.subtitle: South America's Atlantic side
objectives: Compare them with the Andean countries

steps.title: Uruguay
steps.body: Uruguay has a humid, maritime climate influenced by the Atlantic and the Río de la Plata. Tannat, brought by Basque immigrants in the 1870s, is its national grape, giving dark, tannic reds that are often softer than in France's Madiran. Canelones, near Montevideo, is the main region; Maldonado, on the coast, makes fresh whites like Albariño.

steps.title: Brazil
steps.body: Brazil's main region is Serra Gaúcha, in the far south, settled by Italian immigrants. It's wet and humid, which suits early-picked grapes for sparkling wine, now Brazil's strength. Vale dos Vinhedos was its first GI. In the north-east, the São Francisco Valley, near the equator, harvests twice a year with irrigation.

steps.prompt: Why is sparkling wine well suited to Serra Gaúcha?
options: Its humid climate suits early-picked, high-acid grapes
It has very hot, dry summers
steps.explanation: Rain and humidity make full ripeness hard; early picking for sparkling wine keeps acidity and avoids rot.

steps.title: Different from the Andes
steps.body: Unlike Chile and Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil have rain in the growing season, more like Bordeaux than Mendoza. Growers fight disease rather than drought. Their wines tend to be lower in alcohol and fresher, a counterpoint to the ripe, sunny Andean style.

steps.prompt: Uruguay's national grape is Tannat.
steps.explanation: Yes. Basque immigrants brought it in the 1870s, and it covers about a quarter of the vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Uruguay's humid climate gives Tannat a softer style
Brazil's strength is sparkling wine from Serra Gaúcha
The Atlantic side fights rain, not drought

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from South America
objectives: Explain how the Andes and oceans shape the region
Link each country to its grapes

steps.prompt: Match each country to its signature grape.
steps.explanation: Each country built an identity on one grape.

steps.prompt: What is Mendoza's main source of water for vines?
steps.explanation: Mendoza is a desert; Andean snowmelt feeds the irrigation.

steps.prompt: Chilean coastal valleys are warmer than inland ones.
steps.explanation: Not true. The cold Humboldt Current makes coastal valleys cooler.

steps.prompt: Which describe Patagonia's vineyards?
steps.explanation: Patagonia is low; Salta has the very high vineyards.

steps.prompt: Chile's three regional descriptors are Costa, Entre Cordilleras and ____.
steps.explanation: Andes marks foothill vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Andes provide water, altitude and cool nights
The Humboldt Current cools Chile's coast
Argentina ranges from high Salta to windy Patagonia
Uruguay and Brazil face rain on the Atlantic side

modules.title: Australia, New Zealand and South Africa
modules.description: Three southern hemisphere countries, three very different stories of climate and style.

lessons.title: Australia's warm south
lessons.subtitle: Barossa, McLaren Vale and the Riverland
objectives: Explain the importance of old vines

steps.title: South Australia
steps.body: South Australia makes about half of Australia's premium wine. The Barossa Valley, settled by Silesian Lutherans in the 1840s, is famous for rich Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre. McLaren Vale, south of Adelaide, is warm but cooled by the Gulf St Vincent, with Shiraz and Grenache. Inland irrigated areas like the Riverland make large volumes.

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: Phylloxera never reached South Australia, thanks to strict quarantine. So the Barossa has some of the world's oldest producing vines, some planted in the 1840s. Its Old Vine Charter classifies Old Vines at 35 years, Survivor at 70, Centenarian at 100 and Ancestor at 125. Old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit.

steps.prompt: Why does the Barossa have vines over 150 years old?
steps.explanation: South Australia's quarantine rules have kept phylloxera away, so old ungrafted vines survive.

steps.title: Labels
steps.body: Australia uses Geographical Indications: zones, regions and sub-regions. Labels need 85% from a named GI, grape or vintage. Blends list grapes in order of proportion, like Shiraz Cabernet. Large brands often use the broad South Eastern Australia GI, which allows blending across states.
steps.highlight: 85% rule; South Eastern Australia for blends

steps.prompt: Match each Barossa term to its minimum vine age.
steps.explanation: The Barossa Old Vine Charter grades vineyards by age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: South Australia's Barossa and McLaren Vale make rich Shiraz and Grenache
Quarantine kept phylloxera out, leaving very old vines
Labels follow an 85% rule; big brands use South Eastern Australia

lessons.title: Australia's cooler regions
lessons.subtitle: Eden, Clare, Coonawarra and beyond
objectives: Explain why Riesling thrives in Clare and Eden
Describe Margaret River, Yarra and Tasmania

steps.title: Cool by altitude or sea
steps.body: Not all of Australia is hot. Eden Valley and Clare Valley, at higher altitude, make dry, lime-scented Riesling. Coonawarra's red terra rossa soil over limestone gives elegant Cabernet. Adelaide Hills, at up to 700 m, makes Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. Margaret River, on the Indian Ocean, makes Bordeaux-style blends and Chardonnay.
steps.highlight: Altitude and ocean cool the south

steps.title: Victoria and Tasmania
steps.body: Victoria's Yarra Valley, near Melbourne, makes Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. Mornington Peninsula, surrounded by sea, does the same. Tasmania, Australia's coolest state, has become the country's leading source of traditional method sparkling wine and fine Pinot Noir. The Hunter Valley, in New South Wales, makes unique Sémillon.

steps.prompt: Which Australian regions are known for cool-climate wines?
steps.explanation: The Riverland is hot, irrigated and high-volume.

steps.body: Clare and Eden Valley Riesling sealed with screw caps since 2000 has shown how well these wines age. Ten-year-old bottles show toast and lime without losing freshness.

steps.prompt: Which region is famous for Cabernet Sauvignon on red terra rossa soil?
steps.explanation: Coonawarra's terra rossa over limestone gives elegant, minty Cabernet.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Clare and Eden Valley make dry Riesling
Coonawarra and Margaret River make fine Cabernet
Yarra, Mornington and Tasmania lead in cool Pinot and sparkling

lessons.title: New Zealand's North Island
lessons.subtitle: Hawke's Bay and Martinborough
objectives: Describe Hawke's Bay and Gimblett Gravels

steps.title: A maritime country
steps.body: New Zealand's two islands stretch from about 36 to 46 degrees south, and no vineyard is far from the sea. The climate is cool and maritime, with high sunlight and strong ultraviolet levels. Rain can come at harvest, so site and vintage matter. Sauvignon Blanc is over 60% of production.

steps.title: Hawke's Bay
steps.body: Hawke's Bay, on the North Island's east coast, is New Zealand's second largest region and one of its warmest. Gimblett Gravels, an old riverbed of stony soils, stores heat and drains well. It makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah. Chardonnay is also important.
steps.highlight: Gimblett Gravels: Bordeaux blends and Syrah

steps.prompt: What makes Gimblett Gravels good for red grapes?
options: Stony soils that store heat and drain well
steps.explanation: Old riverbed gravel stores warmth and drains, helping red grapes ripen.

steps.title: Martinborough
steps.body: Martinborough, in the Wairarapa near Wellington, is small, dry and windy. In the 1980s, scientists identified its climate and soils as similar to Burgundy's. Its Pinot Noir is concentrated and savoury. Strong winds lower yields but keep grapes healthy.

steps.prompt: Sauvignon Blanc makes up over 60% of New Zealand's production.
steps.explanation: Yes. It dominates exports, though Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are growing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: New Zealand is cool, maritime and bright
Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah
Martinborough makes concentrated Pinot Noir

steps.title: Marlborough
steps.body: Marlborough, at the north-east of the South Island, makes about 75% of New Zealand's wine. Long, sunny days and cold nights give Sauvignon Blanc its intense passion fruit and gooseberry with high acidity. The Wairau Valley is the heart; the Awatere Valley, cooler and higher, gives more herbal styles. Montana planted the first vines in 1973.
steps.highlight: Sunny days, cold nights, Sauvignon Blanc

steps.title: Central Otago
steps.body: Central Otago, around 45 degrees south, is the world's southernmost major wine region. It is New Zealand's only continental climate: hot, dry summers, cold winters, frost risk. Vineyards at up to 400 m, on schist and gravel, make Pinot Noir with vivid fruit and fresh acidity. Bannockburn and Gibbston are key sub-regions.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its signature.
steps.explanation: The South Island has two very different strengths.

steps.title: Contrasts
steps.body: Marlborough is maritime and broad, with large-scale production. Central Otago is inland, continental and small, with mostly boutique producers. Both depend on high sunlight and cool nights. Frost fans and helicopters are used in both to protect vines on cold spring nights.
steps.highlight: Maritime and large; continental and small

steps.prompt: Which features describe Central Otago?
steps.explanation: Marlborough, not Central Otago, makes most of New Zealand's wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marlborough makes about 75% of New Zealand's wine, mostly Sauvignon Blanc
Central Otago is continental and focused on Pinot Noir
Both rely on bright sun and cool nights

lessons.title: South Africa's Cape
lessons.subtitle: Ocean winds and old soils
objectives: Explain the Wine of Origin scheme

steps.title: Between two oceans
steps.body: South Africa's wine regions lie in the Western Cape, at about 34 degrees south. The climate is Mediterranean. The cold Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor, a strong south-easterly wind, cool the vineyards and keep them healthy. The soils are among the world's oldest: granite, sandstone and shale.
steps.highlight: Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor

steps.title: The districts
steps.body: Stellenbosch, near Cape Town, is the historic heart, known for Cabernet Sauvignon and blends. Paarl and Franschhoek are warmer, with Huguenot history. Swartland, to the north, is dry, with old bush vines of Chenin Blanc, Syrah and Grenache. Elgin, Walker Bay and Constantia are cool and coastal. Constantia's sweet wine was famous in the 18th century.

steps.prompt: What is the Cape Doctor?
steps.explanation: The Cape Doctor blows from the south-east, cooling vines and blowing away disease.

steps.title: Wine of Origin
steps.body: The Wine of Origin scheme, since 1973, defines regions, districts and wards. Wines are certified with a seal on the bottle. A named grape, vintage or origin requires 85%. Producers can also make single-vineyard wines from registered sites.

steps.prompt: Match each district to its feature.
steps.explanation: The Cape's districts vary with distance from the sea.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Benguela Current and Cape Doctor cool the Western Cape
Stellenbosch, Swartland and Constantia are key districts
Wine of Origin certifies origin, grape and vintage

steps.title: Pinotage
steps.body: Pinotage was created in 1925 by Professor Abraham Perold at Stellenbosch University, crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault, which was then called Hermitage. It gives dark, red-fruited wines, sometimes with smoky or banana notes. Some modern versions are lighter and fresher; others are oaked and rich. It is South Africa's own grape.

steps.title: Chenin Blanc
steps.body: South Africa has more Chenin Blanc than any other country, about 17,000 hectares. Once used for bulk and brandy, it now makes fine dry whites from old bush vines, especially in Swartland, Stellenbosch and Paarl. Styles range from fresh and unoaked to rich and barrel-fermented. The Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years old.

steps.prompt: Pinotage is a cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.
steps.explanation: Yes. Cinsault was called Hermitage in South Africa, which explains the name Pinotage.

steps.body: Look for the Certified Heritage Vineyards seal on South African labels. It shows the wine comes from a registered vineyard over 35 years old.

steps.prompt: Which country grows the most Chenin Blanc?
steps.explanation: South Africa has more Chenin than France, its homeland.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage, created in 1925, is South Africa's own grape
South Africa grows the most Chenin Blanc in the world
Old vines are certified and drive quality

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Australia, New Zealand and South Africa
objectives: Explain climate and labelling in each

steps.prompt: Match each region to its signature grape.
steps.explanation: Each region has made one grape its signature.

steps.prompt: Why does South Australia have very old ungrafted vines?
options: Phylloxera never arrived thanks to quarantine
steps.explanation: Strict quarantine has kept phylloxera out.

steps.prompt: Which cool influences shape South Africa's Cape?
steps.explanation: The Cape has a Mediterranean climate with dry summers, not monsoons.

steps.prompt: Central Otago has a maritime climate.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's New Zealand's only continental region.

steps.prompt: Pinotage was created by crossing Pinot Noir with ____.
steps.explanation: Cinsault, then called Hermitage in South Africa.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Australia ranges from hot Barossa to cool Tasmania
New Zealand is maritime, except continental Central Otago
South Africa is cooled by ocean winds, with Chenin and Pinotage as signatures
Old vines matter in all three countries

modules.title: Sparkling Wines in Depth
modules.description: From base wine to dosage: every choice that defines a sparkling wine, and the regions that master them.

lessons.title: The base wine
lessons.subtitle: Where quality starts
objectives: Explain what makes a good base wine
Explain the role of reserve wines

steps.title: High acid, low alcohol
steps.body: A good base wine for sparkling is high in acidity, low in alcohol, around 10 to 11%, and neutral in flavour, so the second fermentation and lees can add character. Grapes are picked early, before sugar rises. Cool regions like Champagne, England and Tasmania give this naturally.

steps.title: Pressing fractions
steps.body: Whole bunches are pressed gently to avoid colour and bitterness from skins. In Champagne, 4,000 kg of grapes may give at most 2,550 litres. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the purest, with high acidity. The next 500 litres, the taille, are fruitier and less fine. Top houses often use only the cuvée.

steps.prompt: In Champagne, what is the cuvée?
options: The first and purest pressing fraction
steps.explanation: The cuvée is the first 2,050 litres from 4,000 kg of grapes, highest in acidity and finesse.

steps.title: Reserve wines
steps.body: Houses keep reserve wines from earlier years to blend into their non-vintage, smoothing differences between vintages and adding depth. Some use 10 to 50% reserve wine, stored in tanks, barrels, or a perpetual solera-like system. This is how non-vintage Champagne keeps a consistent house style.
steps.highlight: Reserve wines keep the house style

steps.prompt: Grapes for sparkling base wine are usually picked later than grapes for still wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. They're picked earlier, to keep high acidity and low sugar, since the second fermentation adds alcohol.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Base wines are acidic, low in alcohol and neutral
Gentle whole bunch pressing separates cuvée and taille
Reserve wines keep non-vintage blends consistent

lessons.title: Second fermentation
lessons.subtitle: Tirage and pressure
objectives: Compare full and lower pressure styles

steps.title: Tirage
steps.body: After blending, the base wine is mixed with the liqueur de tirage: sugar, about 24 g/l, selected yeast and riddling aids that help the sediment slide later. The bottle is closed with a crown cap. The yeast ferments the sugar, adding about 1.2 to 1.5% alcohol and producing carbon dioxide.

steps.title: Pressure
steps.body: Each 4 grams of sugar per litre gives about 1 atmosphere of pressure. So 24 g/l produces about 6 atmospheres, typical of Champagne. Crémant has around 4 to 5; Pétillant naturel or frizzante wines much less. Cooler fermentation, around 12 degrees, gives finer bubbles and better integration.

steps.prompt: In the second fermentation, about ____ grams of sugar per litre produce one atmosphere of pressure.
steps.explanation: About 4 g/l per atmosphere, so 24 g/l gives around 6 atmospheres.

steps.title: Pétillant naturel
steps.body: Pétillant naturel, or pét-nat, uses the ancestral method: wine is bottled before the first fermentation ends, so it finishes in bottle, trapping the gas. There's no added sugar or yeast, and often no disgorgement, leaving the wine cloudy. Bubbles are softer. Some appellations, like Gaillac and Limoux, have historic versions.

steps.prompt: How is the ancestral method different from the traditional method?
options: There is only one fermentation, finished in bottle
steps.explanation: The ancestral method bottles the wine while it is still fermenting, so there's no second fermentation.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Liqueur de tirage adds sugar and yeast for the second fermentation
About 4 g/l of sugar makes one atmosphere
Pét-nat finishes its single fermentation in bottle

steps.title: Autolysis
steps.body: After the second fermentation, the dead yeast cells slowly break down, releasing amino acids, mannoproteins and other compounds into the wine. This is autolysis. It begins after a few months and continues for years, adding bread, brioche, biscuit and nutty flavours, and a creamy texture, while the yeast also absorbs oxygen.
steps.highlight: Dead yeast gives brioche and cream

steps.title: Riddling
steps.body: Riddling moves the sediment into the neck. By hand, on wooden racks called pupitres, a remueur turns and tilts thousands of bottles a day, over several weeks. Gyropalettes, invented in Spain in the 1970s, do the same for 500 bottles at once in about a week. Some yeasts are encapsulated in beads to make it faster still.

steps.prompt: What do gyropalettes do?
steps.explanation: Gyropalettes turn and tilt hundreds of bottles at once, replacing manual riddling.

steps.title: When to disgorge
steps.body: Disgorgement ends lees ageing and starts a new phase. Before it, the wine is protected and evolves slowly. After it, oxygen enters, and the wine develops more toasty, nutty notes. Many producers now print the disgorgement date. Recently disgorged, or RD, wines are disgorged after long lees ageing, just before release.

steps.prompt: Put these steps in order.
steps.explanation: The lees age the wine, are moved to the neck, removed, and the wine is topped up.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Autolysis releases bready, creamy notes from dead yeast
Riddling, by hand or gyropalette, moves sediment to the neck
The disgorgement date changes how the wine develops

lessons.title: Dosage and styles
lessons.subtitle: Sweetness and colour
objectives: Explain blanc de blancs, blanc de noirs and rosé

steps.title: Dosage
steps.body: After disgorgement, the liqueur d'expédition, wine with sugar, tops up the bottle. It balances acidity and adds to the flavour development over time through Maillard reactions between sugar and amino acids. The trend is towards lower dosage, but very low dosage can taste austere in a young, high-acid wine.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: Brut Nature has 0 to 3 g/l; Extra Brut up to 6; Brut up to 12; Extra Dry 12 to 17; Dry or Sec 17 to 32; Demi-Sec 32 to 50; Doux over 50. Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes, usually Chardonnay. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes. Rosé can be blended, with still red wine, or saignée.
steps.highlight: Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, Rosé

steps.prompt: Which are true about Blanc de Noirs?
options: It's a white wine made from black grapes
It can use Pinot Noir and Meunier
Its colour comes from gentle pressing
steps.explanation: Blanc de Noirs can be any sweetness level. Its pale colour comes from gentle pressing of black grapes.

steps.body: A Demi-Sec Champagne is underrated with fruit tarts and spicy food. Extra Brut and Brut Nature shine with oysters and raw fish.

steps.prompt: Which dosage term is drier: Extra Brut or Extra Dry?
steps.explanation: Extra Brut has up to 6 g/l; Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/l.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dosage balances acidity and helps flavour develop
Sweetness terms run from Brut Nature to Doux
Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs and Rosé describe grapes and colour

steps.title: The areas
steps.body: Champagne's main areas are the Montagne de Reims, famous for Pinot Noir; the Vallée de la Marne, for Meunier; the Côte des Blancs, for Chardonnay; and the Côte des Bar, further south, for Pinot Noir. The Côte de Sézanne also grows Chardonnay. Chalk subsoils, especially in the Côte des Blancs, give finesse.
steps.highlight: Montagne, Vallée, Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar

steps.title: The échelle des crus
steps.body: Champagne once ranked its 319 villages on a ladder, the échelle des crus, from 80% to 100%. Seventeen villages were Grand Cru at 100%, and 42 were Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The percentage set the grape price. The pricing system ended in 2010, but the Grand Cru and Premier Cru names remain on labels.

steps.prompt: How many Champagne villages hold Grand Cru status?
steps.explanation: Seventeen villages are Grand Cru; 42 are Premier Cru.

steps.title: Houses and growers
steps.body: Houses, or maisons, buy grapes from many growers and blend for a consistent style; they make most Champagne. Growers who make their own wine, called récoltant-manipulant and labelled RM, are a growing movement. Labels show these codes: NM for négociant-manipulant, RM for récoltant-manipulant, CM for co-operatives.
steps.highlight: NM for houses; RM for growers

steps.prompt: Match each label code to its meaning.
steps.explanation: The small letters on the label tell you who made the wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne's areas each favour a grape
The échelle des crus ranked villages; 17 are Grand Cru
NM houses blend; RM growers make wine from their own vines

steps.title: Cava
steps.body: Cava is Spain's traditional method wine, about 95% from Catalonia's Penedès. Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada are the main grapes; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are allowed. The 2020 rules created zones and a top tier, Cava de Paraje Calificado, from single estates aged at least 36 months. Corpinnat producers left the DO for stricter organic rules.

steps.title: Crémant
steps.body: Crémant is France's traditional method wine outside Champagne, made in eight AOPs, including Alsace, Burgundy, Loire, Jura, Limoux and Bordeaux. Rules require whole bunch pressing, a limit on juice yield, and at least 9 months on lees. Each uses local grapes: Chenin Blanc in the Loire, Pinot Blanc and Riesling in Alsace, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in Burgundy.
steps.highlight: Eight crémant AOPs, 9 months on lees

steps.prompt: Match each sparkling wine to its country.
steps.explanation: The traditional method is used worldwide under many names.

steps.title: Other leaders
steps.body: Franciacorta, in Lombardy, needs 18 months on lees for non-vintage and is mainly Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Trentodoc, in Trentino, is mountain-grown. England's south, on chalk similar to Champagne's, has become a serious producer. South Africa's Méthode Cap Classique and Tasmania also make fine examples.

steps.prompt: Crémant must spend at least 9 months on its lees.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's the minimum for all French crémants.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cava is mostly from Penedès, with a new single estate tier
Crémant is made in eight French AOPs with local grapes
Franciacorta, Trentodoc, England and Tasmania also excel

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Sparkling Wines in Depth
objectives: Explain each step of traditional method production

steps.prompt: Put these stages of traditional method production in order.
steps.explanation: Each step builds on the previous one.

steps.prompt: What does autolysis give a sparkling wine?
steps.explanation: Breakdown of dead yeast adds these flavours and texture.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Champagne has precise words for each step.

steps.prompt: Which are Champagne's main areas?
steps.explanation: Penedès is in Spain.

steps.prompt: A grower who makes their own Champagne carries the code ____ on the label.
steps.explanation: RM stands for récoltant-manipulant.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Base wines are acidic and light; pressing fractions matter
Tirage creates pressure; autolysis adds flavour
Dosage sets sweetness; label codes reveal the maker
Champagne, Cava, crémant and others each have their rules

modules.title: Fortified Wines in Depth
modules.description: Sherry, Port and Madeira in full: production, styles, ageing and how to read them.

lessons.title: Fortification
lessons.subtitle: The spirit and the timing
objectives: Explain the chemistry of stopping fermentation

steps.title: The spirit
steps.body: Fortifying spirit is grape spirit, usually distilled to between 77 and 96%. Port uses aguardente at about 77%, which carries some flavour of its own. Sherry and most vins doux naturels use neutral spirit at around 95 to 96%, which adds alcohol without flavour. Less spirit is needed when it's stronger.

steps.title: Stopping the yeast
steps.body: Yeast can't work above about 15 to 16% alcohol. Adding spirit mid-fermentation pushes the wine past that point, killing the yeast and keeping the remaining sugar. In Port, about 115 litres of spirit go into 435 litres of fermenting must, making the classic 550-litre pipe. The earlier the spirit goes in, the sweeter the wine.

steps.prompt: Why does adding spirit mid-fermentation keep a wine sweet?
options: The higher alcohol kills the yeast before it finishes
steps.explanation: Yeast stops working above about 15 to 16% alcohol, leaving the unfermented sugar.

steps.title: Timing and style
steps.body: Spirit added early gives sweet, fruity wines: Port, vins doux naturels and sweet Madeira. Added late, after a dry fermentation, it gives dry wines: Fino, Manzanilla, Sercial Madeira. Each family also uses ageing, with or without oxygen, to shape the final style.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to when spirit is added.
steps.explanation: Timing determines sweetness; strength determines whether flor can grow.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fortifying spirit ranges from 77% for Port to about 96% for Sherry
Spirit above about 16% alcohol stops the yeast
Early fortification keeps sugar; late fortification keeps the wine dry

lessons.title: Sherry: flor and solera
lessons.subtitle: The engines of Jerez
objectives: Explain the solera system in detail

steps.title: Flor
steps.body: Flor is a film of Saccharomyces yeasts that grows on wine in barrels filled only to about five-sixths, leaving air space. It needs 15 to 15.5% alcohol, cool, humid cellars and nutrients. It consumes oxygen, alcohol and glycerol, and produces acetaldehyde, which gives Fino its tangy, nutty, bready aroma. Flor is thickest in spring and autumn.
steps.highlight: Flor feeds on air, alcohol and glycerol

steps.title: The solera
steps.body: The solera system blends wines of different ages. Wine for bottling, the saca, is taken from the oldest scale, the solera. It is refilled from the first criadera, which is refilled from the second, and so on, an operation called rocío. By law, no more than 40% can be drawn per year. Older wine educates the younger; the average age rises over time.

steps.prompt: Flor needs barrels to be completely full to grow.
steps.explanation: Not true. Barrels are left about five-sixths full so flor has air on the surface to grow.

steps.title: The Sherry triangle
steps.body: Sherry must be aged in Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María or Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Sanlúcar, by the mouth of the Guadalquivir, is coolest and most humid, so flor grows thickest there; its Fino is called Manzanilla. Albariza soil, up to 40% chalk, stores winter rain for dry summers.

steps.prompt: Why is flor thickest in Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
options: Its cool, humid sea air favours flor
steps.explanation: Coastal humidity and cooler temperatures keep flor thick, giving Manzanilla its saline freshness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Flor needs air space, 15% alcohol and humid cellars
The solera draws from the oldest scale and refills from younger ones
Sanlúcar's sea air makes Manzanilla

steps.title: Biological and oxidative
steps.body: Fino and Manzanilla age under flor, biological ageing, giving pale, dry, tangy wines at 15%. Oloroso is fortified to 17%, never has flor and ages oxidatively, turning dark brown with walnut, toffee and spice, yet stays dry. As water evaporates, Olorosos concentrate, reaching 20% or more.
steps.highlight: Fino under flor; Oloroso with air

steps.title: Between the two
steps.body: Amontillado starts as Fino under flor, then the flor dies or is killed by fortifying to about 17%, and the wine ages oxidatively. It combines Fino's tang with Oloroso's nuttiness. Palo Cortado is rare: it starts under flor but loses it early, then ages oxidatively, giving Amontillado's aroma with Oloroso's body.

steps.prompt: Match each Sherry to its ageing.
steps.explanation: Biological and oxidative ageing create the range of dry Sherries.

steps.title: Sweet Sherries
steps.body: Pedro Ximénez grapes are dried in the sun until almost raisins, then fortified, giving black, syrupy wines with over 400 g/l of sugar. Moscatel is made similarly. Cream Sherry blends Oloroso with sweet wine; Pale Cream blends Fino with sweetening. These blends are sweet; the dry styles are not.

steps.prompt: Which Sherry styles are dry?
steps.explanation: Cream Sherry is sweetened. Fino, Oloroso and Amontillado are naturally dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fino and Manzanilla age under flor; Oloroso ages with air
Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine both
Pedro Ximénez and Cream are sweet styles

lessons.title: Port: ruby and tawny
lessons.subtitle: Two ways of ageing
objectives: Explain the Douro's role in Port

steps.title: Douro and Gaia
steps.body: Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions: the Baixo Corgo, coolest and wettest; the Cima Corgo, heart of quality; and the Douro Superior, hottest and driest. Vineyards are classified A to F. The wine traditionally travelled down to the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from Porto, for cool, humid ageing.
steps.highlight: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior

steps.title: Ruby and tawny
steps.body: Ruby Ports age in large vats, with little oxygen, keeping colour and fruit. Reserve Ruby is a better selection. Tawny Ports age in small 550-litre casks, called pipes, where oxygen turns them brown and nutty. Aged tawny with an indication of age, 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, is a blend tasted to match that style. Colheita is a single-vintage tawny.
steps.highlight: Vats for ruby; pipes for tawny

steps.prompt: What is a Colheita Port?
options: A tawny from a single vintage
steps.explanation: Colheita is a single-vintage tawny aged at least 7 years in cask.

steps.title: White and rosé
steps.body: White Port, from white grapes like Malvasia Fina and Gouveio, ranges from dry to sweet; mixed with tonic, it's a classic aperitif in Porto. Rosé Port, approved in 2008, is made with short skin contact and drunk young and chilled. Aged white Ports, with age indications, also exist.

steps.prompt: Match each Port to its ageing.
steps.explanation: Ageing in vat or cask defines the family.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions
Ruby ages in large vats; tawny in small casks
Colheita is a single-vintage tawny; white and rosé Ports exist

lessons.title: Vintage Port
lessons.subtitle: Port's greatest wine
objectives: Explain how a vintage is declared
Compare Vintage, single quinta and LBV
Explain how to serve Vintage Port

steps.title: Declaring a vintage
steps.body: Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years, declared by each house, typically about three times a decade. The wine must be approved by the IVDP, the Port institute, and bottled after two to three years. It then ages in bottle for decades. Classic declared years include 1963, 1977, 1994, 2011 and 2017.

steps.title: Single quinta and LBV
steps.body: In good but not great years, houses may release single quinta vintage Ports from one estate, like Quinta do Vesuvio. Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, comes from a single year, bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood, so it's ready earlier. Unfiltered LBV can age further and throw a sediment.

steps.prompt: Vintage Port is bottled after two to three years and ages mainly in bottle.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why it keeps dark colour and fruit for decades and throws a heavy sediment.

steps.body: Stand a Vintage Port upright for a day, then decant it slowly. Young vintages benefit from a few hours of air; very old ones should be drunk soon after decanting.

steps.prompt: What distinguishes LBV from Vintage Port?
options: LBV spends 4 to 6 years in wood before bottling
steps.explanation: Longer time in wood makes LBV ready earlier, unlike Vintage, which ages in bottle.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vintage Port is declared only in exceptional years
Single quinta Ports come from one estate in good years
LBV is aged longer in wood and ready earlier

lessons.title: Madeira
lessons.subtitle: Heat, oxygen and acidity
objectives: Explain estufagem and canteiro in detail
Explain Tinta Negra and the noble grapes

steps.title: Estufagem and canteiro
steps.body: Estufagem heats wine in stainless steel tanks to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, then rests it; this is used mainly for younger wines. Canteiro ages wine in casks in warm lofts, called armazéns, for years, sometimes decades. Canteiro is slower and gentler, giving finer, more complex wines. The best Madeiras are all canteiro.
steps.highlight: Estufagem: fast heat. Canteiro: slow warmth.

steps.title: Age categories
steps.body: Madeira labels show age: 5 years, called Reserve; 10 years, Special Reserve; 15 years, Extra Reserve; and 20, 30, 40 and 50 years. Colheita is a single vintage aged at least five years. Frasqueira, or Vintage, comes from a single noble grape and year, aged at least 20 years in cask.

steps.prompt: What is required for a Frasqueira Madeira?
options: A single noble grape, a single year and 20 years in cask
steps.explanation: Frasqueira is the top category: one grape, one vintage, 20 years minimum in cask.

steps.title: Grapes
steps.body: The noble white grapes, Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia, define sweetness when named on the label. Terrantez is a rare fifth. Tinta Negra, a black grape, makes most Madeira; since 2015 its name can appear on labels. Madeira keeps high acidity, with sugar ranging from under 50 g/l in Sercial to over 100 g/l in Malvasia.

steps.prompt: Order these Madeira age categories from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Each step requires longer ageing; Frasqueira also requires a single grape and year.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Estufagem heats quickly; canteiro ages slowly in warm lofts
Labels show age from 5 years to Frasqueira at 20 or more
Noble grapes define sweetness; Tinta Negra makes most Madeira

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Fortified Wines in Depth
objectives: Compare Sherry, Port and Madeira styles

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its key process.
steps.explanation: Each family relies on a distinctive process.

steps.prompt: What strength of spirit is used to fortify Port?
steps.explanation: Port's aguardente is about 77%, carrying some flavour.

steps.prompt: Which Sherry styles involve oxidative ageing?
steps.explanation: Manzanilla ages under flor only.

steps.prompt: LBV Port is bottled earlier than Vintage Port.
steps.explanation: Not true. LBV spends 4 to 6 years in wood; Vintage is bottled after two to three.

steps.prompt: In Madeira, slow ageing in casks in warm lofts is called ____.
steps.explanation: Canteiro gives the finest Madeiras.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spirit timing and strength shape each family
Sherry relies on flor, oxygen and the solera
Port divides into ruby, tawny and vintage
Madeira's heat and acidity make it nearly immortal

modules.title: Sweet Wines of the World
modules.description: The great sweet wines, how each is made and why they last for decades.

lessons.title: Botrytis in depth
lessons.subtitle: The science of noble rot
objectives: Explain how botrytis changes the grape
Explain why botrytis wines are hard to make

steps.title: What the fungus does
steps.body: Botrytis cinerea pierces the grape skin with fine filaments. Water evaporates, concentrating sugar and acid. The fungus also consumes some acid and sugar, and produces glycerol, which adds viscosity, and gluconic acid. It creates new aromas: honey, apricot, marmalade, saffron and ginger. Laccase, an enzyme it produces, makes the juice prone to oxidation.

steps.title: Why it's hard
steps.body: Infection is uneven and weather-dependent. In bad years, botrytis doesn't come, or grey rot does. Pickers make several passes, called tries, taking only affected berries. Yields can fall to 10 hl/ha or less. Fermentation of such sweet juice is slow, sometimes months, and stops naturally around 13 to 14% alcohol, leaving 100 g/l or more of sugar.
steps.highlight: Several passes, tiny yields, slow fermentation

steps.prompt: Why do pickers pass through botrytis vineyards several times?
options: Infection is uneven, so only affected berries are picked each time
steps.explanation: Botrytis spreads unevenly. Each pass, or trie, takes only the berries that are ready.

steps.title: Fermenting it
steps.body: Botrytised juice is low in yeast nutrients and high in sugar, stressing the yeast. It produces more volatile acidity than normal, so legal limits are higher for these wines. SO2 is needed to protect against laccase and to stop fermentation at the right moment. Many wines then age in oak for 18 to 36 months.

steps.prompt: Which are effects of noble rot on grapes?
steps.explanation: Botrytis weakens and pierces skins rather than thickening them.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Botrytis concentrates the grape and adds new aromas
Uneven infection means several passes and tiny yields
Fermentation is slow, stressed and needs SO2 to stop it

steps.title: Mist from the Ciron
steps.body: Sauternes and Barsac lie in southern Graves, where the cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne. In autumn, this temperature difference creates morning mist, then sunny afternoons, ideal for noble rot. Barsac, on flatter limestone, can label its wines as Barsac or Sauternes.

steps.title: Grapes and making
steps.body: Sémillon is about 80% of plantings: thin skins welcome botrytis and give body and honey. Sauvignon Blanc adds acidity and freshness; Muscadelle adds perfume. Wines ferment and age in barrels, often new, for 18 to 36 months. Alcohol is around 13 to 14%, sugar 100 to 150 g/l. Good Sauternes ages for decades.

steps.prompt: Which grape dominates Sauternes?
steps.explanation: Sémillon's thin skins make it the ideal host for noble rot.

steps.title: The 1855 classification
steps.body: In 1855, Sauternes and Barsac were classified alongside the Médoc. Château d'Yquem was given the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur. Below it are 11 Premiers Crus, like Climens and Suduiraut, and 15 Deuxièmes Crus. Yquem may not make Sauternes in poor years; it skipped 1992, for example.

steps.prompt: Château d'Yquem holds a unique rank in the 1855 classification.
steps.explanation: Yes. It is the only Premier Cru Supérieur.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sauternes and Barsac
Sémillon leads, with Sauvignon and Muscadelle, aged in oak
Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855

lessons.title: Tokaji
lessons.subtitle: Aszú, Szamorodni and Eszencia
objectives: Explain how Aszú is made in detail

steps.title: Aszú
steps.body: Aszú berries, shrivelled by botrytis, are picked one by one and stored as a paste. They're added to a base wine or fermenting must, soaked for 12 to 60 hours, then pressed. Traditionally, sweetness was measured in puttonyos, the number of 25 kg baskets of aszú per 136-litre barrel. Since 2013, Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar.

steps.title: Szamorodni and Eszencia
steps.body: Szamorodni, meaning as it comes, is made from whole bunches with some aszú berries, not separated. It can be dry, aged under a flor-like yeast, or sweet. Eszencia is the free-run juice that drips from aszú berries under their own weight. It can have over 450 g/l of sugar, ferments for years, and rarely reaches 5% alcohol.

steps.prompt: Match each Tokaji to its making.
steps.explanation: Tokaj makes several wines from the same harvest.

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Tokaji Aszú ages at least 18 months in oak, traditionally small Gönci barrels of 136 litres, in cellars cut into volcanic rock, lined with a black mould, Zasmidium cellare, that regulates humidity. High acidity from Furmint lets these wines age for a century or more.

steps.prompt: Tokaji ____ is the free-run juice from aszú berries.
steps.explanation: Eszencia is so sweet it ferments very slowly and stays very low in alcohol.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aszú berries are soaked in base wine, giving at least 120 g/l of sugar
Szamorodni uses whole bunches; Eszencia is pure free-run juice
Furmint's acidity lets Tokaji age for a century

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: Germany's Prädikat levels start with Kabinett and Spätlese, which can be dry or sweet. The sweet wines rise from there. Auslese comes from selected very ripe bunches, sometimes with botrytis. Beerenauslese, BA, uses individually selected overripe berries, usually botrytised. Trockenbeerenauslese, TBA, uses dried, shrivelled botrytis berries, with a minimum of 150 to 154 degrees Oechsle. Eiswein uses frozen grapes.

steps.title: Acidity
steps.body: Riesling's acidity, often 8 to 12 g/l in TBA, balances sugar that can exceed 300 g/l. Alcohol can be as low as 5.5 to 8%. This tension between sugar and acid is what lets German sweet wines feel lively, and lets them age for decades. Without acidity, they'd be syrupy.

steps.prompt: Order these Prädikat levels from least to most concentrated.
steps.explanation: Each level requires riper, more concentrated grapes. Only the top two rely on individually picked, usually botrytised berries.

steps.title: Austria
steps.body: Austria's sweet wines centre on Burgenland's Neusiedlersee, a large, shallow lake whose humidity favours noble rot almost every year. Rust's Ausbruch, a historic style between BA and TBA, is revived as Ruster Ausbruch. Welschriesling, Chardonnay and Scheurebe are common grapes for TBA there.

steps.prompt: Trockenbeerenauslese is a dry wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. Trocken here refers to dried berries, not dryness. TBA is among the sweetest wines in the world.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany's sweet Prädikats rise from Auslese to TBA
Riesling's acidity balances sugar over 300 g/l
Austria's Neusiedlersee makes TBA and Ruster Ausbruch

steps.title: Ice wine
steps.body: Ice wine grapes must freeze naturally on the vine, usually at minus 7 to minus 13 degrees, often in December or January. Picking happens at night while frozen. The press releases only small amounts of concentrated juice, sometimes 15% of normal. Canada uses Vidal and Riesling; Germany and Austria use mainly Riesling.

steps.title: Passito
steps.body: Passito wines are made from grapes dried after harvest. Methods vary: on straw mats, in ventilated lofts, or hanging. Vin Santo is dried for months, then aged for years in small, sealed barrels called caratelli, with some oxidation. Passito di Pantelleria uses Zibibbo, a Muscat, dried in the sun.
steps.highlight: Dried on mats, lofts or racks

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its method.
steps.explanation: Different traditions concentrate sugar in different ways.

steps.body: Vin Santo with cantucci biscuits is a Tuscan ritual: dip the biscuit in the wine. The wine's nutty, dried fruit notes match the almonds.

steps.prompt: Why is ice wine picked at night?
steps.explanation: Grapes must stay frozen until pressed so the water remains as ice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Ice wine grapes freeze naturally and are pressed while frozen
Passito grapes are dried after picking
Vin Santo, Recioto and Pantelleria are classic passito wines

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from Sweet Wines of the World
objectives: Compare the great sweet wine traditions

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its country.
steps.explanation: Each country has its own great sweet wine.

steps.prompt: What is a trie in Sauternes?
options: A pass through the vineyard to pick botrytised grapes
steps.explanation: Pickers make several tries, taking only the berries that are ready.

steps.prompt: Which wines rely mainly on noble rot?
steps.explanation: Icewine relies on freezing, not botrytis.

steps.prompt: Eszencia often reaches only around 5% alcohol or less.
steps.explanation: Yes. With over 450 g/l of sugar, it ferments very slowly and stays very low in alcohol.

steps.prompt: Château d'Yquem is the only ____ Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification.
steps.explanation: Yquem holds the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Botrytis concentrates sugar and adds honeyed aromas
Sauternes, Tokaji and German TBA are botrytis wines
Ice wine and passito use frost and drying
High acidity keeps all great sweet wines fresh

modules.title: Faults and Quality
modules.description: How to tell a faulty wine from one you simply don't like, and how to judge quality without bias.

lessons.title: Cork taint
lessons.subtitle: The musty fault
objectives: Explain what to do with a corked bottle

steps.title: How it smells
steps.body: A corked wine smells of damp cardboard, wet dog or a musty cellar. In mild cases, it simply mutes the fruit, making the wine seem dull and flat. The cause is 2,4,6-trichloroanisole, or TCA. Humans can detect it at just a few parts per trillion.

steps.title: Where it comes from
steps.body: TCA forms when fungi meet chlorine compounds, often in cork bark, but also in barrels, wooden beams or cardboard in wineries. Natural cork producers have cut taint rates by new cleaning methods and screening each cork. A whole winery can be contaminated, affecting wines under any closure.

steps.prompt: What compound causes cork taint?
steps.explanation: TCA gives the musty smell. It can be detected in tiny amounts.

steps.body: A corked wine isn't dangerous, just disappointing. In a restaurant or shop, it's normal to ask for a replacement. Smell first; don't judge by the cork itself, which can smell fine even when the wine doesn't.

steps.prompt: Only wines sealed with natural cork can suffer from TCA.
steps.explanation: Not true. TCA can contaminate a whole winery through barrels or wood, so wines under screw cap can be affected too, though much more rarely.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cork taint smells of damp cardboard and mutes fruit
TCA forms from fungi and chlorine compounds
It's harmless but a reason to replace the bottle

steps.title: Oxidation
steps.body: An oxidised wine has lost its fresh fruit, smelling of bruised apple, sherry or nuts, with browning colour. It comes from too much contact with oxygen, through a faulty closure, poor storage or careless winemaking. It's a fault in a fresh white, but a deliberate style in Oloroso or tawny Port. Acetaldehyde is the main compound.

steps.title: Reduction
steps.body: Reduction is the opposite: too little oxygen, in a wine with sulphur compounds. It smells of rotten egg, struck match, rubber or cabbage. Hydrogen sulphide, the rotten egg smell, forms when stressed yeast lacks nutrients. Light reduction, struck match, can add complexity in some whites; strong reduction is a fault.

steps.prompt: Match each smell to its cause.
steps.explanation: Each fault has a typical smell.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body: Some reduction can be fixed by air: decanting or swirling may blow off struck match or rubber. Persistent rotten egg can sometimes be cleared by a clean copper coin, which binds sulphides. Oxidation can't be undone. Screw caps, which let in little oxygen, can sometimes favour reduction; corks can favour oxidation.
steps.highlight: Air can help reduction, not oxidation

steps.prompt: Which could be signs of oxidation in a young white?
steps.explanation: Fresh lime and green apple are signs of a sound, youthful white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Oxidation brings bruised apple, browning and loss of fruit
Reduction brings rotten egg, rubber or struck match
Air can fix mild reduction; oxidation is permanent

lessons.title: Brett and volatile acidity
lessons.subtitle: Microbial faults
objectives: Explain when each is a fault

steps.title: Brett
steps.body: Brettanomyces is a yeast that can grow in wine, especially in barrels and in reds with higher pH and low SO2. It produces 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol, smelling of barnyard, sticking plaster, sweat and smoked meat. In small amounts, some tasters find it adds complexity; at higher levels, it masks fruit.

steps.title: Volatile acidity
steps.body: Volatile acidity, VA, is mainly acetic acid, made by acetic bacteria when wine meets air, or by stressed yeast. It smells of vinegar and often comes with ethyl acetate, smelling of nail polish remover. Small amounts lift aromas; too much is a fault. EU limits are about 1.2 g/l for reds and 1.08 g/l for whites, higher for sweet wines.

steps.prompt: Which smell is typical of volatile acidity?
steps.explanation: Acetic acid and ethyl acetate give vinegar and solvent aromas.

steps.title: Fault or style
steps.body: The line between fault and character depends on level and context. Some famous wines, like older Châteauneuf-du-Pape, show a touch of Brett; some great sweet wines have higher VA. A fault is when the compound dominates and hides fruit and place. Personal sensitivity varies a lot.

steps.prompt: A small amount of volatile acidity can lift a wine's aromas.
steps.explanation: Yes. At low levels VA can add lift; it becomes a fault when vinegar dominates.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Brett gives barnyard and plaster notes, mainly in reds
Volatile acidity smells of vinegar and nail polish
Level and context decide whether it's a fault or character

steps.title: Heat damage
steps.body: A wine stored too warm, or left in a hot car, can taste cooked: stewed, jammy fruit, flat and dull. The cork may push out or wine may leak around it. The damage is permanent. Even a few hours above 30 degrees can harm a delicate wine.

steps.title: Light strike and refermentation
