steps.body: Light strike happens when light, especially ultraviolet, reacts with riboflavin and amino acids in wine, creating sulphur compounds that smell of cabbage or wet wool. Clear glass offers no protection; Champagne in clear bottles is especially at risk. Refermentation, when yeast restarts in a bottle with sugar, gives unwanted fizz and cloudiness.

steps.prompt: Why are clear glass bottles risky for wine?
options: They let in light that can cause light strike
steps.explanation: Clear glass doesn't filter ultraviolet light, which can create cabbage-like sulphur compounds.

steps.title: Not faults
steps.body: Some things look alarming but are harmless: tartrate crystals, called wine diamonds; sediment in old reds or vintage Port; a slight haze in unfiltered wines; small bubbles in young whites bottled with some carbon dioxide on purpose. Learning these prevents rejecting good bottles.

steps.prompt: Which are harmless rather than faults?
steps.explanation: Light strike and heat damage are real faults.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Heat damage gives cooked fruit and pushed corks
Light strike gives cabbage smells; refermentation gives fizz
Crystals, sediment and slight haze are harmless

steps.title: Quality is not preference
steps.body: You may dislike a perfectly made wine, or love a simple one. Quality judgement asks whether the wine is well made and expressive of its style and origin. Preference asks whether you enjoy it. Professionals separate the two: a great Fino can be outstanding even for someone who prefers fruity reds.
steps.highlight: Quality is not the same as liking

steps.title: Criteria and bias
steps.body: Use balance, length, intensity and complexity, plus typicity: does it taste like its grape and place? Bias creeps in through price, label, reputation, glass colour and even music. In blind tests, wine experts have rated the same wine differently when told it was expensive. Tasting blind removes much of this.

steps.prompt: Match each bias to its source.
steps.explanation: Biases are natural; tasting blind and in a fixed order reduce them.

steps.body: Taste the same wine twice in a flight without knowing. If your notes differ a lot, you've just measured your own consistency, a humbling and useful exercise.

steps.prompt: What is the best way to reduce label and price bias?
options: Taste only one wine at a time
steps.explanation: Tasting blind removes the influence of label, price and reputation.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Quality and personal preference are different questions
Judge with balance, length, intensity, complexity and typicity
Blind tasting reduces price and label bias

steps.prompt: Match each fault to its typical smell.
steps.explanation: Each fault has a fingerprint.

steps.prompt: What causes hydrogen sulphide in wine?
steps.explanation: Yeast short of nitrogen produces rotten egg smells.

steps.prompt: Tartrate crystals in a white wine are a fault.
steps.explanation: Not true. They're harmless salts of tartaric acid.

steps.prompt: Which help reduce bias when judging quality?
steps.explanation: Knowing the price adds bias.

steps.prompt: Cork taint is caused by the compound ____.
steps.explanation: TCA, 2,4,6-trichloroanisole, gives the musty smell.

steps.title: What you learned
points: TCA, oxidation, reduction, Brett and VA are the main faults
Heat and light damage come from poor storage
Level and context decide fault or character
Quality is judged with criteria, ideally blind

modules.title: The Business of Wine
modules.description: How wine is made into a product, priced, sold and collected, and what climate change means for all of it.

lessons.title: How wine is sold
lessons.subtitle: From vineyard to glass
objectives: Describe the route from producer to consumer

steps.title: The chain
steps.body: A bottle passes through several hands. The producer sells to an importer or distributor, who sells to retailers and restaurants, who sell to you. Each step adds a margin. Large producers may also sell directly through cellar doors, clubs and online, keeping more of the price.

steps.title: Three tiers
steps.body: In the United States, a law from 1933, after Prohibition, created the three-tier system: producers must sell to wholesalers, who sell to retailers or restaurants. Each state sets its own rules, and some sell alcohol only through state-run shops. In many other markets, importers and distributors play similar roles, but with fewer legal restrictions.

steps.prompt: What does the US three-tier system require?
options: Producers sell to wholesalers, who sell to retailers
Only state shops may sell wine
steps.explanation: The system separates producers, wholesalers and retailers, though some states allow exceptions.

steps.title: Channels
steps.body: Off-trade means shops and supermarkets, where most wine is sold. On-trade means restaurants and bars, with higher margins. Direct to consumer includes cellar doors, wine clubs and online sales. Supermarkets dominate volume in the UK and much of Europe; on-trade shapes a wine's image.

steps.prompt: Match each channel to its description.
steps.explanation: Each channel has different margins and roles.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wine moves from producer through importers and retailers
The US uses a legal three-tier system
Off-trade, on-trade and direct sales are the main channels

lessons.title: Price and value
lessons.subtitle: Where the money goes
objectives: Explain how a bottle's price is built
Explain why cheap wine has little wine value

steps.title: Building a price
steps.body: A bottle's price includes grapes, winemaking, packaging, transport, duty, tax, and the margins of each seller. In the UK, duty on a 750 ml bottle at 11 to 14.5% was about 2.67 pounds in 2023, plus 20% VAT. On a 6 pound bottle, the wine itself may be worth less than 1 pound. Fixed costs weigh most on cheap wine.
steps.highlight: Fixed costs weigh on cheap wine

steps.title: Why some wine costs more
steps.body: Higher prices reflect lower yields, hand labour, steep slopes, oak barrels, long ageing and scarcity. Above a certain level, prices follow reputation and demand rather than cost. A Grand Cru Burgundy costs hundreds of pounds because the vineyard is tiny and global demand is high, not because it costs that much to make.
steps.highlight: Cost up to a point, then scarcity

steps.prompt: On a cheap bottle, most of the price is the wine itself.
steps.explanation: Not true. Duty, tax, packaging and margins are fixed or proportional, so on cheap bottles they make up most of the price.

steps.body: Spending a little more often buys a lot more wine. Moving from 6 to 12 pounds can more than triple the value of the liquid in the bottle, since fixed costs stay the same.

steps.prompt: What mainly drives the price of the most expensive wines?
steps.explanation: At the top, prices follow reputation, scarcity and demand.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Price includes grapes, making, packaging, duty, tax and margins
Fixed costs dominate the price of cheap wine
Top prices follow scarcity and demand

steps.title: Restaurant margins
steps.body: Restaurants usually mark wine up two to four times the shop price. Margins are often highest on the cheapest wines and lowest on expensive ones in percentage terms. Wine by the glass carries higher margins to cover waste. Some restaurants allow you to bring your own bottle, for a corkage fee.
steps.highlight: Two to four times the shop price

steps.title: Reading the list
steps.body: Good lists are organised by style or region, with vintages and producers. Look for lesser-known regions and grapes, which are often better value than famous names. The second cheapest wine is a classic choice, and restaurants know it, so it's not always the best value.
steps.highlight: Lesser-known regions are often better value

steps.prompt: Where are you most likely to find value on a wine list?
steps.explanation: Famous names carry a premium. Less familiar regions and grapes usually offer more quality for the price.

steps.title: The sommelier
steps.body: A sommelier selects, stores and serves wine, and recommends pairings. Give them a price range and a style you like; it's their job to help. When a bottle is presented, check the label, then taste for faults, not preference. You can refuse a faulty bottle, but not one you simply don't like.
steps.highlight: Give a budget and a style

steps.prompt: What is the right thing to check when a sommelier pours a taste?
options: That it's the wine you ordered
That it's at a sensible temperature
steps.explanation: The tasting is to check for faults, not personal preference.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Restaurants mark wine up two to four times
Lesser-known regions often give the best value
Tell the sommelier your budget and style; taste for faults

lessons.title: Fine wine and collecting
lessons.subtitle: Wine as an asset
objectives: Explain what makes a fine wine collectable

steps.title: What is collected
steps.body: Collectable wines age well and have a track record of price growth. Top Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne, Barolo, vintage Port and a few others dominate. The Liv-ex index tracks prices of these wines like a stock market. Only a tiny share of the world's wine, well under 1%, trades this way.
steps.highlight: A tiny share, mainly a few regions

steps.title: En primeur
steps.body: En primeur, or futures, is a way of buying Bordeaux and some other wines before they are bottled. Châteaux release a share of the wine in spring after the harvest, through négociants. Buyers pay in advance and receive bottles about two years later. The idea is to secure scarce wine at a lower price, but recent prices have often risen little after release.
steps.highlight: Pay now, receive in two years

steps.prompt: Buying Bordeaux before it is bottled is called en ____.
steps.explanation: En primeur lets buyers secure wine early, through the Bordeaux négociant system.

steps.title: Provenance and storage
steps.body: A collectable bottle's value depends on provenance: where it has been stored and by whom. Professional bonded warehouses keep wine at steady temperatures and record each movement. Wine fraud exists: the 2012 case of Rudy Kurniawan, who faked old Burgundies, showed how hard verification can be.

steps.prompt: Provenance, the record of how a bottle was stored, affects its value.
steps.explanation: Yes. Buyers pay more for wine with a clear, professional storage history.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A few regions dominate fine wine collecting
En primeur lets buyers pay early for Bordeaux
Provenance and storage protect value, and fraud exists

lessons.title: Climate and the future
lessons.subtitle: Adapting the vineyard
objectives: Explain the effects of climate change on wine

steps.title: What's changing
steps.body: Harvests in many regions are two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s. Alcohol has risen and acidity fallen. Extreme events, like frost after early budburst, hail, heatwaves, drought and wildfire, are more common. Smoke taint from fires affected California and Australia in 2020.

steps.title: Adapting
steps.body: Producers plant later-ripening grapes, higher or cooler sites, change canopy management for shade, and use drought-tolerant rootstocks. Regulations are changing too: in 2021, Bordeaux approved six new grapes, including Touriga Nacional, for trial in its AOCs. New regions like southern England, Tasmania and Denmark are rising.

steps.prompt: Which are adaptations to a warming climate?
steps.explanation: In heat, growers usually keep leaves to shade grapes, not remove them.

steps.title: Sustainability and packaging
steps.body: Glass bottles are the biggest part of wine's carbon footprint, often around 40%. Lighter bottles, bag-in-box, cans and paper bottles cut emissions. Shipping wine in bulk and bottling near the market also helps. Many producers now measure their footprint and seek certification.

steps.prompt: What is usually the largest part of wine's carbon footprint?
steps.explanation: Heavy glass bottles account for a large share of emissions, often around 40%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Climate change brings earlier harvests and more extreme weather
Producers adapt with new grapes, sites and rules
Lighter packaging cuts wine's biggest footprint, glass

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from The Business of Wine
objectives: Explain how wine is sold and priced

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: These terms describe how wine is sold and valued.

steps.prompt: Why do cheap wines have little liquid value?
options: Fixed costs like duty and packaging make up most of the price
steps.explanation: Duty, tax, packaging and margins weigh heavily on cheap bottles.

steps.prompt: When tasting a wine in a restaurant, you may send it back if you simply dislike it.
steps.explanation: Not true. The tasting checks for faults. Disliking a sound wine isn't grounds to refuse it.

steps.prompt: Which are effects of climate change in vineyards?
steps.explanation: Acidity tends to fall, not rise, with heat.

steps.prompt: In the US, the system separating producers, wholesalers and retailers is called the three-____ system.
steps.explanation: The three-tier system dates from the end of Prohibition in 1933.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Wine moves through producers, importers and retailers
Price reflects costs at first, then scarcity
Fine wine relies on provenance; en primeur sells it early
Climate change pushes new grapes, sites and packaging

modules.title: Final Review
modules.description: Blind tasting, label reading and pairing: everything the previous twenty-nine modules taught.

lessons.title: Blind tasting
lessons.subtitle: Reasoning from the glass
objectives: Explain how to approach a blind tasting
Use evidence from appearance, nose and palate

steps.title: Evidence first
steps.body: Blind tasting is reasoning, not guessing. Gather evidence: colour, aroma intensity and families, structure. Then ask what it suggests. Deep colour suggests thick skins or warmth. High acidity suggests a cool climate or a high-acid grape. Oak suggests ambition and price. Each clue narrows the options.

steps.title: Narrowing down
steps.body: Build the argument in steps. Is it Old World or New World? Fruit-forward and ripe suggests New World or warm sites; earthy, savoury and restrained suggests Old World or cool sites. Then climate: cool, moderate or warm. Then grape. Then region and age. Stop when the evidence runs out, rather than forcing an answer.

steps.prompt: A red is pale ruby, high acidity, low tannin, red cherry and earthy notes. What is the most likely conclusion?
steps.explanation: Pale colour, low tannin, high acidity and earthiness point to a cool-climate Pinot Noir, like Burgundy.

steps.body: In blind tasting, the first impression is often right, but say why. If you can't justify a guess with evidence from the glass, keep looking.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a blind conclusion in order.
items: Decide Old World or New World
steps.explanation: Each step narrows the possibilities using the evidence before it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Blind tasting is reasoning from evidence
Narrow from world to climate, grape, region and age
Stop when the evidence runs out

lessons.title: Identifying grapes
lessons.subtitle: Fingerprints of the classics
objectives: Recognise the main white grapes blind
Recognise the main red grapes blind
Use structure as much as aroma

steps.title: White fingerprints
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc: pronounced grass, gooseberry, high acidity, no oak. Riesling: lime, flowers, high acidity, sometimes sugar and petrol. Chardonnay: neutral fruit shaped by place and oak, often butter and toast. Gewürztraminer: lychee, rose, low acidity, high alcohol. Chenin Blanc: apple, quince, honey, high acidity.

steps.title: Red fingerprints
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin. Merlot: plum, softer tannin. Pinot Noir: pale, red fruit, low tannin. Syrah: blackberry, pepper, deep colour. Nebbiolo: pale but very tannic, rose and tar. Sangiovese: sour cherry, high acidity, tea-like tannin. Structure often reveals more than aroma.
steps.highlight: Tannin and acidity reveal the grape

steps.prompt: Match each wine description to its grape.

pairs.left: Sour cherry, high acidity, tea tannin

steps.explanation: Combining aroma and structure gives the clearest identification.

steps.title: Common confusions
steps.body: Some grapes are easily confused. Pinot Noir and Gamay are both pale and red-fruited; Gamay is often juicier, with banana notes from carbonic maceration. Cabernet and Merlot blend so often it's hard to separate them. Albariño and Grüner Veltliner both show citrus and acidity; Grüner adds white pepper.

steps.prompt: A wine that is pale in colour must be low in tannin.
steps.explanation: Not true. Nebbiolo is pale but very tannic, a classic blind tasting trap.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Each white grape has an aroma plus acidity fingerprint
Red grapes are often identified by tannin and acidity
Know the common confusions, like Pinot Noir and Gamay

lessons.title: Identifying regions
lessons.subtitle: Place in the glass
objectives: Use climate clues to identify regions

steps.title: Climate clues
steps.body: Regions leave marks through climate. Chablis Chardonnay is lean and steely; Californian Chardonnay is riper with more oak. Mosel Riesling is light and off-dry; Clare Valley Riesling is dry with lime. Bordeaux Cabernet is cedar and restraint; Napa is ripe and powerful.

steps.title: Winemaking clues
steps.body: Winemaking traditions also point to regions. American oak's coconut and vanilla suggest traditional Rioja. Long lees ageing and toast suggest Champagne. Carbonic maceration's banana suggests Beaujolais. Dried grape character with high alcohol suggests Amarone. Flor's tangy, nutty character means Fino or Manzanilla.

steps.prompt: Match each clue to its likely region.
steps.explanation: Regional traditions shape flavour as much as grape.

steps.title: Putting it together
steps.body: A lean, mineral, unoaked Chardonnay at 12.5% points to Chablis. A powerful, ripe Cabernet at 14.5% with sweet oak points to Napa. A Sauvignon Blanc with pronounced passion fruit points to Marlborough; with restraint and flint, to Sancerre. Use every clue: climate, grape, winemaking and structure.

steps.prompt: A Sauvignon Blanc with intense passion fruit and grass, very high acidity and no oak. Which region is most likely?
steps.explanation: Pronounced passion fruit and grass with high acidity is classic Marlborough. Sancerre is more restrained; Pessac-Léognan is often oaked.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Climate leaves its mark on the same grape
Winemaking traditions point to regions
Combine climate, grape, winemaking and structure

lessons.title: Pairing under pressure
lessons.subtitle: Fast decisions at the table
objectives: Choose wines for a full menu

steps.title: The quick rules
steps.body: When in doubt: match weight; wine as sweet as the food; acidic food needs acidic wine; salt and fat love acidity and bubbles; tannin needs fat or protein; chilli needs low alcohol and a touch of sugar; umami needs fruity, low-tannin wines. These rules cover most dishes.

steps.title: Difficult dishes
steps.body: Artichokes and asparagus contain compounds that make wine taste sweet or metallic; choose crisp, unoaked whites like Grüner Veltliner or Sauvignon Blanc. Eggs coat the palate; try Champagne. Chocolate needs sweet, fortified wine, like Banyuls or tawny Port. Very spicy curries suit off-dry Riesling.

steps.prompt: Match each dish to a strong choice.
steps.explanation: These pairings follow the core principles.

steps.body: For a menu with many dishes, a versatile wine like dry Champagne, Pinot Noir or a dry Riesling will rarely clash. Bubbles and acidity forgive a lot.

steps.prompt: Which wines are generally versatile across many dishes?
steps.explanation: Very tannic reds clash with many foods, especially fish, umami and chilli.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Remember the core rules: weight, sweetness, acidity, tannin, heat
Difficult dishes have specific answers
Versatile wines like Champagne and Pinot Noir suit mixed menus

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from the path
objectives: Bring together tasting, regions and pairing
Use the vocabulary of the whole path

steps.prompt: A white wine is deep gold, honey and apricot aromas, sweet, high acidity, long finish. What is it most likely?
options: A botrytised sweet wine like Sauternes
steps.explanation: Gold colour, honey, apricot and sweetness balanced by acidity point to noble rot.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its key process.
steps.explanation: Every great wine style comes from a process you've learned.

steps.prompt: Which label terms show minimum ageing?
steps.explanation: Brut is about sweetness; an aged tawny's indication is an average style, not a strict minimum age.

steps.prompt: A pale red with high tannin and rose and tar aromas is most likely Nebbiolo.
steps.explanation: Yes. Pale colour with high tannin is Nebbiolo's signature.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of a systematic tasting.
steps.explanation: Every module started from this method.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Taste systematically and reason from evidence
Grapes, places and processes all leave fingerprints
Labels, pairing and quality judgements follow clear principles
You now have the full path; keep tasting

modules.title: Tannat
modules.description: The most tannic grape of south-west France, which found a softer second home in Uruguay.

lessons.title: Meet Tannat
lessons.subtitle: A grape named for its grip
objectives: Describe Tannat's colour, tannin and flavours

steps.title: Dark and grippy
steps.body: Tannat is a black grape from south-west France, near the Pyrenees. Its name likely comes from the same root as tannin, and it has more than almost any other grape. In the glass it is deep purple, almost black, with blackberry, plum, liquorice and smoky, spicy notes. Acidity is high too.
steps.highlight: Very high tannin, very dark colour

steps.title: Why so tannic
steps.body: Tannat has small berries with thick skins, and unusually many seeds: often five per berry, where most grapes have two to three. Skins and seeds both carry tannin. Tannat is also very rich in procyanidins, a family of antioxidant compounds, and studies have found it among the highest of all red grapes.

steps.prompt: Why does Tannat have so much tannin?
options: Its berries have thick skins and many seeds
It is blended with white grapes
steps.explanation: Tannin comes from skins and seeds. Tannat has thick skins and often five seeds per berry.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: A young Tannat is almost opaque, with a purple rim. On the palate, the tannin grips the gums firmly, more than Cabernet Sauvignon. The fruit is dark, the finish often slightly bitter and spicy. With a few years in bottle, the tannins soften and leather and tobacco notes appear.

steps.prompt: A young Tannat usually has more tannin than a young Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Yes. Tannat is one of the most tannic grapes in the world, firmer than most Cabernet.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tannat is very dark and very tannic, with high acidity
Thick skins and many seeds give it that grip
It shows blackberry, liquorice and smoke, softening with age

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: The Pyrenees and the River Plate
objectives: Compare the climates of both homes

steps.title: Madiran
steps.body: Tannat's French home is Madiran, in Gascony, close to the Pyrenees. Madiran must be at least 60% Tannat, often blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon or Fer Servadou. The climate is mild and fairly wet, with Atlantic influence. Tannat also appears in Irouléguy, in the Basque Country, and in Saint-Mont.

steps.title: Uruguay
steps.body: Basque immigrants brought Tannat to Uruguay in the 1870s; one of them, Pascual Harriague, gave it its early local name, Harriague. Today it is Uruguay's national grape, about a quarter of the vineyard. Uruguay's humid, maritime climate on the River Plate and the Atlantic gives Tannat riper, rounder tannins than in Madiran.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Tannat connection.
steps.explanation: Tannat travelled from the Basque Country to South America with emigrants.

steps.title: Similar yet different
steps.body: Both homes are humid, with rain during the growing season, unlike the dry Andes. Growers must fight disease. Uruguay is warmer and gets more sun, so Tannat ripens more fully. Canelones, near Montevideo, makes most of it; Maldonado, near the sea, and Rivera, in the north, give new styles.

steps.prompt: Why is Tannat from Uruguay often softer than Madiran?
options: It is made from different grapes
Uruguay's warmer, sunnier climate ripens the tannins more
It is blended with white wine
steps.explanation: More warmth and sun bring riper, rounder tannins.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Madiran, near the Pyrenees, is Tannat's French home
Basque immigrants took it to Uruguay in the 1870s
Uruguay's warmer climate gives softer, riper Tannat

lessons.title: Taming the tannin
lessons.subtitle: How winemakers soften Tannat
objectives: Describe other ways to soften Tannat

steps.title: Born in Madiran
steps.body: In 1991, Madiran winemaker Patrick Ducournau developed micro-oxygenation: tiny, controlled doses of oxygen bubbled into the wine. It helps tannins link into longer chains, which feel softer, and stabilises colour. Born to tame Tannat, the technique is now used all over the world.

steps.title: Other tools
steps.body: Winemakers also soften Tannat by picking when skins and seeds are fully ripe, by gentle extraction, avoiding crushed seeds, by shorter maceration and by ageing in oak, where slow oxygen through the wood helps. In Uruguay, some producers make lighter, fresher Tannat with little oak to drink young.

steps.prompt: What does micro-oxygenation do to Tannat?
options: Helps tannins soften and stabilises colour
steps.explanation: Small, controlled doses of oxygen help tannins polymerise, so they feel softer, and fix colour.

steps.title: Blending
steps.body: Blending is the oldest solution. In Madiran, Cabernet Franc adds perfume and lightness. In Uruguay, Tannat is often blended with Merlot or Pinot Noir to soften it, or with Marselan. Some producers even co-ferment a little white Viognier, adding aroma and helping colour.

steps.prompt: Which methods help soften Tannat?
steps.explanation: Crushing seeds releases harsh tannin, the opposite of what you want.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Micro-oxygenation was invented in Madiran in 1991 for Tannat
Ripe picking, gentle extraction and oak soften it
Blending with Cabernet Franc or Merlot adds softness

steps.title: Fat and protein
steps.body: Tannin binds to fat and protein, so Tannat shines with rich meat. In Uruguay, it's the wine of the asado, beef grilled slowly over wood. In Gascony, it goes with duck confit and cassoulet. The fat softens the tannin; the tannin cleans the palate.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Tannat at 16 to 18 degrees. Young, powerful examples benefit from decanting for an hour or two. Good Madiran can age 10 to 20 years, when the tannins soften and earthy, leather notes emerge. Lighter Uruguayan styles are best within a few years.
steps.highlight: Decant young; good Madiran ages 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a young Tannat best?
steps.explanation: Fatty grilled meat softens Tannat's tannin. Delicate fish would taste metallic next to it.

steps.body: Uruguay's sweet fortified Tannat, sometimes called Tannat licoroso, is a good match for dark chocolate.

steps.prompt: Tannat is best served very cold, like a white wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. Cold makes tannin feel harsher. Serve it at 16 to 18 degrees.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tannat loves fatty, grilled meat and duck
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, and decant when young
Good Madiran ages for 10 to 20 years

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Tannat
objectives: Know its homes in France and Uruguay
Explain how it is softened and served

steps.prompt: What makes Tannat so tannic?
steps.explanation: Skins and seeds carry tannin, and Tannat has plenty of both.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Tannat's story.
steps.explanation: Tannat's story spans two continents.

steps.prompt: Basque immigrants brought Tannat to Uruguay.
steps.explanation: Yes, in the 1870s.

steps.prompt: Which help soften Tannat?
steps.explanation: Cold makes tannin feel harder, not softer.

steps.prompt: Madiran must contain at least ____% Tannat.
steps.explanation: At least 60%, often blended with Cabernet Franc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tannat is dark, highly tannic and acidic
Madiran is its French home; Uruguay its adopted one
Micro-oxygenation, oak and blending soften it
It's the wine for grilled meat and duck

modules.title: Malbec
modules.description: Also called Côt or Auxerrois in France. Born in Cahors, reborn at altitude in Mendoza.

lessons.title: Meet Malbec
lessons.subtitle: Dark, plush and violet-scented
objectives: Explain its French origins and names

steps.title: Deep purple
steps.body: Malbec is a black grape with thick skins and deep colour, often inky purple with a magenta rim. It smells of plum, blackberry, black cherry and violet, sometimes with cocoa. Its tannins are usually ripe and soft, its acidity medium. It's one of the most recognisable reds by colour alone.

steps.title: A French grape
steps.body: Malbec comes from south-west France, around Cahors, where it's also called Côt or Auxerrois. DNA shows its parents are Prunelard and Magdeleine Noire des Charentes, the latter also a parent of Merlot. Once widespread in Bordeaux, it suffered badly in the 1956 frost and from rot, and was largely replaced by Merlot.
steps.highlight: Côt in Cahors; parents include a Merlot parent

steps.prompt: Match each Malbec fact to its detail.
steps.explanation: Malbec has deep French roots, though it's now most famous in Argentina.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for very deep purple colour, almost opaque, with a bright violet rim. On the nose, ripe plum and violet. On the palate, plush, soft tannins and ripe fruit, with medium acidity. Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec feels rounder and less gripping, with less blackcurrant and more plum.

steps.prompt: Which aroma is a classic sign of Malbec?
steps.explanation: Violet, with plum, is Malbec's signature aroma.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Malbec is deep purple, with plum and violet
It comes from Cahors, where it's called Côt
It's rounder and softer than Cabernet Sauvignon

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: From Cahors to the Andes
objectives: Explain why Argentina became its home
Name other countries that grow it

steps.title: Argentina's grape
steps.body: Malbec arrived in Argentina in 1853, brought by French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget for Mendoza's new agricultural school. It thrived in the dry, sunny climate, free of the rot that troubled it in France. Today Argentina grows over 75% of the world's Malbec, about 45,000 hectares. April 17 is celebrated as World Malbec Day.

steps.title: Why it thrives there
steps.body: Mendoza is a high desert. Little rain means little rot. Strong sun ripens Malbec fully, giving soft tannins and ripe fruit. Cool nights at altitude keep acidity. Irrigation lets growers control water. In France's wetter climate, Malbec suffers from coulure, poor fruit set, which lowers yields.

steps.prompt: Most of the world's Malbec is grown in France.
steps.explanation: Not true. Argentina grows over 75% of it. France has a small area, mainly in Cahors.

steps.title: Other homes
steps.body: Beyond Argentina and Cahors, Malbec grows in Chile, often blended; in Bordeaux, where it's a minor blending grape; in the Loire, as Côt; and in California, Washington and Australia. Argentina's Salta and Patagonia also make distinct styles: very intense at altitude in Salta, fresher in Patagonia's cool wind.

steps.prompt: Who brought Malbec to Argentina?
steps.explanation: Pouget, a French agronomist, brought cuttings to Mendoza in 1853.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Argentina grows over 75% of the world's Malbec
Mendoza's dry, sunny climate keeps it healthy
It also grows in Cahors, Chile, Bordeaux and the US

steps.title: Cahors
steps.body: Cahors, on the Lot river, must be at least 70% Malbec. Vineyards grow on river terraces and on the limestone plateau, the causse. The wines are dark, firm and often more tannic and savoury than Argentina's, with black fruit, earth and spice. In the Middle Ages they were called the black wine and shipped to London.
steps.highlight: At least 70% Malbec, firm and savoury

steps.title: Mendoza
steps.body: Mendoza Malbec is riper and plusher, with plum, black cherry and violet, softer tannins and often oak. Altitude shapes the style: lower Luján de Cuyo gives rich, round wines; higher Valle de Uco gives fresher, more floral wines with firmer structure. Many producers now use less new oak than in the 2000s.
steps.highlight: Ripe and plush; fresher at altitude

steps.prompt: Match each description to its region.
steps.explanation: The same grape gives a firmer style in France and a plusher one in Argentina.

steps.body: Taste a Cahors next to a Mendoza Malbec. The colour will be similar, but the French one will feel more savoury and firm, the Argentine one riper and rounder.

steps.prompt: Cahors must contain at least 70% Malbec.
steps.explanation: Yes. Merlot and Tannat can make up the rest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cahors makes firm, savoury Malbec, once called the black wine
Mendoza makes riper, plusher Malbec
Altitude in the Valle de Uco brings freshness

lessons.title: Altitude and colour
lessons.subtitle: Why high vineyards make dark wines
objectives: Explain how ultraviolet light affects skins

steps.title: Cooler with height
steps.body: Air cools by about 0.6 degrees for every 100 m of altitude. Mendoza's vineyards lie from about 700 to 1,500 m; in Salta, some reach 3,000 m. Higher sites have cooler nights, so grapes keep acidity and aroma while still ripening in strong daytime sun.

steps.title: Ultraviolet light
steps.body: At altitude, the atmosphere is thinner, and ultraviolet radiation is stronger, rising by roughly 10% for every 1,000 m. Grapes respond by producing more anthocyanins and tannins in their skins, as a natural sunscreen. Skins thicken. That's why high-altitude Malbec is so deeply coloured and structured.

steps.prompt: Why does high-altitude Malbec have deeper colour?
options: Stronger UV light makes skins produce more pigment
steps.explanation: Grapes protect themselves from UV by producing more anthocyanins, the pigments that colour wine.

steps.title: The style it gives
steps.body: The combination of strong light, cool nights and dry air gives Malbec its signature: dark colour, ripe fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannins. In the Valle de Uco, sites like Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira, at 1,100 to 1,500 m, now have their own geographical indications for this reason.

steps.prompt: Which are effects of altitude on Malbec?
steps.explanation: Mendoza is dry at every altitude; rain doesn't increase much with height there.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees per 100 m
Stronger UV thickens skins and deepens colour
Cool nights keep acidity, giving dark yet fresh Malbec

steps.title: Beef and more
steps.body: In Argentina, Malbec is the partner of beef from the asado, from steak to chorizo. Its soft tannins and ripe fruit suit grilled meat, and its plushness handles chimichurri, a herb and garlic sauce. Cahors' firmer style suits duck, lamb and cassoulet. Mushroom dishes work well too.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Malbec at 16 to 18 degrees. Most Argentine Malbec is made to drink within five years. Top examples from high sites, and good Cahors, can age 10 to 20 years, gaining leather, tobacco and dried fruit. Decanting helps young, structured examples.
steps.highlight: Most within five years; the best for decades

steps.prompt: What sauce is a classic partner for Malbec and steak in Argentina?
steps.explanation: Chimichurri's herbs, garlic and vinegar suit Malbec's ripe fruit.

steps.title: Other styles
steps.body: Malbec also makes rosé, often bright pink and fruity, good with empanadas. Some Argentine producers make lighter, fresher, unoaked Malbecs, served slightly cool. In Cahors, some wines are blended with Merlot for softness. The range is wider than the classic plush red.

steps.prompt: Most Argentine Malbec is made to be drunk within a few years.
steps.explanation: Yes. Most is fruity and approachable, though top examples age well.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Malbec suits beef, chimichurri, duck and lamb
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; most is best within five years
Rosé and lighter, fresher Malbecs widen the range

steps.prompt: Which aroma, with plum, is typical of Malbec?
steps.explanation: Violet and plum are Malbec's signature.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Malbec.
steps.explanation: Malbec's history spans two continents.

steps.prompt: High altitude gives Malbec paler colour.
steps.explanation: Not true. Stronger UV makes skins thicker and darker.

steps.prompt: Which describe Mendoza?
steps.explanation: Mendoza is dry, which keeps Malbec healthy.

steps.prompt: Order these places from lowest to highest typical vineyard altitude.
steps.explanation: Cahors is low; Salta has some of the world's highest vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Malbec is dark, plush and violet-scented
Cahors gives firm, savoury wines; Mendoza riper ones
Altitude brings colour and freshness
It's a natural partner for grilled beef

modules.title: Petit Verdot
modules.description: A late-ripening Bordeaux grape that adds colour and spice to blends, and shines alone in warm places.

lessons.title: Meet Petit Verdot
lessons.subtitle: Small berries, deep colour
objectives: Describe Petit Verdot's colour and flavours

steps.title: A dark spice
steps.body: Petit Verdot is a black grape from Bordeaux. Its small, thick-skinned berries give very deep colour, high tannin and high acidity. It smells of violet, blackberry, blueberry, and spices like clove and sage. In a blend, a few percent is enough to add colour, structure and a floral, spicy lift.

steps.title: Why little green
steps.body: Its name means little green one, because in Bordeaux it often failed to ripen fully. It buds early and ripens very late, often after Cabernet Sauvignon. In cool years, it stayed green and harsh. That's why Bordeaux planted little of it, and used it only as a seasoning in the blend.

steps.prompt: What does Petit Verdot mean?
steps.explanation: It means little green one, because in Bordeaux it often stayed unripe.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In a Bordeaux blend, you may not notice Petit Verdot directly, but it deepens the colour and adds a violet and spice note, and firmer tannin on the finish. Alone, it is inky purple, intense, with violets and dark fruit, firm tannin and fresh acidity.

steps.prompt: What does Petit Verdot add to a blend?
steps.explanation: Petit Verdot adds acidity, not lowers it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Petit Verdot gives deep colour, tannin, acidity and spice
Its name means little green one, from struggling to ripen
It seasons Bordeaux blends and can stand alone

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: From Bordeaux to warmer places
objectives: Explain why warm climates suit it
Explain its role in Bordeaux today

steps.title: Bordeaux
steps.body: Petit Verdot is mainly a Left Bank grape, used in small amounts in the Médoc. Château Margaux and others use a few percent. Plantings fell in the 20th century, but warmer vintages since the 1990s have helped it ripen more reliably, and some estates have added more.
steps.highlight: A small part of Left Bank blends

steps.title: Warmer homes
steps.body: In warm, dry places, Petit Verdot ripens fully. Spain grows it in La Mancha and Castilla, sometimes as a single variety. Australia's Riverland and McLaren Vale, California, Virginia and Washington all make varietal Petit Verdot. Argentina and Chile use it in blends.

steps.prompt: Why does Petit Verdot do better in warm climates?
options: It needs a lot of rain
steps.explanation: As a late ripener, it needs a long, warm season to reach full ripeness.

steps.title: Climate change
steps.body: With warmer vintages, Petit Verdot is gaining interest in Bordeaux as a grape that keeps acidity in heat. Growers value its freshness and colour as other grapes ripen faster. It's one reason some see it as part of Bordeaux's future blend.

steps.prompt: Petit Verdot is mainly a Right Bank grape in Bordeaux.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's mostly found in small amounts on the Left Bank, in the Médoc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Petit Verdot is a minor Left Bank blending grape
Warm regions in Spain, Australia and the US ripen it fully
Climate change has renewed interest in Bordeaux

steps.title: A varietal wine
steps.body: Made alone, Petit Verdot gives intense, dark wines with violet, blueberry, liquorice and spice, firm tannin and bright acidity. It can be austere young. Warm regions give rounder, riper styles. In Virginia, it has become a signature grape, ripening well in humid summers thanks to loose bunches that resist rot.

steps.title: Handling it
steps.body: Winemakers often pick it late for full ripeness, use gentle extraction to avoid harshness, and age it in oak to soften tannins. Some blend in a little Cabernet or Shiraz to round it out. Its high acidity helps it age, and good examples develop for a decade or more.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Petit Verdot role.
steps.explanation: Petit Verdot plays different roles in different places.

steps.body: If you find a varietal Petit Verdot, decant it. Its tannins open up with air, and the violet aromas become clearer.

steps.prompt: Why does Petit Verdot handle Virginia's humid summers?
options: Thick skins and loose bunches resist rot
steps.explanation: Loose bunches let air circulate, reducing rot in humid conditions.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Varietal Petit Verdot is intense, floral and firm
Ripe picking, gentle extraction and oak soften it
Virginia, Australia and Spain make notable examples

steps.title: Rich food
steps.body: Petit Verdot's firm tannin and acidity suit rich, savoury food: lamb with herbs, venison, braised beef, hard aged cheeses. Its floral, spicy notes go well with rosemary, sage and black pepper. Avoid delicate fish and very spicy dishes, which clash with its tannin.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, ideally decanted. Young varietal Petit Verdot can be austere; three to five years in bottle softens it. Good examples age 10 to 15 years. In blends, it helps Bordeaux age longer by adding acidity and tannin.
steps.highlight: Decant; three to five years to soften

steps.prompt: Petit Verdot's floral notes pair well with herbs like rosemary and ____.
steps.explanation: Sage and rosemary echo its savoury, floral side.

steps.title: Spotting quality
steps.body: Good Petit Verdot balances its tannin and acidity with ripe fruit; underripe examples taste green and harsh. Look for producers in warm regions or top Bordeaux estates. As a varietal, it's still niche, so it often offers value for its intensity.

steps.prompt: Young varietal Petit Verdot can taste austere and benefits from time.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its tannin and acidity soften with a few years in bottle or with decanting.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Petit Verdot suits lamb, game and herb-crusted meat
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees and decant
It softens with age; the best last 10 to 15 years

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Petit Verdot
objectives: Explain its role alone and in blends

steps.prompt: What does Petit Verdot add to Bordeaux blends?
steps.explanation: Small amounts add colour, structure and a floral, spicy lift.

steps.prompt: Petit Verdot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. It ripens very late, often after Cabernet.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Petit Verdot.
steps.explanation: Its story connects Bordeaux to new homes.

steps.prompt: Which regions make varietal Petit Verdot?
steps.explanation: Champagne grows Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

steps.prompt: Petit Verdot needs a long, ____ season to ripen.
steps.explanation: As a late ripener, warmth is essential.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Petit Verdot is dark, tannic, acidic and floral
It seasons Bordeaux blends in small amounts
Warm regions make it as a varietal
It suits rich, herby meat dishes

modules.title: Syrah
modules.description: Also called Shiraz. Pepper and smoke in the Rhône, ripe dark fruit in the Barossa.

lessons.title: Meet Syrah
lessons.subtitle: Dark fruit and black pepper
objectives: Describe Syrah's colour, aromas and structure

steps.title: Deep and spicy
steps.body: Syrah is a thick-skinned black grape giving deep purple wines with blackberry, blueberry and plum, plus black pepper, smoked meat, olive and violet. Tannins are firm but usually ripe, acidity medium to high. Ripe examples add chocolate and liquorice. It's one of the world's most planted red grapes.

steps.title: Origins and the pepper molecule
steps.body: DNA shows Syrah is a natural cross of two grapes from south-east France: Dureza, from the Ardèche, and Mondeuse Blanche, from Savoie. Its black pepper aroma comes from rotundone, a compound also found in peppercorns. Rotundone forms most in cooler sites and vintages; about one in five people can't smell it at all.

steps.prompt: What compound gives Syrah its black pepper aroma?
steps.explanation: Rotundone is the same compound found in black peppercorns. Pyrazines give green pepper, not black.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep purple, almost opaque colour. On the nose, dark fruit with pepper or smoky, meaty notes suggests Syrah. On the palate, firm but ripe tannins and a savoury finish. Cooler examples are peppery and medium-bodied; warmer ones are fuller, sweeter-fruited and chocolatey.
steps.highlight: Dark colour plus pepper or smoke

steps.prompt: Syrah is a cross between two grapes from south-east France.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its parents are Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, both from the area around the Rhône and the Alps.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah gives dark fruit, black pepper and smoky, meaty notes
It's a cross of Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche
Rotundone gives its pepper aroma, most in cooler sites

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: From the Rhône to the world

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Syrah's classic home is the northern Rhône, on steep granite slopes. It is also a key grape in the southern Rhône and the Languedoc, blended with Grenache and Mourvèdre. As Shiraz, it is Australia's most planted grape. It grows in South Africa, California, Washington, Chile, Argentina and New Zealand's Hawke's Bay.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Syrah needs warmth to ripen, but not extreme heat: too hot, and it loses acidity and turns jammy. Moderate climates give the most aromatic wines, with pepper and violet. Warm climates give richer, fuller, more alcoholic wines. It tolerates drought reasonably well, but its shoots can break in strong wind, like the Mistral.
steps.highlight: Moderate for pepper; warm for richness

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Syrah style.
steps.explanation: The same grape shifts style with climate and tradition.

steps.title: Blending partners
steps.body: In the southern Rhône and Australia, Syrah joins Grenache and Mourvèdre in GSM blends, adding colour and structure. In Côte-Rôtie, a little white Viognier may be co-fermented with it, lifting aroma and stabilising colour. In Australia, a Shiraz Cabernet blend is a classic, invented there.

steps.prompt: Which white grape is sometimes co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie?
steps.explanation: Up to 20% Viognier is allowed in Côte-Rôtie, though most use far less.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah grows in the Rhône, Australia and much of the New World
Moderate climates give pepper; warm ones give richness
It blends with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier and Cabernet

lessons.title: The Northern Rhône
lessons.subtitle: Syrah's original home
objectives: Explain why it makes such distinct Syrah

steps.title: Steep and narrow
steps.body: The northern Rhône runs about 60 km along the river, from Vienne to Valence. Vineyards cling to steep granite slopes, often on terraces held by stone walls. The climate is continental, cooler than the south. Syrah is the only red grape allowed, sometimes with a little white Viognier, Marsanne or Roussanne.

steps.title: The appellations
steps.body: Côte-Rôtie, meaning roasted slope, makes perfumed, elegant Syrah. Hermitage, a single hill facing south, makes powerful, long-lived wines. Cornas makes dark, rustic, firm wines. Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage are larger, more affordable areas. Crozes-Hermitage is the biggest, with flatter vineyards.

steps.prompt: Match each appellation to its style.
steps.explanation: Each northern Rhône appellation shows a different face of Syrah.

steps.body: Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph offer a taste of northern Rhône Syrah at a fraction of Hermitage's price. Look for producers who also make wines from the famous hills.

steps.prompt: In the northern Rhône, Syrah is often blended with Grenache.
steps.explanation: Not true. Syrah is the only red grape in the northern Rhône. Grenache belongs to the southern Rhône.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The northern Rhône grows Syrah on steep granite slopes
Côte-Rôtie is perfumed; Hermitage powerful; Cornas rustic
Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph are more affordable

lessons.title: Barossa Shiraz
lessons.subtitle: Australia's icon
objectives: Explain the role of old vines
Explain how Penfolds Grange changed Australian wine

steps.title: Ripe and rich
steps.body: The Barossa Valley, north-east of Adelaide, is warm and dry. Shiraz there is full-bodied, around 14.5 to 15% alcohol, with ripe blackberry, plum, chocolate, liquorice and often American oak's vanilla and coconut. Tannins are soft and ripe. It's the style that made Australian Shiraz famous worldwide.

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: Phylloxera never reached South Australia, so the Barossa has some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world, some planted in the 1840s by Silesian settlers. Old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit. The Barossa Old Vine Charter classifies Old Vines at 35 years and Ancestor vines at 125 years or more.

steps.prompt: Why does the Barossa have such old Shiraz vines?
steps.explanation: Strict quarantine kept phylloxera out, so the original ungrafted vines survive.

steps.title: Grange
steps.body: In 1951, Max Schubert, Penfolds' chief winemaker, made an experimental Shiraz after visiting Bordeaux. Penfolds Grange, aged in new American oak, was first mocked, then celebrated. It became Australia's most famous wine and showed that Shiraz could make world-class, long-lived wines.

steps.prompt: Which describe classic Barossa Shiraz?
steps.explanation: Barossa Shiraz is deeply coloured and full, not pale.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barossa Shiraz is ripe, full and chocolatey
Old ungrafted vines date back to the 1840s
Penfolds Grange, from 1951, made Australian Shiraz world-class

lessons.title: Syrah or Shiraz
lessons.subtitle: Two names, two styles
objectives: Explain where the name Shiraz came from

steps.title: The names
steps.body: Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape. Shiraz is the name used in Australia and South Africa, possibly from an old local spelling. A popular legend links it to the Persian city of Shiraz, but DNA proves the grape is French. James Busby brought cuttings to Australia in 1832.

steps.title: Names as style signals
steps.body: Today, many producers choose the name to signal style. Syrah suggests a cooler, Rhône-like wine: peppery, savoury, medium-bodied. Shiraz suggests a riper, fuller, fruit-forward wine. Some cool-climate Australian producers now label their wines Syrah for this reason.

steps.prompt: James Busby brought Syrah cuttings to Australia in ____.
steps.explanation: Busby's collection in 1832 included Syrah, which became Australia's Shiraz.

steps.title: Cool-climate Shiraz
steps.body: Australia isn't only warm. The Yarra Valley, Canberra District, Great Southern and Adelaide Hills make lighter, peppery Shiraz. Canberra is known for Shiraz co-fermented with Viognier, inspired by Côte-Rôtie. These wines show that Australia's Shiraz can be elegant as well as powerful.

steps.prompt: An Australian wine is labelled Syrah instead of Shiraz. What does this most likely signal?
steps.explanation: Many producers use Syrah to signal a cooler, Rhône-like style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah and Shiraz are the same French grape
The name often signals style: peppery Syrah, ripe Shiraz
Australia's cooler regions make elegant, peppery Shiraz

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Syrah
objectives: Serve it at the right temperature

steps.title: Meat and spice
steps.body: Syrah's dark fruit and pepper suit grilled and roasted meat: lamb, beef, game and barbecue. Peppery Rhône styles match herbs and black pepper crust. Ripe Barossa Shiraz handles sweet, smoky barbecue sauces. Avoid very delicate dishes, which it overwhelms.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Young, powerful Syrah benefits from decanting. Good Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie age 15 to 30 years, developing leather, game and earthy notes. Top Barossa Shiraz also ages well. Simpler Shiraz is best within a few years.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a peppery northern Rhône Syrah?
options: Lamb with rosemary and black pepper
steps.explanation: Herbs and pepper echo the wine's own aromas; lamb's fat softens its tannins.

steps.title: Beyond the classic
steps.body: Syrah also makes rosé, sparkling red Shiraz, a beloved Australian Christmas wine, and fortified styles in Australia. In blends, it's part of Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Learning to taste for its pepper is one of the most useful skills in blind tasting.

steps.prompt: Sparkling red Shiraz is a traditional Australian style.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's often served with Christmas lunch in Australia.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah suits lamb, game and barbecue
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; the best age for decades
It also makes rosé and sparkling red Shiraz

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Syrah
objectives: Compare the Rhône and the Barossa

steps.prompt: What gives Syrah its black pepper aroma?
steps.explanation: Rotundone, also found in peppercorns.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Syrah.
steps.explanation: Each region shows a different side of the grape.

steps.prompt: Shiraz came originally from the Persian city of Shiraz.
steps.explanation: Not true. DNA shows it comes from south-east France.

steps.prompt: Which are typical Syrah aromas?
steps.explanation: Lychee is typical of Gewürztraminer.

steps.prompt: Penfolds Grange was first made in ____.
steps.explanation: Max Schubert's 1951 experiment became Australia's most famous wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah gives dark fruit, pepper and smoky notes
The northern Rhône is its home; the Barossa its Australian icon
The names Syrah and Shiraz often signal style
It pairs with lamb, game and barbecue

modules.title: Touriga Nacional
modules.description: Portugal's finest red grape: floral, dark and structured, at the heart of Port and the Douro's dry reds.

lessons.title: Meet Touriga Nacional
lessons.subtitle: Portugal's floral red
objectives: Describe Touriga Nacional's aromas and structure

steps.title: Violets and dark fruit
steps.body: Touriga Nacional is a black grape native to Portugal. It gives deep-coloured wines with intense aromas of violet, bergamot, blackberry and black cherry, often with rockrose, a wild herb of the Douro hills. Tannins are firm and ripe, acidity fresh. It's considered the country's finest red grape.

steps.title: Small berries, low yields
steps.body: Touriga Nacional probably comes from the Dão, where it was once called Tourigo. Its small berries and thick skins concentrate colour, tannin and aroma. Its natural yields are low, often under 1 kg per vine, which once made growers reluctant to plant it. Clonal selection since the 1970s raised yields and helped it spread.

steps.prompt: Which aroma is most typical of Touriga Nacional?
steps.explanation: Violet is Touriga Nacional's signature, often with bergamot and dark fruit.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In the glass, look for deep purple colour and a strongly floral nose, like violets and citrus peel, with dark fruit. On the palate, firm, fine tannins and fresh acidity, with a long finish. In blends, it adds perfume and structure that you can often pick out.

steps.prompt: Touriga Nacional naturally gives high yields.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its yields are naturally low, which is part of why its wines are so concentrated.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Touriga Nacional gives violet, bergamot and dark fruit
It probably comes from the Dão and has naturally low yields
It's deep, floral and firm, Portugal's finest red

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Douro, Dão and beyond
objectives: Name countries that have adopted it

steps.title: The Douro and Dão
steps.body: Touriga Nacional is planted in most Portuguese regions, but the Douro and the Dão are its heartlands. In the hot, dry Douro, on schist, it gives powerful, concentrated wines. In the Dão, cooler and granite-based, it gives more elegant, floral wines with fresher acidity. It also grows in Alentejo, Lisboa and Bairrada.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Touriga Nacional handles heat and drought well thanks to deep roots and small berries. Strong sun develops its colour. In very hot sites it can lose some aromatic finesse, so higher or north-facing vineyards are valued. Its vigorous growth needs careful canopy management.

steps.prompt: Match each Portuguese region to its Touriga style.
steps.explanation: Portugal's regions bring out different sides of the grape.

steps.title: Abroad
steps.body: With warmer summers, other countries are interested. Bordeaux approved Touriga Nacional for trial in its AOCs in 2021, as a heat-tolerant option. It also grows in Spain, Australia, South Africa, where it's used for fortified wines, and California.

steps.prompt: Why did Bordeaux approve Touriga Nacional for trial in 2021?
options: It handles heat and drought well
steps.explanation: Bordeaux is looking for grapes adapted to a warming climate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Douro and Dão are Touriga Nacional's heartlands
It handles heat and drought well
Bordeaux, Spain, Australia and South Africa grow it too

lessons.title: Port and dry reds
lessons.subtitle: Two wines, one grape
objectives: Explain Touriga Nacional's role in Port

steps.title: In Port
steps.body: Port is a blend of many grapes. Touriga Nacional brings colour, tannin, structure and its floral perfume, essential for Vintage Port, which must age for decades. It is usually a smaller share than Touriga Franca, the Douro's most planted grape, because of its lower yields. Most Port grapes are foot-trodden or machine-trodden in lagares.

steps.title: Dry reds
steps.body: Since the 1990s, the Douro has become famous for dry reds, often blends of Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz. Barca Velha, first made in 1952, showed the potential. Today single-varietal Touriga Nacional from the Douro and Dão is common, often aged in French oak.

steps.prompt: What does Touriga Nacional bring to Port?
steps.explanation: Touriga Nacional is aromatic, not neutral.

steps.body: Try a Douro dry red and a ruby Port side by side. The violet and dark fruit of Touriga Nacional link both, though one is dry and the other sweet.

steps.prompt: Barca Velha, an early Douro dry red, was first made in ____.
steps.explanation: 1952. It showed that the Douro could make great dry reds.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Touriga Nacional gives Port colour, structure and perfume
The Douro now makes famous dry reds, since Barca Velha in 1952
Dry and sweet styles share its violet and dark fruit

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Touriga Nacional
objectives: Pair dry Touriga Nacional with food

steps.title: Dry wines
steps.body: Dry Touriga Nacional suits roast lamb, kid, game and Portuguese dishes like roast suckling pig from Bairrada or bacalhau with roasted potatoes. Its floral notes go well with herbs and its tannins with fat. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young.

steps.title: Port
steps.body: Ruby and Vintage Ports suit dark chocolate, blue cheese like Stilton, and dried fruit. Serve Port slightly cool, about 16 degrees for ruby and vintage. Vintage Port needs decanting for sediment. Touriga Nacional's structure helps top Vintage Ports age 30 to 50 years.

steps.prompt: Which is a classic partner for Vintage Port?
steps.explanation: Salty blue cheese balances Port's sweetness and power.

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Good dry Touriga Nacional from the Douro or Dão ages 10 to 20 years, gaining earthy, savoury notes while keeping its floral lift. Simpler versions are best young and fruity. Port's age depends on style: rubies are best young; vintages last decades.

steps.prompt: Vintage Port usually needs decanting.
steps.explanation: Yes. It ages in bottle and throws a heavy sediment.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Touriga Nacional suits lamb, kid and roast pork
Port suits blue cheese and dark chocolate
Good dry reds age 10 to 20 years; Vintage Port decades

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Touriga Nacional
objectives: Explain its roles in Port and dry wine

steps.prompt: Which aroma is Touriga Nacional's signature?
steps.explanation: Violet, often with bergamot.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Touriga Nacional.
steps.explanation: Its story runs from Portugal to Bordeaux.

steps.prompt: Touriga Nacional is the most planted grape in the Douro.
steps.explanation: Not true. Touriga Franca is more planted, partly because Touriga Nacional has low yields.

steps.prompt: Which regions are Touriga Nacional's heartlands?
steps.explanation: Rioja and the Mosel grow Tempranillo and Riesling.

steps.prompt: Touriga Nacional naturally gives ____ yields.
steps.explanation: Low yields concentrate its colour and aroma.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Touriga Nacional is floral, dark and structured
The Douro and Dão are its heartlands
It's key in Port and the Douro's dry reds
It handles heat, drawing interest from abroad

modules.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
modules.description: The world's most planted red grape: blackcurrant, cedar and structure, from the Médoc to Napa.

lessons.title: Meet Cabernet Sauvignon
lessons.subtitle: Structure and blackcurrant
objectives: Describe Cabernet Sauvignon's flavours and structure

steps.title: The king of structure
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon gives deep-coloured wines with blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, mint and sometimes green pepper. It has high tannin and high acidity, so it ages well. It is the world's most planted wine grape, about 340,000 hectares, grown in almost every wine country.

steps.title: An accidental cross
steps.body: In 1996, DNA research at UC Davis showed that Cabernet Sauvignon is a natural cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, probably in 17th century Bordeaux. Its small, thick-skinned berries, with a high ratio of skin and seed to juice, explain its colour and tannin. It also resists rot and frost well, since it buds late.

steps.prompt: Which two grapes are the parents of Cabernet Sauvignon?
steps.explanation: DNA testing in 1996 showed it was a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep colour, a nose of blackcurrant with cedar, mint or pencil shavings, and a palate with firm tannin and fresh acidity. In cooler sites, a green pepper or leafy note. In warmer ones, ripe black fruit and sometimes eucalyptus. It often sits in oak, adding vanilla and toast.

steps.prompt: Cabernet Sauvignon buds late, which helps it avoid spring frost.
steps.explanation: Yes. Late budding protects it from frost, but late ripening means it needs a warm site.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Sauvignon gives blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannin
It's a 17th century cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc
Small, thick-skinned berries give colour, tannin and ageing power

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: A truly international grape
objectives: Explain how it adapts to different places

steps.title: Everywhere warm enough
steps.body: Cabernet's classic home is Bordeaux's Left Bank. It's the leading red in Napa Valley, Chile's Maipo, Australia's Coonawarra and Margaret River, Washington State and South Africa's Stellenbosch. In Italy it's key to Bolgheri's Super Tuscans. It also grows in Argentina, China and Spain.

steps.title: Needing warmth
steps.body: As a late ripener, Cabernet needs a long, warm season. In cool places it can taste green, from pyrazines that only break down when fully ripe. Warm, dry sites with well-drained soils suit it best. That's why it does so well on gravel and in sunny, irrigated New World regions.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet character.
steps.explanation: Place changes Cabernet's accent while its core stays.

steps.title: Why it travels well
steps.body: Cabernet's thick skins resist rot, its late budding avoids frost, and it keeps its character in many soils and climates. Growers find it reliable, and consumers recognise the name. That's how it became the world's most planted wine grape, overtaking others in the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Why can Cabernet taste green in cool climates?
options: Pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness
steps.explanation: Pyrazines give green pepper notes; full ripeness reduces them.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet grows in almost every wine country
It needs warmth and drainage to ripen fully
Its resistance and recognisability made it the most planted grape

lessons.title: The Left Bank model
lessons.subtitle: Bordeaux and the blend
objectives: Explain why Cabernet suits the Médoc
Name the key Left Bank appellations

steps.title: Gravel
steps.body: The Médoc and Graves, on the left bank of the Gironde and Garonne, have deep gravel soils left by ancient rivers. Gravel drains well and stores the sun's heat, releasing it at night. That helps Cabernet ripen in Bordeaux's moderate, maritime climate. The best châteaux sit on gravel mounds close to the estuary.

steps.title: The blend
steps.body: Left Bank reds are usually led by Cabernet Sauvignon, often 60 to 80%, with Merlot to add flesh, and smaller amounts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. Blending also spreads risk: in a cool year, Merlot ripens when Cabernet struggles. The result is structured, cedar-scented wine that can age for decades.

steps.prompt: Why is Merlot blended with Cabernet on the Left Bank?
options: To add flesh and reduce risk in cool years
steps.explanation: Merlot fills Cabernet's mid-palate and ripens earlier, which helps in cool vintages.

steps.title: The appellations
steps.body: Pauillac, home to three of the five First Growths, makes powerful, cedar-scented wines. Margaux is more perfumed and elegant. Saint-Julien sits between them. Saint-Estèphe, further north, is firmer, with more clay. Pessac-Léognan, in the Graves, makes both reds and whites, including Haut-Brion.

steps.prompt: Match each appellation to its style.
steps.explanation: Small differences in soil and position shape each style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gravel helps Cabernet ripen in the Médoc
Left Bank blends are Cabernet-led, with Merlot
Pauillac, Margaux, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe are key

steps.title: What pyrazines are
steps.body: Methoxypyrazines are aromatic compounds that smell of green pepper, cut grass and leaves. Humans can detect them at a few parts per trillion. They are found in the Cabernet family: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Carmenère, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc. In small amounts they add freshness; in excess, they taste unripe.
steps.highlight: Green pepper at parts per trillion

steps.title: Sun and ripeness
steps.body: Pyrazines form early in the berry and break down as it ripens, especially with sunlight on the bunches. Cool, cloudy seasons and shaded fruit keep them high. Warm, sunny sites reduce them. This is why a Cabernet from a cool year in Bordeaux may show green notes, while one from Napa rarely does.

steps.prompt: Pyrazine levels in grapes rise steadily as they ripen.
steps.explanation: Not true. Pyrazines are highest before veraison and fall as grapes ripen, especially in sunlight.

steps.title: Managing them
steps.body: Growers reduce pyrazines by removing leaves around bunches early in the season, letting sunlight reach the fruit. They control vigour so the canopy isn't too dense. They pick later for riper flavour, but must watch sugar and alcohol rising. In the winery, careful sorting removes green material.

steps.prompt: Which help lower pyrazine levels in Cabernet?
steps.explanation: Shade keeps pyrazines high.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pyrazines smell of green pepper and grass
They fall as grapes ripen, especially in sunlight
Leaf removal and balanced canopies help manage them

steps.title: Napa Valley
steps.body: Napa Valley has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate, with fog cooling mornings. Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading grape and commands some of the world's highest grape prices. The style is ripe and powerful, with blackcurrant, cassis, chocolate and often new French oak, and alcohol of 14.5% or more.

steps.title: The Judgment of Paris
steps.body: In 1976, British merchant Steven Spurrier organised a blind tasting in Paris. French judges ranked a 1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet ahead of top Bordeaux, including Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion. The result made headlines and showed the world that California could rival France.

steps.prompt: Which wine won the red section of the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
options: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.explanation: The 1973 Stag's Leap Cabernet topped the red wines, ahead of famous Bordeaux.

steps.title: Other New World styles
steps.body: Chile's Maipo makes ripe Cabernet with a minty, herbal note, often good value. Coonawarra, in Australia, on terra rossa soil, gives elegant wines with mint and eucalyptus. Margaret River has a Bordeaux-like, maritime style. Washington State gives ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Stellenbosch blends power with freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet note.
steps.explanation: Each New World region has its own Cabernet accent.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Napa makes ripe, powerful, expensive Cabernet
The 1976 Judgment of Paris put California on the map
Maipo, Coonawarra, Margaret River and Washington add their own styles

steps.title: Red meat
steps.body: Cabernet's firm tannin and dark fruit call for red meat: steak, roast beef, lamb. Fat and protein soften the tannin. Peppercorn sauce and mushrooms go well. Hard aged cheeses like Comté or aged Cheddar work too. Avoid delicate fish and very spicy food, which make it taste harsh.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Decant young, structured Cabernets for an hour or two. Top Bordeaux and Napa can age 20 to 40 years, gaining cedar, tobacco, leather and earth while tannins soften. Everyday Cabernets are best within three to five years.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon go so well with steak?
options: Fat and protein soften its tannin
steps.explanation: Tannin binds to protein and fat, so each softens the other.

steps.body: Old Bordeaux and Napa throw sediment. Stand the bottle upright for a day before opening, then decant slowly in front of a light.

steps.prompt: Which aromas develop in Cabernet as it ages?
steps.explanation: Green apple is a young white wine aroma.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet suits steak, lamb and aged cheese
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees and decant young wines
Top examples age 20 to 40 years

steps.prompt: Which grapes are Cabernet Sauvignon's parents?
steps.explanation: DNA confirmed this in 1996.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its role in Cabernet's story.
steps.explanation: Cabernet is truly international.

steps.prompt: Sunlight on the bunches helps lower pyrazine levels.
steps.explanation: Yes. Pyrazines break down as grapes ripen, especially when exposed to light.

steps.prompt: Which describe Cabernet Sauvignon?
steps.explanation: Cabernet ripens late, not early.

steps.prompt: Left Bank Bordeaux soils are mainly ____.
steps.explanation: Gravel drains and stores heat, helping Cabernet ripen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet gives blackcurrant, cedar, firm tannin and acidity
Bordeaux's Left Bank is its model; Napa its New World star
Pyrazines give green notes when it's not fully ripe
It suits red meat and can age for decades

modules.title: Mourvèdre
modules.description: Also called Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in Australia. A sun-loving grape of dark fruit, game and herbs.

steps.title: Dark and savoury
steps.body: Mourvèdre gives deep-coloured wines with blackberry and plum, plus savoury notes of game, leather, black pepper and the wild herbs of the Mediterranean garrigue. Tannins are high and firm; acidity is moderate. Young, it can be reductive and closed; with age, it opens into meaty, earthy complexity.

steps.title: Spanish origins
steps.body: Mourvèdre comes from Spain, where it's called Monastrell, probably from the region of Valencia or Murcia. In France the name may come from Murviedro, near Valencia. In Australia and California it's often called Mataro, after the town of Mataró near Barcelona. It needs lots of heat and ripens very late.
steps.highlight: Monastrell in Spain, Mataro in Australia

steps.prompt: Match each name to where it's used.
steps.explanation: One grape, three names, all pointing back to eastern Spain.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep colour, dark fruit with a gamey, meaty or herbal edge, and firm tannin. In blends, it adds structure and savouriness. A young Mourvèdre may smell slightly reductive, of struck match or rubber, which usually fades with air. It's often described as the head on its feet and tail in the sun, needing heat but some moisture.

steps.prompt: Mourvèdre ripens early, so it suits cool climates.
steps.explanation: Not true. It ripens very late and needs a hot, sunny climate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mourvèdre gives dark fruit, game and garrigue
It comes from Spain as Monastrell; Australia calls it Mataro
It needs heat and ripens very late

steps.title: Main regions
steps.body: Spain has the most, mainly in Jumilla, Yecla, Alicante and Valencia, as Monastrell. In France, it's the star of Bandol in Provence and a partner in the southern Rhône and Languedoc. Australia grows it in the Barossa and McLaren Vale; California in Contra Costa and Paso Robles.

steps.title: Blending
steps.body: Mourvèdre is the M in GSM blends, with Grenache and Syrah. Grenache brings red fruit and alcohol, Syrah colour and spice, Mourvèdre tannin, dark fruit and a savoury frame that helps the blend age. In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, some estates use a high share, like Château de Beaucastel.

steps.prompt: What does Mourvèdre bring to a GSM blend?
steps.explanation: Mourvèdre adds structure and savoury depth; Grenache brings red fruit.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Mourvèdre needs a long, hot season, often harvested in October. It likes sea breezes and some water near the roots, which is why coastal Bandol suits it. It's drought-tolerant once established, and resists oxidation in winemaking. On its own roots in sandy soils, it survives in parts of Spain.

steps.prompt: Which describe Mourvèdre's needs?
steps.explanation: In cool, short seasons it won't ripen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spain grows the most, as Monastrell
Mourvèdre is the M in GSM, adding structure
It needs heat, a long season and likes the sea

steps.title: Terraces by the sea
steps.body: Bandol lies on the Mediterranean coast of Provence, between Marseille and Toulon. Vineyards climb an amphitheatre of terraces, called restanques, facing south to the sea. Hot, sunny days and sea breezes ripen Mourvèdre fully. Limestone and sandy marl soils keep the vines healthy.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Bandol red must be at least 50% Mourvèdre, with Grenache and Cinsault, and age at least 18 months in oak before release. Most top producers use 75 to 95% Mourvèdre. The wines are dark, structured, gamey and herbal, and can age 20 years or more.
steps.highlight: At least 50% Mourvèdre, 18 months in oak

steps.prompt: Bandol red must age at least ____ months in oak.
steps.explanation: Eighteen months in wood softens Mourvèdre's firm tannins.

steps.title: Rosé and white
steps.body: Bandol's rosé is among Provence's most serious: more structured than most, often with Mourvèdre at its core, and able to age a few years. The small amount of white wine uses Clairette, Ugni Blanc and Bourboulenc. Domaine Tempier, a family estate, helped define Bandol's modern reputation.

steps.prompt: Bandol rosé is often more structured than typical Provence rosé.
steps.explanation: Yes. Mourvèdre gives it more body and ageing potential.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bandol's terraces face the sea, ripening Mourvèdre fully
Reds need at least 50% Mourvèdre and 18 months in oak
Bandol rosé is structured and can age

lessons.title: Monastrell in Spain
lessons.subtitle: Power in the south-east
objectives: Explain how heat and drought shape it

steps.title: Jumilla, Yecla, Alicante
steps.body: In Spain, Monastrell dominates the hot, dry south-east. Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are its main DOs. Vineyards sit at 400 to 800 m on poor, limestone soils, often as old bush vines, many ungrafted because phylloxera struggles in sandy soils. Rainfall is low, often 300 mm a year.
steps.highlight: Old bush vines in the dry south-east

steps.title: Heat and drought
steps.body: The heat gives ripe, dark fruit and high alcohol, often 14.5 to 15.5%. Drought keeps berries small and concentrated. Altitude brings cooler nights, preserving some freshness. Once known for bulk wines, these regions now make concentrated reds at good prices, and some powerful, oaked premium wines.

steps.prompt: Why are many Monastrell vines in south-east Spain ungrafted?
steps.explanation: Sandy soils make it hard for phylloxera to move, so some old vines grow on their own roots.

steps.title: Sweet Fondillón
steps.body: Alicante also makes Fondillón, a historic sweet wine from overripe Monastrell, fermented naturally and aged for at least 10 years in old casks, often in a solera.
