It reaches 16 to 18% alcohol without fortification. It was famous in the 17th and 18th centuries and is now a protected rarity.

steps.prompt: Match each Spanish term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: South-east Spain is Monastrell's home ground.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are Monastrell's heartland
Heat and drought give ripe, dark, powerful reds
Fondillón is Alicante's historic aged sweet wine

steps.title: Game and herbs
steps.body: Mourvèdre's gamey, herbal style suits Provençal and Mediterranean food: lamb with rosemary, beef daube, game, wild boar, grilled sausages. Bandol rosé is a classic with bouillabaisse, Marseille's fish stew. Spanish Monastrell suits roast lamb, chorizo and hearty stews.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees. Young Bandol can be closed and reductive; decant it for an hour or two. Good Bandol ages 15 to 25 years, gaining leather, truffle and dried herbs. Most Spanish Monastrell is best within five years; premium examples age longer.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a classic partner for Bandol rosé?
steps.explanation: Bandol rosé's structure suits the rich, saffron-scented fish stew of Marseille.

steps.body: If a young Mourvèdre smells of struck match, give it time in a decanter. That reductive note usually fades, revealing fruit and herbs.

steps.prompt: Good Bandol red can age for 15 to 25 years.
steps.explanation: Yes. Mourvèdre's tannin and resistance to oxidation help it age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mourvèdre suits lamb, game and Provençal dishes
Decant young Bandol; serve at 16 to 18 degrees
Good Bandol ages 15 to 25 years

steps.prompt: Match each name or place to Mourvèdre.
steps.explanation: One grape with many names and homes.

steps.prompt: What must Bandol red contain?
steps.explanation: At least 50% Mourvèdre, and top producers use much more.

steps.prompt: Mourvèdre ripens early and suits cool regions.
steps.explanation: Not true. It needs heat and ripens very late.

steps.prompt: Which aromas are typical of Mourvèdre?
steps.explanation: Passion fruit belongs to Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.prompt: In GSM blends, the M stands for ____.
steps.explanation: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mourvèdre is dark, gamey, herbal and firm
It's Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in Australia
Bandol is its finest French expression
It loves heat and suits Mediterranean food

modules.title: Aglianico
modules.description: Southern Italy's great red: late-ripening, tannic and acidic, grown on volcanic hills in Campania and Basilicata.

steps.title: Firm and dark
steps.body: Aglianico gives deep-coloured wines with high tannin and high acidity, a rare combination in a southern grape. Aromas include black cherry, plum, leather, tar, smoke and dried herbs. Its power and ageing potential have earned it the nickname the Barolo of the south.

steps.title: Ancient roots
steps.body: Aglianico has grown in southern Italy for centuries. Its name was once linked to Hellenic, suggesting a Greek origin, but DNA hasn't confirmed this, and the name may come from a Spanish-era word. It ripens very late, often in November, which lets it keep acidity even in a warm region.

steps.prompt: Why does Aglianico keep high acidity in the warm south of Italy?
options: It ripens very late, in cooler autumn weather, often at altitude
steps.explanation: Late ripening at altitude, into cool autumn nights, preserves acidity.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In the glass, Aglianico is dark ruby. On the nose, black cherry, plum, smoke and earth. On the palate, firm, sometimes rustic tannins, bright acidity and a long finish. Young wines can be severe; age brings leather, tobacco and dried fruit.

steps.prompt: Which aromas are typical of Aglianico?
steps.explanation: Lychee is typical of Gewürztraminer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico combines high tannin and high acidity
It ripens very late, keeping freshness in the south
It's called the Barolo of the south for its power and age

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Campania and Basilicata
objectives: Explain the role of volcanic soils

steps.title: Two regions
steps.body: Aglianico grows mainly in Campania, around Naples and inland in Irpinia, and in Basilicata, on the slopes of Monte Vulture. Smaller amounts grow in Puglia and Molise. There are some plantings in Australia and California, but it remains overwhelmingly Italian.

steps.title: Volcanoes and height
steps.body: Both key areas are volcanic: Irpinia has volcanic ash over clay and limestone; Vulture is an extinct volcano. Volcanic soils drain well and give a smoky, mineral edge. Altitude, often 400 to 700 m, gives cool nights. Together they explain how a late grape ripens slowly and keeps freshness.

steps.prompt: Monte Vulture, in Basilicata, is an extinct volcano.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its volcanic slopes give Aglianico del Vulture its character.

steps.body: Look for Aglianico from Campania labelled Irpinia or Taburno. They're often cheaper than Taurasi and show the grape's character well.

steps.prompt: What do volcanic soils give Aglianico?
options: Good drainage and a smoky edge
steps.explanation: Volcanic soils drain well and are often linked to smoky, mineral notes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico grows mainly in Campania and Basilicata
Volcanic soils drain well and add a smoky edge
Altitude gives cool nights for slow ripening

steps.title: Taurasi
steps.body: Taurasi, in Irpinia, Campania, became Southern Italy's first DOCG in 1993. It must be at least 85% Aglianico and age at least three years, one in wood; Riserva needs four years, 18 months in wood. The wines are powerful, tannic and long-lived, with black fruit, tar and earth. Mastroberardino kept the tradition alive after the war.

steps.title: Aglianico del Vulture
steps.body: On Monte Vulture in Basilicata, vineyards sit at 200 to 800 m on volcanic tuff. Aglianico del Vulture is the DOC; Aglianico del Vulture Superiore became DOCG in 2010, with longer ageing. The style is often slightly fresher and more mineral than Taurasi, with the same firm structure.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its region.
steps.explanation: Aglianico's great wines come from inland hills.

steps.title: Comparing them
steps.body: Both are serious, age-worthy wines. Taurasi is often fuller and more powerful, with more oak influence. Vulture can be leaner and more mineral, with high acidity. Both benefit from 10 years or more in bottle and are best decanted when young.

steps.prompt: Taurasi became southern Italy's first ____ in 1993.
steps.explanation: Taurasi was the first DOCG of Italy's south.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Taurasi is Campania's DOCG Aglianico, powerful and long-lived
Aglianico del Vulture grows on an extinct volcano
Both need years in bottle and suit decanting

steps.title: Rich, savoury food
steps.body: Aglianico's tannin and acidity suit rich, savoury dishes: slow-cooked ragù, braised lamb, roast pork, sausages and hard cheeses like aged pecorino. Its acidity also handles tomato-based sauces. Avoid delicate fish or very sweet sauces.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Young Taurasi and Vulture are firm and benefit from decanting for two hours. Good examples age 15 to 25 years, softening into leather, tobacco and dried cherry. Lighter Campania Aglianico is drinkable after two or three years.

steps.prompt: Why does Aglianico suit tomato-based sauces?
options: Its high acidity matches the tomato's acidity
steps.explanation: Acidic food needs a wine with at least as much acidity.

steps.body: Pair a mature Taurasi with a Neapolitan ragù simmered for hours. It's a regional match that's lasted generations.

steps.prompt: Young Taurasi is best drunk immediately without decanting.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its firm tannins benefit from air and, ideally, years in bottle.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico suits ragù, lamb and aged pecorino
Its acidity handles tomato sauces
Decant young wines; the best age 15 to 25 years

steps.prompt: Which combination makes Aglianico distinctive?
steps.explanation: It's rare for a southern red to keep such high acidity.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Aglianico.
steps.explanation: Aglianico's story is volcanic and late-ripening.

steps.prompt: Aglianico is grown mainly in northern Italy.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its heartland is Campania and Basilicata, in the south.

steps.prompt: Which help Aglianico keep freshness?
steps.explanation: Hot nights would burn off acidity.

steps.prompt: Aglianico is nicknamed the ____ of the south.
steps.explanation: For its structure, acidity and ageing potential, like Nebbiolo's Barolo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico is tannic, acidic and late-ripening
Campania's Taurasi and Basilicata's Vulture are its great wines
Volcanic soils and altitude shape its style
It ages well and suits rich, savoury food

modules.title: Pinotage
modules.description: South Africa's own grape, a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, in styles from fruity to smoky and serious.

steps.title: Dark and fruity
steps.body: Pinotage gives deep-coloured wines with red and black fruit: plum, mulberry, cherry and blackberry. Many show smoky, earthy notes, and some a hint of banana or coffee. It's medium to full-bodied, with medium tannin and fairly high alcohol. It is uniquely South African.

steps.title: A deliberate cross
steps.body: In 1925, Professor Abraham Perold, at Stellenbosch University, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsault, then called Hermitage in South Africa, hence the name. He hoped to combine Pinot's quality with Cinsault's robustness and yield. The first commercial wine was released in 1961. It inherited Cinsault's vigour and Pinot's red fruit.

steps.prompt: Why is it called Pinotage?
options: It's a type of Pinot Noir
Cinsault was called Hermitage in South Africa
steps.explanation: Pinot plus Hermitage, the local name for Cinsault, gave Pinotage.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep colour and ripe dark fruit with a smoky or earthy edge. Some styles show a sweet, coffee or chocolate note, from heavily toasted oak. Poorly made examples can show acetone or burnt rubber, from volatile compounds, which gave it a bad reputation in the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Pinotage was created by crossing Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its parents are Pinot Noir and Cinsault.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage gives plum, mulberry and smoky notes
It's a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault
It's South Africa's unique grape

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: The Cape's own grape
objectives: Explain how it suits the Cape
Name other countries that grow it

steps.title: The Cape
steps.body: Pinotage is about 7% of South Africa's vineyards. Stellenbosch is its heartland, with Paarl, Swartland and Malmesbury also important. Bush vines on dryland, without irrigation, are valued for concentration. Old Pinotage vineyards, some from the 1950s, are now prized.

steps.title: Suited to the Cape
steps.body: Pinotage buds and ripens early, accumulating sugar fast. That's useful in warm Cape summers, but growers must pick carefully to avoid jammy fruit and high alcohol. It's vigorous and productive, so yields need control. Its thick skins give colour and resist rot.

steps.prompt: Which describe Pinotage in the vineyard?
steps.explanation: Pinotage accumulates sugar quickly, often reaching high alcohol.

steps.body: Look for Pinotage from old bush vines in Stellenbosch or Swartland. They often show more depth and less of the burnt rubber note that hurt the grape's reputation.

steps.prompt: Where else is Pinotage grown, in small amounts?
steps.explanation: Small plantings exist in New Zealand, the US, Germany and Zimbabwe, but South Africa dominates.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Stellenbosch is Pinotage's heartland
It ripens early and needs yield control
Small plantings exist abroad, but it's essentially South African

steps.title: Many styles
steps.body: Pinotage is made in several styles. Light and fruity, for early drinking. Coffee Pinotage, a 2000s trend, aged with heavily toasted oak for mocha and chocolate notes. Serious, structured wines from old vines, aged in French oak. And rosé, even sparkling and fortified versions.

steps.title: Reputation
steps.body: In the 1990s, critics complained of acetone and burnt rubber smells in some Pinotage. Research linked these to isoamyl acetate and to fermentation at high temperatures, stressed yeast and over-extraction. Better vineyard work, cooler fermentations and gentle handling have greatly improved quality.

steps.prompt: What caused the acetone notes in some 1990s Pinotage?
steps.explanation: High fermentation temperatures and stressed yeast created volatile compounds; modern winemaking avoids them.

steps.title: The Cape blend
steps.body: A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of Pinotage, usually 30 to 70%, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Shiraz. It gives South Africa a distinctive blend of its own, combining Pinotage's fruit with Bordeaux grapes' structure. Many Stellenbosch estates make one.
steps.highlight: Cape blend: Pinotage plus Bordeaux grapes

steps.prompt: A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of ____.
steps.explanation: Pinotage gives Cape blends their South African identity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage ranges from light and fruity to serious and oaked
Old faults came from winemaking, now largely fixed
Cape blends combine Pinotage with Bordeaux grapes

steps.title: The braai
steps.body: In South Africa, Pinotage is the wine of the braai, the national barbecue: sausages, called boerewors, lamb chops and steak. Its smoky, fruity side suits charred meat and spicy sauces. It also goes with bobotie, a lightly spiced Cape Malay minced meat dish.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 17 degrees; fruity styles can be slightly cooler. Most Pinotage is best within five years. Old-vine, structured examples can age 10 to 15 years, gaining earthy, savoury notes. Rosé Pinotage is best young and chilled.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a classic South African partner for Pinotage?
steps.explanation: Smoky grilled sausage suits Pinotage's fruit and smoke.

steps.body: Coffee-style Pinotage is a fun match for barbecue ribs with a sweet, smoky glaze. Its mocha notes echo the char.

steps.prompt: Most Pinotage is made for long ageing of 20 years or more.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most is best within five years; only top examples age 10 to 15 years.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage suits the braai and bobotie
Serve at 15 to 17 degrees
Most is best young; old-vine wines age 10 to 15 years

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Pinotage.
steps.explanation: Pinotage's story is South African from start to finish.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are Pinotage's parents?
steps.explanation: Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsault.

steps.prompt: A Cape blend contains a significant share of Pinotage.
steps.explanation: Yes. Usually 30 to 70%, blended with Bordeaux grapes or Shiraz.

steps.prompt: Which styles of Pinotage exist?
steps.explanation: Pinotage is a black grape; it doesn't make botrytised white wine.

steps.prompt: Pinotage's heartland region is ____.
steps.explanation: Stellenbosch is home to the university where it was created, and its main region.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage is South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault
It ranges from fruity to serious and oaked
Better winemaking fixed old faults
It's the wine of the braai

modules.title: Carmenère
modules.description: A forgotten Bordeaux grape, rediscovered in Chile in 1994, with dark fruit, spice and a hint of green pepper.

steps.title: Soft and spicy
steps.body: Carmenère gives deep purple-red wines with blackberry, plum and red pepper, plus spice, paprika, tobacco and sometimes chocolate. Tannins are soft and acidity moderate, so it feels round and smooth. When not fully ripe, it shows a strong green pepper note.

steps.title: Crimson leaves
steps.body: Its name comes from carmin, the French for crimson, because its leaves turn bright red in autumn before falling. Carmenère is part of the Cabernet family; DNA shows it's a cross of Cabernet Franc and Gros Cabernet. Like its relatives, it has methoxypyrazines, which give green notes when grapes aren't fully ripe.

steps.prompt: Where does Carmenère's name come from?
options: The crimson colour of its autumn leaves
steps.explanation: Carmin means crimson; the leaves turn red in autumn.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Carmenère is deep coloured with a purple rim. On the nose, ripe plum and blackberry with a distinctive spicy, green or red pepper note. On the palate, it's smoother and softer than Cabernet Sauvignon, with less grip. That combination of soft tannin and peppery spice is the clue.

steps.prompt: Carmenère usually has firmer tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Carmenère is softer and rounder, with gentler tannins.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère gives plum, spice and a peppery note
Its name comes from its crimson autumn leaves
It's softer than Cabernet, with a green edge when unripe

steps.title: A Bordeaux grape
steps.body: Carmenère was once widely planted in Bordeaux, especially in the Médoc, and valued for its colour. But it suffered from coulure, poor fruit set in cool, wet springs, giving low and irregular yields. After phylloxera destroyed Bordeaux's vineyards in the late 19th century, growers didn't replant it. It almost vanished from France.

steps.title: Chile today
steps.body: In the mid-19th century, Chilean growers brought Bordeaux cuttings, including Carmenère, before phylloxera struck. Chile's dry, warm climate suited it better than Bordeaux's. Today Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère, around 10,000 hectares, especially in Colchagua, Cachapoal, Maipo and Peumo.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Carmenère role.
steps.explanation: Carmenère's map shifted from France to Chile.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Small plantings remain in Bordeaux, and some were rediscovered in northern Italy, where they had been mistaken for Cabernet Franc. China also grows a grape called Cabernet Gernischt, now thought to be Carmenère. Some is planted in California and Washington.

steps.prompt: Why did Carmenère almost disappear from Bordeaux?
options: Poor fruit set and phylloxera led growers not to replant it
steps.explanation: Coulure made yields unreliable, so after phylloxera growers replanted other grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère was a Bordeaux grape, lost after phylloxera
Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère
Small plantings survive in Italy, China and Bordeaux

lessons.title: The lost grape of Bordeaux
lessons.subtitle: Rediscovery in Chile
objectives: Explain why it was confused with Merlot
Explain how this changed Chilean wine

steps.title: Mistaken identity
steps.body: For over a century, Chilean growers thought much of their Merlot was Merlot. Vineyards often mixed the two. The wines tasted different, and some vines ripened weeks later. In 1994, French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot, studying vine leaves and shapes, identified many of these vines as Carmenère.

steps.title: Why the confusion
steps.body: Carmenère and Merlot have similar leaves and bunches. But Carmenère ripens two to three weeks later. When the two were picked together, the Carmenère was often unripe, giving the green, vegetal notes that marked some Chilean Merlot. Separating them improved both wines.

steps.prompt: Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile in ____.
steps.explanation: Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it in 1994.

steps.title: A new identity
steps.body: Chile adopted Carmenère as its signature grape. Producers learned to pick it later, manage the canopy to expose bunches to sun and reduce pyrazines, and lower yields. In 1998, Chile officially recognised it. Today many premium Chilean wines are Carmenère or blends with Cabernet Sauvignon.

steps.prompt: How do Chilean producers avoid green notes in Carmenère?
steps.explanation: Picking with Merlot, earlier, caused the green notes in the first place.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chile's Merlot was often Carmenère, identified in 1994
Carmenère ripens later, so early picking gave green notes
Chile adopted it as its signature grape

steps.title: Spice and grill
steps.body: Carmenère's soft tannins and peppery spice suit grilled meat, roast pork, spicy sausages and dishes with paprika, cumin or roasted peppers. It handles mild spice better than tannic reds. In Chile, it goes with empanadas and pastel de choclo, a corn and beef pie.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Most Carmenère is best within five years, when fruit is fresh. Top examples from Peumo or Apalta, often blended with Cabernet, age 10 years or more. Decanting helps young, oaked examples.

steps.prompt: Why does Carmenère handle mildly spicy dishes well?
options: Its soft tannins clash less with spice
steps.explanation: Firm tannins clash with chilli; Carmenère's soft tannins are more forgiving.

steps.body: Try Carmenère with roasted red peppers or a dish with smoked paprika. The wine's own pepper and spice notes come forward.

steps.prompt: Most Carmenère is made to age for decades.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most is best within five years; only top examples age longer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère suits grilled meat, peppers and mild spice
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees
Most is best within five years

steps.prompt: Who identified Carmenère in Chile in 1994?
steps.explanation: Boursiquot, a French ampelographer, recognised it in vineyards thought to be Merlot.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Carmenère.
steps.explanation: Its history is one of loss and rediscovery.

steps.prompt: Chile grows most of the world's Carmenère.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 95%.

steps.prompt: Which describe Carmenère?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is moderate.

steps.prompt: Carmenère belongs to the ____ family of grapes.
steps.explanation: It's related to Cabernet Franc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère is soft, plummy and peppery
It vanished from Bordeaux after phylloxera
Chile rediscovered it in 1994 and made it its own
It suits grilled meat and mild spice

modules.title: Montepulciano
modules.description: Central Italy's generous red grape, deep in colour and soft in tannin, from Abruzzo to the Marche.

lessons.title: Meet Montepulciano
lessons.subtitle: Deep colour, soft heart
objectives: Avoid the confusion with the Tuscan town

steps.title: Generous and dark
steps.body: Montepulciano gives deep-coloured reds with ripe black cherry, plum, blackberry and dried herbs, sometimes liquorice. Tannins are plentiful but soft and ripe, acidity moderate. It's one of Italy's most planted red grapes and often offers good value.
steps.highlight: Black cherry, soft tannin, deep colour

steps.title: Not the town
steps.body: Montepulciano the grape has nothing to do with Montepulciano the Tuscan town, which makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano from Sangiovese. The grape is grown mainly on the Adriatic side of central Italy. The confusion is so common that it's worth remembering: grape plus region, as in Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.
steps.highlight: Grape in Abruzzo; town in Tuscany

steps.prompt: What is Vino Nobile di Montepulciano made from?
steps.explanation: Vino Nobile is a Tuscan wine made mainly from Sangiovese, named after the town.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep purple-ruby colour, ripe dark fruit and a soft, round texture with plenty of gentle tannin. It's less acidic than Sangiovese, rounder than Aglianico. A slightly bitter, herbal finish is common.

steps.prompt: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is made in the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's made from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo, on the Adriatic coast.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Montepulciano gives deep, ripe, soft reds
The grape is unrelated to the Tuscan town
It's rounder and less acidic than Sangiovese

steps.title: Abruzzo and the Marche
steps.body: Montepulciano dominates Abruzzo, between the Apennines and the Adriatic. It's also important in the Marche, Molise and Puglia. In Abruzzo, the hills between mountains and sea give warm days and cool breezes. Vines are often trained on high pergolas, called tendone, which shade the fruit.

steps.title: Late and warm
steps.body: Montepulciano ripens late and needs warmth; in cooler years it can taste green and harsh. That's why it's rarely grown further north. Its thick skins give deep colour and resist disease. High yields are possible, so quality depends on controlling them.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its region.
steps.explanation: Montepulciano anchors the Adriatic side of central Italy.

steps.body: In Abruzzo, look for Colline Teramane, a DOCG zone in the north of the region, for more structured Montepulciano.

steps.prompt: Why is Montepulciano rarely grown in northern Italy?
options: It ripens late and needs warmth
steps.explanation: Cool climates leave it unripe and harsh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Montepulciano dominates Abruzzo and the Marche
It ripens late and needs warmth
Yield control decides quality

lessons.title: Abruzzo and Conero
lessons.subtitle: Montepulciano's best wines
objectives: Describe Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and its DOCG

steps.title: Abruzzo
steps.body: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC is huge, from cheap and cheerful to serious. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane became DOCG in 2003, requiring at least 90% Montepulciano and longer ageing. Producers like Valentini and Emidio Pepe have shown how long-lived it can be.

steps.title: Conero
steps.body: Monte Conero is a limestone headland on the Adriatic, near Ancona in the Marche. Rosso Cònero DOC must be at least 85% Montepulciano. Conero DOCG, the Riserva, since 2004, requires two years of ageing. Sea breezes and limestone give structured, fresh, dark wines.

steps.prompt: Which wines are based on Montepulciano?
steps.explanation: Vino Nobile is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town.

steps.title: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
steps.body: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep cherry-pink rosé from Montepulciano, its own DOC since 2010. Cerasuolo means cherry-like. Short skin contact with this deeply coloured grape gives a darker, fuller rosé than most, with cherry, strawberry and a savoury edge.

steps.prompt: What does Cerasuolo mean?
steps.explanation: Its deep cherry colour gives Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo its name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Colline Teramane is Abruzzo's DOCG Montepulciano
Conero, by the sea, makes structured Montepulciano
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep cherry rosé

steps.title: Everyday food
steps.body: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a classic pizza and pasta wine: its soft tannins and dark fruit suit tomato sauce, sausages and grilled meat. In Abruzzo, it goes with arrosticini, lamb skewers. Cerasuolo suits fish soups, charcuterie and summer food.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; Cerasuolo chilled at 10 to 12. Simple Montepulciano is best within three years. Colline Teramane and Conero Riserva age 10 to 15 years; some traditional producers' wines last decades.
steps.highlight: Simple wines young; the best for decades

steps.prompt: Which dish is a classic Abruzzo partner for Montepulciano?
steps.explanation: Grilled lamb skewers are Abruzzo's traditional match.

steps.body: An everyday Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is one of Italy's best-value reds for pizza night.

steps.prompt: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is best served chilled.
steps.explanation: Yes. As a rosé, it's served at 10 to 12 degrees.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Montepulciano suits pizza, pasta and grilled lamb
Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees and Cerasuolo chilled
Top wines age 10 to 15 years or more

steps.prompt: Where is Montepulciano the grape mainly grown?
steps.explanation: The Adriatic side of central Italy.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its description.
steps.explanation: Only the first three are Montepulciano.

steps.prompt: Montepulciano has soft, ripe tannins.
steps.explanation: Yes. That gives it a round, generous feel.

steps.prompt: Which are true of Montepulciano?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is moderate.

steps.prompt: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane became DOCG in ____.
steps.explanation: 2003, with stricter rules.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Montepulciano is deep, ripe and soft
It's unrelated to the Tuscan town
Abruzzo and Conero make its best wines
It's an excellent everyday food wine

modules.title: Nero d'Avola
modules.description: Also called Calabrese. Sicily's signature red: dark, ripe and juicy, with fresh acidity.

lessons.title: Meet Nero d'Avola
lessons.subtitle: Sicily's black grape
objectives: Describe Nero d'Avola's flavours and structure

steps.title: Dark and juicy
steps.body: Nero d'Avola means the black of Avola, a town in south-east Sicily. It gives deeply coloured wines with black cherry, plum, mulberry and sometimes chocolate and liquorice. Tannins are moderate and soft; acidity is surprisingly fresh for a hot-climate grape. It's Sicily's most planted red.

steps.title: Why it stays fresh
steps.body: Nero d'Avola keeps good natural acidity even in Sicily's heat, partly because of its genetics and partly because the best vineyards benefit from sea breezes and altitude. It's also called Calabrese, a name that may mean it came from Calabria, or from an old Sicilian dialect word. It was once shipped north to deepen paler wines.

steps.prompt: What does Nero d'Avola mean?
steps.explanation: Avola is a town in south-east Sicily, the grape's historic home.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In the glass, look for deep ruby-purple colour, ripe dark fruit, and a juicy, fresh palate with soft tannins. Unoaked versions are fruity and bright; oaked ones show vanilla and spice. The juiciness and freshness, despite the ripe fruit, are the clue.

steps.prompt: Nero d'Avola was once shipped north to add colour to paler wines.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its deep colour made it a popular blending wine before it became known in its own right.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola gives dark, ripe fruit with fresh acidity
Its name means the black of Avola; it's also called Calabrese
It's Sicily's most planted red grape

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Across Sicily
objectives: Explain how Sicily's climate shapes it

steps.title: South-east and beyond
steps.body: Nero d'Avola grows all over Sicily, but the south-east, around Avola, Noto, Pachino and Vittoria, is its historic home. Limestone and sandy soils there give fresher, more elegant wines. Inland and western areas produce riper, fuller styles. It's also planted in Australia and California in small amounts.

steps.title: Sicilian climate
steps.body: Sicily is hot and dry, with sea breezes and altitude moderating it. Bush vines, called alberello, are traditional, shading the fruit. Many growers now use trellises. Nero d'Avola needs heat but can lose freshness in the hottest sites, so coastal and hillside vineyards are valued.

steps.prompt: Match each Sicilian wine to its grapes.
steps.explanation: Nero d'Avola is found across Sicily, but not on Etna.

steps.title: Cerasuolo di Vittoria
steps.body: Sicily's only DOCG, Cerasuolo di Vittoria, blends 50 to 70% Nero d'Avola with Frappato. Nero gives structure and colour; Frappato gives perfume and lightness. The result is a bright, cherry-scented red, lighter than many Sicilian reds. Cerasuolo here means cherry-red.

steps.prompt: Cerasuolo di Vittoria blends Nero d'Avola with ____.
steps.explanation: Frappato adds perfume and lightness to Nero d'Avola's depth.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola's historic home is south-east Sicily
Sea breezes and hills keep it fresh
Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Sicily's only DOCG, blends it with Frappato

steps.title: Sicilian food
steps.body: Nero d'Avola's juicy fruit and fresh acidity suit tomato-based pasta, pizza, grilled sausages and lamb. In Sicily, it goes with pasta alla Norma, made with aubergine, tomato and ricotta salata. Its soft tannins work with tuna or swordfish steaks too.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 17 degrees. Most Nero d'Avola is best within three to five years, when fruit is bright. Oaked, concentrated versions from top sites age 10 years or more. Cerasuolo di Vittoria can be served slightly cooler.

steps.prompt: Why can Nero d'Avola work with tuna or swordfish?
options: Its soft tannins don't clash with meaty fish
steps.explanation: Soft tannins won't make firm fish taste metallic.

steps.body: Try a lightly chilled Cerasuolo di Vittoria in summer. Its cherry fruit and freshness work like a light red or a serious rosé.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Nero d'Avola?
steps.explanation: Sorbet would make the wine taste sour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola suits tomato pasta, pizza and meaty fish
Serve at 15 to 17 degrees
Most is best within five years

steps.prompt: Where is Nero d'Avola's historic home?
steps.explanation: Around Avola, Noto and Pachino.

steps.prompt: Nero d'Avola is the main grape of Etna Rosso.
steps.explanation: Not true. Etna Rosso is made from Nerello Mascalese.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Nero d'Avola.
steps.explanation: Nero d'Avola is deeply Sicilian.

steps.prompt: Which describe Nero d'Avola?
steps.explanation: It's dark, not pale.

steps.prompt: Sicily's only DOCG is Cerasuolo di ____.
steps.explanation: Cerasuolo di Vittoria blends Nero d'Avola with Frappato.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola is dark, juicy and fresh
It's Sicily's most planted red
Cerasuolo di Vittoria blends it with Frappato
It suits Sicilian pasta, pizza and grilled fish

modules.title: Zinfandel
modules.description: Also called Primitivo in Italy and Tribidrag in Croatia. Ripe bramble fruit, high alcohol and a long American story.

steps.title: Ripe and jammy
steps.body: Zinfandel gives ripe, often jammy wines with blackberry, raspberry, bramble, black pepper and sweet spice, sometimes dried fruit. Alcohol is often high, 14.5 to 16%. Tannins are moderate, acidity medium. The style can range from light rosé to rich, powerful reds and sweet wines.

steps.title: Uneven ripening
steps.body: Zinfandel's bunches ripen unevenly: some berries are still green while others shrivel into raisins. Growers must wait for most to ripen, by which time some are overripe. That raises sugar and alcohol, and gives the mix of fresh and dried fruit flavours. It's also why picking time is so critical.
steps.highlight: Green berries and raisins on one bunch

steps.prompt: Why is Zinfandel often high in alcohol?
options: Uneven ripening means some berries shrivel and concentrate sugar
steps.explanation: Waiting for the green berries to ripen leaves others overripe, raising sugar and alcohol.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium to deep colour, ripe bramble and jammy berry fruit, black pepper and sweet spice, a warm, high-alcohol feel and moderate tannin. A hint of dried fruit or raisin is typical. It's fruitier and less tannic than Cabernet, spicier than Merlot.

steps.prompt: Which are typical of Zinfandel?
steps.explanation: Zinfandel is medium to deep in colour, not pale.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Zinfandel gives ripe bramble fruit, spice and high alcohol
Uneven ripening mixes fresh and raisined berries
It ranges from rosé to rich red and sweet styles

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: California and Puglia
objectives: Name its homes in Italy and Croatia

steps.title: California
steps.body: Zinfandel reached the United States in the 1820s, from an Austrian nursery collection. It spread through California during the Gold Rush and became the state's most widely planted red for decades. Today it's grown in Lodi, Sonoma's Dry Creek Valley, Amador County in the Sierra Foothills, and Paso Robles.

steps.title: Italy and Croatia
steps.body: In Italy it's called Primitivo, grown in Puglia, especially Manduria and Gioia del Colle. Primitivo means early one, because it ripens early. Its origin is Croatia, where it's called Tribidrag or Crljenak Kaštelanski, and today grows in small amounts on the Dalmatian coast.
steps.highlight: Primitivo in Puglia; origin in Croatia

steps.prompt: Match each name to its country.
steps.explanation: One grape with three national identities.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Zinfandel likes warm, sunny climates with dry autumns, which help with its uneven ripening. Cool, damp weather causes rot in its tight bunches. Many of its best wines come from old, head-trained vines, grown without trellises, which give low yields and concentrated fruit.

steps.prompt: What does Primitivo mean?
steps.explanation: Primitivo refers to its early ripening.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Zinfandel is California's heritage red
It's Primitivo in Puglia and Tribidrag in Croatia
It likes warm, dry climates and old head-trained vines

lessons.title: One grape, two names
lessons.subtitle: DNA and identity
objectives: Explain how Zinfandel and Primitivo were linked
Explain how its Croatian origin was found

steps.title: The DNA story
steps.body: For years, Zinfandel was thought to be an American grape. In the 1970s, a professor noticed Primitivo in Puglia looked similar; in 1994, DNA showed they were identical. Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis then searched Croatia; in 2001 she confirmed Crljenak Kaštelanski as the same grape, and later found an older name, Tribidrag, recorded in the 15th century.

steps.title: Labelling
steps.body: Since the EU and the US recognised them as the same, Italian producers can label Primitivo as Zinfandel when exporting to the US, and US producers can call theirs Primitivo. Still, the two are made in different styles: Puglian Primitivo tends to be softer and more rustic; Californian Zinfandel bolder and fruitier.

steps.prompt: Who confirmed Zinfandel's Croatian origin?
steps.explanation: Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis led the DNA research in Croatia.

steps.title: Tribidrag
steps.body: Tribidrag was mentioned in Croatian documents from the 1400s. Phylloxera and neglect almost wiped it out there. Since the DNA discovery, Croatian producers have replanted it on the Dalmatian coast. It's a reminder that wine grapes travel and change names along the way.

steps.prompt: Zinfandel was originally an American grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. DNA shows it came from Croatia, where it was known as Tribidrag.

steps.title: What you learned
points: DNA showed Zinfandel and Primitivo are identical in 1994
Its Croatian origin, Tribidrag, was confirmed in 2001
Labelling rules allow both names, though styles differ

lessons.title: Old vines in California
lessons.subtitle: Heritage vineyards
objectives: Explain why old Zinfandel vines matter

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: Some Californian Zinfandel vineyards date from the 1880s, having survived phylloxera and Prohibition. During Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, Zinfandel was popular with home winemakers, so many vines were kept. Old, head-trained vines give low yields and concentrated, balanced fruit. Lodi and Sonoma have many.

steps.title: Field blends
steps.body: Many old Zinfandel vineyards are field blends: Zinfandel interplanted with Petite Sirah, Carignan, Alicante Bouschet, Mourvèdre and others. Grapes are picked and fermented together. Petite Sirah adds colour and tannin, Carignan acidity. These mixed vineyards reflect how 19th century immigrants planted.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are often found in old Zinfandel field blends?
steps.explanation: Riesling isn't part of these red field blends.

steps.title: Heritage
steps.body: The Historic Vineyard Society, founded in 2011, records Californian vineyards planted at least 50 years ago that still produce. It has helped protect old Zinfandel vineyards from being replanted with more profitable grapes. Producers like Ridge, Turley and Bedrock champion them.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: California's old vines are a living archive.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Many Californian Zinfandel vines date from the 1880s
Old vineyards are often field blends with Petite Sirah and Carignan
The Historic Vineyard Society protects them

steps.title: Barbecue
steps.body: Zinfandel's ripe fruit, spice and alcohol suit barbecue, smoked meats, burgers, sausages and sweet, spicy glazes. Its fruit handles a little sweetness in sauces. Primitivo suits Puglian food: orecchiette with sausage, grilled meats and aged cheeses. Avoid very hot chilli, which clashes with high alcohol.

steps.title: White Zinfandel
steps.body: In 1975, Sutter Home's fermentation stuck, leaving a sweet pink wine. It was sold as White Zinfandel and became the best-selling wine in the US in the 1980s. Its success kept many old Zinfandel vines alive, though it's very different from red Zinfandel.

steps.prompt: How was White Zinfandel born?
options: A stuck fermentation that left sugar
steps.explanation: Sutter Home's 1975 fermentation stopped, leaving a sweet pink wine that became a hit.

steps.body: Serve big, high-alcohol Zinfandel slightly cool, around 16 degrees. A little chill keeps the alcohol from feeling hot.

steps.prompt: White Zinfandel's success helped keep old Zinfandel vines in the ground.
steps.explanation: Yes. Demand for grapes saved many vineyards from being replanted.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Zinfandel suits barbecue and sweet, spicy glazes
White Zinfandel began with a stuck fermentation in 1975
Serve red Zinfandel slightly cool

steps.prompt: Match each name to its place.
steps.explanation: One grape, three identities.

steps.prompt: What makes Zinfandel's ripening tricky?
steps.explanation: Green and raisined berries can sit on the same bunch.

steps.prompt: DNA showed Zinfandel and Primitivo are the same grape.
steps.explanation: Yes, in 1994.

steps.prompt: Which are features of old Californian Zinfandel vineyards?
steps.explanation: Old vineyards are head-trained, not modern trellises.

steps.prompt: White Zinfandel was born from a stuck fermentation in ____.
steps.explanation: At Sutter Home, in 1975.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Zinfandel is ripe, spicy and high in alcohol
It's Primitivo in Italy and came from Croatia
California's old vines and field blends are heritage
It suits barbecue; White Zinfandel is a separate style

modules.title: Merlot
modules.description: Plum, softness and the clay of the Right Bank: the world's second most planted red grape.

steps.title: Soft and plummy
steps.body: Merlot gives medium to full-bodied reds with plum, black cherry, blackberry and, with oak, chocolate and vanilla. Tannins are softer than Cabernet Sauvignon's, acidity medium. It's approachable young and can age well when grown on great sites. It's the second most planted red grape in the world.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Merlot comes from Bordeaux, first recorded in 1784. Its name may come from merle, the French for blackbird, which loves its ripe grapes. DNA shows its parents are Cabernet Franc and Magdeleine Noire des Charentes, so it's a half-sibling of Cabernet Sauvignon. Its large, thinner-skinned berries explain its softer tannins.

steps.prompt: Where may Merlot's name come from?
steps.explanation: Merle means blackbird, a bird that loves its ripe grapes.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium to deep ruby colour, plum and black cherry aromas, and a rounder, softer palate than Cabernet, with less obvious blackcurrant. Cool-climate Merlot can show herbal or green notes; warm-climate Merlot is ripe and fruity, sometimes jammy.

steps.prompt: Merlot has larger berries and thinner skins than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why its tannins are softer and its wines rounder.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot gives plum, black cherry and soft tannins
It comes from Bordeaux; its name may mean blackbird
It's a half-sibling of Cabernet Sauvignon

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Bordeaux and beyond
objectives: Explain why it suits clay and cool soils

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux, about 60% of red plantings. It's important in Italy, especially Tuscany and Friuli, and in Switzerland's Ticino. In the New World it grows in California, Washington, Chile, Australia, South Africa and New Zealand's Hawke's Bay.

steps.title: Early and clay-loving
steps.body: Merlot buds and ripens one to two weeks before Cabernet Sauvignon. On cool, water-retentive clay soils, where Cabernet would struggle to ripen, Merlot thrives. But early budding exposes it to spring frost, and its thinner skins make it prone to rot in wet weather, and to coulure, poor fruit set.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Merlot role.
steps.explanation: Merlot is grown widely, often in Bordeaux-style blends.

steps.body: When a Bordeaux label says Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur, without a famous commune, it's often Merlot-dominated and made to drink early.

steps.prompt: What are Merlot's vulnerabilities in the vineyard?
steps.explanation: Merlot ripens easily; in heat it can overripen, not fail to ripen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape, grown worldwide
It ripens early and loves cool clay soils
Frost, rot and coulure are its weaknesses

steps.title: Pomerol
steps.body: Pomerol is small, about 800 hectares, with no official classification. Its plateau has gravel over clay; the centre has a unique blue clay, rich in smectite, that swells when wet and holds water. Merlot thrives there. Pétrus, almost pure Merlot, grows on this clay. Le Pin and Lafleur are other famous names.

steps.title: Saint-Émilion
steps.body: Saint-Émilion, a UNESCO World Heritage town, has about 5,500 hectares. Its limestone plateau and slopes, the côtes, give elegant, long-lived wines; sandier soils below give softer ones. Merlot leads, with Cabernet Franc often important, as at Cheval Blanc and Ausone.
steps.highlight: Limestone plateau, Merlot and Cabernet Franc

steps.prompt: Which famous Pomerol wine is almost pure Merlot?
steps.explanation: Pétrus grows Merlot on Pomerol's blue clay.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years: Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé. It's controversial and was challenged in court. Cheval Blanc, Ausone and Angélus withdrew from it before the 2022 edition. Pomerol has no classification at all.

steps.prompt: Pomerol has an official classification like the Médoc's.
steps.explanation: Not true. Pomerol has no official classification; reputation alone ranks its wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pomerol's blue clay gives Merlot like Pétrus
Saint-Émilion's limestone gives elegant Merlot and Cabernet Franc
Saint-Émilion's classification is revised; Pomerol has none

steps.title: A boom
steps.body: In the 1990s, Merlot became the fashionable red in the US: soft, fruity and easy to pronounce. Plantings grew fast, often in hot, high-yield sites, giving bland, simple wines. Quality became uneven, and the name grew associated with mass-market wine.

steps.title: Sideways
steps.body: In the 2004 film Sideways, the main character declares he won't drink Merlot. US Merlot sales growth slowed, while Pinot Noir sales rose. Ironically, his treasured bottle is a 1961 Cheval Blanc, a Saint-Émilion with a large share of Merlot alongside Cabernet Franc.

steps.prompt: What wine does the main character of Sideways treasure?
steps.explanation: The irony is that Cheval Blanc contains a large share of Merlot.

steps.title: Great Merlot endures
steps.body: Merlot makes some of the world's most expensive wines: Pétrus, Le Pin, Masseto in Tuscany. Washington State, Hawke's Bay and parts of Chile make excellent, fresh Merlot. Quality depends on site, yield and picking time, like any grape. The backlash was about overproduction, not the grape.

steps.prompt: Which are great Merlot-based wines?
steps.explanation: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot boomed in the 1990s, often overproduced
Sideways, in 2004, hurt its image
Great Merlot, from Pétrus to Masseto, endures

steps.title: Versatile
steps.body: Merlot's soft tannins make it flexible: roast chicken, pork, duck, mushroom dishes, lasagne and medium-rich beef. It handles some umami better than very tannic reds. Lighter styles can even go with salmon or tuna. Avoid very spicy food, which clashes with alcohol.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 18 degrees. Simple Merlot is best within three years. Top Pomerol and Saint-Émilion age 20 to 40 years, gaining truffle, leather and earth. Merlot's softer tannins often make it approachable earlier than Cabernet-based wines of the same quality.

steps.prompt: Why is Merlot flexible with food?
steps.explanation: Soft tannins clash less with a wide range of dishes.

steps.body: An older Pomerol with a mushroom risotto or truffle pasta is a classic match. The earthy, truffle notes of mature Merlot echo the dish.

steps.prompt: Top Pomerol can age for 20 to ____ years.
steps.explanation: Great Pomerol develops truffle and earth over decades.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot pairs widely, from chicken to mushrooms
Serve at 15 to 18 degrees
Top Right Bank wines age for decades

steps.prompt: Why does Merlot suit Pomerol's clay?
options: It ripens early and likes cool, water-retentive soils
steps.explanation: Clay stays cool; early-ripening Merlot still ripens there.

steps.prompt: Match each wine or place to Merlot.
steps.explanation: Merlot makes famous wines in several countries.

steps.prompt: Merlot ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. It ripens one to two weeks earlier.

steps.prompt: Which are Merlot's typical aromas?
steps.explanation: Lime belongs to white wines like Riesling.

steps.prompt: Merlot's name may come from merle, meaning ____.
steps.explanation: Blackbirds love its ripe grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot is plummy, soft and approachable
It's Bordeaux's most planted grape, king of the Right Bank
Its 1990s boom and Sideways hurt its image, not its potential
It's flexible at the table and the best age for decades

modules.title: Dolcetto
modules.description: Piedmont's everyday red: dark, fruity and soft, with a bitter almond finish.

lessons.title: Meet Dolcetto
lessons.subtitle: The little sweet one, made dry

steps.title: Dark and soft
steps.body: Dolcetto is a Piedmont grape giving deep purple wines with black cherry, plum, liquorice and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is low for Piedmont, tannins moderate. It's made to drink young, a daily wine for the Piedmontese while Barolo ages.

steps.title: Why little sweet
steps.body: Dolcetto means little sweet one, but the wine is dry. The name probably refers to the grapes' sweetness when eaten, or to their low acidity compared with Barbera and Nebbiolo. Dolcetto ripens early, up to four weeks before Nebbiolo, so it grows on cooler, higher sites that Nebbiolo couldn't ripen.

steps.prompt: Dolcetto wines are usually sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. The name means little sweet one, but the wines are dry. The name refers to the grape, not the wine.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep purple colour, dark fruit and a soft, round palate with low acidity and moderate tannin, ending in a slightly bitter, almond note. Compared with Barbera, it has less acidity and more tannin; compared with Nebbiolo, much less tannin and darker colour.

steps.prompt: Compared with Barbera, Dolcetto has:
steps.explanation: Barbera is high in acidity and low in tannin; Dolcetto the reverse.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dolcetto gives dark, soft wines with a bitter almond finish
Its name means little sweet one, but the wine is dry
It ripens early, on cooler sites than Nebbiolo

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Piedmont's hills
objectives: Explain its place in Piedmont's vineyards

steps.title: Piedmont
steps.body: Dolcetto grows almost only in Piedmont and nearby Liguria, where it's called Ormeasco. Main zones are Alba, Dogliani, Ovada and Diano d'Alba. Because it ripens early, growers plant it on cooler, higher or north-facing slopes, leaving the warmest sites for Nebbiolo.

steps.title: DOCGs
steps.body: Three Dolcetto zones are DOCG: Dogliani, Diano d'Alba and Ovada Superiore. Dogliani, south of Barolo, is considered its spiritual home, where Dolcetto is the main grape rather than a sideline. Dogliani wines are fuller and can age a little more.

steps.prompt: Match each name to Dolcetto.
steps.explanation: Dolcetto fills the cooler sites of Piedmont.

steps.body: In Piedmont, Dolcetto has lost ground to Barbera and Nebbiolo, which fetch higher prices. A good Dolcetto d'Alba or Dogliani is often a bargain.

steps.prompt: Why is Dolcetto planted on cooler slopes?
steps.explanation: Early ripening means it doesn't need the warmest sites.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dolcetto grows in Piedmont, mainly Alba, Dogliani and Ovada
It takes cooler slopes, leaving warm ones for Nebbiolo
Dogliani is its spiritual home and a DOCG

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Dolcetto
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Everyday food
steps.body: Dolcetto suits everyday Piedmontese food: salumi, vitello tonnato, agnolotti pasta, pizza, roast chicken and mild cheeses. Its soft acidity and moderate tannin make it easy with many dishes. Its bitter finish works well with fatty charcuterie.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 14 to 16 degrees, slightly cooler than big reds. Most Dolcetto is best within two to three years of the vintage, when fruit is fresh. Dogliani Superiore can age five to eight years. It's usually made in steel, without much oak.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Dolcetto?
steps.explanation: Sweet desserts make dry reds taste sour.

steps.title: A mealtime wine
steps.body: In Piedmont, Dolcetto is often the wine on the table at lunch, while Barolo and Barbaresco wait for special occasions or long ageing. It's honest and fruity rather than complex, and that's its charm.

steps.prompt: Most Dolcetto is best drunk within two to three years.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its charm is fresh, dark fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dolcetto suits salumi, pasta and pizza
Serve at 14 to 16 degrees, within two to three years
It's Piedmont's everyday lunch wine

steps.prompt: What does Dolcetto mean?
steps.explanation: But the wine is dry.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Dolcetto.
steps.explanation: Dolcetto is a simple, charming grape.

steps.prompt: Dolcetto has higher acidity than Barbera.
steps.explanation: Not true. Barbera has much higher acidity.

steps.prompt: Which are Dolcetto DOCGs?
steps.explanation: Barolo is Nebbiolo.

steps.explanation: Slightly cooler than big reds keeps its fruit fresh.

It ripens early on Piedmont's cooler slopes
