It's best young, with everyday food

modules.title: Barbera
modules.description: Piedmont's most planted red: deep colour, bright acidity, low tannin and a natural love of food.

steps.title: Bright and juicy
steps.body: Barbera gives deep ruby wines with sour and black cherry, plum, raspberry and dried herbs. Its signature is high acidity with low tannin, an unusual balance for a dark grape. That makes it juicy and refreshing. It's Piedmont's most planted red grape.

steps.title: Why that balance
steps.body: Barbera's skins are rich in colour pigments but low in tannin. Its acidity stays high even when fully ripe, partly due to high levels of malic acid. In the 1980s, producers like Giacomo Bologna began ageing it in small new oak barrels; oak adds the tannin Barbera lacks and softens its acidity.

steps.prompt: Why did producers begin ageing Barbera in new oak?
options: To add the tannin it naturally lacks
steps.explanation: Oak adds structure and tannin, balancing Barbera's high acidity.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep ruby colour, cherry fruit, a mouth-watering acidity and very little grip from tannin. Oaked versions add vanilla and spice. It's darker than Nebbiolo but much softer in tannin, and more acidic than Dolcetto.

steps.prompt: Barbera is known for very high tannin.
steps.explanation: Not true. Barbera is low in tannin; its acidity is what stands out.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera gives cherry fruit with high acidity and low tannin
Oak, since the 1980s, adds the tannin it lacks
It's Piedmont's most planted red

steps.title: Asti and Alba
steps.body: Barbera's two main zones are Asti and Alba. Barbera d'Asti, a DOCG since 2008, is the larger zone, often lighter and fresher, with Nizza, a DOCG since 2014, as its top area. Barbera d'Alba, a DOC, grows on sites not given to Nebbiolo, giving fuller, richer wines.
steps.highlight: Barbera d'Asti and Nizza; Barbera d'Alba

steps.title: Beyond Piedmont
steps.body: Barbera grows in Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese and Emilia-Romagna, where it's sometimes made fizzy. Italian immigrants took it to California and Argentina. Australia has small plantings. Its high acidity makes it useful in hot climates, where it keeps freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each zone to its Barbera.
steps.explanation: Each zone gives Barbera a different weight.

steps.body: Nizza is Barbera's top tier: a minimum of 18 months' ageing, 6 in wood, and grapes from the hills around Nizza Monferrato.

steps.prompt: Why is Barbera useful in hot climates?
steps.explanation: Its natural acidity keeps wines fresh even in heat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera d'Asti and Nizza are DOCGs; Barbera d'Alba is richer
It also grows in Lombardy, Emilia, California and Argentina
Its acidity is useful in warm regions

steps.title: A food wine
steps.body: Barbera's high acidity and low tannin make it one of the most food-friendly reds. It suits tomato sauces, pizza, lasagne, salumi, fatty meats and even mushrooms. It cuts through richness without clashing. In Piedmont, it goes with bagna cauda, a warm garlic and anchovy dip.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 17 degrees. Unoaked Barbera is best within three years. Oaked Barbera d'Alba, d'Asti Superiore and Nizza can age five to ten years. Its acidity helps it keep, but fruit fades before structure develops.
steps.highlight: Unoaked young; oaked five to ten years

steps.prompt: Why does Barbera suit tomato-based dishes?
options: Its high acidity matches tomato's acidity
steps.explanation: Acidic food needs acidic wine.

steps.title: Spotting quality
steps.body: Good Barbera balances its acidity with ripe fruit. Overcropped Barbera tastes thin and sour. Lower yields, older vines and good sites give more depth. In the 1980s, producers' new focus turned it from a peasant wine into a respected one.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Barbera?
steps.explanation: Sweet desserts make dry red taste sour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera's acidity makes it very food-friendly
Serve at 15 to 17 degrees
Unoaked is best young; oaked lasts five to ten years

steps.prompt: What is Barbera's signature balance?
steps.explanation: That balance makes it juicy and food-friendly.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Barbera.
steps.explanation: Barbera's story is one of transformation.

steps.prompt: Barbera d'Asti is a DOCG.
steps.explanation: Yes, since 2008.

steps.prompt: What does new oak bring to Barbera?
steps.explanation: Oak doesn't add sugar.

steps.prompt: Barbera is Piedmont's most ____ red grape.
steps.explanation: It covers more of Piedmont than Nebbiolo or Dolcetto.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera has high acidity and low tannin
Asti, Nizza and Alba are its key zones
Oak gives it structure
It's one of the most food-friendly reds

modules.title: Tempranillo
modules.description: Also called Tinta Roriz and Aragonez in Portugal, Tinto Fino in Ribera. Spain's great red, shaped by oak and time.

steps.title: Red fruit and leather
steps.body: Tempranillo gives medium to full-bodied wines with red cherry, strawberry, plum and dried fig, plus tobacco, leather and earth with age. Tannin is medium to high, acidity medium. Its fruit is fairly neutral, so oak and ageing shape it a lot. It's the third or fourth most planted red grape in the world.

steps.title: The early one
steps.body: Tempranillo comes from temprano, Spanish for early, because it ripens earlier than other Spanish grapes. DNA shows it's a cross of Albillo Mayor and Benedicto, probably from the Ebro valley. It has thick skins, giving deep colour, but naturally modest acidity, so it suits places with cool nights.

steps.prompt: What does Tempranillo's name refer to?
steps.explanation: Temprano means early in Spanish.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Young Tempranillo is ruby, with red fruit and soft tannin. Aged Rioja is paler, garnet, with dried fruit, leather, and vanilla, coconut or dill from American oak. Ribera del Duero is darker and more powerful. The combination of red fruit with leather and oak is a classic clue.
steps.highlight: Red fruit plus leather and oak

steps.prompt: Tempranillo has naturally very high acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its acidity is medium to modest, which is why cool nights or high sites help.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo gives red fruit, leather and tobacco
Its name means early; it's a cross from the Ebro valley
Oak and ageing shape its style

steps.title: Many names
steps.body: Tempranillo grows across Spain: Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Toro, Navarra, La Mancha, Valdepeñas. Each has a local name: Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera, Tinta de Toro in Toro, Cencibel in La Mancha, Ull de Llebre in Catalonia. In Portugal it's Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Tempranillo needs warmth to ripen but cool nights to keep acidity. That's why it thrives on high plateaus, like Ribera del Duero at 750 to 1,000 m, and in Rioja Alta with Atlantic influence. In very hot places it can lose acidity and turn flat. It's also grown in Argentina, Australia and the US.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its region.
steps.explanation: Tempranillo changes names as it crosses Iberia.

steps.title: Thick skins
steps.body: Tempranillo's thick skins give good colour and resistance to rot, but make it sensitive to drought and pests. Its early ripening suits continental climates with short seasons. Higher, cooler sites have become popular as summers grow warmer.

steps.prompt: Why do high plateaus suit Tempranillo?
options: Cool nights keep its modest acidity
steps.explanation: Cool nights balance warm days and preserve freshness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo grows across Spain and Portugal under many names
It needs warm days and cool nights
High plateaus like Ribera suit it well

lessons.title: Rioja and Ribera
lessons.subtitle: Two great Spanish reds
objectives: Describe Tempranillo in Ribera del Duero

steps.title: Rioja
steps.body: Rioja, along the Ebro, is Tempranillo's most famous home. It's usually blended with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo. Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, higher and cooler, give elegant, structured wines; Rioja Oriental, warmer, gives riper ones. Traditional Rioja ages long in American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill.

steps.title: Ribera del Duero
steps.body: Ribera del Duero, on the high Meseta, makes mostly single-variety Tinto Fino. Vineyards at 750 to 1,000 m have hot days and very cold nights. The wines are darker, fuller and more powerful than Rioja, often aged in French oak. Vega Sicilia, since 1864, and Pingus are famous names.

steps.prompt: How does Ribera del Duero Tempranillo typically compare with Rioja?
steps.explanation: High altitude and big diurnal range give Ribera its depth and power.

steps.title: Comparing them
steps.body: Rioja is traditionally a blend, more about elegance and oak-aged complexity. Ribera is usually pure Tempranillo, more about fruit concentration and power. Both have modern producers using French oak and shorter ageing, and traditionalists using long ageing. Toro, further west, is even riper and more muscular.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are often blended with Tempranillo in Rioja?
steps.explanation: Riesling isn't a Rioja grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rioja blends Tempranillo and often ages it in American oak
Ribera del Duero makes powerful, pure Tinto Fino at altitude
Rioja leans to elegance; Ribera and Toro to power

steps.title: National rules
steps.body: Spain's law sets minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: 24 months, at least 6 in oak. Reserva: 36 months, at least 12 in oak. Gran Reserva: 60 months, at least 18 in oak. Joven, young, has little or no oak. These terms appear on the back label, often with a seal.

steps.title: Rioja's rules
steps.body: Rioja sets stricter oak rules. Crianza needs at least 12 months in barrel. Reserva needs 12 months in barrel and 36 months in total. Gran Reserva needs 24 months in barrel and 60 months in total. Tempranillo's thick skins and moderate tannins suit long oak ageing, which softens it and adds vanilla, spice and leather.

steps.prompt: Order the Rioja categories by minimum ageing.
steps.explanation: Each step demands more time in barrel and bottle.

steps.title: Time and taste
steps.body: Long ageing changes Tempranillo: fruit shifts from fresh red cherry to dried fig and prune, colour fades from ruby to garnet and brick, and tertiary notes of leather, tobacco, mushroom and cedar appear. Traditional Gran Reservas, from producers like López de Heredia, can be drunk 30 years later.
steps.highlight: From fresh fruit to leather and tobacco

steps.prompt: How long must a Rioja Gran Reserva spend in barrel at minimum?
steps.explanation: 24 months in barrel, within 60 months of total ageing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spain's law sets Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva ageing
Rioja requires longer barrel ageing than the national minimum
Ageing turns Tempranillo's fruit into leather and tobacco

lessons.title: Tempranillo in Portugal
lessons.subtitle: Tinta Roriz and Aragonez
objectives: Describe Tinta Roriz in the Douro
Explain its role in Portuguese blends

steps.title: Douro
steps.body: In the Douro, Tempranillo is called Tinta Roriz. It's one of the five recommended grapes for Port, with Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca. In dry Douro reds, it adds red fruit, body and fine tannins to blends. It's one of the most planted grapes in the region.
steps.highlight: Tinta Roriz: Port and dry reds

steps.title: Alentejo
steps.body: In the hot Alentejo, Tempranillo is called Aragonez. It's often blended with Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, giving ripe, soft, fruity reds. The heat can make it lose acidity, so cooler sites near the São Mamede mountains are valued. Aragonez is among the region's most planted reds.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its Portuguese role.
steps.explanation: In Portugal, Tempranillo plays a supporting role in blends.

steps.body: Portugal's Dão also grows Tinta Roriz, in elegant blends with Touriga Nacional and Jaen.

steps.prompt: In Portugal, Tempranillo is mostly made as a single-variety wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's mainly a blending partner, with Touriga Nacional in the Douro or Trincadeira in the Alentejo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tinta Roriz is a key Douro grape, for Port and dry reds
Aragonez gives ripe Alentejo blends
In Portugal it's usually a blending partner

steps.title: Spanish table
steps.body: Tempranillo suits roast lamb, especially Castilian lechazo, suckling lamb, a classic with Ribera. Rioja goes with grilled lamb chops over vine cuttings, chorizo, jamón ibérico and Manchego cheese. Aged Gran Reserva suits mushrooms and game. Joven suits tapas.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Joven within two years; Crianza within five; Reserva five to fifteen; Gran Reserva 15 to 30 years or more. Old Rioja can throw sediment; decant gently. Ribera's big young wines benefit from air.

steps.prompt: Which Castilian dish is a classic with Ribera del Duero?
steps.explanation: Roast suckling lamb in wood ovens is Ribera's traditional match.

steps.body: A Rioja Reserva with jamón ibérico is a simple, classic Spanish pairing. The ham's fat and salt soften the wine's tannin.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit aged Tempranillo?
steps.explanation: Sorbet is too sweet and acidic for a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo suits lamb, jamón and Manchego
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees
Gran Reservas age 15 to 30 years or more

steps.prompt: Match each synonym to its region.
steps.explanation: One grape, many names.

steps.prompt: Order Spanish ageing categories from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Each requires more time.

steps.prompt: What does American oak typically add to Rioja?
steps.explanation: American oak's lactones give coconut and vanilla.

steps.prompt: Ribera del Duero is usually darker and more powerful than Rioja.
steps.explanation: Yes. Altitude and pure Tinto Fino give it depth.

steps.prompt: Which describe Tempranillo?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is moderate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo gives red fruit, leather and tobacco
Rioja, Ribera and Toro are its Spanish homes; Tinta Roriz its Portuguese name
Spain's ageing ladder shapes its style
It suits lamb, jamón and Manchego

modules.title: Corvina
modules.description: Valpolicella's leading grape: cherry-fresh when young, rich and raisined as Amarone.

steps.title: Light and bright
steps.body: Corvina, or Corvina Veronese, is the main grape of Valpolicella, near Verona. On its own, it gives light to medium-bodied wines with sour cherry, red berries, almond and herbs. Colour is moderate, tannins are low, acidity is fresh. It's a very different wine before and after drying.

steps.title: Built for drying
steps.body: Corvina has thick skins, loose bunches and good resistance to rot, which make it ideal for drying grapes after harvest. During drying, it develops a compound profile rich in aromatic precursors, and its skins help resist mould. That's why it's the backbone of Amarone and Recioto.
steps.highlight: Thick skins and loose bunches for drying

steps.prompt: Why is Corvina well suited to drying?
options: Thick skins and loose bunches that resist rot
steps.explanation: Loose bunches let air circulate, and thick skins resist mould during months of drying.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: A simple Valpolicella is pale to medium ruby, with bright cherry and a slightly bitter almond finish. Amarone is deep, with dried cherry, raisin, chocolate and spice, and high alcohol. That bitter cherry and almond note links them all.
steps.highlight: Cherry with a bitter almond finish

steps.prompt: Corvina naturally gives deep-coloured, very tannic wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Fresh Corvina is moderately coloured with low tannin. Drying gives Amarone its concentration.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Corvina gives sour cherry, almond and fresh acidity
Thick skins and loose bunches make it ideal for drying
Valpolicella's styles all share its cherry and almond

steps.title: Verona's hills
steps.body: Corvina grows almost only in the Veneto, around Verona. Valpolicella lies north of the city, in valleys running down from the Lessini mountains. The Classico zone, the historic heart, has valleys like Fumane, Marano and Negrar. Valpantena and the eastern zone extend it. Bardolino, on Lake Garda, also uses Corvina.

steps.title: Blending partners
steps.body: Valpolicella wines must be 45 to 95% Corvina, with Corvinone, a separate, larger-berried grape, allowed to replace up to half of it. Rondinella adds colour and resistance; Molinara, once common, adds acidity but is now less used. Oseleta, an old local grape, is being revived for its colour and tannin.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Valpolicella is a blend led by Corvina.

steps.body: Bardolino, from Corvina on Lake Garda's shores, is lighter than Valpolicella. Its rosé, Chiaretto, is one of Italy's best pink wines.

steps.prompt: Valpolicella must contain between 45 and ____% Corvina.
steps.explanation: Producers can use 45 to 95% Corvina, with Corvinone replacing up to half.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Corvina grows around Verona, in Valpolicella and Bardolino
Valpolicella blends Corvina with Corvinone and Rondinella
The Classico zone is the historic heart

lessons.title: Appassimento
lessons.subtitle: Drying the grapes
objectives: Explain how drying changes the grape

steps.title: Drying for months
steps.body: Appassimento is the drying of grapes after harvest. Healthy, loose bunches are picked by hand and laid on bamboo racks or plastic crates in airy lofts, called fruttai. They dry for about 100 to 120 days, losing 30 to 40% of their weight. Sugar, acid and flavour concentrate.
steps.highlight: Three to four months in fruttai

steps.title: Not just water loss
steps.body: Drying is a living process. The berries keep metabolising, changing their chemistry. Some acids decrease, glycerol rises, and new aromas form. Resveratrol and other compounds increase. A little noble rot sometimes develops, adding complexity. The result is dried cherry, raisin and spice flavours.
steps.highlight: Grapes keep living as they dry

steps.prompt: How much weight do grapes typically lose during appassimento?
steps.explanation: About a third, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour.

steps.title: Modern fruttai
steps.body: Traditionally, grapes dried in attics with open windows, at the mercy of the weather. Today many fruttai have fans and dehumidifiers to control conditions and prevent grey rot. Some producers argue that natural drying gives more complexity; others prefer control. Both are allowed.

steps.prompt: What happens during appassimento?
steps.explanation: Fermentation happens after drying, not during.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Appassimento dries grapes for three to four months
Berries lose 30 to 40% of their weight and change chemically
Modern lofts control humidity to prevent rot

steps.title: Amarone and Recioto
steps.body: Recioto della Valpolicella is the oldest style: dried grapes fermented to leave sweetness. Amarone della Valpolicella, DOCG since 2010, is fermented almost dry, reaching 15 to 16% alcohol. Amarone means the big bitter one, compared with Recioto's sweetness. Legend says it was born when a Recioto fermented too far.

steps.title: Ripasso
steps.body: Ripasso, meaning re-passed, is made by refermenting young Valpolicella on the leftover skins of Amarone or Recioto. The skins add sugar, colour, tannin and dried fruit flavour, plus a few degrees of alcohol. The result sits between simple Valpolicella and Amarone, sometimes called baby Amarone.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of making a Ripasso in order.
steps.explanation: Ripasso borrows the skins left after Amarone is pressed, so Amarone comes first.

steps.title: Ageing Amarone
steps.body: Amarone must age at least two years from January after harvest; Riserva at least four. Traditionally, it aged in large Slavonian oak casks; many producers now use French barriques. Producers like Quintarelli and Dal Forno made it famous worldwide.

steps.prompt: How is Ripasso made?
options: By drying grapes for six months
By refermenting Valpolicella on Amarone skins
steps.explanation: The leftover skins add body and flavour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Recioto is sweet; Amarone is dry and powerful, at 15 to 16%
Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on Amarone skins
Amarone ages at least two years; Riserva four

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Corvina
objectives: Pair each Valpolicella style with food

steps.title: A wine for every course
steps.body: Light Valpolicella suits salumi, pizza and pasta, served slightly cool. Ripasso suits risotto, roast meats and polenta. Amarone suits braised beef, game, aged Parmigiano and Monte Veronese cheese; in Verona it flavours risotto all'Amarone. Recioto goes with dark chocolate and dry pastries.
steps.highlight: Light to rich, starter to dessert

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Valpolicella at 14 to 16 degrees, Ripasso and Amarone at 16 to 18, Recioto slightly cooler. Valpolicella is best within three years; Ripasso within eight; Amarone ages 10 to 25 years. Decant young Amarone for its power and alcohol.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to a pairing.
steps.explanation: Corvina offers a wine for each course.

steps.body: Amarone is high in alcohol. Serve it in a large glass, not too warm, and give it time to open.

steps.prompt: Amarone can age for 10 to 25 years.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its concentration, alcohol and structure help it age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Valpolicella suits everyday food; Amarone rich dishes
Serve Amarone at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted
Amarone ages 10 to 25 years

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its making.
steps.explanation: One grape, four wines.

steps.prompt: What is a fruttaio?
steps.explanation: The airy loft where grapes dry for appassimento.

steps.prompt: Amarone means the big bitter one.
steps.explanation: Yes, compared with sweet Recioto.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are used in Valpolicella blends?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo belongs to Piedmont.

steps.prompt: During appassimento grapes lose about 30 to ____% of their weight.
steps.explanation: About a third of their weight, concentrating sugar and flavour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Corvina gives cherry, almond and freshness
Its thick skins and loose bunches suit drying
Amarone, Recioto and Ripasso come from appassimento
Each style matches a different course

modules.title: Cabernet Franc
modules.description: Also called Bouchet in Saint-Émilion and Breton in the Loire. The aromatic parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

lessons.title: Meet Cabernet Franc
lessons.subtitle: Red fruit, violets and leaf
objectives: Describe Cabernet Franc's flavours and structure

steps.title: Aromatic and fresh
steps.body: Cabernet Franc gives medium-bodied reds with raspberry, red currant, violet, graphite and a leafy or green pepper note. Tannins are finer and lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon's, acidity fresh. It's more aromatic and lighter, with a characteristic herbal edge.

steps.title: A parent
steps.body: DNA shows Cabernet Franc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, with Sauvignon Blanc, of Merlot, with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes, and of Carmenère. It probably came from the Basque Country. It buds and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, so it suits cooler places, but it still carries pyrazines, which give green notes when unripe.
steps.highlight: Parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot

steps.prompt: Which grape is Cabernet Franc a parent of?
steps.explanation: Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc to give Cabernet Sauvignon.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium ruby colour, red fruit with violet and a leafy, pencil-shaving or green pepper note. On the palate, fresh acidity and fine, medium tannins. It's lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon and less plummy than Merlot. A leafy, perfumed red with red fruit often means Cabernet Franc.

steps.prompt: Cabernet Franc ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. It ripens earlier, which is why it suits cooler places like the Loire.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc gives raspberry, violet and a leafy note
It's a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carmenère
It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Loire, Bordeaux and the New World

steps.title: France
steps.body: Cabernet Franc's two French homes are the Loire, where it makes single-variety reds, and Bordeaux, where it's a blending grape, especially on the Right Bank. It also grows in the south-west. In the Loire it's sometimes called Breton; in Saint-Émilion, Bouchet.

steps.title: Cool and warm
steps.body: Cabernet Franc tolerates cold winters better than Cabernet Sauvignon, and ripens earlier. That suits the Loire, northern Italy and even Canada and New York. In warmer places, like Argentina's Valle de Uco, California, Virginia and Hungary's Villány, it gives riper, fuller wines, with fewer green notes.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet Franc.
steps.explanation: Cabernet Franc is gaining attention well beyond France.

steps.body: Argentina's Cabernet Franc from the Valle de Uco has become one of the country's most exciting new wines, rivalling Malbec for critics' attention.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Franc suit cooler regions?
options: It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.explanation: It doesn't need extreme heat, and it buds earlier, not later.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc is single-variety in the Loire and blended in Bordeaux
It's cold-hardy and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
Argentina, California, Virginia and Hungary grow fine examples

lessons.title: Chinon and the Loire
lessons.subtitle: Cabernet Franc on its own
objectives: Describe the Loire's Cabernet Franc appellations

steps.title: The appellations
steps.body: In the Loire's Touraine and Anjou-Saumur, Cabernet Franc makes most of the red wine. Chinon, Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil, in Touraine, and Saumur-Champigny, in Saumur, are the key appellations. The wines are medium-bodied, fresh and perfumed, with raspberry, violet and graphite.

steps.title: Soil matters
steps.body: Soils shape the style. Sandy and gravel soils near the rivers give light, fruity wines to drink young. Tuffeau, a soft, white limestone, and clay-limestone on the slopes give more structured wines that can age 10 to 20 years. The same tuffeau was used to build the Loire's châteaux.

steps.prompt: Which soil in Chinon gives the most structured, age-worthy Cabernet Franc?
steps.explanation: Limestone slopes give firmer, longer-lived wines than riverside sand and gravel.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: Loire Cabernet Franc ranges from light, juicy wines, served cool in Paris bistros, to serious, oaked wines from old vines. Rosé de Loire and Cabernet d'Anjou, a rosé often off-dry, also use it. Cooler vintages can show more green notes; warmer ones, riper fruit.

steps.prompt: Which are Loire Cabernet Franc appellations?
steps.explanation: Sancerre Blanc is Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny are key appellations
Gravel gives light wines; tuffeau gives structured ones
Styles range from bistro reds to age-worthy wines

lessons.title: Cabernet Franc in Bordeaux
lessons.subtitle: A blending partner
objectives: Explain Cabernet Franc's role in Bordeaux blends
Name Bordeaux wines with high Cabernet Franc
Explain why it suits the Right Bank

steps.title: A supporting role
steps.body: In Bordeaux, Cabernet Franc is about 10% of red plantings. It adds aromatic lift, freshness and fine tannins to blends. On the Left Bank, it's a minor partner to Cabernet Sauvignon. On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, it often plays a bigger role alongside Merlot.

steps.title: Cheval Blanc and Ausone
steps.body: Château Cheval Blanc, in Saint-Émilion, often uses over 50% Cabernet Franc, on gravel and clay near Pomerol. Château Ausone, on limestone slopes, also uses around half. These show Cabernet Franc can make some of the world's greatest wines, with perfume, freshness and longevity.
steps.highlight: Cheval Blanc: over half Cabernet Franc

steps.prompt: Which Saint-Émilion estate often uses over 50% Cabernet Franc?
steps.explanation: Cheval Blanc is famous for its high share of Cabernet Franc.

steps.title: Why the Right Bank
steps.body: The Right Bank's cooler clay and limestone suit early-ripening grapes. Cabernet Franc ripens before Cabernet Sauvignon, so it does well there. Limestone slopes give it freshness and structure, complementing Merlot's plumpness.

steps.prompt: Cabernet Franc is the most planted grape in Bordeaux.
steps.explanation: Not true. Merlot is the most planted. Cabernet Franc is about 10%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc adds lift and freshness to Bordeaux blends
Cheval Blanc and Ausone use a high share
It suits the Right Bank's cooler soils

steps.title: Versatile
steps.body: Cabernet Franc's fresh acidity and moderate tannin make it food-friendly. Light Loire styles suit charcuterie, pork rillettes, roast chicken and goat's cheese. Fuller styles suit lamb, duck and dishes with herbs and roasted peppers, which echo its own green notes.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve light Loire Cabernet Franc slightly cool, about 14 to 15 degrees. Fuller versions at 16 to 17. Simple Loire reds are best within three years. Top Chinon and Bourgueil from tuffeau age 10 to 20 years. Cheval Blanc ages for decades.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Franc suit dishes with herbs and roasted peppers?
options: They echo its own leafy notes
steps.explanation: Herbal food echoes the wine's leafy, green side.

steps.body: Try a young Chinon slightly chilled with pork rillettes on bread. It's a classic Loire combination.

steps.prompt: Light Loire Cabernet Franc is best served at about ____ degrees.
steps.explanation: Slightly cool brings out its fresh fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc suits charcuterie, poultry and herb dishes
Serve light styles slightly cool
Top Loire and Bordeaux examples age for decades

steps.prompt: Match each name or place to Cabernet Franc.
steps.explanation: Cabernet Franc has French names and famous homes.

steps.prompt: Which grapes is Cabernet Franc a parent of?
steps.explanation: It's the parent of both Bordeaux stars.

steps.prompt: Cabernet Franc ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Yes, which helps in cooler places.

steps.prompt: Which aromas are typical of Cabernet Franc?
steps.explanation: Lychee belongs to Gewürztraminer.

steps.prompt: The soft white limestone of the Loire is called ____.
steps.explanation: Tuffeau gives structured Cabernet Franc and built the Loire's châteaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc is aromatic, fresh and leafy
It's single-variety in the Loire and blended in Bordeaux
It's the parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
It's food-friendly and can age well

modules.title: Carignan
modules.description: Also called Cariñena, Mazuelo, Samsó and Carignano. Once a bulk grape, now prized from old vines.

lessons.title: Meet Carignan
lessons.subtitle: High acid, high tannin, old vines

steps.title: A rustic grape
steps.body: Carignan gives deep-coloured wines with red and black fruit, dried herbs, liquorice and earthy, sometimes meaty notes. It has high acidity, high tannin and can be rustic and astringent when young or overcropped. From old, low-yielding vines, it becomes concentrated and complex.
steps.highlight: Dark fruit, herbs, high acid and tannin

steps.title: Spanish roots
steps.body: Carignan comes from Aragón, in Spain, near the town of Cariñena. In Spain it's also called Mazuelo, in Rioja, and Samsó, in Catalonia. In Italy, mainly Sardinia, it's Carignano. It buds late and ripens very late, so it needs heat. It's vigorous and can yield heavily, which is why it became a bulk grape.

steps.prompt: Match each name to where it's used.
steps.explanation: Carignan takes a new name in each region.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Carignan often appears in blends, adding colour, acidity and structure. On its own, look for deep colour, bright acidity, firm tannin and earthy, herbal notes. Old-vine examples are richer, with dark fruit and spice. Its high acidity sets it apart from Grenache, its usual partner.

steps.prompt: Carignan buds and ripens early.
steps.explanation: Not true. It buds and ripens late, so it needs a hot climate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carignan has high acidity, high tannin and earthy notes
It comes from Cariñena in Aragón and has many names
It ripens late and needs heat

steps.title: France and Spain
steps.body: Carignan was once France's most planted grape, especially in the Languedoc, where it made cheap, high-yield table wine. EU vine-pull schemes from the 1980s cut plantings dramatically. In Spain it grows in Priorat, Montsant, Empordà and Rioja. In Italy, Sardinia's Carignano del Sulcis is its stronghold.

steps.title: Blends
steps.body: In the Languedoc and Roussillon, Carignan blends with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre, adding acidity and colour. In Priorat, it partners Garnacha. In Rioja, as Mazuelo, it's a minor partner to Tempranillo, adding acidity and colour. Carbonic maceration, the Beaujolais method, is sometimes used to soften it.

steps.prompt: Why were many Languedoc Carignan vineyards pulled out from the 1980s?
options: EU schemes to reduce wine surplus
steps.explanation: Vine-pull schemes targeted high-yield, low-value vineyards, many planted with Carignan.

steps.body: Look for Vieilles Vignes, old vines, on Languedoc Carignan labels. Old-vine Carignan is far more concentrated than the bulk wine that gave it a poor reputation.

steps.prompt: Which grapes does Carignan often blend with?
steps.explanation: Riesling isn't a Mediterranean blending partner.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carignan was France's most planted grape; plantings fell sharply
It blends with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre
Carbonic maceration can soften it

lessons.title: Old vines from Priorat to Maule
lessons.subtitle: Carignan's revival

steps.title: Priorat
steps.body: In Priorat, Carignan, called Cariñena or Samsó, grows on steep slopes of llicorella, dark slate. Old vines, many over 80 years, give tiny yields and concentrated, mineral wines. When producers revived Priorat in the late 1980s, old Cariñena with Garnacha was their raw material.

steps.title: Maule
steps.body: In Chile's Maule Valley, old, dry-farmed Carignan vines, some planted after the 1939 Chillán earthquake, were rediscovered. In 2009, producers founded VIGNO, Vignadores de Carignan, requiring at least 65% Carignan from dry-farmed vines over 30 years old, and two years' ageing. It became one of Chile's most exciting wines.

steps.prompt: What does VIGNO require?
options: At least 65% Carignan from dry-farmed vines over 30 years old
steps.explanation: VIGNO is a growers' association protecting old, dry-farmed Maule Carignan.

steps.title: Why old vines
steps.body: Old vines have deep roots that find water in dry soils, so they cope with drought without irrigation. Their naturally low yields concentrate the fruit, balancing Carignan's acidity and tannin. Young, high-yield Carignan is harsh and thin; old-vine Carignan is rich and complex.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Carignan's revival.
steps.explanation: Old vines turned Carignan's reputation around.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Priorat's old Cariñena on llicorella makes concentrated wines
Maule's VIGNO protects old, dry-farmed Carignan
Old vines balance Carignan's acidity and tannin

steps.title: Mediterranean food
steps.body: Carignan's acidity and tannin suit hearty Mediterranean food: cassoulet, grilled lamb, sausages, stews with olives and herbs, and roast vegetables. Its earthy, herbal notes match rosemary, thyme and garlic. Old-vine examples suit game and aged cheeses.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Simple Carignan is best young. Old-vine wines from Priorat, Maule or the Languedoc can age 10 to 15 years, as acidity keeps them fresh. Decant young, firm examples.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits an old-vine Carignan?
steps.explanation: Hearty, fatty dishes balance its acidity and tannin.

steps.body: Carbonic maceration Carignan, light and juicy, is a good chilled red for summer barbecues.

steps.prompt: Carignan's high acidity helps old-vine examples age.
steps.explanation: Yes. Acidity preserves freshness over time.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carignan suits cassoulet, lamb and herby stews
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; decant young wines
Old-vine Carignan ages 10 to 15 years

steps.prompt: Match each name to its region.
steps.explanation: Carignan's names follow its map.

steps.prompt: Why did Carignan get a bad reputation?
options: It was overcropped for bulk wine
steps.explanation: High yields gave thin, harsh wines.

steps.prompt: VIGNO protects old Carignan in Chile's Maule Valley.
steps.explanation: Yes, since 2009.

steps.prompt: Which describe Carignan?
steps.explanation: Carignan is deeply coloured.

steps.prompt: Priorat's dark slate soil is called ____.
steps.explanation: Llicorella forces deep roots and low yields.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carignan has high acidity, tannin and colour
It has many names across the Mediterranean
Old vines in Priorat and Maule revived its reputation
It suits hearty, herby food

modules.title: Sangiovese
modules.description: Also called Brunello, Prugnolo Gentile and Morellino in Tuscany. Italy's most planted red: sour cherry, high acidity and firm tannin.

steps.title: Bright and savoury
steps.body: Sangiovese gives medium-bodied reds with sour cherry, red plum, tomato leaf, dried herbs and, with age, leather and earth. Acidity is high, tannins firm and often slightly drying, like strong tea. Colour is medium ruby, fading early to garnet. It's Italy's most planted grape.
steps.highlight: Sour cherry, high acidity, tea-like tannin

steps.title: Blood of Jupiter
steps.body: Sangiovese may come from sanguis Jovis, Latin for the blood of Jupiter. DNA shows it's a cross of Ciliegiolo and Calabrese di Montenuovo, linking Tuscany and the south. It's genetically unstable, with many clones: Sangiovese Grosso, with bigger berries, is used in Montalcino, where it's called Brunello.

steps.prompt: What does Sangiovese's name possibly mean?
steps.explanation: Sanguis Jovis, Latin for the blood of Jupiter.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium ruby or garnet colour, often with an orange tint even when quite young. On the nose, sour cherry, herbs and earth. On the palate, high acidity and grainy, drying tannin. That combination of sour cherry and tea-like tannin, plus the urge to eat something with tomato, is the clue.

steps.prompt: Sangiovese is usually deeply coloured and low in acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's medium in colour and high in acidity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sangiovese gives sour cherry, herbs and earth
It has high acidity and firm, tea-like tannin
It's Italy's most planted grape, with many clones

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Tuscany and central Italy
objectives: Explain the climate and soils it needs

steps.title: Tuscany and beyond
steps.body: Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany: Chianti, Montalcino, Montepulciano, Carmignano and Morellino di Scansano. It also grows in Umbria, Romagna, the Marche and Lazio. Outside Italy, it's planted in Corsica, as Nielluccio, California, Argentina and Australia, but rarely with the same success.

steps.title: Site-sensitive
steps.body: Sangiovese ripens late and needs warmth, but too much heat makes it flat and jammy. It shows best on hillsides at 250 to 600 m, with good sun and cool nights. Galestro, a crumbly marl schist, and alberese, a hard limestone, give its finest wines. It's prone to rot in wet autumns because of its thin skins.

steps.prompt: Match each regional name to its place.
steps.explanation: Sangiovese takes local names in its best zones.

steps.title: Romagna
steps.body: Across the Apennines, Romagna makes Sangiovese di Romagna, now Romagna Sangiovese DOC, often fruitier and softer. Its sub-zones, like Predappio and Modigliana, are making more serious wines. It shows that Sangiovese isn't only Tuscan.

steps.prompt: Which soils give Sangiovese's finest wines in Tuscany?
steps.explanation: Galestro marl and alberese limestone are prized in Chianti Classico.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany, also grown across central Italy
It needs warm hillsides and cool nights
Galestro and alberese give its finest wines

lessons.title: Chianti Classico
lessons.subtitle: The historic heart
objectives: Explain the difference between Chianti and Chianti Classico
Describe its rules and quality levels

steps.title: Two different wines
steps.body: Chianti covers a large area across Tuscany, with seven sub-zones like Rufina and Colli Senesi. Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, the original zone between Florence and Siena, defined in 1716 by Cosimo III de' Medici. Classico must be at least 80% Sangiovese; white grapes were banned in 2006.
steps.highlight: Chianti Classico: a separate, original zone

steps.title: Quality levels
steps.body: Chianti Classico has three levels: Annata, the basic wine; Riserva, aged at least 24 months; and Gran Selezione, created in 2014, from estate-grown grapes aged at least 30 months. Since 2021, Gran Selezione needs at least 90% Sangiovese, and labels can name 11 villages, called UGAs, like Radda and Panzano.

steps.prompt: Chianti Classico's top level, created in 2014, is called ____.
steps.explanation: Gran Selezione sits above Riserva and Annata, with estate grapes and at least 30 months of ageing.

steps.title: The black rooster
steps.body: The black rooster, gallo nero, is Chianti Classico's symbol. Legend says Florence and Siena settled their border with a race: riders left at the first cockcrow. Florence's black rooster, starved, crowed early, so its rider got further. Every Chianti Classico bottle carries it on the neck.

steps.prompt: Chianti and Chianti Classico are the same DOCG.
steps.explanation: Not true. Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, the original historic zone.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, defined in 1716
It has Annata, Riserva and Gran Selezione
The black rooster marks every bottle

steps.title: Brunello di Montalcino
steps.body: Montalcino, a hill town south of Siena, is warmer and drier than Chianti. Brunello di Montalcino, DOCG since 1980, must be 100% Sangiovese and age at least five years, two in oak, before release; Riserva six years. The Biondi-Santi family created the style in the late 19th century. Rosso di Montalcino is the younger, cheaper version.

steps.title: Vino Nobile
steps.body: Montepulciano, east of Montalcino, makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG from at least 70% Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo Gentile. It ages at least two years. It's often softer than Brunello and more structured than Chianti. Not to be confused with Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a different grape and region.

steps.prompt: What does Brunello di Montalcino require?
steps.explanation: Brunello is pure Sangiovese, aged at least five years before release.

steps.title: Comparing
steps.body: Chianti Classico is often the freshest, with sour cherry and violet. Brunello, from a warmer place and with longer ageing, is fuller, more powerful and long-lived. Vino Nobile sits between them. All three show Sangiovese's acidity and tannin.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its rule.
steps.explanation: Each Tuscan wine sets its own rules.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, aged five years
Vino Nobile is at least 70% Prugnolo Gentile
Brunello is fullest; Chianti Classico freshest

lessons.title: Super Tuscans
lessons.subtitle: Breaking the rules
objectives: Explain how the Super Tuscans began
Explain their effect on Italian law

steps.title: The rebels
steps.body: In the 1960s and 1970s, Chianti rules required white grapes in the blend and limited international grapes. Some producers wanted to make the best wine they could instead. Sassicaia, first sold in 1971, used Cabernet Sauvignon. Tignanello, in 1971, blended Sangiovese with Cabernet in small barrels, with no white grapes.

steps.title: Table wine prices
steps.body: Because they broke DOC rules, these wines had to be sold as Vino da Tavola, the lowest category, yet sold for more than any Chianti. The press named them Super Tuscans. In 1992, Italy created IGT to give them a category; Sassicaia got its own DOC in 2013. Chianti Classico's rules changed too.

steps.prompt: The first Super Tuscans had to be labelled as simple table wine.
steps.explanation: Yes. Breaking DOC rules meant they could only be sold as Vino da Tavola.

steps.title: Today
steps.body: Super Tuscans include Sangiovese-based wines, like Flaccianello and Pergole Torte, which is pure Sangiovese, and Bordeaux blends from Bolgheri, like Ornellaia. Many use small French oak. Since Chianti Classico now allows 100% Sangiovese, some producers have returned to the DOCG.

steps.prompt: Which are Super Tuscans?
steps.explanation: Barolo is a Piedmont DOCG made from Nebbiolo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Super Tuscans broke DOC rules in the 1970s
They led to the IGT category in 1992
They include Sangiovese and Bordeaux-style wines

steps.title: Made for food
steps.body: Sangiovese's acidity makes it perfect with tomato: pasta al pomodoro, pizza, lasagne. Its tannin suits grilled meat, like bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick T-bone. Brunello suits wild boar, game and aged pecorino. It's one of the most food-dependent reds; it can taste austere alone.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Chianti Classico Annata is best within five years. Riserva and Gran Selezione age 10 to 20 years. Brunello ages 15 to 30 years, gaining leather, tobacco and dried cherry. Decant young Brunello.

steps.prompt: What is bistecca alla fiorentina?
steps.explanation: A classic Tuscan match for Chianti or Brunello.

steps.body: If a Sangiovese tastes austere on its own, try it with a bite of tomato pasta. Its acidity and tannin will suddenly make sense.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Sangiovese?
steps.explanation: Sweet desserts make it taste sour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sangiovese's acidity loves tomato
Its tannin suits grilled meat and aged cheese
Brunello ages 15 to 30 years

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its description.
steps.explanation: Sangiovese has several great Tuscan expressions.

steps.prompt: Which soils are prized for Sangiovese in Chianti Classico?
steps.explanation: Galestro marl and alberese limestone.

steps.prompt: The IGT category was created partly because of the Super Tuscans.
steps.explanation: Yes, in 1992.

steps.prompt: Which describe Sangiovese?
steps.explanation: Lychee is Gewürztraminer.

steps.prompt: Brunello di Montalcino must age at least ____ years before release.
steps.explanation: Five years, two of them in oak; Riserva needs six.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sangiovese is high in acidity, with sour cherry and firm tannin
Chianti Classico, Brunello and Vino Nobile are its great wines
Super Tuscans broke rules and changed Italian law
It's made for tomato and grilled meat

modules.title: Gamay
modules.description: Beaujolais' grape: light, juicy and fragrant, from fresh nouveau to serious crus.

steps.title: Light and juicy
steps.body: Gamay, fully Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc, gives light to medium-bodied reds with red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, violet and sometimes banana or bubblegum from winemaking. Tannins are low, acidity fresh. It's pale to medium purple and made to be fresh and drinkable.

steps.title: Banned by a duke
steps.body: Gamay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, from Burgundy. In 1395, Duke Philip the Bold banned it from Burgundy, calling it a very bad and disloyal plant, to protect Pinot Noir. Gamay moved south to Beaujolais, where granite soils suit it far better than Burgundy's limestone.

steps.prompt: Why did Gamay move to Beaujolais?
options: It was banned from Burgundy in 1395
steps.explanation: Philip the Bold banned it to protect Pinot Noir; it found a better home on Beaujolais granite.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for a bright purple colour, juicy red fruit, often floral notes, and a light, fresh palate with low tannin. Carbonic maceration adds banana or bubblegum. Compared with Pinot Noir, Gamay is usually juicier and simpler, with more purple in the colour.

steps.prompt: Gamay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
steps.explanation: Yes. It shares the same parents as Chardonnay.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gamay gives juicy red fruit, low tannin and fresh acidity
It was banned from Burgundy in 1395 and moved to Beaujolais
It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc

steps.title: Beaujolais
steps.body: Beaujolais, just south of Burgundy, grows almost all of the world's Gamay. In the south, on clay and limestone, it makes simple Beaujolais. In the north, on pink granite and schist, it makes Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. Granite drains well and is poor, giving Gamay its best structure and perfume.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Gamay grows in the Loire, in Touraine and Anjou, often for light reds and rosés, and in the Côte Roannaise. Switzerland blends it with Pinot Noir to make Dôle. It's appearing in Oregon, Canada's Niagara and Australia. Burgundy's Coteaux Bourguignons can include it.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Gamay.
steps.explanation: Beaujolais dominates, but Gamay travels.

steps.body: Look for cru Beaujolais rather than plain Beaujolais. The ten crus, on granite, show what Gamay can really do, often at modest prices.

steps.prompt: Why does granite suit Gamay?
steps.explanation: Granite is poor, not fertile, and that helps.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais grows almost all the world's Gamay
Northern granite gives the best wines
The Loire, Switzerland and Oregon grow some too

steps.title: Whole berries
steps.body: In carbonic maceration, whole, uncrushed bunches go into a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, enzymes inside each berry start fermenting sugar into alcohol, up to about 2%, and create aromas like banana, bubblegum and kirsch. Then berries burst, and yeast finishes the job. Colour comes out, but little tannin.

steps.title: Semi-carbonic
steps.body: Most Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Whole bunches go into the tank; the weight crushes the bottom ones, which ferment normally, producing CO2 that fills the tank. The upper berries undergo carbonic maceration. The result: fruity, soft wines with low tannin. Some crus use traditional crushing for more structure.

steps.prompt: What does carbonic maceration typically produce?
options: Fruity, soft wines with banana or bubblegum notes
steps.explanation: Intracellular fermentation gives fruity aromas and little tannin.

steps.title: Beaujolais Nouveau
steps.body: Beaujolais Nouveau is made fast, by semi-carbonic maceration, and released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest. It's light, fruity and meant for immediate drinking. Its fame in the 1980s and 1990s made Beaujolais a household name, but also hurt its reputation for serious wine.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third ____ of November.
steps.explanation: The third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carbonic maceration ferments whole berries in CO2
It gives fruity, soft wines with banana and bubblegum notes
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November

steps.title: Versatile and light
steps.body: Gamay's low tannin and fresh acidity make it very food-friendly. It suits charcuterie, roast chicken, salmon, pâté and Lyon's bistro food, like saucisson and andouillette. It handles light spice better than tannic reds. It's a great picnic wine.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve slightly cool, 12 to 14 degrees; a little chill brings out its fruit. Nouveau within months; Beaujolais and Villages within two or three years. Structured crus, like Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, can age 10 years or more, becoming more like Pinot Noir, a process called pinoter.

steps.prompt: What temperature suits Gamay?
steps.explanation: A slight chill keeps its fruit lively.

steps.body: Aged Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can taste surprisingly like Burgundy. Locals say the wine pinote, becomes Pinot-like, with age.

steps.prompt: Some Beaujolais crus can age 10 years or more.
steps.explanation: Yes. Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent are known for ageing well.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gamay suits charcuterie, chicken and bistro food
Serve slightly cool, 12 to 14 degrees
Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age 10 years or more

steps.prompt: Who banned Gamay from Burgundy in 1395?
steps.explanation: Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, called it a very bad and disloyal plant.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Gamay.
steps.explanation: Gamay has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Gamay has high tannin.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's low in tannin, especially with carbonic maceration.

steps.prompt: Which describe Gamay?
steps.explanation: Gamay is pale to medium purple.

steps.prompt: Gamay is best served at about ____ degrees.
steps.explanation: Slightly cool.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gamay is juicy, light and low in tannin
Beaujolais' granite gives its best wines
Carbonic maceration gives fruity, soft styles
Serve it slightly cool with bistro food

modules.title: Grenache
modules.description: Also called Garnacha in Spain and Cannonau in Sardinia. Red fruit, spice and warmth, from Châteauneuf to Priorat.

steps.title: Ripe and spicy
steps.body: Grenache gives medium to full-bodied reds with strawberry, raspberry, red cherry, white pepper, dried herbs and, with age, leather and toffee. Colour is often paler than expected. Tannins are soft to medium, acidity low to medium, and alcohol high, often 14.5 to 16%.

steps.title: Spanish origins
steps.body: Grenache, Garnacha in Spain, probably comes from Aragón, in north-east Spain; some argue for Sardinia, where it's called Cannonau. It loves heat and drought, and accumulates sugar fast, which explains its high alcohol. Thin skins mean paler colour and softer tannin. It oxidises easily, so it browns early.

steps.prompt: Why is Grenache often high in alcohol?
options: It accumulates sugar quickly in heat
steps.explanation: Grenache ripens to high sugar levels, which become alcohol.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium ruby colour, often with an orange rim early, ripe red fruit, white pepper and herbs, a warm, high-alcohol feel and soft tannins. Compared with Syrah, it's paler and redder-fruited; compared with Pinot Noir, warmer and riper.

steps.prompt: Grenache usually gives deeply coloured, tannic wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its thin skins give paler colour and softer tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grenache gives strawberry, spice and high alcohol
It comes from Spain and loves heat and drought
Thin skins mean paler colour and soft tannin

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: The Mediterranean grape
objectives: Explain why old bush vines matter

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Grenache is one of the world's most planted red grapes. In France, it leads the southern Rhône and much of the Languedoc-Roussillon and Provence rosé. In Spain, it grows in Aragón, Navarra, Priorat, Rioja and around Madrid. Sardinia's Cannonau, Australia's Barossa and McLaren Vale, and California also grow it.

steps.title: Bush vines
steps.body: Grenache has strong, upright wood, so it's often grown as free-standing bush vines, gobelet. They need no trellis and withstand wind. Old bush vines, some over 100 years, with deep roots, survive drought and give low yields of concentrated fruit. Many of Grenache's best wines come from them.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Grenache.
steps.explanation: Grenache thrives across warm, dry regions.

steps.title: Blending
steps.body: Grenache brings red fruit, body and alcohol to blends. Syrah adds colour and structure; Mourvèdre adds tannin and savoury notes; Carignan adds acidity. Rioja adds Garnacha to Tempranillo. Its low colour and tendency to oxidise make it a natural team player.

steps.prompt: Why is Grenache often blended?
steps.explanation: Grenache ripens easily; it's rarely unripe.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grenache is one of the most planted red grapes
Old bush vines give concentrated wines
It's a team player in GSM and Rioja blends

steps.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
steps.body: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, near Avignon, was named after the 14th century popes' summer castle. It allows 13 grape varieties, but Grenache usually leads, often 70% or more. Its famous galets roulés, large round stones, store heat and reflect light. In 1923, Baron Le Roy's rules there helped inspire France's AOC system.

steps.title: The southern Rhône
steps.body: Gigondas and Vacqueyras, nearby, make powerful Grenache-led reds. Côtes du Rhône and Côtes du Rhône Villages offer more affordable versions. Château Rayas is a famous Châteauneuf made almost entirely from Grenache, on sandy soil, showing the grape's elegance.

steps.prompt: What are the galets roulés of Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
options: Large round stones that store heat
steps.explanation: These river stones store heat by day and release it at night.

steps.title: Rosé
steps.body: Grenache is the main grape of many rosés: Provence, Tavel and Navarra's rosado. Its thin skins give pale colour quickly, and its red fruit and body suit dry rosé. Tavel, in the southern Rhône, is a rosé-only appellation, fuller and darker than Provence.

steps.prompt: Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows only Grenache.
steps.explanation: Not true. It allows 13 varieties, though Grenache usually leads.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is Grenache-led, with galets and 13 grapes
Gigondas, Vacqueyras and Côtes du Rhône follow
Grenache is key to Provence, Tavel and Navarra rosé

steps.title: Aragón
steps.body: In Aragón, Garnacha's likely birthplace, Campo de Borja, Calatayud and Cariñena have many old bush vines on poor, stony soils. Campo de Borja calls itself the empire of Garnacha. These areas once made bulk wine but now offer concentrated, good-value Garnacha.

steps.title: Priorat and Gredos
steps.body: In Priorat, old Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate make powerful, mineral wines. In the Sierra de Gredos, west of Madrid, old Garnacha vines on granite at 600 to 1,200 m were rediscovered in the 2000s. Gredos Garnacha is pale, fragrant and fresh, often compared with Burgundy.

steps.prompt: Match each Spanish area to its Garnacha.
steps.explanation: Spain shows every side of Garnacha.

steps.body: Gredos Garnacha shows a lighter, more elegant face of the grape. Try one next to a Châteauneuf to see how much altitude and granite change it.

steps.prompt: Why is Gredos Garnacha often fresher than other Garnachas?
steps.explanation: Altitude up to 1,200 m and granite give freshness and perfume.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aragón is Garnacha's homeland, with old bush vines
Priorat makes powerful Garnacha on slate
Gredos makes fragrant, fresh Garnacha at altitude

lessons.title: Sweet Grenache
lessons.subtitle: Vins doux naturels
objectives: Explain how sweet Grenache is made

steps.title: Fortified Grenache
steps.body: In Roussillon, Grenache makes vins doux naturels: spirit is added during fermentation, stopping it and keeping natural sugar. Grenache's high sugar and red fruit suit this. Banyuls and Maury are the most famous red ones, also Rivesaltes. They have 15 to 18% alcohol.

steps.title: Oxidative or fresh
steps.body: Banyuls and Maury are made in two styles. Rimage or grenat styles are bottled young, keeping red fruit, like ruby Port. Traditional styles age with oxygen for years, in barrels or in glass demijohns left in the sun, giving notes of nuts, coffee, dried fruit and rancio, a complex, nutty, oxidative character.

steps.prompt: What is rancio?
options: A nutty, oxidative character from long ageing
steps.explanation: Rancio develops in wines aged with oxygen and heat.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Banyuls and Maury are among the few wines that match dark chocolate. Rimage styles suit red fruit desserts; aged styles suit coffee, walnut and caramel desserts, and blue cheese. Serve slightly cool, around 14 to 16 degrees.

steps.prompt: Which are sweet fortified Grenache wines?
steps.explanation: Tavel is a dry rosé.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Banyuls and Maury are fortified Grenache from Roussillon
Rimage is fresh; traditional styles age with oxygen
They're rare partners for dark chocolate

steps.title: Warm and savoury
steps.body: Grenache's ripe fruit and soft tannin suit roast lamb, Provençal stews, grilled sausages, roast pork and dishes with herbs and garlic. Lighter Gredos styles suit roast chicken and mushrooms. Its sweetness of fruit handles mildly spicy food, though high alcohol can clash with chilli.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 17 degrees; high alcohol feels hot if served too warm. Simple Côtes du Rhône and Garnacha are best within three years. Top Châteauneuf and Priorat age 15 to 25 years, though Grenache browns early, so colour isn't a reliable guide to age.

steps.prompt: Why should Grenache not be served too warm?
steps.explanation: Warmth makes high alcohol more noticeable.

steps.body: A slightly cool Grenache rosé from Provence is one of the most versatile summer wines, from salads to grilled fish.

steps.prompt: Top Châteauneuf-du-Pape can age 15 to 25 years.
steps.explanation: Yes, especially from top producers and vintages.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grenache suits lamb, stews and herby dishes
Serve at 15 to 17 degrees
Top Châteauneuf and Priorat age for decades

steps.explanation: Grenache, often 70% or more.

steps.explanation: Not true. Altitude and granite make it fragrant and fresh.

steps.explanation: Grenache has thin skins.

steps.explanation: Vins doux naturels: fortified sweet wines.

It leads Châteauneuf-du-Pape and much of Spain
Old bush vines give its best wines

modules.title: Cinsault
modules.description: Also spelled Cinsaut, once called Hermitage in South Africa. A light, perfumed southern grape for rosé and fresh reds.

steps.title: Soft and perfumed
steps.body: Cinsault gives pale to medium red wines with strawberry, raspberry, red cherry and floral notes, sometimes herbs. Tannins are low, acidity moderate. It's light, juicy and fragrant, often used to soften blends and in rosé. It's also a parent of Pinotage.

steps.title: Heat-tolerant
steps.body: Cinsault, also spelled Cinsaut, probably comes from southern France, Languedoc or Provence. It tolerates heat and drought well, with large, juicy berries and thin skins. That gives high yields and pale colour, which is why it was used for bulk wine. From old, low-yielding vines, it gives perfumed, elegant reds.

steps.prompt: Why does Cinsault often give pale wines?
steps.explanation: Thin skins and a high juice ratio give pale colour and low tannin.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale ruby colour, bright red fruit and floral aromas, and a soft, light, juicy palate with little tannin. In blends, it brings perfume and softness. It's often compared with Pinot Noir or Gamay for its lightness, but it's warmer and more southern in feel.

steps.prompt: Cinsault tolerates heat and drought well.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why it's common in the south of France, North Africa and South Africa.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault gives light, perfumed, soft red wine
It's heat-tolerant, with thin skins and big berries
Old vines give its most elegant wines

steps.title: France and beyond
steps.body: Cinsault grows across the Languedoc, Provence and the southern Rhône, mainly as a blending grape and in rosé. It was widely planted in Algeria and Morocco, and Lebanon's Bekaa Valley uses it, notably at Château Musar. South Africa and Chile's Itata Valley have old plantings.

steps.title: In blends
steps.body: In Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Côtes du Rhône, Cinsault adds perfume and softness to Grenache and Syrah. In the Languedoc, it softens Carignan. Its low tannin and freshness make blends more approachable. It's one of 13 grapes allowed in Châteauneuf.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Cinsault.
steps.explanation: Cinsault spread around the Mediterranean and beyond.

steps.body: Chile's Itata Valley has old, dry-farmed Cinsault vines planted long ago. Young producers there now make light, fresh, affordable reds from them.

steps.prompt: What does Cinsault add to blends?
steps.explanation: Cinsault is low in tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault grows across the south of France and beyond
It softens and perfumes blends
Lebanon, South Africa and Chile have notable plantings

steps.title: Rosé
steps.body: Cinsault's thin skins, low tannin and fresh red fruit make it ideal for rosé. It gives pale colour fast, with strawberry and floral notes. In Provence, it's a key partner to Grenache in pale, dry rosé. Tavel and Languedoc rosés use it too.

steps.title: South Africa
steps.body: Cinsault, called Hermitage there in the past, was South Africa's most planted red grape until the 1970s, used for bulk wine and brandy. In 1925, Abraham Perold crossed it with Pinot Noir to create Pinotage. Today, young producers make fresh, light Cinsault from old bush vines, a revival of a forgotten grape.
steps.highlight: Parent of Pinotage, revived from old vines

steps.prompt: Which grape did Perold create by crossing Cinsault with Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: Pinotage, in 1925 at Stellenbosch.

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: South Africa's Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years old, many of them Cinsault. Some, in Wellington and Darling, were planted in the early 20th century. Their low yields give concentration to a grape known for lightness. The wines are pale yet complex.

steps.prompt: In South Africa, Cinsault was once called ____.
steps.explanation: Hence the name Pinotage, from Pinot plus Hermitage.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault's thin skins make it ideal for rosé
It's a parent of Pinotage, created in 1925
South Africa's old Cinsault vines are being revived

lessons.title: At the table

steps.title: Light food
steps.body: Cinsault's light body and soft tannin suit Mediterranean food: grilled fish, salads, charcuterie, roast chicken, mezze and tapas. Rosé suits seafood, salads and summer lunches. Its fruitiness handles mild spice, like Moroccan tagines or Lebanese dishes.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve red Cinsault slightly cool, 13 to 15 degrees, and rosé at 8 to 10. Most is best young, within two to three years. Old-vine wines and blends like Château Musar can age much longer.

steps.prompt: What temperature suits a red Cinsault?
steps.explanation: Slightly cool brings out its fruit and freshness.

steps.body: Château Musar, from Lebanon, blends Cinsault with Cabernet Sauvignon and Carignan, and can age for decades. It's a rare chance to taste old Cinsault.

steps.prompt: Most Cinsault is made for long ageing.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most is best young, though some blends and old-vine wines age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault suits Mediterranean food, mezze and grilled fish
Serve red slightly cool and rosé chilled
Most is best young

steps.prompt: What gives Cinsault its pale colour?
steps.explanation: Thin skins and big berries.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Cinsault.
steps.explanation: Cinsault connects many places.

steps.prompt: Cinsault is a parent of Pinotage.
steps.explanation: Yes, with Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Which describe Cinsault?
steps.explanation: Cinsault is pale.

steps.prompt: Cinsault is best served slightly ____.
steps.explanation: About 13 to 15 degrees for reds.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault is light, floral and soft
It's ideal for rosé and softens blends
It's a parent of Pinotage, with old vines in South Africa
Serve it slightly cool with light food

modules.title: Pinot Meunier
modules.description: Also called Meunier, and Schwarzriesling in Germany. Champagne's third grape: fruity, early and frost-resistant.

steps.title: Fruity and supple
steps.body: Pinot Meunier, often simply Meunier, is a black grape giving fruity, supple wines with red apple, red berries, plum and spice. Acidity is fresh, tannins light. It ages faster than Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, so it's prized for fruitiness and roundness in young wines.

steps.title: The miller
steps.body: Meunier means miller in French. The underside of its leaves is covered in fine white hairs, as if dusted with flour. Genetically, it's a mutation of Pinot Noir, with a different outer cell layer. It buds late and ripens early, which helps it avoid spring frost and ripen in cool places.

steps.prompt: Why is the grape called Meunier, the miller?
options: Its leaves look dusted with flour
steps.explanation: Fine white hairs under the leaves look like flour.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In Champagne blends, Meunier adds fruitiness, roundness and a slightly spicy, bready note, and makes the wine approachable young. On its own, still or sparkling, it's fruity and supple, with red apple and berry aromas. It's less structured and long-lived than Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Meunier is a mutation of Pinot Noir.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's genetically very close to Pinot Noir.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier gives fruity, supple wines with red apple and berries
Its name comes from its floury-looking leaves
It's a mutation of Pinot Noir that buds late and ripens early

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Champagne and Germany
objectives: Explain why it suits cool, frosty places

steps.title: Champagne
steps.body: Meunier is about 30% of Champagne's vineyards, mainly in the Vallée de la Marne, where clay soils and frost-prone valleys suit it. It's also grown in the Aisne and the Aube. Outside Champagne, it's found in England, Germany, Australia's Great Western and California, mostly for sparkling wine.

steps.title: Frost and cold
steps.body: Meunier buds late, after the main spring frost risk, and ripens early. On cold, clay soils and in frost pockets, where Chardonnay and Pinot Noir struggle, Meunier gives reliable crops. That's why growers in the Marne valley rely on it.

steps.prompt: Why does Meunier suit Champagne's Vallée de la Marne?
steps.explanation: Late budding avoids spring frost in the valley's cold pockets.

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: In Germany, Meunier is called Schwarzriesling, black Riesling, or Müllerrebe, though it's unrelated to Riesling. It's grown mainly in Württemberg, for light reds and rosés. Some German producers also make sparkling Sekt with it.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its meaning or place.
steps.explanation: Meunier has names and homes in France and Germany.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier is about 30% of Champagne, mainly in the Marne
It buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost
In Germany it's Schwarzriesling, grown in Württemberg

lessons.title: Meunier in Champagne
lessons.subtitle: From supporting role to star
objectives: Explain Meunier's role in Champagne blends
Explain the change in its reputation

steps.title: The blend
steps.body: In Champagne blends, Chardonnay gives finesse and acidity, Pinot Noir gives structure and body, and Meunier gives fruit and roundness. Because it matures faster, it's especially useful in non-vintage Champagne, to drink younger. Krug is one famous house that has long valued it in its blends.

steps.title: A new star
steps.body: Meunier was long seen as the lesser grape, excluded from Grand Cru village status in the past. Since the 2000s, grower Champagnes made only from Meunier, often from old vines in the Marne, have shown its depth and character. Producers like Jérôme Prévost and Egly-Ouriet helped change minds.

steps.prompt: What does each Champagne grape bring?
steps.explanation: Meunier is known for fruit and early approachability, not austerity.

steps.body: Look for Blanc de Noirs made from 100% Meunier. It's a chance to taste the grape's red apple and spice without Chardonnay or Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Which style can be made from 100% Meunier?
steps.explanation: Blanc de Noirs uses only black grapes, which includes Meunier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier brings fruit and roundness to Champagne blends
It's key for non-vintage, approachable young
Pure Meunier Champagnes have raised its reputation

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Meunier
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Fruity bubbles
steps.body: Meunier-rich Champagnes suit food well: charcuterie, roast chicken, salmon, gougères and mild cheeses. Their red fruit and roundness handle slightly richer dishes than lean Blanc de Blancs. Still Meunier, like Coteaux Champenois rouge, suits light meats.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Champagne at 8 to 10 degrees, in a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute to let its aromas show. Meunier-led Champagnes are often best within a few years of release, though top ones from old vines age well.
steps.highlight: 8 to 10 degrees, in a wine glass

steps.prompt: Why might a white wine glass be better than a flute for Meunier Champagne?
steps.explanation: A wider bowl lets aromas gather.

steps.body: Gougères, little cheese puffs from Burgundy, are a classic Champagne snack. Their richness suits a fruity, Meunier-led Champagne.

steps.prompt: Meunier-led Champagnes are generally drunk younger than Chardonnay-led ones.
steps.explanation: Yes. Meunier matures faster, though top examples can age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier Champagne suits gougères, salmon and chicken
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees, in a wine glass
Most are best within a few years

steps.prompt: What does Meunier bring to Champagne blends?
steps.explanation: Fruit and roundness, especially in non-vintage.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Meunier.
steps.explanation: Meunier has a distinct identity.

steps.prompt: Meunier is related to Riesling.
steps.explanation: Not true. Despite its German name, it's a mutation of Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Which are Champagne's three main grapes?
steps.explanation: Gamay is Beaujolais' grape.

steps.prompt: Meunier makes up about ____% of Champagne's vineyards.
steps.explanation: About 30%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Meunier is a fruity, supple mutation of Pinot Noir
It's about 30% of Champagne, mainly in the Marne
It buds late and ripens early, avoiding frost
Pure Meunier Champagnes have raised its profile

modules.title: Nebbiolo
modules.description: Also called Spanna and Chiavennasca. Piedmont's noble grape: pale in colour, high in tannin, scented with roses and tar.

steps.title: Pale but powerful
steps.body: Nebbiolo gives pale ruby to garnet wines with aromas of rose, violet, red cherry, tar, liquorice and dried herbs, often summed up as tar and roses. It has very high tannin and high acidity, with medium to high alcohol. Its pale colour hides its power, a classic surprise in blind tasting.
steps.highlight: Tar and roses, high tannin and acid

steps.title: Fog and late ripening
steps.body: Nebbiolo's name may come from nebbia, fog, which covers the Langhe hills in autumn when it's harvested, often in October. Or from the white bloom on its berries, like a fog. It's one of the first grapes to bud and the last to ripen, so it needs the warmest, best-exposed slopes. Its skins are low in stable colour pigments, hence the pale colour.

steps.prompt: Why is Nebbiolo pale despite being very tannic?
options: Its skins are low in stable colour pigments
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo has plenty of tannin but few stable pigments, so the colour is light.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale ruby with an orange or brick rim, even when quite young. On the nose, rose, cherry, tar and herbs. On the palate, a striking grip of tannin with high acidity. A pale red that grips like Cabernet is almost certainly Nebbiolo.

steps.prompt: Nebbiolo is one of the first grapes to ripen.
steps.explanation: Not true. It buds early but ripens very late, often in October.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo smells of tar and roses, with very high tannin and acidity
Its name may come from nebbia, the autumn fog
Pale colour hides its power

steps.title: Piedmont
steps.body: Nebbiolo's heart is the Langhe and Roero, around Alba, in Piedmont. Barolo and Barbaresco are its great wines. Roero, across the Tanaro river, makes lighter, more perfumed Nebbiolo on sandy soils. Langhe Nebbiolo and Nebbiolo d'Alba are more affordable regional wines.

steps.title: Northern Piedmont and Lombardy
steps.body: In northern Piedmont, Nebbiolo is called Spanna and grows in Gattinara, Ghemme, Boca and Lessona, on volcanic and acidic soils, giving fresher, more mineral wines. In Lombardy's Valtellina, it's called Chiavennasca and grows on steep Alpine terraces. Valle d'Aosta's Donnas also uses it.

steps.prompt: Match each name or place to Nebbiolo.
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo has several homes in northern Italy.

steps.title: Hard to transplant
steps.body: Nebbiolo is very site-specific: it needs warm, sunny slopes, often south-facing, and calcareous marl to show its best. Plantings in California, Australia and Argentina exist, but few match Piedmont. It's one of the least travelled great grapes.

steps.prompt: What is Nebbiolo called in Valtellina?
steps.explanation: Chiavennasca grows on Valtellina's steep Alpine terraces.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo's heart is the Langhe and Roero
It's Spanna in northern Piedmont and Chiavennasca in Valtellina
It's very site-specific and rarely succeeds abroad

lessons.title: Barolo
lessons.subtitle: The king of wines
objectives: Explain the MGA system and the Barolo wars

steps.title: Eleven villages
steps.body: Barolo DOCG covers 11 villages south-west of Alba. Two soil types matter: Tortonian marl, in the west around La Morra and Barolo, gives more perfumed, softer wines; Serravallian sandstone and marl, in the east around Serralunga and Monforte, gives more powerful, tannic wines. Barolo must be 100% Nebbiolo.

steps.title: Ageing and vineyards
steps.body: Barolo must age at least 38 months, 18 in wood; Riserva 62 months. Since 2010, labels can name 181 MGAs, Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, the officially defined vineyard areas, like Cannubi, Brunate and Monprivato. They work like Burgundy's crus.

steps.prompt: Which part of Barolo gives the most powerful, tannic wines?
options: Serralunga and Monforte, in the east
steps.explanation: Serravallian soils in the east give more structure.

steps.title: The Barolo wars
