steps.body: From the 1980s, modernists, like Elio Altare, used short maceration and new French barriques for softer, fruitier Barolo. Traditionalists, like Bartolo Mascarello, kept long maceration and large old Slavonian casks, called botti. The debate split the region. Today many producers blend both approaches.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Barolo has its own vocabulary.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barolo's 11 villages split into Tortonian and Serravallian soils
It ages at least 38 months; labels can name 181 MGAs
The Barolo wars pitted barriques against botti

lessons.title: Barbaresco and beyond
lessons.subtitle: The queen and other Nebbiolos
objectives: Describe Langhe Nebbiolo and northern styles

steps.title: Barbaresco
steps.body: Barbaresco DOCG covers three main villages, Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso, north-east of Alba, near the Tanaro river. It's slightly lower and warmer, so Nebbiolo ripens earlier. Barbaresco must age at least 26 months, 9 in wood; Riserva 50 months. It has 66 MGAs, like Rabajà and Asili.

steps.title: Compared with Barolo
steps.body: Barbaresco is often described as more elegant and approachable earlier, with softer tannins, while Barolo is more powerful. In practice, site and producer matter more than the name. Angelo Gaja, from the 1960s, raised Barbaresco's prestige worldwide. The Produttori del Barbaresco co-operative is renowned for quality.

steps.prompt: Barbaresco must age longer than Barolo.
steps.explanation: Not true. Barbaresco needs 26 months; Barolo 38.

steps.title: Other Nebbiolos
steps.body: Langhe Nebbiolo and Nebbiolo d'Alba offer younger, fruitier versions. Roero gives perfumed wines on sand. Gattinara and Ghemme in the north are fresher, more mineral. Valtellina's Sforzato is made from dried grapes, like Amarone. Together they show Nebbiolo's range.

steps.prompt: Which are Nebbiolo-based wines?
steps.explanation: Barbera d'Asti is made from Barbera.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbaresco ages 26 months and is often more elegant
Gaja and the Produttori raised its prestige
Langhe, Roero, Gattinara and Valtellina show Nebbiolo's range

lessons.title: Tannin and time
lessons.subtitle: Why Nebbiolo needs patience
objectives: Describe how it changes with age

steps.title: Built to last
steps.body: Nebbiolo's very high tannin and acidity make young Barolo and Barbaresco firm, even harsh. Over years, tannins polymerise, linking into longer chains that feel softer. Acidity preserves freshness. Traditionally, Barolo needed 10 years or more before it was ready.

steps.title: How it changes
steps.body: Young Nebbiolo shows red cherry, rose and fresh herbs. With age, it fades to garnet and brick, and develops tar, leather, truffle, dried roses, tobacco and forest floor. The finest can last 30 to 50 years. Modern winemaking has made many approachable sooner, but the best still reward patience.

steps.prompt: What happens to Nebbiolo's tannins over time?
steps.explanation: Tannins bind into longer chains that feel smoother.

steps.body: Decant young Barolo for several hours before serving. Old Barolo needs only a short, gentle decant to remove sediment.

steps.prompt: Order these colours as a Nebbiolo ages.
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo starts pale and turns orange-brown with age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo's high tannin and acidity need time to soften
With age it develops truffle, tar and dried roses
The finest Barolo lasts 30 to 50 years

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Nebbiolo
objectives: Choose the right Nebbiolo for the occasion

steps.title: Piedmont's table
steps.body: Nebbiolo suits Piedmont's rich food: tajarin pasta with butter and white truffle, brasato al Barolo, beef braised in Barolo, roast game, and aged cheeses like Castelmagno. Truffle and Nebbiolo share earthy aromas. Its tannin and acidity cut through richness.

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve at 17 to 18 degrees in a large glass. Decant young wines for hours. Langhe Nebbiolo can be drunk young, within five years. Barbaresco often from 7 to 20 years, Barolo from 10 to 30 years or more. Choose the younger styles for everyday meals.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a Piedmont classic with Barolo?
steps.explanation: Earthy truffle echoes Nebbiolo's aromas.

steps.body: White truffles from Alba are in season from October to December, the same time Nebbiolo is harvested. That's no coincidence for Piedmont's cooking.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Nebbiolo?
steps.explanation: Delicate fish would clash with its tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo suits truffle, braised beef and aged cheese
Serve at 17 to 18 degrees in a large glass
Choose Langhe Nebbiolo for youth, Barolo for patience

steps.prompt: Which aromas define Nebbiolo?
steps.explanation: Tar and roses is its classic description.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its rule or place.
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo has many expressions.

steps.prompt: A pale colour in Nebbiolo means low tannin.
steps.explanation: Not true. Nebbiolo is pale yet very tannic.

steps.prompt: Which develop in Nebbiolo with age?
steps.explanation: Green apple is a young white wine note.

steps.prompt: Barolo labels can name official vineyard areas called ____.
steps.explanation: Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, since 2010.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo is pale but highly tannic and acidic
Barolo and Barbaresco are its great wines
It needs time; the best age for decades
It suits truffle, braised beef and aged cheese

modules.title: Nerello Mascalese
modules.description: Etna's red grape: pale, perfumed and firm, grown high on the slopes of an active volcano.

lessons.title: Meet Nerello Mascalese
lessons.subtitle: Sicily's mountain red
objectives: Describe Nerello Mascalese's flavours and structure

steps.title: Pale and perfumed
steps.body: Nerello Mascalese gives pale ruby wines with red cherry, raspberry, wild herbs, flowers, smoke and a mineral, volcanic edge. Tannins are firm and fine, acidity high. It's often compared to Pinot Noir for its paleness and perfume, and to Nebbiolo for its tannin and structure.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Nerello Mascalese is named after the Mascali plain, below Mount Etna, in eastern Sicily. DNA suggests it's a cross of Sangiovese and Mantonico Bianco. It ripens late, often in October, which suits Etna's altitude: cool nights and long autumns preserve acidity and aroma.

steps.prompt: Which grapes is Nerello Mascalese often compared with?
steps.explanation: It shares Pinot's paleness and perfume and Nebbiolo's tannin.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale ruby colour, red fruit, herbs and a smoky, stony edge, with firm, fine tannins and fresh acidity. It's paler than most southern reds and more structured than you'd guess from its colour.

steps.prompt: Nerello Mascalese is deeply coloured and low in acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's pale and has high acidity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nerello Mascalese is pale, perfumed and firm
It's named after the Mascali plain below Etna
It's compared with Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo

steps.title: Etna
steps.body: Nerello Mascalese grows mainly on the slopes of Mount Etna, Europe's highest active volcano, at 400 to over 1,000 m. Most vineyards are on the north side, around villages like Passopisciaro, Randazzo and Solicchiata. Smaller amounts grow elsewhere in north-east Sicily, like Faro near Messina.

steps.title: Altitude
steps.body: Altitude cools Etna's vineyards: nights can be 15 to 20 degrees cooler than days, keeping acidity and aroma. Etna receives more rain than the rest of Sicily, and harvest can run into late October. It's one of the few places in southern Italy with an almost Alpine climate.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Nerello Mascalese.
steps.explanation: Nerello Mascalese belongs to north-east Sicily.

steps.title: Partners
steps.body: Etna Rosso DOC must be at least 80% Nerello Mascalese. The rest can be Nerello Cappuccio, which adds colour and softness. Old Etna vineyards are often field blends, with white grapes mixed in. Carricante is Etna's main white grape.

steps.prompt: What does Etna Rosso require?
steps.explanation: Nerello Cappuccio can make up the rest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nerello Mascalese grows mainly on Etna's north slope
Altitude gives cool nights and late harvests
Etna Rosso is at least 80% Nerello Mascalese

steps.title: Volcanic soils
steps.body: Etna's soils are made of volcanic sand, ash and lava, of different ages. They're poor, well-drained and rich in minerals. Each lava flow created different soils, so neighbouring vineyards can taste different. Phylloxera struggles in volcanic sand, so many old vines are ungrafted, trained as alberello, bush vines, on terraces.

steps.title: Contrade
steps.body: Etna's vineyards are divided into contrade, local districts, often defined by lava flows. In 2011, Etna DOC recognised 133 contrade, which can appear on labels, like Burgundy's crus. Producers like Frank Cornelissen, Andrea Franchetti of Passopisciaro and Marc de Grazia drove Etna's revival from the early 2000s.

steps.prompt: Why are many Etna vines ungrafted?
steps.explanation: Sandy volcanic soils protect against phylloxera, so many old vines survive on their own roots.

steps.body: Look for a contrada name on an Etna label, such as Rampante or Feudo di Mezzo. Like a Burgundy cru, it tells you exactly where the grapes grew.

steps.prompt: What are contrade on Etna?
steps.explanation: Contrade are local districts, often defined by lava flows.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Etna's volcanic soils vary with each lava flow
Many old vines are ungrafted bush vines on terraces
133 contrade can appear on labels

steps.title: Versatile and fresh
steps.body: Etna Rosso's freshness and fine tannin suit a wide range: grilled tuna and swordfish, pasta with tomato and aubergine, roast pork, lamb with herbs and mushrooms. Its acidity handles tomato; its moderate weight doesn't overwhelm fish.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 15 to 17 degrees. Simple Etna Rosso is good within five years; contrada wines from old vines can age 10 to 20 years, gaining earth and dried flowers. A short decant helps young, tannic examples.

steps.prompt: Why can Etna Rosso pair with grilled tuna?
options: Its moderate weight and fine tannin don't overwhelm the fish
steps.explanation: Lighter body and fine tannin suit meaty fish.

steps.body: Try an Etna Rosso with pasta alla Norma, Sicily's aubergine, tomato and ricotta salata pasta. The wine's freshness meets the tomato.

steps.prompt: Contrada wines from Etna can age 10 to 20 years.
steps.explanation: Yes. Their acidity and tannin let them develop.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Etna Rosso suits tuna, tomato pasta and mushrooms
Serve at 15 to 17 degrees
Contrada wines can age 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Where does Nerello Mascalese mainly grow?
steps.explanation: On Etna's slopes, especially the north side.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Etna.
steps.explanation: Etna has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Many Etna vines are ungrafted.
steps.explanation: Yes, volcanic sand limits phylloxera.

steps.prompt: Which describe Nerello Mascalese?
steps.explanation: Etna Rosso is dry.

steps.prompt: Etna Rosso must be at least ____% Nerello Mascalese.
steps.explanation: At least 80%, with Nerello Cappuccio allowed.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nerello Mascalese is pale, perfumed and firm
It grows high on Etna's volcanic slopes
Contrade name its vineyard districts
It's a fresh, versatile food wine

modules.title: Pinot Noir
modules.description: Also called Spätburgunder in Germany and Pinot Nero in Italy. Thin skin, high acid and a talent for showing where it was grown.

lessons.title: Meet Pinot Noir
lessons.subtitle: Why the palest red is the hardest to grow
objectives: Explain why Pinot Noir is pale

steps.title: Red fruit and earth
steps.body: Pinot Noir gives pale to medium ruby wines with red cherry, raspberry, strawberry and, with age, earthy notes of mushroom, forest floor and game. Tannins are low to medium and silky, acidity high. Its delicacy and complexity make it one of the most prized grapes, and Burgundy is its home.

steps.title: Thin skins, tight bunches
steps.body: Pinot Noir's skins are thin and low in colour pigments, so its wines are pale and low in tannin. Its tight bunches, shaped like a pine cone, which may give it its name, trap moisture and invite rot. It buds early, risking frost, and mutates easily, with hundreds of clones. It's one of the oldest known grapes, recorded in Burgundy in the 14th century.

steps.prompt: Why is Pinot Noir usually pale in colour?
options: Its skins are thin and low in pigment
steps.explanation: Thin skins with few pigments give pale colour and low tannin.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale ruby, translucent colour. On the nose, red cherry, raspberry and often earthy or floral notes. On the palate, high acidity, silky low tannin and a long, fine finish. If you can read a page through the wine and it smells of red fruit and earth, think Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Pinot Noir's tight bunches make it prone to rot.
steps.explanation: Yes. Tight, compact bunches trap moisture, inviting rot in damp weather.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir is pale because of thin, low-pigment skins
It smells of red fruit and, with age, earth and mushroom
Burgundy is its historic home

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Cool climates around the world
objectives: Explain why it needs a cool climate

steps.title: Cool climates
steps.body: Pinot Noir needs a cool climate. In heat, it ripens too fast, losing its delicate aromas and acidity and turning jammy. A long, cool season builds complexity. Its main homes are Burgundy, Champagne, Germany, Oregon, California's coast, New Zealand, Chile's coast, Australia's Victoria and Tasmania.

steps.title: Clones
steps.body: Pinot Noir mutates easily, so there are hundreds of clones, each with different berry size, yield and flavour. Dijon clones, like 115, 667 and 777, developed in Burgundy, spread worldwide from the 1980s. California's Pommard and Wädenswil clones are also widely planted. Many growers plant several clones for complexity.

steps.prompt: What happens to Pinot Noir in a hot climate?
options: It ripens too fast, losing aroma and turning jammy
steps.explanation: Heat speeds ripening, losing the delicacy Pinot is prized for.

steps.title: Mutations
steps.body: Pinot Noir is the parent or ancestor of many grapes. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations; Meunier is another mutation. Crossed with Gouais Blanc, it gave Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté and Melon. That makes it one of the most important grapes in the history of wine.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are mutations of Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: Cabernet Franc is unrelated.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir needs a cool climate
Hundreds of clones, like the Dijon clones, exist
It's the ancestor of Chardonnay, Gamay and others

steps.title: A thin slope
steps.body: The Côte d'Or, the golden slope, is a narrow strip of east and south-east facing vineyards about 50 km long, from Dijon to Santenay. The north, the Côte de Nuits, is mostly Pinot Noir. The south, the Côte de Beaune, makes both reds and Chardonnay. Limestone and marl soils, and mid-slope positions, give the best wines.
steps.highlight: Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune

steps.title: The hierarchy
steps.body: Burgundy ranks vineyards: Grand Cru at the top, then Premier Cru, then village wines, then regional Bourgogne. Grand Crus like Romanée-Conti, Chambertin and Musigny name only the vineyard on the label. Of Burgundy's 33 Grand Crus, most of the reds are in the Côte de Nuits. Each climat has its own character.
steps.highlight: Grand Cru, Premier Cru, village, regional

steps.prompt: Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each level narrows the area and raises expectations.

steps.title: The villages
steps.body: Gevrey-Chambertin gives powerful, structured reds; Chambolle-Musigny elegant, perfumed ones; Vosne-Romanée rich, spicy and silky, home to Romanée-Conti. In the Côte de Beaune, Pommard is firm, Volnay delicate. Same grape, different soils and slopes, distinct wines.

steps.prompt: Match each village to its style.
steps.explanation: Each Burgundy village has its own personality.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Côte d'Or runs from Dijon to Santenay
Burgundy ranks climats from regional to Grand Cru
Each village, like Gevrey or Chambolle, has its own style

lessons.title: Pinot in Champagne
lessons.subtitle: Black grapes, white wine
objectives: Explain Pinot Noir's role in Champagne

steps.title: Structure and body
steps.body: Pinot Noir is about 38% of Champagne's vineyards, the most planted grape there. It gives body, structure and red fruit aromas to blends. The Montagne de Reims, with Grand Crus like Aÿ, Bouzy and Verzenay, and the Côte des Bar, in the south, are its strongholds.

steps.title: White from black
steps.body: Since the colour is in the skins, gentle pressing of whole bunches gives a pale, white juice from black grapes. Blanc de Noirs is white Champagne made only from Pinot Noir and/or Meunier. It's fuller and fruitier than Blanc de Blancs. For rosé Champagne, a little still red Pinot Noir is often blended in.
steps.highlight: Blanc de Noirs: white from black

steps.prompt: How can Champagne make white wine from Pinot Noir?
options: By gentle pressing that keeps the colour out
steps.explanation: Colour is in the skins; gentle whole-bunch pressing keeps it out of the juice.

steps.title: Still Pinot
steps.body: Bouzy, in the Montagne de Reims, is famous for still red wine, sold as Coteaux Champenois rouge. In warmer years, more producers make it. Its light, crisp style shows Pinot Noir at the edge of ripeness, a reminder of how cool Champagne is.

steps.prompt: Pinot Noir is the most planted grape in Champagne.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 38% of vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir is Champagne's most planted grape, giving body
Blanc de Noirs is white Champagne from black grapes
Bouzy makes still red Coteaux Champenois

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: Germany is the world's third largest Pinot Noir producer, after France and the US, as Spätburgunder. Warmer vintages and better winemaking have transformed it since the 1990s. Baden, the Pfalz and the Ahr make elegant, increasingly respected wines, some rivalling good Burgundy.

steps.title: Oregon and California
steps.body: Oregon's Willamette Valley, at Burgundy's latitude, makes Pinot Noir with bright fruit and earthy notes. In California, the Sonoma Coast, Russian River Valley, Santa Rita Hills and Anderson Valley, cooled by ocean fog and wind, give riper, fuller styles. The 2004 film Sideways boosted US Pinot sales.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Pinot Noir.
steps.explanation: Cool climates around the world grow fine Pinot.

steps.title: New Zealand
steps.body: Pinot Noir is New Zealand's most planted red. Central Otago, the southernmost major wine region, gives vivid, fruity wines with fresh acidity. Martinborough gives savoury, structured wines; Marlborough lighter, fruit-driven ones. Australia's Yarra Valley, Mornington and Tasmania also excel.

steps.prompt: What is Pinot Noir called in Germany?
steps.explanation: Spätburgunder, the late Burgundian.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany's Spätburgunder is now respected worldwide
Oregon and coastal California make fine Pinot
New Zealand's Central Otago leads the southern hemisphere

steps.title: Versatile
steps.body: Pinot Noir's low tannin and high acidity make it one of the most food-friendly reds. It suits roast chicken, duck, salmon, tuna, mushrooms and game birds. Burgundy matches boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin. Its low tannin even works with some fish.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 14 to 16 degrees, slightly cooler than big reds, in a large bowl glass. Simple Pinot is best within five years. Top Burgundy ages 10 to 30 years, developing mushroom, truffle, game and forest floor. Decanting isn't always needed; it can lose delicate aromas.

steps.prompt: Why does Pinot Noir pair well with salmon?
options: Its low tannin doesn't clash with fish
steps.explanation: High tannin can make fish taste metallic; Pinot's low tannin avoids that.

steps.body: Mushroom risotto with an older Pinot Noir is a near-perfect match. The earthy notes in both bring each other forward.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: Very hot curry clashes with most reds.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir suits duck, salmon and mushrooms
Serve at 14 to 16 degrees in a large glass
Top Burgundy ages 10 to 30 years

steps.prompt: Why is Pinot Noir hard to grow?
options: Thin skins, tight bunches and early budding
steps.explanation: Its thin skins and tight bunches invite rot, and early budding risks frost.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its place.
steps.explanation: Pinot Noir has many names.

steps.prompt: Pinot Noir is a parent of Chardonnay.
steps.explanation: Yes, crossed with Gouais Blanc.

steps.prompt: Which are major cool-climate homes of Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: The Barossa is hot, Shiraz country.

steps.prompt: Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Grand Cru is the top.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir is pale, silky, with red fruit and earth
It needs cool climates; Burgundy is its home
It's key in Champagne and thrives in Germany, Oregon and New Zealand
It's one of the most food-friendly reds

modules.title: Gewürztraminer
modules.description: Also called Traminer Aromatico in Italy. Lychee, rose and ginger: the most recognisable aromatic white grape.

steps.title: Exotic perfume
steps.body: Gewürztraminer gives deep golden wines with intense aromas of lychee, rose petals, ginger, Turkish delight and sometimes smoke. It's full-bodied, low in acidity and high in alcohol, often 13.5 to 14.5%. Even dry versions can seem sweet because of the perfume. Few grapes are easier to recognise.

steps.title: Spicy Traminer
steps.body: Gewürz means spice in German. The grape is an aromatic, pink-skinned mutation of Savagnin, the Traminer family, named after Tramin, or Termeno, in Alto Adige, Italy. Its pink to red skin gives white wines a deep golden colour. It buds early and ripens to high sugar.

steps.prompt: What does Gewürz mean in German?
steps.explanation: Gewürz means spice, for its spicy aromatic character.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep gold colour, an explosive nose of lychee and rose, and a full, oily palate with low acidity. A slight bitterness on the finish is common. If you smell lychee, it's almost certainly Gewürztraminer.

steps.prompt: Gewürztraminer usually has very high acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's typically low in acidity, which is why it can feel heavy.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gewürztraminer smells of lychee, rose and ginger
It's a pink-skinned mutation of the Traminer family from Tramin
It's full-bodied, low in acidity and high in alcohol

steps.title: Alsace
steps.body: Gewürztraminer's most famous home is Alsace, where it's about 20% of plantings and one of the four noble grapes allowed in Grand Cru wines. Alsace's dry, sunny autumns, in the rain shadow of the Vosges, ripen it fully. Germany, Alto Adige, Austria, New Zealand and Oregon also grow it.
steps.highlight: Alsace: one of four noble grapes

steps.title: Cool climate needed
steps.body: Gewürztraminer needs a cool climate: in heat, it ripens too fast, losing what little acidity it has and becoming flabby and oily. It buds early, so it's sensitive to spring frost, and it's prone to disease. Picking time is critical: too early, the aromas are weak; too late, the acidity disappears.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Gewürztraminer.
steps.explanation: Gewürztraminer thrives in cool regions.

steps.body: In Alsace, a dry Gewürztraminer and a sweet one can look identical. Some producers use a sweetness scale on the back label; check it before you buy.

steps.prompt: Why must Gewürztraminer be picked at exactly the right time?
options: Too early, aromas are weak; too late, acidity disappears
steps.explanation: The window between aromatic ripeness and flabbiness is narrow.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alsace is Gewürztraminer's most famous home
It needs a cool climate to keep balance
Picking time decides aroma and freshness

lessons.title: Aromatics, explained
lessons.subtitle: Where the perfume comes from
objectives: Explain why Gewürztraminer is so aromatic
Compare it with other aromatic grapes

steps.title: Terpenes
steps.body: Gewürztraminer's perfume comes mainly from terpenes, aromatic compounds also found in flowers and citrus. Geraniol smells of rose, linalool of flowers, and cis-rose oxide, found at high levels in Gewürztraminer, of lychee and rose. These compounds sit mostly in the skins and grow as the grape ripens.

steps.title: Why so strong
steps.body: Gewürztraminer has some of the highest terpene levels of any grape, along with Muscat. Unlike thiols in Sauvignon Blanc, which form during fermentation, terpenes are present in the grape itself. Some are free and smell immediately; others are bound to sugars and released slowly by enzymes, during fermentation and ageing.

steps.prompt: Which compound gives Gewürztraminer its lychee aroma?
steps.explanation: Cis-rose oxide is found at high levels in Gewürztraminer, smelling of lychee and rose.

steps.title: Skin contact
steps.body: Because terpenes sit in the skins, some winemakers give Gewürztraminer a few hours of skin contact before pressing to extract more aroma. Too much, though, adds bitterness and phenolic grip. Muscat, Torrontés and Viognier are other terpene-rich grapes, with their own aroma profiles.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are rich in terpenes?
steps.explanation: Cabernet's aromas come mostly from pyrazines and esters, not terpenes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Terpenes like cis-rose oxide and geraniol give its perfume
They sit in the skins, free or bound to sugars
Muscat and Torrontés are other terpene-rich grapes

lessons.title: Late harvest
lessons.subtitle: Sweet Gewürztraminer
objectives: Explain why Gewürztraminer suits sweet styles

steps.title: Vendanges Tardives
steps.body: Alsace's Vendanges Tardives, VT, means late harvest. Grapes stay on the vine into late autumn, concentrating sugar. Gewürztraminer VT needs a minimum potential alcohol of about 15.3%, around 257 g/l of sugar at harvest. The wines can be dry, off-dry or sweet, rich and intensely perfumed.

steps.title: Sélection de Grains Nobles
steps.body: Sélection de Grains Nobles, SGN, is made from berries affected by noble rot, picked one by one. Minimum sugar is higher, about 18.2% potential alcohol for Gewürztraminer. SGN wines are lusciously sweet, with honey, candied fruit and spice, and can age for decades.

steps.prompt: Order these Alsace Gewürztraminer styles from least to most concentrated.
steps.explanation: Later picking and noble rot concentrate sugar further.

steps.title: Why it suits sweetness
steps.body: Gewürztraminer's high natural sugar and intense aroma suit late harvest styles. Its weakness, low acidity, is a challenge: the best VT and SGN come from top sites and vintages where acidity is preserved. Without it, the wines can feel heavy.
steps.highlight: High sugar, but acidity is key

steps.prompt: What is Sélection de Grains Nobles made from?
steps.explanation: SGN uses botrytised berries, selected one by one.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vendanges Tardives is late harvest, dry to sweet
SGN uses noble rot berries and is lusciously sweet
Acidity decides the best sweet Gewürztraminer

steps.title: Spice and cheese
steps.body: Gewürztraminer's perfume and body suit mildly spiced Asian dishes, especially Thai, Indian and Moroccan food, ideally with a touch of sweetness. In Alsace, it's the classic match for Munster, a pungent washed-rind cheese. It also suits foie gras, smoked salmon and ginger.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 10 to 12 degrees, not too cold, or the aromas close up. Most dry Gewürztraminer is best within three to five years. Grand Cru wines age 10 years or more; VT and SGN can age for decades, gaining honey and dried fruit.

steps.prompt: Which cheese is Alsace's classic match for Gewürztraminer?
steps.explanation: Munster's pungency meets Gewürztraminer's perfume.

steps.body: Pair an off-dry Gewürztraminer with Thai green curry. The touch of sugar calms the chilli, and the ginger and lime echo the wine.

steps.prompt: Gewürztraminer should be served ice cold to bring out its aromas.
steps.explanation: Not true. Too cold, its aromas close up. About 10 to 12 degrees is better.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gewürztraminer suits mild spice, Munster and foie gras
Serve at 10 to 12 degrees
Grand Crus and sweet styles age for decades

steps.prompt: Which aroma is Gewürztraminer's giveaway?
steps.explanation: Lychee, with rose and ginger.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Gewürztraminer.
steps.explanation: Gewürztraminer has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Gewürztraminer has high natural acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its low acidity is its main challenge.

steps.prompt: Which compounds contribute to Gewürztraminer's aroma?
steps.explanation: Pyrazines are typical of Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet.

steps.prompt: Alsace's late harvest wines are labelled Vendanges ____.
steps.explanation: Vendanges Tardives, VT.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gewürztraminer smells of lychee, rose and ginger
Terpenes give its intense perfume
Alsace makes it dry, late harvest and SGN
It suits mild spice and pungent cheese

modules.title: Viognier
modules.description: A perfumed, full-bodied white that nearly vanished, saved by Condrieu and now grown worldwide.

steps.title: Rich and perfumed
steps.body: Viognier gives full-bodied whites with apricot, peach, honeysuckle, violet and orange blossom. Acidity is low to medium, alcohol often high, 13.5 to 14.5%, and the texture oily and round. It's aromatic yet dry, a combination that can surprise first-time tasters.

steps.title: Nearly lost
steps.body: Viognier is difficult to grow: low and irregular yields, prone to coulure, poor fruit set, and powdery mildew. By the mid-1960s, only about 14 hectares remained, mostly in Condrieu. Interest grew from the 1980s, and plantings spread to the south of France, California, Australia and beyond. Today there are over 15,000 hectares worldwide.

steps.prompt: Why did Viognier almost disappear?
options: Low, irregular yields made it unprofitable
steps.explanation: Poor fruit set and disease gave low yields, so growers abandoned it.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium to deep lemon or gold colour, an intense apricot and floral nose, and a full, round, oily palate with low acidity and warmth from alcohol. Compared with Gewürztraminer, it's more apricot than lychee, and less spicy.

steps.prompt: Viognier typically has very high acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its acidity is low to medium, which gives it a round, oily texture.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier gives apricot, honeysuckle and violet
It nearly vanished, with about 14 hectares in the 1960s
It's full, round and low in acidity

steps.title: Rhône and beyond
steps.body: Viognier's home is the northern Rhône: Condrieu and Château-Grillet. It's grown in the Languedoc for IGP Pays d'Oc wines, and in California, Virginia, Australia's Eden Valley and Yalumba, and South Africa. Yalumba, in Australia, pioneered it there from 1980.

steps.title: Ripeness matters
steps.body: Viognier needs warmth to develop its perfume, but too much heat makes it flabby and alcoholic. It must be picked at full ripeness, when aromas peak; picked early, it tastes neutral; picked late, it loses acidity and gains bitterness. Like Gewürztraminer, the picking window is narrow.

steps.prompt: What happens if Viognier is picked too early?
steps.explanation: Its aromas develop late in ripening.

steps.title: With Syrah
steps.body: In Côte-Rôtie, up to 20% Viognier can be co-fermented with Syrah, though most use 2 to 5%. Co-fermentation stabilises colour, through a process called co-pigmentation, and adds floral lift. Australian producers adopted the idea for Shiraz Viognier.

steps.prompt: What does Viognier add when co-fermented with Syrah?
steps.explanation: Viognier is a white grape; it doesn't add tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier's home is Condrieu in the northern Rhône
It needs warmth and precise picking
In Côte-Rôtie it's co-fermented with Syrah

steps.title: Steep granite
steps.body: Condrieu is a small appellation in the northern Rhône, about 200 hectares, on steep granite terraces facing south and south-east above the river. The soil, a crumbly granite called arzelle, drains well. Condrieu must be 100% Viognier. The wines are rich, perfumed and dry, mostly drunk within five years.

steps.title: Château-Grillet
steps.body: Château-Grillet, within Condrieu, is one of France's smallest appellations, about 3.5 hectares, owned by one estate. It's a natural amphitheatre facing south. Its wines are more structured and age longer than most Condrieu. Since 2011, it has belonged to the Pinault family, owners of Château Latour.

steps.prompt: What is unusual about Château-Grillet?
options: It's one of France's smallest appellations, owned by one estate
steps.explanation: About 3.5 hectares, a single-estate appellation.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: Most Condrieu is dry, sometimes with oak for texture. Some producers make late harvest or sweet styles in warm years. Producers like Georges Vernay, who helped save the grape, and Yves Cuilleron are key names. Condrieu is usually expensive because of tiny yields and steep, hand-worked vineyards.

steps.prompt: Condrieu must be 100% ____.
steps.explanation: Condrieu is pure Viognier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Condrieu is pure Viognier on steep granite
Château-Grillet is a tiny single-estate appellation
Most Condrieu is dry and best young

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Viognier
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Rich and aromatic dishes
steps.body: Viognier's body and perfume suit rich dishes: roast chicken with apricots, pork, lobster, crab, creamy sauces, and mildly spiced Asian or Moroccan food. Apricot and ginger in dishes echo it. Avoid very acidic or delicate dishes, which make it seem heavy.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 10 to 13 degrees, not too cold, or its aromas close. Most Viognier is best within three years, when the perfume is fresh. With age, it loses aroma quickly. Château-Grillet and top Condrieu can age a little longer.

steps.prompt: Why is most Viognier best drunk young?
steps.explanation: Its fresh aromas are its charm, and they fade.

steps.body: Try Viognier with a Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots. The fruit and spice match the wine's perfume.

steps.prompt: Viognier generally ages as long as Riesling.
steps.explanation: Not true. Low acidity means most Viognier fades within a few years.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier suits rich, aromatic dishes and apricots
Serve at 10 to 13 degrees
Most is best within three years

steps.prompt: Which aroma is typical of Viognier?
steps.explanation: Apricot, peach and honeysuckle.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Viognier.
steps.explanation: Viognier's story runs from the Rhône to Australia.

steps.prompt: In the 1960s only about 14 hectares of Viognier remained.
steps.explanation: Yes. It was close to extinction.

steps.prompt: Which describe Viognier?
steps.explanation: White wines like Viognier have little tannin.

steps.prompt: Viognier is best served at about ____ degrees.
steps.explanation: Not too cold, to keep the aromas open.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viognier is full, perfumed and low in acidity
It nearly vanished and was saved by Condrieu
It lifts Syrah in Côte-Rôtie
It's best young, with rich, aromatic food

modules.title: Marsanne
modules.description: A full-bodied Rhône white of honey, almond and pear, often with Roussanne, and capable of long ageing.

steps.title: Rich and subtle
steps.body: Marsanne gives full-bodied whites with pear, quince, honeysuckle, almond and, with age, honey and nuts. Acidity is low to medium, alcohol moderate to high, texture waxy and rich. It's less aromatic than Viognier, more about texture than perfume.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Marsanne takes its name from the village of Marsanne, near Montélimar in the Rhône. It's a northern Rhône grape, closely linked to Roussanne, its frequent blending partner. It's more productive and reliable than Roussanne, but can be flabby if overcropped or picked too late.

steps.prompt: What is Marsanne's typical texture?
steps.explanation: Marsanne is full-bodied and waxy, more about texture than aroma.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for medium lemon to gold colour, a subtle nose of pear, almond and flowers, and a full, waxy palate with low to moderate acidity. Young, it can seem quiet; with age, it develops honey and nutty notes. Compared with Viognier, it's less perfumed and less apricot.

steps.prompt: Marsanne is more aromatic than Viognier.
steps.explanation: Not true. Viognier is far more perfumed. Marsanne is about texture.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marsanne gives pear, almond and a waxy texture
It's named after a Rhône village and pairs with Roussanne
It's subtle young and honeyed with age

steps.title: The northern Rhône
steps.body: Marsanne is the main white grape of the northern Rhône's Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray, where it also makes sparkling wine. It's often blended with Roussanne, which adds aroma, acidity and finesse. In the south, it appears in Côtes du Rhône blends.

steps.title: Roussanne
steps.body: Roussanne, its partner, has russet skins, from roux, and gives more aromatic, herbal, elegant wines, with better acidity. But it's harder to grow, prone to disease and irregular yields. Marsanne gives body and reliability; Roussanne gives perfume and freshness. Together they make balanced blends.
steps.highlight: Marsanne for body; Roussanne for freshness

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its contribution.
steps.explanation: Rhône whites are built from complementary grapes.

steps.title: Victoria
steps.body: Australia's Victoria has some of the world's oldest Marsanne vines, at Tahbilk, in the Nagambie Lakes, planted in 1927. Tahbilk's Marsanne is unoaked, lean and citrus when young, turning honeyed and toasty after 10 years. It shows how well Marsanne can age.

steps.prompt: Where are some of the oldest Marsanne vines in the world?
steps.explanation: Tahbilk's Marsanne vines date from 1927.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marsanne leads the whites of Hermitage and Saint-Joseph
Roussanne adds aroma and acidity
Australia's Tahbilk has vines from 1927

lessons.title: White Hermitage
lessons.subtitle: A white that ages for decades

steps.title: The hill
steps.body: Hermitage is a single granite hill above Tain-l'Hermitage, facing south. About a quarter of its wine is white, mostly Marsanne with some Roussanne. The granite and loess, with full southern sun, give rich, powerful whites. Chapoutier and Jean-Louis Chave are famous producers.

steps.title: A strange ageing curve
steps.body: White Hermitage is rich and fruity when young, then often closes up for several years, from about year 3 to 10, showing little aroma. After that, it opens again with honey, nuts, beeswax and dried fruit. The best can age 20 to 50 years, despite modest acidity, thanks to their concentration and phenolics.

steps.prompt: White Hermitage often goes through a closed, quiet phase before opening again with age.
steps.explanation: Yes. Many go quiet for several years, then develop honey and nutty complexity.

steps.title: Oak and style
steps.body: Producers make white Hermitage in different ways: some ferment and age in oak barrels for richness; others use old wood or steel to keep purity. Some sweet vin de paille, from dried grapes, is made in tiny amounts. Crozes-Hermitage whites are lighter and more affordable.
steps.highlight: Oaked or pure; sweet vin de paille

steps.prompt: Why can white Hermitage age for decades?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is modest; concentration and phenolic structure carry it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: White Hermitage is mostly Marsanne from a granite hill
It often closes up, then reopens with honey and nuts
The best age 20 to 50 years

steps.title: Rich dishes
steps.body: Marsanne's body and texture suit rich dishes: roast chicken, veal in cream sauce, lobster, crab, scallops, and dishes with butter or almonds. Aged white Hermitage suits truffle, mushrooms and hard cheeses like Comté. Avoid very acidic or very spicy food.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 11 to 13 degrees, not too cold. Simple Marsanne is good young. White Hermitage is best either within two to three years or after ten. Tahbilk's aged Marsanne shows how unoaked versions develop too.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits an aged white Hermitage?
steps.explanation: Rich, earthy dishes match its honeyed, nutty development.

steps.body: Decant an older white Hermitage. Like a red, it benefits from air, opening its nutty, honeyed aromas.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Marsanne?
steps.explanation: Acidic dressings make low-acid wines taste flat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marsanne suits lobster, veal and Comté
Serve at 11 to 13 degrees
Drink white Hermitage young or after ten years

steps.prompt: What does Roussanne add to Marsanne?
steps.explanation: Roussanne brings perfume and freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Marsanne.
steps.explanation: Marsanne connects the Rhône and Victoria.

steps.prompt: Marsanne is known for intense, explosive aromas.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's subtle, more about texture.

steps.prompt: Which describe Marsanne?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is low to medium.

steps.prompt: White Hermitage can age for 20 to ____ years.
steps.explanation: The best last decades.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marsanne is full, waxy and subtle
It leads Rhône whites, often with Roussanne
White Hermitage ages for decades after a closed phase
Australia's Tahbilk shows old-vine Marsanne

modules.title: Chardonnay
modules.description: The world's most famous white grape: a neutral canvas for place and winemaking, from Chablis to Champagne.

lessons.title: Meet Chardonnay
lessons.subtitle: The winemaker's canvas
objectives: Explain why it's called a canvas

steps.title: Many faces
steps.body: Chardonnay can taste of green apple and lemon, or peach and melon, or pineapple and mango, depending on climate. Winemaking adds butter, toast, vanilla, hazelnut or cream. Acidity ranges from high to medium, body from light to full. With Spain's Airén, it's one of the two most planted white grapes in the world.
steps.highlight: Climate sets fruit; winemaking adds the rest

steps.title: Parents and character
steps.body: DNA shows Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, probably in Burgundy in the Middle Ages. It's named after the village of Chardonnay, in the Mâconnais. Its own aromas are fairly neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking clearly. It buds early, risking frost, but ripens reliably.

steps.prompt: Why is Chardonnay called a winemaker's canvas?
options: Its own aromas are neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking
steps.explanation: Neutral fruit lets climate and winemaking choices show clearly.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Because it varies so much, look for clues: high acidity and green fruit with a chalky edge suggest cool Chablis; nutty, buttery richness with toast suggests oaked Burgundy or California; tropical fruit and soft acidity suggest a warm climate. A lack of strong aromatic signature is itself a clue.

steps.prompt: Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's a sibling of Gamay, Aligoté and Melon.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay's fruit ranges from apple to pineapple with climate
It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc from Burgundy
Its neutral character reflects site and winemaking

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Everywhere wine is made
objectives: Explain the ABC backlash and revival

steps.title: A world grape
steps.body: Chardonnay's home is Burgundy and Champagne. It grows in almost every wine country: California, Australia, Chile, South Africa, New Zealand, Italy, Oregon, Argentina and England. It adapts to cool and warm climates and many soils, though limestone and chalk are prized.

steps.title: Climate and style
steps.body: Cool climates, like Chablis, Tasmania or Sonoma Coast, give lean, citrus Chardonnay with high acidity. Moderate climates, like the Côte de Beaune or Margaret River, give stone fruit and balance. Warm climates, like inland California or Australia's Riverland, give tropical fruit and lower acidity.

steps.prompt: Match each climate to its Chardonnay.
steps.explanation: Climate is the first key to Chardonnay's style.

steps.title: Backlash and revival
steps.body: In the 1990s, heavily oaked, buttery Chardonnays became so common that some drinkers turned away, a trend called ABC, Anything But Chardonnay. Since the 2000s, producers have picked earlier, used less new oak and blocked malolactic more often, giving fresher, more elegant wines.

steps.prompt: What did ABC stand for in the 1990s?
steps.explanation: A backlash against heavily oaked Chardonnay.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay grows almost everywhere, from Burgundy to Chile
Climate shifts it from citrus to tropical
After the ABC backlash, many styles became leaner

lessons.title: Chablis and the Côte de Beaune
lessons.subtitle: Burgundy's white heart

steps.title: Chablis
steps.body: Chablis, in northern Burgundy, is cool and continental, with frost risk. Its Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils, gives lean, mineral, high-acid wines with green apple, lemon and a flinty, saline edge. Most Chablis is unoaked; Grand Crus often see some oak. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Crus.

steps.title: The Côte de Beaune
steps.body: In the Côte de Beaune, south of Beaune, Chardonnay makes some of the world's greatest whites. Meursault is rich, nutty and buttery; Puligny-Montrachet elegant and floral; Chassagne-Montrachet fuller. Grand Crus like Le Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne are fermented and aged in oak, with great ageing potential.

steps.prompt: What is special about Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil?
steps.explanation: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay are full of fossilised oyster shells.

steps.title: Comparing them
steps.body: Chablis is cooler, leaner and more mineral, usually less oak. The Côte de Beaune is warmer, with riper fruit, more body and oak. Further south, the Mâconnais, with Pouilly-Fuissé, gives rounder, fruitier, good-value wines. All are 100% Chardonnay.
steps.highlight: Chablis lean; Côte de Beaune rich

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its style.
steps.explanation: Burgundy shows every side of Chardonnay.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte de Beaune makes rich, oaked whites
The Mâconnais gives rounder, good-value wines

steps.title: Oak
steps.body: Barrel fermentation and ageing add vanilla, toast, spice and a rounder texture. New oak adds more; older barrels mostly add texture and slow oxygen. Burgundy often uses 20 to 50% new oak for top wines. Oak needs ripe, concentrated fruit, or it overwhelms the wine.

steps.title: Malolactic and lees
steps.body: Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, adding a buttery note from diacetyl and lowering acidity. Lees ageing leaves the wine on dead yeast for months, adding creaminess and protecting it from oxidation. Bâtonnage, stirring the lees, increases these effects. Most Burgundy whites use all three.
steps.highlight: Butter from malolactic; cream from lees

steps.prompt: Match each technique to its effect.
steps.explanation: Each winemaking choice leaves its mark.

steps.body: If a Chardonnay tastes of butter and popcorn, it went through malolactic. If it tastes of toast and vanilla, it saw new oak. If it's pure lemon and apple, it was probably made in steel.

steps.prompt: Which techniques make Chardonnay richer and rounder?
steps.explanation: Early picking and steel keep it lean and fresh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Oak adds vanilla, toast and texture
Malolactic adds butter and softens acidity
Lees and bâtonnage add creaminess

lessons.title: Chardonnay in sparkling wine
lessons.subtitle: The finesse of bubbles
objectives: Name other sparkling regions using it

steps.title: Champagne
steps.body: Chardonnay is about 30% of Champagne's vineyards, concentrated in the Côte des Blancs, on chalk. It brings finesse, acidity, citrus and floral notes, and the ability to age long. Grand Cru villages like Cramant, Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Oger give some of its finest sparkling wines.

steps.title: Blanc de Blancs
steps.body: Blanc de Blancs, white from whites, is Champagne made only from white grapes, almost always Chardonnay. It's lean and citrus when young, developing brioche, hazelnut and toast with age. Salon, which makes only vintage Blanc de Blancs from Le Mesnil, and Krug's Clos du Mesnil are famous examples.
steps.highlight: Blanc de Blancs: white from whites

steps.prompt: What is Blanc de Blancs Champagne made from?
steps.explanation: Blanc de Blancs means white from whites.

steps.title: Beyond Champagne
steps.body: Chardonnay is key in traditional method wines worldwide: Franciacorta, Trentodoc, Crémant de Bourgogne, English sparkling wine, Tasmania and California. Its high acidity in cool climates and neutral fruit take on the bready, toasty notes of lees ageing well.

steps.prompt: Which are known for Chardonnay-based sparkling wine?
steps.explanation: The Mosel is known for still Riesling.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay is about 30% of Champagne, mostly in the Côte des Blancs
Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes
Franciacorta, England and Tasmania also use it

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Chardonnay
objectives: Pair different Chardonnay styles with food

steps.title: Match the style
steps.body: Lean Chablis suits oysters, shellfish and goat's cheese. Rich, oaked Chardonnay suits lobster, roast chicken, creamy sauces and pork. Tropical, warm-climate Chardonnay suits grilled chicken and mildly spiced dishes. Blanc de Blancs suits sushi, caviar and fried food.
steps.highlight: Chablis with oysters; oaked with lobster

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve lean Chardonnay at 8 to 10 degrees, rich oaked styles at 10 to 13. Most New World Chardonnay is best within three to five years. Grand Cru Chablis and Côte de Beaune age 10 to 20 years, developing honey, nuts and mushroom. Premature oxidation, or premox, affected some Burgundy from the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Which Chardonnay style suits oysters best?
steps.explanation: Chablis' acidity and saline edge match oysters.

steps.body: Serve rich, oaked Chardonnay slightly warmer than other whites. Too cold, its texture and aromas close up.

steps.prompt: Some Burgundy whites from the 1990s suffered from premature oxidation.
steps.explanation: Yes. Premox affected some vintages, with wines browning and losing fruit early.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Match the Chardonnay style to the dish
Serve lean styles colder, rich ones a little warmer
Top Burgundy ages 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its style.
steps.explanation: Chardonnay takes many forms.

steps.prompt: What does malolactic conversion add to Chardonnay?
steps.explanation: Lactic acid and diacetyl give butter and softness.

steps.prompt: Most Chablis is aged in new oak.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most Chablis is unoaked; some Grand Crus use oak.

steps.prompt: Which are Chardonnay's parents?
steps.explanation: Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.

steps.prompt: Chablis' famous soil is called ____.
steps.explanation: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay with oyster fossils.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay is neutral, reflecting climate and winemaking
Chablis, the Côte de Beaune and Champagne are its benchmarks
Oak, malolactic and lees shape its richness
It suits everything from oysters to lobster

modules.title: Sémillon
modules.description: Bordeaux's golden grape: the heart of Sauternes and the secret of Hunter Valley's long-lived whites.

steps.title: Subtle and textured
steps.body: Sémillon gives medium to full-bodied whites with lemon, lanolin, beeswax, grass and, with age, honey, toast and nuts. Acidity is low to medium, texture waxy and oily. Young, it can seem neutral; its strength is texture and ageing. It's Bordeaux's most planted white grape.

steps.title: Thin skins
steps.body: Sémillon's thin, golden skins make it prone to rot, including noble rot, Botrytis cinerea. That's a weakness in wet years but a gift for sweet wine. It's vigorous and productive. In Bordeaux it's often blended with Sauvignon Blanc, which adds acidity and aroma to Sémillon's body.
steps.highlight: Thin skins, prone to noble rot

steps.prompt: Why is Sémillon so suited to noble rot?
steps.explanation: Thin skins let Botrytis cinerea attack easily.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale to medium lemon colour, a subtle nose of lemon, lanolin and sometimes grass, and a waxy, round palate. In blends with Sauvignon, Sémillon adds weight and texture. Aged Sémillon is unmistakable: toast, honey and lemon curd, even without oak.

steps.prompt: Sémillon has very thick skins.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its thin skins make it prone to rot and noble rot.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sémillon gives lemon, lanolin and a waxy texture
Thin skins make it prone to noble rot
It's often blended with Sauvignon Blanc

steps.title: Bordeaux
steps.body: Sémillon is Bordeaux's most planted white grape. It's blended with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle in dry whites, from Entre-Deux-Mers to Pessac-Léognan, and in sweet wines, from Sauternes, Barsac, Loupiac and Cadillac. Bergerac and Monbazillac, nearby, also use it.

steps.title: Australia and beyond
steps.body: Australia is Sémillon's other great home: the Hunter Valley for unoaked, long-lived dry wines; Margaret River for Sémillon Sauvignon Blanc blends; the Barossa for richer, oaked styles. South Africa once had over 90% Sémillon in the 19th century; now old vines remain. Chile and Argentina grow it too.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Sémillon.
steps.explanation: Sémillon shines dry and sweet.

steps.title: With Sauvignon
steps.body: Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc complement each other: Sémillon gives body, texture and ageing potential; Sauvignon gives aroma and acidity. In dry Bordeaux, the blend can age for decades. In Sauternes, Sémillon usually makes up about 80%, with Sauvignon adding freshness.

steps.prompt: What does Sémillon add to a blend with Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: Sauvignon adds the acidity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sémillon is Bordeaux's most planted white
Australia's Hunter and Margaret River are key homes
With Sauvignon, it balances body and freshness

lessons.title: Noble rot and Sauternes
lessons.subtitle: Sémillon's sweet glory
objectives: Explain how noble rot affects Sémillon

steps.title: The Ciron's mist
steps.body: In Sauternes and Barsac, the cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne, creating autumn mists. Morning humidity lets Botrytis cinerea grow; sunny afternoons stop grey rot. On Sémillon's thin skins, the fungus shrivels berries, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour, and adding honey, apricot and marmalade.

steps.title: Sauternes
steps.body: Pickers pass through the vineyard several times, called tries, choosing only botrytised berries. Yields can be tiny, a glass of wine per vine at Château d'Yquem. Wines are fermented and aged in oak for up to three years, reaching about 13 to 14% alcohol and 100 to 150 g/l of sugar.

steps.prompt: Put the making of Sauternes in order.
items: Mist and sun bring noble rot
steps.explanation: Noble rot first, then careful selection, then slow fermentation and ageing.

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Sauternes is one of the longest-lived wines. Over decades, it darkens from gold to amber, developing crème brûlée, saffron, dried apricot and marmalade. Good vintages last 50 years or more. Château d'Yquem, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855, is the most famous.

steps.prompt: What is a trie in Sauternes?
options: A pass through the vineyard to pick botrytised berries
steps.explanation: Several tries pick only the berries that are ready.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sémillon
Pickers make several tries; yields are tiny
Sauternes ages for decades, darkening to amber

lessons.title: Hunter Valley Sémillon
lessons.subtitle: A dry wine that ages like magic

steps.title: Picked early
steps.body: The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney, is hot and humid, with rain often at harvest. Growers pick Sémillon early, at around 10 to 11% alcohol, before the rain and rot. The wines are fermented in steel, without oak or malolactic, and bottled early. Young, they're lean, lemony and grassy, with high acidity.

steps.title: The transformation
steps.body: With 5 to 10 years in bottle, often under screw cap, Hunter Sémillon transforms: it develops toast, honey, lanolin, lemon curd and nutty notes, as if it had been oaked. It isn't: these flavours come from bottle ageing. The best can age 20 years or more.

steps.prompt: Hunter Valley Sémillon's toasty notes come from oak ageing.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's usually unoaked; toast and honey develop with bottle age.

steps.body: If you find a 10-year-old Hunter Valley Sémillon, open it next to a young one. The difference shows how far bottle ageing can take a simple, unoaked wine.

steps.prompt: Why is Hunter Sémillon picked so early?
options: To avoid harvest rain and rot, and keep acidity
steps.explanation: Early picking keeps freshness and avoids the region's harvest rains.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Hunter Sémillon is picked early, at 10 to 11%, unoaked
Young, it's lean and lemony
With age it gains toast and honey, without oak

steps.title: Dry Sémillon
steps.body: Young Hunter Sémillon suits oysters, sashimi and light seafood. Aged Hunter and dry Bordeaux blends suit roast chicken, crab, lobster, and creamy fish dishes. Margaret River Sémillon Sauvignon suits salads, goat's cheese and summer food.

steps.title: Sauternes
steps.body: Sauternes suits foie gras, a Bordeaux classic, and blue cheese, especially Roquefort, whose salt balances the sweetness. It also suits fruit tarts, crème brûlée and spicy Asian dishes. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Avoid desserts much sweeter than the wine.

steps.prompt: Match each Sémillon to a pairing.
steps.explanation: Each style finds its dish.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve dry Sémillon at 8 to 11 degrees. Young Hunter is crisp and lean; wait 10 years for its magic. Dry white Bordeaux ages 10 to 20 years. Sauternes ages 20 to 50 years or more.

steps.prompt: Roquefort and Sauternes is a classic pairing.
steps.explanation: Yes. Salt balances sugar, and the wine's acidity cuts the cheese's fat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Young dry Sémillon suits seafood; aged suits chicken and crab
Sauternes suits foie gras and Roquefort
Sémillon rewards ageing, dry or sweet

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Sémillon
objectives: Compare its dry and sweet styles

steps.prompt: Why does Sémillon suit noble rot?
steps.explanation: Thin skins let botrytis attack.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Sémillon.
steps.explanation: Sémillon's two great homes are Bordeaux and the Hunter.

steps.prompt: Hunter Sémillon is picked very ripe, at 14% alcohol.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's picked early, at 10 to 11%.

steps.prompt: Which describe Sémillon?
steps.explanation: White Sémillon has little tannin.

steps.prompt: Sémillon is usually blended with Sauvignon ____ in Bordeaux.
steps.explanation: Sauvignon Blanc adds acidity and aroma.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sémillon is waxy, lemony and ages beautifully
It's the heart of Sauternes, thanks to thin skins
Hunter Valley makes unoaked Sémillon that turns toasty
It pairs from oysters to foie gras

modules.title: Pinot Gris
modules.description: Also called Pinot Grigio in Italy and Grauburgunder in Germany. One grape, from light and crisp to rich and spicy.

lessons.title: Meet Pinot Gris
lessons.subtitle: The grey Pinot
objectives: Explain its link to Pinot Noir

steps.title: Pear and spice
steps.body: Pinot Gris gives white wines with pear, apple, white peach, lemon and, in richer styles, honey, spice and smoke. Acidity ranges from fresh to moderate, body from light to full. Its pinkish-grey skins can give a coppery tint. It's one of the world's most popular white grapes.

steps.title: A Pinot mutation
steps.body: Pinot Gris is a colour mutation of Pinot Noir: the same DNA, but with less pigment in the skin, which is greyish-pink. Gris means grey in French; Grigio in Italian. It ripens early and reaches high sugar, so it can give fairly high alcohol, with lowish acidity if picked late.
steps.highlight: Grey-pink skin, a Pinot Noir mutation

steps.prompt: What is Pinot Gris genetically?
options: A colour mutation of Pinot Noir
A cross of Riesling and Chardonnay
steps.explanation: It shares Pinot Noir's DNA, with lighter skin.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Light Pinot Grigio is pale, with neutral apple and lemon and crisp acidity. Richer Pinot Gris is deeper lemon or slightly copper, with pear, spice and honey, and a fuller, oilier texture. If you see a faint pink tint in a white, consider Pinot Gris.
steps.highlight: Pale and crisp, or rich and spicy

steps.prompt: Pinot Gris skins are greyish-pink.
steps.explanation: Yes. That's why Gris, grey, is in its name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Gris gives pear, apple and, when rich, spice and honey
It's a colour mutation of Pinot Noir
Its pink-grey skins can tint the wine

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Italy, Alsace and beyond
objectives: Explain how climate and yield shape it

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Italy is the largest producer, mostly in the north-east: Veneto, Friuli and Alto Adige. Alsace makes its richest versions. Germany calls it Grauburgunder, for dry styles, or Ruländer, for sweeter ones. Oregon, New Zealand, Australia and Hungary, where it's Szürkebarát, grow it too.

steps.title: Yield and picking
steps.body: The style depends heavily on yield and picking time. High yields and early picking give light, neutral, crisp wine. Low yields and later picking give concentrated, rich, spicy wines with more alcohol. The grape itself is the same; the grower's choices make the difference.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its country.
steps.explanation: One grape, several names.

steps.title: Delle Venezie
steps.body: In Italy, the Delle Venezie DOC, created in 2017, covers Pinot Grigio from Veneto, Friuli and Trentino, the world's largest Pinot Grigio appellation. It aimed to raise quality and control the huge volume produced for export. Alto Adige and Collio make more serious examples.

steps.prompt: What gives a richer, spicier Pinot Gris?
steps.explanation: High yields and early picking give the light, neutral style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Italy makes the most; Alsace the richest
Yield and picking time decide the style
Delle Venezie DOC covers Italy's huge Pinot Grigio output

lessons.title: Grigio or Gris
lessons.subtitle: Two names, two styles
objectives: Explain what Pinot Grigio usually means
Explain what Pinot Gris usually means

steps.title: Pinot Grigio
steps.body: Pinot Grigio, in the Italian style, is light-bodied, crisp and neutral, with lemon, green apple and almond. It's usually picked early, fermented cool in steel and bottled young. Its simplicity and freshness made it one of the best-selling white wines in the UK and US. Producers elsewhere use the name to signal this style.

steps.title: Pinot Gris
steps.body: Pinot Gris, in the Alsace style, is fuller and richer, with ripe pear, honey, ginger, smoke and spice, sometimes off-dry. It's picked riper, often from low-yield sites. Alsace's dry, sunny autumns and Grand Cru vineyards give some of the most concentrated versions. Oregon and New Zealand often use the name for richer styles.

steps.prompt: A New Zealand label says Pinot Gris rather than Pinot Grigio. What does it most likely signal?
steps.explanation: Producers use Gris to signal the fuller Alsace style.

steps.body: When choosing, read the name as a style guide: Grigio for a light aperitif, Gris for a fuller wine with food.

steps.prompt: Alsace Pinot Gris can be off-dry.
steps.explanation: Yes. Ripe Alsace Pinot Gris sometimes has some residual sugar.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Grigio means light, crisp and neutral
Pinot Gris means rich, spicy and riper
Alsace makes the most concentrated Pinot Gris

steps.title: Copper colour
steps.body: Ramato means copper-coloured in Italian. It's a traditional style of Pinot Grigio from Friuli and Veneto, made with skin contact. Because Pinot Gris has pink-grey skins, leaving the juice on them for hours or days gives a copper or salmon hue, plus more body, texture and flavour.

steps.title: A Venetian tradition
steps.body: Ramato was traditional in the Republic of Venice, where Pinot Grigio was made this way. Modern, pale Pinot Grigio, pressed quickly, became popular from the 1960s. Since the 2000s, producers have revived ramato, sometimes with longer skin contact, linking it to the orange wine movement.

steps.prompt: Why does ramato have a copper colour?
options: Skin contact with Pinot Gris' pink-grey skins
steps.explanation: The skins' pigment tints the juice.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body: Ramato is fuller and more textured than standard Pinot Grigio, with red apple, peach, dried herbs, and a light tannic grip. It's dry, and works well with food. Its colour sits between rosé and orange wine.

steps.prompt: Which describe ramato?
steps.explanation: Ramato is dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Ramato is copper-coloured Pinot Grigio made with skin contact
It's a Venetian tradition revived since the 2000s
It's fuller and more textured than standard Pinot Grigio

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Pinot Gris
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Match the style
steps.body: Light Pinot Grigio suits aperitifs, salads, light seafood and simple pasta. Rich Pinot Gris suits roast pork, chicken, smoked fish, mushroom dishes and mildly spiced Asian food. Ramato suits charcuterie, risotto and grilled fish. Off-dry Alsace Pinot Gris suits foie gras.
steps.highlight: Grigio light; Gris with richer food

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Pinot Grigio at 7 to 9 degrees, Pinot Gris and ramato at 10 to 12. Most Pinot Grigio is best within a year or two. Alsace Grand Cru Pinot Gris can age 10 years or more, developing honey and smoke.
steps.highlight: Grigio young; Grand Cru Gris ages

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a rich Alsace Pinot Gris?
steps.explanation: Rich Pinot Gris matches pork and fruit.

steps.body: An off-dry Alsace Pinot Gris with smoked salmon or a lightly spiced Thai dish brings out its ginger and smoky notes.

steps.prompt: Most Pinot Grigio is made for long ageing.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's best young and fresh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Grigio suits light food; Pinot Gris richer dishes
Serve Grigio colder than Gris
Grand Cru Pinot Gris can age 10 years or more

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Names signal style.

steps.prompt: What is Pinot Gris' relationship to Pinot Noir?
steps.explanation: Same DNA, lighter skin.

steps.prompt: Italy is the largest producer of Pinot Grigio.
steps.explanation: Yes, mostly in the north-east.

steps.prompt: Which give a richer Pinot Gris?
steps.explanation: Early picking gives the light style.

steps.prompt: Ramato means ____ in Italian.
steps.explanation: For its copper hue from skin contact.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Gris is a pink-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir
Grigio means light and crisp; Gris rich and spicy
Ramato is copper-coloured skin-contact Grigio
Match the style to the food

modules.title: Furmint
modules.description: Tokaj's grape: searing acidity, noble rot and smoky, mineral dry wines.

steps.title: High acidity
steps.body: Furmint gives whites with very high acidity and flavours of lemon, green apple, quince, pear, smoke and a mineral, flinty edge. With age or botrytis, honey, apricot and marmalade appear. Body ranges from medium to full; alcohol can be high in dry styles.

steps.title: Origins and noble rot
steps.body: Furmint is Hungary's signature grape, probably native to the Tokaj region; it's also grown in Slovenia as Šipon. It ripens late, which keeps acidity high. Its thin skins become thinner as it ripens, making it highly susceptible to noble rot, Botrytis cinerea. That's why it's the main grape of Tokaji Aszú.

steps.prompt: Why is Furmint so suited to noble rot?
options: Its skins thin as it ripens
steps.explanation: Thin skins let botrytis attack.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Dry Furmint is pale lemon, with citrus, quince and smoky, flinty notes, high acidity and a firm, mineral palate. Sweet Tokaji is gold to amber, with apricot, marmalade and honey, balanced by vivid acidity. That acidity is the common thread.

steps.prompt: Furmint has low acidity.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its very high acidity is its signature.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Furmint has very high acidity, with quince and smoke
It's native to Tokaj and susceptible to noble rot
Its acidity links dry and sweet styles

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Tokaj and beyond
objectives: Name other places that grow it

steps.title: Tokaj
steps.body: Furmint covers about 60 to 70% of Tokaj's vineyards, in north-east Hungary. The region's volcanic soils, from clay and loess to rhyolite and andesite, give mineral, smoky wines. The Bodrog and Tisza rivers create autumn mists, ideal for noble rot. Hárslevelű and Sárgamuskotály, a Muscat, are its partners.

steps.title: Beyond Tokaj
steps.body: Furmint also grows in Somló, a tiny Hungarian volcanic hill known for powerful dry whites, and in Slovenia, as Šipon, in Štajerska. Austria's Burgenland, around Rust, has revived it. Small plantings exist in Croatia, South Africa and California.

steps.prompt: Match each place or name to Furmint.
steps.explanation: Furmint is Hungary's grape, with neighbours.

steps.body: Tokaj's soils change from hill to hill. Furmint from rhyolite tends to be more mineral and lean; from loess, rounder and fruitier.

steps.prompt: What creates the mists that help noble rot in Tokaj?
steps.explanation: The two rivers meet at Tokaj, bringing autumn mists.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Furmint is 60 to 70% of Tokaj's vineyards
Volcanic soils and river mists shape it
It also grows in Somló, Slovenia and Austria

lessons.title: Tokaji Aszú
lessons.subtitle: The king of wines
objectives: Explain how Tokaji Aszú is made

steps.title: Aszú berries
steps.body: Aszú berries are individually picked, botrytised and shrivelled, almost raisins. They're stored as a paste, then soaked in fermenting must or a base wine for 12 to 60 hours, which extracts sugar and flavour. The mix is pressed and fermented slowly, then aged in small Gönci barrels in cold, damp cellars.
steps.highlight: Botrytised berries soaked in base wine

steps.title: Puttonyos
steps.body: Sweetness was measured in puttonyos: the number of 25 kg baskets, called puttony, of aszú berries added to a 136-litre Gönci barrel of base wine. From 3 to 6 puttonyos. Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, equal to the old 5 puttonyos, and the term puttonyos is optional.

steps.prompt: What did puttonyos measure?
options: Baskets of aszú berries per barrel
steps.explanation: The number of 25 kg baskets added to a 136-litre barrel.

steps.title: Eszencia
steps.body: Eszencia is the free-run juice that drips from aszú berries under their own weight. It can contain over 450 g/l of sugar, ferments for years and rarely exceeds 5% alcohol. It's one of the rarest, sweetest wines in the world, traditionally served by the spoon.
steps.highlight: Over 450 g/l, served by the spoon

steps.prompt: Put the making of Tokaji Aszú in order.
items: Soak in base wine or must
steps.explanation: Selection, soaking and slow fermentation give Aszú its depth.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aszú berries are soaked in base wine, then fermented slowly
Since 2013, Aszú needs at least 120 g/l of sugar
Eszencia is free-run juice with over 450 g/l

steps.title: A modern style
steps.body: Since the early 2000s, Tokaj producers have made more dry Furmint, partly because botrytis doesn't come every year, and partly to show the grape's quality. Dry Furmint has high acidity, citrus, quince, pear, smoky and mineral notes, and can be rich and textured, often compared with white Burgundy or Chenin Blanc.

steps.title: Making it
steps.body: Dry Furmint comes from healthy, non-botrytised grapes, often from single vineyards, called dűlő. Some ferment in oak, which adds texture; others in steel for purity. Its acidity lets it age 10 years or more. Producers like Királyudvar, Oremus and Szepsy helped establish its reputation.

steps.prompt: Dry Furmint is made from healthy grapes without noble rot.
steps.explanation: Yes. Botrytised grapes are kept for sweet wines.

steps.title: Vineyard classification
steps.body: Tokaj's vineyards were classified from 1730, among the first in the world, into first, second and third class. Single-vineyard names like Szent Tamás, Betsek and Mézes Mály are used again on labels, especially for dry Furmint, like Burgundy's crus.

steps.prompt: What is a dűlő in Tokaj?
steps.explanation: Dűlő names, like Szent Tamás, mark single vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Furmint has grown since the 2000s
It's made from healthy grapes, often single vineyards
Tokaj's vineyards were classified from 1730

steps.title: Dry Furmint
steps.body: Dry Furmint's acidity and texture suit rich fish, roast chicken, pork, goose, and creamy Hungarian dishes like chicken paprikash. Its smoky, mineral side suits smoked fish and mushrooms. Serve at 10 to 12 degrees.

steps.title: Tokaji Aszú
steps.body: Aszú suits foie gras, blue cheese, fruit tarts, apricot desserts and even spicy Asian food. Its acidity keeps it fresh with rich food. Serve at 10 to 12 degrees. It ages for decades: Aszú from the 18th century has been found still drinkable.
steps.highlight: Foie gras, blue cheese, apricot tarts

steps.prompt: Match each Furmint wine to a pairing.
steps.explanation: Furmint offers a wine for many courses.

steps.body: Louis XIV is said to have called Tokaji the wine of kings and the king of wines. It was served at European courts for centuries.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Tokaji Aszú?
steps.explanation: Oysters need a dry wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Furmint suits paprikash, pork and smoked fish
Aszú suits foie gras, blue cheese and fruit desserts
Both are served at 10 to 12 degrees and age well

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Furmint
objectives: Explain Tokaji Aszú and dry Furmint

steps.prompt: What is Furmint's signature?
steps.explanation: Acidity links all its styles.

steps.prompt: Match each Tokaj term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Tokaj has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú needs at least 120 g/l of sugar.
steps.explanation: Yes, equal to the old 5 puttonyos.

steps.prompt: Which grapes grow in Tokaj?
steps.explanation: Pinot Noir isn't a Tokaj grape.

steps.prompt: Tokaj's vineyards were first classified from ____.
steps.explanation: Among the earliest vineyard classifications.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Furmint has searing acidity, quince and smoke
It's Tokaj's grape, ideal for noble rot
Aszú and Eszencia are its great sweet wines
Dry Furmint is Hungary's modern white

modules.title: Palomino
modules.description: Also called Palomino Fino and Listán Blanco. A neutral grape transformed by flor and the solera into Sherry.

steps.title: A blank page
steps.body: Palomino, or Palomino Fino, is a white grape with low acidity, low sugar and neutral flavours: a little apple, almond and salt. As a table wine, it's simple and soft. But as a base for Sherry, its neutrality is perfect: flor yeast, oxygen and the solera write the flavour onto it.

steps.title: Why neutral works
steps.body: Sherry's flavours come from how it's aged, not from the grape. A strongly aromatic grape would compete with flor's bready, saline notes or with the nutty notes of oxidation. Palomino's low sugar means base wines at 11 to 12.5% alcohol, easy to fortify to the levels needed for each style.

steps.prompt: Why is Palomino's neutrality an advantage for Sherry?
options: Ageing, not the grape, creates Sherry's flavours
steps.explanation: Flor and oxidation create the flavours; a neutral grape lets them show.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: As an unfortified table wine, Palomino is pale, soft and neutral. In Sherry, its flavour is hidden under flor's bread, almond and salt in Fino, or the walnut and caramel of Oloroso. Palomino's real identity is the Sherry family.

steps.prompt: Palomino is a highly aromatic grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's very neutral, which is why it suits Sherry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Palomino is neutral, low in acidity and sugar
Sherry's flavours come from ageing, not the grape
Its base wines are easy to fortify

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Jerez and the Canaries
objectives: Name other places that grow it

steps.title: Jerez
steps.body: Palomino is about 95% of the vineyards of Jerez, in Andalusia, around Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Sherry triangle. The climate is hot, with over 300 sunny days a year, and two winds: the humid Poniente from the Atlantic and the hot, dry Levante from the east.

steps.title: Albariza
steps.body: The best vineyards are on albariza, a brilliant white soil with up to 40% chalk, formed from marine diatoms. It absorbs winter rain like a sponge and holds it for the dry summer, then forms a hard crust that reduces evaporation. Its white surface reflects sunlight. Pagos, named vineyard areas, like Macharnudo and Carrascal, sit on albariza.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Jerez.
steps.explanation: Jerez has its own vocabulary of land and wind.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Palomino is also grown in the Canary Islands, as Listán Blanco, where it makes dry table wines on volcanic soil.
