Galicia, South Africa, Australia and California grow some, once for fortified wines. Today, a few Jerez producers make unfortified Palomino table wines, showing the albariza in a new way.

steps.prompt: What is special about albariza soil?
options: It stores winter rain for summer
steps.explanation: Its chalky structure holds water deep for the dry summer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Palomino is about 95% of Jerez
Albariza stores water and reflects sun
It's Listán Blanco in the Canaries

steps.title: Flor
steps.body: After fermentation, base wines are classified. The most delicate are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and put into barrels left about five-sixths full. A layer of yeast called flor grows on the surface, protecting the wine from oxygen and feeding on alcohol and glycerol. It adds bready, almond, saline aromas, from acetaldehyde.

steps.title: The solera
steps.body: Sherry ages in a solera: tiers of barrels of different ages. Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest tier, the solera, which is refilled from the next oldest, the first criadera, and so on. New wine enters the youngest. By law, no more than 40% can be drawn per year. The blend stays consistent and gains average age.
steps.highlight: Old tier drawn, refilled from younger

steps.prompt: Why are Sherry barrels left partly empty?
options: To give flor air to grow on the surface
steps.explanation: Flor needs air at the surface to live.

steps.title: Fortification
steps.body: Wines chosen for oxidative ageing are fortified to about 17%. At that strength flor can't survive, so oxygen ages the wine, giving nutty, darker Oloroso. The classification and fortification level decide whether a wine follows the biological path, under flor, or the oxidative one.

steps.prompt: Put the solera's movements in order, starting with bottling.
items: Draw wine from the oldest tier
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill the first criadera from the second
Add new wine to the youngest tier
steps.explanation: Each tier passes wine to the older tier.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Flor grows on wines fortified to about 15%, protecting them
The solera blends wines of many ages
At 17% flor dies and the wine ages oxidatively

steps.title: Biological
steps.body: Fino ages under flor, giving pale, bone-dry wines with almond, bread and salt, at about 15%. Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where cooler, humid sea air keeps flor thick, adding a saline, chamomile freshness. Both are best fresh, soon after bottling.

steps.title: Oxidative and in between
steps.body: Oloroso, fortified to 17%, ages with oxygen, turning amber-brown with walnut, toffee and spice, yet dry. Amontillado starts as Fino, then loses its flor and ages oxidatively, combining both styles. Palo Cortado is rare: it loses flor early, giving Amontillado's aroma with Oloroso's body. Cream Sherry is sweetened, often with Pedro Ximénez.

steps.prompt: Match each Sherry to its ageing.
steps.explanation: The path of ageing defines the style.

steps.body: An opened bottle of Fino or Manzanilla behaves like a white wine: keep it in the fridge and finish it within a week.

steps.prompt: Which Sherry styles are naturally dry?
steps.explanation: Cream is sweetened.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fino and Manzanilla age under flor, pale and dry
Oloroso ages oxidatively, dark yet dry
Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine both paths

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Sherry
objectives: Pair each Sherry style with food

steps.title: A food wine
steps.body: Fino and Manzanilla suit tapas: olives, almonds, jamón, fried fish, prawns and anchovies. Amontillado suits soups, mushrooms, artichokes and asparagus, notoriously hard to pair. Oloroso suits game, stews and hard cheese. Sweet Pedro Ximénez is poured over vanilla ice cream.

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve Fino and Manzanilla well chilled, 6 to 8 degrees, in a white wine glass, not a tiny copita. Amontillado at 12 to 14, Oloroso at 14 to 16. Fino and Manzanilla fade within a week once open; Oloroso lasts weeks. En rama Sherry, lightly filtered, is bottled for fresh drinking.

steps.prompt: Which Sherry is the classic match for jamón and olives?
steps.explanation: Dry, saline Fino and Manzanilla suit salty tapas.

steps.body: Amontillado is one of the few wines that handles asparagus and artichokes. Its nutty, savoury character doesn't clash with their bitter compounds.

steps.prompt: Fino should be served at room temperature.
steps.explanation: Not true. Fino and Manzanilla are best well chilled, at 6 to 8 degrees.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fino suits tapas; Amontillado tricky vegetables; Oloroso game
Serve Fino cold, Oloroso cool
Fino fades fast once open; Oloroso lasts

steps.prompt: Why does Palomino suit Sherry?
options: It's neutral, letting ageing shape the flavour
steps.explanation: Neutrality lets flor and oxidation speak.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Jerez's vocabulary describes its unique process.

steps.prompt: Oloroso ages under flor.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's fortified to 17%, which stops flor, so it ages with oxygen.

steps.prompt: Which are part of the Sherry triangle?
steps.explanation: Rioja is far to the north.

steps.prompt: Order these Sherries from palest to darkest.
steps.explanation: Biological ageing keeps wine pale; oxidation and dried grapes darken it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Palomino is a neutral grape that becomes Sherry
Flor protects Fino; oxygen shapes Oloroso
The solera blends many ages
Sherry is a great food wine

modules.title: Chenin Blanc
modules.description: Also called Steen in South Africa. The Loire's most versatile grape: dry, sweet or sparkling, always with high acidity.

lessons.title: Meet Chenin Blanc
lessons.subtitle: Apple, quince and acidity
objectives: Describe Chenin Blanc's flavours and structure

steps.title: High acid, many faces
steps.body: Chenin Blanc gives whites with green and red apple, quince, pear, lemon, chamomile and, with age or botrytis, honey, beeswax and lanolin. Its acidity is very high, even when ripe. It can be dry, off-dry, sweet or sparkling. Few grapes are as versatile.

steps.title: Why so versatile
steps.body: Chenin ripens unevenly, so a single vineyard can give grapes at different stages, from just-ripe to shrivelled or botrytised. Growers make several passes, picking for each style. Its high acidity balances sugar in sweet wines, supports bubbles in sparkling wines, and lets dry wines age for decades.

steps.prompt: What lets Chenin Blanc make so many styles?
steps.explanation: Acidity supports every style, and uneven ripening gives grapes for each.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for apple and quince, a honeyed or waxy note even in young wines, and a striking acidity. Dry Chenin can seem rich in texture yet sharp in acidity. A slight lanolin or wet wool note is typical. Compared with Riesling, it's less floral and more apple and honey.

steps.prompt: Chenin Blanc is a low-acid grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its very high acidity is its defining feature.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chenin gives apple, quince and honey with high acidity
It makes dry, sweet and sparkling wines
Uneven ripening lets growers pick for each style

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: The Loire and South Africa
objectives: Explain its history in South Africa
Name other countries that grow it

steps.title: The Loire
steps.body: Chenin Blanc's home is the Loire's Anjou-Saumur and Touraine. Key appellations: Vouvray and Montlouis in Touraine; Savennières, Saumur, Anjou, Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume in Anjou. Tuffeau, a soft limestone, and schist give different styles. It's been grown there since at least the 9th century.

steps.title: South Africa
steps.body: South Africa grows more Chenin than anywhere else, around 17,000 hectares, about 18% of its vineyards. Called Steen locally, it arrived with the first Dutch settlers in the 17th century. It was long used for brandy and bulk wine; now old bush vines in Swartland, Stellenbosch and Paarl make some of the country's finest whites.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Chenin.
steps.explanation: Chenin shines in the Loire and South Africa.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Chenin grows in California, once widely for bulk wine, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and Mexico. A few cool-climate producers in the US and Australia now make serious dry Chenin. But the Loire and South Africa remain its two great homes.

steps.prompt: What is Chenin Blanc called in South Africa?
steps.explanation: Steen is the traditional South African name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Loire's Anjou and Touraine are Chenin's home
South Africa grows the most, as Steen
Old bush vines make South Africa's finest Chenin

lessons.title: From dry to sweet
lessons.subtitle: Reading a Chenin label
objectives: Name the sweetness terms on Loire labels
Explain how botrytis affects sweet Chenin

steps.title: Sweetness terms
steps.body: Loire Chenin labels may say sec, dry; demi-sec, off-dry; moelleux, sweet; or doux, very sweet. Vouvray and Montlouis can be any of these, depending on the vintage: in warm years with botrytis, more sweet wine; in cool years, more dry and sparkling. If no term appears, check the back label or producer.

steps.title: Botrytis
steps.body: In Anjou's Layon valley, autumn mists bring noble rot. Coteaux du Layon, and its top crus Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume, make sweet wines from botrytised Chenin. Quarts de Chaume became the Loire's first Grand Cru in 2011. Chenin's acidity keeps them fresh, and they can age for 50 years or more.
steps.highlight: Quarts de Chaume: first Loire Grand Cru

steps.prompt: Order these Loire terms from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Sec is dry; doux is the sweetest.

steps.title: Sparkling
steps.body: Chenin's high acidity makes excellent sparkling wine. Vouvray and Montlouis make pétillant and mousseux; Saumur Brut and Crémant de Loire use Chenin with Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc. They're made by the traditional method, with honeyed, apple flavours.

steps.prompt: Which Loire appellation became the first Grand Cru in 2011?
steps.explanation: Quarts de Chaume makes sweet, botrytised Chenin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux mark sweetness
Coteaux du Layon and Quarts de Chaume are sweet botrytis wines
Chenin's acidity makes fine sparkling wine

steps.title: Vouvray
steps.body: Vouvray, near Tours, grows Chenin on tuffeau limestone and flint-clay, perruches, above the Loire. It makes every style, from sparkling to sweet. Vineyards with aubuis, clay-limestone, give rich wines. Producers like Huet, biodynamic since 1990, made it famous. Montlouis, across the river, is similar but often slightly lighter.

steps.title: Savennières
steps.body: Savennières, west of Angers, on schist and volcanic rock, is famous for dry Chenin: powerful, austere, mineral and long-lived. It has two famous crus: La Coulée de Serrant, a monopole of Nicolas Joly, a biodynamic pioneer, and La Roche aux Moines. Young Savennières can be closed; it needs 10 years to open.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its Loire meaning.
steps.explanation: Each appellation has its own soils and names.

steps.body: Decant a young Savennières. Like a red wine, it opens with air, revealing quince, honey and chamomile.

steps.prompt: Savennières is best known for sweet wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Savennières is famous for powerful, dry Chenin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vouvray makes every style on tuffeau and flint
Savennières makes powerful, dry Chenin on schist
Coulée de Serrant is a famous biodynamic monopole

lessons.title: South African Chenin
lessons.subtitle: Old vines and new energy
objectives: Explain the role of old vines

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: South African Chenin ranges from crisp, fruity, unoaked wines with tropical and apple notes to rich, oaked, textured wines from old vines. The Chenin Blanc Association classifies styles: fresh and fruity, rich and ripe unwooded, rich and ripe wooded, and rich and ripe sweet.
steps.highlight: Fresh to rich, unoaked to oaked

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: Many South African Chenin vineyards are old, dry-farmed bush vines, some planted in the 1960s and earlier. The Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years. Swartland, with granite and schist soils, became the centre of a revival from the early 2000s, led by producers like Eben Sadie and Chris and Andrea Mullineux.

steps.prompt: Which South African region led the Chenin revival from the early 2000s?
steps.explanation: Swartland's old bush vines and young producers drove the revival.

steps.title: Why it suits the Cape
steps.body: Chenin's high acidity is valuable in the Cape's warm climate, keeping wines fresh as they ripen fully. Old bush vines, deep-rooted, cope with drought without irrigation. The result is concentrated wine with acidity, giving South Africa a world-class white style of its own.

steps.prompt: What makes old-vine Chenin special in South Africa?
steps.explanation: Old vines give low, not high, yields.

steps.title: What you learned
points: South African Chenin ranges from fresh to rich and oaked
Old dry-farmed bush vines drive quality
Swartland led the revival from the early 2000s

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Chenin Blanc
objectives: Pair dry and sweet Chenin with food

steps.title: Dry and sweet
steps.body: Dry Chenin suits pork, chicken, river fish with butter sauce, goat's cheese and mildly spiced dishes. Off-dry Vouvray suits Thai food, pork with apples and spicy Asian dishes. Sweet Layon and Quarts de Chaume suit fruit tarts, blue cheese and foie gras. Sparkling Chenin suits aperitifs.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve dry Chenin at 10 to 12 degrees, sweet at 8 to 10. Fresh styles are best young. Top dry Vouvray and Savennières age 20 years or more; sweet Chenin from great vintages 50 years or more, thanks to acidity.
steps.highlight: Sweet Chenin ages 50 years or more

steps.prompt: Which dish suits an off-dry Vouvray?
steps.explanation: A touch of sweetness and high acidity calm the spice.

steps.body: Chenin and goat's cheese is a Loire classic. Try a dry Vouvray or Saumur with crottin de Chavignol or Sainte-Maure.

steps.prompt: Sweet Loire Chenin can age for 50 years or more.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its high acidity and sugar preserve it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Chenin suits pork and goat's cheese; off-dry suits spice
Serve dry at 10 to 12 degrees, sweet at 8 to 10
Top Chenin ages for decades

steps.explanation: Chenin makes every style.

steps.explanation: Doux is the sweetest.

steps.prompt: What is Chenin's defining feature?
steps.explanation: Acidity supports every style.

steps.explanation: Yes, about 17,000 hectares.

steps.explanation: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc.

It makes dry, sweet and sparkling wines

modules.title: Muscat
modules.description: Also called Moscato, Moscatel and Muskateller. The family of grapes that actually taste of grapes.

lessons.title: Meet Muscat
lessons.subtitle: The grape that tastes of grapes
objectives: Explain why it smells of grapes

steps.title: Grapey and floral
steps.body: Muscat is one of the few wine grapes whose wine smells of fresh grapes. Add orange blossom, rose, elderflower, peach and orange peel. Muscat wines can be dry, sweet, sparkling or fortified, from light Moscato d'Asti to rich Rutherglen Muscat. It's one of the oldest known grape families.

steps.title: Terpenes
steps.body: Muscat's aroma comes from high levels of terpenes, especially linalool, floral and citrus, and geraniol, rose. These compounds are present in the grape itself, which is why the wine smells like eating the fruit. Many Muscats are also table grapes and raisins.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Muscat its grapey, floral aroma?
steps.explanation: Terpenes, abundant in Muscat, give floral and grape aromas.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: If a wine smells exactly like fresh grapes, with orange blossom, it's almost certainly Muscat. Dry Muscat is a surprise: aromatic like a sweet wine, but dry on the palate. Compared with Gewürztraminer, Muscat is more grapey and floral, less lychee and spice.

steps.prompt: All Muscat wines are sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. Muscat is made dry, for example in Alsace, as well as sweet and fortified.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Muscat wines smell of fresh grapes and orange blossom
Terpenes like linalool and geraniol give its aroma
It's made dry, sweet, sparkling and fortified

steps.title: A family
steps.body: Muscat is a family of over 200 grapes. The finest is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, small-berried, used in Asti, Alsace, Beaumes-de-Venise and Rutherglen. Muscat of Alexandria, larger-berried and less refined, grows in Spain, Portugal's Setúbal, Sicily as Zibibbo, and Chile. Muscat Ottonel, lighter, grows in Alsace and Austria. Some Muscats are pink or black.

steps.title: Ancient roots
steps.body: Muscat is among the oldest grapes, probably from Greece or the eastern Mediterranean; the Greeks and Romans spread it. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is thought to be the oldest; Muscat of Alexandria is its offspring with a table grape. It grows in Greece, as Moschato on Samos, and across the Mediterranean.

steps.prompt: Match each Muscat to its region.
steps.explanation: The Muscat family spreads around the Mediterranean.

steps.body: Zibibbo, Sicily's name for Muscat of Alexandria, makes the famous Passito di Pantelleria from sun-dried grapes on a volcanic island south of Sicily.

steps.prompt: Which Muscat is considered the finest?
steps.explanation: Its small berries give the most refined wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Muscat is a family of over 200 grapes
Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is the finest
It spread from Greece across the Mediterranean

steps.title: Moscato d'Asti and Asti
steps.body: In Piedmont, Moscato Bianco makes Moscato d'Asti, lightly sparkling, frizzante, sweet and about 5.5% alcohol, and Asti, fully sparkling, around 7%. Fermentation in a pressure tank is stopped by chilling, leaving sugar and trapped bubbles. They smell of peach, grape and orange blossom.

steps.title: Dry and sweet
steps.body: Alsace makes dry Muscat, intensely aromatic yet dry, a classic aperitif. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Muscat de Rivesaltes, in southern France, are fortified, sweet vins doux naturels. Samos, in Greece, makes sweet Muscats, some from sun-dried grapes. Austria makes dry Muskateller.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its style.
steps.explanation: Muscat covers almost every style.

steps.title: Moscato's boom
steps.body: Since the 2000s, Moscato has become hugely popular worldwide, especially in the US, where sweet, light, fruity Moscatos from California and Australia are widely sold. They're often made in Asti's style but from Muscat of Alexandria or other varieties.

steps.prompt: Moscato d'Asti usually has about ____% alcohol.
steps.explanation: Low alcohol and sweetness come from stopping fermentation early.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Moscato d'Asti is sweet, frizzante and about 5.5%
Alsace makes dry Muscat; southern France fortified sweet Muscat
Moscato has become a global trend

lessons.title: Fortified Muscat
lessons.subtitle: Rutherglen and Setúbal
objectives: Explain how ageing changes fortified Muscat

steps.title: Rutherglen
steps.body: Rutherglen, in north-east Victoria, Australia, makes some of the world's richest fortified wines from a dark-skinned Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, called Brown Muscat. Grapes are picked very ripe, fortified, and aged for years in old casks in hot sheds, often in solera-like systems. The wines are dark, syrupy, with raisin, toffee, coffee and orange peel.

steps.title: Classification and Setúbal
steps.body: Rutherglen Muscat has four levels: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare, each older and more concentrated. In Portugal, Moscatel de Setúbal, from Muscat of Alexandria near Lisbon, is fortified and macerated on skins for months, giving orange peel, apricot and honey. Aged versions reach 20 years or more.

steps.prompt: Order Rutherglen Muscat's levels from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Each level is older and more concentrated.

steps.title: Age and oxygen
steps.body: As fortified Muscat ages in cask, it oxidises slowly and concentrates through evaporation. Fresh grape and orange blossom turn into raisin, fig, toffee, coffee and rancio, a nutty, complex character. Old Rare Rutherglen blends can include wines decades old.

steps.prompt: Where is Rutherglen?
steps.explanation: Rutherglen is in Victoria, Australia.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rutherglen Muscat is dark, syrupy and long-aged
It has four levels: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare
Moscatel de Setúbal is Portugal's fortified Muscat

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Muscat
objectives: Pair each Muscat style with food
Know how long to keep them

steps.title: Match the style
steps.body: Dry Muscat suits asparagus, a classic in Alsace, and aperitifs. Moscato d'Asti suits fruit salads, panettone and light desserts, even brunch. Beaumes-de-Venise suits fruit tarts and melon. Rutherglen Muscat suits sticky toffee pudding, chocolate, coffee desserts and blue cheese.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve Moscato d'Asti and dry Muscat at 6 to 8 degrees, sweet fortified Muscat at 12 to 16. Moscato d'Asti and dry Muscat are best within a year or two; their aroma fades. Fortified Muscats, already aged, keep for weeks once opened.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits Rutherglen Muscat?
steps.explanation: Its toffee and raisin notes match rich desserts.

steps.body: Dry Alsace Muscat with white asparagus in spring is one of the few successful asparagus pairings.

steps.prompt: Moscato d'Asti is best drunk young.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its fresh grape aroma is its charm, and it fades with time.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Muscat suits asparagus; Moscato suits fruit desserts
Rutherglen Muscat suits toffee and chocolate
Drink Moscato young; fortified Muscat keeps

steps.prompt: What makes Muscat unique among wine grapes?
options: Its wine smells of fresh grapes
steps.explanation: Terpenes give it a grapey aroma.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its region.
steps.explanation: Muscat has many names.

steps.prompt: Rutherglen Muscat is a light, sparkling wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's dark, rich and fortified.

steps.prompt: Which are Muscat styles?
steps.explanation: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.prompt: Order Rutherglen's levels from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Rare is the oldest and most concentrated.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Muscat smells of grapes and orange blossom, thanks to terpenes
It's a large family, led by Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
It makes dry, sparkling, sweet and fortified wines
Each style finds a match, from asparagus to toffee

modules.title: Torrontés
modules.description: Argentina's own white grape: intensely floral, grown at some of the world's highest vineyards.

steps.title: Perfumed and dry
steps.body: Torrontés gives intensely aromatic whites with rose, jasmine, orange blossom, peach, lemon and lychee. Most are dry, with medium acidity and medium to high alcohol, and sometimes a slightly bitter finish. Its perfume makes it seem sweet, but it's usually dry.

steps.title: An Argentine cross
steps.body: There are three Torrontés: Riojano, the finest and most planted, Sanjuanino and Mendocino. DNA shows Torrontés Riojano is a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, also called Listán Prieto or País, brought by Spanish colonists. That explains its Muscat-like perfume. It's Argentina's own grape, born there.
steps.highlight: Muscat of Alexandria x Criolla Chica

steps.prompt: Why does Torrontés smell like Muscat?
options: Muscat of Alexandria is one of its parents
steps.explanation: Its parentage gives it Muscat-like terpenes.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour and an explosive floral nose of rose and orange blossom, then a dry palate with medium acidity and warm alcohol. A slight bitterness at the end is typical. Compared with Muscat, it's often drier and spicier; compared with Gewürztraminer, fresher.

steps.prompt: Most Torrontés is sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its perfume suggests sweetness, but most is dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Torrontés is intensely floral but usually dry
Torrontés Riojano is a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica
It's Argentina's own grape

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Salta and high altitude
objectives: Explain how altitude shapes its style

steps.title: Salta and Cafayate
steps.body: Torrontés Riojano grows best in the Calchaquí Valleys of Salta, in north-west Argentina, around Cafayate, at 1,700 to over 3,000 m, among the highest vineyards in the world. It's also grown in La Rioja, the province that gave it its name, and in Mendoza and San Juan.

steps.title: Altitude
steps.body: At such altitude, days are hot and sunny, with intense ultraviolet light, while nights are cold. Torrontés ripens fully, developing its aromas, but keeps acidity. The UV thickens skins, adding aroma compounds. Without altitude, in hot lowlands, Torrontés can be flabby, bitter and too alcoholic.
steps.highlight: Sun by day, cold at night

steps.prompt: Match each place to Torrontés.
steps.explanation: Torrontés is at its best high in the north.

steps.title: Making it
steps.body: Winemakers keep Torrontés fresh: cool fermentation in steel, no oak, early bottling. Some pick earlier to reduce alcohol and bitterness. A few producers make oaked, late harvest or sparkling versions, but the fresh, dry style dominates.

steps.prompt: Why does altitude help Torrontés?
options: Cold nights keep acidity while sun ripens aromas
steps.explanation: Altitude gives a large day and night swing, balancing ripeness and freshness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Torrontés thrives in Salta's high valleys, around Cafayate
Altitude keeps acidity while sun ripens aromas
Fresh, unoaked, dry styles dominate

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Torrontés
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Aromatic food
steps.body: Torrontés suits aromatic, lightly spiced food: Thai, Indian, Vietnamese dishes, ceviche, and Argentine empanadas from Salta, filled with spiced beef. Its floral perfume and freshness suit coriander, ginger and lemongrass. Avoid heavy, rich sauces.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 7 to 10 degrees. Torrontés is best young, within one to two years, while its aromas are fresh. With age, it can turn bitter and lose its perfume.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a classic match for Torrontés in Salta?
steps.explanation: Salta's empanadas and Torrontés are a regional pairing.

steps.body: Torrontés is a good choice for sushi or Thai food at a restaurant, when you want something aromatic but dry.

steps.prompt: Which flavours in food suit Torrontés?
steps.explanation: Heavy cream overwhelms its freshness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Torrontés suits empanadas, ceviche and Asian food
Serve at 7 to 10 degrees
Drink it within one to two years

steps.prompt: What is Torrontés Riojano's parentage?
options: Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica
steps.explanation: A natural Argentine cross.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Torrontés.
steps.explanation: Torrontés is Argentina's white signature.

steps.prompt: Torrontés is best aged for many years.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's best young, while fresh.

steps.prompt: Which describe Torrontés?
steps.explanation: Most Torrontés is unoaked.

steps.prompt: Salta's vineyards reach up to about ____ metres.
steps.explanation: Among the highest vineyards in the world.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Torrontés is floral, dry and Argentine
Its parents include Muscat of Alexandria
Salta's altitude gives it freshness
It suits aromatic food and is best young

modules.title: Trebbiano
modules.description: Also called Ugni Blanc in France. A neutral, high-acid grape behind Cognac, Armagnac and Vin Santo.

lessons.title: Meet Trebbiano
lessons.subtitle: Neutral, crisp and prolific
objectives: Explain why it's so widely planted

steps.title: Light and neutral
steps.body: Trebbiano, called Ugni Blanc in France, gives light, crisp whites with lemon, green apple, almond and herbs. It has high acidity and moderate alcohol, and is fairly neutral in aroma. It's one of the most planted white grapes in the world, mostly for brandy and simple wines.

steps.title: Why so widespread
steps.body: Trebbiano is vigorous, productive and resistant to disease, and keeps high acidity even when yields are high. That makes it ideal for distillation, where neutral, acidic, low-alcohol wine is needed. Its many clones and relatives, like Trebbiano Toscano and Trebbiano Romagnolo, share the family name.

steps.prompt: Why is Trebbiano valued for brandy?
options: It gives neutral, acidic, low-alcohol wine
steps.explanation: Distillers want neutral, acidic base wine.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: As a still wine, Trebbiano is pale, light, crisp and neutral, with lemon and almond. It's often blended to add freshness. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, a distinct variety, can be more serious, especially from top producers like Valentini.

steps.prompt: Trebbiano is a low-yielding, delicate grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's vigorous and productive.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Trebbiano gives light, crisp, neutral whites
It's productive and keeps high acidity
It's one of the most planted white grapes

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Italy and France
objectives: Explain its role in French brandy

steps.title: Italy
steps.body: Trebbiano grows across central Italy. Trebbiano Toscano is used in Tuscany, Umbria and Lazio, often in blends like Orvieto and Frascati, and in Vin Santo. Trebbiano Romagnolo grows in Emilia-Romagna. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a separate variety. Lugana, near Lake Garda, uses Turbiana, once called Trebbiano di Lugana.

steps.title: France
steps.body: In France, Ugni Blanc is the main grape of Cognac, about 98% of plantings there, and Armagnac. In the south, it's used in Côtes de Gascogne IGP whites, often blended with Colombard. Local names include Saint-Émilion in Charente, unrelated to the Bordeaux village.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its place.
steps.explanation: The Trebbiano family has many members.

steps.body: In Cognac, Ugni Blanc's local name is Saint-Émilion. Don't confuse it with the Bordeaux appellation.

steps.prompt: Which wines or spirits use Trebbiano or Ugni Blanc?
steps.explanation: Barolo is Nebbiolo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Trebbiano grows across central Italy in several varieties
Ugni Blanc is about 98% of Cognac
It's used in Gascony whites and Armagnac

lessons.title: Cognac and distillation
lessons.subtitle: From thin wine to great brandy
objectives: Explain why Cognac uses Ugni Blanc

steps.title: The base wine
steps.body: Cognac's base wine is made from Ugni Blanc picked early, at about 8 to 9% alcohol, with very high acidity. It's thin and sour to drink, but ideal for distillation: high acidity keeps it stable without added sulphur, which producers avoid because it would taint the spirit, and neutrality lets distillation and oak shape the spirit.

steps.title: Double distillation
steps.body: Cognac is distilled twice in copper pot stills, called alembic charentais. The first distillation gives brouillis, about 28 to 32%. The second gives the heart, la bonne chauffe, around 70%. It then ages in French oak, from Limousin or Tronçais, for years. Distillation must be finished by 31 March after harvest.

steps.prompt: Put Cognac production in order.
steps.explanation: The thin wine is distilled twice, then aged.

steps.title: Age categories
steps.body: Cognac is labelled by minimum age: VS, at least 2 years in oak; VSOP, at least 4 years; XO, at least 10 years since 2018. Cognac's crus, like Grande Champagne and Petite Champagne, on chalk, give the finest spirits. Armagnac, in Gascony, uses Ugni Blanc too, often with single, column distillation.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum oak age for XO Cognac since 2018?
steps.explanation: XO was raised from 6 to 10 years in 2018.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cognac uses thin, acidic Ugni Blanc wine
It's distilled twice in copper pot stills
VS, VSOP and XO mark minimum ages

lessons.title: Vin Santo
lessons.subtitle: Tuscany's holy wine
objectives: Explain how Vin Santo is made

steps.title: Dried grapes
steps.body: Vin Santo, holy wine, is a Tuscan sweet wine made mainly from Trebbiano and Malvasia. Grapes are dried on straw mats or hung from rafters for months, until Christmas or later, concentrating sugar. They're pressed into a thick, sweet must, then sealed into small barrels.

steps.title: Caratelli
steps.body: The must ferments slowly in small barrels called caratelli, often 50 to 100 litres, sealed for three to five years or more. Traditionally they're kept in attics, through hot summers and cold winters. Some caratelli keep a madre, mother, a deposit of old yeast and wine, which starts fermentation. The wine oxidises slowly, becoming amber.

steps.prompt: What is a madre in Vin Santo?
options: A deposit of old yeast and wine left in the barrel
steps.explanation: The madre helps start fermentation and adds character.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: Vin Santo ranges from dry to very sweet, amber to brown, with nuts, dried apricot, caramel, honey and a slightly oxidised note. Vin Santo del Chianti Classico and di Montepulciano are DOCs. Occhio di Pernice, partridge's eye, is a rare version made from Sangiovese.
steps.highlight: Amber, nutty, from dry to sweet

steps.prompt: Vin Santo is always made from red grapes.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's mainly Trebbiano and Malvasia; only Occhio di Pernice uses Sangiovese.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vin Santo is made from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia
It ages for years in small sealed caratelli
It's amber, nutty and from dry to sweet

steps.title: Simple whites
steps.body: Dry Trebbiano suits light, simple food: salads, grilled fish, seafood pasta, fried food and antipasti. Its acidity and neutrality make it refreshing. Lugana, from Turbiana, suits lake fish. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo from top producers suits richer fish and white meat.

steps.title: Vin Santo
steps.body: In Tuscany, Vin Santo is served with cantucci, almond biscuits, dipped into the glass. It also suits blue cheese, nut tarts and dried fruit. Serve at 12 to 14 degrees. It keeps for weeks once opened.

steps.prompt: Which Tuscan biscuits are traditionally dipped in Vin Santo?
steps.explanation: Almond cantucci are the classic match.

steps.body: Serve dry Trebbiano well chilled and young. Its charm is freshness, not complexity.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Vin Santo?
steps.explanation: Oysters need a dry wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Trebbiano suits light seafood and antipasti
Vin Santo suits cantucci, blue cheese and nut tarts
Drink dry Trebbiano young; Vin Santo keeps

steps.prompt: Match each name to its use.
steps.explanation: Trebbiano is a grape of transformation.

steps.prompt: Why is Ugni Blanc ideal for Cognac?
steps.explanation: Distillers want neutral, acidic base wine.

steps.prompt: XO Cognac must age at least 10 years since 2018.
steps.explanation: Yes, raised from 6 years.

steps.prompt: Which describe Trebbiano?
steps.explanation: Its acidity is high.

steps.prompt: Put Cognac production in order.

modules.title: Garganega
modules.description: Soave's grape: almond, lemon and volcanic minerality, dry or sweet as Recioto.

steps.title: Delicate and savoury
steps.body: Garganega gives light to medium-bodied whites with lemon, pear, white peach, almond, white flowers and a saline, mineral edge. Acidity is medium to high. It's the main grape of Soave, in the Veneto. With age, it gains honey and nutty notes.

steps.title: An old Veneto grape
steps.body: Garganega is one of Italy's oldest white grapes, recorded around Verona since the 13th century. DNA shows it's identical to Sicily's Grecanico and related to many central Italian grapes, like Trebbiano Toscano. It's vigorous and late-ripening; yields must be controlled for quality.

steps.prompt: What is Garganega called in Sicily?
steps.explanation: DNA shows Garganega and Grecanico are the same grape.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour, lemon and almond, a light floral note, and a crisp, slightly saline palate with a bitter almond finish. Better Soave has more body and texture. Compared with Pinot Grigio, Garganega has more almond and minerality.

steps.title: Soave
steps.body: Garganega grows mainly in the Veneto, east of Verona, around Soave. Soave DOC must be at least 70% Garganega, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay. Soave Classico, in the hills around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, is the historic core. Gambellara, next door, also uses it.

steps.title: Volcanic hills
steps.body: Soave Classico's hills have volcanic basalt soils, dark and mineral-rich, as well as limestone. Volcanic soils give wines with more structure, saline notes and ageing potential. Vineyards are traditionally trained on pergolas, called pergola veronese, which shade the fruit. Flat land below makes simpler Soave.

steps.body: Since 2019, Soave recognises 33 Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive, named sub-areas, like Foscarino, Calvarino and Monte Fiorentine. These help consumers find the best sites. Producers like Pieropan and Inama helped show Soave's potential.

steps.title: Soave

Soave Superiore DOCG and Soave Classico Superiore require lower yields and longer ageing. Top Soave can age 10 years or more.

steps.title: Recioto di Soave
steps.body: Recioto di Soave, the region's first DOCG in 1998, is a sweet wine from dried Garganega. Grapes are dried for months on racks, appassimento, concentrating sugar, sometimes with noble rot. The wine is golden, honeyed and sweet, with apricot and almond, balanced by acidity.

modules.title: Vermentino
modules.description: Also called Rolle in Provence and Pigato in Liguria. A crisp, herbal, saline white of Mediterranean coasts and islands.

steps.title: A coastal white
steps.body: Vermentino gives light to medium-bodied whites with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, white flowers, Mediterranean herbs and a saline, almond finish. Acidity is medium to high. It's at home by the sea, and its salty, herbal character is often linked to coastal winds and soils.

steps.title: Many names
steps.body: Vermentino probably spread around the western Mediterranean centuries ago. It's called Rolle in Provence and the Languedoc, Pigato in Liguria and Favorita in Piedmont; DNA shows they're the same grape. It likes heat, sun and drought, and tolerates poor, sandy or granite soils, typical of Mediterranean coasts.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its region.
steps.explanation: One grape, several Mediterranean names.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour, citrus and herbs like rosemary and thyme, a crisp palate and a slightly bitter, saline almond finish. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's less pungent and green; compared with Pinot Grigio, more herbal and saline.

steps.prompt: Rolle and Vermentino are the same grape.
steps.explanation: Yes. Rolle is its name in Provence and the Languedoc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vermentino gives citrus, herbs and a saline finish
It's Rolle in Provence, Pigato in Liguria, Favorita in Piedmont
It loves heat, sun and coastal soils

steps.title: Sardinia and Corsica
steps.body: Sardinia is Vermentino's stronghold. Vermentino di Gallura, in the granite north-east, is the island's only DOCG, since 1996, giving fuller, more structured, saline wines. Vermentino di Sardegna DOC covers the whole island. In Corsica, Vermentino, also called Vermentinu, makes Patrimonio and Ajaccio whites.

steps.title: Tuscany, Liguria and Provence
steps.body: Tuscany's coast, Bolgheri and the Maremma, makes fresh Vermentino. Liguria's Cinque Terre and Riviera Ligure di Ponente use it and Pigato. In Provence, Rolle is the main white grape and is often blended into rosé to add freshness and aroma. Australia is planting it as a heat-tolerant grape.

modules.title: Assyrtiko
modules.description: Santorini's grape: bone-dry, steely and saline, keeping high acidity in fierce sun.

steps.title: Steely and saline
steps.body: Assyrtiko gives bone-dry whites with lemon, lime, grapefruit, flint and a saline, smoky mineral edge. Acidity is very high, often with pH around 3, and alcohol can be high, 13.5 to 14.5%. Body is medium to full. It's Greece's most famous white grape.

steps.title: Acid in heat
steps.body: Most grapes lose acidity in hot climates. Assyrtiko is unusual: it keeps very high acidity even when fully ripe under intense Aegean sun. Its tartaric acid is especially stable. This makes it valuable as the climate warms, and it's been planted in Australia, South Africa and the US.

steps.prompt: What makes Assyrtiko unusual?
options: It keeps high acidity even in hot climates
It only grows in cold places
steps.explanation: Few grapes keep such acidity under strong sun.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour, citrus, flint and a sea-salt character, a firm, steely palate with high acidity and fairly high alcohol, and a long, mineral finish. Compared with Riesling, it's less floral and more saline and smoky.

steps.prompt: Assyrtiko loses most of its acidity in hot climates.
steps.explanation: Not true. It keeps high acidity even in intense heat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Assyrtiko is bone-dry, steely and saline
It keeps high acidity even in fierce sun
It's Greece's most famous white grape

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: Santorini and beyond
objectives: Name other Greek regions for Assyrtiko

steps.title: Santorini
steps.body: Assyrtiko's home is Santorini, a volcanic island in the Aegean, formed by a huge eruption around 1600 BC. Its soil, called aspa, is volcanic ash, pumice and lava, with almost no clay or organic matter. Rainfall is very low, about 300 mm a year; vines rely on night sea mist for moisture. Strong winds blow constantly.

steps.title: Phylloxera-free
steps.body: Santorini's volcanic sand doesn't let phylloxera survive, so the vines are ungrafted. Some root systems are over 400 years old: growers cut old vines back and let new shoots grow from the same roots. Assyrtiko also grows in mainland Greece, Macedonia and Crete, and in Australia's Clare Valley.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Santorini.
steps.explanation: Santorini's conditions are extreme.

steps.title: Partners
steps.body: On Santorini, Assyrtiko is often blended with Athiri and Aidani, two aromatic local grapes. Santorini PDO must be at least 75% Assyrtiko. Single-vineyard and old-vine bottlings, like Nykteri, made from grapes picked at night, are increasingly common.

steps.prompt: Why are Santorini's vines ungrafted?
options: Phylloxera can't survive in its volcanic soil
steps.explanation: Phylloxera can't survive in Santorini's volcanic sand.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Santorini's volcanic aspa soil and sea mist shape Assyrtiko
Ungrafted roots can be over 400 years old
It also grows in mainland Greece, Crete and Australia

steps.title: Baskets on the ground
steps.body: On Santorini, vines are trained into low baskets, called kouloura, woven from their own canes, lying on the ground. The grapes grow inside the basket. Each year the basket grows; after decades, growers cut it back and start again from the old roots. It's one of the oldest training systems in the world.

steps.title: Why baskets
steps.body: The kouloura protects grapes from Santorini's strong winds, which can reach over 50 km/h, and from fierce sun and sand. Inside, the grapes catch night humidity from sea mist, the vines' main water source. The low shape keeps the vines close to the ground, where it's cooler and more humid.

steps.prompt: What does the kouloura protect against?
steps.explanation: Santorini has mild winters; frost isn't the main concern.

steps.title: Tiny yields
steps.body: Santorini's yields are among the lowest in Europe, often 10 to 20 hectolitres per hectare, compared with 50 or more elsewhere. Old roots, drought and wind keep them low. Combined with steep land prices from tourism, this makes Santorini expensive and its vineyards endangered.

steps.prompt: What is a kouloura?
options: A basket-shaped vine trained on the ground
steps.explanation: Vines woven into baskets protect the fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Kouloura vines are woven into baskets on the ground
They protect grapes from wind, sun and sand
Yields are tiny, among Europe's lowest

steps.title: Sun-dried grapes
steps.body: Santorini's Vinsanto is a sweet wine made from at least 51% Assyrtiko, with Aidani. Grapes are picked late and dried in the sun for 12 to 14 days, concentrating sugar. The must ferments slowly, and the wine ages for at least two years in oak, often much longer.

steps.title: Ageing and taste
steps.body: Vinsanto can age 10, 20 or even 50 years in barrel, becoming deep amber to dark brown, with raisin, dried apricot, coffee, caramel and spice. Assyrtiko's acidity keeps it fresh despite very high sugar, often over 200 g/l. Its name may come from Santo, for Santorini, wine of Santorini.

steps.prompt: How are grapes for Santorini Vinsanto concentrated?
options: Dried in the sun for 12 to 14 days
steps.explanation: Sun-drying concentrates their sugar.

steps.title: Not Tuscan Vin Santo
steps.body: Santorini's Vinsanto and Tuscany's Vin Santo share a name but differ. Tuscan Vin Santo uses Trebbiano and Malvasia dried indoors and ages in sealed caratelli. Santorini's uses Assyrtiko dried in the sun. The name's origin may link to Santorini or to holy wine, vino santo.

steps.prompt: Santorini Vinsanto and Tuscan Vin Santo use the same grapes.
steps.explanation: Not true. Santorini uses Assyrtiko and Aidani; Tuscany uses Trebbiano and Malvasia.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Santorini Vinsanto uses sun-dried Assyrtiko
It ages for years, becoming amber with raisin and coffee
It differs from Tuscan Vin Santo in grapes and method

steps.title: Greek seafood
steps.body: Dry Assyrtiko suits Greek food: grilled octopus, sea bass, shellfish, fava, Santorini's yellow split pea purée, tomato fritters and feta. Its acidity cuts through olive oil and fried food. Its saline edge suits oysters and sushi too.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve dry Assyrtiko at 8 to 11 degrees. It ages surprisingly well thanks to its acidity: top Santorini wines develop over 10 to 15 years, gaining smoky, honeyed notes. Vinsanto, served at 12 to 14, suits dried fruit, nuts, blue cheese and chocolate.

steps.explanation: Its acidity and salinity suit grilled seafood.

steps.body: Fava, Santorini's yellow split pea purée with olive oil and onions, is a local classic with Assyrtiko.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Vinsanto?
steps.explanation: Oysters need a dry wine.

points: Dry Assyrtiko suits grilled octopus, fava and seafood
Top Santorini Assyrtiko ages 10 to 15 years
Vinsanto suits dried fruit, cheese and chocolate

steps.explanation: It keeps acidity under fierce sun.

steps.explanation: Santorini has its own vocabulary.

steps.explanation: Yes. Phylloxera can't survive in its volcanic sand.

steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is from Piedmont.

steps.explanation: At least 75%.

Santorini's volcanic soil and kouloura vines are unique

modules.title: Grüner Veltliner
modules.description: Austria's signature grape: citrus, green apple and a twist of white pepper.

steps.title: Fresh and peppery
steps.body: Grüner Veltliner, often just Grüner, gives whites with lemon, lime, green apple, pear, green bean, lentil and its signature white pepper. Acidity is medium to high. It ranges from light, crisp everyday wines to powerful, rich ones. It's Austria's most planted grape, about a third of its vineyards.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Grüner Veltliner is native to Austria. DNA shows its parents are Traminer and an old grape found in St. Georgen, near Lake Neusiedl, called St. Georgener-Rebe. Despite its name, it isn't related to Roter Veltliner. It's vigorous and productive, so yield control decides quality.

steps.prompt: What is Grüner Veltliner's signature aroma?
steps.explanation: A white pepper note sets it apart.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon, sometimes green-tinged colour, citrus and green apple with white pepper and vegetal notes like green bean, and a crisp, fresh palate. Richer versions add stone fruit, spice and a creamy texture. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's less pungent and more peppery.

steps.prompt: Grüner Veltliner is Austria's most planted grape.
steps.explanation: Yes, about a third of its vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grüner gives citrus, green apple and white pepper
It's Austria's native and most planted grape
Its parents are Traminer and St. Georgener-Rebe

steps.title: Lower Austria
steps.body: Grüner grows mainly in Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, along the Danube and to the north. Weinviertel, the largest region, makes peppery, fresh Grüner; it was Austria's first DAC, in 2003. The Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal make powerful, structured versions on steep terraces. Vienna also grows it.

steps.title: DAC
steps.body: Austria's DAC system, Districtus Austriae Controllatus, ties regions to typical grapes and styles. A Weinviertel DAC is Grüner Veltliner; Kamptal DAC and Kremstal DAC are Grüner or Riesling. Labels can add Reserve for riper, fuller wines. The Wachau uses its own terms: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd.

steps.prompt: Match each Austrian term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Austria labels by region and style.

steps.title: Abroad
steps.body: Grüner Veltliner is spreading: Slovakia and Czech Republic grow it, and New Zealand, Australia's Adelaide Hills, the US and England have new plantings. Cool to moderate climates suit it best, keeping its freshness and pepper.

steps.prompt: What is Austria's DAC system?
options: A system linking regions to typical grapes and styles
steps.explanation: DAC labels tell you region and expected style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grüner grows mainly in Lower Austria
Weinviertel was Austria's first DAC, in 2003
It's spreading to cool climates abroad

lessons.title: White pepper and loess
lessons.subtitle: Why Grüner tastes as it does
objectives: Explain the role of loess soils

steps.title: Rotundone
steps.body: Grüner's white pepper note comes from rotundone, the same compound that gives Syrah its black pepper aroma and is found in peppercorns. It forms in the skins, especially in cooler sites and years. Like in Syrah, about one in five people can't smell it at all.

steps.title: Loess
steps.body: Grüner grows best on loess, a fine, wind-blown, yellowish silt deposited after the last ice age. Loess is deep, holds water and warms easily, giving full-bodied, rounder Grüner. In the Wachau and Kamptal, loess terraces sit beside primary rock, gneiss and granite, which give leaner, more mineral Grüner, often used for Riesling.

steps.prompt: The compound that gives Grüner its white pepper note is ____.
steps.explanation: Rotundone, also found in Syrah and peppercorns.

steps.title: Light to powerful
steps.body: Light Grüner, like many Weinviertel and Steinfeder wines, is crisp, peppery and best young. Powerful Grüner, like Wachau Smaragd or Kamptal Reserve from loess, is rich, with stone fruit, spice and a creamy texture, and can age 10 to 20 years, gaining honey and toast.

steps.prompt: What does loess give Grüner?
steps.explanation: Primary rock, not loess, gives leaner wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rotundone gives Grüner its white pepper
Loess gives full, round Grüner; rock gives mineral wines
Styles range from light to powerful and age-worthy

steps.title: Versatile
steps.body: Grüner is famous for being food-friendly. It handles tricky vegetables like asparagus and artichokes, and suits Wiener Schnitzel, a Viennese classic, fried chicken, sushi, Vietnamese and Thai dishes, salads and fresh cheeses. Its pepper suits peppery food.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve light Grüner at 7 to 9 degrees, richer styles at 10 to 12. Light styles are best within two years. Smaragd and Reserve can age 10 to 20 years. In Vienna, young Grüner is drunk in Heurigen, wine taverns serving the latest vintage.

steps.explanation: Breaded veal and Grüner's freshness are a Vienna staple.

steps.body: Grüner Veltliner is a safe choice at a restaurant when the table orders very different dishes. It rarely clashes.

steps.explanation: Yes. It's one of the few wines that does.

points: Grüner suits schnitzel, asparagus and Asian food
Serve light styles at 7 to 9 degrees
Smaragd and Reserve age 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Which compound gives Grüner its pepper note?
steps.explanation: Rotundone, as in Syrah.

steps.explanation: Grüner's world is Austrian.

steps.prompt: Grüner Veltliner is closely related to Roter Veltliner.
steps.explanation: Not true. Despite the name, they're not closely related.

steps.prompt: Which describe Grüner?
steps.explanation: Lychee belongs to Gewürztraminer.

steps.prompt: Grüner is about a ____ of Austria's vineyards.
steps.explanation: About a third.

modules.title: Riesling
modules.description: Germany's great grape: piercing acidity, pure fruit and every sweetness level, from bone dry to luscious.

steps.title: Bright and pure
steps.body: Riesling gives whites with lime, lemon, green apple, peach, apricot and white flowers, with a mineral, sometimes smoky edge. Acidity is very high. It's almost never oaked or put through malolactic, so its fruit is pure and transparent. It ranges from bone dry to intensely sweet, and from light to full-bodied.

steps.title: German origins
steps.body: Riesling comes from the Rhine valley in Germany, first recorded in 1435 near Rüsselsheim. DNA shows one parent is Gouais Blanc; the other was a Traminer crossed with a wild vine. It buds late and ripens late, so it needs a long season. Its hard wood resists winter cold well, ideal for northern vineyards.

steps.prompt: Why is Riesling's fruit so pure and transparent?
options: It's rarely oaked or put through malolactic
steps.explanation: Without oak or malolactic, nothing masks its fruit or place.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon, sometimes green-tinged colour, intense lime, apple and flower aromas, and very high acidity. Sweet versions balance sugar with that acidity. Aged Riesling shows honey, toast and a petrol note. High acidity with floral, citrus fruit and no oak is the signature.

steps.prompt: Riesling buds and ripens early.
steps.explanation: Not true. It buds and ripens late, needing a long season.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling gives lime, peach and flowers with very high acidity
It comes from the Rhine, recorded in 1435
It's rarely oaked, so it shows fruit and place clearly

steps.title: Germany and Europe
steps.body: Germany grows about 40% of the world's Riesling, in the Mosel, Rheingau, Pfalz, Nahe and Rheinhessen. Alsace makes dry, fuller Riesling. Austria's Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal make dry, powerful versions on steep terraces. It's also grown in northern Italy and across central Europe.

steps.title: The New World
steps.body: Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys make dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages toward toast. New Zealand's Marlborough and Central Otago, Washington State, New York's Finger Lakes and Canada's Niagara also excel. Riesling needs cool or moderate climates to keep its acidity and aromas.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Riesling style.
steps.explanation: Each region gives Riesling a different accent.

steps.title: Site expression
steps.body: Because Riesling is unoaked and unblended, it shows soil and site clearly. Slate gives smoky, delicate wines; volcanic soils give spice; limestone gives tension; loess gives roundness. That's why Germany and Alsace name single vineyards on labels, like Burgundy.

steps.prompt: What share of the world's Riesling does Germany grow?
steps.explanation: Germany is by far the largest producer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany grows about 40% of the world's Riesling
Australia, Austria, Alsace and North America also excel
Riesling shows soil and site with unusual clarity

steps.title: Ripeness at harvest
steps.body: Germany's top quality level, Prädikatswein, is graded by the sugar in the grapes at harvest, measured in degrees Oechsle. The six levels: Kabinett, Spätlese, late harvest; Auslese, selected bunches; Beerenauslese, selected berries; Eiswein, frozen grapes; and Trockenbeerenauslese, dried, botrytised berries. Minimums vary by region.

steps.title: Ripeness, not sweetness
steps.body: A Prädikat says how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. A Spätlese can be fermented dry, labelled trocken, or left off-dry or sweet. Trocken means up to 9 g/l of sugar; halbtrocken up to 18 g/l; feinherb is an unofficial off-dry term. Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese are always sweet.

steps.prompt: Order these Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Each level demands riper grapes; TBA requires shrivelled, botrytised berries.

steps.title: The VDP
steps.body: Germany's VDP, an association of top estates, uses its own vineyard classification: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. Its top dry wines are labelled Grosses Gewächs, GG, from Grosse Lage sites. Many VDP members use Prädikat terms only for sweeter wines.

steps.prompt: What does trocken on a German label mean?
options: Dry, up to 9 g/l of sugar
steps.explanation: Trocken means dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prädikat levels grade ripeness at harvest, from Kabinett to TBA
They show ripeness, not necessarily sweetness
The VDP's GG means dry wine from a top site

lessons.title: Dry to sweet
lessons.subtitle: Riesling's full range
objectives: Explain the balance of sugar and acidity

steps.title: Dry and off-dry
steps.body: Dry Riesling, from Alsace, Austria, Australia and Germany's trocken and GG wines, is crisp and mineral, with citrus and stone fruit. Off-dry Riesling, like many Mosel Kabinetts, balances a little sugar with high acidity, often at only 7.5 to 9% alcohol, tasting fresh rather than sweet.

steps.title: Sugar and acidity
steps.body: The balance between sugar and acidity defines Riesling. High acidity, often 8 to 10 g/l, makes even 40 or 50 g/l of sugar taste only slightly sweet. The International Riesling Foundation created a taste profile scale, from dry to sweet, that some producers print on the back label to help buyers.

steps.prompt: Why does an off-dry Mosel Kabinett taste fresh rather than sweet?
steps.explanation: Acidity counters the perception of sweetness.

steps.title: Sweet Riesling
steps.body: Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese are sweet, sometimes extremely so: TBA can exceed 300 g/l of sugar, with only 6 to 8% alcohol. Riesling's acidity keeps them lively. These are among the longest-lived wines in the world.

steps.prompt: Which Riesling styles are usually dry?
steps.explanation: TBA is among the sweetest wines in the world.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling ranges from bone dry to intensely sweet
High acidity balances sugar, making off-dry wines taste fresh
Sweet Riesling can exceed 300 g/l and live for decades

steps.title: TDN
steps.body: Aged Riesling often smells of petrol, kerosene or rubber. The compound is TDN, 1,1,6-trimethyl-1,2-dihydronaphthalene. It forms from carotenoids in the grape skins, more so with strong sunlight, heat, drought and low yields. Australian Riesling, under intense sun, often shows it early. Some love it; others find it a flaw in excess.

steps.title: How it ages
steps.body: Young Riesling shows fresh lime, apple and flowers. With 5 to 10 years, it gains honey, toast, beeswax and dried apricot, and colour deepens to gold. High acidity preserves it: good dry Riesling ages 15 to 20 years; sweet Auslese and TBA can age 50 years or more.

steps.prompt: What favours the formation of TDN in Riesling?
steps.explanation: Sun exposure increases carotenoids, which become TDN.

steps.body: If you dislike strong petrol notes, look for Riesling from cooler sites, like the Mosel. Hotter, sunnier regions tend to show more TDN.

steps.prompt: Good sweet Riesling can age for 50 years or more.
steps.explanation: Yes. Sugar and high acidity preserve it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: TDN gives aged Riesling its petrol note, more with sun
With age, Riesling gains honey, toast and beeswax
Dry Riesling ages 15 to 20 years; sweet styles 50 or more

steps.title: Versatile
steps.body: Dry Riesling suits fish, shellfish, pork, sushi and Alsace's choucroute. Off-dry Riesling suits spicy Asian food: Thai, Sichuan, Indian; its sugar and low alcohol calm chilli. Sweet Riesling suits fruit desserts, blue cheese and foie gras. Riesling's acidity cuts fat and salt.

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve Riesling at 7 to 10 degrees; aged and sweet styles a little warmer, 10 to 12. Use a white wine glass with a narrowing rim to focus the aromas. Riesling under screw cap ages well and avoids cork taint.

steps.prompt: Why does off-dry Riesling suit spicy food?
options: Its sugar and low alcohol calm chilli heat
steps.explanation: Sweetness soothes, and low alcohol doesn't amplify the burn.

steps.body: Mosel Kabinett with a spicy Thai salad is one of the great wine and food matches. The wine's lime and sweetness echo the dish.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Riesling?
steps.explanation: Steak suits a red wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dry Riesling suits fish, pork and choucroute
Off-dry Riesling is a top match for spicy food
Serve at 7 to 10 degrees in a narrowing glass

steps.prompt: Order the Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Riper grapes at each step.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Riesling's labels have their own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Why does Riesling age so well?
steps.explanation: Acidity preserves it for decades.

steps.prompt: A Spätlese is always sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. Spätlese measures ripeness; it can be dry.

steps.prompt: Which regions are known for dry Riesling?
steps.explanation: Sauternes is a sweet Sémillon-based wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling is pure, high-acid and unoaked
Prädikat levels measure ripeness, not sweetness
It ranges from dry to TBA, and ages for decades
Off-dry Riesling is a great match for spicy food

modules.title: Verdejo
modules.description: Rueda's grape: herbal, citrus and fennel, with a bitter almond finish.

steps.title: Fresh and herbal
steps.body: Verdejo gives crisp whites with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, fennel, bay leaf and fresh-cut grass, and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is medium to high, body light to medium. It's one of Spain's most popular whites, made mainly in Rueda, in Castilla y León.

steps.title: A revived grape
steps.body: Verdejo has grown in Rueda for centuries, probably brought from North Africa in the Middle Ages. It was long used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines. In 1972, the Rioja house Marqués de Riscal began making fresh, crisp Verdejo in Rueda, with cool fermentation. That modern style made Rueda famous; it became a DO in 1980.

steps.prompt: What changed Verdejo's style in the 1970s?
options: Marqués de Riscal's fresh, cool-fermented wines
steps.explanation: Riscal's modern approach created the fresh style Rueda is known for.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon-green colour, citrus with herbal fennel and grassy notes, a crisp palate and a slightly bitter, almond finish. It's similar to Sauvignon Blanc, with which it's often blended, but more herbal, less pungent and with that bitter twist.

steps.prompt: Verdejo was once used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines.
steps.explanation: Yes. Before the 1970s, Rueda was known for oxidative styles.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Verdejo gives citrus, fennel and a bitter almond finish
It's grown in Rueda for centuries
Marqués de Riscal created its modern fresh style in 1972

steps.title: High plateau
steps.body: Rueda lies on Spain's central Meseta, at 700 to 850 m. Its climate is continental: hot days, cold nights, harsh winters. Soils are stony, sandy and gravelly, with lime. The large day and night swing preserves Verdejo's acidity and aroma. Old ungrafted vines still grow in sandy soils.

steps.title: Night harvesting
steps.body: Because Verdejo oxidises easily, many producers harvest at night, by machine, when temperatures are cooler. Cool grapes reach the winery fresh, keeping aromas. Skin contact and lees ageing can add texture. Most is made in steel; some top wines use oak or concrete eggs.
steps.highlight: Picked at night to stay fresh

steps.prompt: Match each Rueda term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Rueda's rules and practices protect Verdejo's freshness.

steps.body: Look for Rueda Verdejo on the label for a wine made mainly from Verdejo. Plain Rueda may include more Sauvignon Blanc or Viura.

steps.prompt: Why is Verdejo often harvested at night?
options: To keep grapes cool and avoid oxidation
steps.explanation: Cool grapes keep their fresh aromas.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rueda's high plateau gives hot days and cold nights
Night harvesting keeps Verdejo fresh
Rueda Verdejo must be at least 85% Verdejo

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Verdejo
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Tapas and seafood
steps.body: Verdejo suits tapas, grilled fish, prawns, salads, goat's cheese and dishes with herbs. Its herbal notes match green sauces and fennel; its acidity handles fried food like calamari. In Castilla, it's the everyday white with lunch.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 7 to 9 degrees. Most Verdejo is best within one to two years. Oak- or lees-aged versions, and Rueda Dorado, a traditional oxidative fortified style, can age longer.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits Verdejo?
steps.explanation: Its acidity cuts through fried food.

steps.body: Rueda Dorado, a rare traditional style aged in glass demijohns in the sun and then in barrel, shows Verdejo's oxidative past.

steps.prompt: Which describe Verdejo's food matches?
steps.explanation: Rich red meat needs a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Verdejo suits tapas, seafood and herbal dishes
Serve at 7 to 9 degrees
Most is best within two years

steps.prompt: Which finish is typical of Verdejo?
steps.explanation: A slightly bitter, almond finish.

steps.prompt: Match each fact to Verdejo.
steps.explanation: Verdejo's story is old and new.

steps.prompt: Verdejo is often blended with Sauvignon Blanc.
steps.explanation: Yes, especially in plain Rueda.

steps.prompt: Which describe Rueda?
steps.explanation: Rueda is inland and dry.

steps.prompt: Rueda Verdejo must contain at least ____% Verdejo.
steps.explanation: At least 85%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Verdejo is herbal, crisp, with a bitter almond finish
Rueda's high plateau keeps it fresh
Modern Verdejo began in 1972
It's a classic with tapas and seafood

modules.title: Albariño
modules.description: Also called Alvarinho in Portugal. A crisp, saline, peach-scented white of the Atlantic north-west of Iberia.

steps.title: Bright and saline
steps.body: Albariño gives crisp whites with lemon, grapefruit, white peach, apricot, white flowers and a saline, mineral edge. Acidity is high, body light to medium. It's aromatic yet dry. Its home is the Atlantic coast of north-west Spain and northern Portugal.

steps.title: Thick skins
steps.body: Albariño has small berries with thick skins, which resist mildew and rot in its wet, humid homeland. Thick skins also hold aromatic compounds, giving its perfume, and can add a slightly bitter, phenolic finish. Some producers use skin contact or lees ageing for extra texture.
steps.highlight: Thick skins for a wet climate

steps.prompt: Why does Albariño suit its wet, Atlantic home?
options: Its thick skins resist mildew and rot
steps.explanation: Thick skins protect against humidity.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon colour, peach and citrus aromas, and a crisp, saline, mineral palate. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's more stone fruit and less green; compared with Viognier, lighter and much fresher.

steps.prompt: Albariño has thin skins that make it prone to rot.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its thick skins help it resist rot.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Albariño gives peach, citrus and a saline edge
Thick skins resist rot in a wet climate
It's crisp, aromatic and dry

steps.title: Rías Baixas
steps.body: Rías Baixas, in Galicia, Spain's Atlantic north-west, is about 96% Albariño. It's named after the rías, flooded river valleys. Rainfall is high, 1,600 mm or more a year. Five sub-zones include Val do Salnés, coolest and most Atlantic, and O Rosal and Condado do Tea, warmer, along the Miño river. Granite soils dominate.

steps.title: Pergolas
steps.body: To fight humidity, vines are traditionally trained on high pergolas, called parras, on granite posts, two metres or more above the ground. Air circulates under the canopy, reducing rot; grapes stay away from damp soil. Some growers now use wire trellises, which allow more sun on the fruit.

steps.prompt: Match each Rías Baixas term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Rías Baixas' landscape shapes its wine.

steps.title: Portugal
steps.body: Across the Miño, called Minho in Portugal, Albariño is called Alvarinho. It grows in Vinho Verde, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Spain and Portugal share the grape, divided by a river.

steps.prompt: Why are Albariño vines trained on high pergolas?
options: To let air circulate and reduce rot
steps.explanation: Height and airflow fight humidity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rías Baixas is about 96% Albariño on granite
High pergolas fight humidity
Across the river, Portugal calls it Alvarinho

lessons.title: Albariño and Alvarinho
lessons.subtitle: One grape, two countries
objectives: Explain the role of lees ageing

steps.title: Two styles
steps.body: Spanish Albariño from Rías Baixas is crisp, peachy and saline, usually unoaked, around 12.5 to 13%. Portuguese Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço, a warmer, sheltered sub-region of Vinho Verde, is often fuller and riper, with tropical notes. Both share the grape's acidity and perfume.

steps.title: Monção e Melgaço
steps.body: Monção e Melgaço, on the south bank of the Minho, is protected from the Atlantic by hills, so it's warmer and drier than the rest of Vinho Verde. Alvarinho there reaches higher ripeness and gives Vinho Verde's most serious whites. Unlike most Vinho Verde, they're rarely spritzy.

steps.prompt: Why is Monção e Melgaço warmer than the rest of Vinho Verde?
options: Hills shelter it from the Atlantic
steps.explanation: Shelter from Atlantic winds and rain gives more warmth.

steps.title: Lees and ageing
steps.body: Many producers age Albariño on its lees for months, adding texture and creaminess. Some use oak or concrete. Though usually drunk young, good Albariño and Alvarinho can age five to ten years, gaining honey and toasted notes while keeping their acidity.

steps.prompt: Which describe Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho?
steps.explanation: Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is rarely spritzy.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rías Baixas Albariño is crisp and saline
Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is riper and fuller
Lees ageing adds texture; good examples age

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Albariño
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Seafood
steps.body: Albariño is Galicia's seafood wine: pulpo a la gallega, octopus with paprika, mussels, scallops, clams, oysters and grilled fish. Its acidity and saline edge match the sea. It also suits ceviche, sushi and light Asian dishes.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Most is best within two to three years. Lees-aged and top examples can age five to ten years. In Galicia, it's often served in a white ceramic cup, a cunca, for local wines.

steps.prompt: Which Galician dish is a classic match for Albariño?
steps.explanation: Octopus with paprika and olive oil suits Albariño's acidity and salinity.

steps.body: Albariño with a plate of mussels or oysters is about as close to a perfect pairing as it gets.

steps.prompt: Most Albariño is best drunk within two to three years.
steps.explanation: Yes, though top examples can age longer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Albariño suits octopus, shellfish and ceviche
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees
Most is best young; top wines age

steps.prompt: Match each term to Albariño.
steps.explanation: One grape, two countries.

steps.prompt: What helps Albariño resist rot?
steps.explanation: Thick skins protect it in wet weather.

steps.prompt: Rías Baixas is about 96% Albariño.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.prompt: Which describe Albariño?
steps.explanation: White Albariño has little tannin.

steps.prompt: In Portugal, Albariño is called ____.
steps.explanation: Alvarinho, the star of Monção e Melgaço.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Albariño is crisp, peachy and saline
Thick skins suit Atlantic humidity
Rías Baixas and Monção e Melgaço are its homes
It's a natural seafood wine

modules.title: Sauvignon Blanc
modules.description: Also called Fumé Blanc. Grass, gooseberry and passion fruit, from the Loire to Marlborough.

lessons.title: Meet Sauvignon Blanc
lessons.subtitle: Green, zesty and aromatic
objectives: Describe Sauvignon Blanc's flavours and structure

steps.title: Pungent and fresh
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc gives crisp, aromatic whites with gooseberry, lime, grapefruit, passion fruit, cut grass, green pepper, elderflower and sometimes a flinty or smoky note. Acidity is high, body light to medium. Most is unoaked and drunk young. It's one of the most recognisable white grapes.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc probably comes from the Loire or Bordeaux; its name may come from sauvage, wild, for its vigorous growth. DNA shows a close link to Savagnin, of the Traminer family. Crossed with Cabernet Franc, it gave Cabernet Sauvignon in 17th century Bordeaux. It buds late and ripens early.

steps.prompt: Which famous red grape is Sauvignon Blanc a parent of?
steps.explanation: Sauvignon Blanc crossed with Cabernet Franc gave Cabernet Sauvignon.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon-green colour, an intense nose of gooseberry, grass and citrus, sometimes tropical fruit, and a crisp, mouth-watering palate. Compared with Riesling, it's more green and herbal, less floral; compared with Chardonnay, much more aromatic and usually unoaked.

steps.prompt: Most Sauvignon Blanc is aged in new oak.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most is unoaked, to keep its fresh aromas.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sauvignon Blanc gives gooseberry, grass and citrus
It's a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon
It's crisp, aromatic and usually unoaked

lessons.title: Where it grows
lessons.subtitle: From the Loire to the world

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc's French homes are the Loire, especially Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, and Bordeaux, blended with Sémillon. New Zealand's Marlborough made it world-famous. Chile's coastal valleys, like Casablanca and Leyda, South Africa's Elgin and Durbanville, California, Austria's Styria and north-east Italy also grow it.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc needs a cool or moderate climate to keep its acidity and aromas. Cool sites give green, grassy, citrus styles; warmer ones give tropical, passion fruit and melon. Too much heat makes it flat and loses its aromas. Coastal influence and altitude help in warmer countries.
steps.highlight: Cool for green; warmer for tropical

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Sauvignon style.
steps.explanation: Climate and tradition shape each style.

steps.title: Pyrazines and thiols
steps.body: Sauvignon's green notes come from methoxypyrazines, highest in cool sites and shaded fruit. Its tropical notes come from thiols, like 3MH, smelling of passion fruit and grapefruit, released from precursors during fermentation. Winemakers can boost thiols with machine harvesting, skin contact and specific yeasts.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Sauvignon's passion fruit aroma?
steps.explanation: Thiols like 3MH, released during fermentation.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sauvignon grows in the Loire, Bordeaux, New Zealand and beyond
Cool sites give green notes; warmer ones tropical
Pyrazines give grass; thiols give passion fruit

steps.title: Sancerre
steps.body: Sancerre, on the left bank of the upper Loire, makes 100% Sauvignon Blanc whites from hillside vineyards. Its style is crisp and restrained, with citrus, gooseberry, white flowers and a mineral, flinty edge. Sancerre also makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir. Nearby Menetou-Salon, Quincy and Reuilly make similar wines.

steps.title: Soils
steps.body: Three soils shape Sancerre: terres blanches, Kimmeridgian clay-limestone, giving full, structured wines; caillottes, stony limestone, giving fresh, aromatic wines; and silex, flint, giving smoky, mineral, long-lived wines. Pouilly-Fumé, across the river, is known for its flint and a smoky, gunflint character, hence fumé, smoky.

steps.prompt: Match each soil to its Sancerre style.
steps.explanation: Soil shapes each Sancerre.

steps.body: Didier Dagueneau, in Pouilly-Fumé, made some of the world's most celebrated Sauvignon Blanc, showing how long it can age from great sites.

steps.prompt: What does fumé in Pouilly-Fumé refer to?
steps.explanation: Fumé means smoky, linked to its flint soils and the grape's bloom.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sancerre is crisp, restrained and mineral
Terres blanches, caillottes and silex give different styles
Pouilly-Fumé is known for smoky, flinty wines

steps.title: Sun and cool nights
steps.body: Marlborough, at the north-east tip of New Zealand's South Island, has long, sunny days, high UV light and cold nights. That combination gives intensely aromatic Sauvignon with ripe tropical fruit and piercing acidity at the same time. Stony, free-draining soils in the Wairau Valley help.
steps.highlight: Sun by day, cold by night

steps.title: The style
steps.body: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is explosive: passion fruit, gooseberry, grapefruit, cut grass and green pepper, with high acidity. Cloudy Bay's 1985 vintage made it famous worldwide. Today Sauvignon Blanc is about 60% of New Zealand's vineyards and over 80% of its exports.

steps.prompt: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became world-famous with Cloudy Bay's ____ vintage.
steps.explanation: Cloudy Bay's 1985 launched the Marlborough style.

steps.title: Variations
