steps.body: Marlborough isn't one style. The Wairau Valley gives classic tropical, aromatic wines; the Awatere Valley, cooler and windier, gives more herbal, mineral, saline wines. Some producers use barrel fermentation, wild yeast or lees ageing for more complex, textured versions.

steps.prompt: Which describe classic Marlborough Sauvignon?
steps.explanation: Most Marlborough Sauvignon is unoaked and fresh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marlborough's sun and cold nights give intense, fresh Sauvignon
Cloudy Bay's 1985 made it world-famous
The Awatere gives a cooler, more herbal style

steps.title: Bordeaux
steps.body: In Bordeaux, Sauvignon Blanc is blended with Sémillon, sometimes Muscadelle. Sauvignon brings acidity and aroma; Sémillon body and texture. Pessac-Léognan makes the finest dry whites, often fermented and aged in oak, which can age 20 years. Entre-Deux-Mers makes fresh, unoaked versions. Sauvignon is also part of sweet Sauternes.

steps.title: Fumé Blanc
steps.body: In 1966, Robert Mondavi in California named his oak-aged Sauvignon Blanc Fumé Blanc, borrowing from Pouilly-Fumé, to sell a then-unpopular grape. It worked. Today Fumé Blanc in the US often, but not always, means an oaked Sauvignon. The term isn't legally defined.

steps.prompt: Who created the name Fumé Blanc?
steps.explanation: Mondavi borrowed from Pouilly-Fumé in 1966.

steps.title: Sweet and other styles
steps.body: In Sauternes, Sauvignon adds acidity and freshness to botrytised Sémillon. In Styria, Austria, and Friuli, Italy, Sauvignon is made in a mineral, sometimes oak-aged style. Chile's Leyda and South Africa's Elgin give fresh, coastal versions.

steps.prompt: Fumé Blanc is a legally defined style.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's a marketing term, often but not always meaning an oaked Sauvignon.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bordeaux blends Sauvignon with Sémillon, often oaked
Fumé Blanc was Mondavi's 1966 marketing name
Sauvignon adds freshness to Sauternes

steps.title: Green and fresh
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc suits goat's cheese, a Loire classic with Sancerre, salads, green vegetables, asparagus, herbs, seafood, sushi and Thai dishes with lime and coriander. Its acidity cuts through fried food. Oaked Bordeaux whites suit richer fish and white meat.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 7 to 10 degrees. Most Sauvignon Blanc is best within one to three years. Top Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé and Pessac-Léognan can age 10 to 20 years, gaining honey, smoke and mineral notes.

steps.prompt: Which cheese is a classic Loire match for Sancerre?
steps.explanation: Crottin de Chavignol comes from a village in Sancerre.

steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc's green notes make it one of the few wines that pairs with asparagus and green salads.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: Beef stew needs a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sauvignon suits goat's cheese, greens and herbs
Serve at 7 to 10 degrees
Top Loire and Bordeaux wines age 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Match each region to its style.
steps.explanation: Each place shows a different side.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Sauvignon its grassy, green pepper notes?
steps.explanation: Methoxypyrazines, highest in cool, shaded sites.

steps.prompt: Sauvignon Blanc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Yes, with Cabernet Franc.

steps.prompt: Which are Sancerre's soils?
steps.explanation: Llicorella is Priorat's slate.

steps.prompt: Cloudy Bay's 1985 vintage made ____ Sauvignon Blanc famous.
steps.explanation: Marlborough.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sauvignon Blanc is crisp, green and aromatic
Sancerre and Marlborough are its benchmarks
Bordeaux blends it with Sémillon
It suits goat's cheese, greens and herbs

modules.title: Melon de Bourgogne
modules.description: The grape of Muscadet: light, crisp and saline, made richer by ageing on its lees.

steps.title: Light and crisp
steps.body: Melon de Bourgogne, often just Melon, gives light, very dry whites with lemon, green apple, pear, white flowers and a saline, mineral note. Acidity is high, alcohol moderate, often 12% or less; Muscadet is legally capped at 12% for most wines. It's neutral in aroma, which makes lees ageing important.

steps.title: From Burgundy to the sea
steps.body: As its name says, Melon came from Burgundy. It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, a sibling of Chardonnay. After the harsh winter of 1709 killed many vines near Nantes, growers replanted with frost-resistant Melon. It became the grape of Muscadet, near the Loire's mouth. Burgundy later banned it.

steps.prompt: Why was Melon planted near Nantes?
options: It survived the harsh winter of 1709
steps.explanation: After the 1709 freeze, frost-resistant Melon replaced lost vines.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for very pale colour, a subtle nose of lemon, apple and sea air, and a light, crisp, saline palate. Lees-aged versions add bread and a slight creaminess, and sometimes a tiny spritz. Compared with Pinot Grigio, it's more saline and mineral.

steps.prompt: Melon de Bourgogne is a sibling of Chardonnay.
steps.explanation: Yes. Both are crosses of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Melon gives light, crisp, saline whites
It came from Burgundy and replaced vines near Nantes after 1709
It's a sibling of Chardonnay

steps.title: Muscadet
steps.body: Melon grows almost only in the Pays Nantais, near Nantes, where the Loire meets the Atlantic. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, the largest and most important appellation, sits south-east of Nantes. Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire and Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu are smaller. The climate is maritime: mild, damp, with sea breezes.

steps.title: Crus communaux
steps.body: Since 2011, Muscadet has recognised crus communaux, village crus, with specific soils and longer lees ageing, from 17 months to several years. Examples include Clisson, on granite, Gorges, on gabbro, and Le Pallet, on gneiss and gabbro. They show Melon's capacity for complex, age-worthy wines.

steps.prompt: Match each cru to its soil.
steps.explanation: Soils shape Muscadet's crus.

steps.body: Look for a cru communal name on a Muscadet label. These wines spend much longer on their lees and show how serious Melon can be.

steps.prompt: What are Muscadet's crus communaux?
options: Village crus with specific soils and long lees ageing
steps.explanation: They require specific soils and extended lees ageing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Melon grows in the Pays Nantais, mainly Sèvre et Maine
The climate is maritime and mild
Crus communaux, since 2011, show its complexity

steps.title: Sur lie
steps.body: Muscadet sur lie stays on its fine lees, the dead yeast, through winter until bottling in spring. This adds bread and yeasty notes, a creamier texture and protection against oxidation, plus a slight spritz from retained CO2. It gives a neutral grape more depth and character.

steps.title: Oysters
steps.body: Muscadet is the classic oyster wine: its high acidity, low alcohol and saline edge match shellfish perfectly. It also suits mussels, clams, crab, grilled sardines and beurre blanc, Nantes' butter sauce. Serve at 7 to 9 degrees. Most is best within three years; crus communaux age 10 years or more.

steps.prompt: What does sur lie ageing add to Muscadet?
options: Bread notes, creaminess and a slight spritz
steps.explanation: Lees contact adds texture and depth.

steps.body: Muscadet is one of the best-value white wines in France. A good sur lie with a dozen oysters is a classic French pleasure.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Muscadet?
steps.explanation: Roast beef needs a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sur lie ageing adds bread, cream and a slight spritz
Muscadet is the classic oyster wine
Serve at 7 to 9 degrees; crus communaux age longer

steps.prompt: Which wine is made from Melon de Bourgogne?
steps.explanation: Muscadet, despite the name, isn't Muscat.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Muscadet.
steps.explanation: Muscadet's story is maritime.

steps.prompt: Muscadet is made from the Muscat grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's made from Melon de Bourgogne.

steps.prompt: Which describe Muscadet?
steps.explanation: Muscadet is rarely oaked.

steps.prompt: Muscadet is the classic match for ____.
steps.explanation: Its acidity and salinity suit shellfish.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Melon makes Muscadet: light, crisp and saline
It came from Burgundy after the 1709 freeze
Sur lie ageing and crus communaux add depth
It's the classic oyster wine

modules.title: Glera
modules.description: Once called Prosecco itself. The grape behind Italy's famous light, fruity sparkling wine.

steps.title: Light and fruity
steps.body: Glera gives light, delicate wines with pear, green apple, white peach, melon, acacia and wisteria flowers. Acidity is medium to high, body light. Its fresh fruit and floral aromas are best preserved in sparkling wine made by the tank method. It's the main grape of Prosecco.

steps.title: Prosecco to Glera
steps.body: Until 2009, the grape itself was called Prosecco, after a village near Trieste. When Prosecco became a protected DOC and DOCG in 2009, the grape was renamed Glera, an old local synonym, so that only wines from the defined area could use the name Prosecco. Anyone could plant a grape; no one else can use the place name.
steps.highlight: Renamed in 2009 to protect the name

steps.prompt: Why was the Prosecco grape renamed Glera in 2009?
options: To protect Prosecco as a place name
steps.explanation: A grape name can be used anywhere; a protected place name can't.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Prosecco is pale lemon, with light, frothy bubbles, aromas of pear, green apple and flowers, and a fresh, light palate. Compared with Champagne, it's fruitier and less bready, with larger, softer bubbles. Most is Extra Dry or Brut.

steps.prompt: Glera was called Prosecco until 2009.
steps.explanation: Yes. It was renamed to protect Prosecco as a geographical name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Glera gives pear, apple and floral aromas
It was called Prosecco until 2009
It's the main grape of Prosecco

steps.title: Prosecco DOC
steps.body: Glera grows mainly in the Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in north-east Italy. Prosecco DOC covers a large area across nine provinces and must be at least 85% Glera. It's mostly flat land, giving large volumes of fresh, affordable wine. Prosecco Rosé, with Pinot Noir, was allowed from 2020.

steps.title: Tank method
steps.body: Most Prosecco is made by the tank method, also called Martinotti or Charmat: the second fermentation happens in large pressurised tanks, often over a few weeks. This keeps Glera's fresh fruit and floral aromas, without the bready notes of long lees ageing. It's also faster and cheaper than the traditional method.

steps.prompt: Match each Prosecco term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Prosecco has its own rules and words.

steps.title: Sweetness
steps.body: Prosecco is labelled by sweetness: Brut, up to 12 g/l; Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l; Dry, 17 to 32 g/l. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Extra Dry is the traditional style, with a soft touch of sweetness balancing the acidity.
steps.highlight: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut

steps.prompt: Which Prosecco is sweeter: Brut or Extra Dry?
steps.explanation: Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/l; Brut up to 12.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco DOC covers nine provinces, at least 85% Glera
The tank method keeps Glera's fruit fresh
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut

lessons.title: Conegliano Valdobbiadene
lessons.subtitle: Prosecco's hills
objectives: Explain why the hills give better wines

steps.title: The DOCG
steps.body: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG lies in the steep hills between the towns of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, north of Venice. The hills, called hogbacks, are so steep that most work is by hand. The area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019. Asolo, nearby, is a second DOCG.

steps.title: Rive and Cartizze
steps.body: Rive are single-village or hamlet crus on the steepest slopes, 43 in total, picked by hand with lower yields. Cartizze, a single hill of about 107 hectares near Valdobbiadene, is the most prized, with some of Italy's most expensive vineyard land. Its wines are traditionally a little sweeter, often labelled Dry.

steps.prompt: What is Cartizze?
options: A prized single hill in Valdobbiadene
steps.explanation: Cartizze is Prosecco's top cru, about 107 hectares.

steps.title: Why the hills
steps.body: Hillside vineyards drain well, get more sun and cooler nights than the plains, and have lower yields. The wines are more aromatic, more complex and more mineral. Some producers in the hills also make Col Fondo, a traditional style refermented in bottle and left unfiltered, cloudy with lees.

steps.prompt: The Conegliano Valdobbiadene hills are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
steps.explanation: Yes, since 2019.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG is Prosecco's hill heartland
Rive and Cartizze are its top crus
Col Fondo is a traditional, bottle-fermented style

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.subtitle: Serving and pairing Prosecco
objectives: Know how long to keep it

steps.title: Aperitivo
steps.body: Prosecco is Italy's aperitivo wine: with olives, cured ham, fried snacks, cicchetti, Venetian small bites, and light seafood. It's the base of the Spritz, with Aperol or Campari and soda, and the Bellini, with white peach purée, invented at Harry's Bar in Venice. Extra Dry suits slightly spicy Asian food and fruit desserts.

steps.title: Service and age
steps.body: Serve at 6 to 8 degrees. Prosecco is made to drink young, within 12 to 18 months of the vintage, when its fruit is fresh. Unlike Champagne, it doesn't benefit from long ageing. Use a white wine glass to show its aromas, or a tulip glass.

steps.prompt: Which cocktail is made with Prosecco and white peach purée?
steps.explanation: The Bellini was invented at Harry's Bar in Venice.

steps.body: When buying Prosecco, check for the vintage, Millesimato. Drink it within a year or two to enjoy its freshness.

steps.prompt: Which are Prosecco-based drinks or pairings?
steps.explanation: Beef stew needs a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco is the aperitivo wine, base of the Spritz and Bellini
Serve at 6 to 8 degrees
Drink it young, within 12 to 18 months

steps.prompt: Match each term to Prosecco.
steps.explanation: Prosecco has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: How is most Prosecco made?
steps.explanation: The tank method keeps fresh fruit.

steps.prompt: Prosecco improves with ten years of ageing.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's best young, within 12 to 18 months.

steps.prompt: Which describe Glera?
steps.explanation: White sparkling wines have little tannin.

steps.prompt: Glera was renamed from Prosecco in ____.
steps.explanation: To protect Prosecco as a place name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Glera gives fresh pear, apple and flowers
Prosecco DOC is large; Conegliano Valdobbiadene is the hill DOCG
Most is tank-method and best young
It's the wine of aperitivo, Spritz and Bellini

modules.title: Bordeaux
modules.description: Two rivers, an estuary and the Atlantic: the region that defined the red blend and the château.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Rivers, gravel and the Atlantic
objectives: Explain its history as a trading port

steps.title: Two rivers and an estuary
steps.body: Bordeaux lies in south-west France, around the Garonne and Dordogne rivers, which meet to form the Gironde estuary before reaching the Atlantic. It has about 110,000 hectares of vines, one of the largest fine wine regions in the world. Soils vary: gravel on the Left Bank, clay and limestone on the Right.

steps.title: Maritime and variable
steps.body: The climate is maritime: mild winters, warm summers and rain throughout the year. The Atlantic and the Gulf Stream moderate temperatures; the Landes pine forest shelters vineyards from ocean winds. Rain at flowering or harvest can hurt a vintage, which is why vintage quality varies so much, and why blending several grapes spreads the risk.

steps.prompt: Why do Bordeaux vintages vary so much?
options: Its maritime climate brings rain at key moments
steps.explanation: Rain at flowering or harvest can change a year's quality.

steps.title: A trading port
steps.body: Bordeaux's wealth came from trade. From 1152 to 1453, when Aquitaine belonged to the English crown, its light red wine, called claret, flowed to England. Later, Dutch merchants drained the Médoc's marshes in the 17th century, creating the great Left Bank estates. Négociants still sell most of Bordeaux's wine through the Place de Bordeaux.
steps.highlight: Claret, the English and the Dutch

steps.prompt: Which shaped Bordeaux's history?
steps.explanation: Bordeaux's soils are gravel, clay and limestone, not volcanic.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bordeaux sits on the Garonne, Dordogne and Gironde
Its maritime climate makes vintages vary
Trade with England and the Dutch shaped its history

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Blends of five grapes
objectives: Name Bordeaux's red and white grapes

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Bordeaux's reds blend Merlot, the most planted grape, about 60% of red vines, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and small amounts of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carmenère. Since 2021, a few heat-tolerant grapes like Touriga Nacional can be used in small amounts, under trial rules.

steps.title: Why blend
steps.body: Each grape ripens at a different time and suits different soils. Merlot ripens early and likes cool clay; Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late and needs warm gravel; Cabernet Franc adds perfume. In a difficult year, blending lets the winemaker lean on whichever grape did best. Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, sometimes Muscadelle.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Each grape fills a gap in the blend.

steps.body: Bordeaux labels rarely name grapes. The appellation tells you: Left Bank wines lean on Cabernet Sauvignon, Right Bank wines on Merlot.

steps.prompt: Cabernet Sauvignon is Bordeaux's most planted red grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. Merlot is the most planted, about 60% of red vines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc lead the reds
Blending spreads risk and balances flavour
Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon

lessons.title: Left Bank, Right Bank
lessons.subtitle: Two sides of the river
objectives: Compare the Left and Right Banks
Explain how soil drives the difference

steps.title: The Left Bank
steps.body: The Left Bank, west of the Garonne and Gironde, includes the Médoc and Graves. Deep gravel soils drain well and store heat, favouring Cabernet Sauvignon. The Haut-Médoc's famous communes are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux. Graves and Pessac-Léognan, further south, make both reds and whites.
steps.highlight: Médoc and Graves: Cabernet on gravel

steps.title: The Right Bank
steps.body: The Right Bank, north of the Dordogne, includes Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and their satellites, Fronsac and the Côtes. Cooler clay and limestone suit Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Estates are smaller and often family-run. Between the rivers, Entre-Deux-Mers makes mostly dry whites.
steps.highlight: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol: Merlot on clay

steps.prompt: Match each appellation to its bank.
steps.explanation: Geography decides grape and style.

steps.title: Soil and style
steps.body: Left Bank wines are often more structured, with blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannins, built for long ageing. Right Bank wines are often rounder, plummier and softer young. Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau gives freshness; Pomerol's clay gives richness. These are tendencies, not rules.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon dominate on the Left Bank?
options: Gravel soils drain and store heat, helping it ripen
steps.explanation: Gravel's warmth helps a late-ripening grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Left Bank's gravel favours Cabernet Sauvignon
The Right Bank's clay and limestone favour Merlot
Left Bank wines are more structured; Right Bank rounder

steps.title: For a world fair
steps.body: For the 1855 Exposition Universelle in Paris, Napoleon III asked Bordeaux's brokers to rank the region's wines. They used prices. The red list ranked 61 châteaux, all from the Médoc except Haut-Brion in Graves, into five growths, or crus. Sauternes and Barsac were ranked separately, with Yquem on top.

steps.title: Almost unchanged
steps.body: The 1855 classification has changed only twice: Cantemerle was added soon after in 1856, and in 1973 Mouton Rothschild was promoted from Second to First Growth. The five First Growths are Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild. Some Fifth Growths now sell for more than some Seconds.

steps.prompt: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
steps.explanation: Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for decades for the promotion.

steps.title: Other rankings
steps.body: Graves has its own classification, from 1953 and 1959. Saint-Émilion's classification, from 1955, is revised about every ten years and has been controversial. Pomerol has no official classification. The Crus Bourgeois of the Médoc, re-established in 2020, rank hundreds of other estates.

steps.prompt: Which are First Growths of 1855?
steps.explanation: Pétrus, in Pomerol, was never classified; Pomerol has no classification.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The 1855 classification ranked Médoc reds and Sauternes by price
It has changed only twice, in 1856 and 1973
Graves, Saint-Émilion and the Crus Bourgeois have their own rankings

lessons.title: Sauternes and Barsac
lessons.subtitle: Bordeaux's sweet gold
objectives: Explain how noble rot forms in Sauternes

steps.title: The Ciron's mist
steps.body: Sauternes and Barsac lie in southern Graves, where the cold Ciron river flows into the warmer Garonne. On autumn mornings, the difference in temperature creates mist, ideal for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea. Sunny afternoons dry the grapes, stopping grey rot. The fungus shrivels berries and concentrates their sugar and acidity.
steps.highlight: Mist in the morning, sun in the afternoon

steps.title: Making it
steps.body: Sémillon, about 80%, is the main grape, with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle. Pickers pass through the vines several times, called tries, picking only botrytised berries. Yields are tiny. The wines ferment and age in oak, often new, reaching about 14% alcohol with 100 to 150 g/l of sugar.

steps.prompt: Why does the Ciron river matter for Sauternes?
options: Its cold water creates autumn mist that favours noble rot
steps.explanation: Mist plus afternoon sun is the recipe for noble rot.

steps.title: Barsac
steps.body: Barsac, on flatter, limestone-based land next to Sauternes, can label its wines Barsac or Sauternes. Its wines are often slightly lighter and fresher. Climens and Coutet are famous Barsac estates. Nearby Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont make lighter, cheaper sweet wines.

steps.prompt: Barsac producers may label their wines as Sauternes.
steps.explanation: Yes. Barsac can use either name.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sauternes
Sémillon leads; pickers make several tries
Barsac is lighter and can use either name

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Bordeaux and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Bordeaux labels show the château, the appellation, the vintage and often a classification, like Grand Cru Classé en 1855. Appellations run from broad to precise: Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur, then district appellations like Haut-Médoc, then communes like Pauillac. Mis en bouteille au château means estate-bottled. Many châteaux also make a cheaper second wine.

steps.title: Second wines and value
steps.body: Second wines, like Carruades de Lafite or Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux, use younger vines or lots not chosen for the main wine. They offer a taste of a great estate at a lower price. Côtes de Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur from good producers are often excellent value.
steps.highlight: Second wines and Côtes for value

steps.prompt: Order these appellations from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each step narrows the origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Left Bank reds suit lamb, especially roast leg of lamb, and steak. Right Bank Merlot suits duck, mushrooms and beef. Dry whites from Pessac-Léognan suit fish in butter sauce. Sauternes suits foie gras, Roquefort and fruit tarts. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young.
steps.highlight: Lamb with Pauillac, foie gras with Sauternes

steps.prompt: What does mis en bouteille au château mean?
steps.explanation: Estate-bottled, a sign the château controlled the whole process.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show château, appellation, vintage and classification
Second wines and the Côtes offer value
Lamb suits Left Bank reds; foie gras suits Sauternes

steps.prompt: Match each place to its character.
steps.explanation: Bordeaux's sub-regions each have a role.

steps.prompt: How were châteaux ranked in 1855?
steps.explanation: Brokers used market prices.

steps.prompt: Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 60% of red vines.

steps.prompt: Which are Left Bank communes?
steps.explanation: Saint-Émilion is on the Right Bank.

steps.prompt: Pickers in Sauternes make several passes, called ____.
steps.explanation: Each trie picks only the botrytised berries.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Bordeaux is maritime, built on rivers and blends
The Left Bank favours Cabernet; the Right Bank Merlot
The 1855 classification still shapes prices
Sauternes is its noble rot gold

modules.title: Burgundy
modules.description: A narrow strip of limestone slopes where single vineyards, called climats, have been mapped for a thousand years.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Limestone, monks and climats
objectives: Explain the role of the monks

steps.title: A long, narrow region
steps.body: Burgundy, Bourgogne, runs about 230 km from Chablis in the north to the Mâconnais in the south, in eastern France. Its heart is the Côte d'Or, a narrow, east-facing escarpment of limestone and marl. It has about 30,000 hectares of vines, smaller than Bordeaux, but over 1,200 named vineyard sites.

steps.title: Continental and risky
steps.body: Burgundy's climate is continental: cold winters, warm summers and risk at every stage. Spring frost can destroy buds, as in 2016 and 2021. Hail can strip vineyards in minutes. Rain at harvest brings rot. Slopes and east-facing exposure help: they catch morning sun and let cold air drain away.

steps.prompt: Why do Burgundy's best vineyards face east?
options: They catch morning sun and drain cold air
steps.explanation: East-facing slopes warm early and avoid frost pockets.

steps.title: Monks and climats
steps.body: From the 10th century, Benedictine monks of Cluny and Cistercians of Cîteaux studied Burgundy's slopes. They noticed that wines from small plots tasted consistently different and enclosed them with walls, called clos, like Clos de Vougeot. These named plots, the climats, were recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage in 2015.

steps.prompt: Burgundy's climats were recognised by UNESCO in 2015.
steps.explanation: Yes, as a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais
Its continental climate brings frost, hail and rot
Monks mapped the climats, now UNESCO-listed

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Two great grapes and two more

steps.title: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
steps.body: Burgundy's two great grapes are Pinot Noir, for reds, and Chardonnay, for whites. Unlike Bordeaux, Burgundy rarely blends: each wine is usually a single grape from a single place. The idea is that the climat, not the blend, gives the wine its character.

steps.title: Aligoté and Gamay
steps.body: Aligoté, a sibling of Chardonnay, makes crisp, lemony whites; Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, is its own appellation. Aligoté is the traditional base of the Kir, with blackcurrant liqueur. Gamay, banned from the Côte d'Or in 1395, grows mainly in Beaujolais, though it's allowed in some Burgundy blends like Coteaux Bourguignons.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Burgundy is a land of single grapes.

steps.body: Order a Kir in Burgundy and you'll get Aligoté with crème de cassis, named after Félix Kir, a mayor of Dijon.

steps.prompt: Why does Burgundy rarely blend grapes?
options: It aims to show the character of each climat
steps.explanation: A single grape lets the site speak.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are Burgundy's great grapes
Wines usually come from one grape and one place
Aligoté and Gamay play smaller roles

lessons.title: The quality pyramid
lessons.subtitle: Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
objectives: Read Grand Cru and Premier Cru labels
Explain the size of each level

steps.title: Four levels
steps.body: Burgundy's appellations form a pyramid. At the base, regional wines like Bourgogne, about half the production. Then village wines, named after a commune, like Gevrey-Chambertin. Then Premier Cru, named vineyards within a village, about 10%. At the top, 33 Grand Crus, about 1% of production.
steps.highlight: Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A village wine names the village. A Premier Cru adds the vineyard, like Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos Saint-Jacques. A Grand Cru names only the vineyard, like Chambertin or Montrachet. Many villages added their most famous Grand Cru to their name, so Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin. That can confuse: the village wine isn't the Grand Cru.
steps.highlight: Grand Crus name only the vineyard

steps.prompt: Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each level is smaller and more specific.

steps.title: Domaines and négociants
steps.body: Because vineyards are split among many owners, a single climat can appear on many labels. Domaines grow and bottle their own grapes; négociants buy grapes or wine and bottle under their own name. Producer matters as much as appellation in Burgundy.
steps.highlight: Producer matters as much as place

steps.prompt: About how many Grand Crus does Burgundy have?
steps.explanation: 33 Grand Crus, about 1% of production.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy's pyramid: regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
Grand Crus name only the vineyard
Domaines and négociants both bottle; producer matters

lessons.title: The Côte d'Or
lessons.subtitle: The golden slope
objectives: Describe the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune

steps.title: Nuits and Beaune
steps.body: The Côte d'Or runs about 50 km from Dijon to Santenay. The northern half, the Côte de Nuits, is almost all Pinot Noir and has most of the red Grand Crus. The southern half, the Côte de Beaune, makes both reds and the great white Grand Crus, like Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne.
steps.highlight: Nuits for red; Beaune for both

steps.title: Mid-slope
steps.body: The best vineyards lie mid-slope, at about 250 to 350 m. There, limestone and marl mix in thin, well-drained soils, the sun hits from the east, and cold air drains below. The slope's top is too thin and exposed; the bottom, richer and wetter, gives simpler wines. A road, the D974, roughly marks the border of good and lesser land.

steps.prompt: Match each village to its main wine.
steps.explanation: Each village has its own personality.

steps.title: Famous names
steps.body: Vosne-Romanée is home to Romanée-Conti, one of the world's most expensive wines, a 1.8-hectare Grand Cru. Chambolle-Musigny is elegant; Nuits-Saint-Georges firm. In the Côte de Beaune, Pommard is sturdy, Volnay delicate, and Corton is the only red Grand Cru.

steps.prompt: The Côte de Nuits is famous mainly for white wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's almost all Pinot Noir; the great whites come from the Côte de Beaune.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Côte de Nuits makes reds; the Côte de Beaune both
Mid-slope vineyards give the best wines
Each village, like Vosne or Meursault, has its own style

lessons.title: Chablis and the Mâconnais
lessons.subtitle: North and south
objectives: Describe the Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais

steps.title: Chablis
steps.body: Chablis, isolated in the north, about 130 km from Dijon, is cooler than the Côte d'Or. Chardonnay grows on Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils. Wines are lean, mineral and high in acidity. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Cru climats, like Les Clos and Valmur, on one south-west facing slope.

steps.title: Chalonnaise and Mâconnais
steps.body: South of the Côte d'Or, the Côte Chalonnaise has villages like Mercurey and Givry for reds, and Rully and Montagny for whites, offering good value. The Mâconnais, further south and warmer, makes rounder Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages, and Pouilly-Fuissé, which gained Premier Cru vineyards in 2020, and Saint-Véran.

steps.prompt: What makes Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil distinctive?
options: It's full of tiny oyster fossils
steps.explanation: Kimmeridgian marl contains countless fossilised oyster shells.

steps.title: Comparing whites
steps.body: Chablis is lean and mineral, usually unoaked or lightly oaked. The Côte de Beaune is richer, with oak. The Mâconnais is rounder, fruitier and more affordable. All are Chardonnay, showing how much place and climate change it.

steps.prompt: Which are Mâconnais or Chalonnaise wines?
steps.explanation: Pauillac is in Bordeaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais offer value
Pouilly-Fuissé gained Premier Crus in 2020

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Burgundy and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Burgundy label shows the appellation, from Bourgogne to Grand Cru, the producer, the vintage, and whether it's a domaine or négociant. Mis en bouteille au domaine means estate-bottled. Monopole means a single owner holds the whole vineyard, like La Romanée-Conti. Vieilles vignes means old vines, but it isn't legally defined.

steps.title: Vintage
steps.body: Because Burgundy is continental and risky, vintage matters a lot. Frost, hail and rain can halve a crop or dilute it. Warm vintages give riper, rounder wines; cool ones leaner, fresher wines. Good producers make good wine even in difficult years.

steps.prompt: What does monopole mean on a Burgundy label?
options: A single owner holds the whole vineyard
steps.explanation: A monopole belongs to one owner.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Red Burgundy suits roast chicken, duck, game birds, boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin, two dishes cooked with the region's wine. Époisses cheese suits both reds and whites. Chablis suits oysters and snails, escargots de Bourgogne; Meursault suits lobster and creamy chicken. Serve reds at 14 to 16 degrees.

steps.prompt: Vieilles vignes is a legally defined term in Burgundy.
steps.explanation: Not true. It means old vines, but there's no legal definition.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show appellation, producer and vintage
Vintage matters greatly in continental Burgundy
Red Burgundy suits coq au vin; Chablis suits oysters

steps.prompt: Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Grand Cru is the top, about 1% of production.

steps.prompt: Match each area to its wine.
steps.explanation: Burgundy runs north to south.

steps.prompt: Who first mapped Burgundy's climats?
steps.explanation: Monks studied and enclosed the plots.

steps.prompt: Burgundy usually blends many grapes in each wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. Wines are usually one grape from one place.

steps.prompt: Which are Burgundy's main grapes?
steps.explanation: Cabernet belongs to Bordeaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy is continental, east-facing and limestone
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay express each climat
The pyramid runs from Bourgogne to 33 Grand Crus
Producer and vintage matter as much as place

modules.title: Champagne
modules.description: A cold, chalky corner of northern France that turned a winemaking problem into the world's most famous sparkling wine.

steps.title: At the northern limit
steps.body: Champagne lies about 150 km north-east of Paris, at around 49 degrees north, near the northern limit for ripening grapes. Average temperatures are around 11 degrees Celsius. Grapes ripen just enough, giving high acidity and low sugar: poor still wine, but perfect base wine for sparkling. The appellation covers about 34,000 hectares.

steps.title: Chalk
steps.body: Champagne's soils are chalk, often under a thin topsoil. Chalk drains well yet holds water like a sponge, feeding vines in dry summers. It reflects light and heat. The Romans dug chalk pits, crayères, that houses later used as cellars: Reims and Épernay have hundreds of kilometres of tunnels at a steady 10 to 12 degrees.

steps.prompt: Why is Champagne's chalk so valuable?
options: It drains well yet stores water, and its cellars stay cool
steps.explanation: Chalk regulates water, and its tunnels make ideal cellars.

steps.title: From fault to fame
steps.body: In Champagne's cold winters, fermentation often stopped and restarted in spring, making wine fizzy by accident. The English, in the 17th century, bottled it in stronger glass and enjoyed the bubbles. Dom Pérignon, a monk at Hautvillers, didn't invent sparkling wine, but he improved blending and pressing. Houses developed the method in the 18th and 19th centuries.

steps.prompt: Dom Pérignon invented sparkling Champagne.
steps.explanation: Not true. He improved blending and pressing, but bubbles came from accidental refermentation, and the English first bottled it as sparkling.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne is cold, giving high-acid base wine
Chalk regulates water and provides cool cellars
Bubbles began as an accident; houses refined the method

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Three grapes, three roles
objectives: Name the main areas for each

steps.title: Three grapes
steps.body: Pinot Noir is about 38% of plantings, Meunier about 31%, Chardonnay about 31%. Pinot Noir gives body, structure and red fruit; Meunier gives fruit and roundness; Chardonnay gives finesse, acidity and ageing potential. Four other grapes, like Arbane and Petit Meslier, are allowed but rare.

steps.title: Where each grows
steps.body: The Montagne de Reims, with Grand Crus like Aÿ, Bouzy and Verzenay, favours Pinot Noir. The Vallée de la Marne, with frost pockets and clay, suits late-budding Meunier. The Côte des Blancs, on pure chalk, with Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, is Chardonnay country. The Côte des Bar, in the south, on Kimmeridgian marl, grows mainly Pinot Noir.
steps.highlight: Montagne, Vallée, Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar

steps.prompt: Match each area to its main grape.
steps.explanation: Each area favours a grape.

steps.body: Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes, usually Chardonnay; Blanc de Noirs only from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

steps.prompt: Which grape brings finesse and ageing potential to Champagne?
steps.explanation: Chardonnay gives acidity, finesse and longevity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay are Champagne's grapes
Each area favours one grape
Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs use only one colour

lessons.title: The traditional method
lessons.subtitle: How Champagne is made
objectives: Put the steps of the traditional method in order

steps.title: From base wine to bubbles
steps.body: Grapes are hand-picked and pressed whole and gently. The base wines are fermented, then blended, often with reserve wines from earlier years. The blend is bottled with sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage, and sealed with a crown cap. A second fermentation in the bottle creates about 6 atmospheres of pressure.

steps.title: Lees and riddling
steps.body: The wine then ages on its lees, dead yeast: at least 15 months for non-vintage, at least 3 years for vintage. Autolysis adds brioche, biscuit and nutty notes. Riddling moves the yeast to the neck. Disgorgement freezes the neck and removes the plug. Dosage, wine with sugar, tops up the bottle before corking.

steps.prompt: Put the traditional method steps in order.
items: Add sugar and yeast, and seal
steps.explanation: Each step builds on the one before.

steps.title: Why hand-picking
steps.body: Champagne requires hand harvesting. Whole bunches are pressed gently, so black grapes give white juice without colour or bitterness. Pressing is limited: from 4,000 kg of grapes, only 2,550 litres of juice may be used. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the finest; the next 500, the taille, are fruitier.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum lees ageing for non-vintage Champagne?
steps.explanation: Non-vintage needs 15 months in total, with at least 12 on lees; vintage needs 3 years.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne's second fermentation happens in the bottle
Non-vintage ages 15 months; vintage 3 years
Hand-picking and gentle pressing give white juice

lessons.title: Houses and growers
lessons.subtitle: Who makes Champagne
objectives: Explain the role of the houses

steps.title: The houses
steps.body: Large houses, or maisons, like Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Bollinger and Krug, own some vineyards but buy most grapes from about 16,000 growers. They blend across villages and years for a consistent house style, especially in non-vintage. Houses make about two-thirds of Champagne's sales.

steps.title: Growers
steps.body: Growers who make and sell their own Champagne are called récoltant-manipulants, labelled RM. Since the 1990s, grower Champagne has become popular for showing a single village or vineyard. Co-operatives, CM, pool members' grapes. Label codes tell you who made the wine.
steps.highlight: RM grower; NM house; CM co-op

steps.prompt: Match each label code to its meaning.
steps.explanation: The small code on the label reveals the producer type.

steps.title: The échelle des crus
steps.body: Champagne's villages were once ranked on a scale, the échelle des crus, which set grape prices: 17 villages were Grand Cru, 100%, and 42 Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The price system ended in 2010, but the names still appear on labels.

steps.prompt: Most Champagne is sold by large houses that buy grapes.
steps.explanation: Yes. Houses account for about two-thirds of sales.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Houses blend grapes from many growers for a house style
Grower Champagne, RM, shows single villages
17 villages are Grand Cru

lessons.title: Dosage and styles
lessons.subtitle: Sweetness and categories
objectives: Explain non-vintage, vintage and prestige cuvée

steps.title: Dosage
steps.body: Dosage, added after disgorgement, sets the sweetness. Brut Nature: 0 to 3 g/l, no sugar added. Extra Brut: up to 6. Brut, the most common: up to 12. Extra Dry: 12 to 17. Sec: 17 to 32. Demi-Sec: 32 to 50. Doux: over 50. Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, a common confusion.

steps.title: Categories
steps.body: Non-vintage, NV, blends several years for consistency, about 80% of production. Vintage comes from one exceptional year, aged at least 3 years. Prestige cuvées, like Dom Pérignon, Cristal or Krug Grande Cuvée, are a house's top wine. Rosé is made by blending a little still red wine, unusually allowed in Champagne, or by saignée.

steps.prompt: Order these Champagne styles from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut.

steps.title: Reading age
steps.body: Many producers now print the disgorgement date. A recently disgorged wine is fresher; one disgorged years ago has developed more toast and nuttiness. Some houses, like Bollinger with its R.D., release wines disgorged after very long lees ageing.

steps.prompt: How is most rosé Champagne made?
options: By blending in a little still red wine
steps.explanation: Champagne is an exception that allows blending red into white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dosage terms run from Brut Nature to Doux
NV, vintage and prestige cuvée are the main categories
Rosé Champagne is usually blended with red wine

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Champagne and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Champagne label shows the house or grower, the sweetness level, the producer code, NV or a vintage, and sometimes Grand Cru, Premier Cru, Blanc de Blancs or Blanc de Noirs. The word Champagne itself is protected: only wine from the region made by the traditional method can use it.

steps.title: Serving
steps.body: Serve at 8 to 10 degrees; vintage and prestige cuvées a little warmer. A white wine glass shows the aromas better than a narrow flute. Open by holding the cork and turning the bottle slowly, letting the pressure out with a sigh, not a pop.
steps.highlight: 8 to 10 degrees, in a wine glass

steps.prompt: Why might a white wine glass suit Champagne better than a flute?
options: It lets aromas gather and show
steps.explanation: A wider bowl reveals the wine's aromas.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Brut Champagne suits oysters, caviar, sushi, fried food and salty snacks; acidity and bubbles cut fat and salt. Blanc de Blancs suits shellfish; Blanc de Noirs and rosé suit poultry, salmon and charcuterie. Vintage and aged Champagne suit truffle and roast chicken. Demi-Sec suits fruit desserts.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Brut Champagne?
steps.explanation: Sweet cake makes Brut taste sour; choose Demi-Sec.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show producer, dosage, code and vintage
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees in a wine glass
Brut suits oysters and fried food; Demi-Sec suits desserts

lessons.title: Module review
lessons.subtitle: Everything about Champagne
objectives: Describe Champagne's climate, chalk and grapes

steps.prompt: Match each area to its grape.
steps.explanation: Each area favours a grape.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum ageing for vintage Champagne?
steps.explanation: Vintage needs at least 3 years.

steps.prompt: Extra Dry Champagne is drier than Brut.
steps.explanation: Not true. Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l, is sweeter than Brut.

steps.prompt: Which are Champagne's main grapes?
steps.explanation: Riesling isn't a Champagne grape.

steps.prompt: A grower who makes their own Champagne uses the code ____.
steps.explanation: Récoltant-manipulant.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Champagne is cold and chalky, giving high-acid base wine
Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay are its grapes
The traditional method and lees ageing create its style
Labels show dosage, producer type and vintage

modules.title: Loire Valley
modules.description: France's longest river and its garden: crisp whites, fresh reds and every sweetness of Chenin.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: The garden of France
objectives: Explain how climate changes along the river

steps.title: A long river
steps.body: The Loire is France's longest river, about 1,000 km. Vineyards line it for over 400 km, from the Atlantic near Nantes inland to Sancerre and Pouilly. The region is divided into four parts: the Pays Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine and the Central Vineyards. It's known as the garden of France.

steps.title: From maritime to continental
steps.body: Near the Atlantic, the Pays Nantais is maritime: mild and damp. Inland, through Anjou and Touraine, the climate becomes gradually more continental: warmer summers, colder winters. The Central Vineyards, near the centre of France, are continental. Throughout, the Loire is cool, keeping acidity high and alcohol moderate.

steps.prompt: How does the climate change as you move up the Loire from the Atlantic?
steps.explanation: Ocean influence fades inland.

steps.title: Châteaux and kings
steps.body: The Loire was the playground of French kings in the Renaissance, who built châteaux like Chambord and Chenonceau. Many were built from tuffeau, a soft, white limestone. The caves dug to extract it now serve as cellars, especially in Saumur and Vouvray. The valley between Sully-sur-Loire and Chalonnes is a UNESCO site.

steps.prompt: Which are parts of the Loire wine region?
steps.explanation: The Médoc is in Bordeaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Loire has four parts along 400 km of river
The climate shifts from maritime to continental
Tuffeau built its châteaux and cellars

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Four grapes, many styles
objectives: Link each grape to its area

steps.title: Four grapes
steps.body: Melon de Bourgogne makes Muscadet in the Pays Nantais. Chenin Blanc dominates Anjou and Touraine whites, dry to sweet. Cabernet Franc makes most of the reds, in Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny. Sauvignon Blanc leads the Central Vineyards and Touraine. Others include Gamay, Pinot Noir and Grolleau.

steps.title: Every style
steps.body: The Loire makes almost every style of wine: crisp dry whites, sweet botrytised whites, light reds, rosés, including Rosé d'Anjou, and sparkling wine, Crémant de Loire and Saumur. Cool climate and high acidity link them all. Chenin Blanc alone makes dry, sweet and sparkling.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its main area.
steps.explanation: Each part of the Loire has its grape.

steps.body: Most Loire wines are named after the place, not the grape. Learn the four grapes and their areas, and the labels open up.

steps.prompt: The Loire makes only white wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It also makes reds, rosés and sparkling wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Melon, Chenin, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon lead the Loire
Each area has its own grape
High acidity links every style

lessons.title: The western Loire
lessons.subtitle: Muscadet, Anjou and Saumur
objectives: Describe Anjou's whites and sweet wines

steps.title: Muscadet
steps.body: In the Pays Nantais, Muscadet is made from Melon de Bourgogne: light, crisp and saline. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine is the main appellation. Sur lie wines rest on their lees until bottling, gaining texture and a slight spritz. Since 2011, crus communaux, like Clisson and Gorges, show longer-aged, serious Muscadet.

steps.title: Anjou
steps.body: Anjou makes Chenin Blanc in every style. Savennières, on schist, gives dry, powerful, long-lived whites. The Layon valley, with autumn mists, gives sweet botrytised wines: Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume, the Loire's first Grand Cru, in 2011. Anjou also makes rosés like Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou.

steps.prompt: Which Loire appellation became the first Grand Cru, in 2011?
steps.explanation: Quarts de Chaume makes sweet, botrytised Chenin.

steps.title: Saumur
steps.body: Saumur, with tuffeau soils and cellars, makes Saumur Brut, a traditional method sparkling wine, mainly from Chenin Blanc, and Saumur-Champigny, a fresh, fruity Cabernet Franc red. Many sparkling houses, like Bouvet-Ladubay and Gratien & Meyer, are based there, ageing wine in tuffeau caves.

steps.prompt: Which are western Loire wines?
steps.explanation: Sancerre is in the Central Vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Muscadet is crisp Melon, often sur lie
Anjou makes dry Savennières and sweet Layon Chenin
Saumur makes sparkling wine and Cabernet Franc reds

steps.title: Touraine
steps.body: Touraine, around Tours, makes Vouvray and Montlouis from Chenin Blanc, dry to sweet and sparkling. Chinon, Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil make Cabernet Franc reds, from light to structured. Touraine Sauvignon Blanc offers good value.

steps.title: The Central Vineyards
steps.body: Far upstream, the Central Vineyards are nearer Burgundy than the Atlantic. Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé make crisp, mineral Sauvignon Blanc. Sancerre's soils: terres blanches, Kimmeridgian marl, for full wines; caillottes, limestone pebbles, for fresh ones; silex, flint, for smoky wines. Sancerre also makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its grape.
steps.explanation: The Centre and Touraine use different grapes.

steps.title: Pouilly-Fumé and neighbours
steps.body: Pouilly-Fumé, on the opposite bank from Sancerre, is known for flint and a smoky, gunflint character. Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly and Coteaux du Giennois make similar Sauvignon at lower prices. Don't confuse Pouilly-Fumé with Pouilly-Fuissé, a Chardonnay from Burgundy's Mâconnais.

steps.prompt: Pouilly-Fumé and Pouilly-Fuissé are made from the same grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is Burgundy Chardonnay.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Touraine makes Vouvray Chenin and Chinon Cabernet Franc
Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé make mineral Sauvignon
Soils like silex and caillottes shape Sancerre

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Loire and eating with it

steps.title: Reading labels
steps.body: Most Loire labels name the appellation, not the grape. Sweetness terms help for Chenin: sec, dry; demi-sec, off-dry; moelleux, sweet; doux, very sweet. Sur lie marks lees-aged Muscadet. Crémant de Loire and Saumur Brut mark traditional method sparkling wine.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Muscadet suits oysters and mussels. Sancerre suits goat's cheese, like crottin de Chavignol, and fish. Vouvray demi-sec suits pork and spicy food. Chinon suits charcuterie, rillettes and roast chicken, served slightly cool. Sweet Layon suits fruit tarts and blue cheese.

steps.prompt: Which Loire cheese is a classic match for Sancerre?
steps.explanation: Crottin de Chavignol is a goat's cheese from a Sancerre village.

steps.body: The Loire is one of France's best sources of value. Cabernet Franc from Chinon and Muscadet sur lie offer real character at modest prices.

steps.prompt: Order these Loire terms from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Doux is the sweetest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Loire labels name places; learn the grapes
Sec to doux mark Chenin's sweetness
Muscadet with oysters, Sancerre with goat's cheese

steps.prompt: Match each area to its signature wine.
steps.explanation: Four areas, four signatures.

steps.prompt: What soil gives Pouilly-Fumé its smoky character?
steps.explanation: Silex, or flint.

steps.prompt: Saumur makes traditional method sparkling wine.
steps.explanation: Yes, Saumur Brut, mainly from Chenin Blanc.

steps.prompt: Which grapes lead the Loire?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is Italian.

steps.prompt: Muscadet aged on its lees until bottling is labelled ____ lie.
steps.explanation: Sur lie.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Loire runs from maritime Nantes to continental Sancerre
Melon, Chenin, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon lead
It makes every style, always with high acidity
It offers some of France's best value

modules.title: Southern Rhône
modules.description: Sun, stones and the Mistral: Grenache-led blends from Châteauneuf-du-Pape to Côtes du Rhône.

steps.title: A wide valley
steps.body: South of Montélimar, the Rhône valley opens into a wide plain dotted with hills, around Avignon and Orange. The southern Rhône makes over 90% of all Rhône wine. Soils vary: large round stones, galets roulés, sand, clay and limestone. Côtes du Rhône covers the whole region.

steps.title: Mediterranean and windy
steps.body: The climate is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and plenty of sun. The Mistral, a cold, dry wind from the north, blows often, sometimes over 90 km/h. It dries vines after rain, reducing disease, and cools them, but can break shoots. Organic farming is common because conditions are healthy.

steps.prompt: How does the Mistral help vineyards?
options: It dries vines after rain, reducing disease
steps.explanation: A dry wind keeps grapes healthy.

steps.title: Popes and history
steps.body: In the 14th century, the popes moved to Avignon. They built a summer castle, the Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the pope's new castle, and planted vines. In 1923, Baron Le Roy of Châteauneuf drew up rules for the area's wine, which helped inspire France's AOC system, created in 1935.

steps.prompt: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's rules in the 1920s helped inspire the French AOC system.
steps.explanation: Yes. Baron Le Roy's 1923 rules were a model.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The southern Rhône makes over 90% of Rhône wine
Its Mediterranean climate and the Mistral keep vines healthy
The popes at Avignon gave Châteauneuf its name

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Grenache and its partners
objectives: Name the southern Rhône's main grapes

steps.title: Grenache leads
steps.body: Grenache is the main red grape, loving heat and drought, giving red fruit, spice and high alcohol. Syrah adds colour and structure; Mourvèdre adds tannin and savoury, gamey notes; Cinsault adds perfume and lightness, especially in rosé. Carignan also appears. Blends of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre are called GSM.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: White grapes include Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne, Marsanne, Bourboulenc and Viognier. White wines are a small share, about 7%, but growing. They're rich, with stone fruit, herbs and moderate acidity. Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc is the most famous.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Southern Rhône wines are blends.

steps.body: Côtes du Rhône red must be mainly Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre. It's one of France's best everyday reds.

steps.prompt: What does GSM stand for?
steps.explanation: GSM is Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grenache leads, with Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cinsault
GSM blends balance fruit, colour and structure
Whites are a small, growing share

steps.title: Galets roulés
steps.body: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's most famous soil is covered with galets roulés, large, round quartzite stones left by the ancient Rhône. They store heat by day and release it at night, helping ripening, and protect the soil from drying. But Châteauneuf also has sand, which gives elegant wines like Château Rayas, and limestone.

steps.title: Thirteen grapes
steps.body: Châteauneuf allows 13 grape varieties, counted as 18 including colour variants: red, white and pink. Grenache usually dominates, often 70% or more. Château de Beaucastel famously uses all 13. Yields are low, about 35 hl/ha. Wines are rich, warm, spicy, with red fruit, garrigue herbs and leather, often 14.5 to 15.5% alcohol.

steps.prompt: What are galets roulés?
options: Large round stones that store heat
steps.explanation: These river stones warm the vines at night.

steps.title: Bottles and age
steps.body: Many Châteauneuf bottles carry the papal coat of arms embossed on the glass. Most of the wine is red; about 7% is white. Good Châteauneuf ages 10 to 20 years, gaining leather, game and dried fruit. Neighbouring Gigondas and Vacqueyras offer similar, often more affordable wines.

steps.prompt: Châteauneuf-du-Pape may use 13 grape varieties.
steps.explanation: Yes, though Grenache usually dominates.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Galets roulés store heat in Châteauneuf's vineyards
Châteauneuf allows 13 grapes, usually Grenache-led
Its rich, spicy reds age 10 to 20 years

steps.title: Tavel
steps.body: Tavel, across the river from Châteauneuf, is France's only appellation for rosé alone. Its rosé is darker and fuller than Provence's, made from Grenache, Cinsault and others with longer skin contact. It's a rosé for food, able to age a few years. Lirac, nearby, makes red, white and rosé.

steps.title: Sweet wines
steps.body: Beaumes-de-Venise makes Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, a vin doux naturel: fermentation is stopped by adding grape spirit, keeping natural sugar, at 15% or more alcohol. It's golden, with orange blossom, peach and grape. Rasteau also makes a fortified Grenache vin doux naturel, red or amber.

steps.prompt: What is a vin doux naturel?
options: A wine fortified during fermentation to keep sugar
steps.explanation: Spirit stops the yeast, leaving natural sweetness.

steps.title: The crus
steps.body: Besides Châteauneuf and Tavel, the southern Rhône crus include Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Rasteau, Cairanne, Vinsobres, Lirac and Beaumes-de-Venise. Below them sit Côtes du Rhône Villages, sometimes with a village name, and then Côtes du Rhône. Each step up means stricter rules and usually more character.

steps.prompt: Which are southern Rhône crus?
steps.explanation: Hermitage is in the northern Rhône.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tavel is France's rosé-only appellation
Beaumes-de-Venise makes fortified sweet Muscat
Crus sit above Villages and Côtes du Rhône

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Rhône and eating with it

steps.title: The ladder
steps.body: Labels run from Côtes du Rhône, the base, to Côtes du Rhône Villages, to Villages with a named village, like Séguret or Plan de Dieu, to the crus like Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Grapes are rarely named. Prices rise with each step, but good Villages wines are excellent value.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Southern Rhône reds suit Provençal food: lamb with herbs, daube, a beef stew, ratatouille, grilled sausages and game. Tavel suits grilled fish, bouillabaisse and charcuterie. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise suits fruit tarts, melon and blue cheese. Serve reds at 16 to 17 degrees; high alcohol feels hot if served too warm.

steps.prompt: Order these labels from broadest to most specific.
steps.explanation: Each step tightens the rules and the area.

steps.body: Good Côtes du Rhône Villages from a top producer often tastes like a junior Châteauneuf-du-Pape at a fraction of the price.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
steps.explanation: Herbs and lamb echo its garrigue and spice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels run from Côtes du Rhône to the crus
Reds suit lamb, daube and ratatouille
Serve not too warm; good Villages offer value

modules.title: Alsace
modules.description: Between the Vosges and the Rhine: aromatic whites named by grape, from dry to noble rot sweet.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: In the rain shadow of the Vosges
objectives: Explain its French and German history

steps.title: A narrow strip
steps.body: Alsace lies in north-east France, a narrow strip about 120 km long between the Vosges mountains to the west and the Rhine river to the east, on the border with Germany. Vineyards run along the lower slopes of the Vosges, from 200 to 450 m. Soils are a mosaic: granite, limestone, schist, sandstone, volcanic and marl.

steps.title: Rain shadow
steps.body: The Vosges block wet westerly winds, so Alsace is one of France's driest regions; Colmar gets only about 500 mm of rain a year. Summers are warm and sunny, autumns long and dry. That lets grapes ripen fully in a northern latitude, around 48 degrees, giving ripe, aromatic wines with good acidity.

steps.prompt: Why is Alsace so dry and sunny for its latitude?
options: The Vosges block rain from the west
steps.explanation: The mountains cast a rain shadow.

steps.title: Between two countries
steps.body: Alsace changed hands between France and Germany several times: German from 1871 to 1918, and occupied again in 1940 to 1944. Its culture, architecture and grape names show both influences. It uses the tall, slim flûte bottle, required by law, and names grapes on labels, unlike most of France.

steps.prompt: Which show Alsace's German influence?
steps.explanation: Blending 13 grapes is a southern Rhône practice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alsace lies between the Vosges and the Rhine
The Vosges rain shadow makes it dry and sunny
Its French and German history shows in labels and bottles

steps.title: The noble four
steps.body: Alsace's four noble grapes are Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. They're the only ones allowed in most Grand Cru wines. Riesling is the most planted, giving dry, mineral wines. Gewürztraminer gives lychee and rose; Pinot Gris rich, smoky pear; Muscat dry, grapey wines.

steps.title: The others
steps.body: Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois make soft, everyday whites and much of Crémant d'Alsace. Sylvaner gives light, fresh wines. Pinot Noir is the only red, increasingly serious. Edelzwicker and Gentil are blends of several grapes. Most Alsace wines are single-variety, unoaked or aged in old, large foudres.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its character.
steps.explanation: Alsace names each wine by grape.

steps.body: Alsace Muscat is usually dry, a surprise for those who know sweet Muscats. It's a classic with asparagus in spring.

steps.prompt: Which is Alsace's most planted noble grape?
steps.explanation: Riesling covers the most area of the four.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are noble
Pinot Blanc, Sylvaner and Pinot Noir complete the range
Most wines are single-variety and named by grape

lessons.title: Grands crus
lessons.subtitle: Alsace's best sites
objectives: Explain the Alsace Grand Cru system

steps.title: 51 Grand Crus
steps.body: Alsace has 51 Grand Cru vineyards, classified from 1975 to 2007. They cover about 4% of production. Most are limited to the four noble grapes, though some allow Sylvaner or Pinot Noir. Each has its own soil, exposure and rules. Labels show the Grand Cru's name and the grape.

steps.title: Soils and sites
steps.body: Each Grand Cru has a distinct soil: Rangen, on steep volcanic rock, gives powerful wines; Schlossberg, on granite, gives fine Riesling; Hengst and Zotzenberg on marl and limestone; Brand, granite. Producers argue that site matters more than grape, as in Burgundy, and some top estates don't use the Grand Cru label.

steps.prompt: How many Grand Cru vineyards does Alsace have?
steps.explanation: 51 Grand Crus, classified between 1975 and 2007.

steps.title: Premier Cru
steps.body: In 2021, Alsace began recognising communal and Premier Cru levels, aiming to create a Burgundy-style pyramid. Communal appellations, like Bergheim or Ottrott, sit between regional Alsace and the Grand Crus. The system is still developing.

steps.prompt: Most Alsace Grand Crus are limited to the four noble grapes.
steps.explanation: Yes, with a few exceptions.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alsace has 51 Grand Crus, about 4% of production
Each Grand Cru has its own soil and character
A communal and Premier Cru level is emerging

steps.title: Vendanges Tardives
steps.body: Vendanges Tardives, VT, means late harvest. Grapes from the four noble varieties are left on the vine into late autumn, concentrating sugar. Minimum sugar levels are high and set by grape. VT wines can be dry, off-dry or sweet; they're rich, intense and long-lived.

steps.title: Sélection de Grains Nobles
steps.body: Sélection de Grains Nobles, SGN, is made from berries affected by noble rot, Botrytis cinerea, picked one by one. Minimum sugar is even higher. SGN wines are lusciously sweet, with honey, dried apricot and candied citrus, balanced by acidity. They're made only in good years and can age for decades.

steps.prompt: Order these Alsace styles from least to most concentrated.
steps.explanation: Later picking and noble rot concentrate sugar.

steps.title: Sweetness on dry wines
steps.body: Even regular Alsace wines can range from dry to off-dry, which confuses buyers. Many producers print a sweetness scale on the back label, and since 2021 rules encourage clearer terms like sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux. Gewürztraminer and Pinot Gris are more often off-dry than Riesling.

steps.prompt: What is SGN made from?
steps.explanation: Sélection de Grains Nobles uses botrytised berries.

steps.title: What you learned
points: VT is late harvest, from dry to sweet
SGN uses noble rot berries and is lusciously sweet
Check sweetness scales on regular Alsace wines

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Alsace and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Alsace labels show the grape, the producer, and sometimes a Grand Cru, a commune, VT or SGN. Crémant d'Alsace marks traditional method sparkling wine, France's most produced crémant. The flûte bottle is required for still wines. A sweetness indicator often appears on the back.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Alsace wines suit its rich food: choucroute garnie, sauerkraut with sausages, goes with Riesling or Pinot Gris; Munster cheese with Gewürztraminer; tarte flambée, a thin bacon and onion tart, with Pinot Blanc or Riesling; foie gras with VT. They also suit Asian food, especially Gewürztraminer and off-dry Pinot Gris.

steps.prompt: Match each dish to an Alsace wine.
steps.explanation: Alsace wines match its local food.

steps.body: Crémant d'Alsace, often made from Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois and Riesling, is one of France's best-value sparkling wines.

steps.prompt: Alsace still wines must be sold in the tall flûte bottle.
steps.explanation: Yes, by law.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show grape, producer and sometimes Grand Cru
Alsace wines suit choucroute, Munster and tarte flambée
Crémant d'Alsace is great-value sparkling wine

steps.explanation: Alsace has its own vocabulary.

steps.explanation: The rain shadow of the Vosges.

steps.explanation: Yes, unlike most French regions.

steps.prompt: Which are Alsace's noble grapes?
steps.explanation: The fourth is Pinot Gris, not Chardonnay.

steps.prompt: Alsace has ____ Grand Cru vineyards.
steps.explanation: 51 Grand Crus.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alsace is dry and sunny between the Vosges and the Rhine
Four noble grapes lead, named on labels
51 Grand Crus, plus VT and SGN sweet wines

modules.title: Northern Rhône
modules.description: Steep granite slopes above the Rhône, home of Syrah and Viognier.

steps.title: A narrow valley
steps.body: The northern Rhône runs about 60 km along the Rhône river, from Vienne, south of Lyon, to Valence. Vineyards cling to steep slopes on both banks, mostly granite and schist, often on terraces held by dry-stone walls, called chaillées. It's small: about 5% of all Rhône wine.

steps.title: Continental and steep
steps.body: The climate is continental, cooler than the south, with the Mistral wind blowing down the valley. Steep, south and south-east facing slopes catch the sun and drain cold air, letting Syrah ripen this far north. Terraces stop soil erosion. Work is by hand, sometimes with winches, making the wines costly.

steps.prompt: Why do northern Rhône vineyards use terraces?
options: To hold soil on steep slopes
steps.explanation: Terraces prevent erosion and make work possible.

steps.title: Ancient vineyards
steps.body: Vines have grown here since Roman times; Vienne was an important Roman city, and its wine was praised by Pliny. Hermitage takes its name from a 13th century knight, Gaspard de Stérimberg, who, legend says, lived there as a hermit after the Crusades.
steps.highlight: Roman vines; the hermit of Hermitage

steps.prompt: The northern Rhône makes most of the Rhône's wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It makes about 5%; the south makes over 90%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The northern Rhône runs 60 km on steep granite slopes
Steep, sunny slopes ripen Syrah in a continental climate
It's small, about 5% of Rhône wine

steps.title: Syrah only
steps.body: Syrah is the only red grape allowed in the northern Rhône. It gives deep, peppery wines with blackberry, violet, olive and smoked meat. Some appellations let small amounts of white grapes be co-fermented with it: up to 20% Viognier in Côte-Rôtie, 15% Marsanne and Roussanne in Hermitage, though most use much less.

steps.title: White grapes
steps.body: Viognier makes Condrieu and Château-Grillet: rich, apricot and violet. Marsanne and Roussanne make white Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray, where they also make sparkling wine. Marsanne gives body; Roussanne gives aroma and freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its main use.
steps.explanation: The northern Rhône has a short grape list.

steps.body: Co-fermenting a little Viognier with Syrah helps fix colour and adds a floral lift. In Côte-Rôtie, it's typically 2 to 5%.

steps.prompt: Which is the only red grape allowed in the northern Rhône?
steps.explanation: Syrah alone.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Syrah is the northern Rhône's only red grape
Viognier makes Condrieu; Marsanne and Roussanne white Hermitage
Small amounts of white grapes can be co-fermented with Syrah

steps.title: Côte-Rôtie
steps.body: Côte-Rôtie, the roasted slope, lies at the northern end, on very steep schist slopes facing south-east. Its two famous slopes are the Côte Brune, darker, more structured, and the Côte Blonde, lighter, more perfumed. Wines are elegant, floral and peppery. Guigal's single-vineyard La Mouline, La Landonne and La Turque made it famous.

steps.title: Hermitage
steps.body: Hermitage is a single, south-facing granite hill above Tain-l'Hermitage. Its reds are powerful, tannic and long-lived, among France's greatest. About a quarter is white, mostly Marsanne, also long-lived. Famous producers include Chapoutier, Jaboulet, with La Chapelle, and Jean-Louis Chave. In the 19th century, Bordeaux was sometimes hermitagé, strengthened with it.
steps.highlight: A single hill, powerful and long-lived

steps.prompt: What are the Côte Brune and Côte Blonde?
steps.explanation: Brune is darker and firmer; Blonde lighter and perfumed.

steps.title: The others
steps.body: Cornas makes dark, rustic, powerful Syrah on granite. Saint-Joseph, a long strip on the west bank, makes lighter, fruitier reds. Crozes-Hermitage, the largest appellation, on flatter land around Hermitage, offers good value. Condrieu and Château-Grillet make Viognier; Saint-Péray, whites and sparkling.

steps.prompt: Which are northern Rhône appellations?
steps.explanation: Gigondas is in the southern Rhône.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Côte-Rôtie is elegant, on Brune and Blonde slopes
Hermitage is a powerful, long-lived single hill
Cornas, Saint-Joseph and Crozes complete the reds

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the northern Rhône and eating with it
objectives: Pair Syrah and Viognier with food

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels name the appellation, like Côte-Rôtie or Crozes-Hermitage, the producer and sometimes a lieu-dit, a named vineyard. Grapes aren't usually named, but every red is Syrah. Négociants like Guigal, Chapoutier and Jaboulet are important, alongside small domaines.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Northern Rhône Syrah suits lamb with herbs and black pepper, game, duck and grilled beef; its pepper echoes peppercorn sauces. Condrieu suits lobster, crab and dishes with apricot or mild spice. White Hermitage suits rich fish and truffles. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees; decant young Hermitage and Cornas.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a Cornas or Hermitage?
steps.explanation: Rich game and pepper suit Syrah's power and spice.

steps.body: Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph from good producers offer a taste of northern Rhône Syrah at a fraction of Hermitage prices.

steps.prompt: Great Hermitage can age for decades.
steps.explanation: Yes, both red and white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels name the appellation; reds are Syrah
Syrah suits lamb, game and peppercorn sauce
Hermitage and Cornas benefit from decanting and age

steps.explanation: Each appellation has its own style.

steps.explanation: Up to 20%, though most use much less.

steps.prompt: Grenache is a main grape of the northern Rhône.
steps.explanation: Not true. Syrah is the only red grape there.

steps.prompt: Which describe the northern Rhône?
steps.explanation: The north is steep, not flat.

steps.prompt: Côte-Rôtie means the ____ slope.
steps.explanation: For its sun-baked, south-east facing slopes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The northern Rhône is steep, granite and continental
