Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage are its great wines
Syrah here suits lamb, game and pepper

modules.title: Beaujolais
modules.description: Granite hills south of Burgundy, where Gamay makes everything from Nouveau to serious crus.

steps.title: South of Burgundy
steps.body: Beaujolais lies just south of the Mâconnais, north of Lyon, in eastern France. It has about 13,000 hectares of vines on rolling hills. The climate is semi-continental, warmer than the Côte d'Or. Administratively it belongs to Burgundy, but its grape, soils and style are its own.

steps.title: North and south
steps.body: Beaujolais divides in two. The north, the Haut-Beaujolais, has pink granite and schist hills, where the best wines grow: Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. The south, the Bas-Beaujolais, has clay and limestone, called pierres dorées, golden stones, and makes simpler Beaujolais, including much of the Nouveau.

steps.prompt: Where do Beaujolais' best wines grow?
steps.explanation: Granite in the north suits Gamay best.

steps.title: Lyon's wine
steps.body: Beaujolais has long been the everyday wine of Lyon, France's food capital, served in its bouchons, traditional bistros, from a pot, a thick-bottomed bottle. The saying goes that Lyon is watered by three rivers: the Rhône, the Saône and the Beaujolais.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais' northern hills are mainly granite.
steps.explanation: Yes. Pink granite and schist dominate the north.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais lies between the Mâconnais and Lyon
Northern granite gives the best wines; the south is limestone
It's Lyon's traditional everyday wine

steps.title: Gamay
steps.body: Almost all Beaujolais is Gamay, fully Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc. It gives light to medium-bodied reds with red cherry, raspberry, violet and fresh acidity, and low tannin. Beaujolais has nearly all the world's Gamay. Pruned in gobelet, bush style, on the hills, it suits granite's poor, well-drained soils.

steps.title: Carbonic maceration
steps.body: Much Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Whole bunches go into a tank; the bottom ones are crushed and ferment, releasing carbon dioxide. The upper berries ferment inside their skins, giving fruity aromas like banana, bubblegum and cherry, with little tannin. Some crus use more traditional methods for structure.

steps.prompt: What does semi-carbonic maceration give Beaujolais?
steps.explanation: Whole-berry fermentation gives fruity, soft wines.

steps.title: Beaujolais Blanc
steps.body: A small amount of Beaujolais Blanc is made from Chardonnay, mostly in the north, near the Mâconnais. It's fresh and fruity, similar to Mâcon. Rosé is also made from Gamay. But red Gamay is over 95% of production.

steps.prompt: Which are features of Gamay in Beaujolais?
steps.explanation: Gamay is low in tannin.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais is almost all Gamay
Semi-carbonic maceration gives fruity, soft wines
A little Chardonnay makes Beaujolais Blanc

steps.title: Three levels
steps.body: Beaujolais has three main levels. Beaujolais, mostly from the south, light and fruity. Beaujolais-Villages, from 38 villages in the north, with more depth. And the ten crus, named villages on granite, at the top. Crus labels often don't say Beaujolais at all, just the village name.

steps.title: Light to structured
steps.body: The ten crus, north to south: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly. Fleurie, Chiroubles and Saint-Amour are light and floral. Morgon, on decomposed schist, and Moulin-à-Vent, on granite with manganese, are the most structured and age well.
steps.highlight: Fleurie floral; Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent firm

steps.prompt: Match each cru to its style.
steps.explanation: The crus range from light to structured.

steps.body: Aged Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can taste like Burgundy. Locals say the wine pinote, becomes Pinot-like, with age.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais has ____ crus.
steps.explanation: Ten named villages on the northern granite.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais has three levels: Beaujolais, Villages, crus
The ten crus range from light Fleurie to firm Moulin-à-Vent
Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age like Burgundy

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Beaujolais and eating with it

steps.title: Nouveau
steps.body: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest, made quickly by semi-carbonic maceration to be drunk at once. Its success from the 1970s to the 1990s made Beaujolais famous, but also hurt its image for serious wine. Today, crus and natural wine producers, like Marcel Lapierre, have restored its reputation.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Beaujolais is one of the most food-friendly reds: charcuterie, saucisson, roast chicken, pâté, Lyon's bistro dishes, salads, even salmon. Crus suit duck, pork and coq au vin. Serve slightly cool, at 12 to 14 degrees. Nouveau within months; crus from 2 to 10 years.

steps.prompt: When is Beaujolais Nouveau released?
steps.explanation: Weeks after the harvest.

steps.body: On a wine list, a cru Beaujolais is often the best-value red. Look for Morgon, Fleurie or Moulin-à-Vent.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais is best served slightly cool.
steps.explanation: Yes. A slight chill, 12 to 14 degrees, brings out its fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nouveau is released the third Thursday of November
Beaujolais suits charcuterie and bistro food
Serve at 12 to 14 degrees

steps.prompt: Match each term to Beaujolais.
steps.explanation: Beaujolais has its own vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Which soil gives the best Beaujolais?
steps.explanation: Granite in the north.

steps.prompt: Most Beaujolais is made from Pinot Noir.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's almost all Gamay.

steps.prompt: Which are Beaujolais crus?
steps.explanation: Chablis is in Burgundy.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of ____.
steps.explanation: Weeks after harvest, made quickly to drink at once.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais is Gamay on northern granite
Ten crus sit above Villages and Beaujolais
Carbonic maceration gives fruity, soft wines
Serve it cool with bistro food

modules.title: Piedmont
modules.description: At the foot of the Alps: Barolo, Barbaresco and a hillside map as detailed as Burgundy's.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: At the foot of the mountains
objectives: Explain its continental climate and fog

steps.title: Surrounded by mountains
steps.body: Piedmont, Piemonte, means foot of the mountains. It's in north-west Italy, bordered by the Alps on the north and west and the Apennines to the south. The key wine areas are the Langhe and Roero hills around Alba, and Monferrato around Asti. Piedmont has no IGT wines: everything is DOC or DOCG, with 19 DOCGs.

steps.title: Continental with fog
steps.body: The mountains create a continental climate: cold winters, hot summers and autumn fog, nebbia, rising from the Tanaro valley. Fog may give Nebbiolo its name. The Alps block cold northern winds, and a rain shadow keeps the region fairly dry. Hail is a risk. Long, cool autumns suit late-ripening grapes.

steps.prompt: What does Piedmont mean?
steps.explanation: Piemonte: at the foot of the mountains.

steps.title: A hillside hierarchy
steps.body: In the Langhe, grape choice follows the slope. The warmest, south-facing slopes, called sorì, go to Nebbiolo, which ripens last. Cooler slopes take Barbera; the coolest, highest sites take Dolcetto or Moscato. This hierarchy is old and practical, and the vineyard landscapes of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato became a UNESCO site in 2014.

steps.prompt: Piedmont makes many IGT wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Piedmont has no IGT; its wines are DOC or DOCG.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Piedmont lies at the foot of the Alps, around Alba and Asti
Its continental climate has autumn fog and long ripening
The warmest slopes are kept for Nebbiolo

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Nebbiolo makes Barolo, Barbaresco and Roero: pale but powerful, with tar, roses and high tannin. Barbera, the most planted red, gives juicy, high-acid, low-tannin wines. Dolcetto gives soft, dark, early-drinking reds. Other reds include Freisa, Grignolino and Ruchè.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Moscato Bianco makes Asti and Moscato d'Asti, sweet and lightly sparkling. Arneis, revived in the Roero from the 1970s, gives fragrant, pear-scented whites. Cortese makes Gavi, crisp and mineral, in the south-east. Timorasso, near Tortona, is a rising white grape.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its wine.
steps.explanation: Each grape has its signature wine.

steps.body: Langhe Nebbiolo, a DOC, offers Nebbiolo's tar and roses at a much lower price than Barolo, and is ready to drink younger.

steps.prompt: Which is Piedmont's most planted red grape?
steps.explanation: Barbera covers the most area, though Nebbiolo is the most prestigious.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo, Barbera and Dolcetto lead the reds
Moscato, Arneis and Cortese lead the whites
Barbera is the most planted; Nebbiolo the most prestigious

steps.title: Eleven villages
steps.body: Barolo DOCG covers 11 villages south-west of Alba. The main ones are Barolo, La Morra, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba. Western villages, on Tortonian marl, like La Morra, give more perfumed, approachable wines. Eastern villages, on Serravallian sandstone and marl, like Serralunga, give more powerful, tannic wines.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Barolo must be 100% Nebbiolo and age at least 38 months, 18 in wood, before release; Riserva at least 62 months. Since 2010, labels can name one of 181 MGAs, Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, official vineyard areas like Cannubi, Brunate and Rocche dell'Annunziata, similar to Burgundy's crus.

steps.prompt: Which part of Barolo gives the most powerful wines?
steps.explanation: Serravallian soils in the east give more structure.

steps.title: Traditional and modern
steps.body: From the 1980s, the Barolo wars split producers: modernists used short maceration and new French barriques for softer, fruitier wines; traditionalists kept long maceration and large old casks, botti. Bartolo Mascarello and Giacomo Conterno are traditionalist icons; Elio Altare a modernist. Today, many blend both approaches.

steps.prompt: Which are Barolo villages?
steps.explanation: Neive is in Barbaresco.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barolo's 11 villages split into perfumed west and powerful east
It's 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 38 months
181 MGAs name its vineyards

steps.title: Three villages
steps.body: Barbaresco DOCG lies north-east of Alba, near the Tanaro river, mainly in three villages: Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso. It's smaller than Barolo, about 750 hectares compared with about 2,200. It's slightly lower and warmer, closer to the river, so Nebbiolo ripens a little earlier.

steps.title: Rules and style
steps.body: Barbaresco must be 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 26 months, 9 in wood; Riserva 50 months. It has 66 MGAs, like Asili, Rabajà and Montestefano. Its wines are often described as more elegant and approachable earlier than Barolo, with softer tannins, though site and producer matter more.

steps.prompt: How does Barbaresco's minimum ageing compare with Barolo's?
steps.explanation: Barbaresco needs 26 months; Barolo 38.

steps.title: Producers
steps.body: Angelo Gaja, from the 1960s, raised Barbaresco's global prestige, with single-vineyard wines and new ideas. The Produttori del Barbaresco, a co-operative founded in 1958, makes some of the best-value fine wines in Italy, including single-vineyard Riservas. Bruno Giacosa was another legend.

steps.prompt: Barbaresco is larger than Barolo.
steps.explanation: Not true. Barbaresco is about a third of Barolo's size.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbaresco is smaller, lower and slightly warmer than Barolo
It ages at least 26 months and has 66 MGAs
Gaja and the Produttori raised its prestige

steps.title: Barbera
steps.body: Barbera d'Asti, a DOCG, and Barbera d'Alba, a DOC, are its main wines. Nizza, a DOCG since 2014, is Barbera's top area, in the hills around Nizza Monferrato. Barbera is juicy, high in acidity and low in tannin. Since the 1980s, producers like Giacomo Bologna have aged it in small oak for more structure.

steps.title: Dolcetto and Moscato
steps.body: Dolcetto makes soft, dark wines to drink young; Dogliani is its DOCG heartland. Moscato Bianco makes Asti, fully sparkling, and Moscato d'Asti, gently fizzy, frizzante. Both are sweet and low in alcohol: Moscato d'Asti about 5.5%. Fermentation in a sealed tank is stopped by chilling, keeping sugar and bubbles.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its grape.
steps.explanation: Piedmont's everyday wines are just as distinctive.

steps.body: Moscato d'Asti, at 5.5% alcohol and lightly sweet, is a classic with fresh fruit or hazelnut cake, another Piedmont speciality.

steps.prompt: How does Moscato d'Asti keep its sweetness and bubbles?
options: Fermentation in a sealed tank is stopped by chilling
steps.explanation: Stopping fermentation keeps sugar; the sealed tank traps CO2.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barbera d'Asti, Nizza and Barbera d'Alba are juicy, acidic reds
Dogliani is Dolcetto's DOCG
Asti and Moscato d'Asti are sweet and low in alcohol

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Piedmont and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels name the DOC or DOCG, like Barolo or Barbera d'Asti, the producer, the vintage and often an MGA or vineyard name. Riserva marks longer ageing. Langhe Nebbiolo and Nebbiolo d'Alba are more affordable Nebbiolos. The DOCG strip on the neck guarantees origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Piedmont's food is rich: tajarin, thin egg pasta with butter and white truffle; vitello tonnato; brasato al Barolo, beef braised in Barolo; bagna cauda, a hot garlic and anchovy dip. Barolo suits truffles and braised meat; Barbera suits salumi and pasta; Dolcetto suits everyday dishes; Moscato suits hazelnut cake.
steps.highlight: Truffle with Barolo, salumi with Barbera

steps.prompt: Which Piedmont dish is cooked with Barolo?
steps.explanation: Beef braised in Barolo.

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve Barolo and Barbaresco at 17 to 18 degrees, in large glasses, decanted for hours when young. They're best from 10 years and can age 30 or more. Barbera and Dolcetto at 15 to 17, young. Moscato d'Asti well chilled, at 6 to 8.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Barolo?
steps.explanation: Sorbet is too sweet and acidic.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DOCG, MGA and Riserva
Barolo suits truffle and braised beef; Barbera suits salumi
Decant young Barolo; it ages 30 years or more

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its rule.
steps.explanation: Piedmont has precise rules.

steps.prompt: Which slopes are reserved for Nebbiolo?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo ripens last and needs the best sites.

steps.prompt: Barolo must be 100% Nebbiolo.
steps.explanation: Yes, like Barbaresco.

steps.prompt: Which are Piedmont grapes?
steps.explanation: Sangiovese is Tuscany's grape.

steps.prompt: Piedmont's official vineyard areas in Barolo are called ____.
steps.explanation: Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Piedmont is foggy, hilly and all DOC or DOCG
Nebbiolo makes Barolo and Barbaresco on the best slopes
Barbera, Dolcetto and Moscato make everyday wines
Its rich food, from truffle to brasato, suits its wines

modules.title: Tuscany
modules.description: Hills, cypresses and Sangiovese: Chianti, Brunello and the Super Tuscans that rewrote Italian law.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Hills between Florence and the sea

steps.title: Hills and coast
steps.body: Tuscany, in central Italy, stretches from the Apennines in the east to the Tyrrhenian Sea in the west. Most vineyards are on hills between 150 and 600 m, among olive groves and cypresses. The heart is Chianti, between Florence and Siena. South are Montalcino and Montepulciano; on the coast, Bolgheri and the Maremma.

steps.title: Mediterranean with altitude
steps.body: Tuscany has a Mediterranean climate: hot, dry summers and mild winters. Inland, altitude and hills bring cool nights that preserve acidity. The coast is warmer, with sea breezes. Soils include galestro, a crumbly schist-like marl, and alberese, a hard limestone, both prized for Sangiovese.

steps.prompt: Which soils are prized for Sangiovese in Tuscany?
steps.explanation: Galestro marl and alberese limestone give fine Sangiovese.

steps.title: History
steps.body: The Etruscans made wine here before the Romans. In 1716, Cosimo III de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, defined the boundaries of Chianti, Carmignano, Pomino and Valdarno, one of the earliest legal wine regions. In the 1870s, Baron Bettino Ricasoli set a Chianti formula led by Sangiovese.

steps.prompt: Chianti's borders were defined in 1716.
steps.explanation: Yes, by Cosimo III de' Medici.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tuscany runs from the Apennines to the sea
Hills and altitude cool its Mediterranean climate
Cosimo III defined Chianti in 1716

steps.title: Sangiovese
steps.body: Sangiovese is Tuscany's grape: sour cherry, herbs and earth, high acidity and firm, tea-like tannin. It has local names and clones: Brunello in Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile in Montepulciano, Morellino in Scansano. Native partners include Canaiolo, Colorino and Mammolo.

steps.title: International grapes and whites
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Syrah arrived in the 20th century, especially on the coast in Bolgheri. They're used in Super Tuscans and allowed in small amounts in Chianti Classico. White grapes include Vernaccia di San Gimignano, Tuscany's oldest DOCG white, Vermentino on the coast, and Trebbiano and Malvasia for Vin Santo.

steps.prompt: Match each name to its place.
steps.explanation: Tuscany's grapes have local identities.

steps.body: Vin Santo, Tuscany's sweet wine from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia, is served with cantucci almond biscuits.

steps.prompt: Which grape dominates Tuscany?
steps.explanation: Sangiovese is Tuscany's main grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sangiovese leads, with local names like Brunello
Bordeaux grapes thrive on the coast
Vernaccia, Vermentino and Vin Santo complete the whites

steps.title: The black rooster
steps.body: Chianti Classico DOCG covers the original zone between Florence and Siena, with villages like Greve, Radda, Gaiole and Castellina. Its symbol is the black rooster, gallo nero. It must be at least 80% Sangiovese, with native or international grapes for the rest; white grapes were banned in 2006.

steps.title: Three levels
steps.body: Chianti Classico has three levels: Annata, at least 12 months' ageing; Riserva, 24 months; and Gran Selezione, introduced in 2014, from estate grapes, at least 30 months and, since 2021, at least 90% Sangiovese. Since 2021, labels can name 11 UGAs, Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive, villages like Panzano and Radda.

steps.prompt: Order these Chianti wines by minimum ageing, shortest first.
steps.explanation: Plain Chianti is a separate, broader DOCG with lower requirements; Gran Selezione is the top.

steps.title: Chianti versus Classico
steps.body: Chianti DOCG is a separate, much larger area surrounding Chianti Classico, with seven sub-zones like Chianti Rufina and Colli Senesi. Rules are looser: at least 70% Sangiovese. Quality varies, from simple to excellent; Rufina, in the cool hills east of Florence, is often the best.

steps.prompt: What is the symbol of Chianti Classico?
steps.explanation: The gallo nero.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chianti Classico is the historic heart, at least 80% Sangiovese
Annata, Riserva and Gran Selezione are its levels
Chianti DOCG is broader, with seven sub-zones

steps.title: Brunello di Montalcino
steps.body: Montalcino, a hill town about 40 km south of Siena, is warmer and drier than Chianti. Brunello di Montalcino, DOCG since 1980, must be 100% Sangiovese, aged at least five years, two in oak; Riserva six years. The Biondi-Santi family created it in the late 19th century. Rosso di Montalcino is a younger, lighter version.

steps.title: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
steps.body: Montepulciano, east of Montalcino, makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG from at least 70% Sangiovese, here called Prugnolo Gentile, aged at least two years. It's often softer than Brunello and more structured than Chianti. Since 2021, Pieve, a top tier from defined sub-areas, has been introduced.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its rule.
steps.explanation: Each Tuscan red has its own rules.

steps.body: Don't confuse Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, a Tuscan Sangiovese, with Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a different grape from another region.

steps.prompt: Who created Brunello di Montalcino?
steps.explanation: Biondi-Santi in the late 19th century.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, aged five years
Vino Nobile is at least 70% Prugnolo Gentile
Montalcino is warmer and drier than Chianti

steps.title: The rebels
steps.body: In the 1960s and 1970s, Chianti rules forced producers to include white grapes and limited new ideas. Some made wine their own way: Sassicaia, from Cabernet Sauvignon at Bolgheri, first sold in 1971; Tignanello, from Antinori, in 1971, a Sangiovese and Cabernet blend in small barrels. Sold as simple table wine, they cost more than any Chianti.

steps.title: Bolgheri
steps.body: Bolgheri, on the coast, has gravelly soils and a warm, maritime climate, with sea breezes, close to Bordeaux's conditions. Bordeaux grapes thrive: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc. Ornellaia, Masseto and Sassicaia are its icons. Bolgheri DOC came in 1994; Sassicaia got its own DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, in 2013, the only single-estate DOC in Italy.

steps.prompt: What made Sassicaia unusual in 1971?
options: It was Cabernet Sauvignon sold as table wine
steps.explanation: A Cabernet from the coast, outside DOC rules.

steps.title: IGT
steps.body: The Super Tuscans' success led Italy to create the IGT category, Indicazione Geografica Tipica, in 1992, for quality wines outside DOC rules. Toscana IGT now includes many top wines. Chianti Classico's rules also changed, allowing 100% Sangiovese and some international grapes.

steps.prompt: Sassicaia has its own DOC.
steps.explanation: Yes, Bolgheri Sassicaia, since 2013.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Super Tuscans broke DOC rules in the 1970s
Bolgheri's coastal gravel suits Bordeaux grapes
They led to IGT in 1992

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Tuscany and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show the DOCG, like Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino or Vino Nobile, or Toscana IGT for Super Tuscans, plus producer, vintage and sometimes Riserva, Gran Selezione or a UGA. The pink DOCG neck strip and, for Chianti Classico, the black rooster confirm origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Sangiovese's acidity loves tomato and olive oil: pasta with tomato sauce, pappardelle with wild boar ragù, ribollita, a bread and bean soup, and bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick grilled T-bone. Brunello suits game and aged pecorino. Vernaccia and Vermentino suit seafood. Vin Santo suits cantucci.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a Tuscan classic with Chianti Classico or Brunello?
steps.explanation: A thick grilled T-bone steak.

steps.title: Service
steps.body: Serve Tuscan reds at 16 to 18 degrees. Chianti Classico Annata is best within five years; Riserva and Gran Selezione 10 to 20; Brunello 15 to 30. Decant young Brunello and Super Tuscans.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Sangiovese?
steps.explanation: Chocolate mousse needs a sweet wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DOCG or IGT, with Riserva or Gran Selezione
Sangiovese suits tomato, boar and bistecca
Brunello ages 15 to 30 years

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its area.
steps.explanation: Tuscany's wines map its hills and coast.

steps.prompt: What was created in 1992 because of the Super Tuscans?
steps.explanation: IGT gave a home to quality wines outside DOC rules.

steps.prompt: Brunello di Montalcino must be 100% Sangiovese.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.prompt: Which are Tuscan grapes or wines?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is Piedmont's.

steps.prompt: Chianti Classico's top level, since 2014, is ____ Selezione.
steps.explanation: Gran Selezione.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tuscany is hilly, Mediterranean and Sangiovese-led
Chianti Classico, Brunello and Vino Nobile are its classics
Bolgheri's Super Tuscans changed Italian law
Its wines suit tomato, boar and bistecca

modules.title: Veneto
modules.description: Venice's hinterland: Amarone from dried grapes, Soave from volcanic hills and Prosecco from steep slopes.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: From the Alps to the lagoon

steps.title: Mountains, lake and lagoon
steps.body: The Veneto, in north-east Italy, runs from the Dolomites and the Lessini mountains down to the plains and the Venetian lagoon. Lake Garda borders it on the west. Key areas: Valpolicella and Soave, near Verona; Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, north of Venice, for Prosecco.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: The climate is moderate continental, with warm summers and cold winters. Lake Garda moderates the west, and the Alps protect from northern winds. Hillsides give cooler nights and better drainage than the fertile, flat plains, where much simple wine is made.
steps.highlight: Hills for quality, plains for volume

steps.prompt: Why do the Veneto's best wines come from hills?
steps.explanation: Hills give freshness and drainage; plains favour volume.

steps.title: Volume and quality
steps.body: The Veneto is Italy's largest wine region by volume, thanks to Prosecco and Pinot Grigio. But it also makes some of Italy's most distinctive wines. Venice's merchants traded wine for centuries, and the tradition of drying grapes, appassimento, has ancient roots here.

steps.prompt: The Veneto is Italy's largest wine region by volume.
steps.explanation: Yes, thanks largely to Prosecco and Pinot Grigio.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Veneto runs from the Alps to the Venetian lagoon
Hills give its best wines; plains give volume
It's Italy's largest wine region by volume

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Corvina is the main grape of Valpolicella and Bardolino, giving sour cherry and almond, with thick skins ideal for drying. Corvinone, a separate, larger-berried grape, and Rondinella, which adds colour, are its partners. Molinara was once common; Oseleta is being revived.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Garganega makes Soave, with lemon, almond and minerality. Glera makes Prosecco, light and floral. Turbiana makes Lugana on Lake Garda. The Veneto also produces huge amounts of Pinot Grigio, mostly under the Delle Venezie DOC, and international grapes like Merlot and Chardonnay.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its wine.
steps.explanation: Native grapes make the Veneto's signature wines.

steps.body: Look for Lugana, from Turbiana on Lake Garda's southern shore. It's a textured, age-worthy white, less known than Soave.

steps.prompt: Which grape is the backbone of Valpolicella?
steps.explanation: Corvina leads Valpolicella and Amarone.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella make Valpolicella
Garganega makes Soave; Glera makes Prosecco
The Veneto also makes lots of Pinot Grigio

steps.title: Valpolicella
steps.body: Valpolicella lies north of Verona, in valleys running down from the Lessini mountains. The Classico zone, around Fumane, Marano and Negrar, is the historic heart. Simple Valpolicella is light and cherry-fresh. Superiore has more alcohol and ageing.

steps.title: Amarone and Recioto
steps.body: For Amarone and Recioto, the best bunches are dried for about 100 to 120 days in airy lofts, fruttai, losing 30 to 40% of their weight. Recioto della Valpolicella ferments sweet. Amarone della Valpolicella, DOCG since 2010, ferments nearly dry, to 15 to 16% alcohol, with dried cherry, raisin, chocolate and spice. It ages at least two years.

steps.prompt: How is Amarone made?
options: From dried grapes fermented nearly dry
steps.explanation: Appassimento concentrates the grapes; fermentation runs almost dry.

steps.title: Ripasso
steps.body: Ripasso, re-passed, is Valpolicella refermented on the leftover skins of Amarone or Recioto, gaining body, colour and dried fruit flavour. It's sometimes called baby Amarone, sitting between simple Valpolicella and Amarone in weight and price.

steps.prompt: Which Valpolicella wines use dried grapes or their skins?
steps.explanation: Bardolino uses fresh grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Valpolicella is light; Superiore fuller
Amarone and Recioto use dried grapes: dry and sweet
Ripasso is refermented on Amarone skins

steps.title: Volcanic hills
steps.body: Soave lies east of Verona. Soave Classico, in the hills around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, has volcanic basalt and limestone soils. Soave must be at least 70% Garganega, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay. Vines are traditionally trained on pergolas, pergola veronese.

steps.title: From volume to quality
steps.body: Soave was mass-produced in the 1970s, earning a poor reputation. Producers like Pieropan and Inama showed its real potential: mineral, almond-scented, age-worthy wines. Soave Superiore DOCG requires lower yields. Since 2019, 33 UGAs, named sub-areas like Foscarino and Calvarino, can appear on labels.

steps.prompt: What must Soave contain at least 70% of?
steps.explanation: Garganega is Soave's main grape.

steps.title: Recioto di Soave
steps.body: Recioto di Soave, DOCG since 1998, is a sweet wine from dried Garganega. Grapes dry for months, concentrating sugar, sometimes with noble rot. The wine is golden, honeyed and sweet, with apricot and almond, balanced by acidity.

steps.prompt: Recioto di Soave is a sweet wine made from dried grapes.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's Soave's appassimento wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Soave Classico grows Garganega on volcanic hills
Quality rose from cheap volume to named sub-areas
Recioto di Soave is sweet, from dried grapes

steps.title: DOC and DOCG
steps.body: Prosecco DOC covers nine provinces in the Veneto and Friuli, mostly on flat land, making large volumes; at least 85% Glera. Two DOCGs are on hills: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore, north of Treviso, and Asolo. The grape was renamed from Prosecco to Glera in 2009, to protect the place name.
steps.highlight: DOC on plains, DOCG on hills

steps.title: Tank method
steps.body: Most Prosecco is made by the tank method, also called Martinotti or Charmat: the second fermentation happens in a sealed, pressurised tank. This keeps Glera's fresh pear, apple and floral aromas, without the bready notes of long lees ageing. It's faster and cheaper than the traditional method.

steps.prompt: Match each Prosecco term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Prosecco has a clear hierarchy.

steps.title: The hills
steps.body: Conegliano Valdobbiadene's steep hills, a UNESCO site since 2019, are worked mostly by hand. Rive are 43 single-village crus. Cartizze, a 107-hectare hill near Valdobbiadene, is the most prized. Hill wines are more aromatic and complex than those from the plains.

steps.prompt: Why was the Prosecco grape renamed Glera?
options: To protect Prosecco as a place name
steps.explanation: A grape can grow anywhere; a protected place name can't be copied.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco DOC is large; Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo are hill DOCGs
The tank method keeps Glera's fruit fresh
Rive and Cartizze are the hills' top crus

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Veneto and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show DOC or DOCG, like Amarone della Valpolicella or Soave Classico, plus Classico for the historic zone, Superiore for higher ripeness or ageing, and Ripasso. For Prosecco, look for Superiore, Rive or Cartizze, and the sweetness: Brut, Extra Dry, which is sweeter than Brut, and Dry.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Valpolicella suits salumi and pasta; Ripasso suits risotto and roasts; Amarone suits braised beef, game and aged cheese, and flavours risotto all'Amarone. Soave suits risotto, seafood and antipasti. Prosecco suits cicchetti, Venetian small bites, and makes the Spritz and the Bellini. Recioto suits pandoro.

steps.prompt: Which cocktail uses Prosecco and white peach?
steps.explanation: Invented at Harry's Bar, Venice.

steps.body: In Venice, a glass of Prosecco with cicchetti at a bàcaro, a small wine bar, is the local way to start an evening.

steps.prompt: Which dishes suit Amarone?
steps.explanation: Oysters need a crisp white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show Classico, Superiore and Ripasso
Amarone suits braised beef; Soave suits risotto
Prosecco suits cicchetti and makes the Spritz

modules.title: Sicily
modules.description: The Mediterranean's largest island: sun-soaked Nero d'Avola, volcanic Etna and historic Marsala.

steps.title: A large island
steps.body: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, at the toe of Italy, with about 98,000 hectares of vines, among Italy's largest wine regions. It has hills, plains, coasts and Mount Etna, Europe's highest active volcano, in the east. Smaller islands like Pantelleria and the Aeolian Islands also make wine.

steps.title: Hot, dry and windy
steps.body: The climate is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and plenty of sun. Constant winds and sea breezes keep vines healthy, so organic farming is common; Sicily has one of Italy's largest organic vineyard areas. Altitude, on Etna and inland hills, brings freshness. Drought is the main challenge.
steps.highlight: Wind and sun keep vines healthy

steps.prompt: Why is organic farming common in Sicily?
steps.explanation: Wind and dry air keep vines healthy, needing fewer sprays.

steps.title: From bulk to quality
steps.body: For centuries, Sicily made bulk wine, often shipped north to blend, and Marsala, a fortified wine developed by English merchants from 1773. Since the 1990s, producers have focused on native grapes and quality. The Sicilia DOC, created in 2011, covers the whole island; Cerasuolo di Vittoria is its only DOCG.

steps.prompt: Marsala was developed by English merchants.
steps.explanation: Yes, from 1773, by John Woodhouse.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island
Its dry, windy climate suits organic farming
It moved from bulk wine to quality native grapes

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Native grapes
objectives: Explain the role of international grapes

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most planted red: dark, juicy, with black cherry, plum and fresh acidity. Nerello Mascalese, on Etna, gives pale, perfumed, firm wines; Nerello Cappuccio is its partner. Frappato, in the south-east, gives light, floral reds and blends with Nero d'Avola in Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Catarratto is Sicily's most planted grape, used for everyday whites and Marsala. Grillo, a cross of Catarratto and Muscat of Alexandria, gives fresh, citrus whites and is a Marsala grape. Carricante, on Etna, gives taut, citrus, age-worthy whites. Zibibbo, Muscat of Alexandria, makes sweet Passito di Pantelleria.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Sicily's grapes are native and varied.

steps.body: Look for Grillo from western Sicily. It's a fresh, citrus white that offers great value.

steps.prompt: Which is Sicily's most planted grape?
steps.explanation: Catarratto, a white grape, covers the most area.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese and Frappato lead the reds
Catarratto, Grillo and Carricante lead the whites
Zibibbo makes Pantelleria's sweet wine

steps.title: Altitude and lava
steps.body: Etna's vineyards climb its slopes from about 400 to over 1,000 m, mostly on the north, east and south sides. Altitude gives cool nights and late harvests into October. Soils are volcanic sand, ash and lava, poor and well-drained. Phylloxera can't survive easily, so many old vines are ungrafted bush vines, alberello, on terraces.

steps.title: Contrade
steps.body: Etna's vineyards are divided into contrade, local districts often defined by different lava flows. Since 2011, 133 contrade can appear on labels, like Burgundy's crus. Etna DOC, one of Italy's first, from 1968, covers red, white, rosé and sparkling. Etna Rosso must be at least 80% Nerello Mascalese; Etna Bianco at least 60% Carricante.

steps.prompt: What are Etna's contrade?
options: Local districts often defined by lava flows
steps.explanation: Each contrada has its own soil and character.

steps.title: The revival
steps.body: Etna's modern revival began around 2000, when producers like Frank Cornelissen, Andrea Franchetti and Marc de Grazia arrived, and local families like Benanti invested. Its reds, pale and perfumed, are often compared with Burgundy and Barolo. Its whites, from Carricante, are mineral and long-lived.

steps.prompt: Which describe Etna's vineyards?
steps.explanation: Etna's vineyards are steep and poor, not flat and fertile.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Etna's vineyards climb to over 1,000 m on volcanic soils
133 contrade name its districts
Its revival since 2000 made Nerello and Carricante famous

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Sicily and eating with it

steps.title: Labels and Marsala
steps.body: Labels show Sicilia DOC, Etna DOC, Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG, or Terre Siciliane IGT. Marsala, in the west, is a fortified wine from Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia; styles range from Fine, a year old, to Vergine, dry, aged at least five years, often in a solera. It's Sicily's historic wine.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Nero d'Avola suits pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and ricotta, grilled meat and pizza. Etna Rosso suits tuna, swordfish, mushrooms and lamb. Grillo and Carricante suit seafood, raw fish and caponata. Passito di Pantelleria suits cannoli, Sicily's ricotta pastries. Dry Marsala Vergine suits aged cheese.

steps.prompt: Which wine is a classic with cannoli?
steps.explanation: Sweet Zibibbo from Pantelleria suits ricotta pastries.

steps.body: Marsala Vergine, dry and nutty, is very different from the cooking Marsala many people know. Try it as an aperitif with almonds.

steps.prompt: Marsala Vergine is a dry style.
steps.explanation: Yes, aged at least five years.

modules.title: Trentino-Alto Adige
modules.description: Italy's Alpine north: fresh whites, Lagrein and the mountain sparkling wine Trentodoc.

steps.title: Two provinces
steps.body: Trentino-Alto Adige is Italy's northernmost wine region, in the Alps, along the Adige river valley. It has two provinces: Trentino in the south, Italian-speaking, and Alto Adige, or Südtirol, in the north, mostly German-speaking. Vineyards climb from about 200 to over 1,000 m on steep valley slopes.

steps.title: Mountain climate
steps.body: The Alps block cold northern winds, so the valleys are surprisingly warm and sunny by day, with over 300 sunny days a year in Bolzano. Nights are cold, thanks to altitude and mountain air. That large day and night range gives aromatic whites with fresh acidity and ripe reds on the warm valley floors.

steps.prompt: Why are Alto Adige's whites so fresh?
steps.explanation: Altitude and cold air keep acidity high.

steps.title: Two cultures
steps.body: Alto Adige belonged to Austria until 1919, so German is widely spoken and many labels are bilingual, like Südtirol and Alto Adige. Co-operatives, Kellereien, make most of the wine, with high quality; Cantina Terlano is a famous one. Trentino, more Italian in culture, is known for sparkling wine.

steps.prompt: Alto Adige was part of Austria until 1919.
steps.explanation: Yes, which explains its German-speaking culture.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Trentino-Alto Adige is Italy's Alpine north
Warm days and cold nights give fresh wines
Alto Adige is German-speaking, with strong co-operatives

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: About two-thirds of production is white. Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon Blanc, Müller-Thurgau and Gewürztraminer are common. Gewürztraminer takes its name from Tramin, or Termeno, a village in Alto Adige. Alto Adige's whites are crisp, aromatic and precise.

steps.title: Native reds
steps.body: Lagrein gives deep, dark reds with plum, chocolate and firm tannins, and a rosé called Kretzer. Schiava, or Vernatsch, gives light, pale, fruity reds, like Santa Maddalena. Teroldego, in Trentino's Rotaliano plain, gives dark, juicy reds. Marzemino is another Trentino red. Pinot Noir, called Blauburgunder, is increasingly serious.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its character.
steps.explanation: The region grows many grapes in a small space.

steps.body: Schiava is one of the few red wines that's great lightly chilled. Its low tannin and fresh fruit suit summer.

steps.prompt: Gewürztraminer takes its name from which Alto Adige village?
steps.explanation: Tramin, or Termeno, is the grape's namesake.

steps.title: What you learned
points: About two-thirds of the region's wine is white
Lagrein, Schiava and Teroldego are native reds
Gewürztraminer is named after the village of Tramin

steps.title: Mountain bubbles
steps.body: Trentodoc, created in 1993, was one of the first Italian DOCs for traditional method sparkling wine. It's made mainly from Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Meunier, grown in Trentino's mountain vineyards, often at 300 to 800 m. Altitude gives high acidity, ideal for sparkling wine.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Trentodoc must be made by the traditional method, with second fermentation in bottle. Minimum lees ageing: 15 months for non-vintage, 24 months for vintage, 36 months for Riserva. The styles range from Pas Dosé to Demi-Sec. The wines are crisp, fine and elegant, often compared with Champagne.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum lees ageing for Trentodoc Riserva?
steps.explanation: Riserva needs 36 months.

steps.title: Ferrari
steps.body: Giulio Ferrari founded his sparkling wine house in Trento in 1902, after studying in Champagne, and brought Chardonnay to the region. Ferrari, owned since 1952 by the Lunelli family, remains Trentodoc's leading producer. Its Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore is one of Italy's most acclaimed sparkling wines.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are used in Trentodoc?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo isn't used.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Trentodoc is Trentino's traditional method sparkling wine
Altitude gives it high acidity
Ferrari, founded in 1902, leads the category

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Alto Adige labels are often bilingual: Alto Adige or Südtirol, Pinot Grigio or Ruländer, Lagrein or Lagrein Dunkel. Most wines are varietal, named by grape. Trentino labels name the grape or Trentodoc. Kellerei or Cantina means a winery, often a co-operative.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: The region's food blends Italian and Austrian: speck, smoked ham; canederli, bread dumplings; strudel; polenta; and mountain cheeses. Pinot Bianco and Pinot Grigio suit speck and light dishes; Gewürztraminer suits spicy food and cheese; Lagrein suits game, goulash and grilled meat; Trentodoc suits aperitifs and fried food.

steps.explanation: A crisp Alpine white suits the smoky ham.

steps.body: Try Lagrein with goulash, a dish of Austrian heritage still common in Alto Adige.

steps.prompt: Most Alto Adige wines are named by grape.
steps.explanation: Yes, most are varietal wines.

Pinot Bianco suits speck; Lagrein suits game
Trentodoc suits aperitifs

modules.title: Friuli-Venezia Giulia
modules.description: Between the Alps and the Adriatic: precise whites and the modern home of orange wine.

steps.title: A border region
steps.body: Friuli-Venezia Giulia is Italy's north-eastern corner, bordered by Austria to the north and Slovenia to the east, with the Adriatic to the south. The best vineyards are in the eastern hills: Collio and Colli Orientali del Friuli, on the Slovenian border. The flat Grave plain, in the centre, makes larger volumes.

steps.title: Alpine and Adriatic
steps.body: The climate is shaped by both the Alps, which protect from cold northern winds, and the Adriatic, which brings warm, humid air. The meeting creates a good day and night range and plenty of rain. The hills' soil, ponca, a layered marl and sandstone, drains well and gives mineral, structured whites.

steps.prompt: What is ponca?
options: A layered marl and sandstone soil
steps.explanation: Ponca gives Friuli's hill whites their structure.

steps.title: A crossroads
steps.body: Friuli has been Roman, Venetian, Austrian and Italian, and its eastern hills continue into Slovenia's Brda. Collio and Brda share grapes, soils and traditions, divided by a border drawn after the Second World War. That crossroads culture shows in its food and in its openness to new and old winemaking.

steps.prompt: Friuli's Collio continues across the border into Slovenia.
steps.explanation: Yes, as Brda, with similar soils and grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Friuli is Italy's north-eastern corner, near Slovenia
The Alps and Adriatic shape its climate
Ponca soils give its hill whites structure

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: About 80% of Friuli's wine is white. Friulano, formerly Tocai Friulano, gives full, almond-scented whites; it was renamed in 2008 after the EU protected Hungary's Tokaji name. Ribolla Gialla gives crisp, citrus whites and is key to orange wines. Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay are widely grown.

steps.title: Reds and sweet wines
steps.body: Reds include Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, dark and tart; Schioppettino, peppery and fragrant; and Pignolo, tannic. Merlot and Cabernet Franc are also grown. Picolit, a sweet white, made from dried grapes, was once famous at European courts; Ramandolo is another sweet white, from Verduzzo.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its style.
steps.explanation: Friuli grows native and international grapes.

steps.body: Friulano was called Tocai until 2008. Old bottles and older Italian drinkers may still use the name.

steps.prompt: Why was Tocai Friulano renamed?
options: The EU protected Hungary's Tokaji name
steps.explanation: Renamed Friulano in 2008.

steps.title: What you learned
points: About 80% of Friuli's wine is white
Friulano and Ribolla Gialla are key natives
Refosco, Schioppettino and Picolit add reds and sweet wines

lessons.title: Skin-contact whites
lessons.subtitle: The orange wine revival
objectives: Explain how orange wine is made
Explain Friuli's role in its revival

steps.title: White grapes, red method
steps.body: Orange, or amber, wine is made from white grapes fermented on their skins, like a red, for days, weeks or months. Skins give the wine an amber colour, tannin, texture and flavours of dried fruit, tea, nuts and orange peel. It's an ancient method, preserved in Georgia, with its clay qvevri.

steps.title: Friuli's pioneers
steps.body: In the late 1990s, Friuli producers like Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon, in Oslavia in the Collio, began making long skin-contact whites, mainly from Ribolla Gialla. Gravner travelled to Georgia and from 2001 fermented in buried qvevri. Their wines inspired a worldwide orange wine movement.

steps.prompt: Which grape is central to Friuli's orange wines?
steps.explanation: Ribolla Gialla's thick skins suit long maceration.

steps.title: Taste and style
steps.body: Orange wines are dry, with tannin and texture unusual for white wine, and flavours of apricot, orange peel, tea, honey and nuts. Many are made with minimal intervention, little or no sulphur, and natural yeasts. They're often served slightly warmer than whites, around 12 to 14 degrees, in larger glasses.

steps.prompt: What do skins give an orange wine?
steps.explanation: Orange wines are dry; skins don't add sugar.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Orange wine ferments white grapes on their skins
Gravner and Radikon in Friuli revived it from the late 1990s
It's dry, tannic and textured, served a little warmer

lessons.subtitle: Reading Friuli and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Friuli labels usually name the grape and the DOC, like Collio Friulano or Friuli Colli Orientali Ribolla Gialla. Ramandolo and Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit are DOCGs for sweet wines. Rosazzo is a small DOCG for white blends. Orange wines may say macerato or skin contact, or be labelled as table wine.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Friulano is traditionally paired with prosciutto di San Daniele, Friuli's famous ham. Crisp whites suit seafood from the Adriatic; orange wines suit richer dishes, mushrooms, pork, aged cheese and spiced food. Refosco suits game and sausages; Picolit suits blue cheese and pastries.

steps.prompt: Which ham is a classic match for Friulano?
steps.explanation: San Daniele is Friuli's own ham.

steps.body: Orange wines' tannin and texture suit food that would overwhelm most whites, like roast pork or mushroom risotto.

steps.prompt: Orange wines are usually served ice cold.
steps.explanation: Not true. They're often served at 12 to 14 degrees, slightly warmer than most whites.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels name the grape and the DOC
Friulano suits San Daniele ham; orange wines suit richer food
Serve orange wines slightly warmer

steps.explanation: Both in Oslavia, in the Collio.

steps.explanation: Yes, about 80%.

steps.explanation: To avoid confusion with Hungary's Tokaji.

modules.title: Campania
modules.description: Volcanic hills around Naples: Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Volcanoes and ancient vines
objectives: Explain the role of volcanic soils

steps.title: Around Naples
steps.body: Campania, in southern Italy, runs from the coast around Naples and the Amalfi coast inland to the hills of Irpinia. Its key wine areas are inland, around Avellino, at 300 to 700 m. Mount Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei near Naples are volcanic; Irpinia has volcanic ash over clay and limestone.

steps.title: Volcanic and cool
steps.body: Volcanic soils drain well and are rich in minerals; in sandy volcanic areas phylloxera struggled, so some ungrafted vines survive. Inland Irpinia, despite being in the south, has a cool, almost continental climate with snow in winter and late harvests, sometimes in November. That keeps acidity high.

steps.prompt: Why does Irpinia make fresh wines in southern Italy?
options: Altitude gives a cool, almost continental climate
steps.explanation: Height and inland position cool it down.

steps.title: Ancient wines
steps.body: Campania was a centre of Roman wine. Falernian, from northern Campania, was the most famous wine of ancient Rome. The Greeks brought vines here; Greco's name suggests that heritage. Pompeii, destroyed by Vesuvius in 79 AD, was a wine-trading town, and vines have been replanted inside its ruins.

steps.prompt: Falernian, from Campania, was ancient Rome's most famous wine.
steps.explanation: Yes. It was praised by Roman writers.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Campania's best wines come from Irpinia's hills
Volcanic soils and altitude give freshness
It was a centre of Roman wine

steps.title: Aglianico
steps.body: Aglianico is Campania's great red: dark, with high tannin and high acidity, black cherry, smoke and earth. It ripens very late. It makes Taurasi DOCG, often called the Barolo of the south, which must be at least 85% Aglianico and age three years, one in wood; Riserva four years. Mastroberardino kept the tradition alive after the Second World War.

steps.title: Fiano and Greco
steps.body: Fiano di Avellino DOCG gives textured, nutty whites with pear, hazelnut, honey and smoke, that can age 10 years or more. Greco di Tufo DOCG, from sulphur-rich volcanic soils around Tufo, gives firmer, mineral whites with peach and almond. Falanghina, near Naples and Benevento, gives fresh, floral whites; Piedirosso a light red.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its grape.
steps.explanation: Campania's three DOCGs are all in Irpinia.

steps.body: Fiano di Avellino gains honey and smoky notes with age. A five-year-old bottle is often better than a young one.

steps.prompt: Which DOCG is often called the Barolo of the south?
steps.explanation: For Aglianico's tannin, acidity and ageing potential.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico makes Taurasi, structured and long-lived
Fiano is nutty; Greco is mineral
Falanghina and Piedirosso complete Campania's grapes

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Campania's three DOCGs, Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, are all in Irpinia. Other names include Irpinia DOC, Falanghina del Sannio, Campi Flegrei, Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio, from Vesuvius' slopes, and Costa d'Amalfi. Riserva on Taurasi means at least four years of ageing.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Campania's food suits its wines: Fiano with buffalo mozzarella and seafood; Greco with fried fish and pasta with clams; Falanghina with pizza margherita; Taurasi with Neapolitan ragù, slow-cooked meat sauce, lamb and aged cheese. Serve whites at 10 to 12, Taurasi at 16 to 18, decanted.

steps.explanation: Barolo is in Piedmont.

modules.title: Rioja
modules.description: Spain's most famous region: Tempranillo, oak and an ageing system written into law.

steps.title: The Ebro valley
steps.body: Rioja lies in northern Spain, along the Ebro river and its tributaries, including the small Oja river that may give Rioja its name. It spans three regions: La Rioja, the Basque Country, Álava, and Navarra. Vineyards cover about 66,000 hectares, from about 300 to over 700 m. The Sierra de Cantabria shelters it from the north.

steps.title: Atlantic meets Mediterranean
steps.body: Rioja sits where Atlantic and Mediterranean influences meet. The west is cooler and wetter, with Atlantic air; the east is warmer and drier, Mediterranean. The Sierra de Cantabria blocks cold, wet winds from the Bay of Biscay. This range of climates lets growers blend grapes from different areas for balance.

steps.prompt: What shelters Rioja from cold northern winds?
steps.explanation: The mountains block Atlantic winds from the north.

steps.title: The French connection
steps.body: In the 1860s and 1870s, when phylloxera and mildew ruined Bordeaux, French merchants came to Rioja looking for wine. They brought Bordeaux techniques, like ageing in small oak barrels, and the railway linked Rioja to France. Houses like Marqués de Riscal, 1858, and Marqués de Murrieta founded modern Rioja. Rioja became Spain's first DOCa in 1991.

steps.prompt: French merchants brought barrel ageing to Rioja in the 19th century.
steps.explanation: Yes, after phylloxera hit Bordeaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rioja follows the Ebro across three regions
Atlantic and Mediterranean influences meet there
Bordeaux merchants shaped modern Rioja; DOCa since 1991

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Tempranillo covers about 88% of Rioja's red vineyards: red cherry, strawberry, leather and tobacco, with moderate acidity. Garnacha adds body, alcohol and red fruit, especially in the warmer east. Graciano adds acidity, colour and aroma, but is low-yielding. Mazuelo, Carignan, adds acidity and tannin. Maturana Tinta is a revived native.

steps.title: Whites and rosés
steps.body: White Rioja is mainly Viura, Macabeo elsewhere, with Malvasía and Garnacha Blanca, and since 2007, some Tempranillo Blanco, Verdejo and others. Traditional white Rioja is aged long in oak, nutty and oxidative, as at López de Heredia. Rioja also makes rosado, mostly from Garnacha and Tempranillo.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Rioja blends grapes for balance.

steps.body: Traditional white Rioja, aged for years in oak, is one of Spain's most distinctive wines, nutty and complex.

steps.prompt: What share of Rioja's red vineyards is Tempranillo?
steps.explanation: Tempranillo dominates.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tempranillo is about 88% of Rioja's reds
Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo add body, acidity and colour
Viura leads the whites

lessons.title: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
lessons.subtitle: The ageing ladder
objectives: Explain the role of American oak

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Rioja's categories set minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: two years, at least one in barrel. Reserva: three years, at least one in barrel and six months in bottle. Gran Reserva: five years, at least two in barrel and two in bottle. Joven or Genérico wines have little or no barrel age. A coloured seal on the back label shows the category.

steps.title: Oak
steps.body: Rioja's barrels are traditionally 225-litre barricas of American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill. Long ageing in old oak gives traditional Rioja its pale colour, mellow fruit and leather. Since the 1990s, many producers use French oak and shorter ageing for darker, fruitier wines. Both styles thrive.

steps.prompt: Order Rioja's categories by minimum ageing, shortest first.
steps.explanation: Each category requires more time in barrel and bottle.

steps.title: The seals
steps.body: Each bottle carries a back-label seal from the Consejo Regulador: green for Crianza, burgundy red for Reserva, blue for Gran Reserva, and white or no barrel indication for Genérico. This makes the category easy to spot even if the front label doesn't say it.

steps.prompt: What does American oak typically give Rioja?
steps.explanation: American oak's lactones give these notes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva set minimum ageing
American oak gives vanilla and coconut; French oak is now common
Back-label seals show the category

steps.title: Rioja Alta and Alavesa
steps.body: Rioja Alta, in the west, south of the Ebro, is higher, cooler and Atlantic-influenced, with clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils; Haro is its historic centre. Rioja Alavesa, north of the Ebro, in the Basque Country, has chalky clay-limestone on terraces. Both give elegant, fresh, structured Tempranillo.
steps.highlight: Alta and Alavesa: cool and elegant

steps.title: Rioja Oriental
steps.body: Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja, renamed in 2018, is the eastern zone, lower, warmer and drier, Mediterranean. Alluvial and clay soils suit Garnacha, which thrives there. Wines are riper and fuller. Since 2017, labels can name the zone, and from 2018 municipalities, if the grapes come from there.

steps.prompt: Match each sub-zone to its feature.
steps.explanation: Each zone gives Rioja a different character.

steps.title: Blending and place
steps.body: Traditionally, Rioja houses blended grapes from all three zones for balance and consistency. Today, more producers make wines from a single zone, village or vineyard, showing place. This shift from house style to terroir is the biggest change in modern Rioja.

steps.prompt: Rioja Oriental was formerly called Rioja Baja.
steps.explanation: Yes, renamed in 2018.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rioja Alta and Alavesa are cool and elegant
Rioja Oriental is warm and suits Garnacha
Rioja is moving from blends to place-specific wines

lessons.title: Single vineyards
lessons.subtitle: Rioja's new map
objectives: Name key producers of the movement

steps.title: Viñedo Singular
steps.body: In 2017, Rioja created Viñedo Singular, single vineyard, for wines from specific, registered plots. Rules include vines at least 35 years old, low yields, hand harvesting and tasting approval. It aims to recognise the best sites, as in Burgundy. Labels can also name a village, Vino de Municipio, or a zone, Vino de Zona.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: For a century, Rioja focused on ageing and blending, not site. Producers like Remírez de Ganuza, Artadi, Contino and Telmo Rodríguez pushed for place-based classification. Some, like Artadi, left the DOCa in 2015 in protest before the new rules. The debate continues about how far Rioja should go towards a Burgundian model.

steps.prompt: Which is a requirement for Viñedo Singular?
steps.explanation: Old vines, low yields and hand harvesting are required.

steps.title: Old classics
steps.body: Some historic Rioja wines were single vineyard long before the rules: Viña Tondonia, from López de Heredia, since 1913; Contino, the first single-estate Rioja in the 1970s. These show that site has always mattered, even under the blending tradition.

steps.prompt: Which are Rioja's place-based label categories?
steps.explanation: The last one doesn't exist.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viñedo Singular, since 2017, names single vineyards
Village and zone wines show place
Historic wines like Viña Tondonia were early single vineyards

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Rioja and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Rioja labels show the producer, the vintage, the category, Crianza, Reserva or Gran Reserva, and sometimes the zone, village or Viñedo Singular. The back label carries the Consejo Regulador seal. Cosecha or Genérico wines don't follow the ageing ladder and may be young or modern.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Rioja suits lamb, especially chuletillas, small lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings; roast suckling pig; chorizo; jamón ibérico; and Manchego. Gran Reserva suits mushrooms, game and stews. Crianza suits tapas. White Rioja suits fish and oxidative styles suit aged cheese.

steps.prompt: Which dish is a Rioja classic?
options: Lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings
steps.explanation: Chuletillas al sarmiento.

steps.body: An old Gran Reserva may throw sediment. Stand it up for a day and decant gently; its pale colour is normal.

steps.prompt: A pale, garnet colour in old Gran Reserva is a fault.
steps.explanation: Not true. Long oak and bottle ageing naturally lighten the colour.

points: Labels show category, seal and sometimes place
Rioja suits lamb, jamón and Manchego
Old Gran Reservas are pale, mellow and best decanted gently
