modules.title: Jerez
modules.description: The Sherry triangle: white albariza soils, flor yeast and soleras that blend wines across generations.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: The Sherry triangle
objectives: Explain the role of the two winds

steps.title: Three towns
steps.body: Sherry comes from the area around three towns in Andalusia, south-west Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Sherry triangle. The DO is Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Spain's oldest, from 1933. Wines must age in one of the three towns; Sanlúcar's is called Manzanilla.

steps.title: Albariza
steps.body: The best vineyards sit on albariza, a brilliant white soil with up to 40% chalk, formed from ancient marine algae. It soaks up winter rain like a sponge and forms a crust in summer that slows evaporation. Its whiteness reflects sunlight onto the vines. Named vineyard areas, pagos, like Macharnudo, Carrascal and Miraflores, sit on it.

steps.prompt: What is special about albariza?
options: It stores winter rain and reflects sunlight
steps.explanation: Its chalk holds water and its whiteness reflects light.

steps.title: Two winds
steps.body: Jerez is hot, with over 300 sunny days a year. Two winds matter. The Poniente, from the Atlantic, is cool and humid, favouring flor yeast in the cellars. The Levante, from the east, is hot and dry, concentrating grapes but stressing flor. Bodegas are built with high ceilings and thick walls, often facing the Poniente.

steps.prompt: The Poniente wind brings humidity that helps flor grow.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's cool and humid, from the Atlantic.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sherry comes from the triangle of Jerez, El Puerto and Sanlúcar
Albariza stores water and reflects light
The humid Poniente and dry Levante shape vineyard and cellar

steps.title: Palomino
steps.body: Palomino Fino is about 95% of the vineyards. It's neutral, low in acidity and sugar, giving base wines of about 11 to 12.5%. Its neutrality is a strength: Sherry's flavours come from ageing, flor and oxygen, not from the grape.

steps.title: Sweet grapes
steps.body: Pedro Ximénez, PX, and Moscatel are used for sweet wines and for sweetening blends. They're often dried in the sun on mats, asoleo, for one to three weeks, becoming almost raisins. Much PX comes from nearby Montilla-Moriles, which is allowed in Sherry. Fermentation is stopped early by fortification, keeping huge sugar levels.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its use.
steps.explanation: Three grapes, many styles.

steps.body: Pedro Ximénez is one of the sweetest wines in the world, often over 400 g/l of sugar. Pour it over vanilla ice cream.

steps.prompt: Why is Palomino ideal for Sherry?
options: Its neutrality lets ageing create the flavours
steps.explanation: Flor and oxygen write the flavour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Palomino, about 95%, gives neutral base wines
PX and Moscatel are dried in the sun for sweet wines
Sherry's flavour comes from ageing, not the grape

lessons.title: Flor and the solera
lessons.subtitle: Biological ageing and blending
objectives: Explain the classification of base wines

steps.title: Flor
steps.body: After fermentation, base wines are tasted and classified. The finest, palest are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and put in barrels, botas, filled about five-sixths. A film of yeast, flor, grows on the surface. It protects the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol, producing acetaldehyde: bready, nutty, saline aromas. This is biological ageing.

steps.title: The solera
steps.body: Sherry ages in a solera: rows of barrels of different ages. Wine is drawn from the oldest, the solera, a process called saca, never more than about a third at a time; by law, no more than 40% a year. It's replaced from the next oldest, the first criadera, and so on, a process called rocío. Young wine enters the youngest criadera. The result is a consistent blend of many ages.

steps.prompt: Put the solera's movements in order.
items: Draw from the oldest tier, the saca
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill the first criadera from the second
Add young wine to the youngest tier
steps.explanation: Wine moves step by step from young to old.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Base wines are classified by taste. Light, delicate wines are marked for Fino and Manzanilla, fortified to 15%. Fuller wines go to Oloroso, fortified to 17%, where flor can't live. Some wines change paths during ageing, losing their flor and becoming Amontillado or Palo Cortado.

steps.prompt: At what strength can flor no longer survive?
steps.explanation: At 17%, flor dies; the wine ages with oxygen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Flor protects Fino and adds bready, saline notes
The solera blends many ages through saca and rocío
Base wines are classified for Fino or Oloroso

steps.title: Fino
steps.body: Fino ages under flor, usually at least two years, often more, in Jerez or El Puerto. It's pale, bone dry, about 15%, with almond, bread dough, chamomile and a saline edge. El Puerto's Finos, closer to the sea, are often lighter. Fino is best fresh: once opened, drink within a few days.

steps.title: Manzanilla
steps.body: Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Cooler, more humid sea air keeps flor thicker all year, giving lighter, more saline, delicate wines with chamomile notes; manzanilla means chamomile in Spanish. Manzanilla Pasada is an older Manzanilla, with more nutty depth.

steps.prompt: Why is flor thicker in Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
steps.explanation: Sea air at the river mouth keeps flor thriving.

steps.title: En rama
steps.body: En rama, raw, means Sherry bottled with little or no filtration or fining, straight from the barrel. It's more intense and closer to the wine in the cask. Many bodegas release Fino and Manzanilla en rama seasonally, often in spring when flor is thickest. These are best drunk soon after bottling.
steps.highlight: En rama: unfiltered, from the cask

steps.prompt: Which describe Fino and Manzanilla?
steps.explanation: They're pale and dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fino ages under flor: pale, dry, almond and bread
Manzanilla is Sanlúcar's lighter, more saline Fino
En rama Sherries are unfiltered and best fresh

steps.title: Amontillado and Palo Cortado
steps.body: Amontillado starts as a Fino under flor, then the flor fades or is killed by fortifying to about 17%, and the wine ages oxidatively. It's amber, dry, with hazelnut, toffee and saline notes. Palo Cortado is rare: a wine that loses its flor early, combining Amontillado's delicate aroma with Oloroso's richer body.

steps.title: Oloroso
steps.body: Oloroso, fragrant, is fortified to about 17% from the start, never has flor, and ages with oxygen for years. It darkens to mahogany, with walnut, leather, dried fruit and spice. It's naturally dry, despite seeming rich. As water evaporates, alcohol can rise to 20% or more.

steps.prompt: Match each Sherry to its ageing.
steps.explanation: Ageing paths define styles.

steps.title: Sweet styles
steps.body: Pedro Ximénez Sherry is black, syrupy and very sweet, with raisin, fig, coffee and liquorice. Moscatel is sweet and floral. Cream Sherry blends Oloroso with sweet wine; Pale Cream blends Fino with sweetening. Age statements, VOS, 20 years, and VORS, 30 years, mark very old Sherries.

steps.prompt: Order these Sherries from palest to darkest.
steps.explanation: Biological ageing keeps wine pale; oxidation and dried grapes darken it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine flor and oxygen
Oloroso ages oxidatively and stays dry
PX and Cream are sweet; VOS and VORS mark old Sherry

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Sherry and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Sherry labels name the style: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado, Cream or PX. Look for en rama, an age statement like VOS or VORS, or 12 or 15 year old Sherry. Manzanilla always comes from Sanlúcar. Most Sherry has no vintage, being a solera blend; añada Sherries are rare single vintages.

steps.title: Serving
steps.body: Serve Fino and Manzanilla well chilled, 6 to 8 degrees, in a white wine glass; keep open bottles in the fridge and finish within a week. Amontillado and Palo Cortado at 12 to 14; Oloroso at 14 to 16; PX slightly cool. Oxidative styles keep for weeks once open.

steps.prompt: How should Fino be served?
options: Well chilled, and finished within a week
After years in an open bottle
steps.explanation: Fino is delicate; serve it cold and fresh.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Fino and Manzanilla suit tapas: olives, almonds, jamón, fried fish, prawns. Amontillado suits soups, mushrooms and tricky vegetables like artichokes and asparagus. Oloroso suits stews, game and hard cheese. PX suits vanilla ice cream, blue cheese and chocolate.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Fino or Manzanilla?
steps.explanation: Chocolate cake suits PX.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels name the style and sometimes an age
Serve Fino cold and fresh; Oloroso cool
Fino with tapas, Amontillado with soups, PX with ice cream

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Sherry's vocabulary is unique.

steps.prompt: Where must Manzanilla be aged?
steps.explanation: Manzanilla comes only from Sanlúcar.

steps.prompt: Oloroso is naturally sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's dry; sweet versions are blended.

steps.prompt: Which are Sherry's grapes?
steps.explanation: Tempranillo isn't used.

steps.prompt: By law, no more than ____% of a solera can be drawn per year.
steps.explanation: No more than 40%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sherry comes from the triangle's albariza soils
Palomino becomes Fino under flor or Oloroso with oxygen
The solera blends many ages
Each style suits a different dish

modules.title: Ribera del Duero
modules.description: Powerful Tempranillo from a high, cold plateau along the Duero river.

steps.title: Along the Duero
steps.body: Ribera del Duero follows the Duero river for about 115 km across Castilla y León, in north-central Spain. Vineyards sit on the Meseta, the high central plateau, at 750 to over 1,000 m, among the highest in Europe. Soils mix limestone, clay, sand and chalky marl. It has about 26,000 hectares of vines.

steps.title: Extreme continental
steps.body: The climate is extreme continental: long, cold winters, short, hot summers and a huge day and night range, sometimes 20 degrees. Hot days ripen the grapes; cold nights keep acidity and colour. Frost is a constant danger, even in late spring or early autumn; 2017 lost over half the crop to frost.
steps.highlight: Huge day and night swings, frost

steps.prompt: Why does Ribera's Tempranillo keep its freshness?
options: Cold nights on the high plateau
steps.explanation: Altitude gives cold nights that preserve acidity.

steps.title: Vega Sicilia and Pesquera
steps.body: Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864, made Ribera's greatest wine, Único, for over a century before the region was known. Alejandro Fernández's Pesquera, praised by critics in the 1980s, made the region famous. The DO was created in 1982 with only a handful of wineries; today there are over 300. Dominio de Pingus, since 1995, is another icon.

steps.prompt: Which are famous Ribera del Duero producers?
steps.explanation: Château Margaux is in Bordeaux.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Ribera del Duero sits on the high Meseta along the Duero
Its extreme climate brings heat, cold nights and frost
Vega Sicilia and Pesquera made it famous; DO since 1982

steps.title: Tinto Fino
steps.body: Ribera's grape is Tempranillo, locally called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. It has adapted to the extreme climate with thicker skins and smaller berries than in Rioja, giving darker, more concentrated wines with black fruit, liquorice and firm tannin. Reds must be at least 75% Tinto Fino; since 2019, rules allow 100% and blends with Cabernet, Merlot, Malbec, and white Albillo.
steps.highlight: Tinto Fino: thicker skins, darker wines

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Ribera uses Spain's ageing categories: Joven, Crianza, at least 24 months, 12 in oak; Reserva, 36 months, 12 in oak; Gran Reserva, 60 months, 24 in oak. Many wines use French oak and have a modern, powerful style. Since 2019, white wines from Albillo Mayor are also allowed as Ribera del Duero.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Ribera.
steps.explanation: Ribera's rules are close to Rioja's, with local names.

steps.body: Vega Sicilia's Único blends Tinto Fino with some Cabernet Sauvignon and ages for about ten years before release.

steps.prompt: How does Ribera's Tinto Fino typically compare with Rioja's Tempranillo?
steps.explanation: Thicker skins and extreme climate give power.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tinto Fino is Ribera's Tempranillo, darker and more concentrated
Reds must be at least 75% Tinto Fino
Ribera uses Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Ribera and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Ribera del Duero DO, the producer, vintage and ageing category, with a back-label seal. Roble, oak, is an unofficial term for young wines with a few months in barrel. Many top wines don't use the categories at all, relying on the producer's name.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Ribera's classic pairing is lechazo, roast suckling lamb, cooked in wood-fired clay ovens in Aranda de Duero. It also suits grilled steak, game, chorizo, Manchego and aged sheep's cheese. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young; good Ribera ages 10 to 20 years.

steps.prompt: Which dish is Ribera del Duero's classic match?
steps.explanation: Roast suckling lamb in wood ovens.

steps.body: Aranda de Duero has a network of medieval underground cellars, many still used for ageing wine.

steps.prompt: Roble is an official Spanish ageing category.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's an informal term for young wines with brief oak ageing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show the category; Roble is informal
Ribera's classic match is roast suckling lamb
Serve decanted; good wines age 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Match each term to Ribera.
steps.explanation: Ribera's identity is high, cold and powerful.

steps.prompt: What is the main risk in Ribera's vineyards?
steps.explanation: Frost, even in late spring and early autumn.

steps.prompt: Ribera's reds must contain at least 75% Tinto Fino.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.prompt: Which describe Ribera's climate?
steps.explanation: It's cold and continental.

steps.prompt: Ribera del Duero became a DO in ____.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Ribera sits high on the Meseta, with an extreme climate
Tinto Fino gives dark, powerful Tempranillo
Vega Sicilia and Pesquera made it famous
Pair it with roast suckling lamb

modules.title: Priorat
modules.description: Steep slate slopes in Catalonia where old Garnacha and Cariñena make powerful, mineral reds.

steps.title: Rugged hills
steps.body: Priorat lies in Catalonia, about 100 km south-west of Barcelona, in rugged hills surrounded by the Montsant mountains. Vineyards climb steep terraces and slopes from 100 to 750 m. It's small, about 2,000 hectares. The climate is Mediterranean but with continental influence: hot, dry summers, cold winters and very little rain.

steps.title: Llicorella
steps.body: Priorat's signature soil is llicorella, a dark slate and quartz that glitters in the sun. It's poor, holds little water and forces roots to dig deep, sometimes 15 metres or more. Yields are tiny, often under 1 kg per vine on old vines. The result is concentrated wine with a mineral, sometimes graphite edge.
steps.highlight: Dark slate, deep roots, tiny yields

steps.prompt: What is llicorella?
options: A dark slate and quartz soil
steps.explanation: Priorat's famous slate soil.

steps.title: The revival
steps.body: Carthusian monks founded the Scala Dei monastery here in the 12th century, which gave Priorat its name, priory. After phylloxera, the region emptied. In 1989, a group of five producers, including René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios and Carles Pastrana, made wines that stunned critics. Priorat became Spain's second DOCa in 2000, called DOQ in Catalan.

steps.prompt: Priorat is named after a medieval priory.
steps.explanation: Yes, the Carthusian priory of Scala Dei.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Priorat is steep, dry and small, in Catalonia
Llicorella slate forces deep roots and tiny yields
A 1989 revival led to DOQ status in 2000

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Garnacha and Cariñena
objectives: Explain the role of old vines

steps.title: Old natives
steps.body: Garnacha and Cariñena, Carignan, are Priorat's traditional grapes, many from old bush vines over 50 or 80 years old. Garnacha gives ripe red fruit, spice and warmth; Cariñena gives acidity, colour and structure. Together, on llicorella, they make powerful, dark, mineral reds, often 14.5 to 15.5% alcohol.

steps.title: International partners
steps.body: The 1989 pioneers also planted Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot, adding structure and colour to blends. Today many producers focus on the native grapes, especially old Garnacha and Cariñena, and on single vineyards. Whites, from Garnacha Blanca and Macabeo, are rare.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Old natives lead; international grapes support.

steps.body: Neighbouring Montsant, which surrounds Priorat, makes similar Garnacha and Cariñena blends at lower prices, on more varied soils.

steps.prompt: What do old vines give Priorat's wines?
steps.explanation: Old vines on llicorella give very low yields and concentration.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Garnacha and Cariñena are Priorat's traditional grapes
Old bush vines give concentrated, mineral wines
International grapes support some blends

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Priorat and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show DOQ Priorat or DOCa Priorat. Since 2009, Priorat has a place-based classification: Vi de Vila, village wine, from one of 12 villages, like Gratallops or Porrera; Vinya Classificada, classified vineyard; and Gran Vinya Classificada, the top level. It was among the first in Spain to classify by place.
steps.highlight: Vi de Vila to Gran Vinya Classificada

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Priorat's power suits rich, savoury food: grilled lamb, wild boar, beef stews, Catalan dishes like duck with pears, and aged cheese. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted. Good Priorat ages 10 to 20 years, softening its alcohol and tannin into dried fruit and earth.

steps.prompt: What is Vi de Vila in Priorat?
options: A village wine from one of 12 villages
steps.explanation: Part of Priorat's place-based classification.

steps.body: Decant young Priorat for an hour or two. Its high alcohol and concentration open up with air.

steps.prompt: Which are levels of Priorat's classification?
steps.explanation: Gran Reserva Especial isn't a Priorat term.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Priorat classifies villages and vineyards since 2009
Its power suits lamb, boar and stews
Decant young Priorat; it ages 10 to 20 years

steps.prompt: Match each term to Priorat.
steps.explanation: Priorat's story is ancient and modern.

steps.prompt: When did Priorat's modern revival begin?
steps.explanation: With five pioneering producers.

steps.prompt: Priorat is Spain's largest wine region.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's small, about 2,000 hectares.

steps.prompt: Which are Priorat's traditional grapes?
steps.explanation: Albariño grows in Galicia.

steps.prompt: Priorat became a DOQ, or DOCa, in ____.
steps.explanation: In 2000, Spain's second after Rioja.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Priorat is steep and dry, on llicorella slate
Old Garnacha and Cariñena give powerful, mineral reds
The 1989 revival led to DOQ status in 2000
Its village classification maps the best sites

modules.title: Rías Baixas
modules.description: Green, wet Galicia: crisp, saline Albariño from granite and the Atlantic.

steps.title: The rías
steps.body: Rías Baixas is in Galicia, Spain's north-west corner, on the Atlantic coast. It takes its name from the rías, flooded river valleys like fjords, that cut into the coast. Granite dominates the soils. It's green and lush, very different from the rest of Spain. The DO was created in 1988.

steps.title: Wet and mild
steps.body: The climate is maritime: mild temperatures, high humidity and lots of rain, often 1,600 mm or more a year, among Spain's wettest regions. The main challenge is fungal disease. Growers use high pergolas, parras, on granite posts, to keep grapes away from damp ground and let air flow.

steps.prompt: Why are Rías Baixas vines trained on high pergolas?
options: To let air circulate and reduce rot
steps.explanation: Height and airflow fight humidity.

steps.title: Five sub-zones
steps.body: Rías Baixas has five sub-zones. Val do Salnés, the coolest and most Atlantic, is Albariño's historic heart, around Cambados. O Rosal and Condado do Tea, along the Miño river on the Portuguese border, are warmer, and blend Albariño with Loureiro and Treixadura. Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla complete them.
steps.highlight: Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Condado do Tea

steps.prompt: Which are Rías Baixas sub-zones?
steps.explanation: Rioja Alta is in Rioja.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rías Baixas lies on Galicia's Atlantic coast, on granite
It's wet and mild, fighting rot with high pergolas
Val do Salnés is the cool heart; the Miño zones are warmer

steps.title: Albariño
steps.body: Albariño is about 96% of Rías Baixas' vineyards. Its thick skins resist rot in the damp climate. It gives crisp, aromatic, dry whites with lemon, grapefruit, white peach, apricot and a saline, mineral edge. Wines labelled Rías Baixas Albariño must be 100% Albariño.

steps.title: Partners and styles
steps.body: In O Rosal and Condado do Tea, Albariño may be blended with Loureiro, floral, Treixadura, rounder, and Caíño Blanco. Most Albariño is fermented in steel and bottled young. Some producers age it on its lees for months or years, adding texture and allowing it to age; a few use oak. Rías Baixas also allows a little red wine.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Rías Baixas.
steps.explanation: Albariño leads, with local partners.

steps.body: Albariño aged on its lees for a year or more shows how serious it can be: creamy, saline and able to age five years or more.

steps.prompt: What must a Rías Baixas Albariño contain?
steps.explanation: The varietal label requires 100%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Albariño is about 96% of the vineyards
Its thick skins resist rot; it gives peach and salinity
Blends add Loureiro and Treixadura; lees ageing adds depth

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Rías Baixas and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Rías Baixas DO, sometimes a sub-zone like Val do Salnés, and the grape. Rías Baixas Albariño means 100% Albariño; Rías Baixas Salnés, Condado do Tea or Rosal may be blends. Barrica means oak-aged. Most wines are released young, within a year of harvest.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Albariño is Galicia's seafood wine: pulpo a la gallega, octopus with paprika and olive oil, mussels, clams, scallops, razor clams, oysters and grilled fish. Galicia's seafood is famous across Spain. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Cambados holds an Albariño festival every August.

steps.prompt: Which Galician dish is a classic match for Albariño?
steps.explanation: Octopus with paprika suits Albariño's acidity and salinity.

steps.body: Across the Miño river, in Portugal, the same grape is called Alvarinho and makes the wines of Monção e Melgaço.

steps.prompt: Most Rías Baixas Albariño is released young.
steps.explanation: Yes, usually within a year of harvest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show the grape, sub-zone and sometimes barrica
Albariño suits octopus, shellfish and grilled fish
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Rías Baixas' vocabulary is Galician.

steps.prompt: What is Rías Baixas' main challenge?
steps.explanation: It's one of Spain's wettest regions.

steps.prompt: Albariño has thin skins prone to rot.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its thick skins resist rot.

steps.prompt: Which grapes appear in Rías Baixas blends?
steps.explanation: Tempranillo isn't a Rías Baixas grape.

steps.prompt: Rías Baixas became a DO in ____.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rías Baixas is wet, green and granite
Albariño dominates, crisp and saline
High pergolas fight humidity
It's a natural seafood wine

modules.title: Douro
modules.description: Terraced schist slopes above a river: the home of Port and of Portugal's great dry reds.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: A river valley carved in schist

steps.title: The valley
steps.body: The Douro river runs west from Spain to Porto and the Atlantic. Its wine region, in northern Portugal, starts about 100 km inland, behind the Marão mountains, which block Atlantic rain. Vineyards line the steep valley sides and tributaries. It's divided into three sub-regions: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.

steps.title: Heat and drought
steps.body: The Marão creates a rain shadow, so the Douro grows hotter and drier from west to east. Baixo Corgo, in the west, gets about 900 mm of rain; the Douro Superior, near Spain, about 400 mm. Summers often reach 40 degrees. Schist soil, which splits vertically, lets roots dig deep for water.

steps.prompt: What protects the Douro from Atlantic rain?
steps.explanation: The Marão casts a rain shadow over the valley.

steps.title: The first demarcation
steps.body: In 1756, the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro and created a company to control Port's quality and trade, making it one of the world's first legally defined wine regions. Stone markers, marcos, set the boundaries. In 2001, the Alto Douro Wine Region became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

steps.prompt: The Douro was demarcated in 1756.
steps.explanation: Yes, by the Marquis of Pombal.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Douro lies behind the Marão, in three sub-regions
It gets hotter and drier towards Spain
It was demarcated in 1756 and is a UNESCO site

steps.title: Five key reds
steps.body: The Douro allows over 100 grapes, but five are recommended for quality. Touriga Nacional: floral, dark, structured. Touriga Franca, the most planted: perfumed, elegant. Tinta Roriz, Tempranillo: red fruit and body. Tinta Barroca: soft, sweet fruit, early ripening. Tinto Cão: acidity and finesse, low yields.

steps.title: Field blends
steps.body: Many old Douro vineyards are field blends, vinhas velhas, with dozens of grapes planted together, often over 80 years old. They're picked and fermented together, giving complexity. Whites, from Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio and Códega do Larinho, grow at higher, cooler sites and make dry whites and white Port.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Douro blends draw on many natives.

steps.body: Vinhas velhas, old vines, on a Douro label often means a field blend of many grapes, a living record of how the region was planted.

steps.prompt: Which is the Douro's most planted grape?
steps.explanation: Touriga Franca covers the most area.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Five recommended reds lead, from Touriga Nacional to Tinto Cão
Touriga Franca is the most planted
Old field blends give complexity

steps.title: Schist
steps.body: Douro soils are mostly schist, a layered rock that splits vertically. Roots follow the cracks deep, sometimes 10 metres or more, to find water in dry summers. Schist also stores heat. Granite appears at the edges, but the best Port vineyards are on schist; the boundary between schist and granite roughly marks the region.

steps.title: Terraces
steps.body: To plant on slopes up to 60 degrees, people built terraces by hand. Old terraces, socalcos, have dry-stone walls and narrow ledges. From the 1970s, patamares, wider terraces without walls, allowed some machines. Vinha ao alto, vertical planting up the slope, is used where it's less steep. All are labour-intensive.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: The Douro's landscape is built by hand.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Douro vineyards for Port are classified from A to F, based on factors like altitude, yield, soil, slope, exposure and vine age. A and B vineyards receive the most authorisation to make Port, the beneficio, and the highest grape prices. Cima Corgo has the highest share of top-graded vineyards.

steps.prompt: Why does schist suit the Douro?
options: Roots follow its vertical cracks to find water
steps.explanation: Deep roots survive dry summers.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Schist lets roots dig deep for water
Socalcos, patamares and vinha ao alto shape the slopes
Vineyards are graded A to F for Port

steps.title: Making Port
steps.body: Port grapes are crushed, traditionally by foot in stone tanks, lagares, now often by machine or robotic pistons. After two or three days of fermentation, at about 6 to 9% alcohol, aguardente, grape spirit at about 77%, is added, stopping fermentation. The result: about 19 to 22% alcohol and 90 to 110 g/l of sugar. Wine ages in Vila Nova de Gaia or the Douro.

steps.title: Ruby and tawny
steps.body: Ruby styles age briefly in large vats, keeping dark colour and fresh fruit: Ruby, Reserve, Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, a single year bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood, and Vintage. Tawny styles age in small casks, pipes, where oxygen gives nutty, caramel notes: Tawny, Reserve Tawny, aged tawnies with 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, and Colheita, a single-vintage tawny.
steps.highlight: Vats for ruby; casks for tawny

steps.prompt: Match each Port to its ageing.
steps.explanation: How Port ages defines its style.

steps.title: Vintage Port
steps.body: Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years, declared by each house, about three times a decade. It's bottled after two to three years and ages for decades in bottle, throwing a sediment. Single quinta Vintages come from one estate in good, undeclared years. White and rosé Ports add lighter styles.
steps.highlight: Declared about three times a decade

steps.prompt: Which are ruby-style Ports?
steps.explanation: Aged tawny is cask-aged, a tawny style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Port is fortified with aguardente mid-fermentation
Ruby styles age in vats or bottle; tawnies in casks
Vintage Port is declared in exceptional years

lessons.title: Dry Douro reds
lessons.subtitle: The new face of the Douro

steps.title: A new tradition
steps.body: For centuries, most Douro grapes went into Port. Barca Velha, first made in 1952 by Fernando Nicolau de Almeida at Ferreira, showed the Douro could make great dry reds. From the 1990s, producers like Niepoort, Quinta do Crasto and Quinta do Vale Meão built the modern dry Douro. Today dry wines rival Port in volume.

steps.title: Style
steps.body: Dry Douro reds are dark and structured, with black fruit, violet, rockrose and schist minerality, often blends of Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz. Top wines age in French oak and can age 15 to 20 years. Higher, cooler sites give fresher styles. Douro whites, from Rabigato and Viosinho, are crisp and mineral.

steps.prompt: Which wine showed in 1952 that the Douro could make great dry reds?
steps.explanation: Barca Velha, from Ferreira.

steps.body: Some Douro producers make both Port and dry wine from the same quinta, a chance to taste how fortification changes the same fruit.

steps.prompt: Dry wines now rival Port in volume in the Douro.
steps.explanation: Yes. Dry Douro DOC wines have grown greatly since the 1990s.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barca Velha, 1952, began the dry Douro tradition
Dry reds are dark, floral and structured
Douro whites from high sites are crisp and mineral

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Douro and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Dry wines are labelled Douro DOC; fortified wines Porto DOC. Port labels show the style: Ruby, Tawny, LBV, Vintage, Colheita, or an age like 20 Years Old. Quinta means estate. The IVDP, the Douro and Port institute, seals each bottle. Vinhas velhas means old vines.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Dry Douro reds suit roast kid, lamb, bacalhau with roasted potatoes, and game. Ruby and Vintage Port suit Stilton and dark chocolate. Tawny suits crème brûlée, nuts, caramel desserts and Portuguese pastries like pastéis de nata. White Port with tonic is Porto's aperitif. Serve tawny slightly cool.
steps.highlight: Stilton with Vintage; nuts with tawny

steps.prompt: Which is Porto's classic aperitif?
steps.explanation: Porto tónico, white Port and tonic.

steps.title: Serving Port
steps.body: Serve ruby and Vintage Port at about 16 degrees, tawnies at 10 to 14, white Port chilled. Decant Vintage Port and unfiltered LBV for sediment. Opened tawnies last weeks; Vintage Port is best within a day or two.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Vintage Port?
steps.explanation: Oysters need a dry white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Douro DOC is dry; Porto DOC is fortified
Dry reds suit lamb; Vintage Port suits Stilton
Decant Vintage Port; tawnies keep after opening

modules.title: Madeira
modules.description: A volcanic Atlantic island whose wine is heated, oxidised and almost immortal.

steps.title: A steep island
steps.body: Madeira is a Portuguese volcanic island in the Atlantic, about 700 km off Morocco. Its mountains rise to over 1,800 m. Vineyards are small, on steep terraces called poios, mostly on the north and south coasts, from sea level to about 800 m. Volcanic basalt soils are fertile and acidic. There are only about 500 hectares of vines.

steps.title: Subtropical and humid
steps.body: The climate is subtropical and humid, with mild temperatures all year. The south coast is warmer and drier; the north coast cooler and wetter. Humidity brings disease, so vines are often trained on low pergolas, latadas. Water is channelled from the mountains through levadas, ancient irrigation canals.

steps.prompt: What are Madeira's levadas?
steps.explanation: Levadas bring water from the mountains to the terraces.

steps.title: Shipped across the tropics
steps.body: From the 15th century, Madeira was a stop for ships to the Americas and India. Wine loaded as ballast crossed the tropics and came back improved by heat and movement, called vinho da roda, round-trip wine. Spirit was added to protect it. Madeira became the toast of the American colonies; it was used to toast the Declaration of Independence in 1776.

steps.prompt: Madeira improved after crossing the tropics by ship.
steps.explanation: Yes. Heat and movement transformed it, which producers now recreate.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Madeira is a steep, volcanic Atlantic island
Its humid, subtropical climate needs pergolas and levadas
Ship voyages through the tropics shaped its style

steps.title: Tinta Negra
steps.body: Tinta Negra is a black grape making about 80% of Madeira. It's versatile, used for every sweetness level. Until 2015, it couldn't be named on labels; now it can. Most Madeira labelled by age, like 5 Years Old, is Tinta Negra, unless a noble grape is named.

steps.title: The noble grapes
steps.body: Four white grapes are called noble, and each traditionally gives a level of sweetness: Sercial, driest; Verdelho, medium dry; Boal, or Bual, medium sweet; Malvasia, or Malmsey, sweetest. A wine named after a noble grape must contain at least 85% of it. Terrantez, rare, is a fifth noble grape, medium dry to medium sweet.

steps.prompt: Order the noble grapes from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Sercial is driest; Malvasia richest.

steps.body: All Madeira keeps striking acidity, even the sweetest Malmsey. That's what makes it so fresh and long-lived.

steps.prompt: Which grape makes most Madeira?
steps.explanation: About 80%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tinta Negra makes about 80% of Madeira
Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to sweet
Named noble grape wines need at least 85% of that grape

steps.title: Fortification
steps.body: Madeira is fortified with grape spirit at 96%, to about 17 to 22% alcohol. For drier styles, like Sercial, spirit is added late, after more fermentation; for sweeter styles, like Malvasia, early. Then the wine is heated, recreating the effect of tropical voyages.

steps.title: Two methods
steps.body: Estufagem heats wine in stainless steel tanks, estufas, to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, then rests it. It's faster and cheaper, used for younger wines. Canteiro ages wine in wooden casks in warm lofts, armazéns, for years, sometimes decades, heated only by the sun. Canteiro is slower and gentler, giving finer wines. All top Madeiras are canteiro.

steps.prompt: Match each method to its feature.
steps.explanation: Heat is Madeira's signature.

steps.title: Oxidation
steps.body: Madeira's ageing exposes it to heat and oxygen, deliberately. The wine turns amber to brown, with caramel, toffee, nuts, dried fruit, coffee and citrus peel. Because it's already oxidised and heated, it's almost indestructible: once opened, it lasts for months; old bottles from the 18th century can still be sound.

steps.prompt: Which method gives Madeira's finest wines?
steps.explanation: Slow ageing in warm lofts.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Madeira is fortified, then heated
Estufagem heats tanks for months; canteiro ages casks for years
Heat and oxygen make it almost indestructible

steps.title: Four styles
steps.body: Sercial, grown at higher, cooler sites, gives dry, high-acid wines with citrus and almonds. Verdelho gives medium dry wines, with dried fruit and smoke. Boal gives medium sweet wines, with caramel and raisin. Malvasia, or Malmsey, gives rich, sweet wines, with toffee, coffee and orange peel. All keep high acidity.

steps.title: Age categories
steps.body: Madeira labels show age: 3 years, Finest; 5 years, Reserve; 10 years, Special Reserve; 15 years, Extra Reserve; and 20, 30, 40, 50 years and over. Colheita, or Harvest, comes from a single year, aged at least five years. Frasqueira, or Vintage, comes from a single noble grape and year, aged at least 20 years in cask.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its style.
steps.explanation: Each noble grape has its style.

steps.title: Old Madeira
steps.body: Some of the oldest wines still drinkable come from Madeira: Frasqueiras from the 19th century appear at auction and are often still vibrant. Producers like Blandy's, Barbeito, Henriques & Henriques and D'Oliveiras keep stocks of old wine. Rainwater, a lighter style, was popular in the US.

steps.prompt: A Frasqueira Madeira must age at least ____ years in cask.
steps.explanation: Twenty years, from a single grape and year.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to rich
Labels show age from 3 years to Frasqueira
Old Madeira can stay vibrant for centuries

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Madeira and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Madeira labels show the style, by sweetness or grape: Dry, Medium Dry, Medium Sweet, Sweet, or Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia; and the age: 5, 10 or 15 Years Old, Colheita or Frasqueira. Canteiro may be noted. Tinta Negra can now be named. The IVBAM, the island's wine institute, certifies each bottle.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Sercial suits consommé, olives, almonds and sushi; Verdelho suits mushroom soups and pâté; Boal suits cheese, nuts and fruit cake; Malvasia suits chocolate, coffee desserts and Christmas pudding. Madeira is also a classic in cooking, like Madeira sauce for beef. Serve at 12 to 16 degrees, drier styles slightly cooler.
steps.highlight: Consommé with Sercial; chocolate with Malmsey

steps.prompt: Which Madeira suits dark chocolate desserts?
steps.explanation: Rich, sweet Malmsey matches chocolate.

steps.body: An open bottle of Madeira keeps for months. It's the ideal wine to keep on hand for an occasional glass.

steps.prompt: Madeira must be finished within a day of opening.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's already oxidised, so it keeps for months.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show grape or sweetness, and age
Sercial suits soup; Malmsey suits chocolate
Opened Madeira keeps for months

steps.prompt: Order the noble grapes from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Malvasia is the richest.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Madeira's vocabulary is unique.

steps.prompt: Why does Madeira last so long once opened?
steps.explanation: Further air does little harm.

steps.prompt: Which are Madeira's noble grapes?
steps.explanation: Tinta Roriz is a Douro grape; the fourth noble grape is Malvasia.

steps.prompt: Tinta Negra makes most Madeira.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 80%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Madeira is a volcanic Atlantic island with steep terraces
It's fortified, then heated by estufagem or canteiro
Noble grapes run from dry Sercial to rich Malvasia
It's almost indestructible and keeps for months

modules.title: Vinho Verde
modules.description: Portugal's green north-west: light, fresh whites and the serious Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: The green Minho
objectives: Explain the meaning of its name

steps.title: Portugal's largest DOC
steps.body: Vinho Verde covers the Minho, Portugal's green north-west, between the Minho river, on the Spanish border, and the Douro, and from the Atlantic inland. It's Portugal's largest DOC, about 21,000 hectares, divided into nine sub-regions, like Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado and Basto. Granite soils dominate.

steps.title: Wet and green
steps.body: The climate is Atlantic: mild, humid and wet, often 1,200 to 2,000 mm of rain a year. That keeps the landscape green and the grapes fresh, but brings disease. Traditionally, vines grew high on trees, pergolas and tall trellises, called enforcado and ramada, letting air circulate and leaving land below for food crops.

steps.prompt: Why were Vinho Verde vines traditionally trained high?
options: To let air circulate and free land below for crops
steps.explanation: Height reduced rot and allowed farming underneath.

steps.title: Green wine
steps.body: Verde means green, but it refers to youth, not colour: the wine is drunk young and fresh. The name also echoes the region's green landscape. Vinho Verde can be white, red or rosé, though white dominates today. The DOC was demarcated in 1908.
steps.highlight: Verde means young, not green in colour

steps.prompt: Vinho Verde means the wine is green in colour.
steps.explanation: Not true. Verde refers to youth and freshness, and to the green landscape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Vinho Verde is Portugal's largest DOC, in the green north-west
Its Atlantic climate is wet and humid
Verde means young and fresh, not green in colour

steps.title: White grapes
steps.body: Alvarinho, the same as Spain's Albariño, gives the fullest, most aromatic wines, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Loureiro gives floral, laurel-scented, citrus wines, mainly in Lima. Arinto, called Pedernã here, gives crisp, lemony acidity. Avesso, in Baião, gives fuller, nuttier wines. Trajadura adds body and softness.

steps.title: Reds and styles
steps.body: Red Vinho Verde, mainly from Vinhão, is deeply coloured, tart and tannic, traditionally served chilled in white bowls with grilled sardines; it's popular locally but rare abroad. Most white Vinho Verde is light, about 9 to 11.5% alcohol, crisp, often with a slight spritz from added carbon dioxide. Single-grape and single-estate wines are more serious.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its character.
steps.explanation: Vinho Verde's grapes each bring something different.

steps.body: A traditional Vinho Verde's slight spritz once came from malolactic fermentation in bottle; today most producers add carbon dioxide.

steps.prompt: What is Alvarinho called in Spain?
steps.explanation: The same grape across the Minho river.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso are the key whites
Most Vinho Verde is light and slightly spritzy
Red Vinhão is a local, tart, dark speciality

steps.title: On the Minho
steps.body: Monção e Melgaço is the northernmost sub-region, along the south bank of the Minho river, facing Spain's Rías Baixas. Hills to the west shelter it from Atlantic winds and rain, so it's warmer and drier in summer than the rest of Vinho Verde. Granite and alluvial soils dominate.

steps.title: Alvarinho
steps.body: Monção e Melgaço is Alvarinho's heartland. Until 2021, it was the only sub-region allowed to label a wine Alvarinho on the front. The wines are fuller, riper and more aromatic than typical Vinho Verde, around 12.5 to 13.5%, with peach, citrus, tropical fruit and minerality, rarely spritzy. They can age five to ten years.

steps.prompt: Why is Monção e Melgaço warmer than the rest of Vinho Verde?
options: Hills shelter it from Atlantic winds
steps.explanation: Shelter makes it warmer and drier.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body: Producers make Alvarinho in several styles: fresh and unoaked, lees-aged for texture, oak-fermented, and even sparkling, Espumante. Soalheiro, founded in 1974, was a pioneer of quality Alvarinho here. Alvarinho Superior and single-vineyard wines show its potential.

steps.prompt: Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is usually light and spritzy.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's fuller, riper and rarely spritzy.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Monção e Melgaço is sheltered and warmer
It's Alvarinho's heartland in Portugal
Its wines are fuller and can age five to ten years

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Vinho Verde and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Vinho Verde DOC, sometimes a sub-region like Monção e Melgaço or Lima, and often a grape: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Avesso. Regional wines may use Vinho Regional Minho. A sticker seal on the bottle certifies the DOC. Single-estate wines, from a quinta, are usually more serious than branded blends.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Vinho Verde suits light, fresh food: grilled sardines, clams, octopus, salads and sushi. Alvarinho suits richer seafood, bacalhau, grilled fish and white meat. Loureiro suits aperitifs and Asian food. Serve at 7 to 10 degrees. Most is best within a year; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço can age.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits a light Vinho Verde?
steps.explanation: Light, crisp wine suits simple grilled fish.

steps.body: In Portugal's summer festivals, grilled sardines and chilled Vinho Verde are a classic combination.

steps.prompt: Which are Vinho Verde grapes?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is Italian.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show the DOC, sub-region and often a grape
Vinho Verde suits sardines and seafood
Serve cold; most is best young

steps.explanation: Albariño, across the Minho river.

modules.title: Alentejo
modules.description: Southern Portugal's hot plains: ripe, generous reds, cork forests and the Roman clay pots called talhas.

steps.title: Beyond the Tagus
steps.body: Alentejo means beyond the Tagus, the river south of Lisbon. It covers about a third of Portugal, mostly rolling plains with cork oak and olive groves, and some hills like the São Mamede range near Portalegre. It has about 23,000 hectares of vines. Portugal produces about half the world's cork, much of it here.

steps.title: Hot and dry
steps.body: The climate is Mediterranean with continental influence: very hot, dry summers, often over 40 degrees, and mild winters. Rainfall is low. Irrigation is common, especially from the Alqueva reservoir, Europe's largest artificial lake, completed in 2002. Higher sites, like Portalegre, are cooler and fresher.

steps.prompt: What does Alentejo mean?
steps.explanation: The region lies beyond, south of, the Tagus river.

steps.title: Eight sub-regions
steps.body: The Alentejo DOC has eight sub-regions, including Reguengos, Borba, Redondo, Vidigueira and Portalegre. Vidigueira, sheltered by a fault escarpment, is known for whites; Portalegre, at up to 900 m, for fresh wines from old field blends. Much wine is sold as Vinho Regional Alentejano, with more flexible rules.

steps.prompt: Portalegre is one of the Alentejo's cooler sub-regions.
steps.explanation: Yes. Altitude in the São Mamede hills keeps it fresh.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Alentejo covers a third of Portugal, beyond the Tagus
It's very hot and dry, often irrigated
Portalegre and Vidigueira offer fresher styles

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Ripe reds and native whites
objectives: Explain the role of Alicante Bouschet

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Aragonez, Tempranillo, gives red fruit and body. Trincadeira gives spice, herbs and freshness, but is sensitive to rot. Alicante Bouschet, a French red-fleshed grape, called a teinturier, gives deep colour and structure; it found its best home here. Castelão, Syrah and Touriga Nacional are also common. Reds are ripe, round and generous.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Antão Vaz, from Vidigueira, is the main white: ripe tropical fruit and body, tolerant of heat. Arinto adds acidity; Roupeiro adds aroma. Blends of the three are common. White wines are a growing share, especially from cooler sites.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Alentejo blends balance ripeness and freshness.

steps.body: Alicante Bouschet is one of the few grapes with red flesh. That's why wines from it are so deeply coloured.

steps.prompt: What makes Alicante Bouschet unusual?
steps.explanation: A teinturier, with coloured juice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet lead the reds
Antão Vaz leads the whites, with Arinto for acidity
Wines are ripe and generous

steps.title: Roman tradition
steps.body: Talhas are large clay pots, some holding over 1,000 litres, used in the Alentejo since Roman times. Wine was fermented and stored in them, especially around Vidigueira, Cuba and Vila de Frades. The tradition survived in family cellars, adegas, even as modern wineries took over.

steps.title: How it's made
steps.body: Crushed grapes, with skins and sometimes stems, ferment in the talha. The inside is coated with pez, a resin mixture, to seal it. Skins sink to the bottom and act as a natural filter. The wine stays on its skins until about St Martin's Day, November 11, when talhas are traditionally opened and the wine is drawn from a tap at the base.
steps.highlight: Fermented on skins, opened in November

steps.prompt: When are talhas traditionally opened?
steps.explanation: St Martin's Day marks the opening of the new talha wine.

steps.title: Recognition
steps.body: In 2010, the Alentejo DOC created the category DOC Alentejo Vinho de Talha for wines made this way, fermented and stored in clay until at least November 11. Whites, reds, orange wines and rosés can all be made. The style links to the global interest in amphora and skin-contact wines, like Georgia's qvevri.

steps.prompt: Which describe talha wine?
steps.explanation: Flor is a Sherry process.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Talhas are Roman clay pots still used in the Alentejo
Wine ferments on skins until St Martin's Day
DOC Vinho de Talha was created in 2010

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Alentejo and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Alentejo DOC, sometimes a sub-region like Reguengos or Portalegre, or Vinho Regional Alentejano. Reserva in Portugal means higher alcohol and approval by a tasting panel; Garrafeira means longer ageing. Vinho de Talha marks clay-pot wines. Blends are common; grapes may be listed on the back.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Alentejo food is rustic: black pork, porco preto, from acorn-fed pigs; lamb; migas, bread with pork; açorda, bread soup; and sheep's cheese like Serpa. Reds suit pork and lamb; Antão Vaz whites suit bacalhau and grilled fish. Serve reds at 16 to 18, slightly cool in summer.

steps.prompt: Which Alentejo meat is a classic with its reds?
steps.explanation: Acorn-fed black pork suits ripe Alentejo reds.

steps.body: Alentejo reds offer ripe fruit and soft tannins at modest prices, among Portugal's most popular wines at home.

steps.prompt: In Portugal, Garrafeira means longer ageing.
steps.explanation: Yes, longer than Reserva.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DOC or Regional, and Reserva or Garrafeira
Reds suit black pork and lamb
Serve reds slightly cool in hot weather

modules.title: Dão
modules.description: A granite plateau ringed by mountains: elegant reds and Portugal's finest white grape, Encruzado.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Granite ringed by mountains
objectives: Explain how mountains shape its climate

steps.title: A sheltered plateau
steps.body: The Dão lies in central-northern Portugal, south of the Douro, on a granite plateau at 200 to 900 m. It's surrounded by mountains: Caramulo to the west, Buçaco, and the Serra da Estrela, Portugal's highest mainland range, to the south-east. Vineyards are scattered among pine forests, about 15,000 hectares.

steps.title: Protected climate
steps.body: The mountains block Atlantic rain from the west and continental heat from the east. Summers are warm and dry, winters cold and wet, with large day and night swings. Granite soils, sandy and poor, drain well. The result is wines with freshness, elegance and moderate alcohol, often compared with Burgundy in style.

steps.prompt: What shapes the Dão's protected climate?
steps.explanation: Mountains on all sides moderate rain and heat.

steps.title: History
steps.body: The Dão was demarcated in 1908, one of Portugal's oldest regions. For decades, co-operatives dominated, and quality declined. After Portugal joined the EU in 1986, private estates could make and sell their own wine again, and quality rose sharply. Today the Dão is known for elegance and age-worthy wines.

steps.prompt: After 1986, private estates helped lift the Dão's quality.
steps.explanation: Yes, after co-operatives had dominated for decades.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Dão is a granite plateau ringed by mountains
Mountains give a fresh, balanced climate
Private estates revived quality after 1986

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Touriga Nacional probably originated in the Dão and must be at least 20% of the region's red blends. Jaen, the same as Spain's Mencía, gives soft, fruity, floral wines. Alfrocheiro gives colour and red fruit. Tinta Roriz, Tempranillo, adds structure. Dão reds are fresh, floral and structured, with red fruit, pine and spice.

steps.title: Blends
steps.body: Traditionally, Dão wines are blends, often from old field blend vineyards. Touriga Nacional gives aroma and structure; Jaen softness; Alfrocheiro colour; Tinta Roriz body. Single-varietal Touriga Nacional and Jaen are also common now.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Dão grapes balance one another.

steps.body: Jaen is the same grape as Mencía, grown across the border in Spain's Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra.

steps.prompt: Which grape is Jaen the same as?
steps.explanation: Jaen and Mencía are the same grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Touriga Nacional probably originated in the Dão
Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz complete the reds
Dão reds are fresh, floral and structured

steps.title: A Dão native
steps.body: Encruzado is a white grape native to the Dão, and grown almost nowhere else. It gives medium to full-bodied whites with citrus, white peach, pear, flowers and a mineral, sometimes smoky edge, with fresh acidity. It's often compared with white Burgundy for its texture and complexity.

steps.title: Making and ageing
steps.body: Encruzado takes well to barrel fermentation and lees ageing, which add creaminess and nutty notes without masking its fruit. It resists oxidation well. Good Encruzado ages 10 years or more, developing honey, nuts and toast. It's also blended with Malvasia Fina, Bical and Cerceal-Branco in Dão whites.

steps.prompt: Which white wine style is Encruzado often compared with?
steps.explanation: For its texture, complexity and response to oak.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Encruzado shows that Portugal, known for reds and Port, can make world-class whites. It needs careful handling in the vineyard, as it's prone to some diseases, and yields must be controlled. Producers like Quinta dos Roques and Quinta da Pellada helped establish its reputation.

steps.prompt: Which describe Encruzado?
steps.explanation: Encruzado is usually dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Encruzado is the Dão's native white
Barrel fermentation and lees add texture
It can age 10 years or more

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Dão and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Dão DOC, sometimes Dão Nobre, a top category requiring higher quality and ageing, the producer, often a quinta, the grapes and Reserva or Garrafeira. Red Dão must include at least 20% Touriga Nacional. Many wines are blends with grapes listed on the back.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Dão reds suit roast kid, lamb, game, Portuguese rice dishes like arroz de pato, duck rice, and Serra da Estrela cheese, a creamy sheep's cheese from the nearby mountains. Encruzado suits bacalhau, grilled fish, roast chicken and creamy dishes. Serve reds at 16 to 17, whites at 10 to 12.

steps.prompt: Which cheese, from nearby mountains, suits Dão wines?
steps.explanation: A creamy sheep's cheese from Portugal's highest mountains.

steps.body: Dão reds age gracefully. A 10-year-old Dão Reserva often shows red fruit, pine and leather in perfect balance.

steps.prompt: Dão reds must include at least 20% Touriga Nacional.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DOC, Dão Nobre and Reserva
Dão reds suit kid, lamb and Serra da Estrela cheese
Encruzado suits bacalhau and creamy dishes

steps.explanation: The Dão has a clear identity.

steps.explanation: It probably comes from the Dão.

steps.explanation: Not true. It's a granite plateau ringed by mountains.

steps.explanation: Encruzado is white.

modules.title: Mosel
modules.description: Some of the world's steepest vineyards: light, racy Riesling grown on slate above a winding river.

steps.title: The river
steps.body: The Mosel river rises in France and winds north-east through western Germany to join the Rhine at Koblenz. Its German wine region follows about 240 km of loops and bends, with vineyards on the steep banks. It has about 8,700 hectares. It includes two tributaries, the Saar and the Ruwer.

steps.title: Cool, northern climate
steps.body: The Mosel lies at about 50 degrees north, one of the coolest quality wine regions in the world. Average growing season temperatures are low, and ripening is a challenge. The river helps: it moderates temperature, reflects sunlight onto the slopes, and its loops create south-facing banks that catch every hour of sun.

steps.prompt: How does the river help Mosel vineyards?
options: It moderates temperature and reflects sunlight
steps.explanation: Water stores heat and reflects light onto the slopes.

steps.title: Three sections
steps.body: The Mosel is often divided into the Upper Mosel, near Luxembourg, on limestone, growing Elbling; the Middle Mosel, Mittelmosel, the heart, with famous villages like Piesport, Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen and Ürzig; and the Lower Mosel, Terrassenmosel, near Koblenz, with very steep terraces. The Saar and Ruwer join in the south.

steps.prompt: The Middle Mosel is home to villages like Bernkastel and Wehlen.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's the heart of the region.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Mosel winds 240 km through western Germany
It's very cool, at about 50 degrees north
The river and its loops help ripening on south-facing banks

steps.title: Riesling
steps.body: Riesling covers about 62% of the Mosel's vineyards, and almost all its fine wine. It buds and ripens late, tolerates cold winters, and keeps high acidity. On the Mosel's slate, it gives light, delicate wines with green apple, peach, citrus, flowers and a smoky, slatey mineral edge.

steps.title: Other grapes and style
steps.body: Müller-Thurgau, a cross created in 1882, is grown on flatter land. Elbling, an ancient grape, grows in the Upper Mosel, often for sparkling Sekt. Pinot Noir and Pinot Blanc are increasing. Mosel Riesling is famous for low alcohol, often 7.5 to 10%, with sugar balanced by fierce acidity; but dry styles are growing.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Riesling dominates, with supporting grapes.

steps.body: A Mosel Riesling Kabinett at 8% alcohol shows how wine can be intensely flavoured without weight.

steps.prompt: Why does Mosel Riesling often have low alcohol?
options: Grapes ripen slowly, and some sugar is left in the wine
It's made from unripe white grapes only
steps.explanation: Cool ripening and residual sugar keep alcohol low.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling is about 62% of vineyards and most fine wine
Mosel Riesling is light, high in acidity, often off-dry
Müller-Thurgau and Elbling play supporting roles

steps.title: Steep slopes
steps.body: The Mosel has some of the steepest vineyards in the world. The Bremmer Calmont, in the Lower Mosel, reaches about 65 degrees, often called Europe's steepest. Vines are trained on single poles, Einzelpfahl, and work is by hand, sometimes with monorails. Steepness gives more sun and drainage, but costs are high.

steps.title: Slate
steps.body: Most top vineyards are on Devonian slate, grey, blue or red. Slate drains well, absorbs heat by day and releases it at night, helping ripening. Broken slate on the surface reflects light. Many link slate to the Mosel's mineral, smoky character, though the science is debated; its effect on heat and drainage is clear.
steps.highlight: Slate stores heat and drains well

steps.prompt: How does slate help Mosel vineyards?
options: It absorbs and releases heat and drains well
It holds water like a sponge
steps.explanation: Heat storage and drainage help ripening.

steps.title: Famous sites
steps.body: Famous vineyards include Wehlener Sonnenuhr, with its sundial; Bernkasteler Doctor, among Germany's most expensive; Ürziger Würzgarten, on red slate; Graacher Himmelreich; and Piesporter Goldtröpfchen. Labels name the village plus the vineyard, like Wehlener Sonnenuhr, from Wehlen.

steps.prompt: Which are famous Mosel vineyards?
steps.explanation: Clos de Vougeot is in Burgundy.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Mosel has some of the world's steepest vineyards
Slate stores heat and drains well
Labels name village plus vineyard, like Wehlener Sonnenuhr

steps.title: The Prädikat
steps.body: German Prädikatswein is graded by grape sugar at harvest, measured in Oechsle: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, BA, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese, TBA. The levels show ripeness, not the wine's final sweetness. In the Mosel, Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese are often made off-dry or sweet, by tradition.

steps.title: Sweetness terms
steps.body: Trocken means dry, up to 9 g/l of sugar; halbtrocken, off-dry, up to 18 g/l; feinherb, an unofficial off-dry term. Without these words, a Mosel Prädikat wine is usually fruity-sweet, fruchtsüss. The high acidity, often 8 to 10 g/l, balances the sugar, so even sweet wines taste fresh.

steps.prompt: Order the Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Each level demands riper grapes at harvest.

steps.title: Sweet wines
steps.body: In great years, the Mosel makes Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein, from botrytised or frozen grapes, with intense sweetness and acidity. Auctions, like the Grosser Ring auction in Trier, sell rare sweet wines for high prices. These wines age for decades.
steps.highlight: BA, TBA and Eiswein in great years

steps.prompt: What does trocken on a German label mean?
steps.explanation: Trocken means dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prädikat levels show ripeness, from Kabinett to TBA
Trocken means dry; without it, Mosel Prädikats are often sweet
High acidity balances sugar

steps.title: The Saar
steps.body: The Saar joins the Mosel near Trier. It's cooler and windier than the Middle Mosel, and for centuries grapes ripened fully only in good years. In warm years, its Rieslings are among the most precise and electric in the world, with steely acidity. Scharzhofberg, owned largely by Egon Müller, is its most famous vineyard.

steps.title: The Ruwer
steps.body: The Ruwer is a small tributary near Trier, with only a few estates. Its wines are delicate, floral and racy. Maximin Grünhaus and Karthäuserhofberg are famous estates, both former monastic properties. Like the Saar, it was officially part of the Mosel-Saar-Ruwer region until 2007, when the region was renamed simply Mosel.

steps.prompt: How do the Saar and Ruwer differ from the Middle Mosel?
steps.explanation: Cooler conditions give steely, precise Riesling.

steps.title: Climate change
steps.body: Warmer summers since the 1990s have helped the Saar and Ruwer ripen grapes more reliably. What was once a marginal climate now gives balanced wines more often. This has made these cool tributaries even more prized for freshness.

steps.prompt: The region was renamed from Mosel-Saar-Ruwer to Mosel in 2007.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Saar is cool and windy, home of Scharzhofberg
The Ruwer is small, delicate and floral
Warmer summers have helped them ripen more reliably

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Mosel and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Mosel label shows the producer, the village plus vineyard, like Bernkasteler Doctor, the grape, the Prädikat, like Spätlese, the vintage and sometimes trocken. VDP estates use their own classification: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, with GG, Grosses Gewächs, for dry top wines. The AP number shows official testing.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Off-dry Mosel Kabinett suits spicy Asian food, like Thai and Sichuan, and smoked fish. Dry Riesling suits trout, pork and sauerkraut. Spätlese suits roast pork with apples. Sweet Auslese and BA suit fruit desserts, foie gras and blue cheese. Serve at 7 to 10 degrees.

steps.prompt: Which food suits an off-dry Mosel Kabinett?
steps.explanation: Sugar and acidity calm chilli heat.

steps.body: Mosel Riesling ages remarkably. A 20-year-old Spätlese often tastes less sweet and more complex than a young one.

steps.prompt: Which are VDP classification levels?
steps.explanation: Gran Reserva is Spanish.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show village, vineyard and Prädikat
Kabinett suits spicy food; Auslese suits desserts
Mosel Riesling ages remarkably well

modules.title: Rheingau
modules.description: A south-facing slope along the Rhine where Spätlese was born and Riesling grew noble.

steps.title: A south-facing bank
steps.body: The Rheingau lies where the Rhine, blocked by the Taunus hills, turns west for about 30 km between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim. Vineyards face south across the wide river, catching full sun. The Taunus shelters them from cold northern winds. It's small, about 3,200 hectares. Assmannshausen and Lorch extend it north-west.

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: The Rheingau is warmer than the Mosel. The wide Rhine, nearly a kilometre across, reflects light and moderates temperature; the Taunus blocks cold air. Soils vary: slate and quartzite on higher slopes, like Rüdesheim's Berg; loess and marl lower down. Wines are fuller and riper than the Mosel's, often dry.

steps.prompt: What shelters the Rheingau from cold northern winds?
steps.explanation: The Taunus blocks cold air.

steps.title: Monks and estates
steps.body: Cistercian monks founded Kloster Eberbach in 1136 and planted the Steinberg, a walled vineyard like Burgundy's clos. Schloss Johannisberg, on a hill above the Rhine, was a Benedictine abbey. Noble families and monasteries owned most land for centuries, so the Rheingau has many large historic estates.

steps.prompt: Kloster Eberbach was founded by Cistercian monks.
steps.explanation: Yes, in 1136.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Rheingau faces south where the Rhine turns west
It's warmer than the Mosel, giving fuller wines
Monasteries like Kloster Eberbach shaped its history

steps.title: Riesling
steps.body: Riesling covers about 78% of the Rheingau, the highest share of any German region. It gives fuller, riper wines than the Mosel's, with peach, apricot, citrus and spice, firm acidity and often more alcohol. Most top Rheingau Riesling today is dry.

steps.title: Spätburgunder
steps.body: Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir, covers about 12%, mostly in Assmannshausen, on red slate, famous for red wine since the Middle Ages. The wines are elegant, with red cherry and spice. Assmannshäuser Höllenberg is the most famous red vineyard.

steps.prompt: Match each term to the Rheingau.
steps.explanation: The Rheingau is Riesling with a red exception.

steps.body: Rheingau Riesling is often described as a little more serious and structured than Mosel Riesling, with more body and spice.

steps.prompt: What share of the Rheingau's vineyards is Riesling?
steps.explanation: The highest share in Germany.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling covers about 78%, fuller than the Mosel's
Spätburgunder makes elegant reds in Assmannshausen
Most top Rheingau Riesling is dry

lessons.title: The birth of Spätlese
lessons.subtitle: A late messenger
objectives: Explain the role of noble rot

steps.title: The late messenger
steps.body: In 1775, the monks of Schloss Johannisberg needed permission from the Prince-Bishop of Fulda to start the harvest. The messenger returned weeks late. By then, the grapes had shrivelled with noble rot. The monks made wine anyway, and it was remarkable. That late harvest, Spätlese, became a recognised style.

steps.title: Noble rot
steps.body: The story shows the role of Botrytis cinerea: when grapes are left on the vine in misty autumn weather, noble rot concentrates sugar and acidity and adds honeyed aromas. From Spätlese came Auslese, selected bunches, and later Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, picked berry by berry.

steps.prompt: Why was the 1775 harvest at Schloss Johannisberg late?
options: The messenger with permission arrived weeks late
steps.explanation: The delay let noble rot develop, creating Spätlese.

steps.title: Schloss Johannisberg
steps.body: Schloss Johannisberg sits on a hill above the Rhine, on the 50th parallel, with vineyards on a steep slope. It's one of the first estates planted entirely with Riesling, from 1720. A statue of the messenger, the Spätlesereiter, stands in its courtyard. Its wines use coloured capsules to mark quality levels.

steps.prompt: Which developed from the Spätlese tradition?
steps.explanation: Prosecco is Italian sparkling wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spätlese was born at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775
Noble rot concentrated the late-picked grapes
Schloss Johannisberg was planted entirely with Riesling from 1720

steps.title: The VDP
steps.body: The VDP, Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter, is an association of about 200 top German estates, founded in 1910. Its emblem is an eagle with grapes on the bottle capsule. The Rheingau's Charta association, from 1984, pioneered dry, food-friendly Riesling and site classification, ideas the VDP adopted nationally.

steps.title: Four levels
steps.body: The VDP's pyramid, like Burgundy's, has four levels: Gutswein, estate wine; Ortswein, village wine; Erste Lage, first-class site; and Grosse Lage, great site. Dry wines from Grosse Lage sites are called Grosses Gewächs, GG. Sweet wines from top sites still use Prädikat terms, like Spätlese or Auslese.

steps.prompt: Order the VDP levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each step narrows the origin and raises the standard.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: German wine law ranks wine by grape ripeness, not by site. The VDP's private classification brings site to the centre, as in Burgundy. Rheingau sites like Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg, Erbacher Marcobrunn and Hochheimer Hölle are Grosse Lage. Not all great producers are VDP members.

steps.prompt: What is a Grosses Gewächs?
options: A dry wine from a Grosse Lage site
steps.explanation: GG marks the VDP's top dry wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The VDP is an association of about 200 top estates
Its pyramid runs from Gutswein to Grosse Lage
Grosses Gewächs is a dry wine from a top site

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Rheingau and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show producer, village plus vineyard, like Rüdesheimer Berg Rottland, the grape, the Prädikat or trocken, and the VDP eagle if a member. GG means dry top-site wine. Erstes Gewächs was the Rheingau's older term for top dry wines. Spätburgunder from Assmannshausen is labelled as red.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Dry Rheingau Riesling suits pork, veal, river fish like trout and pike, white asparagus, a German spring favourite, and schnitzel. Off-dry and Spätlese suit spicy food and roast pork. Spätburgunder suits game birds and mushrooms. Serve Riesling at 8 to 11 degrees.

steps.prompt: Which German spring vegetable suits dry Rheingau Riesling?
steps.explanation: Spargel season is a German ritual.

steps.body: Good Rheingau GG Riesling ages 10 to 20 years, developing honey, toast and petrol notes while keeping its acidity.

steps.prompt: GG wines from the VDP are sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. GG wines are dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show vineyard, Prädikat or trocken, and the VDP eagle
Dry Riesling suits asparagus, trout and pork
GG Riesling ages 10 to 20 years

modules.title: Pfalz
modules.description: Germany's sunniest wine region: rich, dry Riesling and rising Pinot Noir in the shelter of the Haardt.

steps.title: Along the Haardt
steps.body: The Pfalz, the Palatinate, lies in south-west Germany, a strip about 85 km long between the Haardt mountains, a continuation of France's Vosges, and the Rhine plain. It borders Alsace to the south. With about 23,700 hectares, it's Germany's second largest wine region. The German Wine Route, Deutsche Weinstrasse, runs through it.

steps.title: Warm and dry
steps.body: The Haardt shelters the Pfalz from westerly rain, as the Vosges do for Alsace. It's one of Germany's sunniest and driest regions, with almonds, figs and even lemons growing. That warmth gives riper grapes and fuller wines than further north. Soils vary: sandstone, limestone, loess, basalt and clay.

steps.prompt: What shelters the Pfalz from rain?
steps.explanation: The Haardt, a continuation of the Vosges.

steps.title: Mittelhaardt and Südpfalz
steps.body: The Pfalz has two areas. The Mittelhaardt, in the north, has the most famous villages: Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim and Bad Dürkheim, home of historic estates like Bürklin-Wolf, von Buhl and Bassermann-Jordan. The Südliche Weinstrasse, in the south, near Alsace, is a source of exciting Pinot Noir and whites.

steps.prompt: The Pfalz is one of Germany's sunniest regions.
steps.explanation: Yes. Figs and almonds grow there.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Pfalz runs along the Haardt, bordering Alsace
Its rain shadow makes it sunny and dry
The Mittelhaardt and the south each have their stars

steps.title: Riesling
steps.body: Riesling is the most planted grape, about 25% of the Pfalz, one of the world's largest Riesling areas. The warm climate gives ripe peach, apricot and citrus, with fuller body and good acidity. Most is dry. The Mittelhaardt villages make some of Germany's greatest Rieslings.

steps.title: The Pinot family and others
steps.body: Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir, has grown fast in the south, alongside Weissburgunder, Pinot Blanc, and Grauburgunder, Pinot Gris. Dornfelder, a dark red cross, is popular for everyday wine. Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Scheurebe and Gewürztraminer also grow here. The Pfalz is Germany's most diverse region.

steps.prompt: Match each German name to its grape.
steps.explanation: The Pfalz grows a wide range of grapes.

steps.body: The Südpfalz, near Alsace, is a source of excellent Spätburgunder. Producers like Friedrich Becker grow vines right on the French border.

steps.prompt: Which is the Pfalz's most planted grape?
steps.explanation: Riesling, about a quarter of vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Riesling leads, ripe and mostly dry
The Pinot family is rising, especially in the south
Dornfelder and Scheurebe add variety

lessons.title: Dry German Riesling
lessons.subtitle: The Pfalz's speciality
objectives: Explain the rise of dry German Riesling
Explain the role of trocken and GG

steps.title: A dry revolution
steps.body: For much of the 20th century, German Riesling abroad meant sweet. From the 1980s, Pfalz producers led a return to dry, trocken, Riesling, which had been traditional before. Today over two-thirds of German wine is dry or off-dry, and the Pfalz's warm climate makes balanced dry wines easier.

steps.title: The style
steps.body: Dry Pfalz Riesling is fuller and riper than Mosel or Rheingau Riesling, often 12.5 to 13.5% alcohol, with stone fruit, citrus, spice and minerality from sandstone, limestone or basalt. GG wines from top sites, like Forster Kirchenstück, Forster Jesuitengarten and Deidesheimer Hohenmorgen, can age 10 to 20 years.

steps.prompt: How does dry Pfalz Riesling typically compare with Mosel Riesling?
steps.explanation: A warmer climate gives more body and ripeness.

steps.title: Basalt and sites
steps.body: Forst's top vineyards have basalt, volcanic rock, which absorbs heat and gives intense, spicy, mineral wines. Kirchenstück, a small walled site in Forst, is often considered one of Germany's finest dry Riesling vineyards. Labels name village and vineyard, like Forster Pechstein.

steps.prompt: Which are top Pfalz vineyards?
steps.explanation: Wehlener Sonnenuhr is in the Mosel.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Pfalz led the return to dry German Riesling
Its dry Riesling is riper and fuller
Basalt sites in Forst give some of Germany's best

lessons.title: Labels and the table
