steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show producer, village plus vineyard, like Forster Pechstein, the grape, and trocken or GG for dry wines. VDP estates use Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. Some producers use Prädikat terms only for sweet wines. The Pfalz also makes Sekt, sparkling wine.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: The Pfalz's food is hearty: Saumagen, stuffed pig's stomach, a regional speciality; Flammkuchen, a thin bacon and onion tart; sausages and sauerkraut; and chestnuts. Dry Riesling suits pork, sausages and Flammkuchen; Spätburgunder suits game and duck; Scheurebe suits spicy food. Serve Riesling at 8 to 11 degrees.

steps.prompt: Which regional Pfalz dish is a classic with dry Riesling?
steps.explanation: Stuffed pig's stomach is a Pfalz speciality.

steps.body: In the Pfalz, wine is often served in a Dubbeglas, a dimpled half-litre glass, at village wine festivals like the Dürkheimer Wurstmarkt.

steps.prompt: The Pfalz makes mostly sweet Riesling.
steps.explanation: Not true. Most Pfalz Riesling is dry.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show village, vineyard and trocken or GG
Dry Riesling suits Saumagen, Flammkuchen and pork
Serve at 8 to 11 degrees

modules.title: Burgenland
modules.description: Austria's warm east: Blaufränkisch reds and the noble rot sweet wines of Lake Neusiedl.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Austria's warm east
objectives: Explain the role of Lake Neusiedl

steps.title: On the Hungarian border
steps.body: Burgenland is Austria's easternmost state, a long strip along the Hungarian border, south-east of Vienna. It belonged to Hungary until 1921. It has about 11,700 hectares of vines. Key areas include Neusiedlersee, around the lake; Leithaberg, on the hills to the west; Mittelburgenland; and Eisenberg in the south.

steps.title: Pannonian climate
steps.body: Burgenland has a warm, dry Pannonian climate, influenced by the Hungarian plain: hot summers, cold winters and plenty of sun. It's Austria's warmest wine region, which is why it's the country's red wine heartland. Soils vary: limestone and schist on the Leithaberg, clay in Mittelburgenland, gravel and sand by the lake.

steps.prompt: Why is Burgenland Austria's red wine heartland?
options: Its warm Pannonian climate ripens red grapes
steps.explanation: Warmth from the Hungarian plain helps reds ripen.

steps.title: Lake Neusiedl
steps.body: Lake Neusiedl, Neusiedlersee, is a large, shallow steppe lake, about 320 km2 but only about 1 to 2 m deep, on the border with Hungary. It warms the area and, in autumn, creates mist and humidity that favour noble rot. The lake and its reed beds are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a national park.

steps.prompt: Lake Neusiedl is very deep.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's large but only about 1 to 2 m deep.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgenland is Austria's warm east, part of Hungary until 1921
Its Pannonian climate makes it Austria's red heartland
Shallow Lake Neusiedl brings warmth and autumn mist

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Blaufränkisch is the signature: dark cherry, blackberry, pepper and spice, with fresh acidity and firm tannin. Zweigelt, Austria's most planted red, a 1922 cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, gives soft, cherry reds. St. Laurent gives Pinot-like elegance. Pinot Noir, Merlot and Cabernet also appear in blends.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Welschriesling, unrelated to Riesling, is widely grown, especially for sweet wines. Chardonnay, locally Morillon in parts of Austria, Pinot Blanc, Grüner Veltliner and Furmint, revived near Rust, also grow here. Sweet wines often blend several white grapes affected by noble rot.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Burgenland grows reds and sweet whites.

steps.body: Welschriesling has nothing to do with Riesling. Despite the name, they're not related.

steps.prompt: Which grapes were crossed to create Zweigelt?
steps.explanation: Created in 1922 by Fritz Zweigelt.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Blaufränkisch is Burgenland's signature red
Zweigelt and St. Laurent complete the reds
Welschriesling leads the sweet whites

steps.title: Spicy and fresh
steps.body: Blaufränkisch, called Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany, gives dark, spicy reds with black cherry, blackberry, black pepper and a mineral edge. Its acidity is high, its tannin firm but fine. It's often compared to Pinot Noir for transparency and to Syrah for spice. It ripens late and needs warm sites.

steps.title: Areas and soils
steps.body: Mittelburgenland, called Blaufränkischland, around Deutschkreutz and Horitschon, has heavy clay, giving full, dark wines. Leithaberg, on limestone and schist, gives fresh, mineral, elegant wines. Eisenberg, in the south, on iron-rich schist, gives spicy, firm wines. Each has a DAC for Blaufränkisch.

steps.prompt: What is Blaufränkisch called in Germany?
steps.explanation: Lemberger in Württemberg; Kékfrankos in Hungary.

steps.title: DACs
steps.body: Austria's DAC system links regions to typical grapes. Mittelburgenland DAC, created in 2005, was Burgenland's first, for Blaufränkisch. Leithaberg DAC allows Blaufränkisch for reds and Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay, Grüner Veltliner and Neuburger for whites. Eisenberg DAC is Blaufränkisch. Reserve marks riper, longer-aged wines.

steps.prompt: Which are Blaufränkisch DACs?
steps.explanation: Wachau is for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Blaufränkisch is spicy, dark and fresh
Mittelburgenland is full; Leithaberg mineral; Eisenberg spicy
DACs link each area to Blaufränkisch

lessons.title: Neusiedlersee sweet wines
lessons.subtitle: Noble rot by the lake
objectives: Explain how the lake creates noble rot

steps.title: Noble rot every year
steps.body: Around Lake Neusiedl, autumn mists from the shallow water, followed by warm, sunny days, create ideal conditions for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea, almost every year. That makes the area one of the most reliable sources of sweet wine in the world. Illmitz and Apetlon, on the east shore, are famous for it.

steps.title: Categories
steps.body: Austria uses Prädikat categories similar to Germany's: Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Strohwein or Schilfwein, from grapes dried on straw or reeds, and Trockenbeerenauslese. Ausbruch, between BA and TBA, is a historic style. Grapes include Welschriesling, Chardonnay, Scheurebe and Pinot Blanc. Alois Kracher made the area world-famous.

steps.prompt: Why does Lake Neusiedl favour noble rot almost every year?
options: Autumn mists followed by sunny days
steps.explanation: Mist then sun is the recipe for noble rot.

steps.title: Ruster Ausbruch
steps.body: The town of Rust, on the west shore, has made Ausbruch since at least the 17th century, a sweet wine from botrytised berries mixed with base wine, similar to Tokaji Aszú. Its fame earned Rust the status of a free town in 1681. Ruster Ausbruch DAC protects it today; Furmint is being revived here for it.

steps.prompt: Ruster Ausbruch is similar in method to Tokaji Aszú.
steps.explanation: Yes. Botrytised berries are added to base wine.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Lake Neusiedl brings noble rot almost every year
BA, TBA and Schilfwein are key sweet categories
Ruster Ausbruch is a historic style, like Aszú

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Burgenland and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show the producer, grape, DAC, like Mittelburgenland DAC or Leithaberg DAC, and Reserve for riper wines. Sweet wines show the Prädikat, like TBA or Ausbruch. Austria's red, white and red stripe on the capsule, the Banderole, shows the wine has passed official testing.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Blaufränkisch suits roast duck, goose, venison and goulash, a Hungarian-Austrian dish with paprika. Zweigelt suits Wiener Schnitzel and grilled meat. Sweet wines from Neusiedlersee suit foie gras, blue cheese, strudel and fruit desserts. Serve Blaufränkisch at 16 to 18 degrees.

steps.prompt: Which dish suits Blaufränkisch?
steps.explanation: Paprika and rich meat suit its spice and acidity.

steps.body: St. Martin's Day, November 11, is when Burgenland celebrates the new wine with roast goose. A perfect match for Blaufränkisch.

steps.prompt: Which foods suit Neusiedlersee sweet wines?
steps.explanation: Steak suits a red.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show DAC, Reserve and the Banderole
Blaufränkisch suits duck and goulash
Sweet wines suit foie gras and strudel

steps.explanation: Burgenland's vocabulary mixes Austrian and Hungarian.

steps.prompt: Which is Burgenland's signature red grape?
steps.explanation: Spicy and fresh.

steps.prompt: Burgenland belonged to Hungary until 1921.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.prompt: Which are Austrian sweet wine categories?
steps.explanation: Crianza is Spanish.

steps.prompt: Zweigelt is a cross of Blaufränkisch and St. ____.
steps.explanation: St. Laurent.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgenland is Austria's warm, Pannonian east
Blaufränkisch is its signature red
Lake Neusiedl brings reliable noble rot
Ruster Ausbruch is a historic sweet style

modules.title: Wachau
modules.description: Steep stone terraces above the Danube, with dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling graded by ripeness.

steps.title: A river valley
steps.body: The Wachau is a narrow, 30 km stretch of the Danube valley in Lower Austria, about 80 km west of Vienna, between Melk and Krems. Vineyards climb steep, mostly south-facing slopes on stone terraces. It's small, about 1,300 hectares. Its landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

steps.title: Two climates meet
steps.body: The Wachau sits where cool air from the west, the Waldviertel forest, meets warm Pannonian air from the east. Cool nights from the forest keep acidity and aroma; warm days ripen the grapes. The Danube moderates temperatures. The result: ripe, powerful wines with fresh acidity.
steps.highlight: Cool forest air meets Pannonian warmth

steps.prompt: What gives the Wachau's wines both ripeness and freshness?
options: Warm Pannonian days and cool forest nights
steps.explanation: Two air masses meet over the valley.

steps.title: Terraces
steps.body: The terraces, held by dry-stone walls, were built over centuries, many by monks. They prevent erosion and create flat strips on slopes too steep to work otherwise. Soils on the terraces are primary rock, gneiss and granite, while lower slopes have loess. Maintaining them is costly; work is by hand.

steps.prompt: The Wachau's landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
steps.explanation: Yes, since 2000.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Wachau is a 30 km stretch of the Danube
Cool forest nights meet warm Pannonian days
Steep stone terraces hold its vines

lessons.title: The grapes
lessons.subtitle: Grüner and Riesling
objectives: Describe Grüner Veltliner in the Wachau

steps.title: Grüner Veltliner
steps.body: Grüner Veltliner, Austria's signature grape, covers over half the Wachau. It grows best on deeper loess soils on lower slopes, giving full, peppery wines with citrus, green apple, white pepper and, in riper styles, stone fruit and spice. Its pepper comes from rotundone.

steps.title: Riesling
steps.body: Riesling covers about 20%, but makes many of the most prized wines. It's planted on the steepest, stoniest terraces of gneiss and granite, where Grüner would struggle. Wachau Riesling is dry, powerful and mineral, with peach, apricot and citrus. Famous vineyards include Achleiten, Kellerberg, Loibenberg and Singerriedel.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its soil.
steps.explanation: Grape follows soil in the Wachau.

steps.body: Wachau Riesling and Grüner from the same producer and vintage make a great side-by-side tasting of grape and soil.

steps.prompt: Where is Riesling planted in the Wachau?
steps.explanation: Rocky terraces suit Riesling.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Grüner Veltliner covers over half, on loess
Riesling grows on steep rock terraces
Both are made dry and powerful

steps.title: Three levels
steps.body: The Vinea Wachau, a growers' association founded in 1983, created three categories for dry wines. Steinfeder, named after a feather grass, is light, up to 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel, named after a falconry lure, is medium, 11.5 to 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard, is the ripest, above 12.5%.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: All three are dry, made only from Wachau grapes, without chaptalisation or concentration. Smaragd comes from the ripest grapes, often from top terraces, and can age 10 to 20 years. Unlike Germany's Prädikat, which measures sugar at harvest, these categories reflect alcohol in the finished dry wine.

steps.prompt: Order the Wachau categories from lightest to fullest.
steps.explanation: Riper grapes from the best sites give the fullest wines.

steps.title: Wachau DAC
steps.body: In 2020, the Wachau became a DAC, with three levels of origin: Gebietswein, regional; Ortswein, village; and Riedenwein, single vineyard, with Ried on the label. The Vinea Wachau categories continue alongside. Labels may show both, like Ried Achleiten Riesling Smaragd.

steps.prompt: What does Smaragd refer to?
steps.explanation: The lizard basks on the terraces in the sun.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd grade dry wines by alcohol
Smaragd is the ripest and can age 10 to 20 years
Wachau DAC, since 2020, adds village and vineyard levels

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading the Wachau and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Wachau label shows producer, grape, the Vinea Wachau category, like Federspiel, and since 2020 the DAC level: Wachau DAC, village name, or Ried plus vineyard name. Famous producers include F.X. Pichler, Prager, Hirtzberger, Knoll and the Domäne Wachau co-operative.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Steinfeder and Federspiel suit light dishes: salads, river fish, asparagus, Wiener Schnitzel. Smaragd suits richer food: roast pork, chicken in cream, Asian dishes with spice and fish with butter sauce. Wachau apricots, Marillen, are famous; apricot dumplings suit off-dry wines. Serve at 9 to 12 degrees, Smaragd a little warmer.
steps.highlight: Schnitzel with Federspiel, pork with Smaragd

steps.prompt: Which Wachau fruit is famous?
steps.explanation: Wachau apricots are a protected local speciality.

steps.body: A Smaragd Grüner Veltliner with Wiener Schnitzel is a classic Austrian match. The wine's pepper and body handle the fried crust.

steps.prompt: All Wachau Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd wines are dry.
steps.explanation: Yes. The categories are for dry wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show category, DAC and Ried
Federspiel suits schnitzel; Smaragd suits richer dishes
Serve at 9 to 12 degrees

modules.title: Tokaj
modules.description: Volcanic hills and river mists in north-east Hungary: the wine of kings, and the king of wines.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: Volcanic hills where two rivers meet

steps.title: North-east Hungary
steps.body: Tokaj lies in north-east Hungary, near the Slovak and Ukrainian borders, in the foothills of the Zemplén mountains. The region covers about 27 villages and roughly 5,500 hectares of vines. A small part extends into Slovakia, which also uses the name Tokaj. The town of Tokaj sits where the Bodrog river meets the Tisza.

steps.title: Mist and sun
steps.body: Tokaj has a continental climate: cold winters and warm summers, with long, dry, sunny autumns. The Bodrog and Tisza create autumn mists in the mornings, which burn off into warm afternoons. That combination is perfect for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea, which shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar and acidity.

steps.prompt: What creates Tokaj's ideal conditions for noble rot?
options: River mists in the morning and sunny afternoons
steps.explanation: The Bodrog and Tisza bring mist; the autumn sun dries the grapes.

steps.title: Volcanic soils
steps.body: Tokaj's hills are extinct volcanoes. Soils include rhyolite, andesite, tuff and clay, often covered with loess. Volcanic soils drain well and give mineral, smoky wines. Different hills have different soils, which is why Tokaj's vineyards were classified so early. Its cellars, cut into volcanic rock, are lined with a black mould.

steps.prompt: Tokaj's hills are extinct volcanoes.
steps.explanation: Yes, giving volcanic soils.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tokaj lies where the Bodrog meets the Tisza in north-east Hungary
River mists and sunny autumns favour noble rot
Volcanic soils give mineral, smoky wines

steps.title: Furmint
steps.body: Furmint covers about 60 to 70% of Tokaj's vineyards. It has very high acidity, thin skins that become thinner as it ripens, and late ripening, all ideal for noble rot. It gives quince, apple, lemon, smoke and minerality when dry; honey, apricot and marmalade when sweet.

steps.title: Hárslevelű and others
steps.body: Hárslevelű, linden leaf, about 20 to 25%, adds perfume, honey and spice, with softer acidity. Sárgamuskotály, yellow Muscat, adds floral aromas in small amounts. Kövérszőlő, Zéta and Kabar are also allowed. Most Tokaji blends Furmint with Hárslevelű.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Furmint leads Tokaj's blends.

steps.body: Hárslevelű's name means linden leaf. Its wines often smell of linden blossom and honey.

steps.prompt: Which grape dominates Tokaj?
steps.explanation: About 60 to 70% of vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Furmint, about 60 to 70%, gives acidity and noble rot
Hárslevelű adds perfume and honey
Sárgamuskotály and others play minor roles

lessons.title: Aszú and puttonyos
lessons.subtitle: The great sweet wine
objectives: Explain how Tokaji Aszú is made

steps.title: Aszú berries
steps.body: Aszú berries are grapes shrivelled by noble rot, picked one by one, often in several passes. They're collected and kept as a paste or whole. Then they're soaked in fermenting must or a base wine for 12 to 60 hours, extracting sugar and flavour. The mixture is pressed and fermented slowly, sometimes for months.
steps.highlight: Botrytised berries soaked in base wine

steps.title: Puttonyos
steps.body: Traditionally, sweetness was measured in puttonyos: the number of puttony, 25 kg hods of aszú berries, added to a 136-litre Gönci barrel of base wine, from 3 to 6. Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, equal to the old 5 puttonyos; puttonyos labels of 5 and 6 are optional. Aszú ages at least 18 months in oak.

steps.prompt: Put the making of Tokaji Aszú in order.
items: Pick botrytised berries one by one
Soak in base wine or must
steps.explanation: Selection, soaking and slow fermentation give Aszú.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body: Tokaji Aszú is golden to amber, with apricot, orange marmalade, honey, saffron, ginger and tea. Sugar is balanced by Furmint's searing acidity, so it never feels cloying. It ages for decades, even a century or more.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum sugar for Tokaji Aszú since 2013?
steps.explanation: Equal to the old 5 puttonyos.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aszú berries are soaked in base wine, then fermented slowly
Puttonyos measured baskets per barrel
Since 2013, Aszú needs at least 120 g/l of sugar

steps.title: Szamorodni
steps.body: Szamorodni, a Polish word meaning as it comes, is made from whole bunches with some botrytised berries, not separated. It can be édes, sweet, or száraz, dry. Dry Szamorodni ages under a film of yeast, like Sherry's flor, in barrels not completely filled, giving nutty, oxidative notes. Sweet Szamorodni is lighter than Aszú.
steps.highlight: As it comes: sweet or dry

steps.title: Eszencia
steps.body: Eszencia, or Esszencia, is the free-run juice that drips from aszú berries under their own weight, before soaking. It's extraordinarily sweet, often 450 to 800 g/l of sugar, and ferments for years, reaching only 3 to 5% alcohol. Tiny quantities are made. It's traditionally served by the spoon and was believed to have healing powers.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its making.
steps.explanation: Tokaj makes several wines from one harvest.

steps.title: Dry Furmint
steps.body: Since the 2000s, Tokaj has made more dry wine, mainly from Furmint, from healthy grapes. It's mineral, smoky, with quince and citrus, and can be rich and textured, often compared with white Burgundy. Single-vineyard dry Furmint is now a major part of Tokaj's identity, especially as botrytis doesn't come every year.

steps.prompt: Which are Tokaj wines?
steps.explanation: Amarone is Italian.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Szamorodni uses whole bunches, sweet or dry
Eszencia is free-run juice, extraordinarily sweet
Dry Furmint is Tokaj's modern style

steps.title: Classified from 1730
steps.body: Tokaj's vineyards were classified from 1730, among the first in the world, into first, second and third class, based on soil, exposure and wine quality. In 1737, a royal decree defined the region's boundaries, making it one of the first closed, legally defined wine regions, before Portugal's Douro in 1756.

steps.title: Famous sites
steps.body: Top vineyards, dűlő, include Szarvas and Mézes Mály, once royal vineyards; Szent Tamás, Betsek and Úrágya. Labels increasingly name them, especially for dry Furmint and single-vineyard Aszú. The Hétszőlő and Disznókő estates are also famous names.

steps.prompt: When was Tokaj's wine region legally defined by royal decree?
steps.explanation: Earlier than the Douro's 1756 demarcation.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Tokaji Aszú was served at European royal courts; Louis XIV of France is said to have called it the wine of kings, the king of wines. After 1945, communist state farms took over, and quality fell. From 1990, private and foreign investors, like Royal Tokaji, Disznókő and Oremus, revived it. Tokaj became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.

steps.prompt: Tokaj's vineyards were classified before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.
steps.explanation: Yes, from 1730.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tokaj's vineyards were classified from 1730
A 1737 decree defined the region
Private estates revived it after 1990; UNESCO since 2002

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Tokaj and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show Tokaji, the style, Aszú, Szamorodni, Eszencia or dry Furmint, sometimes puttonyos, 5 or 6, the vintage, the producer and often a vineyard, dűlő. Késői szüretelésű means late harvest, a lighter sweet style. Tokaji Aszú usually comes in a 50 cl bottle.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Tokaji Aszú suits foie gras, blue cheese, apricot tarts and fruit desserts; its acidity also works with spicy Asian food and Hungarian dishes with paprika. Dry Furmint suits fish, poultry, pork and goose. Dry Szamorodni suits nuts and aged cheese, like a Sherry. Serve sweet wines at 10 to 12 degrees.
steps.highlight: Foie gras, blue cheese, apricot tart

steps.prompt: Which food suits Tokaji Aszú?
steps.explanation: Rich foie gras suits Aszú's sweetness and acidity.

steps.body: An open bottle of Tokaji Aszú keeps for weeks in the fridge, thanks to its sugar and acidity.

steps.prompt: Which are Tokaj label terms?
steps.explanation: Crianza is Spanish.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show the style, puttonyos and vineyard
Aszú suits foie gras and fruit desserts
Dry Furmint suits fish, poultry and pork

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Tokaj's vocabulary is precise.

steps.prompt: Which rivers create Tokaj's autumn mists?
steps.explanation: They meet at the town of Tokaj.

steps.prompt: Eszencia reaches high alcohol, around 15%.
steps.explanation: Not true. It usually reaches only 3 to 5%.

steps.prompt: Which are Tokaj grapes?
steps.explanation: Sauvignon Blanc isn't permitted.

steps.prompt: Tokaj's vineyards were classified from ____.
steps.explanation: Among the first classifications in the world.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tokaj's river mists and volcanic soils favour noble rot
Furmint leads, with Hárslevelű
Aszú, Szamorodni and Eszencia are its sweet wines
It was classified from 1730, among the world's first

modules.title: Santorini
modules.description: A volcanic island in the Aegean where vines grow in baskets and Assyrtiko keeps its acidity in fierce sun.

steps.title: A caldera
steps.body: Santorini is a Greek island in the southern Aegean, in the Cyclades. Around 1600 BC, one of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history blew out its centre, leaving a crescent-shaped island around a flooded caldera. Vineyards cover about 1,100 hectares, on the gentle outer slopes.

steps.title: Aspa
steps.body: Santorini's soil, called aspa, is volcanic ash, pumice, lava and pieces of rock, with almost no clay or organic matter. It's very poor and drains instantly. Phylloxera can't survive in it, so vines are ungrafted and roots can be centuries old. The pumice holds a little moisture, helping roots through summer.

steps.prompt: Why are Santorini's vines ungrafted?
options: Phylloxera can't survive in volcanic aspa
steps.explanation: The volcanic soil keeps phylloxera out.

steps.title: Wind, sun and little rain
steps.body: Santorini is hot and very dry, with about 300 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Strong winds, including the meltemi in summer, blow constantly. Vines rely on night-time sea mist and dew for moisture. Yields are tiny, often 10 to 20 hl/ha, among the lowest in Europe.

steps.prompt: Santorini gets heavy summer rain.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's very dry; vines rely on sea mist and dew.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Santorini is a crescent around a volcanic caldera
Its aspa soil keeps phylloxera out; vines are ungrafted
It's dry and windy; vines rely on sea mist

steps.title: Assyrtiko
steps.body: Assyrtiko covers about 80% of Santorini's vineyards. It keeps very high acidity even when fully ripe in strong sun, a rare trait. It gives bone-dry whites with lemon, lime, flint, smoke and a saline edge, with high alcohol. Santorini PDO white must be at least 75% Assyrtiko.

steps.title: Partners
steps.body: Athiri adds citrus and floral softness; Aidani adds floral, honeyed aromas. Both are blended with Assyrtiko and used in Vinsanto. Red grapes, like Mandilaria and Mavrotragano, a rare local grape, are also grown, mainly for reds and some Vinsanto.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Assyrtiko leads Santorini's wines.

steps.body: Nykteri, from the Greek for night, was traditionally made from grapes picked at night and oak-aged. It's a richer style of Santorini Assyrtiko.

steps.prompt: What makes Assyrtiko unusual?
options: It keeps high acidity in hot sun
steps.explanation: Few grapes keep such acidity in heat.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Assyrtiko is about 80% of vineyards, at least 75% in PDO whites
It keeps high acidity in fierce sun
Athiri, Aidani and Mavrotragano complete the range

lessons.title: Basket vines
lessons.subtitle: Kouloura
objectives: Explain the threat to Santorini's vineyards

steps.title: Baskets
steps.body: Santorini's vines are trained into kouloura, low baskets woven from the vine's own canes, lying on the ground. The grapes grow inside the basket. Each year, new canes are woven in, so the basket grows. After 50 to 80 years, the basket is cut off, and a new one grows from the same old roots.

steps.title: Why baskets
steps.body: The kouloura protects grapes from strong winds, which can strip leaves and fruit, from fierce sun and from blowing volcanic sand. Inside, the grapes catch moisture from night sea mist and dew, the vines' main water source. The low shape keeps the vines close to the cooler, more humid ground.
steps.highlight: Shelter from wind, sun and sand

steps.prompt: What does the kouloura protect against?
steps.explanation: Santorini has mild winters; frost isn't the main concern.

steps.title: Threats
steps.body: Santorini's vineyards are shrinking. Tourism has made land extremely valuable, and many vineyards have been built on. Low yields, drought and climate change add pressure. Producers like Hatzidakis, Gaia, Sigalas and Santo Wines work to protect the vines and their heritage.

steps.prompt: What is a kouloura?
options: A basket-shaped vine trained on the ground
steps.explanation: Woven from the vine's own canes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Kouloura vines are woven into baskets on the ground
They protect grapes from wind, sun and sand
Tourism and drought threaten Santorini's vineyards

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Santorini and eating with it

steps.title: Labels and Vinsanto
steps.body: Labels show Santorini PDO, the producer and sometimes Nykteri or a single vineyard. Vinsanto, Santorini's sweet wine, is made from at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani, from grapes sun-dried for about 12 to 14 days, then fermented and aged at least two years in oak, often much longer. It's amber, with raisin, apricot, coffee and spice, balanced by acidity.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Dry Assyrtiko suits Greek seafood: grilled octopus, sea bass, squid, shellfish, and local dishes like fava, a yellow split pea purée, tomatokeftedes, tomato fritters, and feta. Its acidity cuts through olive oil. Vinsanto suits dried fruit, nuts, blue cheese and chocolate. Serve Assyrtiko at 8 to 11 degrees.

steps.prompt: How is Santorini's Vinsanto made?
options: From sun-dried grapes, aged in oak
steps.explanation: Sun-drying concentrates the grapes.

steps.body: Top Santorini Assyrtiko ages well for 10 to 15 years, gaining smoky, honeyed notes while keeping its acidity.

steps.prompt: Dry Assyrtiko is a good match for grilled octopus.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its acidity and saltiness suit grilled seafood.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show Santorini PDO and sometimes Nykteri
Vinsanto is sun-dried and oak-aged
Assyrtiko suits octopus, fava and feta

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Santorini's vocabulary is unique.

steps.prompt: Where do Santorini's vines get most of their moisture?
steps.explanation: Rain is scarce; mist and dew help.

steps.prompt: Santorini's vines are ungrafted.
steps.explanation: Yes. Phylloxera can't survive in its soil.

steps.prompt: Which grapes grow on Santorini?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is Italian.

steps.prompt: Santorini PDO white must be at least ____% Assyrtiko.
steps.explanation: At least 75%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Santorini is a dry, windy volcanic island
Assyrtiko keeps high acidity in fierce sun
Kouloura baskets protect the vines
Vinsanto and dry Assyrtiko suit Greek food

modules.title: Kakheti
modules.description: The cradle of wine: eight thousand years of winemaking in buried clay qvevri.

steps.title: Eastern Georgia
steps.body: Kakheti is Georgia's main wine region, in the east, making about 70% of the country's wine. It lies in the Alazani valley, between the Greater Caucasus mountains to the north and the Gombori range. Its capital is Telavi; Sighnaghi is a famous hilltop town. Vineyards cover the valley and the foothills.
steps.highlight: Alazani valley, about 70% of Georgia's wine

steps.title: Climate
steps.body: Kakheti's climate is moderately continental: hot summers, mild to cold winters and enough rain, with the Caucasus blocking cold northern air. The Alazani river and valley give fertile, varied soils. Long, warm autumns ripen grapes fully. Hail can be a risk.

steps.prompt: What protects Kakheti from cold northern air?
steps.explanation: The Caucasus blocks cold air from the north.

steps.title: 8,000 years
steps.body: Archaeologists have found grape residue in clay jars in Georgia dating to about 6000 BC, around 8,000 years ago, among the oldest evidence of winemaking in the world. Wine is central to Georgian culture: the supra, a traditional feast, is led by a toastmaster, the tamada, with many long toasts.

steps.prompt: Georgia has some of the oldest evidence of winemaking in the world.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 8,000 years old.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Kakheti, in eastern Georgia, makes about 70% of its wine
The Caucasus shelters it; autumns are warm
Georgia has made wine for about 8,000 years

steps.title: Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane
steps.body: Georgia has over 500 native grape varieties. Rkatsiteli, the most planted white, has high acidity and gives citrus, apple and quince in modern styles, or rich, tannic amber wine in qvevri. Mtsvane Kakhuri, green of Kakheti, is aromatic, with tropical fruit and flowers, often blended with Rkatsiteli. Kisi is another fine white.

steps.title: Saperavi
steps.body: Saperavi, meaning dye or colour, is Georgia's main red. It's a teinturier, with red flesh, giving very deep colour, high acidity and firm tannin, with blackberry, black cherry, plum and spice. It ages well. It makes dry reds, like Mukuzani, and semi-sweet reds, like Kindzmarauli.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its character.
steps.explanation: Georgia's grapes are native and diverse.

steps.body: Saperavi's red flesh means even its juice is coloured. Its wines can be almost black.

steps.prompt: What does Saperavi mean?
steps.explanation: For its intensely coloured juice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Georgia has over 500 native grapes
Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane lead the whites
Saperavi is a red-fleshed, deeply coloured red

lessons.title: Qvevri
lessons.subtitle: Buried clay vessels
objectives: Explain how qvevri wine is made

steps.title: Clay underground
steps.body: A qvevri is a large, egg-shaped clay vessel, from about 800 to several thousand litres, buried up to its neck in the ground. The inside is coated with beeswax. The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable, around 13 to 15 degrees, during fermentation and ageing. Qvevri are made by hand by a few master potters.

steps.title: The method
steps.body: Crushed grapes, often with skins, seeds and sometimes stems, chacha, go into the qvevri. Fermentation starts with native yeasts. The cap is punched down, then the qvevri is sealed with a stone or wooden lid and clay. The wine stays on the skins for months, often until spring. The egg shape helps solids settle at the bottom.

steps.prompt: Why is the qvevri buried?
options: The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable
steps.explanation: Underground, temperatures stay steady.

steps.title: UNESCO
steps.body: In 2013, UNESCO added the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri winemaking method to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The method inspired producers worldwide, especially in Friuli, where Josko Gravner began using qvevri in 2001, and in the natural wine movement.

steps.prompt: Which describe qvevri winemaking?
steps.explanation: Qvevri winemaking uses clay, not oak.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Qvevri are egg-shaped clay vessels buried in the ground
Grapes ferment with skins for months
UNESCO recognised the method in 2013

steps.title: Amber, not orange
steps.body: In Georgia, white wine made with long skin contact is called amber wine, karvisperi. In Kakheti, the tradition is full skin contact, with all the chacha, for about six months in qvevri. The result is deep amber, tannic and textured. Western Georgia, in Imereti, uses less chacha and shorter contact for lighter wines.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body: Amber Rkatsiteli tastes of dried apricot, quince, walnuts, honey, black tea and spice, with firm tannin and fresh acidity. It's dry. It's closer to a red wine in structure, so it's served at 12 to 16 degrees and pairs with food. The same grape can also make a fresh, European-style white, with no skin contact.

steps.prompt: What is amber wine?
options: White wine made with long skin contact
steps.explanation: In Georgia, karvisperi.

steps.title: Two styles
steps.body: Today Georgia makes both traditional qvevri wines and European-style wines in steel and oak. Both use native grapes. Amber wines are a small but growing share, and exports have surged. They've inspired the orange wine category worldwide, though Georgians prefer the term amber.

steps.prompt: Georgian amber wines are usually sweet.
steps.explanation: Not true. They're dry, with tannin and acidity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Amber wine is white wine with long skin contact
Kakhetian amber wine uses full skins for about six months
It's dry, tannic, with dried apricot and walnut

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Georgia and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Georgian wines often name a protected place, like Tsinandali, a white blend of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane; Mukuzani, dry Saperavi; Kindzmarauli, semi-sweet Saperavi; or Napareuli. Labels may say qvevri, amber or the grape. Georgia has about 29 protected appellations. Labels may be in the Georgian alphabet, which is unique.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Georgian food is rich and spiced: khachapuri, cheese bread; khinkali, dumplings; mtsvadi, grilled meat; dishes with walnuts, pomegranate and herbs. Amber wines suit walnut sauces, grilled meat and cheese. Saperavi suits lamb and grilled pork. The supra feast, with its tamada and many toasts, is central to Georgian wine culture.

steps.prompt: Who leads the toasts at a Georgian supra?
steps.explanation: The tamada is the toastmaster.

steps.body: Kindzmarauli, a semi-sweet Saperavi, is a popular Georgian style; it pairs with spicy food and desserts.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its style.
steps.explanation: Georgian names identify styles.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels name places like Tsinandali and Mukuzani
Amber wine suits walnuts and grilled meat; Saperavi suits lamb
The supra feast is central to Georgian wine

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Georgia's wine vocabulary is ancient.

steps.prompt: How old is the earliest evidence of Georgian winemaking?
steps.explanation: Around 6000 BC.

steps.prompt: Saperavi has red flesh.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's a teinturier.

steps.prompt: Which are Georgian grapes?
steps.explanation: Tempranillo is Spanish.

steps.prompt: UNESCO recognised qvevri winemaking in ____.
steps.explanation: As Intangible Cultural Heritage.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Kakheti is Georgia's main region, sheltered by the Caucasus
Rkatsiteli, Mtsvane and Saperavi are its key grapes
Qvevri and amber wine are ancient, UNESCO-recognised traditions
Its wines suit rich, spiced Georgian food

modules.title: Napa Valley
modules.description: A small valley north of San Francisco that put American wine on the world map, built on Cabernet Sauvignon.

steps.title: Between two ranges
steps.body: Napa Valley lies about 80 km north of San Francisco, about 50 km long and a few kilometres wide, between the Mayacamas Mountains to the west and the Vaca Range to the east. It has about 18,000 hectares of vines, only about 4% of California's, but a large share of its value. Soils are extremely varied: over 30 types.
steps.highlight: 50 km long, about 4% of California's vines

steps.title: Fog from the bay
steps.body: Napa has a Mediterranean climate: dry, warm summers and mild, wet winters. Cool air and fog come in from San Pablo Bay in the south each night and morning, so the southern end, Carneros, is coolest, and the northern end, Calistoga, hottest. The daily fog keeps acidity in grapes that ripen fully under strong sun.

steps.prompt: Why is Carneros cooler than Calistoga?
options: It's closer to San Pablo Bay and its fog
steps.explanation: Bay fog and cool air reach the south first.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Vines were planted in Napa in the 1830s; by the 1880s, there were over 140 wineries. Phylloxera and Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, nearly ended the industry. In 1966, Robert Mondavi founded the first major new winery since Prohibition, and modern Napa grew from there. In 1968, Napa created the Agricultural Preserve, protecting land from development.

steps.prompt: Napa Valley makes most of California's wine by volume.
steps.explanation: Not true. It has only about 4% of California's vineyards, though its wines are among the most valuable.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Napa is a small valley between two mountain ranges
Bay fog cools the south; the north is hotter
Mondavi's 1966 winery launched modern Napa

steps.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is Napa's star, about 40% of vineyards and most of its value. Napa Cabernet is ripe and powerful, with blackcurrant, black cherry, cassis, chocolate and mint, ripe tannins and often 14.5% alcohol or more, aged in new French oak. Bordeaux-style blends are called Meritage, a trademarked term.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Malbec join Cabernet in blends. Chardonnay is the main white, especially in cooler Carneros. Sauvignon Blanc, sometimes called Fumé Blanc, a name Mondavi coined, and Zinfandel also grow. Pinot Noir thrives in Carneros.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Napa.
steps.explanation: Cabernet leads, with Bordeaux partners.

steps.body: Napa Cabernet grapes are among the most expensive in the world, often over 10,000 dollars per tonne for top vineyards.

steps.prompt: Which grape is Napa's star?
steps.explanation: About 40% of vineyards and most of the value.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Sauvignon is Napa's star
Bordeaux grapes join it in blends called Meritage
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir thrive in cool Carneros

steps.title: A blind tasting
steps.body: On 24 May 1976, British wine merchant Steven Spurrier organised a blind tasting in Paris. Nine French judges compared top Californian wines with top Bordeaux reds and Burgundy whites. Spurrier expected the French wines to win. A journalist from Time magazine, George Taber, was there.

steps.title: The results
steps.body: In the whites, Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay, from Napa, came first, ahead of Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. In the reds, Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon came first, ahead of Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion. Time reported it as the Judgment of Paris.

steps.prompt: Which Napa Cabernet won the red section in 1976?
steps.explanation: Chateau Montelena won the whites with Chardonnay.

steps.title: Impact
steps.body: The result shocked France and gave California, and the New World, credibility. Investment poured into Napa. A rematch in 2006, with the same wines aged 30 years, again placed Californian reds on top. The story became the film Bottle Shock in 2008. Bottles from the tasting are in the Smithsonian museum.

steps.prompt: What were the effects of the Judgment of Paris?
options: It banned French wine in the US
steps.explanation: It didn't ban anything.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Steven Spurrier's 1976 blind tasting compared California and France
Chateau Montelena and Stag's Leap won
It gave the New World credibility

lessons.title: AVAs within the valley
lessons.subtitle: Napa's sub-regions
objectives: Compare valley floor and mountain sites

steps.title: AVAs
steps.body: An AVA, American Viticultural Area, is a defined grape-growing area; a label naming one must use at least 85% of grapes from it. Napa Valley AVA was created in 1981, California's first. Within it are 16 smaller AVAs, each with distinct soils and climate. Napa County law also requires at least 75% Napa Valley grapes for wines naming a Napa sub-AVA.

steps.title: Valley floor and mountains
steps.body: Valley floor AVAs include Oakville and Rutherford, with alluvial soils, famous for rich Cabernet; Rutherford is known for its dusty, earthy Rutherford dust; and Stags Leap District, with softer, elegant tannins. Mountain AVAs, like Howell Mountain, Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain and Diamond Mountain, sit above the fog, with thin, volcanic soils, giving more structured, tannic wines.

steps.prompt: Match each AVA to its feature.
steps.explanation: Each AVA has its own character.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Napa's AVAs show that even a small valley has big differences in soil and climate. Mountain sites, above the fog line, get more sun but cooler temperatures, and lower yields. Valley floor sites are warmer and more fertile. Many top wines blend from several AVAs; others come from single vineyards, like To Kalon in Oakville.

steps.prompt: What must a wine contain to name an AVA on its label?
options: At least 85% grapes from that AVA
steps.explanation: The federal rule is 85%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Napa Valley AVA, created in 1981, contains 16 sub-AVAs
Valley floor AVAs give rich wines; mountain AVAs structured ones
A label naming an AVA needs at least 85% of its grapes

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Napa and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show the winery, the grape, at least 75% of it by US law, the AVA, at least 85%, and the vintage, at least 95% from that year. Estate Bottled means the winery grew and made the wine within the AVA. Reserve has no legal meaning. Cult wines, like Screaming Eagle and Harlan Estate, are made in tiny quantities and sell for very high prices.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Napa Cabernet suits steak, especially grilled ribeye, lamb, beef short ribs and hard cheeses. Its ripe fruit and tannin need fat and protein. Napa Chardonnay suits lobster, crab and roast chicken. Serve Cabernet at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young. Top Napa Cabernet ages 15 to 30 years.

steps.prompt: What does Reserve mean on a Napa label?
steps.explanation: In the US, Reserve isn't regulated.

steps.body: Napa's wineries welcome millions of visitors a year. Many tastings are by appointment, so book ahead.

steps.prompt: Estate Bottled means the winery grew and made the wine within the AVA.
steps.explanation: Yes, it's a regulated term.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels follow 75% grape, 85% AVA, 95% vintage rules
Napa Cabernet suits steak and lamb
Top Napa Cabernet ages 15 to 30 years

steps.prompt: Match each name to its role.
steps.explanation: Napa's history is full of famous names.

steps.prompt: What cools Napa Valley?
options: Fog and cool air from San Pablo Bay
steps.explanation: Fog moves up from the bay.

steps.prompt: Napa Valley was California's first AVA, in 1981.
steps.explanation: Yes.

steps.prompt: Which are Napa mountain AVAs?
steps.explanation: Rutherford is on the valley floor.

steps.prompt: A Napa label naming an AVA must use at least ____% grapes from it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Napa is small, foggy in the south and hot in the north
Cabernet Sauvignon is its star
The 1976 Judgment of Paris made it famous
Its 16 AVAs range from valley floor to mountain

modules.title: Sonoma County
modules.description: Napa's larger, more varied neighbour: cool coastal Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and old-vine Zinfandel.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: From the Pacific to the Mayacamas

steps.title: A large, varied county
steps.body: Sonoma County lies west of Napa, between the Pacific Ocean and the Mayacamas Mountains, about 80 km north of San Francisco. It has about 24,000 hectares of vines, more than Napa, spread over a much more varied landscape: coast, valleys and hills. It has 19 AVAs.
steps.highlight: Larger and more varied than Napa

steps.title: Ocean influence
steps.body: Sonoma's climate ranges from cool and foggy on the coast to warm inland. The cold Pacific creates fog that flows inland through gaps in the coastal hills, especially the Petaluma Gap, cooling valleys like the Russian River. Inland valleys, like Alexander Valley and Dry Creek, are much warmer.

steps.prompt: What is the Petaluma Gap?
options: A gap in the hills that lets cool ocean air in
steps.explanation: It funnels wind and fog inland.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Russian settlers planted vines at Fort Ross on the coast in 1812. Agoston Haraszthy, a Hungarian, founded Buena Vista winery in 1857, California's oldest commercial winery, and brought many European vine cuttings. Italian immigrants later planted Zinfandel. Sonoma is known for family wineries and a relaxed, rural feel.

steps.prompt: Sonoma County has fewer vineyards than Napa.
steps.explanation: Not true. Sonoma has more vineyard area than Napa.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sonoma is larger and more varied than Napa
Ocean fog cools the coast; inland valleys are warm
Buena Vista, from 1857, is California's oldest commercial winery

steps.title: Cool-climate grapes
steps.body: Chardonnay is Sonoma's most planted grape, and Pinot Noir is close behind. Both thrive in the cool, foggy areas near the coast: the Russian River Valley, Sonoma Coast and Carneros. The wines are fresh, with red fruit and citrus, balanced by acidity.
steps.highlight: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in cool areas

steps.title: Warm-climate grapes
steps.body: In warmer inland valleys, Cabernet Sauvignon thrives in Alexander Valley, giving soft, ripe wines. Zinfandel, often from old vines, thrives in Dry Creek Valley and Sonoma Valley, giving ripe, spicy, bramble wines. Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot and Syrah also grow.

steps.prompt: Match each AVA to its grape.
steps.explanation: Sonoma's grapes follow its climates.

steps.body: Old-vine Zinfandel from Dry Creek Valley, some over 100 years old, shows the grape at its most complex.

steps.prompt: Which is Sonoma's most planted grape?
steps.explanation: Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir close behind.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir thrive in cool coastal areas
Cabernet grows in Alexander Valley; Zinfandel in Dry Creek
Sonoma has a grape for every climate

steps.title: Russian River Valley
steps.body: The Russian River Valley is one of California's coolest areas, thanks to morning fog that can last until noon. Goldridge, a fine sandy loam soil, drains well. Its Pinot Noir is ripe yet fresh, with red cherry, raspberry and spice; its Chardonnay rich with citrus and acidity. Producers include Williams Selyem, Rochioli and Kistler.

steps.title: Sonoma Coast
steps.body: The Sonoma Coast AVA is large; its truest coastal areas, near the Pacific, like the Fort Ross-Seaview AVA, sit above the fog line at 300 to 550 m, on ridges. They give lean, high-acid Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, among California's most elegant. The West Sonoma Coast AVA, created in 2022, defines the truly coastal zone.
steps.highlight: Above the fog line, on ridges

steps.prompt: What makes the Russian River Valley so cool?
options: Morning fog that can last until noon
steps.explanation: Ocean fog flows up the river valley.

steps.title: Fog and ripening
steps.body: Fog slows ripening by blocking morning sun and keeping temperatures low, then lifts to let afternoon sun ripen the grapes. This long, slow season builds flavour while keeping acidity. It's why Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, which need cool conditions, do so well here.

steps.prompt: Which are Sonoma's cool coastal AVAs?
steps.explanation: Alexander Valley is warm and inland.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Russian River Valley is cooled by long morning fog
True coastal Sonoma sits on ridges above the fog
Slow ripening gives fresh Pinot Noir and Chardonnay

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Sonoma and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show winery, grape, AVA and vintage. Sonoma County is the broadest appellation; Russian River Valley, Dry Creek Valley or Alexander Valley are more specific. Single-vineyard names, like Rochioli or Bacigalupi, are common. US rules apply: 75% grape, 85% AVA, 95% vintage.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Russian River Pinot Noir suits salmon, duck, mushrooms and roast chicken. Chardonnay suits Dungeness crab, a local favourite, and lobster. Dry Creek Zinfandel suits barbecue, burgers and spicy sausages. Alexander Valley Cabernet suits steak. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees, Zinfandel at 16 to 17.
steps.highlight: Pinot with salmon, Zinfandel with barbecue

steps.prompt: Which local seafood suits Sonoma Chardonnay?
steps.explanation: Dungeness crab is a West Coast favourite.

steps.body: Sonoma's tasting rooms are often smaller and more relaxed than Napa's, with many family wineries.

steps.prompt: Dry Creek Zinfandel suits barbecue.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its ripe fruit and spice match smoky, sweet sauces.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show AVA and often a single vineyard
Pinot suits salmon; Zinfandel suits barbecue
Serve Pinot slightly cooler than Zinfandel

steps.explanation: Sonoma's vocabulary is varied.

steps.prompt: Which Sonoma AVA is known for Cabernet Sauvignon?
steps.explanation: It's warm and inland.

steps.prompt: Sonoma's coastal Pinot Noir benefits from Pacific fog.
steps.explanation: Yes. Fog keeps it cool and fresh.

steps.prompt: Which grapes thrive in Sonoma?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo isn't a Sonoma speciality.

steps.prompt: Sonoma County has ____ AVAs.
steps.explanation: 19 AVAs.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sonoma is larger and more varied than Napa
Pacific fog cools its coast
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead in cool areas; Zinfandel and Cabernet inland
Family wineries define its character

modules.title: Willamette Valley
modules.description: Oregon's cool valley at Burgundy's latitude, where small family wineries made Pinot Noir world-class.

steps.title: Between two ranges
steps.body: The Willamette Valley runs about 240 km south from Portland, Oregon, between the Coast Range to the west and the Cascade Mountains to the east. It's Oregon's largest and most important wine region, with over 70% of the state's vineyards, about 11,000 hectares, and at about 45 degrees north, Burgundy's latitude.

steps.title: Cool and wet
steps.body: The climate is cool and maritime: wet, mild winters and warm, dry summers, with long, cool autumns. The Coast Range blocks much Pacific rain and cold air, but the Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the range, lets cool ocean winds in each afternoon, preserving acidity. Autumn rain at harvest is a risk.
steps.highlight: Coast Range shelter, Van Duzer winds

steps.prompt: What is the Van Duzer Corridor?
options: A gap that lets cool ocean wind into the valley
steps.explanation: It cools vineyards in the afternoon.

steps.title: Pioneers
steps.body: In 1965, David Lett planted Pinot Noir in the Dundee Hills, believing the cool climate suited it; others told him it was too cold and wet. His Eyrie Vineyards 1975 Pinot Noir placed highly in a 1979 Paris tasting against Burgundy. In 1987, Burgundy's Maison Joseph Drouhin bought land in the Dundee Hills, a vote of confidence.

steps.prompt: The Willamette Valley lies at about the same latitude as Burgundy.
steps.explanation: Yes, about 45 degrees north.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Willamette Valley is Oregon's main region, at Burgundy's latitude
Its cool, maritime climate suits Pinot Noir
David Lett planted Pinot Noir there in 1965

steps.title: Pinot Noir
steps.body: Pinot Noir is about two-thirds of the Willamette Valley's vineyards. It gives bright red cherry, raspberry, cranberry and earthy, forest floor notes, with fresh acidity and silky tannins. It's often described as between Burgundy and California in style: riper than Burgundy, fresher than California.

steps.title: Whites and rules
steps.body: Pinot Gris, planted by David Lett in 1966, became Oregon's signature white: richer than Italian Pinot Grigio, with pear and spice. Chardonnay, once a struggle, is now excellent, using Dijon clones. Oregon requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than the US federal 75%, for most varieties.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Oregon.
steps.explanation: Oregon focuses on Pinot.

steps.body: Oregon's 90% rule means a bottle labelled Pinot Noir is almost entirely Pinot Noir, unlike the 75% minimum elsewhere in the US.

steps.prompt: What share of a named grape does Oregon require on most labels?
steps.explanation: Stricter than the federal 75%.

steps.title: The Dundee Hills
steps.body: The Dundee Hills AVA, created in 2005, is the Willamette Valley's historic heart, where David Lett and others first planted. The hills rise to about 300 m, facing south and east, above the valley's fog and frost. Famous producers include Eyrie, Domaine Drouhin Oregon, Domaine Serene and Archery Summit.

steps.title: Jory soil
steps.body: The Dundee Hills' soil is Jory, a deep, red, iron-rich clay loam formed from ancient volcanic basalt. It drains well and holds moderate water. Its Pinot Noir is known for red fruit, elegance and silky texture. Other AVAs have different soils: marine sediments in Yamhill-Carlton give darker fruit, and loess in Chehalem Mountains.

steps.prompt: What is Jory soil?
options: A red, iron-rich clay from volcanic basalt
steps.explanation: It gives the Dundee Hills' elegant Pinot.

steps.title: Other AVAs
steps.body: The Willamette Valley has 11 nested AVAs, including Eola-Amity Hills, cooled by the Van Duzer winds, Yamhill-Carlton, Ribbon Ridge, McMinnville, Chehalem Mountains and Laurelwood District. Each has distinct soils, volcanic, marine sediment or loess, giving different Pinot styles.

steps.prompt: Which are Willamette Valley AVAs?
steps.explanation: Napa Valley is in California.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Dundee Hills are the historic heart
Jory, red volcanic clay, gives elegant Pinot
Eleven AVAs show different soils and styles

Most wineries are small and family-owned; many are certified sustainable, LIVE, or biodynamic.

modules.title: Washington State
modules.description: America's second largest wine state: an irrigated desert east of the Cascades with ripe fruit and fresh acidity.

steps.title: A dry east
steps.body: Washington is the second largest wine-producing US state, after California, with about 24,000 hectares. Almost all vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, far from rainy Seattle. The Columbia Valley AVA covers about a third of the state and contains most other AVAs, like Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley and Red Mountain.

steps.title: Rain shadow
steps.body: The Cascades block Pacific rain, so eastern Washington is a desert or semi-desert, with as little as 150 to 200 mm of rain a year. Summers are hot and long, with up to 17 hours of daylight at about 46 degrees north. Nights are cool. Irrigation from the Columbia, Yakima and Snake rivers makes vineyards possible.

steps.prompt: Why is eastern Washington so dry?
options: The Cascade Mountains block Pacific rain
steps.explanation: A strong rain shadow.

steps.title: Growth
steps.body: Washington's wine industry is young. In 1969, Chateau Ste. Michelle and Columbia Winery began serious winemaking. From about 20 wineries in 1981, there are now over 1,000. Walla Walla, Woodinville, near Seattle, where many wineries have tasting rooms, and the Yakima Valley are centres.

steps.prompt: Most Washington vineyards are near rainy Seattle.
steps.explanation: Not true. Almost all are east of the Cascades, in a dry desert.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Washington is America's second largest wine state
The Cascades create a desert east of the mountains
Its industry has grown fast since the 1970s

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape, giving ripe blackcurrant with firm structure and fresh acidity. Merlot, an early success, gives plush, structured wines. Syrah thrives, especially in Walla Walla and Yakima. Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Grenache also grow. Bordeaux-style blends are common.

steps.title: Whites and style
steps.body: Chardonnay is the most planted white; Riesling is a speciality, from dry to sweet, made in large volume by Chateau Ste. Michelle, one of the world's largest Riesling producers. The common thread: long, sunny days give ripe fruit; cool nights keep acidity. Washington wines are often described as between Napa ripeness and Bordeaux freshness.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Washington grows both reds and whites.

steps.body: Washington Merlot is often more structured than California's, with fresh acidity and firm tannins, a good place to rediscover the grape.

steps.prompt: What gives Washington wines ripe fruit and fresh acidity?
options: Long sunny days and cool nights
steps.explanation: Desert days and cool nights.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah lead the reds
Riesling and Chardonnay lead the whites
Long days and cool nights give ripe, fresh wines

steps.title: Irrigation
steps.body: Without irrigation, most of eastern Washington couldn't grow vines. Water from rivers and the Cascades' snowmelt is applied by drip, giving growers precise control. Mild water stress can be managed to keep berries small and concentrated. The desert air also limits disease, so fewer sprays are needed.

steps.title: Sandy soils and cold
steps.body: Soils are mostly wind-blown loess and sand, over basalt, left by the Missoula Floods at the end of the last ice age. Phylloxera struggles in sand, so most vines are planted on their own roots. The main risk is winter cold: temperatures can drop below minus 20 degrees, killing vines. Growers plant on slopes for air drainage.

steps.prompt: Why are most Washington vines own-rooted?
steps.explanation: Phylloxera struggles in sandy soils.

steps.title: Sub-AVAs
steps.body: Washington has 20 AVAs. Red Mountain, small and warm, gives powerful Cabernet. Walla Walla Valley, straddling Oregon, gives Syrah and Cabernet; its Rocks District, of cobblestones, is famous for savoury Syrah. Yakima Valley, the oldest AVA, from 1983, grows many grapes. Horse Heaven Hills, near the Columbia, is large and windy.

steps.prompt: Which are Washington AVAs?
steps.explanation: Willamette Valley is in Oregon.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Drip irrigation makes Washington's desert vineyards possible
Sandy soils let vines grow on their own roots
Red Mountain, Walla Walla and Yakima are key AVAs

steps.body: Labels show the winery, grape, AVA and vintage. Washington uses US federal rules for AVAs, 85%, and vintage, 95%, but requires 85% for a named grape, stricter than the federal 75%. Columbia Valley is the broadest AVA; Red Mountain or Walla Walla are more specific. Many wineries are in Woodinville but source grapes from the east.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Washington Cabernet suits steak, lamb and burgers; Merlot suits roast pork and duck; Syrah suits barbecue, lamb and game; Riesling suits Asian food, seafood and spicy dishes. Pacific Northwest salmon suits lighter reds and Chardonnay. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees, Riesling at 7 to 10.

modules.title: Mendoza
modules.description: A high desert at the foot of the Andes, irrigated by snowmelt, where Malbec found its second home.

steps.title: At the foot of Aconcagua
steps.body: Mendoza lies in western Argentina, at the foot of the Andes, near Aconcagua, the highest mountain outside Asia, at 6,961 m. It makes about 70% of Argentina's wine, with around 150,000 hectares of vines. Vineyards range from about 600 to 1,600 m in altitude.

steps.title: High desert
steps.body: Mendoza is a high desert, with about 200 to 250 mm of rain a year, in the Andes' rain shadow. Summers are hot and sunny, nights cool, with a large day and night swing. Low humidity means little disease. Hail is the biggest threat; many vineyards use hail nets. The Zonda, a hot, dry wind, can damage vines in spring.

steps.prompt: What is the biggest weather threat in Mendoza?
steps.explanation: Summer hailstorms can destroy crops; nets protect vines.

steps.title: Irrigation
steps.body: Without irrigation, Mendoza couldn't grow vines. Snowmelt from the Andes feeds rivers like the Mendoza and Tunuyán. The Huarpe people built channels before the Spanish arrived; the Spanish expanded them. Today, flood, furrow and drip irrigation all draw on this water. Water rights are precious, and drought years are a growing concern.

steps.prompt: Mendoza's vineyards depend on irrigation from Andean snowmelt.
steps.explanation: Yes. It's a desert without it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mendoza makes about 70% of Argentina's wine, under the Andes
It's a high, dry desert; hail is the main threat
Snowmelt irrigation, via ancient channels, makes it possible

steps.title: Malbec
steps.body: Malbec is Mendoza's signature, with about 70% of Argentina's Malbec. It gives deep purple wines with plum, blackberry, violet and cocoa, and soft, ripe tannins. It arrived in 1853 with French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, hired to found an agricultural school. April 17, the date of the school's founding law, is now World Malbec Day.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Bonarda, the same as Douce Noir from Savoie, not Italy's Bonarda, is Argentina's second most planted red, giving fruity, soft wines. Cabernet Sauvignon is important, often blended with Malbec. Cabernet Franc has become a rising star. Whites include Chardonnay, Torrontés and Sémillon. Criolla Grande and Cereza, pink-skinned, make bulk wine.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Malbec leads, with partners.

steps.body: Argentine Bonarda is not the same as Italian Bonarda. DNA shows it's Douce Noir, from France's Savoie.

steps.prompt: When is World Malbec Day?
steps.explanation: Marking the 1853 founding of Mendoza's agricultural school.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Malbec, from 1853, is Mendoza's signature
Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc follow
World Malbec Day is April 17

steps.title: First zone
steps.body: Luján de Cuyo lies just south of Mendoza city, at about 900 to 1,100 m, along the Mendoza river. It's Mendoza's historic quality heartland, sometimes called the first zone, primera zona, with Maipú. Sub-areas like Perdriel, Agrelo, Vistalba and Las Compuertas have deep alluvial soils with stones.

steps.title: Old vines and DOC
steps.body: Luján de Cuyo has some of Argentina's oldest Malbec vines, many planted before 1950, on their own roots, since phylloxera spreads slowly in Mendoza's sandy, irrigated soils. In 1989, it became Argentina's first DOC, Denominación de Origen Controlada, for Malbec. Its wines are ripe, round and generous, with soft tannins.

steps.prompt: What was Argentina's first DOC?
steps.explanation: Created in 1989 for Malbec.

steps.title: Producers
steps.body: Historic and famous producers include Catena Zapata, whose founder Nicolás Catena pioneered high-altitude, quality Malbec in the 1990s, Achával-Ferrer, Norton and Terrazas de los Andes. Many large wineries are based here, with vineyards both in Luján and in the Valle de Uco.

steps.prompt: Which are sub-areas of Luján de Cuyo?
steps.explanation: Gualtallary is in the Valle de Uco.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Luján de Cuyo is Mendoza's historic quality heart
It has old, own-rooted Malbec vines
It became Argentina's first DOC in 1989

steps.title: High and cool
steps.body: The Valle de Uco lies about 100 km south-west of Mendoza city, at 900 to over 1,600 m, right against the Andes. Its three departments are Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos. Since the 1990s, it's become Argentina's most acclaimed area for fine wine, with major investment, including from French and American producers.

steps.title: Altitude
steps.body: Altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees per 100 m and strengthens ultraviolet light. Cool nights preserve acidity and aroma; strong UV thickens skins, adding colour and tannin. Valle de Uco Malbec is fresher, more floral and more structured than in Luján. Soils, alluvial with stones and limestone, vary greatly.

steps.prompt: How does Valle de Uco Malbec usually compare with Luján de Cuyo's?
steps.explanation: Altitude brings freshness and structure.

steps.title: Geographical indications
steps.body: Since 2013, the Valle de Uco has recognised smaller GIs: Paraje Altamira, in San Carlos, with limestone-rich alluvial soils; Gualtallary, in Tupungato, high up to 1,600 m with limestone; Los Chacayes, in Tunuyán; and San Pablo, very high and cool. These help show terroir in Argentine wine.

steps.prompt: Match each GI to its department.
steps.explanation: The Valle de Uco has a growing map of GIs.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Valle de Uco is high, against the Andes
Altitude gives fresher, more structured Malbec
GIs like Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira show terroir

steps.body: Labels show the grape, often Malbec, the region, Mendoza, and increasingly a sub-region or GI, like Valle de Uco, Luján de Cuyo or Gualtallary. Altitude is often printed. Argentina requires 85% of a named grape. Reserva and Gran Reserva have minimum ageing rules for reds: 12 and 24 months.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Malbec is the wine of the asado, Argentina's barbecue: beef ribs, steak, chorizo and morcilla, blood sausage, with chimichurri, a herb and garlic sauce. Cabernet Franc suits lamb and herbs; Bonarda suits pizza and pasta; Torrontés suits empanadas. Serve Malbec at 16 to 18 degrees.

steps.explanation: Herbs, garlic and vinegar suit Malbec's fruit.

modules.title: Salta
modules.description: Some of the world's highest vineyards, in the Calchaquí Valleys, home of floral Torrontés.

steps.title: High valleys
steps.body: Salta is a province in north-west Argentina, near Bolivia and Chile. Its vineyards lie in the Calchaquí Valleys, between Andean ranges, at about 1,700 to over 3,000 m, among the highest in the world. Cafayate, at about 1,700 m, is the main town and wine centre. Salta has about 3,300 hectares of vines.

steps.title: Altitude and light
steps.body: Salta is close to the tropics, at about 26 degrees south, but altitude makes it cool. Days are hot and very sunny, with intense ultraviolet light; nights are cold, with a day and night range of up to 20 degrees. Rainfall is very low, so vines are irrigated. Sandy, rocky soils drain well and limit disease.

steps.prompt: Why can grapes ripen in balance so close to the tropics in Salta?
options: Altitude cools the air and nights
steps.explanation: Height offsets latitude.

steps.title: Remote vineyards
steps.body: Some of the world's highest vineyards are in Salta's Molinos and Payogasta, above 2,500 m; Bodega Colomé has vines at about 3,100 m. The remoteness, dramatic red rock landscapes and old vines make Salta one of the most spectacular wine regions on earth. Many vines are old, trained on pergolas.

steps.prompt: Salta has some of the world's highest vineyards.
steps.explanation: Yes, above 3,000 m in places.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Salta's Calchaquí Valleys reach over 3,000 m
Altitude offsets latitude, with intense sun and cold nights
Cafayate is its wine centre

steps.title: Torrontés
steps.body: Torrontés Riojano, a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, is Argentina's own white grape and Salta's signature. In Cafayate, it gives intensely floral, aromatic wines with rose, jasmine, orange blossom and peach, yet usually dry, with fresh acidity. Altitude helps it keep acidity and avoid bitterness.

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon thrive too. Intense UV light thickens skins, giving very deep colour, firm tannins and concentrated dark fruit, often with spice and herbs. Tannat also does well. Salta's reds are bold and intense, quite different from Mendoza's.

steps.prompt: Match each term to Salta.
steps.explanation: Salta's grapes are shaped by altitude.

steps.body: Torrontés smells sweet, but taste it: most are dry. That contrast is part of its charm.

steps.prompt: Why are Salta's reds so deeply coloured?
steps.explanation: Grapes protect themselves with thicker, darker skins.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Torrontés is Salta's floral, dry signature white
Malbec and Cabernet give dark, intense reds
Altitude and UV light shape both

steps.body: Torrontés suits Salta's empanadas salteñas, small, juicy beef pastries, as well as spicy food, ceviche, Thai and Indian dishes. Salta's reds suit grilled meat, goat, llama and humita, a corn dish. Serve Torrontés at 7 to 10 degrees, young; reds at 16 to 18.

modules.title: Patagonia
modules.description: Argentina's southern frontier: wind, latitude and fresher Pinot Noir and Malbec.

steps.title: The south
steps.body: Patagonia's wine regions lie in southern Argentina, mainly in Neuquén and Río Negro, around 38 to 39 degrees south, with smaller plantings further south in Chubut, near 43 to 45 degrees. Vineyards are low, about 300 m, in river valleys. It has about 3,500 hectares, a small share of Argentina's total.

steps.title: Cool by latitude, not altitude
steps.body: Unlike Mendoza and Salta, Patagonia is cool because of latitude, not altitude. Summers are sunny with long days, nights are cold, and strong, constant winds blow from the west. The wind keeps grapes healthy, reduces disease and thickens skins. Rainfall is low; irrigation comes from the Limay, Neuquén and Río Negro rivers.

steps.prompt: What makes Patagonia cool, unlike Mendoza?
steps.explanation: It's low but far south.

steps.title: History and growth
steps.body: Río Negro has grown grapes since the early 20th century, with some old vines, like Malbec and Sémillon planted in the 1930s and 1940s. Neuquén's vineyards were mostly planted from the early 2000s, in the desert, with modern irrigation. Producers like Bodega Chacra, Noemía and Familia Schroeder show its potential.
steps.highlight: Old Río Negro vines; new Neuquén

steps.prompt: Patagonia's vineyards are at very high altitude, like Salta's.
steps.explanation: Not true. They're low, about 300 m; coolness comes from latitude.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Patagonia's main regions are Neuquén and Río Negro
Latitude and constant wind keep it cool
Río Negro has old vines; Neuquén is newer

steps.title: Pinot Noir
steps.body: Patagonia is Argentina's best region for Pinot Noir. Its cool climate and long, sunny days give red cherry, raspberry and spice, with fresh acidity and fine tannins. Old Pinot Noir vines in Río Negro, like those at Bodega Chacra, planted in 1932 and 1955, make some of South America's most acclaimed Pinots.

steps.title: Malbec and others
steps.body: Patagonian Malbec is fresher and more elegant than Mendoza's, with red fruit, violet and brighter acidity. Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc also do well. Old Sémillon in Río Negro gives textured whites. Chubut, further south, grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir for sparkling and still wines.

steps.explanation: Patagonia's grapes are fresher than in the north.

steps.body: Try a Patagonian Malbec next to a Mendoza one. The southern wine is usually lighter, fresher and redder in fruit.

steps.prompt: Which grape makes some of South America's most acclaimed wines in Río Negro?
steps.explanation: Old-vine Pinot Noir, like Bodega Chacra's.

modules.title: Maipo Valley
modules.description: Santiago's valley: the historic home of Chilean Cabernet Sauvignon, at the foot of the Andes.

steps.title: Santiago's valley
steps.body: The Maipo Valley surrounds Chile's capital, Santiago, in the north of the Central Valley. It stretches from the Andes in the east toward the Coastal Range in the west, following the Maipo river. It's small by Chilean standards, about 11,000 hectares, but historically the most important for fine red wine.
steps.highlight: Around Santiago, along the Maipo river

steps.title: Mediterranean with Andean breezes
steps.body: Maipo has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, mild winters, rain mostly in winter. Cool air flows down from the Andes at night, giving a big day and night swing. Irrigation from the Maipo river, fed by Andean snowmelt, is essential. Like all Chile, it's free of phylloxera, so vines are ungrafted.

steps.prompt: What cools the Maipo Valley at night?
options: Cold air flowing down from the Andes

steps.title: History
steps.body: In the mid-19th century, wealthy Chilean families, inspired by Bordeaux, brought French grapes, mostly before phylloxera reached Europe's vineyards. They founded estates near Santiago, like Cousiño Macul, 1856, Santa Rita, 1880, and Concha y Toro, 1883, now Chile's largest wine company. Chilean Cabernet's reputation began here.

steps.prompt: Chile's vineyards are free of phylloxera.

steps.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is Maipo's signature: ripe blackcurrant and cherry, often with a distinctive mint or eucalyptus note, firm but ripe tannins and fresh acidity. Many Chilean icon wines, like Almaviva, a Concha y Toro and Mouton Rothschild partnership, and Don Melchor, are Maipo Cabernets.

steps.title: Carmenère
steps.body: Carmenère, brought from Bordeaux in the 19th century, was mixed with Merlot for over a century. In 1994, French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it. It needs a long, warm season; in Maipo it gives dark fruit, spice and soft tannins, with a green pepper note if unripe. Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet Franc are also grown.

steps.title: Foothills of the Andes
steps.body: Alto Maipo, upper Maipo, is the eastern part of the valley, in the Andean foothills, at about 600 to 900 m. Areas include Puente Alto, Pirque and Buin. It's cooler than the valley floor, with strong mountain breezes and a big day and night swing.

steps.title: Soils and style
steps.body: Soils are alluvial, with stones, gravel and clay, washed down from the Andes by the Maipo river. They drain well and limit vigour. Alto Maipo Cabernet is more structured and elegant than the valley floor's, with blackcurrant, mint, graphite and fine tannins. It's often compared with Bordeaux's Left Bank.

steps.prompt: Why is Alto Maipo Cabernet more structured than valley floor Cabernet?
options: Cooler foothill sites and stony soils
steps.explanation: Altitude and drainage give structure.

steps.title: Puente Alto
steps.body: Puente Alto, on an ancient river terrace, is home to some of Chile's most famous Cabernet vineyards: Don Melchor's vineyard, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick. Viñedo Chadwick topped a 2004 Berlin tasting, a Chilean version of the Judgment of Paris, ahead of top Bordeaux.
