modules.title: Casablanca Valley
modules.description: Chile's cool coastal pioneer: crisp Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay cooled by the Pacific.

steps.title: Between Santiago and the sea
steps.body: The Casablanca Valley lies between Santiago and the port of Valparaíso, about 30 km from the Pacific. It runs east to west, opening to the ocean, which lets cool sea air and fog flow in. It has about 6,000 hectares of vines, mostly on gentle slopes and valley floors.

steps.title: The Humboldt Current
steps.body: The cold Humboldt Current runs north along Chile's coast, chilling the ocean. Each morning, fog and cool air move into Casablanca, burning off by midday. Summers are much cooler than in the Central Valley. Spring frost is a major risk; growers use wind machines and sprinklers. Water is scarce, as there's no big river.

steps.prompt: What cools the Casablanca Valley?
options: The cold Humboldt Current and morning fog
steps.explanation: Ocean air and fog cool the valley.

steps.title: A pioneer
steps.body: Before the late 1980s, Chile's vineyards were mostly in the warm Central Valley. In 1982, Pablo Morandé planted vines in Casablanca, then thought too cold. Its success with white wines opened the way for other cool coastal valleys, like San Antonio, Leyda and Limarí. Casablanca showed Chile could make cool-climate wine.

steps.prompt: Casablanca was planted before the warm Central Valley.
steps.explanation: Not true. It was planted from the 1980s, after the Central Valley.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Casablanca lies between Santiago and the Pacific
The Humboldt Current brings fog and cool air
Its success from the 1980s opened Chile's cool coast

steps.title: Sauvignon Blanc
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc is Casablanca's leading grape, giving crisp wines with citrus, grapefruit, passion fruit, cut grass and a herbal, saline note. The cool climate keeps acidity high and green aromas fresh. It's often compared with New Zealand's style, though usually a little less pungent.

steps.title: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir
steps.body: Chardonnay gives fresh, citrus and stone fruit wines, often with some oak and lees. Pinot Noir gives light, fresh reds with red cherry and strawberry. Syrah, from cooler sites, gives peppery wines. About three-quarters of Casablanca's vineyards are white, which is unusual in red-dominated Chile.

modules.title: Barossa Valley
modules.description: Australia's most famous region: rich Shiraz from some of the oldest vines in the world.

lessons.title: The place
lessons.subtitle: A warm valley north of Adelaide

steps.title: North-east of Adelaide
steps.body: The Barossa Valley lies about 60 km north-east of Adelaide, in South Australia. The valley floor is about 250 to 300 m; the hills to the east rise into the cooler Eden Valley. Together they form the Barossa zone. The Barossa Valley has about 13,000 hectares of vines. Soils range from sand to red-brown clay and ironstone.

steps.title: Warm and dry
steps.body: The Barossa Valley has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, often over 35 degrees, and cool, wet winters. Most rain falls in winter. Many old vines are dry-grown, without irrigation, their deep roots finding water. Warmth gives ripe, full-bodied reds.

steps.prompt: What type of climate does the Barossa Valley have?
steps.explanation: Hot summers and winter rain.

steps.title: Silesian settlers
steps.body: In the 1840s, Lutheran settlers from Silesia, then in Prussia, now Poland, settled the Barossa, fleeing religious persecution. They brought farming skills, German food traditions like mettwurst and bienenstich, and Lutheran churches. Many wine families, like Henschke, Hentschke, and Seppelt, have German roots. The heritage is still visible today.

steps.prompt: The Barossa was settled by Lutherans from Silesia in the 1840s.
steps.explanation: Yes, fleeing religious persecution.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Barossa lies north-east of Adelaide
Its warm, dry climate gives ripe reds; old vines are dry-grown
Silesian settlers shaped its culture from the 1840s

steps.title: Shiraz
steps.body: Shiraz, Syrah, is the Barossa's signature, about half of the vineyards. It gives full-bodied, ripe wines with blackberry, plum, chocolate, liquorice and spice, often 14.5 to 15% alcohol, with soft, ripe tannins. Traditional examples use American oak, adding vanilla and coconut. Penfolds Grange, first made in 1951, often includes Barossa Shiraz.
steps.highlight: Rich Shiraz, about half the vines

steps.title: Grenache and Mourvèdre
steps.body: Grenache, often from old bush vines, gives red fruit and spice. Mourvèdre, called Mataro locally, adds tannin and savoury notes. Blends of Grenache, Shiraz and Mourvèdre, GSM, are a Barossa classic. Cabernet Sauvignon and Semillon also grow. Eden Valley adds Riesling.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Barossa blends three Rhône grapes.

steps.body: Mataro, the Barossa's name for Mourvèdre, comes from the town of Mataró near Barcelona.

steps.prompt: What is Barossa Shiraz typically like?
steps.explanation: Warmth gives ripe, rich wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Shiraz is the Barossa's signature, rich and ripe
Grenache and Mataro join it in GSM blends
Penfolds Grange often includes Barossa Shiraz

lessons.title: Old vines
lessons.subtitle: Living history
objectives: Explain why the Barossa has old vines

steps.title: Phylloxera-free
steps.body: South Australia has never had phylloxera, thanks to strict quarantine laws. So the Barossa has some of the world's oldest producing vines, ungrafted, on their own roots. Some Shiraz vines were planted in the 1840s, like at Langmeil's Freedom vineyard and Turkey Flat; Grenache and Mourvèdre vines are similarly old.

steps.title: The Old Vine Charter
steps.body: In 2009, the Barossa created the Old Vine Charter to register and protect old vineyards. It has four levels: Old Vine, at least 35 years; Survivor Vine, 70 years; Centenarian Vine, 100 years; and Ancestor Vine, 125 years or more. Producers can show these on labels.

steps.prompt: Order the Barossa Old Vine Charter levels from youngest to oldest.
steps.explanation: Each level marks older vines.

steps.title: Why they matter
steps.body: Old vines have deep roots that find water in drought, so many are dry-grown. They give low yields of small, concentrated berries, with balance and complexity. They're also a living record of 19th century viticulture, and valuable genetic material, since Europe's original vines were mostly lost to phylloxera.

steps.prompt: Why does the Barossa have such old vines?
steps.explanation: Quarantine kept phylloxera out.

steps.title: What you learned
points: South Australia is phylloxera-free, so old vines survive
The Old Vine Charter registers vines from 35 to 125 years
Old vines give low, concentrated yields and living history

steps.title: Eden Valley
steps.body: Eden Valley lies in the hills east of the Barossa Valley, at about 400 to 600 m. It's cooler, windier and wetter, with granite and schist soils. It's part of the Barossa zone but a separate GI. Its wines are fresher and more elegant than the valley floor's.

steps.title: Riesling and Shiraz
steps.body: Eden Valley is famous for dry Riesling: lime, lemon and floral when young, developing toast and honey with age. Its Shiraz is more peppery and elegant than Barossa Valley Shiraz. Henschke's Hill of Grace, from Shiraz vines planted around 1860, is one of Australia's most famous wines.

steps.prompt: What makes Eden Valley cooler than the Barossa Valley?
steps.explanation: Altitude of 400 to 600 m.

steps.body: Hill of Grace takes its name from the Lutheran church across the road, Gnadenberg, meaning hill of grace.

steps.prompt: Which describe Eden Valley?
steps.explanation: Eden Valley is cool and hilly.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Eden Valley is higher and cooler, in the eastern hills
It's famous for dry Riesling and elegant Shiraz
Henschke's Hill of Grace comes from 1860 vines

steps.body: Australian labels show the grape, the GI, like Barossa Valley or Eden Valley, and the vintage, each at least 85%. Blends list grapes in order of share, like GSM or Shiraz Cabernet. The Barossa zone covers both valleys. Old Vine Charter levels may appear. Wines are often sealed with screw caps.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Barossa Shiraz suits barbecued meat, lamb, beef, kangaroo and rich stews. Its ripe fruit handles sweet, smoky sauces. GSM suits roast lamb and game. Eden Valley Riesling suits seafood, Asian dishes and salads. Barossa's German heritage dishes, like mettwurst, a smoked sausage, suit Shiraz too. Serve Shiraz at 16 to 18 degrees.

modules.title: Margaret River
modules.description: A maritime corner of Western Australia making elegant, Bordeaux-like Cabernet and world-class Chardonnay.

steps.title: A peninsula
steps.body: Margaret River lies in the far south-west of Western Australia, about 270 km south of Perth, on a peninsula between the Indian Ocean to the west and the Southern Ocean to the south. It's about 110 km long and narrow. It has about 5,500 hectares of vines, only around 3% of Australia's, but around 20% of its premium wine.

steps.title: Maritime and mild
steps.body: Margaret River has a maritime, Mediterranean climate, among the most maritime in Australia. Oceans moderate temperatures: small differences between summer and winter, and between day and night. Most rain falls in winter. Summers are warm, not hot. Soils are gravelly, sandy loams over granite, draining well. Strong winds in spring can affect flowering.

steps.prompt: What moderates Margaret River's climate?
steps.explanation: Two oceans keep temperatures mild.

steps.title: Its rise
steps.body: In 1965, Dr John Gladstones, an agricultural scientist, published research suggesting the region's climate was similar to Bordeaux's. Doctors founded the first wineries: Vasse Felix in 1967, then Moss Wood and Cullen. Leeuwin Estate, from the 1970s, made world-class Chardonnay. In a few decades it became one of Australia's top regions.

steps.prompt: Margaret River was compared to Bordeaux's climate in the 1960s.
steps.explanation: Yes, by Dr John Gladstones.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Margaret River lies between two oceans in Western Australia
Its maritime climate is mild and stable
Research from 1965 led to its first wineries

steps.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.body: Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon, often blended with Merlot, is elegant and structured, with blackcurrant, cedar, herbs and fine tannins. It's frequently compared with Bordeaux. Producers like Cullen, Moss Wood, Vasse Felix and Cape Mentelle are famous. Cabernet is the region's most important red.

steps.title: Chardonnay and SBS
steps.body: Margaret River Chardonnay is among Australia's best: rich yet fresh, with stone fruit, citrus, nuts and oak. Leeuwin Estate's Art Series Chardonnay is iconic. Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc blends, called SBS or SSB, are a local speciality: crisp, herbal, citrus and fresh, inspired by Bordeaux whites.

steps.explanation: Margaret River's wines draw on Bordeaux and Burgundy.

steps.body: Margaret River Sémillon Sauvignon Blanc is a refreshing, affordable everyday white, great with seafood.

steps.explanation: SBS, inspired by Bordeaux whites.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Margaret River Cabernet is elegant and Bordeaux-like
Its Chardonnay is among Australia's best
Sémillon Sauvignon Blanc blends are a speciality

steps.body: Labels show the grape or blend, Margaret River GI, and vintage, with Australia's 85% rules. Blends list grapes by share, like Cabernet Merlot. SBS or SSB indicates which white grape dominates. Screw caps are standard. Some producers name single vineyards or sub-regions, like Wilyabrup, an informal area home to several founding estates.

steps.body: Margaret River Cabernet suits lamb, beef and kangaroo; Chardonnay suits marron, a local freshwater crayfish, lobster and roast chicken; SBS suits oysters, fish and salads. The region is also known for surf, forests and seafood. Serve Cabernet at 16 to 18 degrees, Chardonnay at 10 to 12, SBS at 7 to 9.

modules.title: Hunter Valley
modules.description: Australia's oldest wine region: humid and hot, yet home to unoaked Sémillon that ages magically.

steps.title: North of Sydney
steps.body: The Hunter Valley lies about 160 km north of Sydney, in New South Wales, along the Hunter River. It's divided into the Lower Hunter, around Pokolbin, the main wine area, and the Upper Hunter. It has about 2,500 hectares of vines. Soils include sandy alluvial flats, good for Sémillon, and red clay on slopes, for Shiraz.

steps.title: Hot and humid
steps.body: The Hunter is one of Australia's hottest, most humid wine regions, and unusually, much rain falls in summer and at harvest, from February to March. Afternoon cloud and sea breezes moderate the heat. The risk of rot at harvest is high, so grapes are often picked early. It's a challenging, sub-tropical climate for vines.

steps.prompt: What is unusual about the Hunter's rainfall?
options: Much of it falls in summer and at harvest
steps.explanation: Harvest rain brings rot risk.

steps.title: History
steps.body: The Hunter is Australia's oldest continuously operating wine region. James Busby, the father of Australian wine, planted vines there in the 1820s and brought hundreds of cuttings from Europe in 1832. Families like Tyrrell, Tulloch and McWilliam's, with Mount Pleasant, have made wine for generations.

steps.prompt: The Hunter Valley is Australia's oldest wine region still in operation.
steps.explanation: Yes, with vines since the 1820s.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Hunter lies north of Sydney, around Pokolbin
It's hot and humid, with rain at harvest
It's Australia's oldest wine region

steps.title: Sémillon
steps.body: Hunter Sémillon is picked early, at about 10 to 11% alcohol, to avoid harvest rain and keep acidity. It's fermented cool in steel, without oak or malolactic, and bottled early. Young, it's pale, lean and lemony, with grass and high acidity. With 5 to 10 years in bottle, it transforms, gaining toast, honey, lanolin and lemon curd, as if oaked.
steps.highlight: Picked early, unoaked, transforms with age

steps.title: Shiraz
steps.body: Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied, unlike the Barossa's, with red fruit, earth and a savoury, leathery character, sometimes called sweaty saddle in older wines. It's lower in alcohol, around 13 to 13.5%, and ages well. Chardonnay is also grown. Tyrrell's Vat 1 Sémillon and Vat 9 Shiraz are famous examples.

steps.prompt: Match each term to the Hunter.
steps.explanation: The Hunter's grapes have a distinct style.

steps.body: Hunter Sémillon's toasty notes after ten years come entirely from bottle age, not oak. It's one of wine's great transformations.

steps.prompt: Why is Hunter Sémillon picked so early?
options: To avoid harvest rain and keep acidity
steps.explanation: Early picking avoids rot and preserves freshness.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Hunter Sémillon is picked early, unoaked, and transforms with age
Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied and earthy
Tyrrell's Vat 1 and Vat 9 are famous examples

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Young Sémillon suits oysters, sashimi and light seafood. Aged Sémillon suits roast chicken, crab, lobster and creamy dishes. Hunter Shiraz suits lamb, roast beef and mushrooms. Serve Sémillon at 8 to 11 degrees, Shiraz at 15 to 17. Young Sémillon is crisp; wait 10 years for its toasty magic.

modules.title: Marlborough
modules.description: Sunny days, cold nights and stony soils at the top of the South Island: the home of a world-famous Sauvignon Blanc.

steps.title: Top of the South Island
steps.body: Marlborough lies at the north-east tip of New Zealand's South Island, around the town of Blenheim. It's New Zealand's largest wine region by far, with about 30,000 hectares, around two-thirds of the country's vineyards. Its main valleys are the broad Wairau Valley and the smaller, higher Awatere Valley, separated by hills.
steps.highlight: About two-thirds of New Zealand's vines

steps.title: Bright and cool
steps.body: Marlborough is one of New Zealand's sunniest places, with long days and strong ultraviolet light, sheltered from westerly rain by mountains. Nights are cold, so the day and night range is wide. Grapes ripen slowly over a long season, keeping high acidity and intense aromas. Stony, free-draining alluvial soils from old riverbeds limit vigour. Spring frost is a risk.

steps.prompt: What gives Marlborough wines both ripeness and high acidity?
steps.explanation: A wide day and night range keeps acidity while sun ripens the fruit.

steps.title: Fast growth
steps.body: Commercial vines were first planted in Marlborough in 1973, by Montana, now Brancott Estate. In 1985, Cloudy Bay's first Sauvignon Blanc drew worldwide attention. From a few hundred hectares, the region grew to the largest in the country within 40 years, driven by export demand.

steps.prompt: Marlborough is New Zealand's largest wine region.
steps.explanation: Yes, with around two-thirds of the country's vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marlborough sits at the top of the South Island, around Blenheim
Sunny days and cold nights give ripe fruit and high acidity
Planted from 1973, it grew fast after Cloudy Bay's 1985 success

steps.title: Sauvignon Blanc
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc covers about 80% of Marlborough's vineyards and most of New Zealand's wine exports. Marlborough Sauvignon is pungent and zesty: passion fruit, gooseberry, grapefruit, cut grass, green pepper and sometimes a sweaty, tropical edge, with very high acidity. It's almost always unoaked and bottled young.

steps.title: Pinot Noir and others
steps.body: Pinot Noir is the second grape, grown on clay-rich, cooler sites in the southern side valleys, like the Southern Valleys sub-region. It gives bright red cherry and spice, lighter than Central Otago's. Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewürztraminer also grow, and Marlborough makes traditional method sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Sauvignon leads by a long way.

steps.body: Marlborough's Southern Valleys, with more clay, are where many of its best Pinot Noirs come from.

steps.prompt: What share of Marlborough's vineyards is Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: It dominates the region.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Sauvignon Blanc is about 80%, pungent and zesty
Pinot Noir is the second grape, from cooler clay sites
Chardonnay and sparkling wine add variety

steps.title: Thiols and pyrazines
steps.body: Marlborough Sauvignon's tropical notes come from thiols, like 3MH and 3MHA, which smell of passion fruit and grapefruit; they're released during fermentation. Green notes, grass and green pepper, come from methoxypyrazines, kept by cool nights. Marlborough grapes have unusually high levels of both, which explains the intensity.

steps.title: Winemaking
steps.body: Machine harvesting at night breaks some skins, releasing thiol precursors; cool, protective fermentation in steel with selected yeasts keeps them. No oak and early bottling preserve freshness. Some producers make wild-yeast, barrel-fermented or lees-aged versions for texture, but the classic style is pure and pungent.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Marlborough Sauvignon its passion fruit aroma?
steps.explanation: Thiols, released during fermentation.

steps.title: Wairau and Awatere
steps.body: The Wairau Valley, broad and warmer, on stony and silty soils, gives the classic ripe, tropical style. The Awatere Valley, to the south-east, higher, drier, cooler and windier, gives more herbal, mineral, saline wines with tomato leaf and green notes. Many producers blend both for balance.

steps.prompt: Which help create the Marlborough style?
steps.explanation: The classic style is unoaked.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Thiols give passion fruit; pyrazines give grass
Machine harvest and cool steel fermentation preserve aromas
Wairau is tropical; Awatere herbal and saline

steps.body: Labels show the grape, Marlborough GI and vintage, with New Zealand's 85% rules for grape, region and vintage. Some name a sub-region, like Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley or Southern Valleys. Almost all bottles use screw caps; New Zealand led the switch from cork in the early 2000s. Appellation Marlborough Wine is a producer certification for quality and origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Marlborough Sauvignon suits green-lipped mussels, a local speciality, oysters, goat's cheese, salads, asparagus and Thai or Vietnamese food with herbs and lime. Pinot Noir suits salmon, duck and lamb. Serve Sauvignon at 7 to 9 degrees and drink within two years; Pinot at 14 to 16.

steps.explanation: Marlborough is a major source of green-lipped mussels.

steps.body: Drink Marlborough Sauvignon young. Its explosive aromas are at their best in the first year or two.

Drink Sauvignon young and cold

modules.title: Hawke's Bay
modules.description: New Zealand's warm east coast: Bordeaux blends, peppery Syrah and rich Chardonnay.

steps.title: East coast of the North Island
steps.body: Hawke's Bay lies on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island, around the towns of Napier and Hastings. It's New Zealand's second largest wine region, with about 5,000 hectares. Mountain ranges to the west block rain and wind, and the Pacific is to the east. Soils vary greatly, from river gravels to clay and limestone.

steps.title: One of the warmest regions
steps.body: Hawke's Bay is among New Zealand's warmest and sunniest wine regions, which lets later-ripening red grapes ripen. Its maritime climate keeps nights cool and summers moderate. Autumn rain and the occasional cyclone are risks; in 2023, Cyclone Gabrielle flooded many vineyards.

steps.prompt: Why can Hawke's Bay ripen Cabernet and Merlot?
options: It's one of New Zealand's warmest, sunniest regions
steps.explanation: Warmth lets later-ripening reds ripen.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Hawke's Bay is one of New Zealand's oldest wine regions: missionaries planted vines in 1851, and Mission Estate is the country's oldest winery still operating. Te Mata Estate, from 1896, helped show from the 1980s that New Zealand could make serious red wine with its Coleraine blend.

steps.prompt: Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's largest wine region.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's the second largest; Marlborough is the largest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Hawke's Bay is on the North Island's east coast
It's warm and sunny, sheltered by mountains
Mission Estate, from 1851, is New Zealand's oldest winery

steps.title: Bordeaux grapes
steps.body: Merlot is the most planted red, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Malbec, mostly in Bordeaux-style blends. They give medium to full-bodied wines with blackcurrant, plum, cedar and fresh acidity, more elegant than warmer New World examples. Merlot ripens more reliably than Cabernet here.

steps.title: Syrah and Chardonnay
steps.body: Syrah does very well: peppery, floral and medium-bodied, closer to the northern Rhône than to Barossa Shiraz. Chardonnay is Hawke's Bay's most planted grape overall, giving ripe yet fresh wines with stone fruit and citrus, often barrel-fermented. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris also grow.

steps.explanation: Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's red heartland.

steps.explanation: Its moderate climate gives a cooler style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot leads Bordeaux-style blends
Syrah is peppery and Rhône-like
Chardonnay is the most planted grape overall

lessons.title: Gimblett Gravels
lessons.subtitle: An old riverbed
objectives: Explain why it suits red grapes

steps.title: A river changed course
steps.body: Gimblett Gravels is an area of about 800 hectares west of Hastings. It's the old bed of the Ngaruroro River, which changed course after a flood in 1867, leaving deep, stony gravel. The land was once considered useless for farming and was nearly quarried for gravel.

steps.title: Warm, stony soil
steps.body: The gravel soils drain quickly and store the sun's heat, releasing it at night, making the area a few degrees warmer than its surroundings. Low fertility limits vigour. That helps Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah ripen fully, giving concentrated, structured wines. Irrigation is needed, as the gravel holds little water.

steps.prompt: Why does Gimblett Gravels suit red grapes?
options: Stony soil drains and stores heat
steps.explanation: Warm gravel helps late-ripening reds.

steps.title: A defined district
steps.body: In 2001, producers created the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowing District, defined by soil type rather than political boundaries, a rare approach. Wines labelled Gimblett Gravels must come at least 95% from the district. The Bridge Pa Triangle, nearby, is another warm, red-focused sub-area.

steps.prompt: Which describe Gimblett Gravels?
steps.explanation: It's low in fertility and drains fast.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gimblett Gravels is an old riverbed left by an 1867 flood
Stony soil drains and stores heat for red grapes
Its district, from 2001, is defined by soil

lessons.title: Labels and the table
lessons.subtitle: Reading Hawke's Bay and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show the grape or blend, Hawke's Bay GI, and often Gimblett Gravels or Bridge Pa Triangle. Bordeaux blends may list grapes in order of share, like Merlot Cabernet. New Zealand's 85% rules apply. Screw caps are standard, even for reds.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Hawke's Bay Bordeaux blends suit lamb, a New Zealand staple, beef and venison. Syrah suits lamb with rosemary, game and peppered steak. Chardonnay suits roast chicken, crayfish and creamy fish. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees; good blends age 10 to 15 years.

steps.prompt: Which meat is a classic New Zealand match for Hawke's Bay reds?
steps.explanation: New Zealand lamb suits its Bordeaux blends and Syrah.

steps.body: Hawke's Bay is also known for its Art Deco town of Napier, rebuilt after a 1931 earthquake.

steps.prompt: Good Hawke's Bay red blends can age 10 to 15 years.
steps.explanation: Yes, especially from Gimblett Gravels.

points: Labels show the GI and often Gimblett Gravels
Its reds suit lamb, beef and venison
Good blends age 10 to 15 years

modules.title: Central Otago
modules.description: The world's southernmost major wine region: mountains, schist and vivid Pinot Noir.

steps.title: Inland and southern
steps.body: Central Otago lies in the south of New Zealand's South Island, around 45 degrees south, near Queenstown. It's the world's southernmost major wine region. Vineyards sit in valleys and on slopes between mountains, at about 200 to 450 m, on schist, gravel and loess. Sub-regions include Gibbston, Bannockburn, Cromwell Basin, Bendigo and Wanaka.

steps.title: Continental
steps.body: Unlike the rest of New Zealand, Central Otago has a continental climate, far from the sea and sheltered by mountains: hot, dry summer days, cold nights, cold winters and low rainfall, about 350 mm a year in some areas. Frost is a major risk in spring and autumn; growers use wind machines and helicopters. Irrigation is common.

steps.prompt: What makes Central Otago's climate unusual for New Zealand?
options: It's continental, far from the sea
steps.explanation: Mountains and distance from the coast make it continental.

steps.title: Gold and wine
steps.body: In the 1860s, a gold rush brought miners to Central Otago, and a French miner, Jean Désiré Féraud, planted vines around 1864. The industry faded. Modern winemaking began in the 1980s, with pioneers like Rolfe and Lois Mills at Rippon, on Lake Wanaka, and Alan Brady at Gibbston Valley. Bannockburn's old gold sluicings now sit among vineyards.

steps.prompt: Central Otago has a maritime climate.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's New Zealand's only continental wine region.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Central Otago is the world's southernmost major wine region
Its continental climate brings hot days, cold nights and frost

steps.title: Pinot Noir
steps.body: Pinot Noir covers about 80% of Central Otago's vineyards. Its style is vivid: deep for Pinot, with dark cherry, plum, raspberry, thyme and spice, fresh acidity and silky tannins. Intense sunshine and UV light give colour and ripe fruit; cold nights keep acidity. Sub-regions differ: Bannockburn is warm and rich, Gibbston cooler and more delicate.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Pinot Gris, Riesling and Chardonnay are the main whites, with high acidity and purity. Some producers make traditional method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Wild thyme, which grows on the hillsides, is often noted in the wines' aromas.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Central Otago Pinot Noir suits lamb, especially New Zealand lamb, venison, duck, salmon and mushrooms. Its herbal, thyme notes suit herb-crusted meat. Pinot Gris and Riesling suit seafood and Asian food. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees; good examples age 8 to 12 years.

modules.title: Stellenbosch
modules.description: South Africa's historic heart: mountain slopes, ocean breezes, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage.

steps.title: Near Cape Town
steps.body: Stellenbosch lies about 50 km east of Cape Town, in the Western Cape. It's surrounded by mountains, like the Simonsberg, Helderberg and Stellenbosch Mountain, with vineyards on slopes and valley floors. It has about 13,000 hectares of vines and around 150 wineries. Soils are mostly ancient granite and sandstone, among the oldest in the wine world.

steps.title: Mediterranean with ocean breezes
steps.body: Stellenbosch has a warm Mediterranean climate: dry summers, wet winters. False Bay, just to the south, sends cool sea breezes inland in the afternoon. The Cape Doctor, a strong south-easterly wind, cools vines and keeps them healthy. Mountain slopes add altitude and different exposures, so sites vary greatly.
steps.highlight: False Bay breezes and the Cape Doctor

steps.prompt: What cools Stellenbosch vineyards in the afternoon?
steps.explanation: False Bay lies just south of the region.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Stellenbosch was founded in 1679 by Simon van der Stel, the Dutch governor of the Cape, making it South Africa's second oldest town. French Huguenots arrived in the 1680s with winemaking skills. Stellenbosch University, home of the country's main wine science department, created Pinotage in 1925. The Wine of Origin system began in 1973.

steps.prompt: Stellenbosch University created Pinotage.
steps.explanation: Yes, Professor Abraham Perold, in 1925.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Stellenbosch lies among mountains east of Cape Town
False Bay breezes and the Cape Doctor cool it
Founded in 1679, it's the heart of South African wine

steps.title: Reds
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is Stellenbosch's most important red, giving structured wines with blackcurrant, cedar, herbs and fresh acidity, often compared with Bordeaux. Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Shiraz and Pinotage also thrive. Bordeaux-style blends are a strength; estates like Kanonkop, Meerlust and Rustenberg are famous.

steps.title: Whites
steps.body: Chenin Blanc, called Steen locally, is widely planted, giving everything from fresh, fruity wines to rich, oaked old-vine wines. Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay thrive on cooler, higher sites. South Africa has more Chenin Blanc than any other country.

steps.explanation: Stellenbosch grows reds and whites.

steps.explanation: Steen.

points: Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends lead the reds

Sauvignon and Chardonnay thrive on cooler sites

steps.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.body: Stellenbosch Cabernet, especially from the slopes of the Simonsberg and Helderberg, combines ripe dark fruit with herbal, savoury notes and firm structure. Wards like Simonsberg-Stellenbosch and Jonkershoek Valley are known for it. Good examples age 15 to 20 years. Many call Stellenbosch South Africa's Cabernet capital.

steps.title: Pinotage
steps.body: Pinotage, a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, then called Hermitage, gives dark fruit, plum, mulberry and smoky notes. Kanonkop, in Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, is famous for it. A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of Pinotage, usually 30 to 70%, with Bordeaux grapes or Shiraz, giving South Africa its own blend style.

steps.prompt: What is a Cape blend?
options: A red blend with a significant share of Pinotage
A white blend of Chenin and Sauvignon
steps.explanation: Usually 30 to 70% Pinotage.

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: South Africa's Old Vine Project, started in 2016, certifies vineyards over 35 years old with a Certified Heritage Vineyards seal. Stellenbosch has old Chenin, Cinsault and Pinotage vines whose low yields give concentrated wines. The project has helped save many old vineyards from being replanted.

steps.explanation: Riesling isn't involved.

points: Stellenbosch is South Africa's Cabernet capital
Pinotage and Cape blends are its own styles
The Old Vine Project protects old vineyards

A certification seal on the bottle guarantees origin, grape and vintage, each at least 85%. Estate wine must be grown and made on one property.

modules.title: Swartland
modules.description: A dry, rugged land north of Cape Town where old bush vines sparked a South African wine revolution.

steps.title: North of Cape Town
steps.body: Swartland, black land, lies about 65 km north of Cape Town, named after the dark renosterbos shrub that covers its hills. It's a large area of wheat fields and vineyards, around towns like Malmesbury and Riebeek-Kasteel, with the Paardeberg and Kasteelberg mountains. Soils include granite, schist and iron-rich clay.

steps.title: Hot and dry
steps.body: Swartland is warmer and drier than Stellenbosch, with hot summers and about 300 to 600 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Many vines are bush vines, dry-farmed without irrigation, their deep roots finding water. That keeps yields low and fruit concentrated. Atlantic breezes cool some western areas.

steps.prompt: Why are Swartland yields low?
options: Dry-farmed bush vines in a hot, dry climate
steps.explanation: Without irrigation, old vines give small crops.

steps.title: A revolution
steps.body: In the early 2000s, winemakers like Eben Sadie and Adi Badenhorst, then Chris and Andrea Mullineux, came to Swartland, drawn by old, forgotten vineyards. They made natural, low-intervention wines from old Chenin, Syrah and Grenache. In 2010, the Swartland Independent Producers set rules: no added yeast, no acidification, minimal sulphur, no new oak.

steps.prompt: Swartland's revival was led by young producers using old vineyards.
steps.explanation: Yes, from the early 2000s.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Swartland, the black land, lies north of Cape Town
It's hot and dry, with dry-farmed bush vines
A wave of young producers revived it from the 2000s

steps.title: Chenin Blanc
steps.body: Swartland is famous for old-vine Chenin Blanc, from dry-farmed bush vines, some over 50 years old. The wines are concentrated, textured and mineral, with quince, stone fruit, honey and fresh acidity, often fermented in old barrels or concrete. Chenin is often blended with other white grapes, like Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne and Viognier, in Cape white blends.

steps.title: Syrah and Grenache
steps.body: Rhône grapes suit the heat and drought: Syrah gives peppery, savoury reds; Grenache gives red fruit and spice; Cinsault, light, fresh reds; Mourvèdre and Carignan add structure. Blends of these, inspired by the Rhône, are a Swartland signature. Sadie Family's Columella is a famous Syrah-led blend.

steps.explanation: Swartland mixes Chenin and Rhône grapes.

points: Old-vine Chenin Blanc is Swartland's white signature
